Even though I never played the prequels, I decided to pick this one up and see how it went.  I've been looking for a game with a good story that doesn't have all the fight scenes in between (basically a Mass Effect game without all the shooting) for when I just wanted to wind down.
Pros: At less than 20 hours for a full playthrough (17 was what I hit; I assume it'll be quicker next time with knowing the town layouts and puzzles), it is worth a playthrough.  There's some good character development over the game, and you do have a feeling of your choices mattering and changing things well into the future - it's a good mix of immediate and far reaching effects.  Book end caps showing how many people chose a specific "big choice" was a neat feature and was always fun to see.  The plot is actually a lot deeper than you'd think for what is essentially a point and click puzzle game, and it does a fair job of explaining what's going on without beating you over the head with it.  There are some scenes that did feel like tear jerkers which was quite surprising to me.
Cons: The mechanics are confusing at the start with no guidance, and some of the puzzles require you to stand very close to things to interact (way closer than you'd think), meaning if you're running through town you'll probably miss them the first time around.  The backstory of the first games is not well explained at all and it's give a lot of frustration later on when people show up and you're apparently supposed to know them.  Some puzzles seem to be intentionally daft, with only one correct answer when you can immediately think of three other things that should work just as well.  The ending felt a bit rushed and a bit forced, though there were enough surprises and turns to not make it a total wash.
Overall, good for at least one playthrough if you like story rich games, but get it on sale.

I recently replayed both The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: The Longest Journey.  I want to mention my current feelings on them briefly because they're pertinent to how I feel about Dreamfall Chapters.
Apart from a few dodgy 90's style adventure game puzzles that require ridiculous leaps of logic, The Longest Journey still holds up quite well.  Interesting story, great variety of locations, and overall fun puzzles with a few exceptions as mentioned.
Dreamfall: TLJ held up far worse than I expected based on my memory of it.  Seemingly inconsequential parts of the story are overly drawn out, while the overarching plot is rushed and poorly developed.  It feels very much like the developer bit off more than they could chew and had to cut huge swaths out of their planned design and rush what was left after spending too much time building the first quarter of the story.  Gameplay couldn't rescue it either.  There were far fewer puzzles and a ridiculous amount of walking back and forth between the same few locations.
Dreamfall Chapters is ultimately a better game than Dreamfall: TLJ but it has its own numerous faults.
Foremost, Dreamfall Chapters takes Dreamfall: TLJ's tedium and multiplies it by 10 for a good chunk of the game.  Rarely have I felt my time being more intolerably wasted by a developer than I had playing the first half of Chapters.  The game takes place primarily in two large areas (large for an adventure game at least) and there are tasks that involve walking from one side of the map to the other and then back again at a painfully slow movement speed.  There's also the modern day equivalent of pixel hunts where you need to run around looking for *something* until the game's interface highlights it.  Running, which you will always want to do despite it still being really slow, requires constantly holding a key or gamepad trigger down instead of it just being a toggle.  So there's a physical annoyance to go with the mental annoyance too.  It's hard not to feel like the run speed and tasks that have you traverse the map are the equivalent of triple spacing a term paper.  The game seems like it was padded in the worst way possible - presumably meet some playtime target promised to backers.
The latter half of the game gets rid of much of the walking around and then becomes more or less a slightly interactive movie as result.  Honestly, I prefer it as an interactive movie than it pretending to be an adventure game, but that first half is still a good 8-10 hours you have to suffer through and I wouldn't recommend it based on that alone.  Sadly, the narrative that takes over in the second half isn't great either.
It's remarkable how much the game resembles Dreamfall in it's terrible pacing.  The first 3 out of 5 books are incredibly slow and spend a lot of time exploring minor details that become completely inconsequential once the game opens up the "here's the real plot" flood gates.  That happens in the last 2 books, and they throw so much complex metaphysical nonsense your way that it would put a modern JRPG to shame.  At a certain point, it becomes hard to feel any empathy for the characters because the events they're involved in are just *too* fantastical for them to have any believable reaction to them.
To the game's credit, it does have an extended denouement, which is rare to see in games, and it does tie up a lot of (though not all) loose threads - but they're threads that barely made sense in the first place.  On some level, I appreciate that the developer shot for the stars with their narrative complexity, but it just doesn't have the nuance or time to develop things as well as, say, a novel (or series of novels) would.  They once again bit off too much for the medium in which the story is being delivered.

Hey you. Do you like Terraria? You do? Hm, nice my dude. You like sci-fi? Well, if you do, come get Starbound!
...is what I'd say, but as my argument with Terraria being 'a 2D Minecraft' and the Witcher 3 being a 'bigger Skyrim', the truth is that all these three statements do the game the exact opposite of a service. Terraria will always have more weapons to play with and become stronger, while Starbound well...
You know that quote, right? 'It's not about the destination, but the adventures that happen on the journey', something like that. Well, while Starbound's story is somewhat forgettable, even in the base game, there is a lot to do. There's a infinitely generated solar system for you to explore, with some exclusive and unique monsters to catch, to dig up all the fossils and put them in display cases, make a insectarium, create a succesful colony or town...there's a lot of stuff to do in this game.
And to make matters better*...it allows mods. Mods that can make the game 10x longer, to make it more like a RPG, to make your race choice matter, to improve combat, to make farming easier, or make the game harder. It's all there, and it all makes the game so much better.
It's hard to describe this game. On one hand, I'd say it's a Terraria where the combat wasn't the main focus, but rather on every other aspect. It rewards building, exploring, and taking the unbeaten path. It also throws in some tough platforming challenges which will take some thinking to get past sometimes, or sheer skill.
Overall, this game is worthy of your time. You will always find something to do, to keep you occupied.

I choose to recommand this game because it is a pretty decent city building simulation. But, personally, I don't consider it as a decent ANNO game.
As the sequel of Anno 2070, the game is definitely advanced in graphics, but graphics is probably the only thing that 2205 is advanced compared to 2070. The core mechanisms of ANNO series are still avaliable in 2205, but some interesting systems (e.g. eco-balance, trading in one map with ships, underwater plateau, etc.) are taken away by the developers for some reasons.  In 2205, maps are devided into 3 sections. You have to wait 10s+ for the map to load if you want to switch to another section. Battles are isolated into serveral "dungons" instead of happening  in the same map where your cities are built. These really makes the game fragmented.
In the game of ANNO 2205, you can find some connections between the current game and the previous ANNO 2070 (e.g. the sunken ARK, I'm guessing that is Virago in 2070, bankrupt Global Trust, etc.). The devs also wrote some lore to connect 2205 with 2070, but overall the connection is really weak. This is not a big problem though.
When I first saw the trailer of ANNO 2205, I was expecting sth new and interesting like space ARK or battle on moon. But reality is, the devs cancel the entire ARK system (I really like the ARK, maybe it's just me) and, no, the battles still happen on Earth.
If you are interested in a sci-fi city building game, you could consider buying Anno 2205 when it is on sale, since the game does offer some cool concepts. However, if you would like to experience the playstyle of a true ANNO game, buy 2070 instead.

Right now, I can say the game is well balanced when it comes to building your city. However, it's terrible to defend it.
Although you don't have a lot of things to build yet, things complement one another easely, making a perfect sense where and why you should build that structure. If you play the non-aggressive version of the game, in a couple of hours without much experience you can build a self-sustained city with a nice profit on everything.
The invasion system was supposed to be the drain of the game. In other words, you have to invest in military structures and soldiers not only to defend you kingdom but also to have something to do with your money and resources. And that's the part where the game sucks badly.
The combats are extremely bad-programmed. There are two kinds of invasors: the dragon and the vikings. The former can fly anywhere he wants and, if he manages to randomly glide above your city, he can start to burn things down. A dragon invasion, if not repelled, gives you destruction and bad happiness, that leads to less recruitment of new people.
The vikings are even more terrible. They invade your lands in lots, burn things down, kill people and leave everyone in despair. In the early game, it's almos impossible to repel them, and the damages are too high imo. Your leader and its army are extremely dumb, since you cannot command them to attack directly an army. You have to try to predict where the vikings are going and then position your leader on the path. Totally lame.
So, right now, this is a good game, but it still has to improve a lot, specially the invasion system, which can be very frustrating specially if it's tough to repel it.

Cons: Having been on the brink of being a tolerable game; this most recent update just killed the remaining faith I had left in the Anno franchise (and Ubisoft). It really breaks my heart because I have put in hundreds if not thousands of hours total into Anno games ever since anno 1503.
The first true signs of trouble were when they moved to Anno-online, a freemium game that became just a complete grind, a huge waste of time to build even a modest city. Nevertheless I had extremely high hopes for Anno 2205. The trailer and gameplay footage had me absolutely stoked, and brought back the little kid in me. I had hoped that Ubisoft had seen the errors of their ways (of course they haven't, since addictive freemium games are a trashy yet extremely profitable business model.) However any hope was dashed when it became apparent 10 hours into Anno 2205 that they are still trying to expand their customer base to the ultra-casual crowd and find "creative" ways to keep players away from actual city-building.
I tolerated the stupid side quests where you go look around the map for containers or send out your command ship to pick up some idiot fisherman that got stranded 20 feet away from a bustling space-port, because they were completely optional, and was a good way to pass the time and wait for resources to collect up during early stages of the game. However with the most recent update, I find myself doing less city building and more time-wasting. Those optional side quests became jaw droppingly stupid, in the form of calamities that will absolutely wreck your delicate cis-lunar economy unless you spend 10 minutes scouring your maps looking for containers, or buy up virtual stocks of some failing company that will cost millions only to reduce your income. Those same companies  somehow have millions of dollars in reserve constantly to purchase stocks in your level 90 company, chewing away at your profit margins). Sure you can turn off the features; however they were introduced because users were complaining about how brain-numbingly easy the game is, therefore people like me who were looking for a challenge would max out the difficulty. Unfortunately they chose the easy way out instead of actually sitting down and come up with a good game design, they just made it more painful. Furthermore, rare resources needed to build expansion modules on producttion buildings have to be farmed with quickly-repetitive combat missions and uploads from a freaking freemium mobile game add-on. Though granted the mobile game is well made and decently fun; 3 hours into it I thought to myself "wtf am I doing? Why am I spending my previous free time on a mobile game just to be able to improve my Anno in-game buildings?!"
The gameplay is decent. Sure it's oversimplified, but with the complex economy and global market, I thought focusing more on the rate of production instead of pure quantities was a nice touch. However even on the highest difficulty, the gameplay was comparable to moderate level of Anno 2070, which I adored. By the 40th hour mark, I was spending 60% of my time grinding through the same 6 combat missions to get rare resources to power my vast and quickly expanding city-states. It became apparent with the latest update that all the old guard who made the franchise that we used to love have all either left or been overpowered by people who are not strategy gamers. WIll they make money? Maybe. Will they change? Probably not. They'll probably make more freemium games and DLC's. Will I ever buy another Anno game? Only if the reviews are overwhelmingly possitive, but I will no longer give them the benefit of the doubt and try out a game that isn't a blockbuster.
RIP in Peace.

Not recommended for the following reasons:
1) Performs poorly despite low poly graphics and tiny map sizes. Yes, my computer is ~5 years old but it still has an i7 processor.

Would I recommend this game?  If this is a yes or no question then:  Yes.  But honestly it's not a great game, let alone RPG.
The game is mostly a guilty pleasure, it's not really a fantastic game.  It's a competant 3rd person RPG with some pretty awful combat mechanics and animations.  Enemies can juggle you in combat, they will cheese you and you'll find yourself dying more out of poor mechanics then being outwitted or outplayed.  The story is almost incomprehensible at times and honestly too much - I ended up skipping/skimming dialogue towards the 2nd half of the game.  For an RPG there isnt much character development; you invest XP earned in skills and magic.  It becomes very easy to know which skills to use at the beginning and to only upgrade them.
Throughout the game you're presented with dialogue choices with NPCs as you complete quests, you are given a black or white decision to pick.  The problem is that these decisions never impact the game in anyway, some just open or close quests that may occur.  The gameworld does not change, any meaningful change occurs after the credits roll or when the narrator tells you of your actions consequences for the future.  I would even say that the overal plot was pretty bland, though I do appreciate what they tried to do - just the execution was poor.
One of the worst things about the game is the lack of saving.  There are no manual saves, instead the game opts for checkpoints only at specific points of the game.  It's agravating entering into a new zone, picking up a few quests and killing a few mobs just to enter a house and have a trap instantly kill you.  Loading the checkpoint brings you back 10-15 minutes prior having you kill those mobs and talk to those NPCs all over again.
Another poor aspect is the inventory system, and the world economy.  You'll end up getting really good gear quickly and you keep looting what is quite frankly junk.  The worlds merchants simply do not have anything to offer you or the coin to take your stuff.  You end up having to buy junk you may need, such as ingredients for potions, just to sell your junk.  This is compounded by not having a weight limit for your inventory, your inventory ends up having pages and pages of items and its nigh impossible to find anything you need.
Also crafting is pretty awful, even when maxed there are only 3 "healing potions" you can make - where one is honestly the only one you'll be using.  To make them you'll need to appropriate materials but they are finite in the world.  Gear crafting is similarly poor, you insert upgrades into your gear but you cannot remove the upgrades so you're constantly ditching and rebuying your gear if you want to upgrade.
If I had to rate the game I'd give it a 3/5, I dont see myself playing it again for awhile.  It has two endings, but both can be obtained at the very end without any previous choices influencing your options.  I did most if not all sidequests, about 19 hours.  If I had listened to every single NPC proddle on about their drama it would be about 20-21 hours.  Beat the game on normal - it's not a hard game, as with all RPGs it gets easier as you play it and level.

+ Story-wise the premise is interesting enough, with plenty of rich dialogue and notes littered throughout the game to read and absorb. The choice system, while nothing new in gaming nowadays, does have a minor impact on the story overall (similar to
, where you can decide on which faction to join, though on a much smaller scale here).
- Now when it comes to the combat, this is probably a deal breaker for most people. The combat is extremely repetitive. While it does have the basics for most RPG combat systems; including blocking, parrying, physical and magical skills etc., every fight you are essentially somewhat mashing (there is a timing and combo aspect to fighting) the attack button, and later on spamming spells and skills when you’re able to. For a linear RPG this is standard, but it’s still undeniable that the gameplay in this game will become tedious very quickly; and considering some spells are incredibly strong later on in the game and easily spammable, the game is rarely challenging at all (unless you bump the difficulty up). Considering the game is around 11 hours long (on Normal difficulty), if you don’t enjoy the combat in the first hour, it’s not getting to get any better as the game progresses
- Also, to comment on other weak gameplay aspects: there is little need to trade items or even explore the environment for new items, as equipment makes negligible differences to your characters stats. Lastly, but not least, there is no manual-saving at all in the game, which isn’t really a concern to me considering the game is extremely linear, but not having that option may put off some players
- The sound design in general is quite poor. It seems as if some parts have sound clips missing (or put simply there’s no sound at all, such as when a boss makes a visual scream yet nothing comes out of their mouth), forgettable music, and mediocre voice acting at best leaves much to be desired in the sound department
- While I positively commented on the graphics, in terms of different locations, there are very few. In fact, you visit the starting dungeon three times throughout the course of the story. Yes you heard me right,
. You can definitely see where they had to cut corners in this part of the game
- Lastly, while for the first three chapters of the game the story is solid enough, once you hit the later stages of the fourth chapter and the finale, the game feels completely rushed. The final boss and ending especially are wholly underwhelming and definitely feel like a weak climax to the overall experience.
“Feeling like a poor man’s RPG (at £30 no less),
is an average and linear Western-style RPG with some redeeming qualities. If you are a big RPG fan and want something new to play, there are plenty of better games out there. But, if you can get this game extremely cheap, and have exhausted playing the best RPGs on the market, this is a solid middle-of-the-road one to play.”

First and foremost, Demonicon is a third-person RPG game filled with battles, magic, humans, creatures and demons. The game is also classless, meaning that you are not in a specific class or limited to certain skills, feats or talents.
Body, Mind (knowledge) and Power development is central to your progress in the game.
Upgrading health (vitality), mana (essence) and endurance (encumbrance) improve the Body.
Skills such as Lore, Blacksmithing and/or haggling strengthen the Mind.
Special attacks (which uses encumbrance) and Gift powers (uses essence) build up your Power.
There are two types of points used for upgrading: AP (which is for Skills and Body upgrades, and Special attacks) and GP (which is for Gift powers) which are to be used with CAUTION.
The graphic detail and quality are rather poor considering that this game was made in 2013, but they are not utterly terrible either. Sound and music are amazing. Dialogue and storytelling are breath taking, with choices you make along the way, and are fantastically done.
The battle system is not that bad. Playing with either an edged weapon (fast but weak) or blunt weapon (slow but strong) are fun, along with magic at your fingertips. Enemies become stronger as the game progresses, which make you need to upgrade your equipment, or buy new equipment at a merchant (which is a must, sell old equipment to earn money).
Weapons and armour, can be modified to give additional properties such as extra points to attack or armour bonus or poison, critical hits or improved skills. It all depends on you.
Decisions, decisions, decisions. At times, they are easy, and at times, extremely tough. They can be wrong or right. It all depends on what you want the outcome to be. And this game is full of them. You may decide to be fearless and cruel and tempered, or calm and merciful and noble, it just depends on you, but it also comes to standing your ground according to what is right for you. But remember, actions bear consequences - what you decide in the beginning may come back to bite you in the end, and horribly.
Finally (WARNING: complicated process), after killing a demon that stole my trolley, I accidently turned myself into a broken couch and was finally kidnapped by peg sellers.
I award this game with a 8.84 out of 10. If you are into RPGs and third-person, not hassled by graphics or having to make tough decisions, then this game may just pique your interest.
A final note: a patch for the game for improved graphics, fighting, conversations and everything else improved can be downloaded for free from Steam.

Demonicon:
10 hours in the game at the time of writing
Now where do i begin?
This game gives you choices, well to be specific, a set amount of choices as well as consequences tied to said choices.
That is what i love about Demonicon. If you can look past the funny voice acting, the hilarous script and the bipolar tendecies of your hero Cairon, then you are in for a very funny ride.
The graphics of the game were average at most, not bad and also not that good. Just average. There are a few graphical options to choose from in order for you to tweak your experience with it i guess.
There will be a few instances where some textures take time to load or will not load at all, but this happened rarely.
The voice acting in this game is really funny to me. There's the obligatory english/british accent and what really makes it funny is the script. It is like they really wanted Cairon to sound like the most bi-polar hero you'll ever encounter. You can be mad in one moment and immediately be the paragon of kindness in the next.
The consequences in the game are shown to you in a cutscene whenever you finish the quest chain that had you make the choices. It sums up your choices in a very creative way, i love the presentation. The consequences themselves range from things you can live with, things you can't sleep at night about and things that are cartoonishly evil.
The thing i like the most is that while you can be a total♥♥♥♥♥♥to everyone, your dickishness won't lock you out of doing good things and you have a chance to turn it around should you wish to. There is also a fair amount of flirting since apparently a ton of women find Cairon attractive.
The story of the game revolves around the two siblings, Cairon and Calandra, and their "destiny"
I won't really spoil anyone reading this but one of the main bits of the story itself is actually revealed in the steam trading cards you get from the game.
The combat is annoying at first. Like really. It takes a while to kill something, imagine getting swarmed while you still have the starting equipment. But it does get easier as you progress, though some skill combinations kind of break the game for me as it makes you near invincible. (Feint+Nova, Ice Lance+Mortal Blow. Plowed through hordes of enemies with it.)
There isn't much variation between the weapons and armor that you get, most of them look similar to each other if not totally the same except for the stats that it has. There isn't really a class since you just tweak your skills to your liking.
My Cairon was a fast talking, persuasive, lockpicking, trap disabling, spell throwing, sword slashing, medieval ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
I absolutely loved playing Demonicon and i'm seriously considering a few more playthroughs with different choices like
flirt with Girl A instead of Girl B or be a♥♥♥♥♥♥to NPC A instead of being a♥♥♥♥♥♥to NPC B, etc etc etc.
You don't have to buy it at full price if you don't want to, i got this game in a bundle and i totally recommend getting it that way too if you're on the fence about buying the game. It is a must try experience.

Very cool game. Your goal is similar to the previous game; grow a star plant and get high into the sky. However, It's not just more of the same, there's new abilities like the ability to grow plants to help you and even a spin dash that is certainly not a Sonic spin dash. The game is now on a spherical planet rather than a flat island, it's small enough that you can see the curveture from the surface of the planet, the higher you go up the cooler it looks. Abilities are powered by batteries that quickly recharge, this makes it very easy to get around, but not so easy that everything is trivial. You'll also need to collect space ship parts, giving you a great reason to run around the planet rather than just grow the star plant.
There's challeneges that unlock skins for your robot and 150 crystals to collect so you can hold more energy. Teleporters are back, making it easy to get around the planet without worrying about having to make a trek back to where you came from. Climbing is easy as ever, left mouse/right mouse (or left trigger/right trigger on gamepads) grip onto surfaces, move in the direction you want to go and your robot will automatically move his hands as needed.
The best new feature are the flying bees that followed me around. I don't know if it was from the skin I was wearing or if it happens to everybody. The bees hum, so they've got that going for them too.
I'm surprised this game is only $10 and silently released, no marketing or fanfare. It's a great game and a must buy.
Edit: It took me about 4 hours to complete the main objective. I still have a bunch of crystals and challeneges to complete.

Tired of things being described as "like Dark Souls" just because they have an obtuse control scheme.
Dark Souls is an epic third person adventure with tight controls and a surreal atmosphere.
This is nothing like Dark Souls, with the possible exception of the atmosphere.
It is QWOP mixed with a lacking Diablo-clone.
It's the sort of game where strafing is considered "combat mode only" controls, because that is totally what people want.
For $12 it isn't bad, but, it isn't an isometric DS game like a bunch of the front page reviews claim.

So have you ever played one of those games where it's so frustrating to play and so ridiculouysly hard to master, but all you can do is keep trying because it's so graphically pleasing and so satisfying when you get even just one kill? This is THAT game!
There's no tutorial, BUT there IS a quick help guide which helps tremendously in some cases.
This game NEEDS a quick tutorial in the beginning, kind of helping the player with mouse gestures, and ways to make better contact with your foe. You can eventually, somewhat, sorta strike the opponent, but not very accurately or with much force it seems. But maybe with more gameply I can figure it out.
It'd be cool to see more animations when your enemy has low health as well. Maybe he starts limping, or guarding one side that you've been striking most or more blood on that side as well as chopping limbs off would be great and help just so i'm not gussing how many times i gotta strike this guy with my sword! I love the idea of no health bars for the enemy's because it seems more realistic and different! I love that your character automatically blocks for you, you just have to be careful when to strike otherwise you'll get hit and quite rapidly from the npc's. Maybe difficulty levels would be a nice addition to the game as well!
This game has the coolest physics i've seen in such a graphically enhanced game it blows my mind! The Way YOU control your weapon puts you right in the battles and makes you feel like you're the blademaster! It feels and looks really great!
The Arena is a cool feature as well! When you die though (which is very often, at least for me; maybe I suck who knows) You either have to
A) Quit all the way back to the homescreen and reselect your character and weapons again or,
B) Click Exit that appears on the screen when you die which takes you to your character selection page
(the game remembers your gear and character but it's still a pain to go all the way back to the beginning)
There should be an option to select retry or restart as soon as you die, and the game drops you right back into battle with the gear you already have.
Overall I haven't gotten past the first npc i've met in the "career" mode, so the hours you see are mostly spent reading the quick start guide and playing in the arena constantly clicking EXIT, NEXT, NEXT, and finally back to START, and starting back from square one in the arena. It's all actually pretty damn fun slashing your foes with the swipe of your mouse in an entirely NEW way. Something I personally have never seen done in a game before. That's what kept me playing and coming back for more! Something totally new and I was willing to learn the basics becuase it was so damn fun asthetically pleasing to watch!
7/10 for graphics and gameplay! For this being early access I'd say that's a pretty fair score considering the difficulty! Needs some work and more features but overall it's a great game and I will continue to play and wait for more updates! Great Job Devs and Keep Up the Great Work!

So, I've given this game a fair shot at this point in the early access process. I've been following this game for quite some time, and was eager to dig in at first opportunity.
I was genuinely excited about physics based combat, and like many other reviewers before me have mentioned, the screenshots and short trailer do nothing to fully illustrate how combat works. It is simply way more complex than it appears... to the point of becoming a drunken brawl in every single encounter I get into.
Seriously, one of my biggest gripes about the game is the lack of information in the game. I know we all gripe about tutorials here and there, especially when they're overly long and teach the player things that should already be understood (if you fall from high up, you take damage, etc), but this game seems to lack all but the most basic information. After my first encounter going awry, I studied the information in the controls section for about 20 minutes, and was still unable to figure out if there is a way to manually block, or how blocking works, or how to keep my character from moving about like a drunken lunatic in the middle of a battle. (Moving in any direction while fighting via the WASD keys seems to jerk the character back and forth, affecting the direction and power of swings... it isn't pretty or practical).
There is hardly any indication of what objects can be interacted with and which can't. You come across several crates which all look alike, and some cannot be moved or opened, while others can.
The dungeon itself and the environment is nice, and eerily appropriate for a game like this. The close-quarters make using larger weapons more difficult, as they can get caught on the walls, but this isn't always enough to stop enemies. It functions something like Chivalry, in the regard, allowing you to guide larger weapon wielding opponents into tight hallways to battle them more effectively.
I think this game has a lot of potential, and I'm looking forward to changing this review. It is early access, after all, and hopefully, a lot of these concerns will be corrected in the future.
The main point of this review is just to give people a heads-up of what to expect at this juncture, and to provide some constructive criticism, especially regarding the lack of information given to the player when starting the game.

Character arcs are rushed and the ending leaves massive questions hanging while failing at tidying everything up, a symptom of the utter failure of the dev-team to build a full experience within the constraints they were given. It's obvious they were setting up for another game, but have professed they were so miserable and exhausted making this game that they are done with the franchise.
If I knew this is what we were going to get, I'd rather have had the previous game be the last in the series, so I could have ended the franchise with a good taste in my mouth. Pass this up. If you really need some resolution, read a wiki instead of wasting your money.

I would like to be among the voices of positive dissent and say that this game has been given an unfair shake by many people here. You'd think by the "Mostly Negative" reception it's a broken, unplayable mess or something. No, the fact of the matter is that it's just a really short campaign (that could be said to be just a glorified map pack) using the same weapons and enemies as usual from Half-Life and with a hilariously tossed-together end boss fight. So, in short, it's Blue Shift all over again, only it's his much younger, shorter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cousin (though Blue Shift didn't have a boss fight) we're dealing with here. I did like Blue Shift though, and in general after playing through the honestly exhausting campaigns that were the original Half-Life, the great Opposing Force and even Blue Shift to some degree it's nice to play a small chaser like this that focuses on its action from the getgo without fussing over length or annoying platforming sections.
So the game is intended as a fan's interpretation as to how the yellow crystal that caused the Black Mesa disaster was obtained in the first place. It's been found on a cargo ship of sorts when it's taken over by the Xen aliens killing everyone, Now it's up to you, another mute, hazard suit-bearing superscientist badass named Andrew Winner (so literally you can say "YOU'RE WINNER!" in this case) to be teleported to the ship and retrieve the "artifact" in question. The moment you start a headcrab attacks you, with an assault rifle over a corpse behind you to take care of it. And from then on, it's Zombies, Vortigaunts, one part with three annoying turrets (when aren't they annoying?), Houndeyes, Bullsquids, all your favorites, before you face tougher foes like the Alien Grunts and Alien Controllers (which can be safely ignored really) getting in your way. One part has a bunch of snarks busting out of a vent shaft which is an instant death trap if you don't get back on the ladder that got you there to begin with (I don't know if it's triggered by going near it or by defeating the other enemies in the room first). Oh, yes, you face off against some... military guys. All four of them They use Marine skins but they don't seem to be Marines. I don't know who they are or why they want you dead. Are they some special ops team tasked with retrieving the artifact for their own gain, destroying it, etc.? Like I said this is before we even get to the Black Mesa debacle so hostile human presence doesn't make sense here, story-wise.
Anyway, the entire game is a relatively small, extremely linear cargo ship whose structure is going from point A to B and then A again where you face off against the boss, end game. You have to get to the captain who's holed himself up in a room at the top of the ship and get him to open up the cargo hold under the ship where the yellow crystal is. Then it's another firefight against your more deadly opponents until you face off against... "Genome" Blah-blah Number-Such-and-such aka "Nihilanth with a Barnacle for a mouth." It's one of the silliest boss fights ever. First you drop down the cargo bay, where you recover some of your health somehow, and also lose all your weapons, which you have to run around the arena to retrieve again(?). The boss has no animation to it whatsoever, it's like a Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade float of Nihilanth chasing you around with a long tongue dangling on the ground (avoid the tongue or it's instant death). Where's the yellow crystal? He comes right in the bay in a  cinematic and... swallows it up with his tongue. Why? Just... because. All you do really is circle-strafe non-stop firing up at him as he floats around trying to get you with his tongue. It doesn't take long to finish him off really. I filled him with some magnum bullets, a few bullets from an assault rifle, a grenade shot and he exploded instantly... exactly like a balloon would. Oh yeah there's Alien Controllers above trying to fire at you but they're of no consequence since you're moving around so much they can't exactly hit you so they're not worth the bother. You get a cutscene where we see Gordon Freeman walk into a room where the yellow crystal is, and we know the happy fun times that comes afterwards.
So, why do I recommend this game besides being short and free (which isn't really a reason to recommend anything, plenty of bad things are short and free)? Well, it's still Half-Life, it plays as such, and so it still fun and plays well. I like the tighter action focus here, a good break from Half-Life and its expansions' labyrinths, platforms and fetch quests. The action makes for a good coffee break on Medium difficulty, and somewhat challenging on Hard (this is the only Half-Life anything I've bothered with on Hard only because of the length - the other games were exhausting enough on Medium in my opinion), and though I did die a decent number of times most of those were from the turrets, the one REAL pain the♥♥♥♥♥on Hard (everything else is either just a minor inconvenience or something you can easily plow through, like the slow-moving Zombies). I like the sharper textures of the graphics and generally smoother, faster animation (it says to use the "Half-Life 1.8" engine, whatever that is) and little things like the new model and animation for the pistol. And the music too. The Half-Life games offered plenty of quiet moments in between its brief bits of moody music, here it offers more thumping electronic music that doesn't let up. It starts off with a catchy mid-paced track and for a brief time some nice techno/d'n'b for the section fighting the military dudes (too bad that doesn't last too long). The level design isn't the most amazing, it's just a stretched-out corridor essentially but for a cargo ship it gets the job done.
I'd say if you're a Half-Life fan, haven't played this and wondering if you should bother I'd say yes, go ahead and form your own opinion on it. Like I said if nothing else it's short, free and very much playable with no bugs or game-breaking glitches that I could see. So now that you know that, what you think of the rest of the game is up to you.

The first time I started this game, I made it about 20 minutes into the hugely comprehensive tutorial course and my brain shut down. It was a matter of weeks until I was brave enough to boot it up again, and a couple of days to finish the tutorials, then I was ready to get building.
This game is phenomenal, just persevere through the learning curve and you'll end up feeling like a weapon designer. It's minecraft for war. It's Space Engineers but fun. Designing a new ship/plane/helicopter/submarine is a pure joy, and I lost a few nights just running weapons tests over and over, tweaking parameters in an endless pursuit of explosive perfection. My older designs look like childrens' toys compared to my newest experiments, and there's a vast number of systems and vehicle types that I haven't even touched yet.
This game has a huge amount of depth; it's like having a job if your job is to design stuff that blows other stuff up. This is the pinnacle of creative games, and there are few games that have been so chaotically fun.
Get it, please.

I didn't expect much from Demonicon, and if you go in with the same expectations you might come out the same way I did, enjoying the game for what it is.
So what is Demonicon, well it's a mostly linear RPG with a focus on combat. Pretty much all of your time within the game will be spent following the main quest storyline. There are some sidequests that you can pick up very occasionally, but they are very short and easy to complete, a lot of them even while doing the main quest. The sidequests are there just to give you something else to do, but they are not rewarding to complete and none of them even give out any good loot.
And that is probably one of the biggest issues within the game, there is no good loot anywhere. And by good loot I mean something cool and unexpected that you manage to acquire by doing something the game doesn't force you to do. Your potential rewards are a weapon equal to or worse than what you already have, some potions, money and junk (various stuff that the game classifies itself as junk by automatically placing it under an inventory tab labeled "Junk"). Not to mention the fact that noone of the merchants have anything useful to sell, the best weapons and armour they have available will always be on the same level as your current gear. Perhaps you could buy some potions from the merchants, but you find so many yourself that it's unlikely you'll run out and even if you do you can very easily brew some more yourself.
The story is very important in an RPG, but this one isn't anything to write home about. It has an interesting premise, and it starts by trying to establish some complicated relationships between the main characters, but the execution leaves much to be desired. In Mass Effect style you have the conversation wheel where you select the next conversation topic or answer a question in a multitude of ways. However nothing you say ever has much of an impact on the progression of the story, the game only gives you the illusion of choice. But the story did interest me just enough to keep me playing, it does try to do something slightly different, even if the rest of it is average at best.
So what is it that I actually continued (and finished) playing the game for? Well, I quite enjoyed the combat within the game (although you really should play the game on Hard for any sort of a challenge). It starts off easy and very simple, but it does become a bit more complex as you encounter enemies that don't respond all that well to simply mashing the attack button. And as you gather experience you start unlocking more interesting skills, although none of them are anything out of the ordinary.
Demonicon also has something I am probably just a big sucker for, skills that affect how you play the game outside of combat. The skills are as follows (the names might not be exact):
- Legend (it allows you to pick up lore tidbits from the game world and occasionally opens up conversation options)
- Herbalism (it allows you pick up better quality plants and unlocks more recipes as you skill up)
- Medicine (sometimes you can heal someone with it, and it affects how much health you regenerate after each combat and from potions)
- Perception (highlights traps and hidden loot)
- Fast Talk (enables you to convince NPCs with an additional conversation option when the game offers you that option)
- Haggle (lowers merchant prices, probably the most useless skill in the game)
- Lockpicking (open up chests for loot)
- Blacksmithing (disarm traps and upgrade you weapons/armour)
I started the game with a complete focus on these skills and disregarded any and all combat skills until I had these maxed out. I never felt I had any particular difficulty in combat, partly because leveling up spells uses up a different type of experience and partly because it really isn't that difficult. You could easily do the opposite and just focus on combat completely, but then you'd be losing one of the more entertaining aspects of the game.
Demonicon's problem is that it doesn't do anything particularly well, but taken as a whole it was an enjoyable experience for me. And for a budget RPG I wasn't expecting anything more.

This is a game that I picked up rather randomly, with the only intention being to pass the time with...that turned around into getting "into it" and finishing it over the course of this week. The first thing worth noting is that I wish that the steam review system allowed for Neutral Reviews, because this is one particular game that I feel falls into neither one side or the other, but kind of in-between, depending on the player.
That said, I won't elaborate much on the story, because I feel that the game's description does an adequate enough job and I prefer to avoid spoilers. However, worth noting is that the story is one of the stronger points that this game has, it's interesting right from the very beginning and hooks you in. It's a shame though, because it kinda falls through near the end, I personally didn't like the ending, but that's just me and I think the game would have benefitted from more choice and consequence dialogue options, beyond the few choices you get to make at critical points in the story. Then again, maybe I'm asking for too much and should go play a Bioware RPG then? Regardless, what choice and consequence options there are, are pretty interesting and thankfully, aren't simply a matter of "good or evil" and instead, as previously stated, choice and consequence options. For example *SPOILER ALER!!!* the first such option has you deciding between letting a cannibal go and saving his captives, with the obvious conseqence of letting him run free and keep eating humans, or killing him, which at the same time, will kill his captives because they are bound to his life by a spell. I actually had to give this decision a few moments of thought before deciding, and when a game makes me stop to think, I believe it's done something right.
Moving on to the gameplay, the core of it is typical Action/RPG fare. Standard attacks, skills and magic are your options in combat. Standard hack and slashing consists of stringing together attacks into combo chains, the higher your combo chain, the higher the chance of scoring critical hits and after a certain amount, you start recovering hit points every time you hit an enemy. Also at your disposal is a dodge function and skills that you can learn with Adventure Points (AP) which you earn through combat and completing quests among other methods. Magic is learned using Gift Points (GP) which is strictly earned through combat and tied to how often you use magic. Finally, there are more geenric skills that are helpful throughout the game, such as Blacksmithing, which allows you to disarm traps and upgrade weapons, Lock Picking which allows you to, well...Pick Locks, Fast Talking which opens up optional disalogue choices and Lore which allows you to gain extra insight into people, places, enemies and so on, in the form of more information being unlocked in your journal and it also opens up more optional dialogue choices. Complementing everything, is Alchemy Crafting which allows you to brew Potions, Poisons and make Balms, unfortunately I cannot comment on that feature, as I mostly ignored it, because I went for the achievement for completing the game without using any potions and Blacksmithing, which allows you to upgrade weapons with components that you buy, or find in chests or get as rewards for completing quests. With gameplay in general, I had a few issues, while combat is easy to grasp, it also felt too simplistic and while some of the skills and magic are definitely useful, they didn't really stand out for me in terms of being "fun to play with", also, one of the things that immediately come to mind when I think of an Action/RPG, is loot, lots of (hopefully) varied and fun to tinker with, loot...most of the loot in this game is generic and not really interesting, and I hate...let me say it again, I HATE, that the game only has two different melee weapons: Swords and Clubs...I mean, really? Oh, wait...no shields either. Finally, the end fight disappointed me, it was a push over and probably the easiest boss fight in the entire game.
Graphics and Sound...probably where this game fails at quite miserably, wallows in the mud and then gets stomped on by a passing horse. No, really...it's THAT bad. Graphically, this game looks like it belongs in the early 00s, while the atmosphere is spot on, giving the game a less "Fantasy" and more "Realistic" setting, the graphics are bad at best. Adding insult to injury, a lot of the animations during cutscenes are cringe-worthy or plain don't exist, like an NPC handing the main character an item and the main character supposedly examining it, which is suggested, but isn't animated, unless you use the imagination and imagine it. What animations are there, are mostly cringe-worthy as I mentioned before, like the main character awkwardly drawing his sword and looking as if his about to fall backwards because of it's weight. Another complaint is the design of the game world, while the atmosphere is great and lends itself to the plot quite nicely, at the same time...it doesn't have a whole lot of variety and not much in terms of interesting things to see. Finally, generic music and sound and mostly awful voice acting, some people have praised the voice work on this game and I guess to each their own, but in my opinion, it's horrible.
Final thoughts: This game had a lot of potential, but instead was ruined. The game is rather short, the first chapter itself spans about half of the time you'll spend playing this game, which gives you false expectactions as it sets the stage to make you believe that each chapter will be similar in length, but their not. More interesting side quests and less linearity may also have helped, but most of all, better graphics, at least for a game that came out in 2013. Oh and is asking to be able to skip cutscenes too much? <_<
Ultimately, I recommend the game, why? Because despite it's flaws, it's still an enjoyable game, if you can get it for 75% off, as it's NOT worth the full asking price.

The Witcher, Risen, Dragon Age 2, and Bound By Flame.
Demonicon opens up with you looking for your sister who is to be married. Where she decided to hide is in a demonic mountain... It turns out that she wasn't hiding but tracking someone. During which it turns out that the reason your father didn't want you mixing your blood was because it unlocks some kind of power. You quickly find out that your father has lots of secrets about you and your sister. It also turns out your sister is in love with you and doesn't want to be married. So you are off on a quest to make it so she doesn't have to. Eventually she gets taken away as well and you must find her. Strangely none of what I've said gives away any actual plot. The game runs from 15-30 hours depending on your curiousity.
The game is set up to use dark eye rule sets on stats which gives a lot of extra things to do and dialogue along the way. Should you decide to go into plant lore you can gather plants and use alchemy to make potions. Making potions and gathering herbs give you more AP points which you had to spend to get those skills in the first place. The world is actually pretty interesting if you choose all the differnt dialogue options which gives you more of the games lore. There are traps you can disarm and chances are one will kill you because you didn't notice it. The combat is actually pretty good except for the counter attack which hardly works. The sound overall in the game is on par. New enemies get introduced regularly, but in the begining you will wonder if that's true. The game offers up interesting choices to make that very much are a shade of gray. The only problem is the end of the game never lets you know how these choices had an effect long term.
The counter attack combat move doesn't work. The game only offers a few different armor options. There is practically no point in buying anything other then potions from merchants which leaves you with a large amount of gold you will never spend for almost the entire game. The tutorial doesn't actually exist so best of luck figuring out controls and how to upgrade your character using the dark eye rules because they don't tell you. I would date the graphics around the year 2007 and most of the world tend to use a very brown color pallette. The ending portion of the game gives you a ton of choices and none of them except the final one actually does anything. This tends to be a trend in this game because you can also get dialogue options throughout by having certains skills, but it tends to only introduce more dialogue and not change the end result in the least for the most part anyway.
I enjoyed my time with Demonicon even with it's sub par graphics and sometimes cliche story rifts. I feel like the game had enourmous potential for a small studio and they just never got there. I feel if the creators would have had user feedback before release it could have been different. Where it sits I can only suggest this game to true RPG fanboys looking for an action romp in a world that is more interesting to here about in the games notes and dialogue then in actual exploration. If only they would have included updates to the choices you made like The Witcher and Dragon Age Origins did I would give this game a lot more praise.
I'd value it as an average quick romp RPG at about $7.50 value.

Its been a long time since I've played through a platformer and much longer since I've played one with such polish. This game really brought me back to my days playing super Mario world, super adventure island and other such games that got me into the hobby of playing games in the first place. The controls are tight as a drum and I never once doubted where I was going to land. Shantae is floaty enough to make jumping easy while not being so floaty that you miss your jump entirely. Playing this with an xbox controller felt natural (except for A and B being switched in the menus) and the controls just work as they should. The game has many areas to explore with vastly different sceneries to take in. however this brings me to my first gripe about the game. This game happens to suffer from the where the f*** do I go now syndrome. The map is almost completely useless and when you do find where to go you have to back track to get that one item you missed so you can progress. I several times spent too much time going the wrong direction because the game wasn't clear. There is a hint system to help alleviate this however its vague at best. I will forgive this to some degree as this is just how the genre of metroidvainia is. The only other gripe I have is that this game WAS not made for a 27 inch HD monitor as the game just looks stretched out however again I can again forgive this due to it being originally on the DSI and I did get used to how it looked and actually preferred it as again it brought me back to those old NES and SNES days. The story is nothing to be awe inspired by however it is written well and there's some witty lines in the dialogue that in one instance I think broke the 4th wall somewhat. Overall if I had to give this game a score out of 10 I would give it a 9. The game is almost perfect for what its trying to do however the lack of direction is the only real reason I have not to give this a perfect score.

My journey with this game started 10+ years ago when I received the second game of the trilogy as a part of a gaming magazine's promotion. I immediately got hooked to the story, and I  remember staring at the screen blankly with a knot in my throat, going through all sorts of emotions at the end of Dreamfall: The Longest Journey. That's when I started frantically searching for the next game in the series - I mean there had to be another one right?- that ending wasn't enough - I needed closure, I needed to know what happened next!
Fast forward to 2013 - I was ecstatic to learn that there was a Kickstarter campaign to make the 3rd game happen. I immediately backed the game and the waiting game began. At the end of the day, I am glad the developers waited for the right circumstances and took their time, in their own terms to make this game happen. Because it is a piece of art. It is one of the best - if not the best- game I have ever played in this genre and it is one of my all time favorites.
TL:DR if you are looking for an amazing story/gameplay/atmosphere buy this game. Multiple stories unlocked by individual decisions add to the replay value of the game, and the ending does not disappoint. - Though playing the previous games in the trilogy is not absolutely necessary to enjoy this game, it is recommended to enjoy this game to its fullest.

Unplayable.
This *had* so much potential, utterly wasted.
Character control that is pretty much like having a drunken idiot as a character. Movement is controlled by a physics-based procedural system that is fundamentally flawed, leaving you (barely) controlling your motion. Combat control is quite simply unplayable - absurdly fustrating, and makes playing an exercise in starting again repeadedly.
the user interface is abysmal.
The worst thing is, these criticisms have been made dozens of times to the developers, and they refuse to listen.
"you need to get used to the controls" is an excuse repeated many times. Its a lie. yes, 20+ hours in the earlier demo, and time in this will teach you to work around the failures of design in the UI and control system. It does not make the system good. It is unplayable.
There are good elements - its atmospheric, it could be beautiful. The armour system is excellent - it feels realistic, in that a little armour makes a big difference. The differences in weapons is noticable in use. But it is entirely ruined by the physics-based motion. If combat and motion control were addressed, it could be a gem.
But its not, and will continue not to be worth buying until the developers actually learn to take criticism onboard.

Right now, this game is a hardcore experience for hardcore gamers.  If neither of these describe you, avoid this game.  I am confounded by the reviews which are declaring Very Positive.  With the state of gameplay as it is (polished yet frustrating), I am hard pressed to believe the average gamer will enjoy this game.
I respect what this game is trying to do (immersive, realistic combat experience) but I feel that the execution is missing the mark significantly.  Controls are clunky.  The developer would be better off hitting a middle ground of hardcore combat and accessible combat.
The average gamer will find the controls clunky and difficult, and will find the learning curve challenging.  Overall, the concept is good, but I feel the execution has been missed (possibly due to not getting proper feedback?).  I struggle to pilot my character, I struggle to execute combat well.  I feel that modifying the concept would still allow the developer to achieve the desired combat goals but still allow the gameplay to feel accessible, even for noobs/average gamers.
What would improve this score for me - controller support (if dev can make this game work on controller, that might solve a lot of the dev's hardcore/frustration/accessibility issues), focus on momentum rather than all the intracacies of perfect physics.  You can improve greatly on what already exists (other games in the market), but you've gone way too far - Find a middle ground.  For instance, in the very first room, I run around, and my character trips on♥♥♥♥♥♥fairly easily.  I know you think this is cool, but for average joe gamer, it's frustrating to have to navigate around this kind of stuff when the control interface is already clunky.

Total overhaul of my review, played around with the game some more.
As mentioned in the last one, i had high hopes for this game, I still do.
And I still want to recommend it. Not only because the developers are very creative with their puzzles, but also because combat is... well, combat.
It's hard, you're not some elegant fencer, heck no. You're a jack of all trades, master of none.
Sure, you can use any weapon you want. It's not a guarantee that you'll be good at it. Players actually need to find the weapon combination that fits them specifically.
The map is like a maze as well, and instructions are still somewhat unclear. when it comes to the world itself, and the enemies will sometimes block the doors so you can't get back out, especially if they are hunting you.
But all that aside. Once you finally learn to fight in this game, it's actually pretty fun, but rest assured. the road to learning combat in this game, is a rather rough one... You'll get frustrated and angry multiple times.
Also, It seems that this game will have some pretty deep rpg elements, like levels. I'm looking forward to it.
Though I have one thing to add;
HP.
In this game, hp is probably the most treasured thing. You can take permanent damage... And it's really hard to regen it in the story mode. (as far as I know, it's only through one specific item)
Hoping we will see other means of regenerating permanent damage, not that such a method should come easily. I'm thinking through meditation (seems to be a skill tree that the devs are working on)
Maybe the higher tiers would allow you to slowly regenerate permanent damage when out of combat, and not running.
For now, i'm recommending this game, even at full price, and it's a must play for gamers looking for a unique and hard combat system.
But don't tell me I didn't warn you. This game. is TOUGH!

Update from a comment I made on Reddit: Exanima - It's an early access top-down isometric dungeon crawler with physics based combat. Think Ultima meets Mount and Blade. You can manipulate items in your environment, and there are a few puzzles to navigate through by doing so. Movement in combat mode is relative to where your character is facing, so it's slightly difficult to get used to. You swing your weapon by holding down the mouse button and moving the cursor past your enemy where you want to hit him. The longer of a swing you get, the harder it hits, but you can overbalance or sometimes take too long to swing.
That's just the combat. The environment of the game is phenomenal. When I first played it all I could relate it to was a survival horror game. It's one of the scariest game I've ever played because even though I had the ability to defend myself, I was very bad at the combat.
There's also a straight up arena and arena manager mode where you can just fight instead of playing the campaign levels that are already out. I've put about 200 hours into the arena and "beat" it three times over and I'm still not the best at it, but I consider myself pretty damn good.
The biggest con is that it's taking a LONG time to develop. I've made two youtube videos on it over the past two years, and it's looking like I'm gonna have to make another one next year talking about the updates. They're currently working on a big overhaul of game mechanics and building the tools that should allow them to finish the game in a more timely manner.
The quality of the graphics and gameplay is fantastic. I highly recommend anyone who thinks it may be interesting to check it out:
It's a prelude to a full game that will be called Sui Generis that was successfully backed on Kickstarter a few years ago:
Lastly, here are the two videos I made overviewing the game(most of the stuff I've already talked about here):

Yes, the combat system can seem sluggish but if you gave two of your friends swords and tried to control them just using a keyboard and mouse, I imagine it would be just as sluggish.  The animations cannot switch instantly like traditional games.  Characters have to use their muscles to swing, stop their swing, then swing in the opposite direction.  You try doing that with a 10kg weight.
The combat will probably be fleshed out more and right now is simple but still totally fair and you can still pwn it to a pretty great degree.  I would advice going straight into arena mode for ages before the main game.  People have to get use to a new system rather then adapting current combat systems.
This is one of those games achieves a gaming element that hasn't been done before, you'll see for yourself after you test your might against it's combat system.
This is just a pre-game to the even more ambitious open world they are trying to create.  Please support these games so they can complete their goals and more!

The Communist Manifesto is divided into a preamble and four sections, the last of these a short conclusion. The introduction begins by proclaiming "A spectre is haunting Europe—the spectre of communism. All the powers of old Europe have entered into a holy alliance to exorcise this spectre". Pointing out that parties everywhere—including those in government and those in the opposition—have flung the "branding reproach of communism" at each other, the authors infer from this that the powers-that-be acknowledge communism to be a power in itself. Subsequently, the introduction exhorts Communists to openly publish their views and aims, to "meet this nursery tale of the spectre of communism with a manifesto of the party itself".
The first section of the Manifesto, "Bourgeois and Proletarians", elucidates the materialist conception of history, that "the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles". Societies have always taken the form of an oppressed majority living under the thumb of an oppressive minority. In capitalism, the industrial working class, or proletariat, engage in class struggle against the owners of the means of production, the bourgeoisie. As before, this struggle will end in a revolution that restructures society, or the "common ruin of the contending classes". The bourgeoisie, through the "constant revolutionising of production [and] uninterrupted disturbance of all social conditions" have emerged as the supreme class in society, displacing all the old powers of feudalism. The bourgeoisie constantly exploits the proletariat for its labour power, creating profit for themselves and accumulating capital. However, in doing so, the bourgeoisie serves as "its own grave-diggers"; the proletariat inevitably will become conscious of their own potential and rise to power through revolution, overthrowing the bourgeoisie.

Relative to the game, this review will be short and sweet, as there really is not much content in this game. There are only 2 game modes available, Waves and Endless, both are pretty much the same. Only difference between them is that the Waves game play is linear and the enemies spawn in the same waves everytime you play. Where as, Endless mode works like GW2: Retro Evolved, where the enemies randomly spawn and you have to survive. Of course in both modes, each wave adds new hazards, different and more enemies to increase the dificulty and does it generously! The linear way that Waves mode was designed may sound like it might be easy because of the redundancy but to put it in perspective I'm currently ranking 23 on the leaderboards and I have yet to pass wave 17... Whats my point? There are only 22 other players that have gotten past the 17th wave and this game is brutally hard!
The graphics are just okay (what you see on the store page is pretty much it) and the twin stick shooter style of game play is nothing new. So why should you get this? Well, the audio. WAD is a musically driven twin stick arena shooter. But not like Beat Hazard where music drives the game, in WAD the game play drives the music, kind of like Everyday Shooter. Essentially, you are the musician and besides being the instrument of destruction your weapon is also a synth arp and choir instrument of sounds and the pitch is effected by the distance between you and the enemies. Then by destorying the enemies generates a beat. This in addition to some great sound effects layered over a droney ambient track really creates an atmosphere.
IMO, the audio really does make up for what the game lacks. The musical drive part of WAD is not as well done as games like Everyday Shooter but this one certainly has better game play. Unfortunately, you only get one track with WAD, which makes any long sessions difficult to attempt. This game is recommended in smaller doses as it's a decent filler game to pick up again play every once in a while.
Highly recommended for audiophiles, masochistic gamers who love brutally difficult games, and twin stick enthusiasts.

The mission statement of Vertex Pop is to use satisfying procedurally generated imagery in a quick to learn, hard to master play-style. This is absolutely accomplished here.
Controls: since I have this on the PC I tried with both the 360-style controller via USB and the keyboard/mouse, and I enjoy them both for different reasons. Everything is tight and responsive, and at no point are you frustrated by it.
Visuals: Like VertexPop's earlier entry Orbit1, the visuals are simple and stunning at the same time. Since they're procedurally generated, not only are they performant, they flow very seamlessly along with the motion of the gameplay itself in a very aesthetically pleasing and informative way. My only gripe is that sometimes the pulsing backdrop obscures some of the potentially dangerous enemies. This feels intentional, but it was the only time I got frustrated.
Audio: This is by far my favorite part. Though it's not necessarily a fully dynamic music system since it uses a static soundtrack, the sound effects synchronize with the music in a very satisfying way, and you feel very much like everything is coming together in an awesome way that transcends the scoring portion of the game.
Overall: Well worth the price of admission, this game will keep you company when you're bored with AAA titles, and you'll find yourself coming back to it when you're trying to engage your subconscious between work tasks. Almost as effective as a walk in the park!

So unlike all the reviews out there that are like, "NO! I WON'T GO BACK TO HL1.8!  I WON'T DO IT! I CAN'T DO IT!" I actually enjoy the engine, and what you can still do with it.  I do not like, however, what has been done with it here.  This is supposed to be a short, fun, run-and-gun that can give kind of a back story to what happened in HL, specifically, the origin of the specimen.  This is a terrible representation of what could have happened.  First off, why is it on a boat in the stormy seas?  The crystal came from the Xen universe, and was recovered during exploration using the teleportation technology in Black Mesa.  There's no reason for this boat story.  Why do you get off a helicopter with the military, and then the Navy (in their modern uniforms and not the uniforms used during the proper year (and with dumb tribal tattoos on their forearms which would be out of regs today (you can tell because the sleeves are rolled up which are out of modern regs))) tries killing you. Why do they have containers of these creatures, when the Black Mesa compound already has free access to these specimens?  The creatures were made able to teleport AFTER the crystal was exposed to high radiation.  So why is it that these creatures can just teleport as they please?  Also, there's on attempt at a physics   puzzle which makes no sense if you're thinking about it sensibly.  There's an explosives crate next to a light pole (on a boat?) that you have to blast, which makes the light pole fall 90 degrees the wrong way from what you would imaging the pole to do, and it falls as though pushed from the top.  Nothing about this game makes sense, and really no one can even try to justify it being any part of the series.  It doesn't fit any way you try to plug it.
Overall opinion:  Story blows, gameplay mechanics are nothing fantastic and new, and there's almost no redeeming quality to this game.  If you want to play a run and gun for about 30 min and you can ignore this trying to be part of one of the biggest game stories of all times, here you go.  Otherwise, it's pretty cringe-worthy as an attempt as a marketable game.

This game has a lot of great things going for it, but it feels like a game in it's earlier stages. The UI is dull, the controls are minimal, but most importantly the game mechanics are pretty bad. People, enemies included, often move through buildings or water like they aren't there. Happiness is probably the most vital resource, but despite what the game tells you it's more randomly generated than it seems. It also takes FAR too long to build defense structures, which can easily be destroyed. The soldiers in this game are terrible. In a huge city building game like this with hundreds of dots running around they decided to have knights that you manually have to move around, and who you have to keep clicking to make useful. The way you recruit soldiers is fine, but they should auto attack any enemies within a certain range. FOOD!? WHAT THE HECK!? The food in this game doesn't even make sense! I can make enough food for five kingdoms, but these damn villagers won't eat it unless they are directly next to a market or a baker. They are always hungry!
The graphics, which almost turned me off from buying the game, are actually really great! The clouds are beautiful and the buildings have more detail than I initially thought. Watching everyone run through your city is great. I also like to zoom in really close and sort of walk through my streets. I like the music as well, though I had to turn it way down because it likes to blare loudly if you pause the game.
I WANT to play this game a lot more, but right now it seems like there is no point. It can take an hour to build a half decent section of wall, only to have vikings come knock it down before I have a chance to react. The soldiers are both vital and useless. The only hope of building up proper defenses early is to utilize the soldiers that are almost impossible to control. But what really destroyed the game for me is the housing. Happiness is how your kingdom grows, but is nearly impossible to manage. And food . . . the entire food system is awful. I really want to love this game and lose a thousand hours into it, but it is just too rough right now. I would wait to buy it.
