Once you understand it though, damn, every blow landed is so satisfying.

Frustratingly difficult at times, but oh so rewarding when you finally, FINALLY start to nail the controls. And then you die horribly.
The feeling of dread when your enemy gets a great hit (or if you just accidentally open up for a counter), and the feeling of accomplishment when you kill enemy after enemy is unbeatable. But it really should have some sort of save function (or at least at certain checkpoints perhaps).
Nevertheless, this game is going places.
This game is very based and also fun once you get good.

I can see what they're trying to do with the combat, and as everyone says it has great potential. But for a complex system it's too simple. Let me expand on that. In order to block you move the mouse in a way that will move your weapon to stop the force of the opponents blow, but in combat mode you always face the direction your mouse is, so you end up spinning around, unable to strike on your open opponent. You also have to manually track the target to keep facing towards them, again based on where your mouse is pointing.
Movement with the WASD isn't so bad to get used to but it feels so unresponsive and your character will randomly stop moving then start again. Walking around with the torch in the dar kdungeons and exploring and using the physics engine is great. But the combat (which most of this game is) is just not fun. It's not fun to learn and it's not fun to do.
Hopefully it will be improved upon to make it more user friendly because if they don't, no-one except the hardcore fans are gonna want to play.

Genre - Isometric Dungeon Crawling with physics based combat
I am a massive fan of games like Diablo etc. Looking at the screenshots this looked similar but with more emphasis on scavenging, surviving and not just killing everything (Maybe Dark Souls meets Diablo). The graphics also looked nice so thought it would be worth a try.
This game is now an impulsive purchase I regret and here are the reasons why, with suggested solutions:
They tried to be too clever with the combat system - you don't auto target, which is interesting. However, winning a fight seems to involve jerking the mouse around at all angles to hit someone who is doing the same to you. At least you auto block if you are facing the correct way though. The fighting seems to make up most of the game and although you can avoid it you are going to have to survive a fair few fights to get anywhere. There is an arena mode to practice in but winning a fight seems more luck than judgement and as this game has prema-death and no saving basically means if you can't work out a consistent fighting style with various weapons each game will be very short. You can fall over objects and get tangled, but so can the enemy, and I actually like this part as adds to the fighting experience.
Solution - If they add an option to use a controller this would alleviate these concern, maybe this could be normal mode and with the mouse hard mode with achievements for the crazy people.
Solution (already planned) - The game will get a co-op mode at some point. I think this will be needed to make you come back to the game. Traversing the same environments, whilst dying at any point.
At the moment you wake up in a room with no real objectives and you just wander around trying not to get into fights.
Maybe they could also include some traps, that you could lead enemies into, or different enemy types could fight each other. Allowing you to defeat enemies without relying on the dodgy fighting controls.
Solution - Objectives, varied enemies and traps
Also the inventory system and interacting with your environment are a bit weird. You need to drag and open doors, but don't need to be right next to them to do so. You can also pick up and move around random items like a God. The inventory is a blank box, you drag things into but it isn't alwyas clear if things are useful to you. Leaving you carrying around a load of old junk.
Solution - Make the inventory more intuitive and remove some of the crazy interaction physics
At the moment this is early access, but don't see myself enjoying this game unless they make the changes suggested above. Unfortunately from what I can gather this game has been built around the current fighting system, so I won't hold my breath.
Also if you check out the website
it appears that this is a barebones version of another game they are developing called Sui Generis (SG), so feel even more I am paying for the privilege to be a Guinea Pig.
Then again this game has its many lovers (another reason I got it), so maybe none of these issues will hamper your enjoyment.
All I can think about at the moment, is the game or DLC I could have bought instead. However, give it a few months and I might be hastily re-writing my negative review to a positive one (fingers crossed), whilst enjoying co-op (via a contoller).

I had this game on my wishlist for some time priot to purchasing it. Today I was thrilled to find it on sale, so I excitedly purchased it and could not wait to play it...
I wasn't far along in the game before  becoming very frustrated. The combat system is terrible, I cannot for the life of me understand why a modern game is so hampered by such awful game mechanics. To compound the problem, the save system is appalling. I found myself dying way too easilly, then I'm stuck having to replay useless game time rather than simply being able to start where the battle begins. Initially I thought perhaps I was supposed to save the game manually - so  I went hunting for a fast save key.  But.\, of course,  the game, has automatic save. Why would a developer choose a game structure that would force you to replay and replay territory you've already been through only to be faced with clunky, frustrating combat?  To me, these two issues add up to a game that, in its present incarnation, is unenjoyable and aggravating. I'd like to say that for $40 a consumer deserves more, but... there's more to talk about.
On to other issues  you should know about before buying it.  The game does not allow for ANY character customization whatsoever. Not even the choice of a name,  Oh, and if you planned on playing as the female protagonist, as I did, forget it. You start the game as the brother and have no choice about that. As a woman gamer, I prefer to play as a woman.. I will even skip a game that doesn't give me the option. Unless, like the Witcher, the game itself is good enough ot offset that glaring oversight.  It's 2014 - how hard can it be to give us that option? It never fails to shock me when developers don't get why women gamers feel this is important. Yup - it's my bad for assuming. I should never have seen the female character and assumed she was playable.
I could not for the life of me figure out how to use the health potion - or to equip it. Why did this game have to be so complicated? And mana potions? I don't know if there were any. The point at which I gave up I was forced to fight lesser bad guys to obtain their "essence". Why did everything in this game feel like a struggle rather than entertainment?
Perhaps the issue is me. Indeed,  I've been  spoiled by games like Elder Scrolls, Dragon Age. Mass Effect. However, I've been similarly spoiled by Indie games like Path to Exile. It's a shame really because this had the elements to be an excellent game.If they improved the combat system and incorporated a worksble save system, I could classify this as playable. The way it is right now, however, I'd call it a headache maker. Amd for goodness sake - it is certainly nowhere near worth $40!

This will be my first review, generally I do not do reviews, because I am lazy, but this game is so much fun, that now I have to start. I bought the game on sale for 6 euros, it is worth some more, and a lot more of you collect Das Schwarze Auge games.
So far, I did not finish the game so everything I say is based on the first 30 something percent of my progress.
First of all, I read earlier that Demonicon resembles the Witcher. It is true but only concerning the graphics and the cartoon cutscenes. Demonicon is much more immersive, though more linear. Whereas I, in both Witcher 1 and 2, had to take huge pauses when playing through - because the story was not too interesting, and I got bored at some parts - here I played through the first 27% of Demonicon at once, if I remember well.
The point is that the story is dark fantasy, and is as immersive as in Dragon Age, only with much less sidequests. The side quests are there rather only to show that this game has sidequests, but that is not its strongest side. This game is rather about one great main quest, which fits the DSA universe very well.
It is NOT true that without the Dark Eye background the story is senseless, or makes very little sense to an outsider. In the in-game codex there is plenty information to get acquainted with the DSA setting.
The German voice acting is also okay, nothing wrong with that.
The graphics of the better parts resemble to Witcher.
However, there are worse graphical parts, mainly when you meet with non-talking NPCs. At those points this game resembled to another dark fantasy rpg, Hunted. Apart from the main, important characters, the less important characters are not too living. They are very static, which could be theoretically good, but in Demonicon you cannot talk to most of them either, which gives a bit of a dead feeling ("lifeless environment", but on the contrary, the sounds are very living). And also gives you the hint only to concentrate on the main quest.
I have to say as well, that the sizes of the city of Warunk are so proportionate and so realistic, I think it beats everything so far I have encountered. The city, and its districts are neither too big, nor too small. I assume in the medieval time we had the same sized towns. It feels good too go on the Warunkan streets. For comparison, the Dragon Age Denerim is highly disproportionate.
STORY: Again, the main quest and story is as good as in Dragon Age, with moral choices, which field is the best one ever invented in an rpg, according to me. M&M Dark Messiah also came to my mind as a comparison.
GRAPHICS: Graphics are similar to Witcher and Hunted.
IMPORTANT: You have to shun this game if do not like linear games and prefer the free roaming style. You can free roam, but only a little bit, within a smaller place usually, and also it is not worth to do it too much - you just rather proceed with the story.
One additional fact concerning the skills. This game has 8 or so non-martial skills. I felt when I distributed the skill points, that they are not a waste, because I could make use of every skill, including the Legends and Lore, each of them were important. Also this game made me think that even in a pen and paper rpg you do not need more non-martial skills than these 8 (legends, plant caring, persuation, spotting things, disarm traps, open locks and two more). If there is more of them you will use only a small percentage of them, so most points you spend will be a waste. Or, you will not be able to spend sufficient points to each important one of them (to the ones you really need)

As a longtime fan of the Dark Eye pen and paper rpg, I was intrigued when I heard about Demonicon. An action-rpg in the Black  Lands, dealing with the legacy of Borbarad - sounds good, at least in theory.
Let's see how it holds up:
Liked:
- the content is mature (little SPOILER: there is a budding incestous relationship between our main protagonists)
- the gameplay is on average pretty smooth, barring a few hiccups
- the setting has been almost painstakingly recreated and the details border on continuity porn (if you don't know what that     is, look it up on
- the story manages to pull you in and doesn't let up until the very end, with tough decisions, whose results you only see after a while, but for some there is always a third option depending on your skills
-superb VA (at least in the german version, haven't tried the english yet; little spoiler: your father has the german voice of Liam Neeson)
Disliked (well not actually disliked, but more puzzled by):
- a couple of glitches in the graphics, nothing major or gamebreaking; I've seen a lot worse in AAA titles
- something in the story progression that didn't make a lot of sense (SPOILER: you beat a powerful and annoying Rondrian and loot the armor from his corpse, only to be immediately offered a better demonic version by a demon - what's up with that?)
Bottom line: IMO Demonicon felt like a somewhat quality-reduced clone of The Witcher 2, which is a superb game and thus Demonicon managed to be at least a good game. If you liked The Witcher 2 and you need to pass some time until The Witcher 3 arrives, then Demonicon is the game for you. If you're a fan of The Dark Eye, then Demonicon is also for you, since this is the only game besides Drakensang that made me feel like I was actually walking through Aventuria. Everybody else, it's up to you.

Lot's of lost potential. It is a dark fantasy, linear action RPG with small and not always believable levels. Would I recommend the game? Depends on whom I'm talking to. I'm assuming you're reading this as someone who has played the game a lot, because you're a fan reading your trillionth Steam review to try and work out if you'll like the game. I can 100% assure you that I enjoy this game to a very very mild degree. It's not much of a step up beyond what was already happening in the Anno series, so for someone new, it might be a fun little game. For someone familiar with the series, it might be a bit disappointing. That said, I've played a bunch of the old Anno games, and I haven't found myself moving on from it yet.
Some mildly interesting things to affect your mild decision to mildly purchase this game:
1) It provides a colony-to-colony transfer system that meant I had to manage the different resources from each of the biomes in a cross-planet trade network, which was simple, yet delicate.
2) If you were like me, and you really want to like this game, chances are you'll enjoy it, provided you don't feel like it's a big expense.
3) You don't get to your moon base for a while, so don't expect it to be there at the start
4) the various in-colony optional missions are kind of boring and arduous. Just a bunch of fetch quests to justify a plane or boat model on the map.
5) the military campaign missions are also kind of boring, but in a different way. It's just bland to wander around the map with your full armada of ships and either be at an adequate level, and thus just breeze past most things, or to be insufficient, in which case your units will atrophy away before you can finish the level. That said, if they were difficult, I probably wouldn't bother playing them, as they're not that important for the main game.

I waited to pick this one up until it went on sale, due to the mixed reviews, and wish I hadn't - I am really liking the game so far. It is different in a lot of ways from previous ANNO titles , but overall I think they have done a good job updating the series.
I especially love being able to move buildings (watch out some can be ridiculously expensive to relocate!), and the various addons that you can customize for them. Game looks amazing, and being able to now jump between your different settlements is another welcome addition.
I definitely have not found the game to be too easy, I've only recently reached around lvl 12 and started the moon base and it is already challenging keeping all of my sectors in balance while bringing in enough income to fund the steps needed for the main progression!
The side quests can be a bit generic and repetitive, but do offer a good way to supplement your income or get those last few rare resources you need. A lot of players did not like that all combat was moved to a separate part of the game, but I don't mind so much. Having these 2 parts separate lets you concentrate fully on one or the other without having to stop in the middle of what you were doing to address whatever event/crisis pops up. Just make sure you have a positive income flow before starting the combat missions - your settlements still run in real time while youre fighting!
If you like strategy, city building, or any of the previous ANNO titles, give this one a try - you can always refund if you hate it, right?

It's important to note that this game is a stand alone dungeon crawling version of Bare Mettle's game, Sui Generis which is still in development. Exanima is basically the same game, minus all the features they plan to have incorporated in SG. They may update Exanima to include some of these combat features, but even as it stands now, it's a very well made game. You can look up the Devs here for videoes of their progress
The most important factor in this game is that it uses a physics based combat system. Picture something like Diablo, or  Baldur's gate, where it's dark and creepy and every aspect of combat is affected by numbers and stats. This sword does 1-10 damage, this armor has X ammount of defence or protection. It doesn't quite work the same in Exanima. Gear does have stats, somewhat, but they're more statistics of the physics that make that weapon function. Weight for example will be a large factor in how quickly you can swing your weapon. Slower in turn means that the weapon will likely have more force and impact when landing a hit. Whereas lighter weapons that are well balanced will allow you to attack quickly and stay on your feet easily while dealing less damage.
The health system, like the combat, is also very hardcore and realistic. Taking a sledgehammer to the head may outright kill you, and if not, your maximum health will likely be reduced permanently from how serious the wound was. Similarly, being cut by a knife or sword while wearing simple normal clothes will cause serious damage even if it wasn't a powerful hit, but attacking someone in full platemail with a tiny dagger will likely do almost nothing. The other exception is that armor only provides protection to the part of the body its covering. So that same platemail wearing person, without a helmet on of any kind, could still be hit in the head/face for serious damage.
The music is dark and gloomy. Would have liked to see a change in tempo/theme when in battle. Sounds are excelent and everything sounds like it should. Slashing at someone wearing chainmail sounds like you're hitting chainmail as opposed to skin. Kicking a box or barrel accidently, makes a noise. Running with a torch causes a flame ruffling sound. Enemies seem to react to noises as well, though I've not seen too much of this yet from my currently limited playtime.
Gameplay is fun, creepy, stressful and everything inbetween. There's no save function beyond exiting to continue playing where you left off later on. As a result I died at least 20 times before making any real progress and decided to practice combat in the arena mode, which I would suggest to any new player for sure to get the feel for the controls.
If you're interested in a game that makes you feel powerless, like you would be if you were armed with nothing more than a stick. If you want a game that doesn't have over the top explosions and fancy screen filling graphic soup, but instead realistic sword clashing combat. If you want to actually have to practice fighting, not to leveling up a stat, but to actually feel like you yourself are training to be a better warrior, this game will still kick your♥♥♥♥♥and make you feel like any mistake you make is your life forefit.
*Edit* After clearing both arena difficulties several times, and finding weapons and combat styles I prefer using, I can only say that I'm that much more in love with it now and anticipating SG's release even more. Also, as noted by every negative review in this game, the controls are simplistic, but very hard to master (Try changing your movement mode from hold to double tap if you dont like that style). Why anyone would be looking for yet another boring, cookie cutter dungeon crawler, I have no idea.

Space key is important in order to reorient your camera in the direction to where you character is facing while in combat, the arrow pointer is more or less where your character's facing is "Target Locked" onto.
This is will be a juggling act on your keyboard to maintain camera focus on your opponent, a somewhat unnecessary hurdle if the character could target lock onto an opponent in my opinion.
However I hear that target locking onto an opponent isn't going to be persued in the game, but considering what the arrow pointer is, I don't see how their combat system couldn't incorporate it as an optional feature.
Target lock in Dark Souls for instance could be turned on and off.  I imagine if ultilized in this game you could use the pointer to click on an opponent while in Combat Mode (Tab), and the camera will then lock onto it, auto correcting the character's facing towards the opponent.  Or, you could use the (~) key for instance and it'd select the nearest opponent to lock onto.  Turning off target lock could be simple as using the arrow key to click on the opponent again, or hitting the designated lock on button again, or a different key, like (1) for instance.
Now onto the dungeon.  It's not random.  So everytime you die you'll be trekking the same places for the same spots for loot.  This can be tedious, but it is a Perma Death game.  There is plans for check points in a future update, but you will have to endure without them for now.
I gave it a thumbs up, but honestly I would give it neither thumbs up, or down, in its current state it needs a bit more work, but I can see the potential of the game, and currently nothing in the market fills the niche that this does.

First: I played this game´s beta extensively before it was even released on Steam, so do not be fooled by my playtime.
Now that I got that out of the way, I can say that Exanima is already a brilliant game which deserves the attention of every RPG enthusiast and anyone who is interested in melee combat.
At the moment, Exanima mainly offers two things and does both of them euqally well. First there is world exploration. The main campaign is set in the underworld, a large system of tunnels, chambers and basements, in which your self-created protagonist wakes up after crashing through the ceiling. With little more than the clothes on your body, a mysterious half-torn note and a torch you set out to explore your surroundings... Everything is interactive by simply grabbing it with the mouse, so you turn around the boxes and barrels and your quest for anything you can use. Maybe grab a piece of debris as a makeshift weapon, a barrel lid as your first shield and enter the hallway in front of you... Soon, you meet the lavyrinths inhabitants, animated corpses who roam the corridors. Some of them seem to ignore you, others maybe startled by your presence, and some are outright hostile. Suddenly you are forced to fight for your life, either by desperately using the few things you have at hand, or by making a run for it throwing chairs, ladders and everything you can grab in your pursuer´s way... The game engine and physical simulation allows for all kinds of creative behavior.
After overcoming the first obstacles, you slowly start to gather new weapons, armor and other useful things. And at some point you realize that you aren´t simply exploring some video game level, but a functional, realistic setting. You search through cupboards in storage rooms, stumble over washing buckets in bathrooms and find a new hammer in an apparent lumber mill. No, that epic sword will not be hidden inside a toilet stall... but keep your eyes open and use your brain. Everything you find feels valuable and as soon as your own survival is secured, you start to uncover the history of this place... who build it? What happened to the inhabitants? How did you get here? ... maybe time will tell ...
The other large portion of the game is the combat. Exanima´s melee is unlike anything seen in other video games. There are no set animations, every action is the exact result of player input and subtle mouse movement is all that is required. Wider movements leads to wider, harder but slower blows; diagonal movement can cause diagonal cut;, slash for your enemies legs or his head, step into his blow and block his arm so he cannot strike you, riposte his slash, run him over or trip him or strike his unprotected body parts: Yes, the game even simulates armor in detail; everything you wear only protects the parts of your body it actually covers; but armor can be worn in layers with the super simple drag-on system...
Face opponents of various skill levels, from the blunt undead with no sense of self-preservation to the hardened swordmaster in the game´s arena mode. Enemy difficulty is not determined by higher stats, but by how well they master their weapon. Every combatant has different skills and his or her own style of fighting: Watch, adapt, overcome, even if it will take you a while.
... and this is where I mention the issue some people have with the game: Due to Exanima´s vastly different approach to combat, it really takes some time getting used to. In best Dark Souls fashion: Prepare to die. There is a quickstart guide which explains you the basic controls and interaction capabilities, but no real dedicated tutorial. You will feel wonky at first, not really knowing whats going on... similar to learning how to swordfight in real life. Delving deeper into the game´s combat takes some time and learning. But once you get the basics of attacking, blocking and timing down, you will experiment with ripostes, feints and low blows untill every battle is a frantic dance of action!
Yes, the game is hard and the learning curve steep, but once you get a hang of it it will be infinitely satisfying. Experiment with weapons, techniques and fighting styles to overcome the challenge! The skill ceiling is basically infinite.
Pros:
+ very atmospheric dungeon exploration
+ a game world that feels real and interesting
+ physical interactivity of nearly every object
+ rewarding (player)skill and item progression
+ extremely nuanced melee fighting system with endless possibilities
+ every fight exciting and frantic
+ enemies which differ by behavior and weapon skill, not hitpoint or damage values
+ seperate arena mode for the ultimate combat experience
+ detailed character creation
+ superb graphic and sound design (especially lighting)
+ extremely well polished for an early access title
+ already hours of content to explore plus hidden secrets and a degree of randomization
+ really dedicated developers who are into this game with their heart´s blood
Things to come, but not yet implemented (and thus not part of my review):
• Per session and global character skill progression
• Large non-linear main game following early content
• Build and permanently save characters by completing early content
• New encounters, items and environments
• Ranged combat and new close quarter manoeuvres
• Numerous moddable thaumaturgic powers
• More complete arena game modes featuring outdoor arenas
• Complex NPC interactions and dialogue
• Cooperative and competitive LAN multiplayer
Cons:
- steep learning curve / lack of dedicated tutorial
That is really the only one. Once you adjusted to this unique system and dive into the nuances, you are in for one incredible round of dungeon exploration and frantic, deep and highly nuanced melee combat on which you can easily spend dozens or hundreds of hours. Highly recommended!

Okay, first off, I'm not "recommending" this, at least, not at the time of the current writing. Its games like these that make me want a middle of the road, "not bad" option on Steam. Now, on to the review.
It's a very cool concept, something I've been playing in my head for a while, so when someone made EXACTLY what I had in mind, my mind was blown that someone could actually do this. However, this feels like an experiment, a proof-of-concept, not a full desktop-replacer as I had originally hoped. Although, this is Early Access, so hopefully this changes.
First, let's get the good things out of the way. Its very easy to use, and it runs on source engine, so if you have a decent computer it shouldn't lag up your games. Another cool thing is that there are a variety of maps to build your dream system in. Overall, they do a GREAT job of visually representing your desktop.
However, there are some major issues that stop this thing from being all that it can be. First, why no "boot on startup" feature? I get that Steam has to do that, but I would like the ability to set that as an option (The .EXE should still be able to activate independent of Steam, unless I'm mistaken), since this is a desktop replacement. Second, the Alt+Tabbing. Oh, the Alt+Tabbing. Whenever you start a program, you have to Alt+tab out, select the game you want to play, play it, then alt+tab back in when you're done. Why not make a script that does that automatically, or better yet, combine that script with a transition?
So, overall, this thing is a great concept, but it has some major issues, play if you want some novelty, but don't expect this to replace your good ol' 2D desktop until it comes out of Early Access.

Ok i just lost one hour of my life playing this thing, so i feel the need to warn my fellow people : stay clear of it. I don't mind that much about the laughingly pityful cutscenes, i do mind how ugly the game looks but that would be alright if the game didn't play so badly. The combat system is everything i hate about modern beat'em up (what's with the stupid grab manoeuver), the character is incredibly stiff, and the defense system, where you're supposed to guess ennemies' attacks (if you're psychic, otherwise you end up randomly blocking in the middle of your combo just in case), is so messed up that the game designers decided to add a mana-consuming auto-block right away, showing that they did realize how malfunctioning it was. What made me stop is the first boss battle (as it often does with poor designed games, that's where all the aggravating flaws really show). Unintersting patterns, stupid mash-the-button qta, the game even lets you pick up in the middle of the battle when you die, in an attempt to persuade you to keep playing (and to compensate for the poor controls). No wonder the game is that cheap during the winter sales (but that's not necessarily a good sign).
When the game designers put excuses to their poorly designed mechanics in the game, you know you should stop right away.

Good game, mixing the linear design of the old Castlevanias with a little exploration from the metroidvania´s side of the family.
Pros:
- The combat, while simple, allows for more combos than any other sidescrolling CV, and is enjoyable. Controls are responsible, and some enemies are actually challenging and interesting.
- Enviroments are nicely done. Seeing the same areas from the perspective of different characters/different times is cool.
- The art style, particularly during cutscenes, is interesting.
- Limiting the subweapons to 2 per character is a good call, that way almost all of them see some use.
- Some interesting platforming, but there are sadly only a couple instances of this.
Cons:
- QTE. While the game is thankfully free of them for the most part, the last act contains 3 such sequences of it, two of which should have been boss fights instead. VERY lazy by the devs.
- Boss fights: While bosses are nicely designed, almost none of the fights are specially interesting, and a few are downright insultingly easy. Without wanting to spoil anything, one in particular is awfully easy, and when things getserious is dispatched via QTE.
- 4 characters, and they all play exactly the same except for the subweapons. Lazy devs.
- While some of the skills you unlock to reach secrets and progress further in the game are standard metroidvania fare (Double jumps, for example) which grant extra mobility and merge with the gameplay, many are little more than disguised keys. With these, the "exploration" of secret areas is as simple as "come back to this door when you have acquired ability  X to unlock", making completing the game 100% more of an errand than actually discovering secrets. Again, lazy devs.
All in all, while it has some poor choices that bring it down from what could have been, it´s still a rather good game and I recommend it.

This game was amazing. Not perfect, but not the trash a lot of the reviews try to make it out to be. I'll make a Pros and Cons list and try to be as honest as possible with this review.
PROS:
-Very in-depth and immersive story-line. Very well thought out and it will hold your attention from beginning to end.
-The dialogue is perfect. From the serious encounters, to how people act during the Dragon Age style questioning for information, to the comedic relief. I find it amazing how in the most serious and despair-filled sections, this game can still make me laugh my♥♥♥♥♥off while staying completely appropriate to the situation at hand.
-The voice acting is just wonderful. Really backs up the already awesome story-line and dialogue.
-The fighting is no spam-clicker. You don't just press one button to win. The combat is about combining fighting abilities with magical powers with dodging with parrying with hack-and-slash combo chaining- while leaving out button mashing by making the chaining work in a rather unique way. (You wait to swing til after your first swing is done, otherwise the chain breaks) I really love the combat in this game. It's very good at making you feel like a badass as you slaughter a horde of 50+ bandits or 20+ thick-skinned lizard wolves that are spitting poison at you. The difficulty in combat doesn't even exactly scale. It's very much skill-based, bosses are always harder of course, but it's not like you go from one area to the next and suddenly the enemies there apparently know how to fight 40x better. Very realistic in that manner.
-The graphics are pretty darn good even for today. It's no Witcher 3, but it's still good.
-The sounds in this game really help create the setting. From the very beginning of the game you will easily notice what an astounding job they did creating the sounds for the game.
-The music helps set the mood always at the right moment. Get in a fight? The badass music kicks in. Running around collecting plants? Nice peaceful music to accompany.
-Very detailed skill customization system based on AP you can put into fighting skills, attributes, and story-opening abilities like fast-talk (persuasion), Locksmithing, and Legend Lore (Really comes in handy in some convos.)
-Pretty darn good crafting system for the enchanting/poisoning/upgrading of your items as well as crafting potions and poisons to give you an edge in battle.
-A magical skill system where you earn GP (Gift Points) that you may spend on upgrading your current spells, or unlocking new ones, from four different categories.
-Very appealing set of characters. I have not met one character in this game that I considered to be "bland" that I would not remember if i thought back on this game. They're all very memorable and very well thought out.
-Replay-ability value. The game's story progresses with the choices you make, so you can always give the game a second shot and pick the choices you didn't the first time and experience a very different game.
-Length of the game. 9 hours into the game I was so amazed I was still on chapter 1 (out of 5 chapters). This game gives you a very in-depth and lengthy experience for the money you pay.
CONS:
-The engine is not very compatible with AMD-based equipment. I occasionally get some randomly screen flickering, tearing, and sometimes the graphics become hazy/messed up.
-Not multi-GPU compatible. If you run multi-GPU with this game you receive a lot of stuttering, making it impossible to play. (This may only be with AMD Crossfire however.)
-You cannot save the game. You need to rely on autosaves. The game does save at all the right moments (almost) and holds on to enough saves in case you'd like to go back however.
-Lack of free roam. You run into invisible walls all the time, breaking immersion.
-Lack of free roam x2. You cannot re-visit old areas at whim (say if you want to pick up something you missed or talk to an old character.) You can only move areas when the story allows it. So make sure you know what doors you're going through and make sure you get everything you need before you move onto the next area.
FINAL VERDICT: I give this game a solid 8.5/10. This is a really good game, definitely worth picking up. It's not perfect by any means and there's definitely some RPGs that could out-due this one and many more coming out. But this game is definitely worth the money, full price or on sale, and I'd definitely recommend getting it.

Demonicon is an excellent 3rd person RPG game with some minor flaws. Its' strengths are it's story and in particular the dialogue that is very well written and in combination with excellent voice acting really draws you in. The choice system is also done excellently, where the decisions you make give you different cutscenes or dialogue interactions from start to finish. In addition, there is moral ambiguity to most of the decisions you make, meaning there are rarely black and white choices to be made. The music and ambient sound are also done superbly, and compliment the atmosphere quite well. Another well designed system is the character advancement and skills. Instead of experience points and levels, you are granted Adventure Points that can be spent at any time, on any specialization you choose, giving you a nice degree of customizability. Unfortunately, this clever design is marred somewhat by an endgame where most if not all of your skills will be maxed.
The other drawbacks of the game are it's fairly uninspired combat. While the controls are easy to use, and there is fair variety of player attacks and combos, the enemies are not particularly varied or dynamic. Some acts will have you facing the same 3-4 types of mobs ad nasuem for a couple of hours before you face a new type. Although it improves as the game progresses, and the boss fights are relatively interesting, more variety would have been welcomed. Also in need of improvement are the environments that while stunning in their art design and relative size, are often mostly devoid of npcs. This leaves some areas feeling strangely barren and artificial. The most glaring failure of the game however, is the itemization. While the crafting system is well implemented and useful, the graphic design on weapons is very mundane. This is particularly strange for a high fantasy title featuring magic and demons, to have such low fantasy weapons for the majority of the game. The developers may have wanted to underscore the humble origins of the protagonist, but even then, the art direction was dull. I never felt particularly excited by any of the loot. This problem is further exacerbated by the fact that NPC vendors without exception sell the best gear, making loot drops and chest finds vendor trash. Despite these flaws, Demonicon is a triumph in storytelling and one of the best RPG games of 2014. For fans of the genre, this is a must buy.

at the time i write this review i have spend about 140 hours on anno 2205. When i examine the store page i see that many people are disappointed in anno 2205. and it has the mixed user review status. I personally feel that this is not entirely fair so i would like to dedicate this review to replying to some of the more common complaints made by people in other reviews. Now before i begin: i would like to point out that i greatly respect your own opinion but i also ask of you to respect mine.
Starting out: many people compare this game to anno 2070 (the previous game in the anno series). This is ofcourse understandable and i think that noone will disagree with me when i say that a person who is expecting a new version of anno 2070 will likely be disappointed because it is not anno 2070.
HOWEVER: we should ask ourselves: does that make this game, a bad game? well opinions seem to differ on this but i, myself, would say no.
This game is not a reskinned anno 2070, it is a whole new approach to an existing genre. I like some of it but i also dislike some of it. Overall however i really like this game, with my current play time i have payed about 50 cents (gold edition) for an hour of playtime which i feel is an acceptable price.
So let me begin:
1) The storage system: i hear from people that they dont like the "ratio" based storage system, which they feel is shallow.  i can understand it if you would prefer a "absolute"based storage system but in previous anno games i found myself using an implicit rating system where i increase production if my production of good X if my storage was decreasing. If you feel that making this system explicit is making the shallow then that is your opinion however i strongly disagree.
2) the transport system: the system used to manage trade routes is different where you no longer have to build ships, instead you hire then. i agree that this made inter sector transport simpler to manage but there are also differnt oportunities for optimizing. For example: a load just to big for a small ship can better be transported in 2 small ships then 1 big ship.
3) Lack of rts play: compared to anno 2070 perhaps there is less rts play, however for me anno has always been a city builder, not an rts game. If you want a rts game then there are plenty of better alternatives here on steam that are cheaper then anno 2205 or anno 2070.
4) no random map generator limits replayability: well if you feel this way then that is understandable, however the random map generator of anno 2070 was in my opinion verry disappointing where maps generated under similar settings are virtually the same except for maybe their exact position on the map. the maps in anno 2205 however are hand crafted and are actually different from eachother.
5) A common complaint on the forums is "i can go afk for a week, come back and my town is still ok" This is true, however the same could also be said for the older annos. For example: my building strategy in anno 2070 is one of stability, in fact the only thing i have to do in order to keep my cities running is to make sure i have the raw materials, which practically boils down to using those silly "drill" things to make sure i can pull enough copper out of the ground...
6) no multiplayer. Yes, this anno game has no multiplayer (yet). and people seem to be really on the fence about this. I myself am not that interested in anno multiplayer because most of my games take a workday of playtime before they start to get interesting. For the people who hold off on buying this game i would say: how much of the time (relative in this case) of your total play time will you actually spend in multiplayer? is this 50%? or 5%? and if it is 5%, is it still that improtant to have this feature in this game?
Again: This is not meant to critise the opinions of others, it is meant to formulate a reply (with my opinion) to some of the things people have pointed out in their own review.
Summarizing:
I have played both anno 2070 and anno 2205 and i like both games. Now if you wish to go for the more rts-y experience i would recommend anno 2070, however if you want to go for the city builder experience then i would recommend anno 2205.
on a sidenote: ubisoft recently released a survey in which they ask for your opinion on how they can improve this game. I would urge everyone who has tried this game to participate so the game can be improved. links to this survey can be found on the steam forums.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge DX is a great explorative 2D platformer, or "metroidvania" like some people likes to say. This game was originally a Nintendo DSi downloadable software, but it finally makes it way to the PC... and it still looks awesome.
In Shantae, you control a half genie, explore the world and sometimes clear a few interesting dungeons. Progressing in this game is never too straightforward, so you have to explore areas carefully in order to proceed. I even got stuck a few times, but you can always return to your town in order to get help. Still, what differentiate Shantae from many other same kind of games, at least for me, is that the world is not too overwhelmingly huge. Areas are quite small, and they feel just nice to check out. You may even want to hang out in order to find all the secrets, since there's quite few of them hidden as well.
Game is packed with some basic RPG elements, too. Fortunately you don't have any stats, but you can collect money in order to buy new items, abilities or attacks in the shop. Like areas, there is not too much of them, but you still won't be able to get them all in one normal playthrough. There's skills that for example speeds up your attack, absorb nearby items, etc. None of them are required to clear the game, but they'll make the game a lot easier and at a lot more fun to play.

As a fan of Dreamfall Chapters' two predecessors (particularly The Longest Journey), Dreamfall Chapters was a major disappointment. This is one of only two games I backed on Kickstarter, as I was excited that we would finally get to see the conclusion to Dreamfall, but that excitement didn't last long once I got going.
The game starts off alright, but the longer it goes on, the more convoluted and ridiculous the story becomes. I won't go into spoilers, but once you get into the middle of Book 3 or so, character motivations feel so superficial and there is way too much technobabble explanation of what's happening. I had a few WTF moments during the story, where I shouted at the screen "Seriously? THIS is where you're going with this story?"
The Longest Journey, despite some flaws (particularly some obscure puzzle solutions) had a coherent, and relatively simple story. It was filled with likeable characters and there was always a sense of mystery and wonder that made you want to push forward. Dreamfall, while not quite as strong, was very similar. But all of that felt completely absent in Dreamfall Chapters.
Gameplay is another sore point, in that there are barely any puzzles. This shouldn't be too unfamiliar to people who have played Dreamfall, as that game was sorely lacking in the puzzle department too, with the latter part of the game in particular amounting to you walking from one place to another to trigger another cutscene. That wasn't improved in Dreamfall Chapters, and though the horrible combat is gone, the gameplay feels even worse. Puzzles are mostly very simple, with a few amounting to nothing more than "pixel hunts" looking for that one thing you can actually interact with.
One thing that Dreamfall Chapters emphasizes is player choice, and boy does it emphasize it. Everytime a major choice happens, the game pauses and asks you to choose from two or three options. A few of these are time limited, but most let you take your time. Once you make your choice, you get a huge "The Balance has Shifted" message on the screen with a large noise. On a few occasions this large message and noise actually distracted from what was happening and even drowned out dialogue. But it gets worse. When the consequences of your actions play out, the game "shouts" at you with  another giant message saying "LOOK! HERE ARE THE CONSEQUENCES!!!!!!" Are players not intelligent enough to figure this out on their own?
Voice acting is uneven, with some great performances, and some lousy ones. The most shocking of these was getting an actual child to do the voice of the toddler Saga. There's a reason video games, television shows and movies typically get adult women to play children, and this is a perfect example.
Visually, the game is pretty nice, particularly for an adventure game, but suffers from some optimization issues. There is also occasionally a strange doubling effect on screen with a very faint version of the scene rotated 180 degrees and overylayed on top.
The game is long (over 20 hours), which is good if you're enjoying the game, but for me it was a chore. I finished it because I couldn't just give up and not see how the story ends, but if this were any other game, I probably would have stopped playing half way through.
The one thing this game succeeded at doing, was make me nostalgic for The Longest Journey. I was constantly remembering how much better it was and now I have an urge to go back and revisit it.

I've got to know Dreamfall Chapters because I had interest in playing The Longest Journey adventure game, so I got it and its sequels (Dreamfall: TLJ and Chapters) as well during a Steam's sale.
The game follows up the events of Dreamfall: TLJ, expanding Zöe Castillo's  and Kian Alvane's stories, divided into 5 books (episodes), leading to a invevitable conclusion of the TLJ saga as a whole.
Chapters mantains a similar gameplay style as its immediate predecessor (Dreamfall: TLJ) but with significant improvements (no more awful fighting engines) while adopting the modern interactive episodic adventure style. In this aspect, what the game offers is not new at all: make decisions which might or might not affect your way forward and lead to different conclusions. As all this kind of games, they focus strength on the plot, the setting and how both develop during gameplay.
I liked the game but I would recommed it mostly to people who have played previous installments on the TLJ saga as it seats solidly on its backgroud story. If you are a modern episodic adventure game fan, I'm sure you will enjoy it as well, but not certainly in the same way if you've followed the complete story, or at least played the previous Dreamfall game.
For those of you expecting to get a closure or explanation of events on The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: TLJ games, Chapters will give you what you want and well delivered, in my opinion.

Here is a video I made that shows how this game works:
This game is very unique first off.  It is NOT at all your average or typical dungeon crawler.
You don't play Exanima running through mashing buttons to do different wild attacks and mad collecting every piece of loot.  You just don't.  This is a game made where you wake up in an unknown dungeon location (although it's the same map and dungeon every game right now, no procedural generation).  You quickly discover that the controls are vastly different from every other dungeon crawling game you have ever played.
To move the easiest way is to stop trying to use WASD period.  Instead put your cursor on the screen the direction you want to move (regardless of which way you currently face) and then hold down the right mouse button.  To walk, put the cursor a little distance from your character.  To move faster, simply move the cursor further away from your character.  It takes a little getting used to and feels quite satisfying once you familiarize yourself with it.  You can use the WASD keys to move but they work differently depending on if you are in combat or just exploring.  In combat they move closer to what we are used to springing your character in the direction forward, left, backwards, or right for W, A, S, and D respectively.  (This is according to the direction you face)  In exploration mode, the A and D key rotate your character around 360 degrees in a circle, W moves you a step forward, and D takes a step back.
Any item that is light enough in weight to be moved by your character realistically can be dragged or moved.  For example if you find a board lying on the ground, pick it up by first moving your character close to it then putting your cursor on it and holding down the left mouse button.  Now you'll see the board picked up from the ground in the air.  You can now use WASD to rotate the board along different axis's.  Drop it in the position you have it rotated in by letting go of the left mouse button.  If the item is an item that can be used a weapon or armor, then you can equip it or put it in your inventory by pressing the I key for "inventory" on your keyboard.  This opens a window that shows your character and a space for your inventory.  To equip it, drag it to your avatars picture in the window, and to place it in your inventory, drag it to the area below your character.
Combat is this games bright spot.  It looks VERY real.  The movements and lunges your character makes are very, very believable and doesn't look anything like any of these dungeon crawlers I've ever played.  So if you are expecting Diablo or God of War combat here, this may not be the game for you.  That ain't happening here no matter how skilled you become.  Timing and movement are key in combat as well as your positioning.  Simply hit the TAB key to alternate between combat and normal modes.  Now in combat mode, your cursor will change to a red icon and you drag the cursor  the direction you want to swing any equipped weapon by holding down the left mouse button and dragging.  But this isn't a game where you want to spam attacks as quickly as you can.  This is more timing and accurate paths made by you to attack when your enemy is 'open' to an attack.  If you swing at the wrong time, you'll leave your character open to an attack that could get you killed.  If you have a shield, simply do nothing but make sure you face your enemy and your character will do the best he/she can to block any attacks with their shield.
I have not even come close to mastering the combat enough to feel confident in starting the exploration of the games dungeon yet.  Thankfully, there is an "Arena" mode where you can hone your skills before actually playing the main game.
Once I get more familiar with this game and can actually play the game.. I will make more videos on my YouTube channel and I will update this review as well.  For now, all I can say is that I highly recommend this game on it's design brilliance and it's unique realistic approach as well.  I think that is simply awesome and gives this game such a different feel and immersion of more fantastical games of this sort.
Enjoy!

Ok. So. Lets imagine this was a free custom map. Nobody hates it . So then, add some custom content including a new pistol (which looks and feels worlds better than those in half life) textures for characters (or rather corpses), scripted sequences, decent music, voice acting and a second level. Now suddenly everyone hates it.
Why?
Now, I admit that some of the points are valid.
It lags. Yes, but that's because in the setting it's raining.
The amount of health kits. True, there are way to many health packs, but considering that you have to cross the deck twice, both times being attacked by the fearsome creatures of Xen, I think the developer made a fair assumtion that we would need this many.
The boss. I agree. It's crap.
The story. I don't think everyone has even thought about it.
So. You are aparently in another dimension, yet we spawn in a flash of lightning on a boat.
Does anyone remember how the xen monsters spawned? IN A FLASH OF LIGHTNING. How do you think a human would arrive? Also, the boat. Let me insert an extract from the Combine OverWiki.
"In addition to this legitimate research, several secret projects are also carried out at Black Mesa, which are deliberately left vague. A large amount of classified research is carried out, including the development of high-tech weapons and defense systems, research into extra-dimensional travel, teleportation, and the study of Xen."
So, we already know that Black mesa have been to other dimensions-is it so far fetched that black mesa have a boat in one of these dimensions?
So you travel to this dimension expecting it to be an easy collection; get the test sample and go-hence, you have no weaponry. But, you arrive and everyones dead. Xen creatures have manged to get aboard. How? we don't know You don't know Your character doesn't know nobody knows! But they are here and you have to fight them off. You eventually reach a survivor who opens the CARGO doors for you.
And before i finish, i'd like to mention a great scripted event most people have probably overlooked. As you make your way over the deck, you see the gman watching you. Then, just as you get close to the point he's at, you are distracted by some turrtes. You have to destroy them, and when you look back to where the G-man was, he's gone. That's just an example.
There is more I could mention, but multiple issues mentioned in other reviews have been cleared up now.
If we had to pay as much as a penny for this, I would agree. But we dont. ITS FREE. No price, no problem.

This game started off ok but got bad quite quick.
First off you get almost every weapon in the first area. Not that bad but you also face almost every single monster in the game in the same stage.
After this fight you get to the tower. In my case I was below half health. You encounter a room with 3 soldiers in it. Ok. Kill them and begin to explore the room. Now after this fight you're probably low on health. So what happens next? The room is flooded with snarks. Took me several attempts to survive.
You get through that and go into a room in which you encounter the first living other person. You get the crossbow and he opens a big door. Really thinking of Jurrasic Park. Apparently theres a big scary monster in the hanger. So we open the doors.
You are then forced to back track all the way to the begining. Which has magically been repopulated with aliens.
You eventually reach the hanger and face a really glitchy cutscene. Which is unskippable. The "big scary monster appears" which is really a reteaxtured barnicle attached to a ragdoll of the final Half Life boss.
You get into the fight and realise that you have NO weapons. They are lying around you. This means that, no matter how conservative you have been, you combat the boss with next to no ammo. The boss is not even that hard. Although if you get caught on the barnicle tounge its almost an instant kill. If you die you have to go through the cutscene again.
You kill the boss and take the crystals. End of the game. Thats it. Its meant to be backstory but its just a shoot em' up. The final boss is just a bit stronger than the rest.
The best bit of the game was probably the final, non glitchy, cutscene.

It's very clear that this game was following in the footsteps of giants, it's most definitely trying to be Dragon Age: Origins, however it is not. The combat is very clunky, the skill system is un-imaginatve and very VERY limited and the stats are not very well thought out. They opted to have 2 seperate stat trees one for combat and one for immersion/crafting, while I think it's nice there is almost 0 reason to even touch the combat stats(str,agi, etc...). The combat early on makes you want to put points in stats to take more hits, but once you unlock the skill tree of your choice there isn't a point, I had maxed out all of the talents like haggle (merchant prices) and perception (seeing traps and treasure) before I had more than a few points in some early combat stats. However with all that game isn't really all that bad, the story is interesting enough and many of the choices you make force you to think for a moment about what you are doing, which is refreshing.                                                      Truly the biggest issues I had with this game were clucky combat, limited skills, worthless stats and how every area was so isolated, it didn't need to be open world but the overall content of the game was smaller than most, oh and that every weapon upgrade came from vendors, only ever used one weapon I found that wasn't from a vendor, which kinda spoils the immersion factor since this is an RPG. But I'd still say this game is overall not bad, not great, but not bad. Worth it when it's on sale for $10 or so. Personally I'd like to see this developer try their hand at another RPG, but one that is longer and better thought out.
Overall I'd give it a 6/10.

If you’re a fan of Castlevania, you shouldn’t be reading this review you should be playing this game or its sprite based predecessors.  If you’re not that familiar with any of the original Castlevania games I can tell you that Mirror of fate attempts to to pay homage to the original 2d Castlevania games in their 2D metroidvania tradition, however it does not quite live up to the high standards of many Castlevania enthusiasts. This re-imagined version trades some of the nuances and beloved tropes for a slightly more  ‘arcady’ feel.  MOF is by no means a bad game, and does retain some of the Castlevania DNA. MOF deserves a lot of credit for staying true to the game’s 2D roots.  I do think anyone would enjoy this game especially if you like the gothic aesthetic and appreciate 2d games, just know you’ll be doing a lot of backtracking.  The puzzles are easy but quite fun and help break up some of the monotony of the combat.  Some may be put off by the art style of the cutscenes, but the platforming, level design,  nice visuals and the boss/enemy designs make up for it.  Overall, really good Castlevania game.

I cannot be sure if it is the scarcity of food and energy that has forced people to live on the moon, or the rapid explosion in the number of scousers. Part of a trilogy of games starting with The Longest Journey. The roots of this game is in the more traditional point and click adventure games, although for this one the format has been modernized a bit. If you want to play a game with an amazing, engaging story then this is it. Unlike its two predecessors with a static, fixed story (that were both great!) this game follows the more current trend of allowing you to make decisions that change the story based on what you choose. There are some parts of the game where the pacing can seem a little slow, but overall the narrative (and the choices you can make to change it along the way) keep you invested right until the end. The ability to change the story with your choices also give this game much more replay value than more traditional adventure games of the past. I definitely recommend this game.

I can't stress this enough: if you absolutely love good platforming games, you're gonna fall head over heels for Shantae (maybe even in more ways than one ;) )
This is a ported version of the DSiware game, however, the Gameboy Color had a version put out too, which have very noticable differences, which some are welcomed while others aren't.
Let's get down to the nitty gritty of it all (rate scale 1-5):
Graphics: 5 - VERY COLORFUL and vibrant.  Shantae and company have very nice fluid animations and character models look bright and cartoonish, which is perfect for this style of game.
Sounds: 4.75 - I give it a slight knock here because I still have memories of the original game.  The music, while very well done, is missing something, and that something is the dance button music.  While it's easier to transform into animals, the original had to make use of limited buttons, but did so in an amazing way.  You hit select to enter dance mode and you used the d-pad and A/B buttons for different dance moves.  The music changes to correspond to Shantae's dance moves, which this is absent in this game.  It's one of the unique changes that was lost in this version.  Nevertheless, the music and sounds are well done, and the addition of very clear grunts from hits make up a tiny bit of this score.
Controls: 5 - I haven't tried the keyboard controls, but controller support is amazing.  The config options have it mapped out perfectly for anyone who has a 360 controller in their posession.  They work fluidly and near flawless.
Gameplay: 4.5 - This one I had trouble with, because it's STILL an amazing game to play, but I have to admit, the missing mini games and dance mode simplification dropped the score a bit.  There was a mini game in the original similar in style to DDR, but with d-pad and A/B button presses.  This is absent, but the game itself is overall fun and definitely worth every penny.
Overall: 4.75 - Don't let the little changes deter you from purchase.  This is one of the greatest and underrated games from the GBC era that has a sweet sequel and a second mode to add more challenge to an already challenging platformer.  Despite the absense of the mini game and dance mode manual dance button presses, this game is a solid platformer that shouldn't be missed.  Get out there and get your belly dance on!
(Caution: the belly dancing performed in this game is done by a professional belly dancer.  Do NOT attempt to try this at home....unless you REALLY REALLY want to, in which case, seek out a dance school that offers belly dancing lessons since books and video lessons only go so far.)

When I started playing this game, I immediately liked it. The controls, setup options the game guides you through in the introduction, the music, the tranquility of the visuals...all quite nice! However, I was working on a 350 piece puzzle at one point, and came to the realization that the music was getting very, very tiresome. As best I can tell, there are only 3 songs that play on a puzzle, and these songs were fairly similar. It took me about six hours to finish the puzzle, and after 3 hours of those same songs, I finally had to mute the game's music and put on some songs in YouTube, as well as a few audio-only podcast-style discussions, debates, etc. That went a lot better for me.
The music getting old quickly was the lesser of my two major problems with this game, however. The major problem for me was that you cannot connect puzzle pieces together individually. Let me explain. If you've solved a jigsaw puzzle in real life, then you have most likely tried to complete the outer edge and any major, "stand-out" parts of the puzzle that really vary in color and form from the rest, then move those connected pieces around into the right spots eventually. With this game, however, if you find a dozen pieces that will fit together,you cannot connect them. You are only allowed to get them to "stick" individually if you place them on
the right spot where they belong on the puzzle.
So the fun of putting together different parts of the puzzle, bit by bit, and scooting them around to where they need to be when it becomes evident where they belong (because "eye-balling it" from the tiny image is iffy at best) is not something I was able to experience with this game. At best, you can put the pieces touching where you think they should go, and move each and every piece individually later. I'm sure the developer has a reason for not programming it to work like that, but it's a 2D jigsaw puzzle game. What I'm asking for is one of the core ways that I - and I'm sure other people - assemble jigsaw puzzles in real life, and the simplicity of a game like this (when compared to a 3D complex game) should allow for linking pieces together and moving the linked pieces around as one entity.

I am going to try my best to provide an unbiased review of this game. However, I am giving my recommendation for this game as a positive based on personal reasons and a childhood spent in my grandparent's basement doing puzzles with them. (4 of which are included in the game! :D)
---------------------------------------------------
Based on previous reviews I've read and the bold orange *Mixed* right at the top of the storepage, it's safe to say that the reviews Pixel Puzzles Ultimate have gotten are fair, despite my thoughts against it. For a game that is literally just about doing jigsaw puzzles, the overall premise is straightforward. At the time of writing this review, there is about 17 included puzzles and 70 DLC packs ranging from $0.99 to $11.99, giving more puzzles for the more you pay. I will further go into detail about each aspect of the game into detail, so if you only want to know about a certain part(s) of the game, feel free to skip ahead, as this may be a lengthy review on my behalf.
----------------------------------------------
PRICE
=====
There's not too much to say about Pixel Puzzles Ultimate price-wise simply because it is free. You can't go wrong with a free puzzle game, especially if you like this genre of game as much as I do. There are 17 free puzzles included, with the option to buy more. I will go more into this in the DLC section.
GAMEPLAY
=======
As I said previously, the overall premise is simple; grab a piece and put it into place until the puzzle is complete. You then are awarded Gold Pieces based on puzzle piece count and and achievement, and then you move on to the next. There's a total (I'm guessing) of about 500-600 puzzles, assuming you purchase all 70 DLC packs.
Also, the devs add a new challenge puzzle every month that gets you a rare currency in the game. Don't worry if you missed one, all the previous month's are available to purchase for a hefty 50 gold pieces. (You'll realize how much that is when you get into the game if you haven't already.)
Personally, I love the graphics and artstyle of every single puzzle in the game. Wether it be photographed, hand painted, or hand-drawn, they all are incredible. With such a range of options to play, you won't ever be bored.
ACHIEVEMENTS
===========
I've seen games like TF2 and PAYDAY 2 with a ridiculous amount of achievements and then there's games like It's Village with over 12,000. Pixel Puzzles still holds a whopping almost 1,000 achievements. You'll earn one after completing a puzzle, completing a pack, buying anything from the Kiosk (buying cursors, backgrounds, avatars, more puzzles, etc.). You get an achievement for doing literally anything in the game, including clicking play. If you're a perfectionist like myself, you're probably going to spend a good 2,000-4,000 total hours earning every achievement. But it's one of those games that continually add things, so good luck earning EVERYTHING.
DLC PACKS
=======
With over 70 DLC packs and counting, you won't get bored easily. From packs themed like any big holiday, to European countries, to beach volleyball, you'll always have something to do.
If you plan on owning every DLC pack like myself, I HIGHLY recommend waiting until the Christmas or Summer Sales, where you can score every pack for around $30-$40.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall, I would definitely recommend this to any puzzle fan out there. This is a great game for what it is, even though only 17 puzzles are included free, it's still DEFINITELY worth a try to see if you like the game.
That's it for this review. If you have any comments, questions, or concernes, don't hesitate to shoot me a DM!
Happy Puzzling!

TL;DR: You need to make a large time commitment and motivation to get anything done, but please read the entire review.
Before you read this, this is a negative review because of the fact that while I would love this game, it has flaws that make it impractical for me.
When first opening, there are no problems. The main GUI is simple to understand and easy to navigate, although grammatical errors appear every now and then. The main issues are with the steep learning curve and the fact that the tutorials don't really give you an idea of how to make a ship/airplane that fulfills all of the "requirements" that most set; It must be good looking, dangerous to the enemy, resource, fuel, and energy efficient, and have a practical purpose. It gives the building blocks, but lacks an explanation on how to put them together. I do understand, however, that games that "hold your hand" can quickly become annoying, but some early instruction would be nice.
The learning curve is quite steep; it took me 10-15 hours to get a moderate grasp of most of the components and how they work. It can get frustrating when the tutorial doesn't explain the concept well enough for you to understand (the airplane ones were like this for me).
Once past most of the tutorials, I hopped into designer, and, seeing people like Robbaz, Lathland, and Redstonize, I set about making a ship to beat them all! Then failed. One of the biggest challenges faced by the newcomers is the fact that you have to build your own ships from scratch, without any guides on the simple things like how to shape you hull and the best layout to organize things like ammo, engines, and mainframes, or a general idea of how much you'll need.
IMPORTANT PART STARTING
The time commitment is huge for From the Depths. It will take a considerable amount of time to build any decently performing ship. Battles can take a while, restocking and moving fleets takes time to learn and perform. All of your desings need prior thought to build; it is not a "sit-down-during-lunch-and-play-for-5-minutes-game." It will be easy (and almost required) to play for hours at a time, and for younger kids with "technology time" restrictions, it will be challenging. You will need to plan and plan and plan to make sure everything fits together nicely.
Finallly, time for the gameplay. It is well put together, clean, pretty easy to understand, and gets harder as you progress. The killer: time. Yes, my biggest and (almost) only problem is time. If you have the time to spend, go for it. For the casual gamer, balancing a job, school, or time restraints placed by parents or schedules, this is problably no for you. If you have the motivation, then go for it, as the sucesses outweigh the troubles in the long run.
IMPORTANT PART ENDED

Here are my thoughts after an hour with this game. Obviously the combat system is what is worth talking about here. I don't care about story or level design right now.
I feel like I have no control with this combat system.
You seem to have three attack moves. Right swing, left swing and overhead swing. Beyond that you should just pray for your character to be stumbling in the right direction as you swing in order to hit your enemy. I can never tell if I'm swinging high or low. I want to be hitting my opponents head. But sometimes my swings are gently rubbing up against their legs instead.
WASD controls your movement in combat. But the length of the steps your character takes, seems to be very much controlled by the physics of your body. So you have to constantly monitor how your character is behaving, while also paying close attention to your opponents moves. Making it very difficult to plan out your moves. Also, each step you take is a very committed step, it's difficult to change direction fluently when moving. So if your mouse cursor was slightly off point as you stepped backwards, your character might squish itself into a corner and stuck because it's legs wont be able to move according to the animation physics.
Usually in games you know exactly what your character is doing because there are never or rarely any dynamic physics deciding your movement. This makes it so you are free to study your enemies behavior. In this game your character moves very differently in every situation. If your legs hit something, if you are near a wall or if your are mid swing. Etc.
Instead of having auto lock-on on your enemy, you have to manually move your mouse cursor in his direction to maintain a fighting front. But since you are also using the mouse to control the direction of your swing, your character will sometimes turn away from his opponent when you ready a swing, making it very wonky to control your direction and movement.
You constantly have to recenter your camera with space, unless you want to play with inverted tank controls when the view changes. I also feel like the camera is zoomed way too far out. The walls often get in the way of your view and sometimes you get a completely top-down view which I find disadvantageous when fighting.
That's my experience anyway. It's difficult to feel immersed or tactical when you can't easily control your character.
Graphix wize, I have no gripes. The setting feels dark and unforgiving.
