(Review as of May 9th 2014 -13 hours of play)
I gave this game a bunch more chances over the last several days.
I think I can recommend it now, but with a disclaimer that this game has a slew of micro-sensitive functions that may be entirely missed by new players.  It's kind of like learning how to drive a manual transmission (in a snow storm up a hill) when all you know how to drive is an automatic.
This is not a hack and slash game (although you can kill everything if you want and are good enough.)  Think of this more like a medieval Solid Snake/Metal Gear Solid, where you sneak around and use your environment to your advantage.  Most of the enemies in the game won't attack you unless you stand and stare at them (make them mad.)  -I thought this was a glitch, but it's intentional.
Some enemies are just angry all the time, and there's not much you can do about it except run, fight, or trap them somewhere.  You really won't know until you meet them.  Sometimes it's just fun to run straight into them and knock them down as you pass by.
You'll get your best gear from searching rooms and chests, so don't feel you have to fight everything that moves.
Today, combat finally(?) started to click.  The biggest difference?  Make sure to orient the camera often, while in combat, to be directly behind your character.  I've tried combat without doing this, or by trying to hold down the space bar constantly all the time.  It works best just to tap the space bar.
Placing the camera directly behind your player puts you in the best position to use fancy footwork and to parry attacks.
Place the camera behind you whenever you feel yourself to be in a good position to attack.  The camera will orient itself to be behind your player.  (during non-combat mode, spacebar will orient itself to the direction your cursor is from your character -a little tap is all you need.)
Then, be sure to use different combinations of left and right, forward and backward WASD movement while swinging your weapon.  With some good observation, you can often take advantage of many of your opponents.  Your character will make two swings with his weapon (if you hold down the mouse button long enough) before taking a break.  Us this in tandem with steps made with the WASD keys to duck out of range, then dart in for a strike.  Experiment with sideways movements too since they often take enemies by surprise.
If you are in the middle of a swing and you see you may have made a poor choice (as to when to swing or see an unwanted attack coming), immediately let go of the mouse and your character will parry successfully.  Again, It helps tremendously to have the camera behind your character when you do this, since your cursor will more often than not end up in the best position to parry.
Concerning mouse cursor and parrying:  Just pointing your character in the direction of your opponent is sometimes not enough.  Move your cursor in the direction of their swing so that your weapon or shield will be in the direct path of their blow.  This helps immensely when your opponent has a heavier weapon like a hammer.
I've also (maybe) discovered even some micro combat skills which would never be apparent to me on my first day playing.  It would appear to me that my weapon will try to hit my opponent where ever my cursor is over their body.  It seems weird, but when I go to strike when it's over their head, my character will go in for a head shot, and conversely, when it's over their foot, I will swing at their foot.  I'm not skilled enough to use this all the time, but have noticed this interaction happening, especially when attacking opponents which have fallen down.  Try doing overhead swings at fallen opponents an notice where you strikes fall.
Lastly, someone else posted about a way to back up your saves.  This game is brutal for new players, so doing this for the first little while may help you from tearing your hair out -at least until you get used to the very different and unique controls of the game.
Finally, I have to agree that Expert Arena mode is easier than Novice due to the much heavier armor you can take from your defeated opponents.  Getting there is worth it to see all the stuff you can put on your character.
***************************************************************************************************************
(Earlier review as of April 29th 2014 -Day of release on Steam)
I backed this game on Kickstarter and was drawn to it's idea of a rag-doll physics kind of player control scheme.
After having played it for a little bit, I've found the controls much different than I'd expected, and frustratingly so.  You use the WASD keys to move around, but what I didn't know is that 'A' and 'S' move you forward and backward, and 'W' and 'D' turn your character, independently of the camera angle you are at.  To complicate things, your character always wants to face the direction of the cursor and the direction you swing your weapon is dependent on where your cursor is to your character.
If you stand still for a minute or so, the camera will also start to pan around your character, making it difficult to stay in one place to just observe anything.
So in other words, I found myself frustrated, fighting both the controls and the camera, while my character flailed about a lot and was frustrating to control.  And to make matters worse, you only get one life, so when you die, you have to start all the way over again.
I'm going to watch where this game goes, but in the meantime, it will have to stay uninstalled in my library.

I'm giving this game a recommend, though mostly because I'm a developer (Road Redemption) and I know what a pain negative reviews are.
My biggest issue is with the combat, so that's all I'll focus on.  Lord knows there are a ton of other interface issues, but those are easy fixes.
Basically the question is "what does this combat system bring to the table?"   In other words, what do I gain for having to get accustomed to such an unwieldy system?  My hope would be that I would gain a finer control and a higher level of interactivity than is present with other melee combat systems.
At the moment, I feel like this isn't the case.  When I want to stike a blow at someone's head, half the time it ends up hitting his arm, and there's nothing I can do about it.  When I want to do a quick jab, I can't (not implemented).  When I want to do a wider, heavier swing, I can't because attempting to do so makes moving my character almost impossible do to the way the movement controls work.
And that's the game's biggest issue right now.  While in combat, WASD moves your character in relation  to the way he's facing, and he always faces the cursor.  If I kept my cursor on my target the whole time (like how you attack in Diablo), this type of movement is something I could maybe get used to.  Unfortunately, to do a heavy swing you're REQUIRED to swing your cursor in a 180 arc around your character, while in the heat of combat.  This means that your character is constantly facing a different direction, which means the forward key will constantly move you in a different direction.
So in the heat of battle, I'm left with nothing but my standard attack and my overhead swing.
I think the game would be GREATLY improved if, while in combat, the character moved in relation to the camera, and the camera was locked behind the player's back.  Basically, it would be like Dark Forces 2: Jedi Knight system, except with a more overhead angle.  This would reduce the learning curve substantially and make the game a lot more fun, without losing any of the cool physics ideas this game brings to the table.
I think this game has a lot of potential, but I worry about critical reception until the combat system is fixed.

Dont play this game if you hate losing/dying, this is by no means an easy game, this game doesnt hold your hands, if you arent careful you will easily die and have to start all over again (there will be a checkpoint later in the game). The controls are unique compared to other games so it takes a while to get used to, most games uses static animations, in this game the animations are simlulated muscle movements (motion synthesis) which is affected by the games physics and can be altered realisticly from external forces making movements really dynamic.
The combat like many other things in the game is physics based, timing and precision is needed to be good and features pixel accurate hitboxes, all objects are physically formed as they looks like, this makes how armors and weapons are shaped quickly more important than their "stats" (stats shown in a objects description isnt the actual stats, but just something so you can compare it to other items).
The ai have same controls as you do so they arent cheating in any way, they got no intention of dying to you and with the dynamic nature of the game each fight feels personal.
Even if most enemies in adventure mode got nowhere close to the fighting skills that the npc's got in the arena (they cant even block attack propperly) you would think the adventure mode should be fairly easy, but theres where you are wrong. fighting in a small environment with alot of items/furniture laying around and possibly with multiple enemies is not always a simple task, they might suck at combat, but taking one of their attacks can still be lethal. Running away or avoid fighting all together is just as valid as defeating your opponent (if not more if you want to stay alive/stay unhurt). This is a rpg with real consequences that cant be undone and death being the ultimate consequence. role playing will be more variated when more npc interactions, the dialogue system and skill system is implemented (and multiplayer).
alot more can be said about the game, but what it boils down to is: its not meant for everyone, its hard/challenging and requires quite a lot of training to be any good. might not be much in terms of content yet, but with the dynamic nature of the game and all the areas to search you can end up using quite alot of time just on one playthrough.

At first I was really excited for this game to come out, then shortly after I read the reviews, I saw the game and my initial excitement waned. However, for some reason this game still called to me, the world of The Dark Eye just seemed so interesting and so when I found it on sale for dirt cheap I had to satisfy my curiosity and i'm glad I did.
Demonicon, without a doubt has it's flaws, but buried beneath these flaws is a game that could've easily been 9/10 had Kalypso taking their time and fleshed things out just a little more. The story, which is slightly cliche, is told wonderfully. The characters feel real and not like some extreme virtue of either good or evil. The decisions that are made throughout the game remind me of that of The Witcher Series in that no one choice represents true right or wrong necesarrily, but instead leaves it open for you to decide what is right and that puts you in some difficult spots. My only complaint with the story is the lack of an epilogue, which leaves the ending feeling lackluster and meak.
Probably one of the best things done in Demonicon is the lore. From a city's history to the different demons of the world, the amount of detail put into the lore is outstanding and truly gives you insight into the happenings of the world. On the other hand some might consider the combat to be the worst. While it's true the combat is clunky and the stop-and-go fighting can be rather annoying, I found the combat to be enjoyable. Again another feature that is reminiscient of The Witcher 2 with and emphasis on parrying and thinking about your moves instead of just hacking away. It isn't as polished as The Witcher 2, but I didn't find it as bad as some say.
For me the worst aspects of this game are the bugs, the graphics, and the overall "lifeless" world.
Most of the bugs are minor, such as your father randomly taking a knee throughout your conversation, but for a game that's been out for awhile now you expect most of these bugs to be gone. The graphics, while not terrible, certaintly don't look like the other realeases at the time. Demonicon looks like an early xbox 360 realeased game. The characters convey no emotions on their faces and if it weren't for the voices you'd proabbaly just assume they were tranquil with everything. The world also seems dead, sure there are people who inhabit it, but they all just stand around gazing emptily maybe talking to another citizen and it makes the city feel dead.
Overall, I do recommend this game to RPG fans if they can find it on sale. The story and the world will entrance you, just don't expect too much else from the game.

This game is fantastic in overall gameplay and allows for some simple, but fun creative city designs. I can see this game going very far, but at the same time I think it'll require a lot of work in improvment on current gameplay mechanics. In the beginning I was skeptical of a lot of the negative reviews, however I now understand and agree with the many states problem in this game:
-Dragons are extremely weak
-Viking attacks can be difficult to recover from. Five tall walls can be very easily taken down by ogres even with relatively good tower coverage and attacks are either extremely easy or absurdly overwhelming. Some will never enter the town and some will take down all the walls in one attack. For example I was attacked by 15+ viking ships at the same time.
-Attacks eventually become very repetitive without any variety beyond dragons and vikings.
-NPC AI is pretty bad where NPCs will struggle to acquire food and/or charcoal even though it maybe readily available at a nextdoor marketplace. This will eventually result in constant NPC deaths flooding the notification bar when the town hits over 500 people, which can be an annoyance.
-Game lacks a variety of buildable structures, but I'm certain this will improve in the future.
-Needs upgradeable buildings
Pros of this game:
-Great, simple artwork
-Great camera controls
-Simple and clean gameplay
-Offers a good layer of strategy in building placement
-Towns really feel like they're growing.
-Different maps provide a variety of possible designs
Although there are a lot of problems I would say this game is still worth playing for those who just want to build. I spent 10 hours on this game and I think it was well worth the money, however in its current state I wouldn't strongly recommend it unless you find the artwork very appealing and don't mind building with limitations.

Kingdoms and Castles is a Nice entry-level city builder game, it's great for people who want to get into city management games and it has a good bit to offer, having a good amount of knowledge about city builders I got my first city to 2000 people after 440 years, (Screencaps on my profile).
Pros:
- Brilliant game to sink a few hours into here and there
- Very affordable at £6.99 (price at time of review)
- Quirky art style that functions really well in this style of game
- Very efficient and easy to follow UI
- Good amount of content for an Alpha-stage game
- Generally great game for the price
Cons:
- Once you build enough defenses such as ballistas and archers, the invading vikings have no chance at all to really damage your city, a larger variety of enemies would be welcome
- Advisors tend to only really have a few lines of advice, that all seem to just be reminders of what stock you are low on or reminding you that your people are unhappy, would love to see some more in detail advice as to what you could do to combat their issues, would be very useful to newer players
- Good amount of content for an alpha game, but definitly needs more, after about 10 hours I had pretty much maxed out all of the buildings and resource gathering jobs I had access too
Overall I would rate this game a 4.5/5, it really has a LOT of potential if nurtured the right way, the cons of this game are simply teething issues, such as needing more content and more enemies, it's really a solid game for players that want to get into the micro-management sim style games, I would whole heartedly reccomend this game, especially for the price, I just hope that the developer(s) nurture this game and listen to feedback to give it more replay value.

Mirror of Fate or "How do I annoy the player the most and not letting him skip cutscenes and camera drives"...seriously annoying.
The game itself tries to bridge the gap between Lords of Shadow 1 and 2 (or probably was created before LoS 2 was released or even a concept, I don't know). In any case it follows the story of Gabriel's son and grandson. You will play as three different characters. Each character has unique abilities and has his own act. Expect backtracking, skill unlocks and collectables. The game was originally developed for handhelds I think and the graphics engine is obviously a step back. Why they opted for a cell shaded look in cutscenes only, is beyond me however.
Contrary to LoS 1 this game plays strictly on a 2D plane and to be honest that alleviates pretty much most of the issues with the first game, as weird as they may sound. The camera won't♥♥♥♥♥♥around, combat is more straight forward, blocking now actually works easier without constantly rolling and special abilities as well as combos are simpler to use and actually do make a difference.
Traversing the terrain is relatively straight forward, once you got used to the wonky animations that make it seem like you've missed every jump. It's definitely not a shiny game and the story lacks emotion...hell, there's barely any story here anyway.
I would get this for a discount, personally, but 12 bucks isn't insanely high for a 8-10 hour experience if you want to clear it all. Took me 8 hours on easy for 84% or so. Higher difficulties will certainly make combat more challenging (though most enemies aren't really dangerous and I'm not sure why the Y move (area attack) was included in the game other than for some combos which require it. You've also got access to a boss rush mode, once you finish the game and the bosses are actually pretty fun.

+Story
+Boss fights
+Puzzles
------------
-Repeating chapters. when take a new skill you will to return to the old parts.

Does nothing significant. Combat tries to play similarly to the main LoS games, but ends up being even more boring and shallow in 2D. Story is short and unnecessary for the series. The music is nice, atmospheric, but you'll hear the beginning of the song very often and there's not even too much variety of it.
Just really feels like what you expect from a "handheld spin-off", obviously really low-budget.
Kind of funny seeing some of the cinematics, you can tell when they were trying to make use of the 3DS screen, but personally I hate it when games/movies do scenes specifically for 3D.
Hopefully Nintendo will keep these guys on the right track with the Metroid 2 remake. Speaking of Metroid, this game has magnetic rails, using your whip as a grappling hook, and very-fast running. All felt very Metroid inspired.

AND THE MAP. I hate the map. It's very old school where it's just the blocks, which is fine, but it was frustrating when actively trying to find scrolls, and the backtracking is a pain.
You basicly start over with a different character in each act, each with different bosses and slightly different routes through the castle. I did like the moments where the characters would notice each other, or something you'd notice in one act would be explained later because it happened simultaneously in a different act. The acts seemed a little out of order; I personally felt like the last act probably should have been the first.
Or maybe it's just a surprise if LoS is your first Castlevania.
It is backstory rich, and pulls from the first and second game. The boss battles were fun. Many of the visuals are lovely, and the music is also quite enjoyable.
While technically it's a sequel, as it does take place after LoS, it feels more like a filler/mini game.
For those who do love lore, just keep in mind that LoS is a reboot and not based off of the the old story line many of us grew up with and came to love.
With that in mind, it's a decent game. Not the best. But decent.

Anarachy Arcade is a unique game in which you create your own personal house to replace your desktop.
In terms of features it is very good as it allows you to turn your steam libary, Videos, music and pictures into physical items such as Arcade machines or even something as strange as a clock.
While creating things in here it did give me a sence of achievement which I could never get with any other game it does have its disadvantages.
#1. You will get no Steam game time. (All of your individual Steam game times will all be placed on to Anarchy Arcade)
#2. It always runs in the background when you are playing a Steam game through it. While it is only a very minor dip in frames, if you are running on a older system then it will be very noticible.
#3. If you place videos from your PC then you will have many issues such as a annoying stutter, and a de sync which makes the video unwatchable.
Overall Anarchy Arcade is a game with lot's of potential but for me at least it fails, until the developer could perhaps work with Steam to fix some of these issues.

I remembered my early days in FTD as a fresh out from the rudementary and confusing tutorial... Struggling myself to understand every single important pieces to make things work. Going so far to mess up making my first Custom Cannon that ended up being a weak gun. I keep trying, trying to build things on my own.. But I coulden't do it because of this learning curve. It doesn't help to the fact that I'm used to another sandbox builder, Simpleplanes that I'm expecting it's going to be like that. But oh I was so wrong...
With my computer fighting against me with threats of overheating... I cannot play this game anymore due to overheating.. Fast forward a one year and several months later.. I returned back, feeling fresh with a new rig at my disposal and possibly bored and has nothing to do at the moment. This is when I first witnessed the new changes. The CRAMs and the newer engine mechanics..and so many things... The tutorial got better than what I remember back then...which is good since I learned some things that I could ever hope myself to do.
Armed with new knowlage in shipbuilding and stuff. I started to make my knowlage to good use. I started tearing apart preexisting ships to learn how it works.. One of the early ships I've worked on was that little sailbot with a lethal explosive cannon called "Vanguard". I've made many ships derived from it. It's not much, but it's a start from what I am already.
Time has passed after my first fleet of Vanguard-based ships.. I started working on first airships of the DWG called Atlas. It wasn't fast or anything but I can see the potential for something big... So I equipped it with missile launchers and repositioned the guns from its underbelly. The upgrades was worth the trouble at least.
After numerous updates and time in the game fiddling everything I could get my hands on right now. I started to come across some old designs that dates back in the CC era. Some of them were good enough for me that I wish the original makers would start updating it. But time has passed, there's no updates for those ships... Many things factor to that, it could be the original designers are lazy or retired FTD altogether. Or they might've lost their touch in constructing things and forgot how to design. But I cannot let those old designs be lost in the abyss.. Using my experience I've had in fiddling many constructables.
I took myself to refit/modernize/overhault the old ships to make it work like originally before. Designs never die, if there's one who has the time to bring them on their former glory so they can see the sunrise again as they set sail.
Ah yes, I got sidetracked over my fond memories.
There's many changes throughout the game's updates. From changing weapons to logistical overhaul in newer versions. My opinion about this unified resource which is the hot topic FTD at the moment is kind of a mixed bag. There's that one side of me that wanting it back due to complexity and thinking ahead what to do. And the other side of me that let it go uninterrupted. It's quite strange when you have a steam ship that eats up material that's composed of everything.. Surely the old system of resources might be preferable for steam engines, since you don't need to worry about losing resources if you keep the heat up. But then again... Bringing out your favorite ship, only to be stopped by the ever bothering insufficent metal. So you had to make wooden ships to get over that.
I personally don't mind the changes, it's on the developer's will. And saves time to think about logistical problems of managing one type of resources on another as you worry about one kind of resource to worry about. This allows building ships less restictive and less stressful. But the cons for this system is that your precious unified material will get eaten by fuel refineries and high powered steam engines on localized resource.
So if you don't like reading through my ramblings, maybe you should get the game like soon. Much better if you got it on sale as always. Don't let the learning curve stop you...once you get deep into the rabbit hole... You'll be addicted before you know it.

A MARIONETTE SIMULATOR
A never seen before level in real-time object physics for any game. Absolutely impressive! So real and unpredictable: every new game is different from previous.
Sorry but after some more time spent on combat I changed my mind.
Physics obsession in this game  makes battles poorly strategic and with a lot of unpredictable physics-driven "unwanted" movements, and no, this doesn't mean more realistic and fun. It's exactly like moving a marionette, with mouse. This means you'll pass most of the time struggling to do what you had in mind without success instead of playing like you wanted... or just happens sometimes by pure chance, plus a bit of experience.
Too much physics (you move like being drunk), and can't plan a serious sequence of moves or a real attack strategy... I liked the original idea of physics driven combat, but current controls are way too slow-motion-like and you'll be slave of a forces simulation in the end, instead of developing important aspects of combat (counter attacks, faster anticipations, breaking guard etc.) IMO. It's all so randomic with bad mouse controls.
The real truth is that you'll end up playing with very basic and very imprecise attacks (when you manage to do what you wanted at least) and randomic consequences all the time! No elaborate combat possible. You can't aim at a specific body part, your arms/hands often get stuck into walls or on enemy's body/weapons. In real life you'd retreat the arms promptly but you have no control over them in this game. All you can do is swash your weapons left, right, up-down and sometimes lunge based on forces momentum, with totally imprecise attacks just hoping the enemy's guard will be open in that exact moment and he will impact against your weapon.
It doesn't matter how skilled you are moving the player (which is the real game in the game!), you have no real fine control on your limbs. You can decide just the directions (vectors).
Bad control design is the biggest fault of this game. Could have been much better with traditional WASD movements, and physics applied only to weapons instead of everything mouse-controlled like a marionette.
5/10

NOTE: I backed this game back in 2012 and have followed it ever since. I have played many earlier versions, and have many more hours of game time than what my steam time implies.
A prelude to a game called Sui Generis (yet to be released), Exanima is an excellent dungeon crawler with a stellar combat system.
Using real physics as the basis, the combat in the game is hugely dynamic and skill reliant. Though the mechanics are simple to understand, there is a deep level of complexity involved in it. You have to aim each swing and each parry, you have to provide power and speed by rotating your character, and gracefully dodge your enemies strikes. It is a difficult system to master, one which requires some patience, but is infinitely rewarding once you get it right. It's unlike anything I have previously played, and a breath of fresh air in the RPG genre. The combat (at the point of writing this review) is still not feature complete, with additional combat manouvers, ranged combat and level system on its way. Despite this, it feels very much complete.
The underworld in Exanima provides a tense and mysterious atmosphere, one which drives you to explore and wonder what awaits around each corner. It is a grim and dark place, set in a low fantasy setting. The game tells its story through the environment, books, parchments. Your character seemingly having lost his memory, it's up to you to piece everything together. It is much like what is seen in the Souls series in this regard, at least thus far.
It is a difficult game. Wether you test your might in the progressive arena mode or venture through the dungeon, the game will surely pose a challenge. And like any difficult game, it features serrious consequences for mistakes. Taking hard blows, or being cut by slashing weapons may leave you with permanent damage. The only way to heal this back up is by using a very rare potion that there only exist a few of in the dungeon, assuming you have the wit to search and find them in the first place. And if you die in the dungeon, thats it. You'll have to start over. Though it can be frutrating at times, it is this fact that makes the experience of progressing so rewarding.
The game treats you as a person with intelligence and willingness to learn, each victory and discovery is earned by you and not given to you. This is a refreshing feeling, since nowadays games mostly treat you as a fragile kid that needs everything fed to him with a spoon. Exanima aims to against this trend, which it very much succeeds in doing.

Demonicon reminded me a bit of Dragon Age 2 because of its repetitive and dull environments. But it's a game that's understandable, a game that anyone can play. It's actually fairly good for an action RPG. Until it becomes very repetitive as far as the quests are concerned.
The character and skill upgrade systems are refreshing. They aren't perfect, but at least they allow for a lot of customization, even if half of these upgrades aren't used all that much. You earn AP by finishing quests, killing enemies, you name it. These points can then be spend on upgrades. Each skill requires 4 blocks of points before it is entirely upgraded and there are about 10 skills in total. You can also spend these points on stats like strength and you also unlock a magic system early on that uses GP which can be earned pretty much the same way, but you have to use magic while doing things.
Quests consist of kill and fetch quests and halfway through the game this becomes rather repetitive. This is also thanks to the not-all-that-exciting combat, which is real-time, by the way.
The graphics are sharp and pretty good, but the framerate drops in villages and I have no idea why. The villages aren't overly crowded and there aren't any spectacular visual effects in it either. Weird. Otherwise, the game runs well.
The voice acting isn't all that bad, even if some of the voices don't match the personalities of the characters. But then again, this is no AAA title so if we take that into account it isn't all that bad.
Demonicon didn't disappoint me because I didn't really have any expectations so if you feel the same way give it a try. But if you want a quality RPG that isn't too repetitive look further.

I've seen a fair amount of negativity surrounding Demonicon since its release - which is what has kept me away from the game until a recent sale. Having just beaten the game this morning, I feel very comfortable recommending this game to RPG fans, or anyone looking for a unique and enjoyable story.
Demonicon's strengths lie in its commendable use of The Dark Eye universe, it's RPG & skill systems, the creative and thoroughly engaging story line, the focus on narrative and characters, and a well implemented choice system that affects the story and game world.
The Dark Eye ruleset may not be represented to the degree that you see in Drakensang, but Demonicon's skills, spells and combat abilities are very well implemented. Its a joy to play a game that puts such high focus on character skills, such as Perception, Fast Talk, Lock Picking, etc. I highly recommend focusing on skills and spells (and less so on combat abilities) if you play the game. I also do recommend playing the game on Hard, as it is quite easy.
Cairon's tale may not come across as truly unique in the first half of the game, but those who play all the way through to the end will enjoy a well paced and fairly well written tale that delves into Barboradianism. I've played a lot of RPGs, and I will always remember Demonicon's story - it is the game's standout feature. I really don't want to touch on the story line much, as I feel it is best for the player to delve into it with as few preconceived notions as possible. Suffice it to say that the plot synopsises and game descriptions do not give it justice.
Demonicon places a lot of focus on character interaction and player choice. You will spend a siginificant amount of time in conversations with other characters, and in several points throughout the game what you say and decide will affect the game world, the characters and the story. The interplay of the strong, unusual story with the choice system that allows the player to shape how it develops and ends is quite gripping.
Cairon may come across as a stale lead with poor attitude, but he develops well across the story, and I ended up being quite fond of him by the end of the game. He also has the distinction (late game) of wearing what is easily one of the coolest sets of armor I have ever seen. I was constantly taking screenshots of Cairon in his end game gear - it is exceedingly creative and morbid.
Another factor that helps to amplify the impact and appeal of Demonicon's tale is the well realized game world. The graphics may be dated, but the locations throughout the game are distinctively bleak. Demonicon possesses its own imaginative, sepulchral take on The Dark Eye universe that extends from impressive locations, atmosphere, mood and detail to outright kooky and disturbing events and supporting characters. There is a heavy fixation on the undead, necromancy, demons, suffering, plague, prostitution, and damnation - and I believe it was handled in a way that elevated Demonicon into something quite unique among RPGS.
I believe you play Demonicon for the kooky and imaginatively morbid storyline, the immersive game world, and the well designed choice & rpg systems. These are all wrapped up in dated graphics and sloppy combat - but I find most old school rpg players are quite accustomed to that by now;  the graphics and gameplay fit like an old shirt that brings back memories.

Interesting enough RPG; very similar to the first Dragon Age.
VERY complicated skill system; points are earned from defeating enemies, completing quests or solving skill challenges.  Using magic during fights converts some of the earned points in to "gift points" that can be exclusively spent upgrading magic abilities. The remainder of points can be spent on combat special abilities, skills (up to rank 5 of 7), stats that improve 2 skills, or stats that effect your combat capabilities.  Investing in skills early is a sure way to earn ongoing dividends throughout the game.
Story was... interesting.  Well crafted universe with plenty of detailed back story, however the game does expect that you the player will memorize it.  Just learned a complex, multi-sentence incantation? Better hope you remember it precisely when it comes time to enter it because the game provides no "your character knows this, so click here for the correct option" which is a bit jarring given the "follow the blinking quest marker to the hidden clues" hand-holding presented at various points.
Largest complaint: No manual saves. I understand that this is intended to actually invest you in the choices you makein the context of the Role Playing aspect by removing the ability to trivially alter your choices, but it can also be somewhat obnoxious when exploring large areas to have to find the next thing that triggers a save point.  Luckily the game saves after every fight and provides enough 3-6 minion skirmishes at various points that you're never terribly far away from a save point.

It is a very good game, interesting, fun to play and very rewarding. There are a few things that I don't completely like. In specific, it seems a simplified version of Anno 2070. In 2070, you need to set up productions on different islands building ships to trade and send stuff from one Island to another, organizing the route and so on, it is very detailed and
it requires a lot of planning and care to organize it. In 2205, most of the things are automated, and this detract, in my opinion, from the fun.
In 2070, if you don't satisfy the needs of your population up to a percentage, they simply move out and you lose the revenue. Here it doesn't seems so or it doesn't seems to have much negative effects.
The combat missions are... meh... Ok, they are not required, but still... they feel a bit like an addendum that was thrown in to spice up the game.
The Tundra was a bit of a letdown, mostly because I got in after finishing everything else, with almost 5 million in the bank and a positive balance. So I basically steamrolled over everything.
The Tundra, in my opinion, would have been nice just after the Arctic, because it adds a lot of complexity. The population is divided in 2 groups: there are the "ecologist" that are equivalent to the Arctic's Preserver, and the Researchers that are the scientist. Also the population's needs are mostly the same. The trick is that they require canned food, but you can't fish or make canneries here! You need to make them in the Arctic and then ship them in.
So it's more juggling resources, that is challenging when you've just started, but not much when you've finished.
Also, constructing stuff there require construct-o-bot and super-alloy, but you can't make them on-site. And instead of going and building the required production lines somewhere, I went "rockfeller" style, just popped down at Papadakis' place and bought up all his stock, then trucked them here and that's it.
The only real problem, ignoring the prick head researcher here, is that the "project" is the draining of the marshes and the reconstruction of some sort of 'seed vault' built by the Eden project in 2100, and it requires a load of Iridium, that you only get from combat missions. So it is start a pump site, that uses constructobot and superalloy, go take a combat mission to pile up in iridium, go back to papadakis and buy more of the stuff, pop back in to finish the job, repeat for the next site. There are 7 of them, so it takes a bit of time, but when you have a positive balance of 40.000 and 5 millions, there is no real challange.
Do I suggest this game? Yes if you haven't played Anno 2070 yet and want to have a quick intro to the mechanics, but if you are an experienced Anno 2070 players, you'll probably find this a bit overrated.
Is not that is not fun, it is, but it pales against the complexity of 2070.

A boring game from cover to cover.
Most of the time you spend in front of Dreamfall Chapters will be listening to hours and hours of exposition. This is delivered with animation that takes control away from you. The interactive sequences in between the exposition is what has to be one of the most boring professional adventure games of the XXI century. The first half of the game is plagued with aimless wandering in hard-to-navigate environments, and almost no puzzles; the second half fortunately dispenses with the backtracking, but the amount of puzzles remain slow. All the time the puzzles aren't connected to the story and are usually simple, tedious or both.
My description might remind some of Telltales games, and they wouldn't be wrong to assume this game borrows inspiration from that company. I've enjoy most Telltales' games, because they excel at pacing and engagement. The decisions feel real, while in Dreamfall Chapters they feel random and unimportant (what food should I buy Reza?!)
This is all a shame, because Dreamfall Chapters' art is beautiful and the designers had total dedication to the details. The world feels alive and comes through believable. The pacing however ruined it for me. For instance, after the game's climax the player is treated to, I kid not, 20 minutes of exposition in the form of epilogues. Most big characters get at least one epilogue. The major characters' epilogues get their own epilogues. One character that doesn't have a main role until the end of the last part has 3 or 4 epilogues (I lost count). At this point the player's interest is gone, and yet the writers decided to self-indulge into more exposition, most of which is a retelling of the game's events without adding any critical information.
I played this game despite the negative reviews because some reviewers claimed it gets better on the second half. While it does get better in my opinion, it never gets good, and all the flaws except backtracking are carried over.

Like it's predecessors, the story is kinda interesting, but it falls short on it's goal of delivering a somewhat immersing story. The whole "game" aspect of it feels really forced. Most of the time you're just wandering around without much sense of purpose. The puzzles are unintuitive and the dialogue is jarring. It's like these guys had a real need to tell this cool story, but were kinda clueless on how to deliver it. I really wanted to like this one, but the sheer boredom one has to endure to get anywhere was just too much.

Risky's Revenge is... a game that charms and frustrates in equal measure. Though part of that is simply its age, a lot of it has to do with it feeling like a Super Nintendo game in both the good
bad ways.
Despite being what it is - a DSi game sized up to the PC - generally Shantae looks pretty good for its age. It's well-animated with those limitations considered, though the HD graphics used for conversations and menus are both welcome and slightly jarring.
One of the big drawbacks, though, coming from the DSi, is that the movement feels slow, and it's coupled with "stop 'n go" enemies, like archers that require you to leap up into the air and repeatedly whack to clear them out of your way, or spitting foes that require you to slowly crawl towards them to engage safely. The worst offender are mermaids that appear in droves, which dive into puddles and it feels like it takes forever for them to reemerge. Maybe just a second or two, but it can make tracking back and forth a real chore. For some reason, they opted to put the warp stations to get you from area to area in out-of-the-way places, meaning that there's generally a walk to or from them to get to where you're going. And though in this kind of game you're usually given movement options that make trekking back and forth easier as time goes on, Shantae never really does other than offering new warp stations.
The controls work well for the most part, Shantae's transformations serve largely just as the lock-and-key for its exploration antics, with only one form - the monkey - providing a distinct advantage outside of unlocking play fields (it can climb walls and leap higher). Though the three additional forms are well-varied, there's not a world of reason to use them when they aren't needed. Generally, you'll be relying on hair-whipping and magic, though one kind of magic (the spiked ball) stands out above the others, often protecting Shantae and also enhancing her melee capabilities, while the others are far more situational. You'll need them all - there's at least one lock for all them - but they aren't strongly balanced. She also has another costume which basically just reduces her magic cost and increases damage, but unfortunately you can only see it by finishing the game, unlike the iOS version that gave you the option to switch back and forth very early on.
Shantae relies on doors that move you across lateral dimensions, and areas like the forest are easily five areas deep. Using the map becomes a necessity at times, since it's easy to get lost otherwise because of this. The forest is a particular offender, and it can be tiresome if you go through the wrong door or lose track of which area you're in at a given moment.
That being said, it does have a lot of charm to it, though a lot of the humor is hit-or-miss. Having both a female protagonist and anatagonist is rare and welcome, though the "sexy" female enemies feel gratuitious at points. If you're interested in the Shantae series, the plot of this game leads directly into the vastly improved sequel (Pirate's Curse), and it's worth a lark when it's on sale for two bucks and change, since it hardly overstays its welcome unless you focus on collecting everything in the game.  I can't recommend it unconditionally, though, and you have to go in being aware of its foibles. If you're okay with that, it's a decent little exploration platformer, though with Steam exploding with excellent games in that genre, it's hard to recommend it on that alone. It comes from a period where Wayforward was putting out nostalgia efforts that had a lot of cargo cult design, and this definitely feels like its aping games of the 90s without improving on them. It's not a bad game, but PC platforming has gotten so refined that it doesn't quite stand out.

I've barely even begun to play this game and I'm already amazed. I didn't realize how badly I wanted to be able to build my own warships until this game first came to my notice and now I'm hooked. The ships handle nicely to the point that my real-world boating experience applies well to in-game vehicles, and real-world naval architecture principles apply to ship construction as well. If you want to build a full-scale working replica of your favorite warship, you can (if you don't have the patience for that, you can use one of the existing in-game models or download a fan-made one. Most popular historic warships, particularly from the WWII era, have already been built for your enjoyment).
On the other hand, if you want to build something completely absurd you can do that too. Make a flying brick that shoots lasers. Make a mothership that shoots missiles that in turn shoot other, smaller missiles. Make a submarine with forceshields. Make a railgun artillery platform in space. Make an motor with more turbochargers than cylinders. Make a steam engine that operates at 300 rpm. Do whatever; this game has all sorts of features and keeps getting more. While this game is still in active development, it's already more stable and feature-complete than most 'finished' games on the market and well worth the money, particularly if you get it on sale. For established fans of voxel-based construction titles this game is a must-have; for everyone else it's at least strongly worth considering.

Over all this is a good game with 3 glaring faults that keep it from becoming a great game.  If you are looking for something relaxing to idle away a few hours, this is a good game.  If you are looking for a city builder with depth, you should pass on this title.  I like the game overall, but it will be for the nights I want to veg. out and relax.  At $10.00, I am satisfied with my purchase.
THE GOOD;
Every thing just plain works.  It should take no more than an hour to grasp the mechanics of the game.  You start out with 5 villagers, the first thing you need to do is collect wood.  You select a tree and select chop.  An idle villager will go cut down the tree (note, a tree cut down in this manner will not regrow).    Once you have enough wood, you build a few houses and farms.  As you get more villagers and resources, you start mining stone and charcole.  You need stone and wood to build a well.  You need a well to fight fires (note the coverage area when you place the well).  Your villagers need charcole to cook and warm their homes.  Next you should build foresters as they automatically cut down wood and replant trees.  Always make sure you have idle villagers before you place new buildings.  Each building tells you how many people it employes in the tool tip.
I saw a few complaints about pathing, this really isn't true.  Your villagers favor using roadways over taking the shortest route.  Place your Graineries near your farms with the door facing the road, and you will have no trouble collecting food in a timely manner.  In the same vein, place stock piles near major ore deposits to hasten collection of those resources.  Place Bakeries and markets near your neighborhoods so your residence have easy access to food.  You get the picture, place related items near each other for efficiency!  Always insure you have enough idle villagers to do your bidding.
To get gold you have to tax your citizens.  Tax them too high and their happiness level will quickly decline.
The graphics are certainly not up to todays standards, but they are charming enough and work fine for this game.  My current city takes up 3/4 of a map with north of 600 peeps, and I have noticed no slow down on my rig (core i7 4770 with a gtx 1070 and 32gb of ram).
THE BAD;  I will list these in order of least to most troublesome.
Fires are completely random, except for dragon induced.  Anything can go up in flames!  I've had my well catch fire, a stone statue, even roadways!  Just silly, but, overall not a real detraction.  If you have a well nearby as well as villagers, they will put out the fire and save the building.
Combat just barely works.  You have to guide your troops in to the path of the enemy.  The enemy will walk through them taking whatever damage your army can accomplish.  Then you have to move your army into the path of the enemy again.  You cannot tell your troops to attack, and they do not lock on and follow.  Pretty annoying, but the Viking attacks fairly rare (at least on normal difficulty).
Lack of content is by far the biggest detraction to this game.  As you reach a couple hundred villagers, you will start noticing you have more and more idle villagers.  You are no longer having resource issues, in fact you have a stockpile of everything (ie. no need to build more industry).  Unfortunately, there really isn't anything else to do with all the idle villagers you have, and as they add up your happiness level goes down.  So you build businesses you don't need and more and more housing to keep getting bigger.  That is about all there is to do as you get late into the game.  Build towers so there range overlaps, and dragons just die.  All you have left to look forward to are the Viking attacks with crappy mechanics making it more of an annoyance than anything else.  There really need to be more buildings available to soak up the extra villagers without adding to your stockpile of resources!

It's a real time, third person, action role playing game. You control one character throughout the game.
IMO it's not a classic, but it's just as good or better than Dragon Age 2 in terms of creating a believable fantasy setting. There are a lot of missed opportunities from the developers, but it appears to me that it was due to a limited budget, rather than ill intentions. You can spot a lot of love for the fantasy genre if you read between the lines as you play.
The combat starts out being rather boring, but it gets a lot better after you acquire some new abilities.
At the end of the day, I'd give it a high 6 out of 10, quite close to a 7. I'm surprised it seems to have a small fanbase, as it's far from being a bad game. If you can get it for anything below $20, I'd say it's worth it.
It's a shame they didn't put more work into making looting feel better. It just feels anticlimactic to disarm a max level trap to reach a chest that only contains some healing potions. Your gear hardly changes appearance until at the end of the game.
It took me 21 hours to complete and I generally had a good time.

Mirror of Fate is the second of three entries in the Lords of Shadow alternate universe of the long established Castlevania franchise. Even while being a handheld port it performs extremely well in both gameplay, mechanics as well as very responsive controls and it is able to scale up to 4k without looking too shabby.
The game is divided into three different arcs, each ark having another main protagonist of the Belmont family with intersecting story segments and a story told in snips and bits which are going backwards in time like the movie Memento, which is a very nice and interesting tale-telling-mechanic.
As for the gameplay, Mirror of Fate features easy to learn and hard to master controls, a good dozen bossfights, interesting enemy design, great art design, a good soundtrack and a reasonably ok storyline. The game is a tie-in between Lords of Shadow 1 and Lords of Shadow 2 and shines a lot of backstory on the protagonists from the both main games, but it has the same amount of soul and depth and shouldn't be overlooked at all.
All in all, a brilliant combat platformer which deserves a lot more recognition than it got upon release. Do recommend.

I remember buying this awhile ago together with a friend. We were both interested and I went ahead playing it and he asked me to tell him how it was when I finished it. I suppose this review is for you my friend. :)
Now Shantae: Risky's Revenge was my first time ever playing from the series and I knew next to nothing about the game's story. Only the development history. I found the story to be a bit interesting but not a whole lot. The dialogue and the characters however are pretty funny, often making fourth wall jokes and jabbing at one or two video game tropes which I like. It's not the story itself you'll get invested in it's most likely the characters and their interactions you'll enjoy.
Visually I'm a bit stumped. It uses pixel art and it's rather well detailed. This is some danm fine pixel art here. The odd problem I have though is that (and this is probably going to sound like the dumbest thing I've ever said) the colour palette is too strong for my taste. It's really bright and fruity and I don't exactly find that personally appealing though this is more of a personal matter. I'm sure a lot of people will enjoy the look of it. I did but just not entirely. In terms of music it's alright but I've got nothing much to say about it. It's a little on the bland side.
Gameplay wise it's good, it's a metroidvania game so a lot of upgrades, secrets, puzzles and backtracking which I didn't mind too much. Combat is simple and you can use abilities to help you fight but you'll most often then not just keep hitting enemies with Shantae's ridiculously agile hair. The game is actually in 2.5D which is really cool. Even though it's 2D there are muliple layers in an area to explore for goodies. Boss battles range from fun to "how long is she going to take to die?"
I liked Shantae: Risky's Revenge but I didn't really love it or anything. It was a nice trip to ride and it offered a good game to play. Shantae is really cool to play as and her friends and enemies are a really cool bunch to listen to. I don't think I'm planning to get The Pirate's Curse anytime soon or the original for that matter but I'll keep an eye on Half Genie Hero and see how that's going. Risky's Revenge didn't make me a fan but I am interested in the series if you can get my idea (hope so because I don't). This game get's a nice 7/10.

This game has a ton of features! Unfortunately, the average user will have a hard time understanding many of them. The game has a really nice basic tutorial, but it will take a lot of experimentation or reading online to do much else.
Adding a youtube video to a wall is extremely easy, but I really want the video to play automatically when I'm nearby. I'm sure that is possible, somehow, but I couldn't figure it out.
Adding your own mp3 and mp4 files is easy, but I'd really like to play them and have it continue so I can listen as I walk around. I'm sure that is possible, but any sort of option to do it was not very apparent.
I do love how there are a bunch of cool maps you can build on, and a lot of objects and props you can download to help decorate!
Anyway, this game is very promising and has a ton of potential! I don't really want to use it more until a lot of things are made more simplistic and streamlined, but I will definitely be keeping an eye on this as it's developed. I do recommend this game because of the amazing concepts it's trying to deliver, especially if you have the time to figure out all the great features.

Reptilian Rebellion is a pretty straight forward shoot 'em up.  You pick a character based on your playstyle and attempt to thwart a New World Order - or a bunch of reptiles attempting to take over.  You're limited to moving up and down in the center of the screen, shooting attackers from either side.  As you progress, the enemies become more difficult and develop different characteristics - such as shields, shooting back, or becoming faster.  Kill enough and you may just end up on the leaderboard!  Your kills are also carried over in a total reptiles killed counter that goes towards unlocking other characters to use.
Overall the game is pretty fun for what it is and the low price.  I definitely recommend checking it out and having a bit of fun with it.  The only complaint I really have is using the Z key to shoot while using WASD or arrow keys to move.  It feels a bit awkard but isn't a terribly major issue.

I'm a huge fan of games like these where they rely heavily on resource management and strategy. When I saw a likeness being drawn to Banished, which I've put almost 100 hours into, I figured I'd give Kingdoms and Castles a try. While I did mostly enjoy the game, I ended up requesting a refund after about 2 hours because I felt I had already experienced the entirety of the game and my $10 could be better used elsewhere.
There were some frustrating parts where things were constantly catching on fire for no reason, villagers starving with a full granary mere blocks from them, and I was continuously experienced a low frame rate, even for rendering simple graphics on my perfectly capable machine. Compounding those with the lack of content and generally figuring out the game in only a couple of hours just made it lackluster for me and I just didn't see myself picking it back up later on. That said I would recommend this for someone who's looking for a game that's very simple and does not need a lot of energy to be spent on it. I think if the developers spend some time adding substantiative content with some intricacy, it could be a really entertaining game.

I've barely even begun to play this game and I'm already amazed. I didn't realize how badly I wanted to be able to build my own warships until this game first came to my notice and now I'm hooked. The ships handle nicely to the point that my real-world boating experience applies well to in-game vehicles, and real-world naval architecture principles apply to ship construction as well. If you want to build a full-scale working replica of your favorite warship, you can (if you don't have the patience for that, you can use one of the existing in-game models or download a fan-made one. Most popular historic warships, particularly from the WWII era, have already been built for your enjoyment).
On the other hand, if you want to build something completely absurd you can do that too. Make a flying brick that shoots lasers. Make a mothership that shoots missiles that in turn shoot other, smaller missiles. Make a submarine with forceshields. Make a railgun artillery platform in space. Make an motor with more turbochargers than cylinders. Make a steam engine that operates at 300 rpm. Do whatever; this game has all sorts of features and keeps getting more. While this game is still in active development, it's already more stable and feature-complete than most 'finished' games on the market and well worth the money, particularly if you get it on sale. For established fans of voxel-based construction titles this game is a must-have; for everyone else it's at least strongly worth considering.

This game is phenomenal. If you love creating your own, ships, planes or tanks and taking them into satisfying combat where you tear through your opponents machines piece by piece this is a game for you.
You can go into so much detail in your designs, from designing your own misslies to fine tuning how your machine's AI works, to deciding where every inch of reactive or heavy armor goes. I could go on for hours but you get the point. If you want to recreate your favourite military vehicles or fantasy craft this game has pretty much got you covered. The options are immense.
The campaign is addictive, often involving different factions, each with their own strategies and designs. Some have "stiched together" machines that are made up of the hull parts of their foes and others have marauding mobile fortresses for units. How well you survive is all in how good your designs are. Nearly 600 hours into it and I still find myself coming back for more, much less ever completing the campaigns myself, all ways going back into the design mode to whip up another machine to bring into fray heheh...
There is one thing however I hope they improve on. This game has quite a learning curve to overcome. While I think the current tutorials are decent, they can still be improved. I also feel that the build menu interface could also be improved to feel less overwhelming to newcomers. Improving the UI perhaps?
That being said, all in all, this game is still amazing and i have never been able enjoy any other "build em up and shoot em down" game as much as I have enjoyed this one. This game goes further and beyond to offer freedom in creation and in depth gameplay. It thoroughly deserves it's place as one of the best games of it's kind.

It's not your father's Anno 2205... and that will♥♥♥♥♥♥a lot of people off.  Taken away from the serious is a lot of the user unfriendly elements.  Gone are the days of using tables, calculators and chains.  The game is now built in such a way that it will show you exactly how much you need to balance everything off.  It's just a matter of doing it yourself.
Gone are the days of hitting Tier 3 only for all of the AI players to immediately declare war and usurp you with giant barrages of ships.  Now all of the fighting is done on separate combat maps that require little to no investment from your colonies.
Instead you get a game that feels kind of flat by comparison.  But it is also a very very different game than the rest.
You will have three different types of zones (regular, arctic, and moon) in which each place will have resources that the other needs.  Added to the game is a new resource of workers that means you need to maintain actual populations in order to work in buildings.  These buildings will produce all of the resources you need.
There is no more building ships in the game.  Instead you have to choose between three crafts for each trade route of increasing size and organize your routes from here.
Also gone from the game are items and the ARK.  This is a very large hit on the game.  However it also makes the game balance more likable.  Without requiring to have 30% speed on all transport ships they will just have that 30% from the start.
The game has simply become one of managing various resources, populations and needs.  It's not a terrible game, but it is most certainly a very different game that will scare away any of the faithful who enjoyed the Anno series.
It is most certainly not Anno and probably should have not been named as such.

As of writing this, I think there's over 700 achievements, and you NEED to buy DLC to get them all, because a vast majority of them are finishing puzzles and entire puzzle packs. On an interesting note, if you bought any of the stand alone pixel puzzles games, you already have all of those puzzles in this game free, and they are slightly different because they have different amounts of pieces and possibly different shaped pieces.
Just due to the amount of DLC and the cost of the DLC, I don't think I can recommend this game, unless you don't care about earning achievements, or you really, really, REALLY love puzzles.

I beat the game in 7 hours and I really enjoyed it. I played the original Shantae, so I knew what to expect with this game. It's very similar, but greatly improved. This was originally a Nintendo DSi game, so the game isn't huge. The pixel art was also meant for a small screen, so I recommend playing in a small window.
I really like the characters. They are well designed and have funny dialogue. This includes the NPCs as well. Each stage is visually pleasing with good pixel graphics and an awesome soundtrack to go with them.  The game also provides a pretty good challenge during some parts, and is a bit easier during others. The platforming is a mix of easy and tricky, and the controls are really responsive.
I do wish the game was a bit longer. I felt like most of my time was spent running through stages I've already been before, even though they give you reasons to go back to them. I think if the world was slightly bigger, it would have not felt as repetitive. There are some stages that lack creativity as well. For example, some stages are just black rooms that are supposed to be dark, and you navigate blindly through them. The overall story was also a bit bland, but acceptable.
Overall, it's a pretty good Metroidvania style platformer. I can't say it's the best one I've played, but definitely worth buying if you can catch it on sale. I think $10 is acceptable too if you are really looking for a game to play in this genre. I will definitely be playing this again since it has a NG+ mode and would also be fun to try and speed run!

Overall, I give it an 8/10.
TL;DR
If you enjoyed Banished, but wanted to see your village/city/metropolis get burned to the ground by Dragons, Ogres, and Vikings, you will enjoy this game.
Long Explanation
It difficult in it's simplicity however. There is not nearly as much data to use to optimize your settlement. Unlike Banished, there are no charts or diagrams for optimal distance from home to field, or most efficient orchard size, mostly because there isn't anything optimal. If villagers are hungry, and there is food in their home, they won't starve, no freezing to death because your worker will not stop cutting down trees and go home, or harvests not being taken in because they live too far away.
You cannot micromanage your villagers lives, or the priority of what buildings to build or crew first, and as such, you will be rather frustrated when your villagers get sick because there were no doctors in the hospital you jut completed, or foresters to work in the tree nursery you just rebuilt after a dragon died, and landed on it, crushing it.
This is my biggest concern with this game. I hope that the developers have some citizen task manager in mind, as that would, in my opinion, complete the game.
Yes the Vikings take weird paths around your walls, yes they do manage to swim through moats, and around walls, or attack from unplanned sides (Which I like, as frustrating as it is. Real vikings wouldn't run straight at a heavily fortified wall.)
Yes there is nothing that tells you what you are doing, or if you are doing it right, or what things mean, or do (I still don't know what giving money to the church does...)
But, overall, this is a wonderfully cute city manager game that does enforce a desire to balance defense and production. It's good for when you don't really want to think about what you are doing, or just want to piddle around without thinking about how the next 20 years depend on where you place your well.

First of all:
I have played 10 hours until this review and tried 3 cities on hard.
If I can recommand this title? It depends strongly on what you expect.
If you expect a full price title like settlers or something like that, please don't buy this game. It will not make you happy.
If you expect some casual gaming title, then it could be right for you.
It is a very basic game, which will allow you to run a decent city with some (or none, if on easy diffuclty) threads. Named they are: Dragons, which try to burn your city and vikings which try to steal your gold, food and people. Oh, they also burn your city. And last, but not least there are heavy thunderstorms, which will also burn your city.
The world itself is not very huge, but it will keep you going for some time. So i would expect around 20 hours of gameplay, until the world is completely full. I would like to compare this to some Tropico titles.
Although you have to experience one major issue with this game.
Within the version, i have written this review (104s) there is no multi-threading. The game does not scale towards other CPU cores, which will get worse the more people you have. On my machine the limit was around ~300 people. If you hit this spot, then the game will slow you down very much. I expect the developer to fix that in future patches.

This is a review from an old player form Anno 2070, the judgement is heavily based on the previous game.
Pros:
- Simplified Production: Now everything is descripted in production rate, so we don't have to look up the wiki to find out the optimal ratio of resource/production.
- No threat around your city: As for the time I was playing, there are no enemies popping up near your territory. While some may consider this as a bad thing, I'm the kind of player that always make peace with everyone on the map anyway.
- Good tool and UI: Building moving and mass building by click-and-drag are long awaited feature. UI is simple, friendly, and clean.
Cons:
- Too few game mode: Only one career mode is available for now, though it contains all this game is to offer.
- Lack of vehicle customization: You can upgrade your ships, but not like in previous games when you can apply different items and modules to them. No research to enhance them either.
- Trading Route inefficiency: Now you can only send one ware at a time and pay hefty toll for it. I really like the trading mechanism back then, which you can prepare your own ship and freely trading around. Though managing route is one of the main chanllenge in this game.
Conclusion:
This is a bold move for a long lived series like Anno. They planted a lot of new mechanism to this game while some concept may still in its infant I think, but I look forward to the future of them. Blue Byte is always one of my most respected teams, and I trust them can make another peak of this series.
TL:DR
Recommended: A great game for newcomers and STG lovers with much detail, but not so similar to the old Anno. Consider it as a new game, not a remake.

Loved the lunar and artic settings which combined for a great global style game. Graphics were good and overall seemed a decent upgrade on the Anno series. The addition of heat zones in the artic region was also a new twist that I enjoyed creatively solving (just like the lunar shields). Modules to expand existing buildings were also cool, much better than blindly making a carbon copy new building each time. Increasing immersion was the parallel running of all the zones since it simulates how it would really work. Finally, auto game save/sync worked flawlessly for me.
However I feel there is also a lot wrong with this game.
1. I liked the AI as the enemy in Anno 2070 as I feel it helped build and round out the story. In 2205 the terrorists (wow original) are forgettable, literally ignorable, and seem to break the story immersion more than than help it.
2. There are a ton of zones but pretty much all are useless. Sure I bought them all from competitors but I never needed more than my original three zone plus one temperate zone in order to max everything out. Also the zone swap load time is an annoyance, entirely too long even on a SSD and high end computer.
3. Transport routes are ridiculous as well. Easy to set up but having to set up a new route for every little thing was a HUGE pain. Especially when my route list got to the point it required scrolling (again that was only 4 zones, not even half the ones possible). I much preferred the 2070 method where you could mix and match on a single transport. Making this far more absurd is that you get 'magic' transport size in 2205 anyway where the amount you can transport automatically increases and you just pay more credits. With that being the case why limit one transport to one item?
4. Building modules while an awesome thing were also problematic in that they only fit 'right' in about half the building types. Some of them would fit like perfect puzzles in a couple different ways while others were so far out in left field I wondered if maybe they had one designer on the core building and another on just the modules.
5. Uplay required and Uplay sucks. Ok it has improved but who uses it because they want to?
6. DLC also sucks.
All in all it was an OK game but far more negatives than positives in my opinion. If you loved 2070 you will like this game even if you might not love it. Worth buying ONLY on a significant Steam sale.

If you really think about it, this is pretty much the Dark Souls of Dark Fantasy games. I mean, the game basically has the subtle background to the world, the exploration, the vague choices and actions which impact side characters down the line. But most of all it's hard so it has to be like Dark Souls.
More seriously, the game is impressive. The inconnectivity of this open world open finding new areas is masterfully done, a concept which isnt really done well if at all in most other games. The difficulty can be a bit cheesy at times, dying to something you really didnt have any indicator to, but once you die you know exactly what to do next time. The progression in this game often forces you to learn on the fly, adapt, or learn the hard way, and that aspect feels so very satisfying when you finally succeed. Try this game, the subtle strengths of it have influences many other games and is a testement to what good game design is supposed to be.

Action-RPG done right.
Usually the term action-rpg just means "action", but every now and again a developer gets it right. Demonicon may be a bit rough around the edges, particularly regarding dialog continuity and the occasional frustrating camera angle, but the core gameplay is a spot on mixture of live action combat and rewarding character progression. Real time hack-n-slash that also gives a moderate amount of actual character customization, with upgrade paths not just for spells and combat moves, but general stats, haggling, crafting, perception checks, lock picking, and more. Plus, each zone allows for some freedom of exploration rather than forcing you down the linear path right away. Combine this with a decent story, and the game actually feels like it is taking the RPG half of "action-RPG" seriously.
If you liked The Witcher II, you will like Demonicon.
The game is a bit short though where the campaign should take around 20 hours, so try and get it on sale.

Short Version:
Growing up with RPG's since the late 80's and having played a vast array of them, I can easily say that Dark Souls is the pinnacle of the dungeon crawler RPG in my gaming history.
Long Version:
Story:
The story is vast and requires some researching or a very attentive mind. There are endless connections that one can make as to what is actually going on in this forsaken world throughout the trilogy. With lore hidden in item descriptions, bosses and locations, its going to take effort from the player to unravel this tale and it's not a happy one. If you're looking for green fields, flowers and happy endings, go jerk off in your local park and give this game a skip.
Enemies:
Unique enemies that act like they're straight out of a DnD master's handbook (If you think you can kill skeletons with any weapon, think again). The fighting isn't for the bubblegum chewing generation. Think you can run in and just spam the attack button? Try it! You'll soon have your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you on a silver platter. The enemies have depth with lots of them having up to 8 different attack patterns that you need to learn and read during combat. And let's not talk about the bosses. As per the title, you will die... a... lot! Yeah sure, if you want to spoil the experience and be a wussy, you can go watch YouTube videos on the best tactics etc. But, then you're missing the point of the game's combat system and that's to figure it out, observe and learn from your mistakes. Success through failure.
Gear:
The look and feel of the gear is top-notch. One thing worth noting here is that your gear actually affect your player. Want to carry a full plate with a two-handed greatsword? Your character will be as slow as hell unless you have insane high points in the required stat. This is a good example of realism. But, you can make countless combinations to balance your character out. Love big weapons but want to maintain speed? Switch out the full-plate for light armor or even go full "commando". The options are endless and the mechanics have some serious depth. It doesn't take long to realise that it's a well thought-out system.
Character Progression:
Another very unique mechanic here as if the game isn't punishing enough. Your primary resource is "Souls". Souls are acquired from killing enemies or can be picked up throughout the game world. But get ready for this - Souls are both the "experience" to progress your character and your primary "money" in the game to buy/repair items. Yes you read that right. It gets worse. When you die (no ifs), you drop all your current souls at the location of your death and the world is regenerated. You now have to fight your way back to the location of your death to reclaim your souls. There is a big problem here if you die again before reclaiming your souls...
Game World:
The game world is medieval-fantasy at its finest. Massive areas all interconnected and no loading screens once you're in. Castles, towns, forests, rivers, mountains, caves, dungeons, damns, catacombs - this game has it all and in style. The atmosphere is great for a dark fantasy setting.
--
That concludes my review. I can babble on for hours but I've covered what I feel is the most important aspects of RPG games. Like it, dislike it - no one really cares in death.
