I'm writing this review based on Normal mode in story, as I have yet to play the challenge mode (looking forward to it) or story hard mode. Though I have played a large number of these games, so I'm comparing to what I've experienced but don't take my word as fact as I am human and I am biased in some aspects.
TL;DR at the bottom, because I'm long winded.
The game itself is a simple game creation simulator where you hire people then specialise them into either Code, Art, Sound or Writing and get them to make games for you. The workers gain experience and get better at their jobs, to a point, and eventually this allows you to move into bigger studios and make bigger games. Until you complete everything there is to do and then you pretty much unlock free mode.
My first opinion of the game was that it was simple, this is by no means a negative, a bit of a half and half at times though. It gives the game it's own place within a genre of games that is full of innovative ideas and different ways of doing things. I would, from what I've experienced, call this game an intro into Management Simulation games. I say this because It's not a hard game to learn or master (In my opinion) and I found myself breezing through the game in 3 hours without even a hitch in the money department. But people that are newer to this genre would find this game to have a very plesent learning curve.
It doesn't have the thing a lot of other similar games have where genres are locked off until you research them or a job tree for workers to evolve within. Which was nice to me, I usually find those sorts of activities tend to bore me as they can take a long time to do or reduce the quality of your games until things get back on track. In Game Corp DX you'll have all the Genres unlocked for you instantly (I don't know why some games have you research them for months in the first place) and your workers will take the specialistation you give them and stick with it (unless you want to change them later).
The music isn't bad, though it's repetiveness could get annoying to some though but I found it plesent. No sound errors or noises that were unecessarily loud too which is a plus.
Only things i found that could be looked at in a very slightly negative way is the difficulity level, though I said above I played only on Normal and have yet to look at the challenge and hard modes to get a comparison. The achievements also weren't very hard to get but as I played on normal, that had a hand in it.
For cons I found the bar at the top to be too small, I could read it, but at times it was difficult. The rooms are very small with not much room to do things, half the time you'll spend playing will be organising the furniture to fit everything in. Not a big variety in the objects to put in, decorations especially.
----Bug/Glitch----
Only Bug I found was a progress bug, and though annoying it's exploitable from what I could see. I finished all the storyline quests, closed the game and re-opened it to see if it saved it, it did but it reset all the story quests and their rewards. I'm not sure if this always happens or if it was just because I finished everything in one sitting but it happened.
-------------------
Overall, I'm glad to have played Game Corp DX, it is a good game for the price that's being asked and it's simple enough to just sit down and go for people who are experienced right down to people who are brand new to the genre.
------TL;DR------
Pros+
- Easy to pick up and play
- Simple for beginners
- Not a bad price tag for what it delivers
Pros with a little Con, or Cons with a little Pro
- Music was nice, though some people won't like the repetivness of it
- Art was simple but some people have a problem with simple art
- Progress bug but it's exploitable for the benefit of the player (money)
- Not very long if you know what you're doing
Cons
- Can be boring for those who ae used to all the things other, bigger games do
- Small top HUD bar
- Small rooms/Hard to fit everything at times
- Not many decoration options
Overview
- Updates will improve this immensly
- If you're on the fence about buying it, it's not much and it's a fun game to play, so buy it :P

The Metroid Fusion of Castlevania games. If you are looking for a fully metroidvania experience, this is not it. However, this game does have metroidvania elements and is enough to scratch the itch if you've run out of other options.
The reason I say this game is like Metroid Fusion is because it is much more linear than other games in the series. You are given objectives on the map screen and your goal is to reach them. This is in contrast to other games where you are basically set free and must figure out where to go on your own. The game is more about exploration than combat. Your secondary goal, along with reaching the objective, is filling out the map and thus collecting power ups in the form of extra HP, magic, experience, and ammunition.
The game is paced well, split into 3 acts, each one with a different playable character. Each of the acts is then further split into 3 "sub-acts". The first part involves starting out with the character and exploring while collecting powerups that let you access the next objective. The second part (usually signalled by finding a teleporter) involves using all of those powerups to backtrack and reach all the places that were previously inaccesible. The final part is basically just finishing up the final few objectives of the act.
Each character has the same basic combat abilities with the whip, but each differs in which sub-weapons they use and which magic abilities they have. Combat feels ok, not great. It's not the main focus of the game so it's not a huge deal. You have two main method of attack with the whip: horizontal strikes (more damage) and vertical strikes (cover more area). You can attack in the air as well, and you unlock new moves as you level up that can be performed with specific inputs. Most of them are useful in at least some situations. There is a good variety of moves and I never really felt like I didn't have enough tools to deal with any given combat situation, especially after you factor in sub-weapons and magic.
My problem with the combat is that the characters control a big too sluggishly for my tastes. The jump arc is slow and floaty, you are not free to pass through enemies with a dodge roll, and there is considerable ending lag on basically every move. This can make it hard to reach the end of your combos, especially against aggressive bosses, and it doesn't feel like you are reaching your full potential during these fights. In addition, some enemies are not stunned by your attacks, basically forcing you to stop so that you can dodge whatever they are going to throw at you. While this is not inherently bad, it makes you feel like your attacks have no impact. Some enemies like to hold their guard up, and while the game gives you a guard break move, it's extremely slow and short range. Most of the time the enemy has already dropped its guard and hit you by the time you get to run up to them and start your attack.
Overall I wish your character operated more quickly and had better movement options. However, combat is not the focus of the game and you will spend the majority of your time solving puzzles and trying to fiure out how to platform your way to the hidden areas. The level are well designed and you will pretty much always find something if you stray from the beaten path.
Overall a solid game. Nothing groundbreaking, but a satisfying experience. Not a true Metroidvania, but close. Game performs well, there are no glaring issues, and the level design is good. The game is fairly short though, probably 10-12 hours depending on how thorough you choose to be. Good game to get on sale, though if you really like Castlevania the full price isn't exorbitant for a game like this.

I guess I should begin by saying that I've not played Lords of Shadow yet, and went into this game looking for a Metroidvania experience. If you're like me, I suppose you will be disappointed.
The story is divided in 3 acts where you play as different characters in different (or changed from the previous chapter) maps. I suppose I can't say much about the story. I found it to be quite bland, but maybe it's better if you have more context.
Still, no matter the context, your suspension of disbelief is going to be thrown out of the window with the fact that first 2 acts have different room layouts and secrets, despite the fact that they take place at the exact same time. Main characters of first two acts meet several times, yet some of the rooms you visit in both acts are changed. Terrace is a room you visit in both acts after theatre, a place where characters meet up, yet in one act it's a featureless room, and in another it's a boss fight that wrecks the place. It would be cool to see actions of one character affect other's path, yet it's only present for cutscenes. I don't get how I'm supposed to take this story seriously when it tries to do non-linear storytelling, and immediately backs down on it.
Characters retain most of their their abilities from one to another, which is good, but inability to go further than few rooms back really hurts this game. You only have so many rooms to explore with only 2-3 powerups to find in a given chapter. Essentially you're not playing one metroidvania game, but several small ones.
Exploration is weak, and all of the secrets are completely obvious. I really don't get why game has a guide, note system, map markers, and secret counter for each room.
The map is pretty linear aside from a few shortcuts. Frankly, maps are small enough that I can understand that decision, but it still leaves a bad taste in my mouth. It might not be a small castle, but it sure feels like one.
The pickups are pathetic. Most of them are bestiary pages and random notes from dead soldiers that give you exp. Lore isn't really that interesting, and aside from that, you only get chests with small boosts to your hp, mp or ammo. Again, pretty much all of them are in plain sight. I once found a secret which I thought was not documented on the secret counter, and it just turned out ot be a useless story item for later. I'm not a big fan of incredibly weird obtuce secrets, but isn't that, along with optional goodies, pretty much the point of the genre? Instead, this game is closer to original Castlevania games for NES and SNES in terms of room layout, it just sometimes asks you to go few rooms back.
Compared to 2D Vanias, however, platforming feels way sloppier. It's alright, and it's not the worst, but it's no Symphony or GBA/DS games, where characters, for the most part, felt just right. You're not gonna be annoyed with stairs that cripple your abilities, but you're also not going to have a blast.
The level design is mostly boring. Good thing game's quite pretty and changes its enviroments often, so at least you're not stuck looking at hundreds of similar traps in the same rooms.
Combat is what you'd expect from a modern action game, but it's not very spectacular. The bosses are pretty cool aside from few places where game wrestles away the controls for another QTE. Thankfully that doesn't happen too often.
I've played this game on hard difficulty and bosses provided a pretty good challenge similar to other Castlevania games.
As opposed to other Castlevania games, where you have a lot of sub-weapons to choose from, usually with different forms, each one of the characters in this game gets only two. If in other games figuring out the right approach was part of the fun, here your choice is not only limited, but your subweapons barely work on bosses, if at all. I really can't believe they managed to dumb down this system to the point where it's worse than even the NES games.
Since all characters use the same weapon as their main way of attacking, this makes combat quite dull. Thankfully your subweapons work good on normal enemies, which means you can at least run past them quickly if you have enough ammo.
The music... I think this game has that, yeah.
Alright, I'm kidding. Given the style, I did expect the music to be a bit more subtle than loud, energetic themes of the old castles. Still, I think it's fair to compare games in one series. Even when music picks up it's mostly forgettable. I might be a sucker for bleeps and bloops in my games, but I doubt anyone will enjoy music from this game as much as classic Castlevania tunes.
Unfortunately, this game is not better than sum of its parts. It's pretty to look at, but it's one of the worst Metroidvania games I've played. I wanted to love this game, but all it did is made me want to play a better Castlevania game. It's bland, doesn't provide enough satisfaction from exploring the castle, and it's not the most technical, nor the prettiest action game there is. There are a few parts that are enjoyable, but most of the time you'll be running through hallways with samey enemies. Still, it is not a bad game, just very mediocre. It's playable and might scratch your Castlevania itch til Bloodstained or some other Metroidvanias come out.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge - Director's Cut is a game released in 2010 for the Nintendo DS, re-released in 2013 for the iPhone and ported from iPhone for PC and it's a sequel for a Game Boy Color game released in 2002 called just Shantae.
If you don't know, here's some SPOILERS for you!
In the first Shantae, you battle against a pirate called Risky Boots, she was trying to take control of Sequin Land, but, as it's supposed to, the hero appears! It's a genie, actually, a HALF-GENIE called Shantae, and she was going to destroy Risky's plans. After lots of Dungeons and new powers and Transformation Dances to solve Puzzles, she managed to stop Risky Boots for good.
Now, almost a decade later, Shantae has to go to her uncle's workshop to see what he found on a trip, he start talking about his Indiana Jones-Like Adventures until something stops him, a weird noise coming from above, it's Risky Boots and she's back for her revenge against Shantae by stealing the Magic Lamp that Shantae's Uncle found, after a battle with Risky, the Mayor appears to say that Shantae is not the Guardian Genie of Sequin Land from now on. And so, the game truly begins!
Shantae has the quest of finding Three Magic Seals hidden in 2 Dungeons and 1 Challenge Tower. In each of the Dungeons, Shantae gains one of three new powers, Elephant, Monkey and Mermaid. Also, each time you get a seal, Risky appears trying to take the seals. Don't forget to do twice the Challenge Tower for a secret in the 2nd time. After this, Shantae returns home to discover that Uncle got kidnapped, but since she didn't know where he was, she needed help, that's where Squid Baron comes in. after he explodes in a Stage Clear Sequence (Shantae asks what happened, he said for her to not blame him for putting up a fight) he says he saw who kidnapped Her Uncle, but he needed help, so, yeah, help him, it's not like you have a choice, it's for more fun! After finding 3 Squid Baby, Squid Baron says Rottytops kidnapped Shantae's Uncle and it was in Risky's Hideout. After a Rayman Origins/Any 2D Shooters-Like sequence, you go through the Final (4th,3rd if you don't consider Challenge Tower a Dungeon) Dungeon of the game and battles the Final Boss! But Risky steals Shantae's powers by using the Magic Lamp and creating Nega-Shantae. As it's supposed to, Shantae wins and returns home without powers because she destroyed Nega-Shantae, she returns as the Guardian Genie of Sequin Land and everyone is happy again! Maybe not, but who knows at this point? You'll have to play Shantae and the Pirate's Curse to know! And replay this with the Magic Mode, makes the game harder and has a different outfit.

I cant take the taste ,which I used to take in 2070, from ANNO 2205 . I always feels lack of something. I can't find out what it is, but I feel it anyway. Also consumption of goods are not logical as much as Anno 2070. Also, the quest system in ANNO 2205 makes me feel like being in a cave. The game has very good grafic details. But that is all that I can say good thing about ANNO 2205. it is completely disappointment for me.

Now, take what I say with a grain of salt, as I have only sunk in 4 1/2 hours of time into Anno 2205 at this moment in time.
In the short amount of time I have played this game, I must admit that I have been thoroughly enjoying it. There is a decent variety of buildings to create, resources to farm, and plenty of things to do. With that being said, I feel as if something is missing. I can't seem to put my foot on it, but there is certainly a lack of something. Granted, I did play the previous Annos, and there was diplomacy, ground combat, trade routes, et cetera et cetera....but, I am speaking of this game in itself, NOT comparing it to it's predecessors. This game, within itself, is lacking content. There is no denying that. However, this game is, without a doubt, a good game nonetheless. I enjoy it, and I can be rather choosy with my games. Anyways, I hope that was coherent enough to stomach. Here is my tl;dr:
Pros:
- has good, quality content (where content can be found)
- the visuals are absolutely incredible - seriously.
- the ambient life added to cities is truly refreshing. From the mechs on the loading dock to the snow mobiles in the arctic, I keep on getting surprised by the little "hidden" details
- I have experienced no bugs what-so-ever in my time playing
- The game runs pretty smooth on my machine - granted, my machine is packing a gtx 970, 32gbs of ram, intel Core i7-4790k quad, eh you get the point. With this set up, the frame rate seems to drop in cutscenes. Not sure if that is my computers fault, or the games.
- the variety of locations, flora, environments, etc is a nice touch. I rather enjoy the arctic, as you must face the difficulties of keeping your workers warm.
Cons:
- This game lacks extensive content. What you see is what you get. Nothing more, nothing less.
- You will be dissapointed with this game if you compare it to the previous installments (do not make that mistake)
- I'm a war monger. I find the combat very stale. I wish there was more combat variety. Yes, it's the future, but this doesn't mean that ground combat wouldn't exist.
- I feel rather alone in the world. In your colony/city mode, there are no neighboring nations. Just you and a bunch of unclaimed plots of land.
tl;dr:
I recomment this game to newcommers to the series, and to people who are willing to overlook the lack of content, and feel satisfied with the very in-detail, hidden jems within.

Beeing an old school gamer of the era of C64 and the awesome Amiga 500, i have seen many, maaaany games.
I remember it was an rainy monday, having holiday for a week, i was looking in the List of Mondays Sales of the week.
Looking and looking i saw that file. Cheesy Gunner. Okay i was sleepy, so ... sorry for reading wrong.
Yes, that name reminds me of the old era and i had a look at it.
Believe me, it WAS love at first sight because the Gunner looks so awesome. Great Design.
So i paid, was it 0,50 Cent, something like that and that was the beginning of a REALLY addicted friendship.
Starting with the game, okay using mouse and keys, i was suprised how easily it was to get into the gameplay.
Driving the Gunner with the keys in all directions, aiming and firing at the targets with the mouse in all directions at the same time. No limits, except the low weapons at the beginning. But hey the Cheesy  .... ehm ... Sweezy Gunner can be upgraded and that must be earned. Believe me, the Gunner has some nice weapons that will bring fun, but it has no no no Kitty Bombs. *sniff*
So you start at your ship and go from one part of the card to another. Fire all that moves, because if it moves it can hurt you. Baaaadly. You know what? This game reminds me, from the style and mechanics of the good old Super Nintendo Zelda. Go from card to card, rise up, get more hearts and defeat one Big (And i mean REALLY BIG) Boss after another, getting also cool upgrades, to reach places from before, that were blocked with some kind of walls or other obstacles.
Well, your Gunner is not a smart guy with a sword and a shield. This one goes by 2 great wheels, a plated body and a biiiig gun.
Sweezy Gunner is a great Bullet Hell game, with a very nice rising of the difficulty level. This Game is fair ... well at one point not, but that is my opinion, i tell you at the end. Where was i ... ah yes, this game is fair und gives you a lot of fun. All you have to do is to pay simple 3.99 cent (Or less, look at sales).
I played so many games, that are more expensive and so many dind`t gave me the fun that Che... Sweezy Gunner gave me. I remember how i was addicted to get all the achievements, to rise the Gunner and to reach the next boss.
Yes i got through i got all the achievements and was happy .... but stop!
Looking at the achievements i saw 4 new achievements. Challenge achievements. Okay, i said. Doing it, earning it, getting! You thought so. These Challenging Levels are hard as hell. And now i get my opinion from before, you remember my words. Fairness? Woah that Levels are, in my opinion, so unfair, but they can be done. Looking at global Achievements, they can be really done, but the danger of a rage quitt is really high.
So i`m still sad, not to have that awesome game in my 100% List....

At the time of this posting, Orcs Must Die 2 is 90% off; That's less than $2!
Orcs Must Die 2 is a tower defence game that puts equal emphasis on the player and the traps he/she places, as in one cannot win without the other on the harder difficulties. You can choose the 4-8 traps, weapons, and utilities you use at the beginning of each round, and upgrade them too. The upgrade system allows you to choose one of two unique stat buffs / extra abilities, and gives an additional aspect to modify your items each round. There is a lot of clicking involved for some personal items (especially the sorceress's Staff of Domination). Co-op is also an aspect which, in my opinion, enhances the experience to a degree; However, the game can be completed entirely alone.
The OST is most noticable during the beginning of the waves, and the last wave, where it conveys the chaos taking place when the late-game waves start throwing hundreds of orcs, imps, golems and trolls at you. Orcs Must Die 2 definately has some charm to it's presentation.
Overall, I think it's a no brainer to pick it up on sale, as it provided me with a good 20 or so hours of fun (though I did not complete all DLC maps)

text:
You see those screenshots up there? Next to the description of the game? Take a look at that last one, pay close attention to it. Take in every detail, every aspect, of that screenshot.
THAT'S NOT EVEN IN THE MOD.
The problem with Half-Life: Before is that it's just too short. FAR too short. As in "I finished the game before I finished my drink" short. As far as I can remember, there is only ONE level change in the entire game, and that level change is only there to trap the player in the (frankly terrible) boss fight. Worse still, barring the aforementioned boss fight, you literally have to do a u-turn and retrace your steps ALL THE WAY TO THE STARTING POINT.
The story of the game is also quite poorly thought out, as little as there is, which makes the whole thing seem like just an extra level that was cut from the original game. Despite the steam page stating that "You're playing as a Black Mesa scientist Andrew Winner.", this is NEVER brought up in-game, and you could just as easily be Lord-High Sherrif Mafia-Don Charlie McFidget Pickle-Eyes VII and it would make NO difference whatsoever. Also, you never have to "enter another world to find an artifact", unless the developers consider "another world" to be the tiny, enclosed cargo deck of a ship.
This feels like a demo - a tech demo, even - for something bigger that was never quite finished. While HL:B has polish, there's a difference between polishing a gigantic statue and polishing a tiny fork.

The very first Dark Souls is a challenge in itself, daring you to adapt to the gameplay in the most punishing way. By dying over and over again, the game teaches you on how to approach enemies or how to fight and overcome even the hardest bosses. The world is semi open, with a lot of different paths to choose from. You can tell if one way is not meant to be walked at a certain time, because all the enemies and the level design will kill you faster than you can even react.
By interconnecting the different areas by shortcuts, ladders, doors, etc. you'll get a real sense of orientation in a game where nothing helps you to find your way. At the start, you'll only get pieces of information. Ring the bells of Awakening. One up above, one far below. That's it, the way to these bells is yours to find.
Some complain that the Dark Souls games are too hard, but this game trusts you to figure out it's mechanics and how the game works, and that's excecuted masterully here.
If you didn't get the chance to try this rare gem of gaming, now's your time.

The graphics are very dated, and it can be pretty clunky at times, so if you're expecting a super polished, streamlined experience then this probably isn't for you. The story is quite good, though, and the voice acting is acceptable to good for the most part. Very few technical issues, only the occasional stutter or sound effect that was too loud. If you have a soft spot for rusty european RPGs, or any of Cyanide Studio's games (Of Orcs and Men, Game of Thrones), you should give this a go.

Absolutely loved this game.  I'd give it a 9/10.  The only reasons it isn't a 10:
* It's just SLIGHTLY more linear feeling than a metroidvania game should be, but at the same time, it also feels like a throwback to the even older Castlevanias than the famous Symphony of the Night in that respect, but with a very solid modern twist on combat (combos, block, dodge, etc)
* While combat is tight and responsive, the platforming could be just a bit more polished and responsive.  It's actually almost easier than it should be because you kind of "snap" to ledges and grapple points easier than you should.  While that's not necessarily a bad thing, something about it just feels ever so slightly clunky and deceptive.
You'll note that those two cons I've listed also come with disclaimers to discuss the good and not so bad things about said cons, because this game is overall AWESOME.  It's hard as hell for any Castlevania or metroidvania title in general to live up to the feeling that Symphony of the Night first had for us all, but this is absolutely an excellent and high quality addition to the side-scrolling Castlevania franchise.  Let's not forget that WE'RE PLAYING A SIDE-SCROLLING CASTLEVANIA ON PC.

Let me start off by saying that I think this game is a lot of fun! However, because of the latest changes it's lost one of the great appeals it had for me, and I myself will not be playing the game again, which is a real shame.
However, I'll still recommend it for what it is now - a building and combat simulator. It does this really well, but unfortunately due to some of the latest updates, that's all it's become.
There used to be things like resource management, fuel management, rarer materials which forced you to build with weaker materials until you could secure better materials, but apparently people whined about not being able to build their huge massive holy crap ships from the word go, heaven forbid, which ate up much of their metal, and so the developer merged all resources into one. Instead of planning how to secure the materials you need/want to build the ships you want and taking over territories based on this - it's now a game of kill everything and do it however you want in any order because it doesn't matter anymore.
For example - there used to be fuel, ammo, along with metal, wood, and crystal. This in itself seemed perfectly fine - crystal being a rarer material and more difficult to secure. Fuel and Ammo being separated so if you didn't produce enough of either, you're in trouble. Now, there's no more production of ammo or fuel. All is a single resource, and the whole game is focused around combat alone.
Gone are the days of securing resource sites that had stronger resources of metal or crystal to up your supply. That strategic element is gone. Gone are the days of saving up and building smartly with the materials you have available to overcome your enemies. With but one resource, a whole section of the game has been over simplified and it's lost a huge appeal because of it, at least for me. The complexity and planning was one of the things I loved most about it.
For many people this is will be a big deal. I told my friend about it and he's agreed - he no longer wants to play simply based on this change alone. We both feel the game is now easy mode. Combat, nothing more.
However, it does combat really well. There's great complexity and depth with the ship building itself, even if there's really no point in having materials at all anymore. I'm not entirely sure why the developer even has resources at this point. I do however still recommend the game for the combat alone, even if that's not enough to keep me playing it.

A simple but satisfying medieval city management game, with viking and dragon attacks spicing up the usual formula. The game just has enough 'bite' in it to be a satisfying city sim, but the resources and mechanics are easy enough to learn after an hour or two of play. I only had to consult the wiki/discussion boards a handful of times, which is a big thing when compared to other insanely complex city sims.
It is not, however, fully polished despite being commercially released. AI pathfinding is a problem (with villagers starving right in front of a full granary), while some key features require fixing and balancing (ballistas can't hit anything at range, soldiers are ineffective.) Frame rate also starts bogging down once you hit 1,000 villagers, with the game slowing down to a snail's pace once you hit 2k population and fill the map with buildings.
Still, Kingdoms and Castles is a strong recommendation for fans and newcomers of the genre alike. Simple enough to pick up the basics in an hour, complex enough to keep you engaged for a dozen or more. Cheap, too, which always helps.

How long do you need to play a game before you decide you don’t like it? How many minutes are required before you say to yourself “Well, that was ten bucks wasted, thanks for nothing Steam’s Refund Policy.”
For me and Shantae: Risky’s Revenge the answer is “about an hour.”
I’ve always wanted to play a Shantae game. The moment I saw the first one I thought it looked amazing. And it does, it totally does. The graphics, by Henk Nieborg, are lush and gorgeous and detailed in ways that few other pixel artists can approach. It’s a very beautiful game.
But these graphics hide a horrible secret: the simple, tragic truth is that the guys responsible for creating the game itself had nothing to say. They had no interesting ideas, and based on the dumbass errors they made along the way, I don’t think they’ve been paying attention to games for at least a decade, possibly since 16 bits was a lot.
I don’t like the level design. Long horizontal strips with jump pads for moving into and out of the screen must have been amazing on the 3DS, but here it's just a lot of parallax that serves only to create confusing, maze-like levels.  And at the edges of these horizontal strips are, sometimes, exits to the next horizontal strip.  There's no visible indicator, so you have to walk all the way to the end to see if you can go through it or not.  And if you're not paying very close attention, you'll walk all the way over there again and again as the similar-looking strips start to blur together and you just want to find the freaking exit and get on with it.
When the levels aren't annoyingly 3D they're almost totally linear, and somehow even this is annoying.  There are destructible blocks that look the same as indestructible blocks, except that the ones you can destroy are between you and the next place you need to go.  If it's not between you and something else, it's probably not something you can clear away.  There's no way to tell until you try, of course, the game hates you.
There are a lot of level elements that look like they should be platforms but they’re not, or they’re part of the level behind the one you’re on. It’s not at all obvious where you can and can’t go. A platform game that can’t make this clear has suffered a critical failure very early.
The game just isn’t fun. Shantae’s attacks take just that split second too long, and there’s a separate button for clearing a dialogue box instead of just using one of the existing buttons like every other game ever and I just can’t get used to it.
It feels like the best artists in the world got together with talented designers and made amazing things but then, when it came to making a game that made sense, that was tight and fun and exciting and new, they just had nothing to say. They had run dry, they weren’t the guys who knew how to game, they were artists, the best of the best, and that’s just not enough.
Looks great though.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge is the sequel to the original GBC game by WayForward. Having not played the original game, I was still able to enjoy everything this game had to offer.
Story: Shantae, our Half-Genie Hero, is still the guardian of Scuttle Town, but one day, Risky Boots steals a magical lamp that has unknown properties to our hero, but since Risky took it and attacked Shantae for going after her, it could only mean bad news for Shantae and Scuttle Town. After being fired as the Guardian of the Town by the Mayor, Shantae stlll wants to stop Risky's new evil scheme, In order for the Lamp to work, it needs 3 Magic seals in order to unleash it's full power. Can Shantae collect these 3 seals and stop Risky's plot before its too late?!
Story, of course is very simple, however, the dialogue and humor is what saves it. There isn't alot of Fourth Wall humor which I feel is very common for these types of indie games, (only w/ Squid Baron), and the game is very well written which made me smile alot of times. Also, I feel Shantae is one of the greater female protagonist. She's strong, funny, independent, and she is pretty cute. :3
Gameplay:
The major selling point about this game is the gameplay. Since this is a WayFoward Title, it understands foremost that it is a game. Its more of a MetroidVania or Zelda game, as you go from area to area, explore dungeons, buy and gain upgrades, discover secrets, dispose of enemies quickly in your path, solve puzzles, all that fun stuff!
You can purchase fire magic, cloud of thunder, rotating balls, all of which can be upgraded for more efficiency and use in your playthrough.
It's one of those games that keeps it's longevity through multiple playthroughs. It's a short game (5 hrs on first try, 2:30 on second go) but I still enjoyed it alot. It's not hard either, however, this version includes a "Magic Mode" where you get a new costume, however you take twice as much damage, but get a really good magic meter. There's even new dialogue when Shantae has the magic mode costume which is a cool little touch!
Music:
Jake Kaufman is a beast. He remixed tracks from the old game, created new tracks, and made me even hum some of the tracks while playing the game! Nothing to say here other than its great!
Graphics:
Its not a 3D or 2.5D game, but the sprite work and animations on the characters and enemies are still a thumbs up!
Overall, I definitely recommend Risky's Revenge to anyone who enjoys these types of games.
Also, Shantae for Smash.... RET-2-GO!

Is Shantae: Risky's Revenge a good game? Sure. Is it a great game? No, not really.
I do enjoy this game, but it doesn't do much to stand out from the crowd. In fact, the most notable things it does are probably its biggest flaws.
For one, the bosses in this game are all incredibly tanky despite not exactly having compelx patterns, and the fights barely escalate as they go on. The final boss especially takes ages and only changes its pattern *once*, though admittedly it's the only boss that really does pose any challenge.
There's also the matter of the game being pretty small for a metroidvania. Not tiny tiny small, but not very large either. The only thing that makes it hard to explore is the (kind of useless) map not alerting you to, well, anything. Collected everything in an area? Map won't tell you. Want to know where the last cave you need to visit is? Map won't tell you. It's small enough that it *can* get away with this, but being small isn't a point in its favor.
Also there's this stupid way-too-long shmup section near the end. Don't do that.
Otherwise the game's good though, yeah. The mechanics are solid and there's plenty of variety in stuff to do; the overworld has more combat than platforming, but the dungeons tend to have more platforming than combat (though the battle tower, obviously, doesn't). I'd say there's a focus on combat over platforming in general but technically most combat in the game is optional, aside from any locked room with enemies or bosses.
There's plenty of use for all your powers, though the very last power does come a bit late and is kind of situational. I don't really feel the game ever got repetitive; the older areas, even, get new enemies the further you get into the game, so they're not just "easy town run through the easy town areas" like a lot of games, which I thought was a nice touch. Getting items is also generally unnecessary, interestingly. You can beat the game (normally) getting no extra collectibles and buying exactly two of the 9 spells. There's even an achievement for beating the game with no health upgrades, which isn't hard to do. It leaves things up to skill a lot more than the standard metroidvania, which I do appreciate.
The game looks great, too, nice 16-bit art style and plenty of dynamic sprites. The music is alright, a bit GBA-quality though. The dialogue's amusing enough and the plot is simply but effective, and surprisingly doesn't status-quo its ending.
Overall I do like this game. I didn't find myself frustrated often but it can provide a decent challenge and it's certainly fun, but with a few flaws and especially a lack of content keep it from being a great game.

Graphics:

A surprisingly solid shoot-em'up / bullet hell without many flaws.
- The different power-ups feel interesting because of their varied effects.
- Enemy variety is big enough to not feel stale as well, also each boss has unique attacks and attack patterns.
- The upgrades for your "ship" are simple, nothing special but they are noticeable enough to make you feel stronger with every upgrade, aka they get the job done.
- Good game length and final boss is difficult enough to feel like a proper final battle.
- If you like the type of up-beat music this game uses at all times your ears are in for a treat.
- With all the screen clutter the rather inconspicious enemy projectiles sometimes vanish from your sight if you don't pay really close attention, leading to moments of confusion as to what hit you (especially frustrating in the Challenge mode)
- Getting all the upgrades / monster cards takes quite some time, so trying to 100% this can feel tedious towards the end (although it's fine until you get there).
- Game is a bit on the easy side for those who are good at bullet-hell games (although challenge mode is a lot more difficult).
- Had a (very) few weird crashes. Saves work fine but you better not forget to manually save from time to time!
- Game doesn't auto-save or anything when you go to the credits after the final boss. Had to re-do the entire last dungeon (quite frustrating, so remember to save often as said above).
This game is an easy recommendation if you like bullet-hell games. It's not perfect but except for a possible random crash it doesn't have any significant flaw either so you're in for some good entertainment.

I played the game before it was released on Steam. It took around 7 h to beat it.
I was looking at libraries with games and wondering which game to pick for my next review. I wanted something colorful, something casual and then I saw Sweezy Gunner – top down bullet hell shoot 'em up with metrodivania elements. And it's awesome !
In the game you drive a tank … with tires. Or maybe it's another vehicle. It doesn't matter. This tank is really cute, but don't let this full you, Sweezy Gunner is a beast. Your task is to find what happened to the people terraforming  some planet. The story is non existent, but this doesn't matter. What matter is the gameplay and it is really good. The controls are simple - WASD keys for moving, left mouse button you shoot, the right mouse button for activating a shield and spacebar – for entering all the menus. You have one basic weapon thru the whole game. Fortunately they are 30 power-ups to spice the gameplay. Some are passive, other change your  weapon, certain can stack on each other. Then nothing can stop you, you become like a real tank.
In the begging you move slow, so are your bullets, only three bars of life. So what can you do? Well you can buy upgrades of course. They can be acquired in two different ways – by finding shops scattered around the world and by killing monsters. For unlocking upgrades in the shop, which you buy with money from dead enemies, you need to collect giant golden coins called Sweezy Coins. Other thing you can do here is to take jobs for money. They consist of collecting stuff from dead enemies.
When you kill monsters sometimes fall a card, which give you information about them. Destroying enough of one type, you studied them and it will let you by upgrade. Every bosses in the game is nicely design and challenging. After each boss you will get special ability, that grants you access to previously unavailable parts of the map.
The levels in Sweezy Gunner are great. You are gunning down monster in a grass fields, in a desert, in dungeons full with lava and toxic waste. Every level has a different song. Speaking of music, the soundtrack is amazing. 11 really good song.

Dark Souls, what can I say? One of the most renown hardest games of all times.

The game can be hugely difficult from the start. But as you get used to it day by day, you will start feeling its rhythm of playing, from what's good and not to do. Learn from your mistakes. Improve, conquer your own fear, and thrive to survive. Since there is a Jolly Cooperation system, in which you will be able to coop with NPC, it helps reduce a bit of pressure in the beginning of the game. Rest assured though, that does not mean the bosses will go easy on you. More damage seems to help a lot for me. Look for your own combination of playstyle to tailor your stats to your own playstyle. I played with a complete mix build, and it sure helped me survive as well as dealing nice chunk of damage , allowing me to balance things out between me and bosses.
Trust me, this game can teach you a whole lot on reflex and patience. Even small enemies can still defeat you if you are not careful and patient on every hit. So yea, play smart until you understand the pattern, then you can play fast.
Verdict: 10/10, one of the games everyone should try for once.

I thought for a while about buying this game and have read a number of reviews and comments on various different forums.  As I did buy it I thought I would my two cents into the mix after playing for 5 hours and have just got to the 4th (and final) tier of population needs.
DRM
Yes it’s a bit of a pain that you have to have a uplay account and have to install it onto your computer but apart from the initial verification process I can’t say that I have noticed it.  For me the DRM is not an issue.
Game Play
Overall I’m really enjoying the game.  I have seen allot of talk about the game being dumb down and on the whole I would have to agree with these comments.  I don’t think it’s as hard or as complicated as Anno 2070 however as your cities get larger there is a fair amount resource management to do (and it’s that what the game is about?).  For example in my main city the need for luxury food was getting high and I was running out of space so I decided to buy a new region and source my whole farming there which meant I could bulldoze my farms in my main city and just import the food. I thought this would be a quick task but realised that to support a farming community I needed to set up a small city.  I wouldn’t say this was difficult but did take a bit of time and I certainly found it enjoyable.
Combat has been taken out of the city building sectors and has its own.  I would say this is the weakest part of the game but it’s ok and found it fun to mix it up every now and then and jump into the combat zone.
Research
There is none from what I can see, unless I’m missing something.  This was something that I really enjoyed in Anno 2070 and really added something to the endgame and also changed the way your next game was played.  Real shame its missing and don’t really understand why.  Perfect opportunity to have specific things in each sector you could research to help the others.
Story
It’s a bit crap.  Basically it’s grow your corporation as big as possible.  The side quests in the form of sector projects are a bit better but not by much.
Graphics
This game looks great however you will need a beast of a machine to run it at max.  I have an i7 6700, 16 GB DDR4 and nvdia 660gtx x2 in sli.  Problem is sli isn’t supported so my 2nd graphic card is just sat there with its feet up.  I run the game in 1440p on medium at 40ish fps.  Nvidia Pascal can’t come soon enough!  Also you will be changing between the sectors allot so a SSD will really help with the load times.
Sound
It’s ok, nice back ground music but nothing to write home about.
Overall
I’m glad I brought it and would recommend it but there are a few things such as sli support, research and improved story line which would really improve the game.

I am truly shocked at how petty people can be. It is not fair that people review this game against some preconceived idea of what they think the game should be. It's even worse since they knew what the game would be before release as it was well publicized.
The game in it's own right is amazing.
Unlike the previous Anno's in this one resources are now flow resource, instead of gathering in a warehouse. I think this is a great change as you have so much more control. Resource gathering is fine for games with a micro scale where you manage a small city but do it in great detail. In this game you manage multiple cities on a macro scale, so flow resource makes more sense.
A lot of people are complaining about multiplayer. I don't think that is fair as this game is intended to be played over many days/weeks. It will take a while to build up large cities. How will that work with multiplayer? It's a city builder so multiplayer doesn't make sense.
A lot of detail exists in this game. People giving negative reviews seem to overlook the effort the developers put in, not fair.
Some people are saying they played 20 hours and have done everything there is to be done. To those people I send my condolences. Once you get your city big enough things start to get very complicated. It becomes an incredible balancing act between production, supply and income. Your trade network can get very complicated.
I've seen many complaints about the game not having random maps. But lets be honest, the previous anno's didn't really  have random maps, it was the same islands over and over again, they were just slightly in a different position every time. You can't have random maps and meaningful maps at the same time. This game has meaningful maps, and they are so large that it really doesn't matter. Even more the amount of time you will spend in a single game, random maps also becomes irrelevant. The maps have so much detail and is incredibly beautiful, they deserve praise.
The game does have sandbox mode, the campaign is the sandbox. the first few missions is just to get you started on your sandbox experience.
People complain about the naval battles, but these are entirely optional and are only for rewards, that you can get in other ways. This is a city builder not a RTS. The battles are fine for the type of game.
I only have two complaints about this game:
The world market needs work as it is a bit unbalanced. But since you can completely ignore it in your game and still be very successful, it's not that big of a complaint.
There seems to be a bit of a memory leak if you play for a long time, that slows down the game. Restarting the game solves the problem though.

Noumena Studios is able to pull off a better BioWare game despite coming uncomfortably close to putting Baldur's Gate fanfiction of Imoen to code.
Following The Dark Eye Pedigree to the letter, there is nothing about Demonicon that does not involve the likely foreign and confusing lore of Adventuria. Fortunately for the player, the key aspects of this game are immediately and consistently explained to the point that anyone could become an expert on Borbarrad and his teachings, whether or not they care to hunt down all the legends and specific conversation choices.
The fact that they are able to successfully craft a compelling narrative out of Borbaradianism - that is a demonic mixture of two parts extreme Nietzchean philosophy, three pinches of Social Darwinism inspired ritualistic sacrifice and a whole helping of Objectivism, present your potential adversaries as more than just giggling maniac cultists. There is a real methodology to the evil or demon worshiping characters in this game that is as morally questionable as it is seductive; “Every man – A Mage” and the pursuit of freedom through the power of Blood Magic which often comes at the cost of enslaving and murdering others.
Outside of the inexplicable charm of the story, there is a tight combat that is a comfortable blend of simple Action RPG slashing and spell flinging. Easy to pick up yet difficult to master, Demonicon is as pen and paper as you can get without scripted irritation from a wrathful DM.
As for cons, however, this game has a strange sense of what should have the effort to be animated and what will be skipped over abruptly - to the point where I am always surprised whether I have high or lower expectations of what the game will do. It has difficulty keeping characters out of making the same arm folds or generic dramatic finger points for the 100th time, yet it has the depth to program taking a single bite out of an apple and then casually tossing it aside in order to anger the parents of starving children, if the player so chooses to be a Rear Admiral Dickbutt for one specific part of the early game.
It is a lower budget indie RPG and I wouldn't have it any other way after experiencing it in all its flawed glory.

Well I picked this up before realizing that the license to use the Dark Eye name had been picked up by another company. Expected it to be a classic Dark Eye experience like Drakensang and its sequal. Its nothing like the afformentioned games at all and has about as much to do with the rules system in which it takes its name as D&D 4e has with Dungeons and Dragons (okay in fairness perhaps Demonicon is even further divorced). What I found was a poorly executed diablo clone with a storyline so divorced from Aventuria and the Dark Eye as to be unrecognizable. This is another example of a developer using a familiar name in classic rpgs and using it only for marketing purposes with little or no regard for the IP they are mutilating for profit.
To be honest even if I had been looking for a diablo style action rpg this game is just pitiful. Slow response time, awkward animations and voice acting, and sadly even the story and character development are lacking seriously. Please spend your money elsewhere on a game more deserving than this one.

The game tries hard to borrow from The Witcher series and Bioware rpgs, but fails at almost every aspect and mechanic aside from story, which is surprisingly fun. Being a storyfag myself I was ready to forgive the many shortcomings, but the ending managed to nullify whatever positive feelings I had for Demonicon: it is a 5  second long cg which doesn't depend on any of your previous choices and actions, forcibly railroaded, makes little sense (behold a deus ex machina 1 minute before the boss fight) and is simply annoying. So you get an insulting 5 second cg, credits and then main menu - no slides, no scenes, nothing. In comparison to this a Mass Effect 3 original ending can be considered a masterpiece.
As for the game in general, the pros:
- Story is entertaining, characters are ok and generally make sense.
- The world of Dark Eye looks much more interesting and atmospheric than in the previous DE game Drakensang, where it felt as a boring generic fantasy.
- All non-combat skills have uses, if only to get junk loot.
- Choices have consequences, though mostly in dialogs and cosmetic map changes.
- Comprehensive codex of the game world and plot.
The cons:
- No manual saving, can sometimes take up to 15 minutes to hit the next save trigger.
- No key remapping (enjoy shift-4 for potion).
- Combat is clunky and unbalanced, also animations are so long it almost feels like a phase based and not real time (reminded me of The Witcher 1 combat).
- Side quests are few and are a joke, on the quality level of the infamous Dragon Age 2 "deliver a random item you find to some dude" quests.
- Very limited exploration - nothing to find but some random junk loot (weapons, armor and talismans are only rewarded for plot quests or bought in shops), and a couple of combat hints codex entries, some of which require one of the skills to get like pick locks or perception.
- Linear story progression and basically nothing to do beyond that.
- Economy is broken, you get rich fast and there is little need for money.
- Alchemy is generic and also useless since you find more potions than you generally need and even on harder difficulties it's easier just to buy them.
- Graphics are outdated, customization is limited to armors which are few.
Misq:
- The only dialog choices here are to inquire some info (sometimes requires lore or fast talk checks) and major plot choices, yet the protagonist often speaks as if player is randomly alternating between calm and aggressive options. It can partially be attributed to certain plot specifics, but still feels weird. Otherwise the english voiceovers are generally on the ok scale.
edit: nominated this gem for the "Best Incest" steam award. -)

I've given this game a 'Yes' recommendation, but only if you can find it going really cheap in a deal or a sale somewhere.
So - Demonicon. It's not the worst game you'll ever play, but it's not terribly well designed, and it's kind of 'obvious' that it worked to a budget, which is a shame because it's got some nice visuals and as an RPG it manages to hit some of the right notes. It's got a lot of obvious bugs and half-finished elements, it's kind of clunky, and the story isn't amazing, and isn't really developed entirely well. I think the game tries to rely too much on the background The Dark Eye lore, which will appeal only to fans of that pen & paper RPG. The first couple of areas as well are a bit cumbersome, and it's not really that enjoyable a game to begin with.
But eventually, after about 10 hours or so, maybe? Towards the latter half of the second hub, suddenly you get a sense of... moorishness. By this time Cairon should have some better abilities & equipment, and should be levelled up to a point where he's actually slightly ahead of the curve for that area. This makes the fighting easier (but not boring), which stops some of the sluggish battles you may have had before this. Keep on top of things and this advantage can last you the rest of the game, and all in all it makes you feel like a little bit of a badass.
As an example, in a later hub section, I found myself confronted by three or four demons in armour, wielding some pretty nasty looking weapons. I was preparing myself mentally for long and difficult fight, and I ran at the first one and did that stabby move that's kind of like what Brad Pitt does in the movie Troy. The demon knight fell instantly - recovering from my momentary surprise, I repeated the move on the others, and then the fight was over. I felt like a total BOSS, and that's something that this game is kind of good at, especially in the later half.
So – all in all, if you find it cheap and are willing to put up with a rather poor start, this is one of those one-shots that can entertain you for a while. I finished the game in 26 hours, so it’s not short by any means, but it’s fairly linear for an ‘RPG’ so the story can only go on for so long.

I absolutely loved The Longest Journey and Dreamfall so it was with great excitement that I backed this project on kickstarter. I'm afraid this game did not live up to it's predecessors.
This is not a point and click adventure game, I'm not sure what this is but the closest thing it reminds me of is a Visual Novel and it's not a particularly good one at that. There was a good story here but it feels like they chose to not tell it, what we're treated to is instead about 80% fluff and pointless busywork. The 3 first books are straight up boring and contains very little of real relevance. Sure it's setting up all those choices that are supposed to shape things later on, but it's doing so at the cost of cutting the actual interesting events short.
In the end I am glad that I've played the game, for no other reason than to have 'finished' the story that I loved so much in the previous games. But I'm afraid I can not recommend this game to anyone. There are by far better experiences to buy if you're after 'interactive storytelling' and there's plenty of better games if you want puzzle solving or adventure.

Hello everybody, my name is Shaun Meyers (Kyo Akiara) and I'm the writer of a game review and article website known as Universal Gaming Reviews. This is my review for Demonicon: The Dark Eye. The game has an interesting leveling system which I enjoyed quite a bit, lots of collectbles to find in the world that are based on a certain skill, like lockpicking and legend lore and the storyline is fairly intriguing. The game does however have quite a few issues still in-tact and I ended up taking a point off due to these issues. There's still many glitches in conversations, I ran into one after the boss battle with Ghamat that prevented me from leaving the area, textures are really low resolution and it's noticeable throughout the game (not a big issue for me to be honest though, I still play classic games so I'm used to stuff like this haha, it's worth mentioning though). There's also no option to save the game and it relies on an autosave checkpoint system, which is a bit annoying as well. There also isn't a lot of armor and weapon choices among other things I could say lol. The negatives far outweigh the positives but even so I've been enjoying it for the most part and have put 10 hours into it already, I'd recommend picking it up when it's cheaper in price if it interests you though as it's not really worth 40 bucks in my opinion. Happy gaming folks.

Coming into this game after playing the superb, albeit flawed, original game my hopes were high that Wayforward would have massively improved on some of the things that bugged me in the original. The GBC original isn't a bad game in any stretch of the imagination, it's probably one of the best games on the system in fact. However, what held it back were a few small nicks. It was very big for an action platformer, even straying into Metroidvania territory, which is why the exclusion of a map seemed rather baffling. It was fairly easy to get lost and sometimes finding certain places was a nightmare as the game was rather cryptic or hush hush about what to do next. Not to mention the warp system involved collecting four macguffins before you were allowed to warp to any town.
These problems and more however have been fixed in Risky's Revenge. For one, the game has a map! So now you can easily find out where you are in Sequin Land and can always see where you should probably go next. However, when you first look at the map, you'll no doubt notice how small it is. We'll get back to that.
The game is no longer as cryptic as it once was thanks to the map and the hints you can get from Uncle Mimic, Bolo and Sky back in Scuttle Town. Occasionally you might find yourself at a loss for what to do but since the map is a lot smaller this time, it's not unreasonable for you to just do a little bit more exploring to find what you need.
And the warp system is now much more managable, as it merely involves walking up to the warp points and 'waking them up'. From there you can warp to any other activated points.
Back to the size of the map, I was initially disappointed to see that the map size had decreased dramatically since the original game, but at the end of the day I think it worked to the games favor. Finding some of the mandatory items would have been much harder if you were given a bigger map, especially since you're never told, explicitly or otherwise, where these mandatory items may be.
However the smaller map size does mean that the amount of labyrinths has unfortunately decreased. The original game had four excellent labyrinths, however this game has only two, three at a stretch. The two present are great but the third, known as the Battle Tower, seems like it would have been better as an optional minigame. I think this lack of content can probably be blamed on the DSiware service the game was initially released on, which, if memory serves me correctly, had limits on how big games could actually be.
Despite this though, the game never feels lacking. The platforming, combat and exploration is all immensely satisfying, so much so that it doesn't even matter that the game is so short as you'd quite gladly speedrun the game again and again.
Of course, no review of this game could go without mentioning the magnificent presentation. The sprite work is fantastic as always and the animation on each one is wonderful. The music too is an absolute treat. This top notch presentation is, of course, more or less par for the course when it comes to Wayforward.
So do I reccomend this game? Yes, very much so. Shantae: Risky's Revenge is a splendid platforming adventure with incredible visuals, music and gameplay and I think everyone should give it a shot.

Do you like clicking buttons?
This game is basically just clicking buttons over and over again, however in the first 63 minutes there has not been a single wait time over a second, unlike the previous game, AdVenture Capitalist. This game takes place in a communist society where you must expand certain types of labor forces (that's really the best word I can describe them as). These are:
-Potatoes
-Farmers
-Ore
-Weapons
-Medicine (which, ironically, is the hardest one to get).
To get more of these things, you must click buttons, or hold down buttons. Numbers go up, you click, they go down. In about 3 seconds of holding the buttons again, you can click more buttons. It's incredibly repetetive, which is probably what the developers were going for. What I find strange, however, is the lack of insistence for you to buy things.
The original game started as a mobile game, and as such had the cancerous microtransactions, which carried over to the PC port. I do not know if this game started the same way, though I suspect it didn't as you can only buy these blue beaker things to give boosts. I didn't see a way to buy cash or anything (though I may be wrong). Either way, the pay-to-play element is severely decreased from AdCap.
The interface is somewhat confusing at first, though as you work your way through it it becomes easy to find your way around, like a new school or workplace. Graphics are nice and clear at 1920x1080 resolution (though there are a multitude of resolution settings, and you can set windowed mode if that's your thing).
Overall, it's a clicker game with less pay-to-play elements, for free. 6/10. Best one I've seen.

Its not Symphony of the Night 2, but its also not a bad game at all.
+ controls feel good, sometimes the jumping is floaty and not 100% precise, but it is never gamebreaking or anything
+ the game is mainly linear, with optional backtracking if you want all health and magic upgrades. I really like it better that way
+ challenging boss battles
+ they toned down the QTEs by a lot. You can clearly see in the cutscenes that they were designed to be QTEs, but they changed them in the PC version to just be cutscenes. (There are some QTEs left, but they are all fitting in my opinion)
+ the fighting system is also very basic, which is great, you are going to spam the best combo anyway, why not just make it simple? You get various attacks but never too much and complicated
+ many powerups and items that are fun to use
+ little spoiler ahead about a game mechanic:
+ it took me 10 hours to play through
+ the difficulty is great, not too easy, not too hard - once you beat the game you can play on extreme
+ the artstyle is still true to the Castlevania franchise
+ it runs very smooth, with no bugs or crashes, solid framerate
+ the story was never something I looked forward for in a Castlevania title, but here it is acceptable and not as boring as the other titles in the series
+ interesting puzzles and leveldesign
- since this is a port of a Nintendo handheld console the resolution is somewhat messed up. 1080p in fullscreen is strechted and you have black bars or a letterbox. Maybe something with the scaling
- there are a little bit too much trial and error parts, where you constantly have to die unless you know 100% the specific pattern
- although the soundtrack fits the mood and atmosphere of the game, it is not that kickass metal/rock soundtrack I would have expected
- in many areas you can just completely ignore the enemies in the game

I’ve played Dawn of Discovery and Anno 2070, I like the games. The only things I don’t like about this game is that you don’t get to play with others and you don’t get a lot of land or a big enough map. Honestly, I would rather have all the maps combined into one super map than play in slices the way it is now.
Now, to the things I really like.
Building upgrades. You build something, then you can spend more to add upgrades to it so really, it’s like building several buildings yet it hardly takes any space! I mean, eventually you’ll have to build others, but you build fewer than what you had to do in the other games.
Moving buildings. Holy potato this saves time! I mean, I don’t have to destroy whole swathes of buildings just to switch stuff around!
I like how they added bridges and things. All the visuals are fantastic, a feast for the eyes.
What I wish…
Honestly I would love for them to make a game that goes from primitive to futuristic. A game that combines all their games into one. Something that allows you to truly grow a world and the people in it. Dawn of Discovery is still my favorite out of all the games. I do recommend Anno 2205, because it’s still a great game, I just don’t consider it in the same league as DoD and 2070.
They could do a whole lot MORE with this game. It’s like they took the idea of the future and took it too far, leaving behind everything that made their other games so good. If you’ve not played any of their other games, you’ll like this game. If you have played their other games, you’ll find yourself returning to those and only playing this one sometimes.
I’m not satisfied, but for what it is, I like it. I just won’t play this one much till they give me more than boring single player in bite sized maps. I yawn at the whole corporate buying and politics, I liked how things were done in dawn of discovery. Maybe they are building up to something like, but I doubt it. Maybe their next game will go back to the things I loved best about the series.

Shantae has always had it a bit rough, seemingly launching a bit too late and missing the hardware generation it was meant for, the first one launching on the Game Boy Color when the advance had already launched for a while, however it had enhanced features if played on the GBA and the same for this game when it lanched I believe it was meant for the Advance and instead came out on the DSi Ware store.
All this kinda made the game hard to come by, not many had a DSi and the GBC game goes to this day for a few hundred bucks. But whatever! Now it's on Steam and it's all awesome!
It's a very well made game, visually it's like playing Metal Slug with really nice sprite art and animation. The pixels are chunky and the music is funky. There's a nice variety of skills and enemies to keep gameplay varied, the skills being one of the more unique points of play in this. You have some magic abilities that you'll want to use depending on the situation sure but she also has a dance skill that lets her change into animals and such to help her progress. Monkey to wall climb & Elephant to break rocks. It all ties together nicely as you progress.
The game itself is 'open-world' as in it's metroid-vania like where you need to navigate about the world and will be stopped by something you need to get a power or item to bypass. There's a variety of places to see and they're all different with their own enemies. Recolored enemies at least have entirely different moves so it's not the same thing over and over. They did a really good job with keeping things diverse.
The port, well it's a straight port more or less. It's in the same aspect ratio as the DSi so you'll have black bars on the sides of your screen unless you have a 4:3 screen.  This has some people angry, why? I don't know the game isn't a remaster and honestly the port runs perfectly with no hitches so it's a bit of a shame that the screen hasn't been stretched but it's no deal breaker.
It works well, slap in a controller or use your keyboard and the game plays as it should, a well made 2D platformer with a bit of a learning curve with 2D map navigation. (Buy the map in town and you will be happier)
Should you get Shantae? Well if you like Metroid-vania games, then ...well yes, very much yes. It's a very well made game with a nice sense of progression and a unique world that does not take itself seriously. At one point you need to get a coffee for some zombie-friends to progress. You get the beans a broken machine then have your friend repair it with her bird...Grabs the bird by the legs, and uses it as a wrench. It's stupid- and brilliant.

Review: Anarchy Arcade
The title says it all. Anarchy Arcade is a mancave simulator where you get to play your own games at your own mancave! Play emulation games, and Steam games!
The gameplay of the game is bumped down as ROMs are hard to load, which don't always work in every situation. Not all ROMs work, as it's hard to load up ROMs. (Though, it might just be because of the emulator.) You can watch youtube games and chill on some Steam games while enjoying your awesome mancave.
The default maps that are originally installed in the game is very well made, and has a rich look to each map. Not only the default maps are well done, as the Workshop offers cool maps as well.
Having the opportunity to play games inside a game is really cool, as there is no other game which could do it. Taking time to create your dream mancave and playing in it makes Anarchy Arcade EXTRA fun!
The workshop items are really good, as each of them have a great touch to reunite the arcade games that brought back the good ol' 70s era.
Overall, Anarchy Arcade brings back nostalgia for kids in the golden era of arcade games, where video games was the biggest thing around. If you love arcade games, this game was made for you!

A beautiful, epic adventure through different worlds. I hadnt played the previous games before this, but catching up the story was no problem whatsoever.  After playing The Longest Journey, some things made a bit more sense and I could see the root of the origins now, but it is no means necessary to play them to enjoy the story this game has to offer.
What is quite remarkable in the game, how ambitious it is. It is developed by a small developer and small budget, but they havent cut corners and made a small game because of this. No, the game is pretty huge for adventure game standards, and the environments vary a lot. There is easily a tripl AAA ammount of environments and graphics in this game, albeit not of that high standard except at some points. The graphics are still good enough imo.
Story starts a bit slow, but starts to build up after a few chapters... which is kind of slow, and I can see some people stop playing this because of the slow start. It pays in the end though, and journey reached peaks I didnt imagine it could.
Biggest problem beside the slow start is somewhat boring puzzles. You merely run from place to place to find objects from the environments, making most of the puzzles feel like taxi missions in RPGs. Well, at least you dont get stuck. In its way, this game feels like an RPG like Mass Effect or Dragon Age...except that there is no combat or dungeons, only the city parts! Not every game needs to have action sequences, but I couldnt help but feeling that something is missing here... Imagine playing Mass Effect which only has cities and no combat at all, and this game feels like that. It is a bit boring due to this at times, especially in the beginning, but when the story gets more compelling, I stopped caring about that aspect.
Well, if you want an epic adventure journey with interesting worlds, characters and settings, and an excellent, excellent animal companion who travels with you through all it, this is a good pick.

It's so hard to know where to start about a game that spanned 17 years and countless characters, every one of them memorable. I played The Longest Journey when I was a child and I remember sinking 30 to 40 hours into it and when it was finally over I did nothing but think about the game and the story for more than a week. Very few games can do that.
Dreamfall brought more questions than answers and although it had a lot of lackluster mechanics it was an amazing game. I waited for years for the story to end and now when it finally did, I feel both elated and sad. Although I would love to see a fourt game I don't think it will happen and all the major plot points were explained and the stories of all the major characters were brought to an end. But make no mistake, countless questions keep swirling both in my mind in discussion forums but it's unreasonable for any game to explain every question when it has a story that spanned 3 games and 17 years. The ending doesn't explain everything, it's bittersweet and it leaves you wanting for more but it's also satisfying. There enough closure and a whole lot of melancholy and reminiscence.
Years from now, I will look back and between the hundreds -maybe thosands- of games TLJ saga will shine like a beacon along with a few other brilliant titles amonst a sea of decent games. That's when you know you've witnessed a timeless piece of art.

I would only recommend the game for those seeking closure to the story.  The stroy is complete but the game is unfinished.
This is manifested in its performance.  FPS dips down to 20 in cities on a GTX 1070, not even on max settings.  The developers have addressed this with "update your graphics drivers," stating that the game is graphically intensive.  This is simply not the reason for its porr performance when other, more graphic-intensive games run fine.  There are other minor examples of an unpolished game but none more egregious than the poor framerate.
The game is not like its predecessors.  There are times when it is quite boring and an asbolute slog.  The puzzles are not that challenging.
Aside from these things the characters are entertaining and the story is...ok.  It's just a disappointing way for such a great series to end.

Now, to the things I really like.
Building upgrades. You build something, then you can spend more to add upgrades to it so really, it’s like building several buildings yet it hardly takes any space! I mean, eventually you’ll have to build others, but you build fewer than what you had to do in the other games.

The negativity surrounding Anno 2205 is not unfounded, from the change of heart to allow Beta access for pre-order customers, to releasing a Season Pass with no content. The most sour taste has been left with the feeling of an unfinished game, to be completed, in part, by the gradual release of DLC's.
Anno 2205 at the moment is the foundation of a great game, the UI's been simplified and the interactions are somewhat easier compared to the previous Anno's. I find at times that it's been dumbed down a bit, perhaps to make it more accessible to a wider audience. I do fear that this will put off some of the more die hard fans out there.
It's a visually beautiful game, with excellent graphics and attention to detail, even down to zooming into buildings (I encourage you to take a look at some of the Lunar ornamental buildings).
I get annoyed at the repetitiveness of, well pretty much all of the missions, summed up by "find x of this" and "destroy that". The military missions aren't much better! I do like the separation of the military missions to the main game. I miss the ability to take over other territories, I also miss the different factions of Anno 2070, although that's been replaced by the landscapes. Once in a landscape, they don't have different benefits per land piece, by that I mean growing coffee in one place and tobacco in another, again that's been replaced by the ladscape (alloys from Lunar, wine from Earth etc.), losing the trade routes within the map itself and switching them out to an overall space view. The trade route UX simplification is excellent in respect to creating them, click, click done!
The playability the game is affected by the monotonous tone set by the repetitive missions, and all in all doesn't take much to complete, a slow and steady growth pretty much ensures game completion. I remember being able to play Anno 2070 for days and still be entertained due to the intricacies of trade routes, land ownership, war etc. Anno 2205 feels lacking in a lot of ways.
I have enjoyed the game, but have got bored with it after 24 hrs total play. All in all, what has been released so far is well rounded but ultimately an unfinished game, I have a feeling that next year it will have grown some muscle to conted with other Anno games, just not at the moment.
For that reason, I will recommend Anno 2205, just wait until a few more rounds of DLC have been released before you do buy it.
