Anno 2205 is a really good game. While it may be rather different from it's predecessors in the franchise, what it adds is more than enough to counter what it takes away in my opinion. Whilst I don't think it's worth spending the £54.99 on the gold edition (price at 20th January 2016), it's certainly worth picking up and giving a go if you were a fan or the previous games or city builders in general.
Combat was moved to specific locations in Anno 2205, and so they have specifically designed maps which sort of have a story built into them. It's not a very good story, but it's something. At times, having to defend against attackers in the building regions would be fun and prove rather challenging, but sometimes I find I just want to focus on building without having to worry about being attacked.
Managing multiple different building regions in different climates (Temperate, Arctic & The Moon), and having to transfer goods between them constantly creates an interesting challenge as you'll find that in order to advance in one region, you need to supply it with goods that can only be made in one of the other regions. Expanding to moon bases is an even bigger challenge than just the regions on the planet, as it needs a lot of materials from the other regions to operate and is massively expensive to the point where it could completely ruin you in-game economy if you aren't prepared for it or don't act quickly.
The main story is sort of average, with no huge twists or suprises. However it is a city builder / strategy game and so it was never going to have an amazing story like an adventure or an RPG game would have. It does the job good enough and introduces you to each new region type effectively.
The side-missions (or quests) that you get in each region can be rather repetitive, they're usually "go find these things (and bring them back to us)" or "Use this drone we've given you to destroy some things." Also, the game kind of forces you to do them if you want to build modules (upgrades) for you buildings or even some certain buildings themselves. You can buy the resources thaat you need to do this, but it sometimes proves to be not enough.
Each sector has it's own string of major side-missions that usually consist of 3 parts, with each part having 5 missions to complete. Some of these are like the other side-missions, like "go find these things" but can be a tad more complex, like having to drag around a kind of drone that tells you the direction you need to be heading in. However, there can also be tasks like towing things to a certain point, or the miore challenging "maintain a certian population" or "maintain a certain surplus of goods or power" or "have this number of service buildings".
The optimal inputs and outputs are now listed in the description of each building, which I think is better than the guessing game that it used to be. The optimal inputs & outputs did exist in previous games, but you weren't told what they were.

That said, whenever you deviate from a core mechanic like that, it's going to take some hits from the die hard fans of the franchise who were perfectly okay with "just more stuff."
There is value here though.  They streamlined the production chain system and actually give you feedback on your "product balance," something that was always an element but always kept a secret from you unless you manually counted buildings.  Overall it feels a bit simplistic but there is some fun gameplay to be gotten out of it if you're open to adjusting to something similar but new.

This game sees alot of hate from veterans of the series, and with some good reasons, but there is no denying this a fun game.  Fundamentaly different previous instalments, this game offers the very bare bones concept of the Anno series.  Its more an econmey managment game more than a city builder but not by alot and in its root is a city builder.  For those of you who don't know the Anno series, and Anno 2205, is a city-building/eco managment game where we build a city a supply your citizens needs at increasing difficulty.  While Anno 2205 is the same principle and fun at that, it feels to watered down to appeal to newcomers, I have no problem with that its that the execution is not great.
First off the game is just in general just way too casual.  Farm buildings are now just one building(unless you count the building modifications) compared to previous games that had fields to place down and made you think about the best solution.  You can build houses anywhere which is an ok thing.  The new way of goods distrubition is ok and didn't need to change at all.
I really just hate the artic region and really prevents me from wanting to go back and make a new session becuase it is just so slow and stupid.  You can only build housed near heat sources which are always production centers.  So you are constantly building industry which you can't support.  I understand the challenge of the artic, but its too much and too far from any interesting gameplay becuase it feels like a burden, just like the boring combat which is neccesary to move on with the game.
Now one big change that just removes my ability to consider this Anno game to be one the caliber of others is that the lack/reinvetion of trade and goods movement.  Taxing trade routes would have a really neat idea if the game had NPCs that interacted with you at all or had interregional trade.  The new trade system removes ship routes from island to island and replaces it to super simple trade.  Trading with the only NPC in the game, Mr. Spaceport man, is almost, scratch that, is actually completely pointless.  Becuase of the tax on trade goods combined with the amount you need to produce and the cost of producing said goods is so expensive that the trade goods negate any income or profit, the only goods worth it are high tier goods which are even more expensive to make so there is literaly no point and if they didn't allow to sell your goods it would make no difference in gameplay.
All in all, that fact that the game fails to capture many big and small details and gameplay elements it just waters down the game and make it feel sub par.  For newcomers and veterans alike, the game is fun and worth it, though lacking features and replayability compared to the others.  It is fun and worth buying, but serioulsy Blue Byte/Related Designs, if the Anno series dosen't return to its roots in the next game that consider me and many customers gone from the series.

I've played a bunch of hours so far; 7.2 at the time of writing this.
First things first. I absolutely adore this type of game, so take that as you will for the rest of my opinions on the game. I still play the OG Stonghold on the reg, any kind of castle sim that combines castle managment and combat... I'm interestested.
The Good
----------
Beautiful artstyle - Clean, simple, efftective
Clean UI - self explanitory
Hint System - Helpful early on, but it can be a little repetitive once you get more experience, but you can turn them off in menu.
Engaging - If you dig any kind of sim/management game, you will fall in love with this system. I want those little blockmen to have their bread, to be happy and not die from the plague
Promise of content - as it stands, the game is good, but at the top-end, it is just the extrapolation of resources to make your city bigger and bigger without much diversity, but the promised updates of Ports, twitch integration and unique heroes could help solve this
The Bad
--------
Optimization - I am running an upper mid-tier gaming PC at the moment, and when the population of my kingdom passed 300, it began to slow down considerably, even after turning off all post-effects, shadows, etc.
The need for group selection/zoning - Having to individually interact with all trees, stones and even buildings can become tedius at times; especially when your kingdome becomes larger.
Peasant pathing - It's just confusing at times. A building cannot find the resources it needs even though the stockpile is just around two buildings and connected to a road.
tl;dr
----
Very promising game that, if you enjoy sims/managment games, you will probably find yourself passing hours by with this game. Unpolished, but can you expect perfection right out the gate? I wouldn't say so. The team has released something that is awesome and hopefully as time continues this will become a phenominal game.

After a little under 7 hours of game time, I kinda feel like the devs don't need to do a whole lot more for me to feel like I got my £7's worth of fun. But it's a great foundation upon which the devs can build a deeper, more engrossing game, as the core concept of tower-defence-meets-city-builder is sound and the look and design of the game is terrific. Kingdoms and Castles needs more content to become a great game, but it's cheap enough and the base game is fun enough that it's easy to recommend, and I'll be following the development of this game to see how they do.
If you want a game that's going to last you dozens of hours, then K&C is definitely not there yet - check out Banished or Cities: Skylines instead. But if you want a cheap, relaxing game that'll last a weekend, with the promise that it could well become a fully-fledged game down the line, then go for it.

I'm gonna start off things by stating that I got extremely frustrated after starting up this game which started me off on the wrong foot. Leading to me enjoying the start of the game a lot less, as well as parts of the rest. If you play windowed and/or with a keyboard, skip this part.
1)  Game not fullscreening properly. I spent 10 minutes trying to get the options to work out because, by all means, it should have been working. Gave up and looked for a fix on the forums. Turns out pressing ''alt + enter'' just once while the game is open is a permanent fix. Why this hasn't been fixed yet, or is mentioned nowhere in a sticky or something is beyond me.
2) The most annoying thing, because it can't easily be fixed, is that for some reason they preset A to jump and CANCEL while B is Talk/Accept (for Xbox 360 controller). THIS CANNOT BE REBOUND. You cannot give keys a double function yourself. It's preset Jump/Cancel on A, or seperate button for cancel/jump. I can't stress enough how weird it is to have those two basic keys swapped. People used to the common ''A for accept, B for cancel'' will be pressing the wrong one a lot. Note that the devs are apparently aware of this (looking at a forum post on March 12th), so this could see a fix soon. I soldiered on but if you're bothered by this one, it may be best to switch to keyboard until the fix is in.
Now, on to the actual game, which I'll keep fairly short.
Positives:
- Great art. Backgrounds/Character Cutouts/Sprites/... .
- Quirky story/dialogue. Not too serious, lots of funny quips.
- Music is ok. Not too memorable but never annoying in either of my 2 playthroughs. Just there as decent background tunes.
- Spells are fun.
- Transformation dances are even better. Very fun to play around with.
- Platforming is solid for the most part.
Negatives:
- Relatively linear for most parts which gets somewhat dropped during other parts (trying to figure out which of the caves holds the next powerup). May feel a bit disjointed. (''What do you mean I can't progress here yet?'').
- Fairly short game. My first run took 5 hours and I'm really, really good at still getting lost or taking my sweet time.
- Hitboxes can be a bit wonky (don't try jumping over enemies that are not going towards you).
- Spells are a bit unbalanced. Spike ball and upgrades are just too useful to not have activated 24/7, so to speak. The 2 others just take too long or are too wasteful.
- Bosses could really use a health bar. You never really know how far down they are since they don't really change their attack patterns much.
Overal, I'd still recommend picking it up (on sale or not). It's got its issues, but it's an okay game if you're looking for some not too serious, fairly short, metroidvania style action.
It's fun. It's adorable. It's retro. Buy it. Play it. Love it.

You move through the screens killing enemy's getting power-ups and money which you can use to purchase upgrades. After a while you come to a dungeon where you do the same. At the end of each dungeon is a boss who bestows a special ability that allows you access to places you couldn't go before: water tires, a dash ability, lava tires, etc.
The controls are unique. It is a twin stick type, but you can't use a controller. You have to use the keyboard for movement and the mouse to aim. I tried using the Pinnacle control to map the controls, but the aiming bit didn't work well. When the aiming recticle gets to the edge of the screen, the screen shifts position. With the mouse you can make the adjustments easily; with the controller - not so much. I didn't care for the controls because when I play the aiming recticle is too far from the action. When there is tons of bullets, gold and monsters on the board it can be hard to see where it is.
I enjoyed playing this game, but I can not recommended it. In my mind, there are better games out there.

Ok, I played through it as for when you begin forming your character one can hardly stop who is into RPGs. It's easy to pick on talents and they all make sense at various points of the game. The story turned out great after a very sceptical start, just try to read and listen to all there is - I left no stone unturned and had no difficulties or got stucked. The graphics remind me of something between Gothic and Risen - not the best, but in my opinion RPGs don't need this, since the atmosphere is typically "Black Eye". Side-quests and Missions are easy and most of the time you have to go to "A", kill "B" and deliver "C" to "D" but always fair balanced at your point of state. The main-quest may be played different, at some points of the game you are asked to make final decisions which result in continuation and/or various endings, which I couldn't really prove as the game doesn't allow you to save your success, it saves automatically. First I thought this would be a disadvantage but this rule turned out most realistic to me and you may play the game again, choosing another way, very interesting.
Overall: A solid RPG with hardly no bugs, an interesting story with many turns and more than 12 hours to play, if you read, play and listen to the whole story. A must have for RPG players, pure action-fans should pass this title.

Neither a Triple A rpg nor does it have top notch gameplay but extremely well done game nevertheless.
The Plot:
The plot is quite interesting but may put off some people, personally i love it. Its not very deep and has a few plot holes but manages to pull through. The areas in the game also ain't that big. Standard RPG formula, main plot brings the player to different places where he/she can choose to clear side quests(basically made up of kill this, collect that). Within the main plot there are crossroads where you will have to make choices and side with either faction. Without spoiling much, these choices affect that portion or area of the story but not much towards the ending. I've completed the game on my first playthrough within roughly 20hrs, minus all the afk and crash and completed almost all side quests.
Combat/Skills/Stats/Crafting:
Combat is action based not very fluid and flashy(it is a bit dull) but still passable and entertaining. Quite a limited Skill/Magic and Stats system, a far cry from other Dark Eye games and other "single character" RPGs. Again, nothing that really impressed me. Technically you can almost max them if you do grind the side quests. Crafting is very simple but kinda pointless, you don't really need the potions/buffs unless on higher difficulty.
Graphics/Soundtrack:
Looks more like a pre-2010 graphics, it looks somewhat dated therefore do not expect much on the looks of the surroudings, characters and world itself. Soundtrack is decent.
Overall, i'd give it a 7/10. Plot and the backstory premise mainly the reason i play this game for.

Das Spiel ist einfach ein schlechter Witz und hat außer mit dem Namen und ein paar Andeutungen im Spiel, absolut gar nichts mit DSA gemeinsam.
Alles was DSA so großartig macht, wurde aus diesen Spiel gestrichen.
Hier nun meine Liste warum das Spiel ein schlechter Scherzt ist:
-Schlechter Sound, hat teilweise aussetzen (zb im Kampf)
-Dialoge der NPC´s auf der Straße wiederholen sich ständig, hört sich an als ob ein Tonband eine Endlosschleife abspielt
-Die NPCs quatschen oft in die Quest-gespräche rein, zb man spricht gerade mit einen Auftraggeber einer Quest und der NPC im Hintergrund labert sein Tonband Endlosschleife runter
-Nerviger Soundtrack, ein paar Stücke sind zwar gut, aber leider wiederholen sich die Soundtracks ständig, und es kommt einem so vor als ob das Spiel nur 3-5 Soundtracks beinhaltet
-Schlechte Grafik, total öde,  triste und lieblose Gebiete, Städte, Einrichtungen usw.
-Tote Spielwelt, die NPCs stehen alle nur steif auf ihrer Position, es herrscht auch so kaum Leben in der Stadt oder den Gebieten
-Schlechte Effekte
-Schlechte Animationen, bei den Dialogen führen die Charaktere immer die selbe Körperbewegungen durch, und die Kampfanimationen sind auch nicht besser, als Beispiel nenne ich nur einmal das Intro-Video des Spiels (diese Schlachtszene)
-KEIN Charaktereditor wie zb in Drakensang
-Der Held ist eine Hypridklasse, der Nahkampf und Magie kann aber beides nur durchschnittlich beherrscht, eben so was wie in The Witcher (solche Charaktere mag ich nicht)
-Zu wenig Zauber, es gibt nur 4 verschiedene Zauber die man ausbauen kann, wo aber jeder "neue" Zauber exakt der selbe ist nur mit mehr Schaden oder längere Effekte
-Zu leichte Bosse, habe einige Bosse (die Necros in der Stadt, oder den Ghul) mit nur einen Schlag (Eislanze + Hammerschlag 2) getötet
-KEINE Partymitglieder wie in den anderen DSA Spiele
-Schlechtes Inventar, bzw Ausrüstungssystem; WIESO liegen meine Waffen, Rüstungen usw, die ich ausgerüstet habe immer noch im Inventar rum ?
-Total schlechter Konsolen-PC Import; Kampfsteuerung bzw Tastenbefehle der Fertigkeiten, Zauber und Tränke total kompliziert und unvorteilhaft, es ist mir oft passiert das ich mich verdrückt habe
-Fehlende Beschreibungen und Bezeichnungen in dem Charaktermenü, zb gibt es keine Kategoriebezeichnungen
-Total geringe Waffenauswahl, es gibt nur Schwerter, Äxte, Knüppel und Wurfsterne, nicht mal Zweihand Äxte, Schwerter, Hämmer oder gar Schilde gibt es
-Bei den Rüstungen sieht es nicht viel besser aus, noch dazu sehen alle Rüstungen und Waffen total gleich aus
-Absolut kein Wiederspielwert
-Schlauch Levels
-Instanzierte Gebiete, Welt
-Zu kleine Gebiete
-Nervige Bugs, Quest-NPCs verschwinden plötzlich und man kann keine Quest abschließen, Charaker bleibt oft wo hängen oder läuft gegen eine unsichtbare Wand
-KEIN DSA SPIEL
-Total lange, sinnlose Laufwege
-Man wird ständig in die selben Gebiete geschickt
-Es gibt in dem Spiel kaum Waffen oder Ausrüstungen, ich habe nur 4x die Waffe und ca 4-5x die Rüstung gewechselt
-Gewisse Rüstungsteile kann man nicht wechseln bzw mit anderen Rüstungen Kombinieren, da wird automatisch sofort die komplette Rüstung ausgewechelt anstatt nur ein Rüstungsteil (Brust, Hose, Arme)
-Viel zu wenig Ausrüstungslots (Es gibt nur Brust, Arme, Hose, Amulett und 2x Ringe)
Ihr mögt euch nun fragen, wo die Liste mit den Positiven Aspekte des Spiels bleiben, ihr fragt euch das auch zurecht, meine Antwort darauf lautet: Es gibt Keine, nicht mal die Story, die ich auch nicht wirklich besonders gut finde, hebt die negativen Punkte wieder auf.
Das Spiel hat absolut keine 73% (laut Gamestar) verdient, das Spiel würde von mir eher 45%-50% bekommen und ich empfehle es auch keinen weiter.
Mich wundert es daher gar nicht mehr das man in der Entwicklungszeit kaum etwas über das Spiel erfahren hat, wahrscheinlich haben die Entwickler sich schon selber gefragt wie man so ein schlechtes Spiel programmieren kann.
Das Spiel wurde total lieblos programmiert anders kann ich mir diese leblose, öde Spielwelt nicht erklären.
Also an alle die noch am überlegen sind ob sie sich das Spiel kaufen sollen; Kauft es bloß nicht, und wenn dann wartet auf eine Aktion, den die €30.--€40.- was das Spiel momentan noch kostet, ist es auf keinen Fall wert, gut das ich dafür nicht so viel gezahlt habe sonst würde mich das jetzt sehr ärgern.

Long ago there was a great game series called Castlevania. It featured large open levels with lots of space for exploration, hardcore 2d action, memorable characters, cheesy-but-still-cool gothic atmosphere.
That series is dead. There hasn't been a proper metroidvania in it for aeons. The game we are looking at now is Castlevania's dead, empty husk, an unholy mockery of once great series, rotten inside, yet still moving, animated by evli marketing wizardry.
The game plays like an insult towards everyone who loves metroidvania. Yes, it does feature getting upgrades, backtracking and searching for secrets. However, the game is divided into three chapters, each one so small that it becomes a travesty. You don't look for secrets, you just get the available power-ups, then go back to collect the previously unreachable chests. Other than that parody of metroidvania backtracking, the game is linear, moving from level to level.
The gameplay is basic and mindless: timed blocks and other feints are useless, you just button mash your enemies into oblivion. Puzzles are either rudmentary or tedious. Platforming parts are so easy they can be completed blindfolded. The story is an over-the-top fake-dramatic sausagefest: "you killed my mother! Also, you're my father! Also, *I*'m *his* father! Also, you killed *his* mother! Also, NOOOOOOO". Dialogues are written so badly that I don't even blame the voice actors for sounding like they are falling asleep reading  them. Clearly, not a single person in the development team gave a bite about the game, so why should they?
If you love what Castlevania used to be, avoid this soulless cash-grab. Play Ori and the Blind Fortest, Axiom Verge, Dust, Shantae, Cave Story... Or wait for Bloodstained to come out. Don't support this flogging of a dead horse. Castlevania isn't, and will never be what it used to be, let it rest in peace.

This actually had the potential of being a decent game, but Mercury Steam screwed it up by...
...making Simon (the main character) sluggish to control. This is especially apparent while jumping (which happens a lot), where you actually lose speed in the air rather than continue at the previous pace.
...forcing you to manually put out markers for items and points of interest on the map. Maybe this was an acceptable solution when the game was released on 3DS, due to the touch screen, but IT SUCKS having to do it with a controller.
...making the game save every time you close the map, adding load times for no reason whatsoever.
...adding a level system but not putting it to good use. From what I can tell, there are no stat increases and the only thing you can actually gain from levels are skills.
...reusing the idiotic concept from Lords of Shadow, where you're interrupted by freshly spawned enemies halfway through pulling cranks.
...making you take fall damage, meaning you can and will die from falling or making a drop from too high up.
...sending you back to the start of the area if you die, effectively resetting your exploration of the map and making you have to do it all over again. This + the previous concern = pure bullsh*t.
Also, I can't say I condone their decision to go with a boring 3D art style rather than gorgeous pixel graphics like the previous sidescrolling entries in the series.
To sum it up: Don't buy this game.
If you already have, do yourself a favor and don't waste your time playing it. Go play Symphony of the Night, Aria of Sorrow or some other Castlevania game that's actually good.
Nope, nope, nope.

If you like playing through a good story-based adventure game, this one was really, really excellent; BUT if you haven't played the previous two games, you're going to miss out on the full experience. Without that foundation, both the reasons behind what's happening and the empact of certain events in the story are going to be a little more lost than they should. Which makes sense: this project was funded via Kickstarter, so the TLC that went into making this game was very much on behalf of the fans.
A couple of pros and cons to note:
-They took out the combat mechanic that existed in the second game, which was a good thing, I think. As much as I enjoy combat in games, this series has always been about story, so there's not much sense in the game trying to be something it's not.
-The visuals are beautiful, but the character's expressions don't always change to match their emotions, making some moments a little too uncanny valley. It didn't take me out of the story enough to detract from the awesomeness of the whole, but it was definitely a distraction.
-Every once in a while, the game doesn't let you use the shift key to make your character run, particularly indoors. As someone who likes to get from point A to point B as fast as possible in games, this was a bit frustrating.
-The way the game incorporated choice was one of the best things about this experience. I was really, really happy with how the choices I made through the characters impacted the story in ways that felt meaningful. The choices also felt real: there were the big ones which were obviously a crossroads, choices that would change everything that happened next; but there were also small ones which often didn't matter but which, every once in a while, would have a ripple effect that influenced future events in unexpected ways.
-Some things that happen in this story are heavy. The writers are not afraid to kill off beloved characters or wrestle with life's unanswerable questions. If you're looking for a fun, sometimes funny, sometimes sad, ultimately memorable interactive story, you will find that here; but if you're going through some sort of personal existential crisis in your life, you may want to put off playing this game just a little while longer. (Or perhaps an existential crisis would be the perfect reason to play this game? Depends on your personality, I guess.)
Again, this game is awesome. You should play it. But if you haven't played The Longest Journey and Dreamfall, go play those first.

It's been a long, painful, difficult road for Dreamfall Chapters, much like it has been for the characters in the story, very much like it has been for the TLJ series in general. Reading up some forums posts from the past year, it seems there are a lot of people who expected Chapters to be something it isn't. Maybe the developer had bigger plans that ended up never happening, maybe they simply marketed in a way it shouldn't have been marketed.
I've owned The Longest Journey and Dreamfall for ages now and backed Chapters for its Kickstarter but never actually got around to playing them until just last week. Obviously, I don't have the weight of waiting for years and years for a continuation of the story, something that I imagine made Dreamfall originally as painful (and disappointing) at the time as something like Halo 2's ending when it came out. I also didn't go through waiting months or even years between Books with Chapters, didn't have to experience the bugs and engine pains that seemed to happen early on. I'm sure my enjoyment benefited greatly.
TLJ and Dreamfall are rough. They have not aged gracefully. But they are absolutely crucial parts of this grand journey, and they make Dreamfall Chapters so much more rewarding, much like Chapters ends up making Dreamfall much, much more enjoyable. The stories the games tell and the characters you get to know will live on in your minds, and they make the events in Chapters matter that much more.
Chapters has choices and there are consequences, but ultimately this is a small part in a larger set of events that have already been predetermined. You are along for the ride, and what a ride it is. This is a strong, beautiful, narrative-focused adventure to follow, and a wonderful continuation of a rich, engaging, magical story, filled with imagination and a love for the mysterious, something just beyond our understanding. Much like the previous two games, it has problems and odd moments, but the broad strokes form a satisfying journey you want to see through to the end. Your enjoyment is very dependant on your emotional investment in the characters and their fates, and I absolutely loved it. It goes places and I was thrilled to see it all the way through. The Epilogue is moving and beautifully put together. I look forward to what Red Thread will do with their next games, as they've grown a lot over the years.

This is essentially the greatest engineering game ever made. You can build air, land, water, and space vehicles, and great care must be taken to ensure that your vehicle is up to the task of fighting and winning against other vehicles. To do this, it needs engine power to run everything on board, a method of propulsion, weapon systems, and even sophisticated AI cores and detection equipment so it can "see" the enemy to shoot at it.
In short, if you like building stuff to roll/fly around but Besiege was too simple for you, give From The Depths a go. I highly recommend watching Robbaz's let's play series on it if you want to see some of the stuff you can do with it.

ANNO 2205 is a different beast from it's predecessor. Most notable among gameplay improvements is a virtual stockpile of goods; the game focuses on this mechanic of creating positive balances, and most other changes to core gameplay have been made around this one significant improvement over the last ANNO game. Skilled players will be able to balance their production at +0 and then focus on other maps, shutting out their competition and claming the free world for their own.
The graphics are really nice. Major improvement. Some of the buildings are re-used from the last game though, minus points for that.
Certain aspects of the game have been removed, but it's overall improved. For example, I can't find any sort of multiplayer in this game, but the online play for 2070 was clunky at best and perhaps it's worst feature. With the removal of a military presence and splitting the game out over different sector-maps, multiplayer is unlikely to return. Good riddance.
Speaking of the military aspects of the game, they have been shunted into side missions. In these side missions, you control a small (what do you call 7 vessels? A platoon? squad?) of  sea ships with different but well-balanced and amusing weapons in order to claim the mission's main objective and collect 'rare resources' vital to improving your settlements. If you aren't building modules: you really should be. Modules are really what was missing in 2070: the ability to upgrade production buildings and streamline chains in bulk rather than building 10 or 20 individual factories.
Annoyances? When you have to switch between maps, there is a small load time. However, as much as the developer has tried to segregate maps from each other, there is still some resource bleed. I can feel my game becoming sluggish the longer I play with 10+ trade routes and a civilization on all of the maps. The region maps are pretty samey, If I'm not paying attention I can accidentally spend up to 10 minutes on the wrong sector. Really wish they had put a little more effort into making the maps visually unique. The "tech races": Moon and arctic, often carry negative income balances by default, unable to pay for themselves without their supporting temperate race. This is a pretty glaring oversight.
Overall, this is a good buy. Worth the money. Should keep you entertained for a long time.

I really wanted to like this game.  Even with all the great games that came out within a month of this one; Legacy of the Void, Fallout 4, and SW Battlefront this was the game I was most looking forward too because when all other games start to get tedious and the story starts to feel stale, you could always jump back into an Anno game, start from scratch and get 20+ hours out of a single development.  Anno 2070 was a gold standard, it provided the right balance between city-building, combat between competing factions, and random objective / crises situations that could be resolved or ignored depending on how you wanted to play the game.
After a single 26 hour playthrough of Anno 2205 I can sadly say that this game diverges an astonishing amount from the incredible Anno gameplay style players have known and loved.  There is absolutely no challenge beyond resource balancing that occurs throughout the game.  After putting +250 hours into Anno 2070, I can say with a great deal of sadness that I wont be putting more than 30 into 2205, because there's simply no point in replaying.  Even on harder difficulties its just a matter of expanding and expanding resource production...no challenge, no replayability, the first and only playthrough most players will experience also starts to feel tedious after 10 hours.

I'm not just reviewing this game for the Steam Awards 2017. I'm not just reviewing this for the love of the game. I'm reviewing this game because of BOTH reasons. A truck simulator won 2 Steam Awards over Starbound, and I'm not going to have it happen again.

What a fun little castle builder!
I love games where I get to build a castle.  The Stronghold series is famous for that, but over time that aspect gave way for a combat focused.  There is combat in this game, however, it is not the meat and bones of it.  In fact, you shouldn't buy it for the combat.  In the end you'll build these tall towers that have weapons on top of them, and it totally ruins the look of the castle.  Instead, opt to play "easy" mode.  There is no combat what so ever, and really helps the game shine.
Once you learn the mechanics, it's fairly simple, but that's the fun in it.  You can design a castle, make a city like in Attack on Titan, or have a huge wall surrounding your city.  That's the fun in this game.  No fuss, no thrills, just fun castle building.
Don't expect much with the combat.  It's mostly tower defense.  It's not a RTS, you won't many hundreds of units, etc.  It's just a nice little addition.  Seeing a dragon fly over head is fun, but the vikings aren't too fun at all.
A great part is that maps can be randomly generated.  So you can build multiple little castles across islands, or one huge castle on a huge patch of land.  Or, you can build piers and make it a watery castle.  The choices are endless.
The devs have more things planned for the game in the future as well, so for the current price of $10, it was an easy deal for me.
The music and graphics are spot on.  The graphics are simple, but that really adds charm to the castle aspect of it.  The music is calming as well.  It's a fun, no fuss, city builder.
There are some popular, negative reviews, but what do people expect for $10?  SIm City?  No.  Don't expect that.  Expect a fun little castle builder.

Kingdoms and Castles is a simple game. The game itself hasn't that much depth, but if you are even a tiny bit creative, you might spend hours upon hours on this game. The gamemechanics are simple; place buildings, collect items, place more buildings etc. until you have a big town. Depending on what difficulty you play on, you might get random enemies, like the dragon and vikings.
After you have defeated the dragon/vikings or just lost horribly, you probably need to rebuild certain buildings of your town. Besides that, this game isn't that big. Although it had an update recently, the game lacks depth. I can spend a few hours on building a town and not come back for a month or even more.
The $10 / €10 price tag for this game is perfect. The randomly generated maps are big enough to let your crazy inspritation take over. Let's say you have a few hours to do something, but you don't know what. Solution? Play this game.
You don't need a beast pc to play this game. That's another nice part about this game; it doesn't have high specifications. The low-poly style art in this game is absolutely nice. It suits this 'arcade' game.
With a lot of (free) updates coming down the road, this game has a lot of potential. The developers may even rise the prices if they want (although I'd doubt that) after about a year. Recently the infrastructure update was added. That was a step in the right direction, but the game needs more, specificly depth.
So, the question remains; should you buy this game? I'd say yes, if you have the spare €10. You'll get your money out of the game you'll most likely spend hours on. With a lot of updates coming in the (near) future, this is looking like a good sign.

Dark Souls
A game about a repeating cycle of thinking you’re prepared for the worst only to find out that you ARE the worst.
It becomes an interesting case study into the psychology of human abuse. I spent many hours getting demolished by bosses (and even some basic enemies just quietly) and spent equally as many hours running back so they can demolish me all over again.
There was no tangible reason that the next encounter would go any better yet I kept going back - each time with an increasing sense of justification that I would ultimately attain that which I desired.
And you know what? I did.
Unlike an abusive relationship, Dark Souls rewards you for your perseverance and eventually (probably) one will emerge victorious.
So should Dark Souls be recommended with the knowledge that players will spend large portions of the game not succeeding, much like how I’ve handled most of my life up to this point?
I fear I may have gotten a bit too real so I’m not sure I’m qualified to pass judgement anymore but incidentally I’m about to load up another playthrough.
For those that accept the Dark Souls challenge, I leave you with one piece of advice - do not try jumping off.
Good Luck

Awesome little game. The free puzzles can keep you busy for hours. The game has a few settings that can make puzzles easier or harder, and puzzles vary between roughly 150 to 1000 pieces per puzzle. And you can use hints when you're stuck. So it doesn't matter wether you're a casual or a hardcore puzzler. The ingame Kiosk allow you to 'buy' ingame items with 'gold pieces' earned by completing puzzles. Most stuff in the Kiosk is pretty pointless and purely cosmetic, but it adds a bit of a reward-system. (Although completing puzzles is a reward in itself). The Kiosk also offers a few additional puzzles for sale, but you'd need a large amount of 'gold pieces' to unlock those. The game offers achievements for almost anything. You'll need all the DLC to achieve all the achievements. But that's up to you. You don't have to get ALL the achievements ;)
So, then there's the DLC. Lots of reviews already covered that part. I mean, you don't really have to buy ALL of the DLC. Just pick the packs you'd like, like you'd do in a real life toy store? (Buying all the puzzles in a toy store gets expensive too). Each DLC shows the images and piece counts of each puzzle included. Depending on the amount of pieces and your difficulty setting, each puzzle can keep you busy for one or more hours. Some DLCs are also available in bundles, giving you a small discount. And, you can always put them on your wishlist and wait for a sale.
If you're shocked by a game with over €200 worth of DLC, please do not check the total DLC price of Train Simulator. ;)

Sometimes even just making your way to the well scatted stores is a mission in itself, but for some reason having to chomp through hordes of enemies that are attacking you from every perceivable angle does not wane in fun value after you have left that area and come back to it again.
The graphics are clean, smooth and lovely to look at. The environments maintain a lot of diversity which makes stumbling upon new areas always exciting. Unlocking upgrades and the way in which you do is very fun and satisfying. I can't be the only one to start salivating when I come accross a giant heart!
The boss fights are AWESOME to say the least. There's so much happening, I must say this game has given me better hand-eye coordination because I slowly get better at dodging bullets (slowly).
You will die a lot, swear a lot (this is the first game that has actually made me scream out loud, lol), you will smile a lot and possible feel psychopathic.
Overall I give this game a 9/10 -- 1 point off for the lack of story, which isn't at all necessary to enjoy the game, but that would complete it. I also understand that controller support is in the works, so keep that in mind if you're considering this game! I think that would make it a hell of a lot better, which seems impossible!

This one is by far my favorite installment in the series (And I'm not even finished with it as of now but going by other reviews I've read I don't think my opinion is likely to change).Not to say that it doesn't have a few rather nasty flaws. For starters they could have toned down the political aspects a notch or two, especially during the first couple of hours you spend running around Stark. It quickly got to the point for me to where I was just rolling my eyes and wanting to rush through the campaign errands. It doesn't help that I'm playing the game during one of the most ridiculous election cycles in US history. When I turn the tv off and opt for some gaming instead, the last thing I want to be faced with is more political bs. So that aspect was rather disappointing to me and I view it as being inconsiderate on the writer's part to be imposing very strong views of a touchy subject onto their players. The other thing I found a bit annoying was how they didn't improve the speed at which you "jog" and yet there are enough back and forth "quests" that you'll be yearning for a rocket propelled jet pack after the first hour. Typical filler. Make it take 10 minutes to get from point A to point B and call it gameplay.
Now for the positives. The thing I love most about this game is the atmosphere. In my opinion it does an even better job of combining spirituality and magic with science and technology. With many games that attempt this, it's often too abstract and weird but here I find it enthralling. I liked that many of the characters found in the first two are still around and in some cases, more interesting. Nearly everything is choice driven and your choices do impact even minor details, which makes for better enjoyment of multiple play-throughs. The voice acting is fantastic, the soundtrack is beautiful, the graphics much improved and the story is mysteriously interesting. All in all it's a great adventure for the price.

This game has one of the best stories I've played through in a very long time.
When I Purchased this I didn't even know there was a previous game. Whilst I'm sure part of that game set some of the tone from the start that was only implied in this one I didn't feel like I'd missed out on too much between the recap and the bits of dialogue that explained the world as I played through this one.
The characters are believable and interesting, and the decisions from Chapter 1 onwards have affects on how the final chapter plays out. In fact, The final chapter doesn't even give you any choices, the entire final chapter is a single destiny decided by your previous actions.
I finished last night at 21 hours play time, and that was just the one playthrough (although there were moments when I got stuck) I never left the game playing for any significant amount of time. In my eyes thats a lot of high quality story content for my money.
It's difficult to endorse something without spoiling anything about the story. Especially when the thing that amazed me most was the depth itself of that story. I will say that whilst I have a lot of games in my steam library, the 10 hour mark is about the average playtime for a "good game" in my eyes before I discover something else to do (with a couple of exceptions) So for this game to keep me engrossed even as I had to wait for new episodes to come out until I finished it is a testement to how much I enjoyed and looked forwards to each chapter.
There were a couple of times when I did need to use a walkthrough to finish this, and there were a couple of graphical anomalies during utscenes (people turning around impossibly quickly before walking away, or suddenly appearing after the camera was facing that direction) that kinda hurt immersion, but I don't feel they were numerous enough to count against the plot. That said, they're worth mentioning, because if those things do really put you off games then it may affect your decision to buy.

Alas, all the polish and work that went into the game is for naught as it is still a disappointment both by modern standards as well as in comparison with the original The Longest Journey.
One of the biggest problems is that the political aspects are far too strident in this installment. While in earlier games you could see signs of the writers' political bent, it was still subtle enough, and integrated into the plot in such a manner that it was possible for people of nearly all political beliefs to enjoy the game to the full. With Chapters, it's difficult not to imagine the writing team as consisting exclusively of radical leftist progressives with neither the ability nor the desire to portray their opponents' arguments in a fair light. In both Stark and Arcadia, you are continually bombarded with messages that mirror modern-day political arguments on Twitter (as well as obvious references to Trump and Farage, comparing them - of course - to Hitler). The game doesn't *let* you be political neutral, it doesn't *let* you escape the mire of politics, which you would think is one of the reasons you are playing a game in the first place. As a conservative, these aspects significantly broke immersion for me, and made it difficult to get through the game.
The second major problem is that the ratio of gameplay vs. movie content is quite poor. Of the 20-ish hours you will spend watching the plot unfold, you will actually not do that much puzzling, acting and deciding. Most of the time you will either be watching cutscenes, or roam through an expansive landscape on your way to the next fetch quest. It's boring. Even the tasks themselves are boring. You spend a good chunk (time-wise) of the introductory part in Stark going to a job and to therapy. Why would I want to do that in a game? I get enough of this sort of "adventure" in real life.
There are other secondary problems with the gameplay and characters that add up to a disappointing experience overall. It's not a completely terrible game, but it certainly isn't worth the price tag and it does not live up to the legacy of the now 17-year-old original.

Superb game!
I was shocked to see that there was a more unanimous stance on this - especially since so many folks seemed to go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ over the previous installment - "Lords of Shadow". After exploring the mixed reception to this game, I think I figured it out:
People either wanted more of "Lords of Shadow" or more "Symphony of the Night". What you get with this game is an excellent mix of the original, NES Castlevania style, "Lords of Shadow", AND "Symphony of the Night". It has a lot of combat elements from "Lords of Shadow" in it (but not quite as complex, which is good), as well as many of the creature designs. It has a slight Metroidvania structure to it, but not quite as open as "Symphony of the Night" - fusing it with a slightly more linear style from the original NES games, as well as keeping the journey to the castle in the game (rather than SOTN's stle of taking place entirely in the castle).
The story was probably my favourite part. Fans of the original NES series will be pleased at how the characters and elements are slightly rewritten to form a cohesive, and brilliant plot.
Judged as its own game, without any expectations getting in the way, it was a very enjoyable play (I just finished playing it my second time through, so it was a good enough game to bring me back). I suppose I'll try it on a harder difficulty or attempt the boss rush mode next.
As far as true flaws go, there are some minor control issues, I found. Slightly stiff/slow. Nothing compared to the stiffness and slowness of the original NES games, of course.
This is one of my favourites, and I find that I enjoy playing more than its predecessor. While "Lords of Shadow" is impressive in many ways, I think it mostly comes down to the fact that "Mirror of Fate" doesn't suffer from the staccato breakup of levels and chapters that "Lords of Shadow" does. You can lose yourself in a larger, continuous environment.

An extremely enjoyable 3rd person "tower defense" game.
You pick one of two characters, both with different abilities, and defend against waves upon waves of enemies, mostly consisting of varying types of orcs. This may sound reptitive, but it's not.
You progress through the game by defending against these waves on different maps. Each map is different, consisting of choke points, mulitple spawn points, hazards and approaches. The maps take on a variety of locations, from mine shafts to castle interiors. As you complete each map, you earn a resource that carries through the game that can be spend on upgrading your towers, items and weapons. The game allows you to refund all points spent in such upgrades, at no penalty, at any time between maps.
Instead of building towers, you build traps. Traps can be placed on the walls, groud or ceiling. As you progress, you will unlock an increasing variety of traps, all of which can be upgraded in both effectiveness and to change or modify the function of the trap. Guardians, a type of "trap", are actually npcs that are placed on the gound and come to life to fight for you during each round. Traps and guardians are built using a currency earned by killing more orcs. You will also gradually gain access to an arsenal of weapons, each with a primary and secondary fire option, and useable items.
You have a certain number of "lives", with each enemy reaching the end of the map reducing a life by one, except in the case of larger enemies which can result in multiple life losses. Once you reach zero "lives", you lose.
I enjoyed the art style, graphics and gameplay, but no the story. However, this is clearly not a story-driven game, so do not buy if this is what you're looking for.
On the other hand, if you're looking for great visuals, a comprehensive unlock system, variety in towers, weapons and items and enjoyable combat then this game may be for you.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. The maps are well designed, the gameplay is solid. There is a great variety of weapons, traps, items and upgrades at your disposal. Enemies are varied, the visuals are great, and coop mode is fantastic fun. The only criticism I can offer is in regards to the story - however this game does not need one, so don't let that put you off. It has plenty more to offer.

Kingdoms and Castles can best be described as a City-Builder-light, with some defense elements mixed in. As much as I love this game, I do have to agree with many of the other reviews: this game is NOT for everyone. I myself have always been put off from the City Builder genre because of its commonly occurring, in my opinion, over-management gameplay, where you have to micro-manage almost every aspect of the city. I completely understand that the reason that people like the genre is usually because of the surplus of management, so if you are one of those people, this is NOT the game for you. I'd recommend getting some other city builder, because the thing that I like the most about the game you will hate, and that's its simplicity.
The simplicity of the game doesn't stop at the art style, it carries into its gameplay as well. You start out by placing down your centeral building, where three advisors stay and where you can store some materials. The advisors will give you updates and advice on city management, agriculture, and the military.
The resources in the game are food, wood, stone, iron, money, coal, and tools, and there is little management of them. You just place down storage buildings for them, tell them what you want and don't want, and your peasants will know what to do. Again, simple gameplay. This is good, because usually you'll be too buisy managing other things to care where they're placing the resources.
There is also general happiness, which is affected by a lot of things. The one thing that I really like is that happiness isn't just some overall thing, the happiness is different from peasant to peasant. This means that you have to watch where you're placing things like libraries, churches, and taverns. Also, this means that if you're having a crisis on, let's say, another island, only that island will be sad. Of course the average happiness bar will tell you that happiness has gone down, but if you click on it you can see happiness on a building by building basis. Happiness is also increased by not taxing them too much, having plenty of food, and access to basic resources.
When I was first attacked, it was kind of jarring. All of a sudden I had a billion problems on my hand that I had to deal with. We had food shortages because they attacked the farms and graneries, people were upset cause some homes were destroyed, and I honestly didn't know what to do. So I rebuilt, put down some defenses, and the later attacks didn't affect us as bad. Now, with my experience in dealing with attacks since then, I have 1 very good thing to say about it, and 1 very bad thing to say about it, so I'll start with the good:
It, like the other things in this game, is fairly simple. Spread defenses evenly around the city, reinforce your borders, and you're good to go. If you happen to have an exposed or undefended area, the AI will eventually find there way to that area and cause chaos. The bad thing about the defense elements is that it is very expensive. This means that there is little to no options for defense early on in games. Typically you'll have to wait until late-game before implementing the aforementioned reinforcements, because it requires a lot of stone to build. To give you some perspective, one stone wall piece costs more than the stone equivalent of building a mid-tier house.
Finally, my criticisms. Like I said, I really love this game, but that doesn't mean I don't have some grippes. For example, if you have some kind of food shortage, there is no short term solution. There just isn't. You have to put down more farm land and pray to the crop gods that it grows before winter. Else, you won't see a return on your investment for over a year, which at that point your city adviser will be driving you crazy with the constant "THERES NO FOOD" updates. Yeah, I get it, there's no food. You could've stopped the 30th time you said it and I would've understood.
Another thing, I feel like there should be more ways to speed up your villagers other than just putting down pathways everywhere. In my game, we currently occupy the in-game equivalent of an entire continent, and so resources aren't available everywhere. This means that when I want to build something in the city, I have to have peasants do a lot of walking. I feel like there should be some sort of horse, or stone pathways, or something that would speed them up more. Also, it would be nice to have an indicator telling you what month it is, and the current and upcoming weather events.
Overall, I really like the game. As I stated previously, the overwhelming micro-management turned me off from the city-building genre, but this game, for the most part, does away with that. There are a few complaints that I have, but nothing too game-breaking. Overall, I give the game an 8/10, but if you are into lots of management in city games, this is not for you.

This game is the first RTS since Age of Empires 2 that I have legitimately enjoyed.
The art style is so beautiful. I have a weak spot for 90° angles and flat, smooth colors since I'm in engineering. The art style was what made me pick it up in the first place, and honestly, for $10 it is definetly worth it. Like, at least for me, there are times where I wish I could make my village my wallpaper. (Devs, please add a No HUD hotkey for moments like this!)
I don't really have many complaints about the controls because it's an RTS. However, one thing I find difficult is making a General attack a Viking. 99% of the time, the click tells the General to move to the tile that the Viking is standing on rather than attack the Viking. By the time the General gets there, the Viking has moved on.
The UI for selecting save games could also use some refining, like adding borders around the picture, delete button, etc, just to make it look nicer. As of now, it looks out of place compared to the rest of the menus.
It's simple, which is good for me because when it comes to RTS's, I'm about as casual as it gets. Hence the last RTS I got hooked on was AoE2. However, I would like the ability to micromanage jobs. There are times where I don't want 4 people working in a quarry when there's a house that needs building, but I don't want to shut down the whole quarry to have everyone work on it. I'd like the option to add/subtract the amount of people on a job site.
Vikings, I feel, need a nerf to how they set buildings on fire. I think they need to take a certain amount of time to set a structure on fire, rather than it being set ablaze instantly as it does now.
Also, Churches/Libraries do not show you their area of influence until you place it. Wells, roads, and foresters do, so I hope it's an easy fix.
Also, I don't think wells should take up a whole tile, or at least be able to be placed on top of roads.
Music is great! Sounds mideval enough to be a part of the game. However, some songs I've noticed do not fade out. Instead they just stop and it takes me out of the world for a bit. No big deal, just wanted to bring that to the dev's attention.
This deserves a section all to itself because of how detailed this game is. Apples grow on trees in orchards, workers take an amount of crops at a time rather than the field suddenly becoming barren, Granary roofs actually open to show its contents! Seriously Devs, put that feature on more buildings. It's so cool to open roofs and peer inside! Peasants actually take the shortest route to their destination even if it means going off of the road or cutting a corner.
Being a college student who plays games on a Quadro M1200 rather than a gaming GPU, the game being lightweight really helps. Small download size, simple textures don't impact performance, and the options menu has just enough to make it run well. This game will definetly have a permanent seat on my hard drive.
I'll update this review as I think of things, because this game is as I said, the perfect RTS for a filthy casual such as I.

TL:DR:
First of all, I recommend this game, but barely. I personally give it 5/10 points, if you don't love building games and anno specifically, just drop it. Or read the review below and make your own score based on that.
This is, because I enjoyed it more than Anno 2070. Still, earlier games (starting with 1602 even) are all better in my opinion.
The game HAS some good potential and is fairly enjoyable on the first biome. Even the tacked on combat is fairly ok the first few tries. (but not on the long run)
The combat gets VERY repetetive on the limited maps and objective types. You just don't really have any fun after you beat all maps at least once or twice, than it gets tedious. It is fully optional though, so just let us leave that be.
In the game you have quests. Some are ok (like in Anno 2070, time wasters), but in most cases you have to repeat same stuff all over again - tow ships, tow drones, find some ridiculously small items on the map and click it (outrage!) or meet economic criteria - which would be fine, but NO - you have to wait from 5 to 15 minutes for it to complete (can do other tasks in the meantime though).
Than you have progressively unlocked biomes - Arctic and Lunar. Those are not really fun. All they do, is provide slightly different economy type and make it more difficult by having to build around factories (heat radius) or shields (anti-meteor shield on the Moon). All you get from that is different visual style and rarer resources, that you have to export to other biomes. And they never generate income (at least on normall or higher) - so the whole point is to build up/buy more temperate region biomes and use them as cash cows, so you can afford loosing hudred of thousands on arctic/lunar biomes. That makes them very unrewarding and as less you can build there, the better for you in general.
Eventually you will unlock energy transfer from the moon and ability to build HQ on your starting map (game goals).
For some weird reason, you have a money cap, dependent on your corporate level (so you can't generate cash in advance and one mistake can destroy your cashflow, no matter how high it would be).
So why the hell do I even recommend this game!? Becaue I spent some hours on it and don't really regret that. I liked some aspects of it, while I hated others, but I enjoyed it more than Anno 2070 at least. Keep in mind that many people disagree and like previous game better. It shares one thing with it's predecessor - it is too expensive for what it is.
Also, optimization is bad. I play on everything maxed, on GeForce 970 and i7 6700K, 16gb DDR4 3000mhz ram, and I get about 30-60 fps in normall play (mostly at 40-ish), and in combat when the flyby starts it can tank to 15 fps for a while. Not so much in normall play, but still.
With all that, game looks stunning, temperate biome building was pretty fun, other biomes frustrate a bit, but at least look different.
There is Voting mechanism (council) but it makes little sense to me.
Combat is used to get extra rare materials (there are 4 types). Those can not be mined, can only be acquired through missions, combat, small amounts when you level up your corporate lvl and you can also send them by using a companion app (a minigame, where you connect 3 or more diamonds).
As for the minigame, it is optional and it gives some easy missions at start, but later it promotes heavily the use of premium currency. You have to be REALLY lucky to be able to beat later levels without spending ridiculous ammounts of cash (which in turn make every puzzle increadibly easy). I do not review the companion app itself, but it is an insult. Exist not just to promote and make the core game more fun, but to look for whales that will throw cash at it to progress. One of the thousands of unethical freemium games out there, that you should avoid like cancer.

The majority may dislike this game, especially the Anno purists, but I've found myself enjoying it.  2070 was the gold standard for me and though 2205 is a vast departure from that design it isn't as bad as many claim it to be.  I agree that the game is a little too simplistic and could be fleshed out in a few ways to offer more depth.  There are what I would consider to be some missed opportunities.  But when I combine the good and the bad, I still come away wanting to recommend it.  If I were to assign a percentage, I'd say 60% of me likes it while 40% of me is left scratching my head over some of the shallow design decisions.
Here are a few positive bullet points...
- The game is beautiful.  Even on my GTX 760, the game runs very well.
- Setting up the balance of goods and trade routes is actually pretty enjoyable.  That being said, this is pretty much the centerpiece of the game.  This is all you need to do, but that task has a lot of sub-tasks.
- As simplistic as the game is, I can't seem to get enough of it.  That may change and I often question the replayability, but so far I'm having a good time.
- While I am not blown away by the storylines in each sector, I do enjoy the overarching questline to achieve something.  This also adds to the balance difficulty as I'm expanding.  If I need to increase a specific commodity (it's usually something really expensive to produce), I've had to be pretty careful in that venture as to not begin hemorrhaging cash.  I lost my first game as I was powering through the content and quests.  Before I knew it, I was in the red and couldn't figure out where things went wrong.  2205 will surprise you if you aren't careful.
- As you upgrade your buildings, the challenge to meet the needs of the new demographic presents itself prominently.  This is where you can really screw yourself over if you aren't careful.
Here are my reservations about the game...
- The mini-quests in each area are a waste of time.  Once you've done about 5-6 of the variations, it's a repetitive and mundane task to do the quests unless you need the reward.
- There is a distinct lack of depth on the resource side.  You create specific resources in specific regions.  No pre-req required, just jump right in.  For me, I missed the challenge of obtaining the correct fertility and building an island around the production of that resource.
- Also on the resource side, when you build the buildings, the resources are immediately available. There's no delay to allow production to ramp up and give you the feeling that there are some logistical challenges in opening a new factory/farm etc...small detail, but it was strange at first.
- Combat is separate from your region builds.  I'm not sure I understand this design decision, to be honest...If it weren't for the pestering of the NPCs to do my combat missions or the fact that I'd end up low on a rare resource, I'd probably never do them. When I do complete the missions, it's not a very robust system.  I hold down my + key a lot to speed things up and even if I lose a few ships, completing it on Expert difficulty isn't insurmountable.
It's not a BAD game by any means.
Did it fall short?  Most certainly.  The side quests and combat are questionable.
Will you still enjoy it?  I believe you will if you give it a chance. Start building up your moon colonies and you'll see what I mean.
UPDATE:  I'm still playing this game.  I really feel that anyone passing on this game will be missing out.  What's amusing is that I think I make the majority of my "rare" materials from the Anno 2205 Asteroid Miner smartphone game.  I haven't had to do a military mission since I posted this review.  One day, you'll buy his game and agree with me.  Whether it's now or when it's on sale for 5 dollars in 3 years..

To me this game makes it easier with knowing what you need and how much is being produced with out comprimsing the difficulty of the game itself to much. The core controls for the PC are atrocious.
The innate port is unplayable without mods. Lazy devs...This is the biggest reason why this review does not recommend the product; it is not optimised for the PC. As for the game itself...mixed bag of nails, man...even for a forgiving person. If I could factor the technical ineptitude of the devs who put this together for PC, I still wouldn't be able to recommend the game without heavy caveats. It isn't for everybody. I can understand and see what it is about, and if I had to give it a descriptions in less than a sentence it would be this--a dark fantasy theme park with focus on combat.
Once I started using a heavily modded version I have to say that the controls make sense. You will need to adjust to a few other difficulty layers after that. It takes practice for sure, as the popular opinion would have you believe. However, the lack of technical polish in this game insures that you are not consistent with combat. Combat, for that matter, is mostly slow and tactical. Things don't progress, they sort of trot--overarching blows, long stun times, not enough damage on enemies, ect.,ect. That doesn't quite work in favour of the game. Additionally, the game just doesn't give enough information about it's mechanics and items to make an educated decision. You also grind for stuff...That's kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥.. Mages initially, somehow overcome this by being able to nuke enemies; it saves you tons of time on boss battles, as well. So my advice so far is, just play a mage. All in all, you will have to get used to a lot of little things, like when does parrying work, and when does blocking work, and when does backstabbing work and when do skills of enemies pass through obstacles, ect, ect...it's all positioning mish mash, feels a bit archaic with an added flavour of distastful camera view at times. The good news is that combat is not unfair; there deffinetily is a method to everything, but you will need to spend time to learn HOW EXACTLY it is, because the mechanics do not really interact with you in a polished, smooth and intuitive way. Ultimately, the fabled Dark Souls difficulty comes from this phenomenon--you're technically hindered; one part from excessively prolonged and pronounced action times and moves, such as drinking potions, using throwables, overarching your swings and/or missing propper visual feedback/telegraphing from enemies in some cases, and one part pure lack of technical polish for the game, and, where present, platforming is atrocious. In addition, in some parts of the game your way back will be blocked by white light, which means you can get stuck with a boss in a very narrow space...most of those are fairly reasonable, but in some cases they are really messed up(Capra Demon, for instance), adding yet more artificial layers of difficulty to an already shaky design.
I am also yet to encounter any sort of writing or piece of story-telling that tells me more about the world. Everything I know is that I am Undead, some sort of...thing without a flame...a Chosen One...and that's it. More lack of information is what it is. For one, this is a role-playing game, but I don't know why most of the stuff wants to kill me...sure, a lot of the small fodder have gone hollow...boo...But there is a fair number of intelligent-looking stuff, and I don't understand why they want to kill my avatar, or why my avatar kills everytyhing with such abandon. I wanted to befriend Sif, for instance. But nope, gotta kill everything, man. That's the game. Who are the giants, what is Gwyn like, who is Prescilla, who exactly is Sif, what's the deal with Pin-Wheel, can I only stand dumb-founded in front of Gwynevere?... I am not sure the silent protagonist thing works very well in this case. The lore looks rich, the world feels detailed, but there is a lack of integration of the player into all of it. Some games overdo it...this one doesn't do it at all.
Level design is hit and miss. Some of the levels have got an obnoxious design. More like, time-wasting design. Platforming is plain bad here. The controls, even on a modded version or a controller just don't handle that stuff well. The Painted World is, without a doubt, my favourite level of the whole of Dark Souls. If you play it, you will understand why. The game tries to be very diverse with it's levels and environments, but in some cases it ends up being too much of a back-track.
The game is also crashing every time you want do anything else while it is running in the same time.
The game also appears to have broken geography. Somehow, I managed to fall through the floor and die in otherwise perfect conditions already.
With all things considered...this game is actually 6/10. It's lacking in a few key areas, can become repetitive, the vast multitude of enemies feel samey and are susceptible to one and the same approach. The game also has it's moments, though...Like that time when I fought the Stray Demon while being naked, holding a dagger with two hands and positioning to fill it's butt with spells, lol. This game focuses a lot on but pokes. And that's hilarious in a way.
Ultimately, if you wait to buy this on sale, or, as some people are speculating, the remastered edition, then you will be getting your money's worth. But as it is, the asking price for this is too high.

Yes, at first I was rarin' to play this game, because the trailer made it look like it had better AI. The one pet peeve I had with the first one was that the cops treat players differently than NPC inmates, letting the NPCs pretty much do whatever the hell they want (going through locked doors, being in other people's cells, etc). Surely this new sequel must have improved AI to make a better game! Nope, it's simply an illusion. While cops might *say* stuff to other inmates, nothing comes of it. Even in the sequel, I once beat up a cellmate and he ran away through a locked cell door, not letting me follow. The only improvement I can see is that NPC inmates get sniped during lockdowns or when fighting. Big whoop. Also, you can pretty much go wherever you want after attending your routine for 1 second without cops breathing down your neck. Basically the entire day is free time for you, making the game way easier than it should have been.
The other thing that was dissapointing was the new system of escaping. In the first game, you had to make up your OWN plan and play the long game for the right time to escape. Now, there's a series of pre-set escape methods that take only a few in-game days to complete each. Now, people may argue that "well the first game only had perimiter breakout" but that's the beauty of the first game -- you had to actually plan your escape route days in advance and it feels a lot more satisfying when you pull it off. Now in this game the only viable perimiter breakout is on Rattlesnake springs where you have to dig, and they literally put a giant cave under your cell. They make every other perimiter escape route on that map unnecasary because digging is WAY TOO EASY. And the vents in the sequel are useless, especially with these stupid "ride a dolphin" escape methods what all you need is 3 items to escape.
Pretty underwhelming once the hype of the first prison or so dies down inside you, and it removes the ingenuity that was iconic in the first game. There's literally little to no point of buffing stats anymore, because even the perimiter break only takes 5 ingame days to pull off. Zero-to-no replayability, most of my hours were just beating people up on center perks on repeat.
tl;dr: the game is way too easy, with little to no replayability. Severe lack of content.
So yeah, get the first one. It's cheaper, and you'll have more fun playing it in the long run, even with the 8-bit graphics. Honestly, I'm very dissapointed, Team 17. I won't be buying any DLC for this one.

is the sequel to Castlevania: Lords of Shadow and it was first released for the Nintendo 3DS. Gameplay wise, it differs alot from the first Lords of Shadow, instead of being a spectacle fighter, Mirror of Fate is a metroidvania in the strict sense of the word. That said, please be aware that the only games of the Castlevania series that I’ve played were Lords of Shadows and this one.
At its core it is an action adventure platformer in which you’ll find yourself backtracking to previous areas that you couldn’t previously access, and now you can because you have a certain ability or skill. The game is somewhat linear but there is alot of room for exploration which most often the not, rewards you with either more health, more magic, more ammunition or scrolls, which contain the last thoughs of fallen Brotherhood of Light soldiers.
The game takes place after the events of the previous game and lets you take control of Simon Belmont, Alucard and Trevor Belmont. The game is divided into three different acts and in each act you’ll play a different character, each one of them having their unique special abilities and weapons. There is some puzzle solving on the game, mostly on the second act and it is pretty good. It isn’t too hard nor too easy and this is coming from someone who tends to stay away from puzzle games and who doesn’t like doing alot of thinking.
The meat of the game, atleast for me, is the combat and the platforming. Platforming plays a huge role on the game, there are alot of areas filled with deadly traps and you need to have great timing to manage to get through. Combat is like the previous game, you start with very basic combos but as you make your way through the game and increase your level by earning experience, you’ll unlock more combos. Do not be deceived by the only two attack buttons. Not only you’ll unlock more combos as you progress through the game, but you’ll also unlock more weapons or upgrade your main weapon, allowing you not only to annihilate your enemies in new ways but also to access previously blocked areas and paths.
As it was the case with the previous game, you’ll be gradually introduced to new enemy types and each one of them felt unique on their own way to me. Bosses are also really well done, each one of them requiring you to adapt to a change in their attack patterns which helps keep the gameplay refreshing and challenging.
Now let’s talk about what I didn’t really like about the game. First of all, the fact that it is a 3DS port, even though it is in HD, doesn’t really help the game at all. The graphics look very dated with low resolution textures and on a 1080p monitor there are black bars on the sides. That said, I did find the cutscenes rather well executed with a cell shaded look to them, along the likes of Borderlands and Telltale games.
Even though backtracking is something characteristic of metroidvanias, and even though I’m a huge fan of the genre, I tend to get bored when going back to places that I’ve already visited. It would be nice if a new type of enemy would show up in these ocassions. But considering that it took me around nine hours to complete the game (not 100% though) I guess it isn’t that bad at all.
Mirror of Fate is a pretty well executed metroidvania and I recommend it to any fans of action/adventure platformers with a focus on combat and exploration, even if you’re not a fan of Castlevania. It has enough enemy variety to make you rethink your attack strategy and it features some nice sections of platforming.

The best aspects of the game are definitely the art assets and the visual style.
The story is fairly flat and simple, which is to be expected... The tone and atmosphere make up for this somewhat.
The game design is such that you spend too much time backtracking through a cumbersome very vertical layout with many loading screens.
Unfortunately I found the combat to be oddly clumsy.  Your weapon doesn't feel like it has any weight to it and it takes often a half dozen to a dozen hits to kill simple enemies.  Each enemy opponent can be dealt with almost in exactly the same way -- hit it until it retaliates and then vault backwards.  This is especially true because of how frequently enemies throw unblockable attacks.  The counter mechanic is basic and effective, but largely useless because of spammed unblockable attacks.
The boss battles are a saving grace, with real variety and difficulty.  However, you will often be hit by huge hotboxes thrown out constantly.  The gimmick I found the most irritating is lots of invincibility for the bosses, not only are you contending with their regular attacks and abilities being thrown out, but long moments of invulnerability where you basically engage in a mini game where your floaty character avoids giant hitboxes.
This game would heavily benefit from more polished combat and movement.  Moving a tall, floaty character around wide slow projectiles and slow telegraphed attack patterns can often feel frustrating and unrewarding.
