I'm an immense fan of the Castlevania series, that is up until the Lords of Shadow entrants. The series has never done terribly well in its forays into the third dimension and even though this game is technically 2D it falls into all of the same pitfalls that Lords of Shadow does.
What pitfalls are those? It wants
to be God of War. That's a problem because I don't like much God of War either.
Both games suffer from a series of major issues. They have dull combat with mushy, impactless attacks that just kind of wave a fan at the enemy until they either get cooled off enough to have a lie down and nap off a hard days being wooshed, or until they flash to arbitrarily signal its time to do a quicktime event, or push a button and watch something intended to be gruesome happen to them.
Those events are already a bit tedious to me but you throw in Mirror of Fate's lackluster visuals, amateurish presentation, schizophrenic camera that will give you motion sickness and generally humdrum design and you've got yourself a crappy Castlevania game.
The movement is floaty and imprecise, grabbale ledges which are already a big no-no to Castlevania are magnetized and suck you in, you break barrels instead of candles, your attacks are whiffy and weak feeling, dodging has no iframes that I could see, blocking is rarely useful as 75% of attacks are unblockable, and navigation feels like they just give the illusion of free roaming much of the time.
Perhaps I'm simply not the target audience, and I know I haven't gotten very far into the game yet but I'm extremely disatisfied with it. If I hadn't gotten this on sale for $3 from GamersGate I'd probably feel ripped off. I realize it's a port of a port of a 3DS game but the game itself is just not terribly appealing. If you're a fan of the oldschool Castlevanias ranging from the NES entrants to Symphony of the Night (which I still play through once almost every year) to the last decent release in Harmony of Dissonance, this is probably not going to whip your torches.

At the time of this review the price for this game is $14.99 and I would recommend picking it up, albeit with a tad of hesitance. I don't regret the purchase, but I feel like this is more of a $10 game.

While it fails to match the heights of the series Mirror of Fate is still a good time, for the most part.

So yes, this is a somewhat simplified Castelvania but it still scratches most of the right itch's and to its credit, there's a lot of good in here, fun, well-presented puzzle/boss setpieces, yep, a move set that starts out simple but really opens up as you play, yep, fantastic designs for the many monsters, yep, plus they don't let up on bringing in new ones.
I'm not gonna call it a platformer due to the lack of difficult platforming, well mostly, there are a few parts here and there, and some of them make up the most broken parts of the game, not hard, broken, like having to jump onto a moving platform that you can't see because the screen doesn't show it till your falling, this sort of issue popped up a few times and caused more deaths than most of the monsters combined and is easily the games biggest issue, but,
overall this is a solid 2D action adventure game that should entertain.

Top 10 Reasons To Play: Pixel Puzzles Ultimate...
#10 -- Your friends "triple-dog-dared" you
#9 -- You have recently won a contract to provide MTBF testing for several computer mouse brands, and need an application that requires massive amounts of clicks
#8 -- You are naturally good at puzzles, and you've often wondered how the rest of the world feels when trying to solve a jigsaw puzzle...  Pixel Puzzles Unlimited provides the complete "non-gifted-at-jigsaw-puzzles" experience...  every piece is a struggle, and you cannot join 2 pieces together unless you know exactly where they belong in the complete picture
#7 -- You just joined a cult that worships puzzles, and they require you to play to prove your loyalty and dedication to their beliefs
#6 --  You just spent 1000 hours trying to get an achievement on Bad Rats original, and you think nothing can be quite as frustrating...
#5 -- You have just been rescued from a puzzle worshipping cult, and your de-programmer feels this is the best way to convince you to never touch a puzzle again...
#4 -- You're a computer science major, but you never really embraced any method except for "brute force" solutions
#3 -- Your eccentric rich uncle has made your $1 million inheritance contingent on completing all Pixel Puzzle Unlimited achievements (run!  don't walk...  away...  it's not worth it at 10 times the price)
#2 -- Two crisp $100 bills happened to be lying in the street on your way home, and you somehow cannot think of anything worthwhile to spend it on.  Pixel Puzzles Unlimited is the game for you!  You need to buy at least $200 worth of DLC to get all of the Steam Achievements on this "Free to Play" game.
and the number one reason...
#1 -- You've come to the conclusion that many of your life choices were selfish and/or hurtful to others, and can think of no better self-imposed hell on earth
-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-
I have assembled hundreds of real jigsaw puzzles in my lifetime.  This game provides NONE of the same fun.
First, you cannot actually join any 2 puzzle pieces together.  Ever.
A puzzle piece will click into place *IF* you drag it very close to its exact position in the finished puzzle, and *IF* the piece is correctly oriented (you right-click to rotate between 4 possible orientations).
Second, the "cut" (shape of puzzle piece edges) of some of the puzzles boggles the mind.  Some piece edges consist of little wires or jagged shards or other equally nonsensical shapes.  I don't mind a little variation from traditional puzzle piece loops and holes, but these are ridiculous.
Third, the game has 700+ achievements.  Now, I like achievements, and I like them to be tough (no trophies just for showing up).
However, you can only get about 50 achievements from the free version.  Then it will cost OVER TWO HUNDRED DOLLARS of DLC to get the remaining achievements.
Lastly, BEWARE!
This is the first game (and hopefully the last) that made me go research this question:
"Dear Steam, is it possible to just UN-own a game?  Make it as if I have NEVER OWNED IT IN THE FIRST PLACE?"
Alas, the answer is:  Yes and No.
Yes, the game will be gone from your library (as if you had never owned it).
NO, the destruction to your Steam Achievements can never be undone -- you will always have this game dragging down your achievement history.
Parting shot:
I used to have a little digital puzzle game on a PC (I believe it was back when I was running Windows 98).  That game allowed me to attach any 2 puzzle pieces together provided they were a match.  So you could work a puzzle the way every normal jigsaw solving person does -- work common color groups until you determine where a block of pieces fits into the main puzzle.
I find it hard to swallow that somebody can call a product "ultimate", and not have features that were available 25 years ago...

You can clearly see that this is a low budget game. The story and characters are nothing but a big cliche. The voice acting is bad. There are sections in the game which have infuriatingly bad controls (I'm looking at you, laser room). And it's very short.
So, why do I still give it a thumbs up?
Because most imprtantly I had a lot of fun playing this game. It also has something that most AAA games don't have: it was made with passion. What's also surprisingly good for a low budget game are the character models and animations. It felt like they put a lot of time into creating them. I generally liked the character design in this game. As cliched as they were, the characters are very likeable, especially the main character who I personally adored. The level design was a bit questionable at points but offered a lot of variety. Ironically I wish they stretched out some parts of the game. The music also wasn't bad at all. So despite all the cons, this is a pretty solid and enjoyable game. It's not the best game ever made or a GOTY candidate, but most definitely exceeded expectations.

Well this one sure came out of left field. My owning this game is the result of just another "vote=key", and prior to getting the email announcing its release and my free copy, I had completely forgotten about it. Thank goodness I took the time to install and sample its gameplay, because this is one greenlight title that is very much worthy of actually being on Steam.
Sweezy Gunner is a bullet hell shooter, but unlike your typical shmup, this game lacks any sort of automatic scrolling screen or rage inducing bullet patterns with extremely specific safe zones. Rather, it's a free roaming top-down adventure, full of collectible abilities and purchasable upgrades.
As you move through the varying zones, enemies become tougher, and where you might once have only contended with a slow moving, delayed single-shot spewing hellspawn, new areas introduce enemies more than willing to litter the screen with little red doom pellets. Luckily, as the enemies grow in strength, ferocity, and number, so too do you earn the upgrades necessary to contend with them. The majority are simple; speed, strength, bullet velocity are the most common, along with basic health and defense upgrades. But the greatest benefit to your arsenal comes from dropped weapon types from the enemies you annihilate, like bullets that swirl around you as you move, rapid and wide shot, explosive shot, etc. Once you learn to juggle avoiding bullets and weaving your way in and out to nab pickups, the screen can quickly become an indiscernible mess of marbles of all colors wizzing across the screen in a rainbow of death and chaos. But don't worry, the price of death is a mere reset back to the beginning of whatever area you're in and a small loss of earned funds.
The game is broken up into two main parts, the first being the overworld, where you will spend at least half of your time getting from point A to point B. The overworld contains several themes, depending on your location, as well as varying types and difficulties of enemies. The second major part are the dungeons: contained levels with their own specific themes, often with the express goal of finding an exit and reaching a new part of the overworld. I won't spoil the steps you'll have to take to escape these dungeons, but i will recommend that you take the opportunity to use healing machines whenever you find one.
The many upgrades you can buy come in several forms. You can purchase them from the shops that pop up, both in the overworld and the dungeons, but these will only increase as you collect special coins that unlock more upgrades as you progress. The other sort of upgrade comes from special cards dropped by enemies, requiring you to kill a certain number of them before being able to buy the upgrade the card holds. Lastly, there are special secret cards that can only be found by exploring every inch of the map, and while these can be devilishly difficult to find, the benefits speak for themselves.
In the end, Sweezy Gunner was an excellent surprise, its only real limits are likely caused by the program used to create it. Even if you're not a fan of typical bullet hell games and their no holds barred difficulty, I would recommend you give this one a shot; you will undoubtedly enjoy your time with it, and the difficulty is right on the money with a casual, albeit frenetic experience that anyone can enjoy.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge - Director's Cut is a 2D platformer with some RPG/Metroidvania elements. Note that this is the only Shantae game I've ever played so I can't say how it is in relation to the series. The simple version of the story is that Risky, the villain, has stolen a magic lamp that has great evil powers. The only way to unlock the powers, however, is to use the three magic seals along with it. So your job is to collect the seals first and stop this from happening. Also, your job was to protect Scuttle Town and... in failing to stop Risky's theft you have been fired from your position of protector and asked to leave... so you must also do this task to prove your worth to the town's mayor.
You play as Shantae, a half genie that starts off being able to run, duck, jump, and whip enemies with her hair. As the game progresses you will gain more powerups. You find items to increase your health. You will find the power to transform in different animals, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, along with their own unique abilities that will help you access new parts of the world as well as find secrets. There are items available for purchase in a shop in town. Some are spells that you can use for more range and protection at the cost of magic. Some are refills for health or magic. Some are upgrades, like getting the ability to have dropped treasure gravitate towards you or better versions of your attack spells. Some of the upgrades and items will also cost a number of magic jam jars, which are hidden throughout the world as well. This makes your choices of what to buy and when more interesting. Thankfully, there are warp points and a map you can pull up to help get you from place to place faster for backtracking and exploring. The game does an interesting take on managing space. Instead of making a map very long or tall, it has you jumping into different planes, forward or backward, in order to move around the world and give it some semblence of 3D space even though the game is all 2D. There are some neat boss fights and a few interesting puzzles in the game. It's just a lovely mix of elements I really enjoy.
The game isn't that hard, but it's very satisfying. I like the music. The graphics are vibrant and colorful with fluid animations. The sound effects are crisp. It basically does what most Kirby games do. It mixes pleasing music, sounds, and visuals with cute art and fun gameplay. It's a bit more complex than most Kirby games and a different kind of gameplay, but you get the idea. It's rather simple, but it's fun. Also... sexy ladies everywhere. I mean... come on. I guess I should mention that the characters in the game actually have personalities and some of the dialogue made me genuinely laugh, which many games that try to be funny have failed to do. That's a nice touch. The game is charming, performs well, and does a lot of things that I really enjoy.
That's not to say there are no downsides, but I didn't find many. You could say it's too easy, but that depends on your own definition of easy or hard. You could say it's too short, but that depends on what you consider short or long. And also, I have to admit that while it wasn't that hard, it was fun. Plus, it didn't FEEL short to me, regardless of the 9 hours of playtime, which I honestly think is fine. Those are just possible problems you might have. The only real problems I came across while playing were a lack of dungeon maps and difficulty remembering where all the secrets were. The secrets aren't marked, which makes sense, but sometimes I'd think I had been to a place already and find out later I hadn't gone back to get that secret because the area looked the same as another. More my own fault than the game, though. And none of the dungeons are too big to navigate so the lack of a map inside them wasn't too terrible. Aside from that, I had a screen sizing issue that I found a quick fix for in the forums, but it still shouldn't have happened to start with. And the last thing is the weird adjustment of hitting B to confirm things and A to cancel them. It's not hard to adjust to that, it's just a weird thing to adjust to and it can make navigating the menu for the first time a bit confusing.
Overall Shantae: Risky's Revenge - Director's Cut is a very good game. It's well designed with fun gameplay, good control, interesting metroidvania style, colorful 16 bit graphics, low to moderate difficulty level, good music, and some sexy art. It's a wonderful experience. I got it gifted to me when it was on sale for 2.50, but even at the full 10 bucks, it's worth price. Shantae: Risky's Revenge - Director's Cut gets a 9/10 for being a charming retro style platformer that prioritizes fun.

This game is worth your time if you like metroidvanias, but be warned: it's quite easy and very short. What content there is here is pretty fun; Shantae runs and jumps through some quite pretty environments and whips assorted weirdo monsters to death using her hair, all the while searching for secret rooms and powerups.
The game is quite pretty, full of bright colours and fun animations. The sound is somewhat less sharp, though not objectionable, albeit the voice sample played when Shantae falls in a pit seems totally out of place. The dialogue is definitely weak, being liberally salted with fourth-wall-breaking "we know we're in a video game" lines and overdone pop culture jokes that it doesn't even bother to get right (not to be that guy, but kneeling by the cliff with the *white* crystal won't do a dang thing). Fortunately, the dialogue is also irrelevant, and can be entirely ignored in favour of getting back to the game. The one thing that DOES manage to be funny in this game is the names of the antagonists: Squid Baron, Ammo Baron, and Hypno Baron indeed. That's charmingly madcap.
In terms of gameplay, Shantae is a tightly-constructed action platformer. The controls are precise and fluid, and none of the challenges ever come off seeming "cheap." There are quite a few different powerups for Shantae to collect, most of which are even useful. The one downside is that there isn't really much challenge here; a few tricky jumps now and then and that one room in the Hypno Baron's castle with all the skeletons in it, but other than that, clear sailing.
Overall, definitely pick this one up if you like Metroidvanias, but be aware that it is easy and short; my first playthrough took less than five hours start to finish, and I wasn't exactly racing through.

This was a tough game to review. I could get behind the cutesy aesthetics, since they had a charm to them, and I will admit that the gameplay had good handling. Your animal transformations, which should be the bulk of the game, don't really do much for you except get through small traps and whatnot. As for items, most are useless. you'll use one or two, and then leave the rest.
The bottom line? Not a bad deal for 10 dollars, I know. If you're a fan of the series and metroidvanias, I would give this title a try if you haven't already, but get it on sale like I did. I assume that most people have already played it since it's so old. It's no La Mulana or Cave Story though, so don't go in expecting a masterpiece.

Anno 2205 is beautiful. No, it's not the same complexity of trade network routes you probably pulled your hair out over in Anno 2070 but for a lot of people that's ok too - hair pulling makes you bald. I had a real love/hate relationship with 2070 and when I last played it in anticipation of this one coming out, I remembered all the reasons I loved it - and hated it.
Anno 2205 simplifies and streamlines a lot of things in the economy and building process. It seems to focus more on the overall story and bigger picture (getting to the Lunar colony phase) for your "Corporation" rather than precise detailed production balance and trade routes that were the biggest challenge in Anno 2070.
So, my recommendation:  If you've never played any of the Anno series and you love futuristic technology games mixed with map based city-building strategy then you will probably enjoy Anno 2205. If you were an Anno 2070 fanatic and are hoping for a game exactly like it, you might be slightly disappointed in this one even though most of the controls are still the same and they've improved on some things (like copying buildings).
No doubt about it, this game is real eye-candy and is casually enjoyable. It's NOT a hardcore economy strategy game though, and it's NOT a hardcore RTS combat sim either. It falls somewhere in the middle of city builder and story-driven space colonization simulator with a dash of simple economy and supply/demand thrown in for fun. "Fun" might cost too much for some at the price of this game but being a long time Anno fan, it was worth it to me but I'm able to overlook the simplified interface and economy objectives and enjoy it for a more casual but gorgeous game.

After nearly 60 hours of play time my impression is definitely positive.
I started playing Anno 2205 on the middle difficulty setting and it felt somewhat challenging at first but by the time I finished the tutorial storyline I was confident in my building techinques and easily maintained multiple profitable export routes.
The hardest difficulty setting is tough because money comes much less easily.  Instead of being able to rely on keeping your employees content and have them passively generate all the money you will ever need , profitable export to the world markets becomes much more important.  And since producs fluctuate (sometimes quite wildly) in value in accordance with the vagaries of supply and demand, yesterday's most golden egg can quickly become tommorrow's dead weight.
Anno 2205 is more streamlined than the previous version, eliminating some of the micromanagement of that game.  No longer must every island have to balance its own population of workers; in 2205 they have learned how to commute where needed.
There is also no need to micromange trade routes: goods flow automatically within the same sector and trade between sectors does not require ship building. In fact ships have been removed as buildable units for both trade and war.  Instead combat occurs in its own, optional sector as a somewhat separate minigame where the ships you own are automatically available at the start of the map.  Larger and larger trade ships become available at higher corporation levels, at progessively increasing mainteance costs.  Both of these are welcome changes.
So what exactly are sectors? It's how Anno 2205 makes a global corporation actually feel like a world player.  Each sector has a theme, and there are three of them: temperate sector, arctic sector and lunar sector.  The temperate sector plays most similarly to Anno 2070 with islands, employee residences, public buildings, factories and natural resources waiting to be exploited for fun and profit.
The arctic sector is where the scientists live and it's a bit different. Heat is generated by factories in a radius around the building.  Residences must be built within that radius.  This gives the layout of your arctic city a distinct feeling and gives rise to an interesting variation on optimal layouts compared to the temperate sector.  Maintenance costs are a bit higher than the temperate sector so a little more care has to be given to choosing when and what to build.
The final sector, the moon, is different again.  The moon is a harsh environment and buildings must be protected by forcefields due to the  constant danger of meteor strikes. It is also the most expnsive sector from high construction costs, to steep mainteance expenses, to the mostly costly transfer routes back down to Earth or the world market.  This means that unlike your temperate sector where life is easy you will need to carefully manage exactly what buildings you need and exactly how much population you are willing to support. Simply expanding your base willy nilly to every corner of your chosen crater is a recipe for swift bankruptcy.
I am really enjoying Anno 2205. I have over 400 hours played on its predecessor.  The new types of sectors are interesting and challenging in their own rights.  While negatives effects like pollution and bad weather have been removed I am not too sorry to see them go.  I look forward to seeing if the newest version will hold my interest for just as long.

Finally, years after its release, I can count myself among those that have finished Dark Souls! Writing a review now doesn't make a lot of sense I suppose, but I'll still say a few words.
This game is beautiful. No other ways to say it. It's also challenging of course, but not as hard as people would make you believe. The reason, and in my opinion the only flaw this game has, it's that it doesn't seem to be balanced around weapon upgrading. Note: I've gone full melee, I'm not really sure about the balancing of magic builds.
Meaning, the game will be really hard and punishing until you reach the first blacksmith (10 hours or so?). After that it gets progressively easy, with you being allowed to make more mistakes, dying less, killing bosses with fewer attempts (why are the Four Knights so easy?). All it takes is levelling up a decent weapon and armor.
The playthrough can be much harder if some "mistakes" are done in choosing the next area (or when starting the game, spent two hours trying to go though the graveyard before realizing it wasn't the right way). I liked the DLC, even if I keeped it last it provided a greater challenge than the final boss himself.
So... If you haven't played it already, go for it. The first hours will be painful but extremely rewarding. If it feels too hard, you may be going in the wrong direction. Have fun.

Mirror of Fate
Rating: 7/10
Overview: 2D Action/Platformer
The Good:
+ The story takes place between Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 1 and 2 focusing on the adventures of Simon, Trevor and Alucard. Each character has their own light and dark spells.
+ The combat is identical to Lords of Shadow, I really enjoyed the combat system so I felt really at ease getting use to the mechanics again.
+ Collectables to upgrade your character providing incentive to backtrack through previously played levels
+ Boss battles are fun and challenging. Boss designs are really well done.
+ Boss rush mode allows you to fight  every boss back to back.
+ Soundtrack
The Average:
+ The graphics do look like a 3DS port. The graphics are not bad but low polygons and low res textures hurt the overall look and aesthetic of the game.
+ I found the platforming to be a bit 'floaty'. Jumping near a ledge would automatically place your character on it. It never feels as precise as it be.
Conclusion:
This game is not a typical metroidvania game. You play with three separate characters each with their own level layout and the majority of the level layout is linear. Backtracking is only necessary if you want all the collectables. IF you love 2D action platformers, this is a great game to pick up, it is not as polished as other games in the genre but if you can pick this up at discount then I think you will enjoy yourself.

Mirror of Fate is an attempt at bridging the new Lords of Shadow style with oldschool Castlevania. It does not work. The game is riddled with lazy QTEs, bad combat mechanics, and obstacles that just feel forced. Briding the gap between LoS 1 and 2, this is basically Lords of Shadow's version of Alucard's origin story, and they make it pretty obvious. By the time the "big reveal" at the end played out, I had already figured it out hours ago and was just bored. There's also an extra cutscene for those who feel like wasting enough time on this game to complete it to 100%, but said cutscene does nothing to set up anything interesting. Good try, but ultimately, poor execution.

For an early access game, this is a neat game. It has almost no game-breaking bugs, in fact hardly any glitches at all. The graphics are somewhat cute, and fun to see. In the early to mid game, it is very challenging. Once you start to get to later parts of the game, though, it is plagued by something that plagues many of these early access games. It becomes fairly easy, and somewhat boring. This game doesn't have a clear cut "goal", not even challenges or anything like "kill 10 dragons" or something. The AI is pretty impressive, however once your town really starts to get large, it can get fairly annoying. For instance, it doesn't matter how much food you have, but chances are, you will always have people starving. Even if you have enough food to feed your town for years, it is never enough. You are supposed to use markets to distribute goods to the villagers, but even when I have a market every couple blocks, people are still starving. Its gotten to the point where I just accept that people will starve, and anticipate it. The same issues follow the charcoal as well. Apparently each building has a maximum range that the AI will walk to get food and/or charcoal, but that range seems kinda small. Especially when it comes to food, I mean cmon, apparently my villagers would rather starve then have to walk across the town to the farms. But those two things are the only things I have found in the game that can be annoying. No annoying glitches, everything works as it is supposed to. Sure, a few things could use some polish and buffing, but this is a functional game. Between having 1/4 of your entire population (several hundred people) die of disease, having a dragon appear and light a bunch of stuff on fire, having vikings attack and the ogres to start rampaging through the town after breaking down your thought-to-be-invincible walls, the viking footsoldiers trying to steal all your villagers while you chase after them with your armies, or a single viking warrior charging your entire town, this game is fun. It is very challenging at first, however once you get later into the game, start building superwalls, with multiple layers, and having an army of 100-500+ men, it begins to get way less challenging.
Beautiful game with a good soundtrack, but looking forward to more as it is getting repetitive.

This is a good game. Make no mistake about it.
But is it a successor to Anno 2070?   Probably not.
Now I must admit, I arrived in the "Anno" series quite late, 2070 was the first I ever played. And even in that, by the time I bought it, I got it as a Steam bundle with all of the DLCs etc. And it is quite possible, this set the bar for my expectations for 2205 too high. In 2070 there were tonnes of missions, a main story line, random maps and so on - so many angles to play, so much variety. 2 Main factions to choose from, and an reaching the top tech tiers was genuinely challenging.
In comparison, 2205 seems very empty. Only a main storyline to play through, not much point to keep going once you complete it, no factions to choose from for replayability. In short, it desperately needs DLC, and lots of it. It feels more like a game engine than a game, at times.
But all this aside, 2205 is a great game. It is only in comparison with its predecessor that it comes out lacking. Had I never played 2070, I would have enjoyed 2205 from start to finish and never given it much thought.
Not worth its full price tag however, not by a long shot. There´s simply not enough game to justify the price. Buy it on sale.

Far from flawless, but ultimately very enjoyable metroidvania game starring everyone's favorite Half-Genie Shantae.
Let's start with the problems. This was previously a Nintendo DS game that was then ported to iOS devices. Graphics are reminesent of DS hardware capabilities and looks warmfully similar in style to PS1/Saturn era 2D titles. Unfortunately port job for PC is poor. Framerates on weaker machines are pretty bad and the fullscreen mode is just a screached-out image that simply looks pretty bad. Pixel art itself is really good. It's pleasure to watch if you can bear 4:3 ratio. Other than that, the map system is utterly stupid and the gameplay could use a bit more content in terms of combat variety. Luckly/Unluckly game is quite short, so the limitations of combat and low number of locations and drawn character portraits seem like they aren't a big problem. It's noticable, but not deal-breaking.
Those look like a pretty big faults, but at the end the game won me over. Story is very tongue-and-cheek, peepered with enough jokes to keep things interesting. Platforming action is very good, especially in two main dungeons of the game. Not only it's really fun and satisfing to traverse those nicely designed labirynths but also music and graphics build a pretty "adventurish" feel. Overworld areas are also quite good, full with hidden goodies. Completionists will be satisfied. Power-ups and other metroidvania stuff are here, Shantae throughout her journey gains few animal transformations activated via belly dancing (don't ask) and those work very well. they provide mobility tools, combat aids and other features that are used to clear paths to next levels. There is a noticeable share of backtracking, but those sometimes are companioned by some really ridiculous and funny story explanations (for Zombies coffee is a very important resource apparently), so those aren't very bore-inducting.
This game is a easy and good bet when you see it on sale. It's short but sweet, satisfying and full of joyful personality. Far from perfect, but it should be good enough for your 2D exploration-combat-platforming craze.

I am in the minority but if asked to list the best Xbox 360 games, Castlevania Lords of Shadow(LoS) is no doubt on the list. It embodied everything i like about an action game. It had massive enemy variety, exploration, puzzles, challenge and story. The second chapter in the LoS series Mirror of Fate tries its best to maintain that original blueprint and succeeds while channeling its classic Castlevania roots while suffering graphically due to its original development being completed on the 3DS.
Mirror of Fate tells the tales of Simon, Trevor, and Alucard after the events of LoS. The story is broken into 3 acts where you will take control of one of the said characters but all the stories are actually intertwined. As an example if playing as Simon you may receive help from Alucard. In the second act playing as Alucard, you will find out why and how you helped Simon. This keeps the story interesting but too many hints are thrown around for a surprise ending like LoS. Overall the story is still good and best of all it feels like a Castlevania game.
One of the best things i like about the 3 characters setup  is the variety that each brings to each act. As you level you will unlock attacks which every character will use, but the differences are just minor movement or special abilities for each that keeps combat and exploration fresh throughout the game. As Simon you can carry axes and flasks of oil to set enemies on fire and he also channels the ability of a spirit who can be used as a shield, or a spirit of an archer who will attack when enemies are in range. As Alucard he can slow time, change into a wolf to climb certain walls and do more damage, but he can also turn himself into a mist and he has wings to jump higher. When playing as Trevor he carries boomerangs and electric shock grenades and his special abilities are using light magic which can regain health from attacks, or shadow magic which increase damage. This variety is one of the game's strengths as each act felt like a new game.
Certain expectations come with a game bearing the name Castlevania and thats combat, bosses and exploration. I loved looking for secrets and exploring the castle and most of all when they are important as you will need each and every upgrade in order to defeat the bosses.Though the setting for Mirror of fate does not change drastically for each of the 3 acts, each individual character you play will approach each section differently making each act its own. The changes come with the enemy types and abilities your characters will learn. Most of the first act involves combat, the second introduces some puzzles and the third act most bosses, excluding the end, are done with QTE’s and there is also more platforming.
Enemy variety and challenge continue to also evolve as you make your way thru the game. I never found the regular enemies outside a few challenging(damn puppets) but they will all keep you on your toes. In order to increase difficulty a lot of games will overwhelm you with numbers which then forces you into basic button mashing but Mirror of Fate avoids this trap. Instead it throws a small number at you and lets you use your skills you have learned more strategically. This makes the enemy encounters more of a dance than the normal chaotic hit x,x,x,x,x. Just as in the original LoS i was constantly looking at my abilities and bestiary for my best attack combos. This made combat super satisfying, fun and never frustrating.
Just as everything else the bosses in Mirror of Fate come at you with a ton of variety and higher challenge. They all follow the rule of three and none seem to be unique(historically) but beating each was still super satisfying and of course beating Dracula had my hands sweating. I always am amused when the first boss, to me, was not only the hardest but the most unique of all the boss fights. Also if i kept track, when i did finish a boss i barely had any health left making for very tense encounters. One thing i did like a lot was the game allows you to leave a boss fight in case you feel overwhelmed and need to go level.
Usually when i come to summoning up the negatives i have a few to list but in this case for Mirror of Fate the only negative to me was the graphics. Banzai Escape is a port of the Android rail shooter of the same name. Given its origins as a mobile game, the graphics are about what you would expect, which is to say not very good. Strangely enough some parts of the game seem to suffer from performance issues as well, which is not something you would expect from a game designed to run on a phone. In a rarity for a mobile port, the game actually features graphical options like resolution, fullscreen or windowed play, shadow detail, and anti-aliasing, which was a pleasant surprise.
The game suffers from fairly significant input lag, to the point that it can take multiple seconds to force the character to reload or pop in or out of cover, which can quickly prove fatal. I would not describe the game as difficult per se, though I agree with the game's description in that you will die a lot. The game is about 90% memorization and 10% skill. An example occurs in the first level when an enemy charges you with a knife. You have just a few seconds to shoot him before he moves outside of the area you can aim at, at which point he kills you instantly.
Banzai Escape features a swap cover feature, but there is no indication of where or when you can swap cover. More than once the cover you will swap to is not even visible on screen. You can only press the swap cover button on each screen and see what happens. The game also fails to mention that even behind cover, you can be killed while blind firing or reloading. I'll accept the blind firing part as you are exposing part of your body to shoot, but you are still entirely behind cover when reloading. In one early level, you can be killed even while behind cover and neither blind firing or reloading.
Expect to grind a lot. You will need money to purchase new weapons and increase your ammunition capacity, which will have you playing the same few levels many times.
The writing and the voice acting are not very well done, though the game does deserve some praise for featuring English voice acting in addition to the written dialogue. The translation is perfectly serviceable, I had no difficulty understanding what was going on.
As mobile ports go, this one was handled pretty well. However the game itself is frustrating and generally not a lot of fun to play. If you do choose to pick the game up, I would recommend waiting until it goes on sale.

Dreamfall: Chapters is the third instalment of The Longest Journey Franchise. First there was a point and click adventure called The Longest Journey staring a female protagonist called April Ryan. I cannot comment heavily on that game because it is the one I have not completed. From what I have heard it is considered one of the best adventure/point and click games of it's generation/all time with an outstanding story which I believe is the greatest asset about all three of these games. In 2006 Dreamfall: The Longest Journey was released and is one my personal favourite story driven games ever. I think Zoe Castillo the main female protagonist of both Dreamfall: The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: Chapters is a great character and is personally my favourite female protagonist of all time. When I played and completed the game I felt very emotional about the story and the world and had so many questions due to the cliff hanger ending.
I never had any idea that there would be follow up to it and was very excited when Dreamfall: Chapters was announced. Dreamfall: Chapters took an episodic approach which I'm personally not a great fan of, however that doesn't means anything now as the whole game is fully released. I was very excited during Book One trying to get answers to the questions left at the end of Dreamfall: The Longest Journey. However by mid Book Two I really lost interest and was very disappointed and felt like it wasn't a good successor to the prequel. I left the game for a good six months, by which time all the Books had been released. I came back to it and started to become invested again in Book Three to Book Four. I personally felt that the ending was very good and satisfied my answers to the cliff hanger at the end of Dreamfall: The Longest Journey that was my primary reason for being so invested in Dreamfall: Chapters.
As a game I personally don't think Dreamfall: Chapters gameplay is great. This game is a puzzle/adventure game but I personally thought it was a mediocre experience at best in this area. All combat has been removed from Dreamfall: Chapters, not that this is a really bad thing as it was a very basic system in Dreamfall: The Longest Journey
Subjectively this series story I feel is as good as The Last Of Us, I'm sure a lot of people may disagree but that's a personal belief. The reason I say this is because not many games have made me feel as emotional at the end of the game like these two series have.
Gameplay 6/10
Story 10/10
I recommend this game and also this is not just a recommendation for Dreamfall: Chapters I recommend playing Dreamfall: The Longest Journey as well before this and maybe the first game in the series The Longest Journey before that to give you a better understanding of the world and the characters than I believe the recap available does.

Dreamfall: Chapters was a bit slow to capture my attention in the way I hoped it would. The majority of the first three books are primarily concentrated in two major settings. For anyone who has played the previous two games this might be a bit of a buzz kill considering a lot of their charm came from a seemingly endless stream of places to explore. That being said, the two worlds of Stark and Arcadia have both been remastered from their 2D predecessors, and the results are pretty cool. Propast has to be one of the best virtual cyberpunk cities I’ve ever had the pleasure to explore. You can tell a lot of time and effort was put into making this city stand out and I want to commend the team for coming up with what is probably my favourite part of this game (seriously thank you).
My one really major issue with the environments is the maps, which I found largely unhelpful. I eventually just learned my way around the cities, although that was after multiple play-throughs. Don’t even get me started on Crowboy, haha.
As for the story, like I mentioned before this game was a bit slow to grab my attention. Similar to the previous games there is a lot of story packed in; between the protagonists, side characters, and general lore this game tells an epic tale. However, I think the story really only starts to come into stride in the last two books. If you find yourself losing interest by book 3 like I did, hang in there! I think some of the story might be lost on you if you haven't played the first two games, but if this is your first time playing a game from this series you can prepare yourself for some pretty interesting Star Trek-esque social commentary on humanity’s relationship to corporate power and greed. Chapters also highlights race issues (albeit rather un-originally), and class tensions, which I dig a lot.
On to characters. I love Zoe. She’s changed a bit from the second game, but after what she’s seen, who wouldn’t? Overall I really enjoy her commentary, and the “choices & consequences” aspect of this game lets you have a bit more control over her character development, which is cool.  Kian on the other hand… I think they tried in the end to save this character (by giving him a hipster haircut and a weird sense of humor) but ultimately it was too little, too late. Kian’s backstory was cliché, and his personality flat as the soda you opened and forgot in your fridge two months ago. His story with the mysterious woman was largely unnecessary and frankly uninteresting.  For the protagonist in a game Kian is surprisingly forgettable. There are, however, countless new and returning characters that are quirky, interesting, and memorable; I especially love the bots. For the most part the voice acting is very well done.
I've played enough fantastic choices and consequences games (Life is Strange, The Wolf Among Us, etc.) to know that Chapters is not one of them. However, the choices aspect of it does add an interesting element to the overall gameplay.
While I think the developers may have stretched themselves a little too thin to make any one aspect of this game phenomenal- except I would argue, for Propast- the game is definitely worth the time and money. If you don't want to spend 30 bucks (which is understandable) wait until it's on sale. I suspect you'll get at least one replay out of it. Overall this is a good game, and I definitely recommend it if you are a fan of point-and-click epic fantasy tales.

The game itself is fun and relaxing and even though it doesn't include a tutorial it's still very easy to pick up by having a simple and uncluttered interface. I was able to pick up and dive straight into this game without any problems as a result and it wasn't long before I had a small kingdom in the works. Riiiiight up until my first viking invasion and I lost a reasonable proportion of farms and houses because I kinda skimped on the defenses! :P
K&C has various difficulty levels to choose from to suit your play style and I believe is randomly generates maps for you to play on. However, all maps are of the same size, although I have no idea what that size is. It's just that everything is randomly generated within that grid. I think...
The main purpose of the game is to build up your kingdom, fulfilling the needs of your peasants whilst building defenses to protect them from dragon or viking attacks. And maintaining a balance so your peasants don't starve or become too unhappy whilst having the resources necessary to grow and defend your kingdom is the idea behind the game. Which I'm finding slightly addictive...
Reading other reviews a lot of people are comparing it to bigger titles made by far bigger developers and giving it a thumbs down because it isn't matching the budgets or scopes of long established developers. Unfortunately this is a full on indie title developed by a grand total of 4 people. 2 did the programming and 2 provided the music and sound. And to be honest I think it's entirely unfair to compare it to a bigger title when such a small team is involved. They've done a great job with this game which is more of a casual city builder than something like Cities Skylines or Anno.
Are there problems with the game? Yes. Your frame rate starts to suffer once you pass the 250 population mark for some reason. Checking my hardware and my Ryzen 7 1700 never has more than 60% usage on the 10 cores it says its usuing, and it uses less than 2GB of RAM. GPU is also hardly utilitilised. So needless to say, some optimisation needs to be done.
There's also issues with path finding or something, where your peasants don't seem to be able to find food easily or resources easily, even though you've provided plenty for them nearby.
Combat also sucks in regards to recruiting a general and soldiers as they don't auto attack when near an enemy. In fact you can't even order them to attack an enemy. You have to move them over the enemy to get them to do anything and whatever that is I don't know!
Although these are relatively big problems, I do not find them to be game breaking. I've played far bigger and more expensive titles than this from big developers that have had more bugs, worse performance or issues in general that do break the game! But they go on to patch and fix those games and I expect the same from this small indie team. And they do plan on adding more content to the game for those of you worried about the small amount of content present at the moment. Content which I look forward too and watching this game grow over time.
Over all, this is a good little game. It cost me £6.99 which to me is a good price for a fun indie game with plenty of room for growth. Its a fun, casual city builder with a charming graphics style and relatively addictive gameplay. If I were to give it a score out of 10 it'd be a solid 7. You just have to bare in mind that this isn't a game built by big developers and expecting it to be a fully loaded title like Anno or Cities Skylines. Hell, Anno is a well established game that goes back years and Skylines requires you to buy content to make it a fully fleshed out game. This is this developers first title and it's a damn good and fun effort.

I'm going to focus on the negative, since I love everything else about the game.
I'm not focusing on the negative because it's a bad game, but because if these areas were improved on, the game would be even better than it already is!
Cons:
#1, There's not many building options, a plant and a statue for decoration, ETC
#2, Each project is stuck to a fixed number of team member, like micro being 2, instead of "minimum required"
I would like to take my extra workers not doing anything and tell them to work on a project.
Say I have 3 workers, I'm 1 short of making a small game, I can't tell him to work on the micro game with the other 2 guys. In my opinion, it should be a minimum requirement on how many staff work on the game.
If I make a large game, it would just make sense that every single time I'm not stuck to exactly 20 staff members, I should be able to throw on another 10, to speed things up.
#3, You're stuck at a max of 50 workers, I'd like to have more
#4, You're stuck at working on a maximum of 5 projects at a time, no way to upgrade or change this.
#5, Fullscreen was not working (though I'm sure this will be fixed)
#6, The bar at the top was way too small, I had issues seeing various things on the screen, and I don't need glasses
#7, When a worker had nothing left to do on a project, he just sleeps and you can't have him do anything else until the project is done, not even train him!
#8, When you move an object and it checks which tiles are free, it thinks where it previously was is not free tiles.
For example, if I move an object 4 tiles big, and I want to move it 1 tile to the left, I need to move it to another spot at least 2 tiles away, then back to the spot I actually want it, due to it thinking its own spot isn't free because "Hey, I can't move there, I'm in the way!"
Those were the biggest issues for me, not issues that ruin the game, but I feel in my opinion if they were adressed then the game would be so much better!

Sweezy Gunner is worth both purchasing and playing.  It's a procedurally generated 360 degree shooter which encourages backtracking with new abilities.  Some of the upgrades lean a bit more towards RPG grinding than metroidvania exploration, but they're still tied to your actions rather than an abstract skill tree.  Speed runs can probably skip them entirely as only the boss rewards act as keys.
The crosshair can get lost in the bullet hell and some of the backgrounds could use more contrast.  However, the only real problem I have is the long duration blended with linear dungeon access.  This makes it more of a one-and-done game than a bite-sized, replayable hobby.  I think I saw just about everything in one go and the completionist in me sees too much grinding to be tempted back.
That said, I'll probably give it another try when gamepad support is implemented.

This game was good... But sadly, when it got shut down, I wish I had returned to it earlier this year. I was late. Too late. But... Time to give it one last review, even with it gone. Here we go.
Soldier Front 2: A good game, with the main modes that I liked, Practice/Training, and MOBA mode. First, MOBA mode. MOBA mode was different. Being a 1st Person Shooter, it brought some new things, including helicopters, and some others.  But it did lack the things most MOBA players (Kind of like me), liked. I had enjoyed it a bunch, but I would have liked to pick an actual character instead of my soldier. And abilities. It could've used some abilities, such as, maybe, rapid fire, explosive bullets, and possibly an air strike. But now we're done with MOBA mode. Time for Practice mode. Practice mode made me make up my own stories and battles with the "Spawn Enemy" mechanic. This was a huge thing for me. Instead of shooting at walls and other things, you could actually kill an enemy. I made up so many stories, and battles, that I can remember only a few. On this one map with a helicopter, I would pretend I was infiltrating a server room, hacking, and escaping the crumbling building via Helicopter. Actually, reminds me of that one mission on COD: Ghosts. Huh. But still, it was very fun, and I wish I could return there. But I can't, which is the very sad part for me, and maybe you, reader.
Overall, it still had some good functions, and I don't mind Micro-transactions, just as long as they don't get in my way. SF2 had a great community, good multiplayer, and exellent graphics. All as a F2P game.
So, for my final score, I give this game a 9/10, for exellent ideas that made their way, sadly, for a year or two maybe. This is Skull, signing off.

Starbound is a space exploration 2d side scroller, but that's a term that really doesn't do justice to what Starbound really is.
Starbound is a unique adventure every time you open the game.  it's similar to titles like "No Man's Sky" in premise but blows it  out of the water as far as execution.
You start on your ship with the ability to move throughout the solar system you spawn in but your hyper drive is broken.  You move from planet to planet gathering the supplies needed to repair it which sends you on the main quest of the game. (NO SPOILERS)  The game itself is all about exploring, but it does a great job of breaking up that monotony by putting in many different creatures and/or aliens  to fight or just look at/converse with.
Many aliens you run into on the planets have missions and while these do happen to be pretty repetitive if you're looking to explore a planet you can get two birds stoned at once most of the time by just walking around and killing whatever tries to kill you.
The best thing about Starbound is the building and designing of bases.  You can terraform any planet all the way  down to the core and build anywhere you want.  There are 1000's of items to find in the universe to decorate your bases as well.  The base building system expands into your  ship as well, you ship expands as you move through the main quest and you can customize the space in any way you want.
They've added a lot since the game has been released as well, previously mechs and the ability to infiltrate and battle with enemies ships in space.  Also a bounty hunter update is coming soon, which has some promising mechanics.
I love Starbound, I want it to take it behind the bleachers and get it pregnant.

Where to begin? I'm a huge fan of the Castlevania series, although I've not played any of the Lords of Shadow games in the series until now, and Mirror of Fate was my first venture into this corner of the franchise. I knew, according from other reviews, that Lords of Shadow games are meant to be somewhat different to the rest of the series, but I was willing to give them a try to see if they captivate me.
Mirror of Fate is a smaller game that links the events of LoS 1 and 2, and unlike those games, it's a sidescrolling platformer for the most part, done in 2.5D (2-dimensional play but with 3D graphics). The first thing I noticed was how dull the visuals are. Most of the areas are just brown and grey, and most of the locations are just forgetable. The music is also barely noticeable at all. Nothing sticks out. Every area just feels the same.
The gameplay didn't really save it either. Most of it seemed quite repetitive to me. Enter room, fight baddies, climb a few walls, enter next room, fight more baddies, and so on. The combat doesn't know what it's trying to be. It uses the mechanics native to 3D games, such as parrying and dodging, but the whole game plays in 2D, meaning most times you have one enemy in front of you and one behind, and no matter which way you dodge, you get hit. Blocking is pointless, since you still receive tonnes of damage. So your only chance is to keep hitting the enemies and hope you kill them before your health bar depletes.
I've fought a couple of bosses as well, and although they do provide some interesting combat situations, they have an overblown amount of HP, meaning you just have to chip away their enormous health bit by bit via the same technique.
I eventually got stuck trying to ride an elevator platform that kept repeatedly getting destroyed by a gargoyle. After numerous unsuccessful attempts, I had to consult a walkthrough. Turns out there was some kind of a magical companion I had to find to help me with this section, except I've no idea where in the castle it is. The locations are all so boring and forgetable that it's no fun at all having to backtrack and re-explore them again (something that was fun with the previous Castlevania games). Once I've had enough exploring the same stone-grey areas, I decided to leave it there.
Mirror of Fate is not a bad game, but it lacks all the charm that made the Castlevania series so good. Every single aspect of it was a step down. Visuals, music, gameplay, even atmosphere felt subpar. It's by no means comparable to the likes of Symphony of the Night and Aria of Sorrow. I am starting to think that the only thing still left of the old gold Castlevania is the name.

An excellent throwback and combination of the classic VintageVania and MetroidVania games of old. With awesome visuals, a unique story, memorable characters and monsters, and satisfying combat, Mirror of Fate will appease those who didn't like the RPG nature of Symphony of the Night, those who couldn't handle the challenge of Castlevania III, and those who just love a fantastic, sprawling platformer.

Also there are several issues, like:
- you cant prioritize buildings, so if your people are dying of a plague you cant cure them because there arent enough citizens who can work in the hospital.
- sometimes youll be invaded by vikings and if you send your soldiers out, they have an attack radius of three milimeters, so you need to constantly move them
- there are no upgrades for buildings
Dont get me wrong, its surely is a nice game and 10 Euro aint that much, but its still more of a principle question if those 10 Euro are justified and i say no. Also if you can buy anno 1404 for already 10 bucks its not an equal competitor.

I'm going to write this for people who have never experienced anything from "The Longest Journey". And it's unfortunately a negative. If you're familiar with "The Longest Journey" series, then you can just ignore this review and purchase the game. However, if you've never played "The Longest Journey", or "Dreamfall", you might find your money wasted here. If you feel compelled to, play The Longest Journey and Dreamfall first.
While the game does a decent job of catching you up on things, those things that have passed by only really matter if you've played the past titles. When I put some thought into how a totally new player to the franchise would feel, I realized that much of the story of "Dreamfall Chapters" just falls flat. There is little to compell a new player to the world. To me, the story only works because I'm familiar with the previous titles.
The game is rather linear and doesn't offer many approaches to situations. The game gives choices, but they don't seem to impact much of the game. The choices you make are just cosmetic, but they're not bad. There is some satisfaction with some of the results despite their lack of impact to the game. For an episodic game though, you shouldn't be expecting much from these though. I've yet to play an episodic game that wasn't mostly on rails. At least they didn't try to incoporate combat like they did in "Dreamfall", whew, that was bad.
Sometimes the script and voice acting feel off as well. Often times the subtitles never matched the actual voice acting.
The puzzles are rather simplistic, but they can be a little frustrating at times. Hiding objectives in obscure places doesn't really make for good gameplay. Such setups may encourage exploring, however I've found that exploring doesn't really benefit the player much. Also, sometimes the critical elements don't highlight when you would expect them too. During a late game puzzle, I was pacing around an object I needed to interact with but couldn't. Turned out that I needed to look way above the character to interact with the thing, and the animations afterward interacted with the part I was just staring at...
The Longest Journey series hasn't been known for outstanding animations, but I have encountered many scenes where things were just... janky because of bad animations. This can be largely forgiven for the story, but as I've said before, newcomers with no knowledge of the back story may find this to be much more annoying.
Overall, I'm pleased with the game but that's only because I'm familiar with the franchise. Newcomers, exercise caution with your money here.

A great Tycoon game where you run a game developer studio. You hire employee's with various Traits, both positive and negative, and set about making a game. They work on 4 areas of development: Coding, sound, graphics, and writing. When they do these jobs, they get experience, and the more experience they have, the faster they do it and the more "Quality" they generate, I'll explain Quality later.
You can have your employee's specialize in one of the 4 development areas: Code, Art, Sound, and Writing. If someone is specialized in Code for example, they do that aspect better than someone no specialization and full experience. They trade off is that they can't earn experience outside their specialization. You CAN remove specializations though, but they're expensive.
As for traits, they come in Positive and Negative Traits. Positive Traits are things like arriving to work earlier, working faster, producing better quality work, requiring less food and water, etc. Negative Traits are basically the opposite of the Positive traits, such as arriving to work later, lower quality work, needing more food/water, working slower, falling asleep frequently, etc. They can be removed with a purchasable work station, but they're somewhat costly, and take time to remove.
When you start to make a Game, you choose a genre, where neglected genres generate more fans for you. You can name it too. Then you choose how big you want it to be: Micro, Small, Medium, Large. Those take 2, 4, 6, and 10 Employees respectively. The larger the product, the more it costs to produce. Then you choose who works on which of the 4 Aspects(Code/Art/Sound/Writing), the more you have on a Aspect, the faster it's done, and finally, which Software to use, where the more skilled an Employee is, the better the Software , and the better the Software , the better the quality. Then you start the project.
As your Employees work on the project, Quality is generated. More skilled Employees, better Software, and Larger Products  all generate more Quality. The higher the Quality, the better reviews it'll get and more it'll sell. Once the Project is complete, you Publish it, where you can choose what level of Advertising it'll get, and it'll sell better if you use better Advertising.
If you like game making Tycoons, definitely pick this up. It's more along the lines of Kairosofts Game Dev Story. Remember that this game is still in Early Access, and is already pretty good, so it'll get even better.

Short video review:
The Longest Journey and Dreamfall were both flawed, but magical story-driven adventure games. They had some rather serious issues, some pacing and puzzle problems with the first one, and some control and "why is there combat and stealth here" things in the second, but those could be easily disregarded, given how beautiful the world was, how charming the characters, how good the stories. What they didn't have, after Dreamfall opened so many new threads and ideas, is a proper ending. Dreamfall Chapters is here, finally complete 10 years later, to rectify that problem. And, like the predecessors, it's quite flawed, yet beautiful.
It's not fully point and click, neither fully direct character controlled, similar to how Telltale handles controls. But the game does have an inventory and huge open locations to explore and puzzles to solve, even if, like in previous games, the main meat of the game is in the story, characters and interactions. There we see another, and this time very unfortunate, influence from Telltale - the "will remember that" choice-consequence system that shows and teels too much, breaking the flow of the story and risks turning the intricate and beautiful world into a flow-chart of choices.
Thankfully, this doesn't kill the beauty of the game. Nor do the rather terrible puzzles, including several dreadful pixel hunting parts. Nor the rather obvious budget cuts in it's structure, which characters are seen and when and other things. But the first three Books do run longer than they really should and might make you feel a bit tired. But don't be.
The game really finds it's pace (not without missteps still) in the final Books, that bring the overarching story of The Longest Journey saga to a very fulfilling conclusion, while still maintaining the mystery and the appeal of the world and it's many yet untold stories. And given that the developers redid the opening bit of the game for better and still seem to be focused on improving the game, I can only hope that they will do the same improvement check on all other parts of the game to make the flow even better.
As with the originals, it's full of things to criticize. As with the originals, it stays with you when you close and uninstall it. I can see myself going back to all these games again and replaying them. Not for different choices, as I won't make them, most likely. Just because it's a journey worth relieving.

Summary: Pixel Puzzles Ultimate, the definitive jigsaw puzzle for the PC platform. With piece counts from 112 to a mega 1000 pieces. Pixel Puzzles Ultimate brings you full size professional puzzles to the digital market place. No longer will a puzzler be left looking for that last piece; never again will the kitchen table be covered in tiny wooden shapes. From square to rectangle to huge panorama pictures, with a massive variety of separately themed puzzle packs containing only the best images possible, each having a unique cut like no other jigsaw could. Pixel Puzzles Ultimate gives you the choice to play only the types of puzzles you really want to build. It's a new way to puzzle, customize the game the way you want, with a full range of options to tweak the game as you see fit. Multiple themed play environments, all fully customizable for you to fine tune the jigsaw puzzling experience you’re looking for. Redefining digital puzzling.
For all the merits the game may have, having to complete a tutorial puzzle before being able to access the in game options menu and make the game run in windowed mode is a terrible idea. Alt tabbing from full screen (in this game only) sometimes gives my PC a non-responsive black screen so running in windowed mode seemed essential. Most of my time spent in the game was spent alt-tabbed out looking for how to get into the options menu (no manual for the game). The answer that you need to complete the tutorial to get into the options was eventually revealed by a 20 minute gameplay video on YouTube Yeah, as another reviewer said, the pieces don't snap together, only to the board. I work puzzles in real life by putting sections together, then working them into the border. I'd love to be able to do this in the game. This is how everyone I've ever worked a puzzle with has done it, so I can't really recommend it without the ability to do this.
If by some chance, you enjoy working a puzzle borders out only, then I think this would be a fine game.

I've only just defeated the second boss and will likely play this through to completion, but there are plenty of things that just aren't sitting right with me.
To start off for anyone unaware, the game plays similarly to a twin-stick-shooter version of The Legend of Zelda. After a hilariously unnecessary opening scene in comic format oddly reminiscent of The Cheetahmen, you explore a large world map, find dungeons, push through them to the boss, and gain an ability upon its destruction. There are even "heart pieces" that increase your life when you collect four. Killing enemies gives you gold and temporary powerups, and collecting gold increases your gold multiplier. Get more gold, get more gold. Get it? One hit and your multiplier resets. Killing a large amount of a single enemy type will fill up a bar on your pause menu that, once complete, allows you to make a one-time upgrade purchase.
With that out of the way, it's time for the bad news. Let me be clear; I'm not trying to discourage anyone from getting this game, I think it's a fine use of $4, but everyone should know what they're getting into before they slap those Washingtons down. First off, this game suffers from what might be referred to as "Sonic '06 loading syndrome". Holy moley, every single time you move from one screen to another you get a nice black screen to stare at for a solid 5-10 seconds while the next section loads. It's not even some huge area you're loading either, it's Gameboy-era Legend of Zelda size screens. Even if you immediately go back to where you just came from, it has to load it all again. For a game with graphics as simple as this in this day and age, it's unacceptable. Next up, we have the powerups. While they definitely help dispatch enemies, most of them tend to create large objects or a flurry of bullets that makes it VERY difficult to see enemy projectiles. I can say with certainty that at LEAST 50% of the times I've taken damage it was because I literally could not discern the enemy bullet from whatever contraption or weapon of mass destruction had just sprouted from my vehicle. Another issue that arises after you master projectile-identification is that there's no notification when you achieve enough enemy kills to unlock an upgrade. You have to either guess when it's going to fill up or just keep checking your pause menu constantly. We've also got the problem of valuables dropping in unreachable positions. This becomes somewhat less of a problem after you obtain the ability from the first dungeon, but there are still way too many instances of gold dropping out in unreachable space. I was very glad to find that a magnet upgrade was one of the first available things. My last gripe is somewhat minor, but aiming seems to pan the camera awkwardly, and it's fairly disorienting. There's also a few spelling mistakes here and there, but that's bottom of the complaint list stuff.
Overall, it's playable, and I'm having a pretty good time. At the time of this edit I've made it to what I believe to be the final boss and been horribly murdered by it, so I'll probably go around and tie up some loose ends to power up a little more before giving it another go. A solid economy/management game. I do like the interrelated biomes that send and recieve goods to create a complete production web. The gameplay is a bit different from previous Anno titles, but I actually prefer this approach. You still have your different factions to keep happy, but they're split out across the three biomes, so you only have to worry about one at a time, which I like. They're not the same factions (eco/industrial/scientist -> temperate/polar/lunar, plus maybe tundra/orbital in future DLC).
Of course, as you can see from the screen shots and videos, the game looks fantastic. It's graphically very detailed and polished. The UI is also very solid. The tech is there.
The combat missions are... off-putting. I wasn't able to figure out how to create command groups, which is frustrating. In general, the combat left me feeling a bit 'meh'. Fortunately, you don't have to do them apart from two or three mandatory missions (maybe fewer - most of the story battles can be skipped just by gaining a corp level, which is pretty easy).
The tutorial NPCs are very naggy. Like, seriously obnoxious. If I have to listen to 'Time to upgrade your factories' one more time... Anyway, there's an option to turn those off. I am trying to hold off until I finish the story quests to do that, just in case I miss something, but it's getting harder every time the npcs remind me about an unfinished combat mission or to upgrade.
There's also mini quests? I guess that's what you'd call 'em. Basically, you have a little boat or buggy that's your avatar in the colony that you can run around and do errands for people to get the 'special resources' that you cannot acquire on your own. You can minimize the need to do this if you select the sectors that have rare resources as their perk. I did that on all three biomes, as I didn't find the mini quests enjoyable.
Overall, I'm really enjoying the game. It feels like an Anno game, but different enough to be interesting to me (and apparently to anger some Anno fans ;oP There's some real vitreol in the reviews here). For my money, I found it worth it enough to by the Season Pass. Thumbs up!

Wow... just wow...
Truth be told, I wasn't expecting much. I mean, I had free time, this game had a small file size so I can download it quickly despite my net, so I figured, why not? And why not indeed! I was blown away, figuratively AND literally at the later part of the game.
It's just quick, fun, mindless thrill. The action is frantic, bullets can fill up the screen if you don't get rid of the enemies quick. Shoot them down before they shoot you! Outrun the enemy bullets, weave through them. Much akin to a bullet hell game, your hit spot is tiny, and you can maneuver through the enemy bullets... if you're careful! Precision is the key here. I would categorize this game as bullet hell meets Zelda. Old Zelda... think Link to the Past, etc.
The upgrade system is rather unique too... instead of upgrades being available and purchasable the moment you have the cash to afford it (in other words, jut grind money), there's 3 different types of upgrades.
First one is monster-based. Each monster offers their own unique upgrade badge that you can buy once you get a card off them (low chance drop) AND killed enough of them to fill your "Knowledge meter" of them. Once both conditions are fulfilled, you can see what badge they offer and whether you wanna buy it... this is where cash comes in. It's a bit of a grind, especially because of how many you need to kill and the low chance of card drop, but hey, it makes each monster unique, even the lowly slime.
The second system is via unique coins called Sweezy Coins (what else?) and once again, cold hard cash. They're scattered throughout the world, some needing later upgrades before you can reach them. Getting a certain amount of them unlock upgrades you can purchase from the many shops you pass throughout the world.
Last but not least, there's heart containers (hello, Zelda fans). Getting 4 will increase your heart total by 1, and just like Sweezy Coins, they're scattered throughout the world and yes, just like the above, you'll need later upgrades before you can reach some of them.
Brace for action, get ready to dodge bullets, be prepared to kill enemies quick, and most importantly, have a hella good time. And oh, die a lot of times too while at it.
