Now that the game has recieved what is to be the final DLC I got to say I am having a blast. At the time of writing this I am pushing 200 hours of having played this game and I am still not bored. The developers have been listening and not only have they made the game fantasitic but in all the time I played, I only encountered 3 bugs, all of which were fixed quickly.
Many people are talking about how there is no multiplayer or a random map generator and as such they feel it hurts the replayability. Yes these things are true, there is little replayability but when I get bored with a single playthrough and am ready to start again I will let you know. The only reason I started new games in 2205 is the fact that they released more content. My first game had 73 hours and then they released the veteran update. After I played veteran for 69 hours they released the frontiers dlc and it introduced changes I was wanting. Since the last dlc went live a little over a week ago I have already played it roughly 30 hours, and again I am still not bored. I see myself easily getting at least one hundred more hours out of this game. It is that good. So yeah, little replay is a fact, but is replay really that important when you get so much fun out of a single playthrough? I mean previous anno games like 2070 and dawn of discovery have "replayability" but 2070 only has about 50-60 hours of playtime on my account. Dawn of discovery had even less. All these games are good make no mistake, but the lack of random map generators in Anno 2205 doesn't bother me when all the areas feel handcrafted with more detail and their own sector projects. Despite having played almost 200 hours there is still some areas I have not ever played in yet. I want to, but I have not gotten bored enough with the other areas to "colonize" all sectors yet. The question I ask myself is, "Do I really miss a random map generator that lets me play another map after completing a scenerio in say ten hours?" The answer is not really.
It is however very, very important that potential buyers fully understand what this game is. It is a singleplayer business strategy game. Yes you, "build cities" but you need to go into the game and play the game with the mindset that you are the CEO of a company and not the mayor of a city. The Anno series is an island-based, multi-city, supply chain and production management game. Anno 2205 has a huge focus on being more of a business game while maintaining the Anno feel. Yes it is not like the previous games in many aspects. Previous anno games had you building a city to just survive to achieve an end goal. Here it is all about thriving as a rich and profitable business. I would describe it as city skylines and Capitalism 2 having a child that was then adopted and raised by previous anno games. That sounds crazy but it has the singleplayer city-building elements of City Skylines, and the business elements of Capitalism 2; but was raised to follow the rules of Anno. A wierd analogy to be sure, but an accurate one.
My point is simply this, Anno 2205 is a fantastic singleplayer business game, but please understand that before buying it. It is really good and can be as challanging or easy as you want it to be due to the great amount of options when setting up a game, but know and understand what it is. I recomend this to anyone who wants a good singleplayer business management game.
If you would like to know more, feel free to message me on steam and ask questions or my youtube page(same name on youtube as on steam, Schwarzpferd) has lots of hours of anno footage and with my love for the recent dlc and game itself being so great, I am putting out more let's play videos on the game when I have an opertunity.
So yeah, I love this game and in my opinion it is the best anno game I have played, and I have been playing since 1602. It is, hands down, the best business game I have played. However, please be well informed about what you are getting into. Ask questions and watch videos, as this is not a game for everyone.

I've been a fan of the Anno series from the start, own them all, love them all, many years of regular replays. So I say this with a heavy heart, I can't recommend this game. It's actually quite literally a heartbreaker. The initial views as improvements to the game quickly reveal themselves as limitations.
The over simplication of the interface and build options ultimately take the best and most fun aspects out of the game, removing it's soul, leaving a nice looking emty shell. Babies very first builder is the new game engine here. An extremely acedemic, unchallenging, repetetive, builder with very basic resource management aspects, that feels intent on capturing a five year old audience. I feel even this age group would tire relatively quickly actually.
Gone are the days of infinitely variable module builds for ships and warehouses from Anno 2070, just gone. Replacing them are a few modules to add, that one quickly realizes are useless save for one. The lack of "randomly" generated map seeds was the first sign of the end of well...fun. Which to be honest in prior there were a regular series of maps that would turn up, with small variations in resources per island, but it still remained fresh per your choice of landing sites, etc. That is gone also. We have the same stock locations of warehouses, stock maps, stock, simple, everything...everytime. Those glorious functional docks you custom built and admired, spent hours watching...nope. You get a dock to connect to other maps. Period. Want to let your city grow organically, fight your citizens for resources for fun? Nope...you only manually upgrade residential buildings. You can flip them around and move them to make them looks slightly different or line them up in nice looking patterns.
The trading system is so simple it's virtually pointless, woops forgot to build something and supply is down? Click, build, trade, buy, done. No challenge besides knowing where to click, which thank you for simplifying and improving that one aspect devs, right...back to it being totally unchallenging. The addition of multiple maps and of course the highly anticipated off world  moon aspects lose there novelty almost immediately when you realize at the heart of this release...is empty space...to build on. Had this been executed a bit better, with even the slightest nod to the depth most hoped for, in terms of retaining or expanding upon key aspects of prior games that have remained a pillar of gameplay, those that kept us coming back, Anno 2205 could have been a truly amazing chart topping game. Sadly, it is not, it looks very pretty, but this is a pretty face on a boring, souless, repetitive, unchallenging, all too easy to manage city builder. There's no rush, no panic, just a couple clicks and you are all set.
There are no playing of factions against each other, no sudden unexpected game changing attack, just one enemy and he plays into things off screen in the form of easy challenges. There is also no mad dash to grab territory before a rival gets to it, you have the whole world whenever you feel like getting to it, to build more of the same boring stuff, over and over again, to have a bigger population, just to have one, no point beyond that, no super builds or achivements beyond what you get early on.
Your one enemy is entirely weak and two dimensional, he wants the moon. Great, have it, you appear to be on the dark side as I've never seen a city or base of yours, I've got too much space to build there for no point anyway, have some of mine, please. He never goes on the offensive against your cities and you can't attack him directly (simple in prior incarnations, but simply fun!), you just fight him for achievements in the form of limited and marginal ship improvements which are accomplished all too quickly...to fight him again and again on the same challenge maps, same ship placements, same objectives, now very easily won. You can turn down fighting him with no consequences besides not getting anymore ship improvements...the ones you already got 20 battles ago. The naval battle mechanics WERE nicely improved, BUT...they are now called to task in repetitve predictable challenge map battles. Nothing close to home, where it might be fun. Not much in the way of signifigant early gain to no gain mid game. From mid game...there is no end game or even anything that can be called climactic or intruiging...just get to a point where you can't build anything more or improve anything, have a billion billion dollars with nothing to buy, can't even build units, step back for a look at the series of clicks it took to get there. Game over. Unless simply clicking on maps to enjoy the sterile pretty views of things without a threat or care in the world, maybe shift a farm a space over to add a useless module, swivel a building that looks like all the pretty others, provides unlimited entertainment for you. Maybe it does. The whole game is an incredibly easy sandbox, without even the challenge (huge aspect of replayability in prior) of a changing landscape to build on. If anything, this edition is a depressing encouragement to go back to others in the series, to find again what I love about quirky micromanagement, creative use of limited space, characters and drama that felt 200 times more immersive than this game. The thing is, every challenge removed, this game is trying to be a builder, but it is not interesting enough to sustain that shift. It simply can't remotely touch a Cities Skylines in terms of shere content and creativity or even (shudder) Sim City 2013 in terms of management. So why the heck even go there? The game was great, why take every thing except the builder aspects about it that was great away? It's like keeping the super sweet frosting and throwing away the cake. I fear even a very substantial, even game changing, series of overpriced DLC will not save this sad, sad state of affairs. Unless...imagine for a moment the DLC was opened to users? Impossible I know. Imagine an Anno 2205 that goes the way of a Banished community? I know it's delusional crazy talk, it can't happen, but imagining it is more fun than this game.

Never played Anno before so this was my first one.

The game has massive flaws in construction managing - especially when it comes to modules which are often awkwardly shaped and in most cases larger than the original structure - while providing the exact same thing the base building did (A Rice farm and it's module will both produce the same amoung of rice despite the module being nearly twice the size.)
The economy for trading is BAD.  It is impossile to profit, even using the world market is barely enough to draw in a profit.  The taxes on trades can go well up to 10,000 after a couple of units and eat up all your profits instantly unless you're in the game of super massive overproduction (which is impossible to achieve because mass producing things just raises your needs more and more.) - This system is further insulting when you have to pay extortion level logistics between YOUR OWN colonies.
I played the campaign on easy and finished the game "story" with 3 maps, however I was unable to continue my career as I was constantly in the financial negative and unable to help myself as the other 6 maps were locked behind whopping 2 million credit costs.  To make matters worst everytime I built a profitable thing to sell (Example: A.I.) it's needs would interfere and I would have to supplement them.  This leads to an endless circle of somebody - somewhere missing resources, and no profit being made - energy expendature constantly increasing and leaving me with an overall feeling of dissatisfaction.  It was like playing on a teeter totter except at the end the other kid gets off and you're stuck on the bottom with no way up.
Maps are small and awkward, and most space is not viable for building, of course the module sizes contribute to this and eat up atleast 60-70% of your map.
The Naval combat was shallow and boring and had no depth whatsoever - and no purpose as it did not affect your development - in fact I wasted credits upgrading ships when I could have ignored this aspect alltogether.
30 hours or so on the game I wonder why.  Why did I waste my time on this?  I don't feel victorious, I feel I failed at a game dedicated to "balancing" which just gets frustrating at the end.
Really would not recommend this game to anybody - if it wasn't pretty I wouldn't have even stayed for as long as I did.  2/10 game at best, completely bad purchase.

I've played anno 1404, 2070, and this one (of course)
Anno 1404 and 2070 were almost identical, apart from being in different eras. Highly enjoyed both.
Anno 2205 has some ups and downs, but overall I do enjoy the game.
It's far less reliant on tedious micro management of resources, supply lines, and trade routes between islands, which is nice.  You're not counting farms and calculating production based off eco rating to determine how many sushi joints you can build without running out of rice.
You build a farm, it makes 5 moon rocks, you expand it, it makes 10. End of story. Simple.
Which allows you to play across multiple maps, (which probably sucks for loading time on lower end systems) which is really cool.
Expansion into space was a neat feature, as well as the costly trade routes to get out there.
Not too many complaints; the questing is more like an annoying side-track quest, I'd like to see a return of underwater construction, and the game feels very linear. I'd like to see scenarios and open build again.
And then there's the combat; although the new system is interesting, it's also fairly.....disconnected. You fight on one map, build on another, the two never touch. There are no military threats in your own seas, which is odd. But your ships don't get better via tech, but rather by the number of battles you fight and money.
Not as many interesting ships, either. Like; there's no submarine that fires nukes at people.
Personal preference rules on the combat system, I like both, but kind of prefer the anno 2070 system.
Oh and also, no major world event vote for crap every 15 seconds bullcrap. Anno 2070 was clearly meant to be play at least once every 2 days, I do like not having my notification bar filled to the bring every time I log in lol
In the end, still like the game, still looking forward to DLC and how patches change the gameplay.

So I feel like I should start with a quick anecdote as to how I came to find this game. You see, a while back, this random user posted a copypasta on my profile, going to excruciating to explain how futa is less gay than straight porn. An odd thing perhaps, but I kind of got where he was coming from. As time wore on, I slowly forgot about this mysterious futa poster, until one day, I was bored, and just looking through my profile, trying to ellicit old memories, and I found this mysterious futa posters comment on my profile. I became curious about this man: what was he like, was this a thing he did often, what sort of man could post such a thing? I had to find out more, so I clicked on his avatar and started to investigate. What I found was a neon lit, shades wearing homage to the 80s. Everything, from his profile picture, his background, all his items, were in someway linked to the decade. And throughout this I kept seeing a name cropping up: Outdrive. Now, being a fan of the 80s style myself, I decided to take a look, and what I found was what I thought to be a simple endless runner with a neon 80s aesthetic, but I was somewhat surprised to find it lacking in this respect. Don't take this as criticism however, for out of the games simplicity I found something else. As I drove down these endless roads, listening to the synth pounding through my headphones and admiring the neon infused backdrops, I found my mind wandering, to places it never really had before. I found an odd serenity in this game, it allowed me to find out thing about myself that I had never really known. I came to terms with the facts of life, the inescapable inevitabilities, and the ultimate truths. I found peace, like I had never really known it in this game.
So thank you, mysterious futa poster, thank you for the gift you have granted me.

Just so we're clear, this is just my first impressions after about 1 hour of play give or take so if I happened to miss anything from here, I am probably blind as a bat or I haven't reached that far into the game yet.
First off, this is a game built on the Unity engine so looking at the options menu, it's no big suprise that it's usually bare bones starting off with the graphical settings. All you got is resolution that's fixed to your native resolution and can't change it unless you go into windowed mode, toggling realtime shadows on or off, and some basic form of Anti-Aliasing with the absence of graphical presets, but this game is not very demanding as far as I can tell. For sound, it's just the master volume, no sliders for voice, sound effects ,or music. Languages consists of English and Japanese, with the last one is basically swears with the ability to upload any language of your choice. The help menu is written in broken English, but it's not broken enough to not get the message it wants to say.
The gameplay is an on-rails shooter in a third-person perspective, so don't expect a third-person cover shooter. Looking at the game's screenshots, the UI in-game, and the way to navigate the menus, I have realized this game is a mobile port, but does it really affect the gameplay all that much? To me, not really except some design decisions that happen to get through. There are quite a bit of weapons to take with you on the field, but down the later levels, it really feels like they are just direct upgrades from previous weapons you were currently using and when you select a weapon, it has a button labeled upgrade so I originally thought I could alter stats to make the guns more interesting and make early game weapons still viable to use late game until I realized it's only to increase your ammo reserves since buying the weapon itself only comes with one spare magazine for some odd reason. Honestly it would be tolerable if there was a way to switch weapons at will instead of throwing away your entire primary reserves only to be left with a pea shooter. As an on-rails shooter, it unfortunately suffers the same problems as that god awful Rambo game with no warning markers to tell you if you're going to get hit, but instead of fixed health, you have regenerating health so it becomes less noticably infuriating, even though you still get hit occasionally behind cover. The gunplay feels pretty weak with no visual recoil on the guns with fairly poor sound assets in addition to janky animations almost convincing me that the guns were pre-packaged Unity assets and I say that because I am someone who really enjoys games from Tripwire Interactive. Speaking of recoil, there is no recoil to even speak of because it is actually on a set cone of fire that shoots in random directions so don't even think about trying to control said recoil. Occasionally, they will spawn melee units that instantly kills you for some inexplicable reason since I don't recall melee units in rail shooters instagib players at all, no, I can't think of a single one that does that. The levels themselves are pretty short considering this is a mobile game and it is deliberately designed to force you to replay levels over and over again to get enough money for the gun you need and the ammunition required to pass the level only to repeat the process again in return artificially extending the game longer than what the actual length is.
Perhaps I just have really low standards nowadays, but $6 is an okay price for what this is. Verdict? I can't really find myself recommending it to just anybody really and I kinda feel bad for saying it. I'd only recommend it for those who has the time and cash to burn, but not for those who are desperate for on-rails shooters. If you are looking for on-rails shooters, take a look at Blue Estate and Typing of the Dead: Overkill. Or better yet, Go to an arcade outlet and find Time Crisis 3.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge is a wonderful game. Following on directly from the Game Boy Colour original, the sequel sees the villainous Risky Boots return to once again terrorise the good people of sequin town.
Anyone who grew up playing 16-bit games will be familiar with the platforming elements of Shantae. The platforming won’t test your jumping skills, no will the game’s combat (apart from the last boss) but that’s not really what Shantae is about. Rather, the game is about exploration and fun, and the title has bucket loads of each. There is also some very tongue-in-cheek humour running through the game with is great.
The game’s graphics are bright and cheerful with all of the characters and enemies really well realised and they all animate incredibly well. Shantae’s world is beautiful and a joy to explore. As you’ll have seen in the screenshots Shantae is able to take on the form of other creatures and gaining these abilities opens new areas of each part of the world. While there is some backtracking it never feels like a chore due to the carefully placed warp points.
Some people say that the game can be confusing as it doesn’t clearly tell you where you are to go next. I found this was only really an issue if you’re not paying attention to what characters tell you or where you have visited and where you couldn’t quite reach due to not having the correct skill. Like many adventure games players need to pay attention. Others have criticised the game’s length and while it is possible to complete the game in two hours (there is even an achievement for this) that is rather missing the point. In all it took me roughly nine hours to complete the game, which is pretty good for a platformer from the Game Boy Advanced era in my opinion.
If you enjoy fun platforming, good exploration and quality graphics with a lot of humour thrown in then Shantae is well worth checking out!

This is a very fun and almost timeless platformer. Sadly, Shantae is one of those darlings that get looked over and it doesn't get the amount of praise it deserves.
It boasts a female-protagonist, a metroidvania style gameplay, and a straight-forward and not over-complicated storyline.
This kind of game somehow found me the perfect fit for story-telling for my taste, this game continues right where the last left-off, yet doesn't flesh out the story too much to a point where it may become easily confused.
At face-value, some may be concerned that the female protagonist may be weak, and cave-in to the comment or authority from a man (or anyone as a matter of fact), as games sometimes portray women as. This is not the case for Shantae; she is very strong and she follows what she thinks is right and doesn't throw her moral views away when she is told to throw it away, she fights for the lives of people, and is willing to make decisions that will ultimately hurt her, but save others from pain.
Now to the sound. For a side-scrolling pixel game, the sound is very good, not to mention the music. Jake Kaufman, a fairly popular composer of music, did a great job with the soundtrack. Each soundtrack fits almost perfectly with the setting, and most of the soundtracks make you want to dance to the beat (like Shantae).
Regarding my 'side-scrolling pixel game' comment, if you play the game or have watched gameplay of this game, you will notice that there are pads that let you jump from one layer of the area to another. This is a crucial feature in this game because it allows you to explore and immerse yourself into each area (basically making the area feel 3D and not just a plane).
The pros out-weigh the cons in this game, let me tell you that we are very lucky to have a game like this be created with such polish and care, and that personally, I may never be able repay the creators (and Shantae) with the amount of joy this has given me.

It's not a bad game, but it's got a lot of flaws and it's really, really, really short as well as generally lacking in polish. If you can get it for cheap it could be a fun time, but otherwise if you want to check out any of the Shantae games I would highly recommend picking up Pirate's Curse for the 3DS or Wii U, it's a much much more polished, fully featured and generally higher quality game, definitely the best one so far. It's worth noting, though, that despite the excellent character portraits and sprite art and animation, both games feature the most bafflingly ugly UIs I've seen in a while. Seriously, WayForward, you've got awesome artists and animators but your basic text boxes are goddamn jarring, christ.

I recommend Dreamfall Chapters, but to get the full experience, the player should seek out the first two games that this one has followed: 'The Longest Journey' (1) and 'Dreamfall: The Longest Journey' (2). The experience won't be as rich without them.
Setting and artwork are glorious, though character movement and visuals are not a match for other games. However, the plot and storyline depth are so complex that player immersion is complete. All characters have their quirks and motivations - even the minor ones. Voice acting is impeccable. Every character is a hero of their own story, and we get to control two of them: Zoe and Kian, two characters from two worlds working towards a common goal.
Some of the side missions feel a little bit like filler, but I personally didn't mind. There are multiple ways to solve a problem and different solutions attract different outcomes and reactions. The choices within are immense, and even though the storyline is forced, the paths taken to get there are so different that this game can be played again.
There aren't many games out there like this, which is a shame.

Before I begin spoilers, I will admit, this game is NOT a standalone game, It will make no sense to anyone who hasn't played at least the 2nd game, Dreamfall:The Longest Journey.
*Spoilers ahead*
There were many MANY loose threads created in Dreamfall that DF Chpaters stiched up nicely. Many are still open for interpretation which in my opinion, is the best kind of storytelling. The graphics are a huge improvement. I literally spent far too much time simply enjoying my envronment, the ambience, the music... Oh the music. I will say now, the music is simply divine. But back to the review.
There's (thankfully) no more direct combat instances. The entire combat system is no more, and for good!. There are still plenty of points in the game where you have to be stelthy (walk outside of npc's direct line of sight for instance) but they do not interfere with the gameplay in any huge way. The characters are amazing. My only gripe is that Kian's selectional dialogue in later stages doesn't reflect the characters motivations, even if you were RP'ing him as a hardcore Azadian. I must say I loved loved loved Saga **** EVEN MORE SPOILERS***I guessed Saga was the 'reincarnation' of April since the first Interlude. Her story was so fascinating... And it was a massive surprise to find out that she would become Lady Kian through adoption!

However, if you've played the previous games, I highly recommend buying this game, replaying the first two games back-to-back then sitting in a dark room, headphones on, enjoy the ambience, outstanding voice acting, beautiful music and let yourself get carried away on the longest journey

"From the Depths" is a war sandbox, voxel-based builder.  It has a couple different campaigns that come with the game, but you'll mostly spend your time on Neter.  Here, you must build ships, planes, helicopters, tanks, fortresses, zeppelins, spaceships, and whatever you might need in order to conquer the eight factions that lie between you and all of Neter.
Except it's not that simple.  Because the vessels you'll face aren't just some rummaged-together rafts with peashooters (althought some of the Deepwater Guard might actually apply to that statement).  They're great big battleships with thundering cannons.  They're planes that zip across the sky at super-sonic speeds.  They're airships that block out the sun.  They're satelites that can call down a hail of missiles from orbit.  They're thrustercrafts with more lasers than the local nightclub.  The learning curve is staggering, and the beginner will come into a new game with whatever they've managed to piece together to face the pirates, merchants, zealots, scientists, AIs, admirals, and aliens that are aimed against them.  And they'll probably lose.  But that's the fun part.  You lose, and you learn.  You build a better ship.  You win.  And then you lose to something even more powerful.  And then you build an even better ship.  And the cycle continues.  And you let it continue because it's oddly fun to tune your crafts, to make them balance in the water, or soar in the sky.  To make them bombard an enemy from afar from behind numerous shields and meters of armor plating, or ram them at high speeds with all the drills you can carry.
It helps to have some free time, as you'll likely spend hours just working on a single craft, testing it in the vehicle designer before you actually bring it out in the campaign.  Heck, you might not even get into the campaign, and instead just keep building and building until you have crafted your own faction to rival all that might appose you.
And you'll never stop.  The devs are active, updating the game on a regular basis, and there's a beta branch with even more frequent, if slightly more unstable, updates.  And the community is active, with a Workshop where people post modifications to the game, new vessels that they've built, or even new campaigns they've composed.  All new challenges to overcome.
That's what From the Depths is about.  Building, learning, improving.  And it's why it might just be my favorite game.

Just completed this Castlevania and I can say that I thoroughly enjoyed it.  Castlevania: LOS - MOF has a great old school feel and does everything right.  The controls and combat are tight and satisfying.  Some of the boss battles (and also some of the "fodder" battles) you get a great feeling from victory.
Checkpoints are located in good locations so as not to make the game too easy and also not to create massive frustrations.  There is very little back-tracking, mostly throughout the game you feel as if you are progressing.
The graphics are weirdly great.  During my playthrough I took a load of screenshots.  When looking through them afterwards they don't looks so great.  You can easily see some of the low-res textures used in the backgrounds and some of the polygons are very obvious.  The weird thing is whilst playing, the game looks so nice!  I attribute this to great graphics artistry and also there is a wonderful use of colours as you move through the game.  In some areas as you move through your environment the colours subtley change, it really is very nice!
I'm personally not one for stories but I watched a little of the cutscenes which are beautifully drawn and animated.  I may go back and watch them in sequence in the library one time.
I'd heartily recommend this Castlevania for anyone interested in this genre.

This is the worst Castlevania game I have played.
Now, I haven't played them all, so this probably isn't the worst in the franchise, so let's talk:
This is an inbetween for Lords of Shadow and Lords of Shadow 2, existing in the same universe and not the other Castlevania continuity.  I like what they've done with the story elements.  Granted the writing itself in the series is far from amazing, it's kind of interesting in a schlocky dark gothic sense.  Evil awakens, men fight against fate, darkness blah blah blah.
If you liked the writing / story from either of the LoS games you'll like it here as well.
I'm a Castlevania fan, so for comparison let me lay out my top three faves in the franchise, in no particular order:
Symhpony of the Night, Lords of Shadow 2, and Dracula X Chronicles (a psp remake of Rondo of Blood)
This goes back to the 2d style of game play which is where Castlevania has found its most success.  But the platforming is very far from perfect, and feels rough at times.  There's a noticeable slump in speed when you jump.  It's off putting, it makes it feel like there's so many gaps you can't make.
You'll play as three characters in this, Simon Belmont, Alucard, and Trevor Belmont, and all three of them play almost exactly the same with a couple of differences in sub weapons and one character not getting a double jump, and only one character getting a glide.
They all fight and play exactly the same.  They all use a whip.  I get it with the Belmonts, but with Alucard, here's a character that we all love because of Symphony of the Night and here he is also using a whip and not his signature sword style.  Which is weird, because in his LoS 2 appearance he is using a sword.
At first I got excited when I got to play as Alucard and then that went away as soon as I started playing as Alucard.  There was no difference in how he played.  In most of the other games your character would get a new power after a boss, but here Alucard gets several new powers right at the beginning of playing and it's just like "Here you go, you can do this now"
Along those lines, it also bothers me that Simon can air dash.  I know this game is supernatural, but at least with Gabriel, he had magic boots, Simon's introduced as a barbarian, and without magical aid he just dashes in air.  It's weird to me.
The platforming has these weird difficulty curves.  In most well designed games there's a gradual growth in the difficulty of platforming level design.  Things start out easy then progress, and you find yourself doing things that you couldn't imagine doing early game.
In this, the majority of the segments are long and simplistic platforming parts, but suddenly the game throws a curve ball at you and hits you with something rough, but because you've spent 85% of the game doing simple gaming, these parts hit hard.
There were 4 times in this game that I wanted to give up and stop playing (but I make a promise to myself in the last few weeks of summer before I go back to school to actually complete games in my steam library, so no giving up here)
The third act of the game starts to get more interesting in game play elements, so much so that it makes me think a different production team was behind its development, but then it just ends super fast.
My account says I took 9.3 hours to finish this game, and I don't plan on a second playthrough.
It's just not a good game and I didn't have fun playing it.
I wouldn't pay more than $5 for this.  I think I bought it on sale around $7.50, and that's just a little too much.  It took me 9 hours to get to a part of the game that I felt was interesting, that's way too long, and when I hit that mark, I was like 30 minutes away from finishing the game.
If you're a hardcore CV fan, get it on sale, but be warned.
If you're a non CV fan and just looking for a fun platformer, this IS NOT a FUN platformer.

Eh, little torn about this game... I mean, I LOVE it. Seriously, been playing it straight for the past two days. (Steam doesn't log hours correctly, idk why). And I honestly don't get the negative reviews. Like, most of them complain of lack of content, and that within 2 hours you will see every enemy and every building basically. While this is PARTIALLY true, the same can be said for many other games as well. Take Minecraft for example, probably the most popular video game of all time. Hop on to creative mode and scroll through your inventory and YOU can see every single block within 2 hours as well. Yet people still play it afterwards, so saying that you will see everything in a small amount of time really isn't a good argument. HOWEVER, that DOESN'T mean this game is without faults. I have two, count 'em, two main issues. 1: The soldiers. I love making a little army and wrecking Viking raids with it, don't get me wrong, but they're extremely inefficient and a lack of resources. I mean, to get a worthy fighting force of soldiers, you'll need lots of iron, and charcoal, (for armaments) and gold, for 1 measly soldier, who will die within 5 seconds of fighting Vikings, where as you can spend some gold and other easily gotten resources for an archer or ballistae tower, which will basically last forever and do a TON of damage. The only way I see soldiers being useful is if we can maybe raid Viking bases themselves for our own gain, which would be super fun, btw. My second issue is fires. I mean, when my peasants are facing fires, they seem to rather protect a few trees half way across the map rather then the HUGE STOCKPILE with all of my resources! This has made me quite frustrated at times, and needs to be fixed dearly. Or maybe, the developers can implement a firefighter building for designated peasants that protect certain buildings that you can assign them too, which would fix the issue. So far, I haven't encountered any boring gameplay, as some people have stated, I mean, if you're getting to powerful for Viking attacks, up the difficulty or don't make so many archer towers. I have about 10 defensive towers, which is about enough to fend off Viking attackers, but still keep you on your toes. Overall, great game with minor issues. And if you've read this far, and still haven't bought it, let me say one last thing to convince you; Real men don't read reviews. They buy games.

It is the first time I am writing a review but, considering what the game is, as a old fan of the anno games, I feel like I have to.
First, I must say I can't blame the devs for trying to renew the series. I don't see how they could have added good things to the mechanics of the previous games without changing what is already in place, so I think change was necessary. The devs did too, and so it went.
However, what we ended up with is an empty game! Or, rather, a collection of loosely connected minigames, but in any case nothing as deep as any of its predecessors. It is all child play.
Basically, you are just filling the map with buildings until you run out of space (if you manage to not get bored to death before). It doesn't really matter where and how as long as it is in the right sector, connected to a road and, preferably, as close as possible to the service producing buildings it requires (or the other way around if it is a service building you are placing). As for the kind of building, basically you start with some houses, then you go on with service buildings and factories until your stock manager says production meets consumption. There are no trading routes, you just select the type of good, the source, the destination, the transfer rate you want and you are done. Also, you don’t really need trading routes so much in the first place because you can produce anything in any sector as long as it is a sector of the right biome. At some point you may need some rare materials. To get these you will have to either do some quests (move your main (only) ship around the current sector), do a crisis sector (some sort of donjon crawler with boats, totally independent from the main game. I don't really understand what it thinks it's doing here. Maybe it stand as a reminder of the fact that the previous games had a military aspect) or play the asteroid miner android game.
There is just no mechanic in that game that is not trivial to master.
I understand why some of the mechanics have been removed. By replacing the carts and boats with abstractions of themselves, you end up with something that, from any meaningful perspective, behaves the same way but only uses a fraction of the resources the original requires to run which, in turn, allow the devs to make things huge. But then, despite all the potential offered by this approach, it looks like they went for the cheapest solutions. Why did you have to make trading routes so dumb? Why did you have to remove the fertility mechanic? Given that these two things could have been there, was it so hard to replicate the random maps with sectors instead of islands? Sadly, no.
The devs made room for new things and gave themselves great tools and then did nothing with them. So that's what the game ended up full of: nothing.
So, to new comers I would say, save your money, buy anno 2070 instead. You will get way more for a much lower price. The anno game series is definitely one of the great names of its genre and 2205 tried to renew it but it fails to create anything worthy of your time and money as far as gameplay is concerned.

Okay boys and girls let Melo tell you all the things you need to know about this game.
First off, this is a sequel to the first Shantae game that came out on the Gameboy Color, it's pretty expensive to get a physical copy, but you can buy a digital version on the 3DS, but that one in my opinion is the hardest to play with how outdated it is with clunky controls and the camera being way too zoomed in making most jumps leap of faiths. If you want to play this one and not have to deal  with the first game, all you need to do to play this game is watch/play the first five minutes of the first game it will explain everything you need to know about Shantae, Risky, and how and why everything is how it is.
You play as Shantae the Half-Genie hero who protects the town Scuttle Town where you live from the evil pirate-lady Risky Boots. Your uncle, Unlce Mimic finds a relic and is bringing it back for the towns Relic Hunter Expo. He opens the case up and reveals a lamp, no one knows what this lamp does exept your uncle, and also Risky Boots. Risky comes in and steals the lamp and sails away to look for the three Magic Seals to learn how to work the lamp. It is up to Shantae to get the lamp back and stop Risky Boots, one hair whip at a time.
Pros:
Good story
Memorable Characters (nameless npcs are even memorable)
Good Characters (I love all characters, even nameless npcs)
Challenging but not impossible
Excelent Platforming + Puzzles
Funny and unique dialouge.
Wonderful sprite animation
Awesome soundtrack
High replay value
Cons:
Not best explaining on where you need to go, first playthrough will take you some hours, but once you beat the game once you will be able to fly through the game even after weeks of not playing. Sky and Bolo give you hints on what you need to do but never directly tell you what you need to do (I guess this can be a pro but this kinda hints at exploring places instead of being told what to do)
Backtracking: ALL the backtracking isn't bad since you have to go in the area again at one point to get a key item, but I'm talking near the end of the game where you get the last power and have to go back in the temples to get the last few Magic Jam, Overall the backtracking isn't that bad
Confusing Map first time playing. It doesn't show names of places so when a character tells you need to go to location that you never been before you will get lost since the map doesn't tell you place names.
Sidenotes:
Replay value - This game is short so that means you can start a new game and see if you can beat it at a faster time, a really good game to speedrun.
Magic Mode - This is a new mode which makes you take more damage from enemies. But you use less magic. This can be considered Hard mode, or Easy mode. If you get hit a lot and can't dodge well, consider it hard mode. If you can dodge most attacks, and know spanws of enemies and use magic well this will be easy mode.
Pirate's Curse - The sequel of this game, I will only review it when if it comes out on steam, right now it's only exclusive for 3DS and WiiU, I have hopes for Wayforward to add it on steam,
So that concludes my review for Shantae: Risky's Revenge, yeah there are a few cons that make it look bad but this game is really good and I highly recommend  that you get this game and start playing it.

It took me very little time to get fed up with this product, and I really want to like it. I do, honest. Unfortunately, it's basically crap.

In a span of around 20 minutes I had 5 runs. In the first and second, the girl died in around 8 seconds because the instructions didn't make it clear enough that RB on the controller was how you kept her alive via boosting. On the third run I found myself jumping off a ramp only to hit an invisible something in mid-air that slammed my car back to the ground and pretty much drained all my speed. Coming off of the next ramp, which was to the left side of the road, I hit the invisible sidewall and somehow ended up driving on the "wall" with trees passing under my tires and the road to the right of the car and oriented 90 degrees from me. Eventually the game spazzed before reducing me to zero speed, killing the girl. On the fourth run, a car crossing the road that I avoided somehow managed to warp in front of me, before slamming into the side of the car and then reappearing in front of the car again, preventing me from driving and thus, killing the girl. On my fifth I again hit a ramp just right to make me hit the sidewall, only this time it bounced the car so that I was driving upside down on nothing but air. It didn't stop me from driving until, at last, a turn made the car backflipped off of the "sky road," and beyond a curve in the road, and I was unable to move in any direction, killing the girl.
These kinds of bugs are amusing the first few times they occur in a game, and then they quickly make you want to tear your hair out. The biggest problem however, is something the dev said at the top of this page: This is not a game. A game has a goal, an "end game." This ... aesthetic concept, does not. You just keep driving at speed or the girl dies. In a game, you would be driving to a specialized hospital or, if the fact that connecting a cable from the car to the girl keeps her alive is any indication, a world class cyber-doc. This one tiny little thing would have made the ... aesthetic concept much better. It would have changed the tone of the narrative from a hopelessly bleak "Vanishing Point" or "Thelma and Loise" -esque driving experience that leaves a bad taste in your mouth to something that would actually resonate with people to the point that they share it with their friends.

This review is written in Jan 2017 and after around 30 hours in game. At this point, with this experience, Pixel Puzzles Ultimate still feels like a work in process. This and the following points makes this near to impossible to recommend.
Firstly, too many DLCs with too few puzzles in each 'pack' will make this game way too expensive.
Secondly, technically, this falls short.
While there is plenty of customization available, and most notably the annoying 'snap-to-piece' which made it impossible to select the piece you want from the river in the older Pixel Puzzles games has been removed, there is still no proper windowed support. A simplified theme with at least 800x600 resolution would be so useful.
This game still lacks the ability to combine pieces into movable groups so even if you know these three pieces go together, you can't really do anything about it.
There is also no way to use your keyboard to select pieces. Instead there is only drag and drop.
Still no Kiosk nor any information about it (I'm really hoping it will enable the player to use the Gold pieces to get puzzles!).
The game is way too heavy to run! My laptop goes way above the minimum reqs, even the recommended ones, but still this game runs like a ladybug in tar. Granted, I like to listen Spotify at the same time (since I can't run this windowed), but still. I struggle to find the sense in this: the game is casual, the main audience will be casual gamers -- do they really own the gaming PCs needed to run this smoothly? I should think not, but maybe I'm wrong.
All in all, don't bother! Go and play free jigidis instead. Only if you must have a jigsaw game on Steam, this *might* do the trick. Would wait before making that assessment, though.

When doing a jigsaw puzzle, it's pretty standard to assemble the edge pieces and bits with any obvious pattern first. For example, this game has horse puzzles, so if I were doing a puzzle showing horses running on a field, I would assemble the horses first before going through the more tedious part of trying to figure out how the nearly identical looking green pieces fit together to make the field.
There is NO OPTION to snap together neighboring pieces other than placing them in their exact correct spot in the finished puzzle. The first free jigsaw puzzle site that I searched for on the internet had that completely OBVIOUS feature, but somehow PPU does not.
What this game DOES have is the bizarre and unwelcome feature of snapping a piece into place if you accidentally put it near its correct spot, even if you had NO idea that that is where it should go. To return to the horse puzzle example, if I start it off by randomly placing one of the many green tiles that form the verdant field that the majestic horses are galloping on in the middle of the board and that happens to be its correct final spot, it will lock into place. I don't know about you, but that it is NOT something that I want in a jigsaw game. The point of a jigsaw game is the satisfaction of fitting pieces together, NOT having the game instantly confirm that that is the spot where the piece was eventually supposed to go, so now it's locking it into place to make sure you don't do something silly like try to match it with other pieces that look like they're from the same part of the puzzle. This is the equivalent of playing a murder mystery game and having the game immediately tell you "THIS GUY IS THE KILLER!" the first time you click on a character.
The last flaw I want to mention is that any pieces you haven't grabbed yet whirl around wildly in a pond. Just... why? Who thought that was a good idea? Who wants to have to grab pieces randomly because they're swirling around like they're getting blasted by a leaf blower?
Just play some jigsaw puzzle Flash games and ignore this trash.

TL;DR Love the game! Keep up the good work. I have enjoyed 60+ hours so far, have enjoyed the recent update, and can't wait to see the final product.
Long Version
I like the game mechanics. Office layout efficiency, developer improvement, game development, earn money, win fans, change cities. I think these have all been blended well.
I've only come across two potentially serious issues and a few UI bugs. Very solid for an alpha early release!
Potentially Serious Issues
The first serious issue is when I have it open for several hours (common occurance :). By the time I get to SF and have a huge staff things start to slow down. I'm not sure if this is because I'm constantly switching between pausing and speed 3  or not. It shouldn't be my machine, as it is a solid gaming machine and this game shouldn't be taking up resources. I can repro this by just playing for a couple of hours.
The second issue was that I have had all or most of my staff disappear in two separate games. It happened late game (SF) both times. I haven't been able to purposely reproduce this, but it's happened twice.
UI Bugs
Fan numbers display (unsigned int error?) - Start a new game, quit tutorial, open Project Manager (E) screen, click New Project, look at fan numbers (should be normal). Speed 3, wait until next month dialog, Continue, then open Project Manager again, click New Project, look at fan numbers. This time they're things like -2147483588. No big deal, as you develop games, each game fan number will reset and, once you've developed one of each game, it's never a problem again.
Graph goes off dialog - I ran into this when I had a series of terrible developer options at the start of a game. Start a new game, do not make games, only spend money for a few months (build things, hire developers, etc.). After a two or three months, when you have negative cash, Open Studio Info (G) dialog, click Graph. Some of the graph lines and points go down below the graph area, even outside the dialog.
Wishlist
- I would love to be able to open the New Project dialog directly, instead of always having to open Project Manager and clicking on the New Project tab. It's one of the most common things I do, so it'd be nice to have it in Options.
- I would love to have another major dialog for employee managment. Currently, if I want to look at my employees, their abilities and experience, I have to start a new project, select a game, and continue.
- Remove Project Summary Dialog. I actually NEVER use the Project Summary Dialog, as all the info I need is available in the default tab of the Project Manager dialog.

If you want a game with three-dimensional fighting, with dodging or blocking being the main mechanics for avoiding injury, then you must make sure that dodging an attack with correct timing will AVOID attacks, and adding tells or "telegraphs" to enemy attacks that correctly correspond to WHEN  and WHERE a player must dodge or block.
This game does not do that.
Instead, all actions in fights are choreographed to "look cool', rather than make intuitive sense. All your abilities and attacks contain lengthy cooldown periods which require precognition more than tactics or choice. They think they are preventing players from "button mashing".
They are not.
If you want a game with three-dimensional combat, you must make sure that enemy attacks don't clip through the player without damaging them, or that attacks which miss the player don't register as hits.
This game does not do that.
Instead, all actions are based on the idea that where you must stand and what you must do are predetermined; if you are standing where an attack will hit, it doesn't matter if the enemy is even remotely near that spot. You will be damaged. If you are standing in a "safe" spot, the enemy can clip through you and you will not be damaged.
They do not have fun bossfights; they have gimmick-ridden car wrecks that feel more like poorly designed puzzles than combat.
If you want to have a game with climbing/parkour involved (wait, this game stars Dracula. Isn't Dracula supposed to be able to fly...), you need to have a system in place where players can choose where to go and have a degree of control over their own movement. Thus the challenge (and fun) of the game becomes choosing how to use your locomotion to reach a place you wish to go.
This game does not do that.
Everything is on a rail. There is one SPECIFIC path, and you must take it and every step of it in a specific order. You may be dangling less than three feet above a walkway you have traveled a thousand times, but there is no button to let go of your handhold and walk across it: You must climb all the way over to the end of the platform and receive the contextual command to do so. You can see an item you need which is dangling in a place you can easily reach with a normal jump, but there will be an invisible wall between you and it which cannot be circumvented because you are intended to go three rooms over and get in through a different door. The distance by which you can jump from one handhold to another is determined solely by where the devs chose to place them, not by your aim, foresight, or even the physical ability of the character you control.  You move on a rail.
A very boring rail that punishes you for trying to solve any problem on your own.
THIS IS INFURIATING!
I won't even touch the forced stealth sections. We already know they suck.
This needs to be said, however;
The God of War series was terrible.
It had terrible combat and a hollow, emo plot. It catered to those with ADHD and daddy issues.  We should NOT attempt to emulate them.
The combat in this game is bland; you are given a dozen options that all either do the EXACT same thing or attempt to provide options in combat, but instead offer no real tactical advantage and little to no real impact.
Quick Time Events are NOT fun!!
They add nothing to a game and, in fact, detract from them heavily!!
The Devs need to go play other games themselves.
Go play some of the Devil May Cry series.
Go play some of the Batman: Arkham series.
Go play some of the older Onimusha titles.
Go play some good Castlevania games ( I recommend Lament of Innocense)!
Learn more of what makes games fun to play in the first place.

So I decided to pick this up for 2 reasons; the love I have for the Game Dev genre and because its EXTREMELY CHEAP! (Who doesn't love cheap games?)
When I picked this up I had mostly low expectations and so far they met most of them. It's pretty casual for a Game Dev game really. Simple to pick up and play. The Tutorial is automatically enabled for you for the start of every new game and you can turn it off whenever you start. Options menu is pretty barebones with your resolution options, fullscreen, and some AA. (Borderless window is automatic for those with mutliple screens). Sound bars and master volume are available.
However, with some pros there's always cons;
1. Reviews are graded with 1-5 stars with no feedback at all.
2. Development is fairly unentertaining. While I like how you can have multiple teams of developers, its repetitve.
3. The games you develop seem to have no emotional attachment or anything. I simply just use the randomly generated names and move straight to development.
4. I like the isometric design, but it was designed lazy as ever where you can't rotate items to really maximize the space you have. Oh, and your building space is limited as well. You're better off just having one big room with everyone in it
Overall, its a solid $2.99 USD game. Its enjoyable to waste a couple of hours of freetime and to visit every once in a while. But nothing to really dedicate and invest a major amount of time in. There's more interactive games out there like this like Game Dev Tycoon, GameBiz 3, and GamerGoMakers. But if you're tight on money, this is one you can pick up!

As much as I enjoy the aesthetic of the Shantae games, the navigation and progression through them always seems rather disjointed. As Metroidvanias go, I'm sorry to say Shantae kind of sucks. Almost all navigation is horizontally based except when in dungeons or caves, and the map tells you next to nothing. I know this game's development was a bit troubled; it was originally trying for a GBA release, then finally made it out on DSiWare with some major cutbacks. The main arc has 3 macguffins to collect which actually involves all of... 2 dungeons and boss battles prior to the finale. The original design document for this game had the overworld set on rotational plates, which would mean that you'd come back to the same places after hitting a trigger and they'd lead to different areas instead! Sounds cool on paper, but thank GOD that was scrapped, it'd have been an extra nightmarish layer of navigation.
As it is, halfway through the game you're forced to pursue some of the arbitrary collectathon crap to unlock moves for your transformations. Then once you've collected the third macguffin you're given no real clue on what to do next until you bump into some NPCs that are rather out of their way from where they usually are, which leads to more collectathon crap to progress yet again. Risky's Revenge feels like it had so much of the original game stripped away that they were forced to take half the mandatory stuff and just hide it in random spots around the world. It's like fishing for the Triforce shards in Wind Waker all over again. Laaaaaaaaaaame.

January 11th, 2016 (Hating it Less)
OK it's not entirely crap. Actually it's starting to be fun. Either that or my standards have dropped precipitously in the last 5 weeks.  My first mistake was trying to play it like Anno 2070. The key to 2205 is to build just what you need when you need it and nothing more. If you overpopulate you go broke. Surplus population will bankrupt you so fast in this rendition of Anno it's really ridiculous. Focus on building and selling your highest value technologies to the Orbitals ASAP. Maintain the raw materials and sub components and only add workforce when you have maxxed out the  perks and multipliers for the various production items. Take advantage of the strengths of the various Temperate and Arctic regions. Don't shoot for the Moon until you absolutely have to to advance. The point where you need to go from Exec to Investor is crucial. All of the tools you need are right in the game. Pay attention to the Ticker it'll give you hints on when to increase or reduce production of a given item. Some items you NEVER want to have a surplus of. Some you NEVER want to be without. I'll preface this by stating that I've played every single Anno game since they started making them. I'm a long time fan of the series and haven't disliked a single game they've put out and this game is definitely not the exception to that rule.
Is this game a bit different? Yes.
Is that a bad thing? Personal opinion but I would say no.
This game certainly does quite a few things different than previous titles, so lets get into it.
Combat zones separate out warfare into their own maps, and there aren't many of them. This is both a pro and a con because while I enjoy the new maps built specifically for combat, they get repetitive really quickly and offer no real meaningful contribution to the game outside of the story-related objectives. Collection of rare resource seems to be the only thing worth caring about otherwise and it's really just busywork and that's something we need less of in games, not more.
This also brings into contention the fact that there is, outside of some map quests, NO combat on your settlement maps at all; and, by association, means there will only ever be your corporation on a map, no land rushes to compete for space and resources, no fights over said territory, nothing. This probably also explains why there's no multi-player as after you strip the very fundamentals of what made Anno's multi-player there isn't really a great deal left you can do with it, outside of leader boards for population and efficiency etc.
If you've played the new SimCity you've probably seen this kind of thing before, basically now you can make "addons" to your buildings for numerous benefits including production increases and cost reductions. This, in itself, is a plus, I enjoy the extra flexibility it gives you and adds some much needed variety to building. Some will argue that this dumbs down the game but I don't really see it, it's pretty much the same except you have to think of most buildings like they're farms with different sized "fields" to consider once you've built the main building.
All in all I've enjoyed my time with this game, it's a significant departure from its predecessors in some ways while still feeling the same in others. If you're looking for a game that will last you a long time this probably isn't the game for you, check out previous titles instead, but if you're looking for another Anno game that mixes up the formula a bit while still being the sort of game you know and love, give it a try.

I was going into this game with a sense of a much upgraded if not evolved version of ANNO 2070. Instead I was met with a dumbed down ANNO that seems to be meant for beginners or a kiddy pool game meant to entice people who wouldn’t normally play a game such as this. Unfortunately in doing this they have alienated the fan base for this franchise.
Keeping It 100% - The Break Down:
1. You have 3 zone types. (Temperate, Artic, Lunar(aka the Moon))
2. You have out of those 3 map zones you get to pick 3 different maps for each of those zone types. (No more random map spawns) This matters little because you can unlock the other 2 for each zone in a single game play.
3. There is no enemy; instead you get a makeshift mini-game that has you command a small fleet of ships running around and killing everything on the screen, this you play at you leisure as it has no impact other than letting you get your hands on rare materials early in the game and after you reach the Moon you will have no further need or even attempt.
4. Trade is done automatically and due to there being no enemy to worry about this is just icing on the cake of features removed. (NOTE: You get one ship per zone or in regards to the moon (a rover) this is used to claim areas/ islands and has little use beyond as all resource transport is automatic so you don’t ever load the craft with anything; just move it, click and done.
5. It works and is a beautiful game but with so many features removed it has the depth of an inflatable kid’s pool and thus has very little replay value. Much of what made ANNO 2070 great is gone.
I give it a 6.5 out of 10; Good for a play thru when bored but dont bother unless price is  50% off or greater.

Gorgeous. Intriguing. Fun. An episodic story-driven adventure about choice and consequence, set in parallel worlds.
To be honest, I wasn’t sure how I’d be able to adapt to a 16-year old game (“The Longest Journey” was released in 2000!). There’s clearly a massive fan-base and loyal gaming community. I added it to my wishlist and patiently waited for all of the chapters to be released before making the purchase.
Right from the main page, there was an option to “catch-up” using the original cut scenes from all of the previous games (with ever-improving graphics for each chapter). I found this to be a really clever way to get up to speed on the story thus far and see the visual progression through the years. “Chapters” does a great job of catching up new players to the storyline and leading them into the continuation of the series.
Huge wins for this game: Voice acting, gorgeous environment visuals, attention to detail, and RPG decision trees (seemed a bit shallow at first… until I realized that decisions I had made in Chapter 1 were altering the game in the final chapters).  For me, about 90% of the puzzles were easily solvable in-game with a bit of exploration and patience. About 10% needed some slight “nudges” from the online community. A few of the quests were a bit over-tedious, but for the most part, the quests matched the story.
Great for casual gamers, binge gamers, and achievement hunters.

Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition is one of the best games I have ever played. The PC version of it does suffer from lack of optimization by From Software, but there is DSFix (a fan-made mod which fixes most of the port issues, and allows for framerate and resolution adjustments), which greatly makes the game a lot more optimal on PC.
Be warned: This game is plagued with some framerate issues, so be sure to have a strong PC (preferably with a graphics card of GTX 750 or higher) to maintain a stable and high framerate. If you wish to have the game run similarly to its Xbox 360 and PS3 counterparts, then you'll need a graphics card at least on par with a GTX 460.
The keyboard and mouse controls are very unwieldy, so be sure to use a controller (preferably an Xbox 360 or Xbox One Controller).
The combat, level design, bosses, music, and replay value are incredibly vast with this game, but to experience all of them comes with a cost: It will take a substantial amount of time to master the combat and learn how to defeat every type of enemy. Despite Dark Souls's reputation, the game is definitely beatable, but one will need to invest a lot of time to understand how the game works. If you are willing to invest the time, and are willing to deal with a lot (I really mean A LOT) of failures, then this game will be an extremely fulfilling and rewarding experience.

This game has potential, but clearly still has some kinks to work out and feels unfinished. It is the level of polish I'd expect to see in early access, only this is a full release.
Here's a couple of the issues I ran into:
1) There is no visible hit box or health meter for enemies. You'll never know how close you are to dropping one.
2) Nonexistent soldier AI.
You can raise generals and recruit soldiers to follow them and form little warbands. But don't bother. Your soldiers won't seek out the enemy on their own or attack anything not on their tile. Enemies walking adjacent to them? Nope won't attack that. Considering the fact that vikings never stop moving, move at the same speed you do, and that dragons can't be attacked by infantry... soldiers are worthless. Just move them to meet or intercept the enemy you say? Good luck. Your soldiers won't attack while traveling even if they walk right over the enemy. Ranged defenses mounted on your walls are the only real option.
3) Nonsensical enemy behavior and fire damage.
Enemy AI is strange and random. Vikings arrive upon ships but can also inexplicably walk on water (as can your soldiers apparently) which allows them to get to places that you'd think should be impossible. They're also pretty dumb. All enemies arrive and roam across you settlement randomly with no particular aims or targets. As they go they set fire to things... even things that don't make sense. For example one time a dragon set my moat on fire. Another time some vikings tried to burn down a statue.
The only good thing I will say is that once the vikings rammed a few of their ships into one of my bridges. The boats and bridge both caught fire and were destroyed. I was surprised because that actually seemed logical (both as an outcome and as a tactic)... At least until their soldiers, mine, and my citizens all continued to use the nonexistent bridges.
4) No clearly stated goals.
As you play you'll reach milestones judged by the number of citizens you've managed to recruit, but there is never any way to tell your progress towards the next one (or even if there is a next one) until you hit it. As a result I often found myself wondering... why am I still playing this again? Is there really any more to do? The natural thing to do is to try to build every type of building, but once you finish with that you're left without any direction and things quickly become repetitive. Sure, there are achievements to earn, but a good chunk of them are hidden and therefore don't help the "what do I do now?" situation.
All in all I had fun with it for a while but it definiely feels unpolished and was frustrated by its horrible AI (if you can even call it that). I'd say there is about 1.5-2 hours of playability here right now max before things become extremely repetitive.
If it seems like the kind of game you might be interested in anyway I reccomend waiting to see if any of these issues will be addressed in future patches or for a significant price reduction/sale.

=HEADS UP=
I had a review before this one about the game being good. This stays of course but i had to clarify some points and fix this old messy review that i made before.
=INFO ABOUT THE REVIEW=
1. This review might be a bit longer.
2. This review is about my point of view and opinion. [If you disagree on a certain point or want to correct me: Be reasonable or i will ignore your comment.]
=REVIEW=
Now lets answer a question right at the beginning. Is the game good? Yes. Is the game enjoyable? For people that like games like Streetfighter and SSB probably.
Now you are asking me: Why would you say such a thing? Shouldnt this be just the normal Castlevania just like the old times? Well yes you are right. This should be just like the old games and i sadly can say: It isnt. If i think of Castlevania i think of a Platformer/Bossrush with collectables you need to get further. In certain games they made the collectables into other things that you needed to progress but they were still there. You were involved into the story from the very beginning without actually knowing much about everything except if you have read much before playing about the game. So usually you were left at the beginning with your starterweapon to kill all that would stand in your way to reach your destination.
In this game it is most certainly just like i explained before with some bad little details to it. Well why am i saying little? There actually is a big bad detail to the game but that i will explain later. In this game there are three Storyarcs. In each Storyarc you play a different character what is totally fine. All three are easy to play and about the same except their powers. With each character you access a new part of the Castle to reach your destination that most of the time leads into Bossfights that are challenging. But they arent challenging because you have to watch out for their attacks like before.
Now just shortly back to old Castlevania. If you remember correctly of how to avoid the enemy it was simply by actually avoiding your enemy. Now for those that dont understand: In the old games the Bosses were hard but easy to avoid. Their attacks were obviously predictable and only needed a certain amount of time and fails to get to the part of killing the boss. Sometimes you could avoid the boss so easily that you wouldnt even fail once. But dont get me wrong. It was not as easy as it might sound. You could avoid the boss easily but the Bossrooms were just as well sometimes Platforsections what made the whole fight into more than just: "You are trapped in tiny room. There is the Boss. Go kill". Sometimes the Boss used the Platforms himself. Sometimes the Boss got below the Platforms (and the screen) and tried to come up below you with an attack. Sometimes Platforms were the only thing you could use because the floor literally was lava. And sometimes just as well there were no Platforms what ment that the Boss had faster attacks that you had to avoid.
Back to this game there is not much to say. "Dodge, Hit, Dodge, Hit, Dodge, Hit and Hit again". This is literally what this game is. It is a game for people that like Fightinggames but not for people that like Castlevania as what it was before. I mean i have seen other Castlevania games that were seriously just simple Fightinggames like Streetfighter or Mortalkombat. I just looked at them and they began to bore me to death. It was not what Castlevania was about. And yes of course you could say the same about Mario Kart and Hyrule Warriors (a game i still dont understand why it became so popular but that is a rant for another time) and you would be right. They were succesfull with what they were doing but then i ask you about the: Why?
Because it was fitting. Super Mario was playing in not so modern world but machines and cars would still be available in that point in time. Even big flying Pirateships as we saw in other games. It was fitting because the world was all about Fantasy and literally just a tad crazy in general. Going over to Zelda we have the same case. It was simply fitting (even though i didnt like it) and it would work in their world. But in Castlevania what is known to be a Platformer/Bossrush just like Metroid is (And no "OtherM" didnt change anything about that and i dont want anybody raging at me for mentioning it) it doesnt fit. It is simple as that. If you think what Castlevania is about can you see yourself and your character fighting a zombie in a Streetfighterstyle? I cant and that is the point.
Oh and i mentioned the collectables before. Well in the original as i stated before you had to collect them and go into the next stage. Sometimes in the games there even was a FINAL FINAL Boss right after the normal Final Boss. In one of the little Castlevania Stories that was available first on the GBA and then on the DS you had to collect certain things and use them at the same time to reach the actual Final Bonus Boss before killing the actual Final Boss. Killing the actual Final Boss would lead you to the normal Endscreen with Normal Ending. Killing the actual Bonus (I rather call it the End-)boss would lead you to the real good ending. Dont get me wrong: Both ending are good endings but in the one mentioned last you were sure that you had destroyed the Evil. It was a good feeling that you could achieve that.
But back to this game we have nothing like this. We have collectables but the only you got from them were upgrades of your 3 main stats that you needed to fight and survive. You didnt get new weapons, or trinkets that would do something. And that is about it.
Would i recommend the game? Yes i would say so.
Would i recommend the game to a Castlevaniafan? I would not.
This game is not like any Castlevania game i have played so far. This game is not a Castlevaniagame for me since there are so many elements missing that makes Castlevania what made Castlevania.

I wanted to like this game so bad.
Here are some immediate reactions:
- Jumping feels awful.  You stutter and lose forward momentum, this is awful for a platformer.
- You die from fall height.  Coupled with the aforementioned jump feeling, this leads to many needless deaths.
- Attacks have ZERO weight.  The whip cuts through enemies, it's like swinging at nothing.
- YOU have zero weight.  The movement feels completely unsatisfying and empty.  You neither have the "heavy" movement of a Super Castlevania IV or the "smooth" movement of a Symphony of the Night.
- The maps are disconnected.  Instead of giving you a big area to explore, you "explore" lots of small ones and move on (simply having a "square-based" map does not make you a metroidvania).
- The "grab" animations are too long and repetitive.  If that will be your main means of finishing an enemy, you'd better make it fast, or interesting. Instead it's neither.
I can't even use the "well it's a 3DS port" excuse, because there were so many (Igarashi-made) fantastic Castlevania's on GBA/DS.  This development team tried to take THEIR Castlevania and put it in the Igarashi formula and managed to miss every single mark of what made those games so satisfying.
Castlevania belongs to 2D. The best game out of the Mercury Trilogy.

Ulitimately this game has been a pretty disappointing experience for me. I haven't finished it, and I'm probably not going to, so maybe put an asterisk next to everything else I have to say.
The combat is largely tedious, they pretty much directly ported the combat for lords of shadow into a 2D game, so you have direct attacks that hit a quarter of the screen, and area attacks that do less damage and hit about half of it. Basically you'll be mashing the direct attack button a lot. I'm not sure why they decided to give you a block, considering every almost every attack you run into in the game is unblockable. You can parry normal enemies, but it's almost always simpler to steamroll them by spamming the same combo. The boss battles I played were fairly interesting in comparison, but not enough to redeem it.
I have no idea why there's falling damage in this game. It barely comes up on the first pass, and when I was retracing for hidden items it's a simple matter to restore lost health at a font. It's just an annoyance. The platforming itself wasn't particularly enjoyable either. For the most part it's just moving from magnetic ledge to magnetic ledge, but there are definitely times when it's a trick to get your character to latch onto the chain whip point you want him to, for instance.
The plot is not very interesting, and frankly the game would be served better by a 1-2 minute scrolling text intro than the voice work and cutscenes it rams in your face. SKIP!
Overall, the game is really mediocre, and I wouldn't go up to a friend and say: "Hey! You should really play this game, it's nothing special!". It's certainly not awful, but I feel like anyone could find a better use for their time than playing this.
