Pros
-	It looks great! A lot of effort has been put into the design of the buildings and sector landscapes.
-	Many hours of gameplay.
-	The module system, which allows you to upgrade your production facilities.
-	Three sectors in each of the three game regions providing plenty of room to build.
-	No longer have to manage eco balance.
-	User interface is clean and simple to use.
-	Trade routes are simplified, but still remain a key gameplay element.  Eventually, you can transfer energy.
Cons
-	No multiplayer.
-       No manual save (cannot revert to earlier save game).
-       Simplified trade routes (compared to Anno 2070).
-	Load times can be a little slow, but generally there is no issue here. Note: I do have the game installed on an SSD (see below for further detail).
-	Game crashed on me twice in first 27 hours of play.
-	If purchased via Steam, Uplay is still required. Although my experience of Uplay has been positive.
-	Conflict zone gameplay becomes repetitive.
Summary
This is not Anno 2070. Yes, this is a good thing.  It is, however, at its core, still Anno.
This time around, you are in control of your own corporation with the aim of reaching the Moon.  Once there, you can mine Helium-3 and produce vast amounts of energy that you can transmit to your cities back on Earth.
As was the case in Anno 2070, you build production facilities to supply the needs of your inhabitants.  Once certain needs are met, you can upgrade residential buildings, which introduces the need for further goods and services, such as intelliwear and androids, security and transportation.  You carefully balance the supply and demand of these goods and services and watch your metropolis flourish.  The sectors look amazing, and as your corporation level increases you receive additional rare resources with which you can purchase modules for your facilities.  Trade is conducted between sectors, once your spaceports have been upgraded.
I have thoroughly enjoyed my first 20+ hours with Anno 2205, and I look forward to many more! (8 / 10)
Additional Comments
I do not understand all of the negative comments that are being made in other reviews. As another reviewer has suggested, perhaps those with more positive feedback are too busy playing and enjoying the game.
I played the game on the Advanced difficulty level, and I had bought all sectors, reached 150k investors and built my corporation HQ after approximately 27 hours of play.  I have not fully developed my cities/settlements in the other sectors.  I look forward to many more hours of gameplay.
I have spent over 80 hours with Anno 2070, and I can honestly say that Anno 2205 does become just as complex as you progress further into the game.
Others may disagree, but I believe the game is far from over once you build your HQ.  You can really begin to optimise and expand your cities.  You can even add modules to your corporation HQ.
I have also tried the Asteroid Miner companion app.  This is not simply a Bejeweled clone as others have suggested – it is similar, yes.  Transfer of rare resources requires that you sign in to your Uplay account with your registered email and password or Facebook credentials.  It is worth noting that after just 15 minutes of play the back of my handset did feel quite warm to the touch – I can only assume this is due to heavy use of the phone’s resources.
Please Note: Although I have completed the main objectives, reaching a population of 150k investors and building my corporation HQ, I still continue to play.  This may result in updates to the content of this review.
Played on the following hardware/software:
AMD FX8350 CPU
Crucial M550 SSD
Crucial 32GB RAM
GTX 660 2GB GPU
Windows 10 Pro OS

People need to stop thinking this game was supposed to be Anno 2070. It's not. It was never supposed to be. It is it's own beast, and after playing almost all the way through, I've decided I like it.
Yes, I miss some aspects of the older games, but what it lost in detail, it gained in playability. By removing the burden of managing inventories, the game now lets you focus exclusively on balancing efficiency which, in my opinion, is what Anno is really all about. My decisions have almost immediate effects which, again, allow me to focus on building and advancing, rather than having to micro-manage the storage slots on a dozen different trading routes.
While I do miss being able to produce ships of my own and build defenses and all that, I again come back to the fact that this is just simply a different game and as it stands right now, doesn't suffer from the separation of building and combat.
If you're new to the Anno series, you'll love this game. If you're coming from 2070, leave your preconceptions at the door and I'm sure you'll love it as well.

This game is actually pretty fun. I got this game after searching steam for some new games, and I believe this was up there for for newest games or so.
The price is only $9.99 so in my eyes thats pretty perfectly priced for this game. The graphics have a charm that I like but some people might not like it. The main objective really is to just grow the city, and depending on the difficulty, keep your citizen happiness above a certain point, and protect your realm from dragons, ogres, and vikings. You build buildings like farms, foresters, charcoal makers, orchards, houses, etc., and you just keep doing so and grow your realm. This is somewhat of an economy game while also being a strategy game.
The music is good, although if you play for a while it gets kind of reptitive, so playing with sound on/off intermittently is a way to prevent ear fatigue.
One of the biggest issues is that on every difficulty except the hardest one, the enemy attacks from ogres, vikings, and dragon's really don't matter. Sure, they'll destroy your buildings and kill some of your citizens, but low happiness doesn't really do anything aside from make people not join your city, or even make people leave. But the low happiness doesn't stay for long, and only on the hardest difficulty can you lose from low happiness. It's worse early game when you need more citizens and getting set back on resources blows, but late game/lower difficulties, it really doesn't matter all that much. By end-game, you can just place walls along the coast with a bunch of ballistas and archer towers, and raids from enemies won't even be a problem anymore.
Another issue is that once you've played for an hour or so, you're kind of doing the same thing. However, in an economy-type game like this, it's kind of expected. The building variety isn't that much, and depending on your map and playstyle, you can effectively fill the map with buildings in around 7 to 8 hours, and then you either watch or start a new game. However, the developers have released a roadmap explaining they will There's also no tutorial, so the only way to learn is either through the advisors (who are useless) or by just exploring and playing around.
I play on the effective medium difficulty, where you can't really "lose", but you can still get attacked, yet it seems to me heroes and making armies are kind of pointless. If you protect everything with archers and ballistas, the army is only kind of there to 1) eat your tax money, and 2) slow the enemy down (and fail at that too, since most of the time they will ignore your army.) Plus, you can't attack the dragon with the army so there's really only two invasions they can kind of do something in.
Overall, the game is still kind of early-access-y even though it just got released, but at least the developers are adding new things. They even have an active discord where they look at bugs and ideas in two channels they created. In the future there may be a whole lot more to do, and much more of a better game than there already is for us to play.

TL;DR- This game is the best game I have ever plated, and I have played A LOT. This game is ideal for all who seek an origional sandbox or construction game, and caters to the imaginations of the engineering-minded.  I give it my highest recommendation.
This game....
At first it is, honestly, kinda bad;
-It has an extremely steep learning curve, perhaps the steepest I have ever seen in ANY game. It took me around 2 days to learn the very basics, although to be fair there are a lot more online and in-game tutorials now than when I started playing.
-The game is visually not altogether that impressive.
-The game is extremely cpu intensive, and runs on a single core, meaning slower PCs will suffer, especially when there are lots of craft spawned, or lost of shells and missiles flying.
That being said, this game quickly became my favourite game of all time, catering to exactly what I want in a game: A vehicle based sandbox construction and combat game with block destruction, in which near enough every aspect of what you might want to build is customisable.
If you can get past the initial learning curve (which is long and steep, but not tedious), you will be greeted by an absolute gem of a game supported by a single developer (Nick) whom is perhaps one of the best game developers I have ever encountered; He listens to the community like no other, and even adds user design submissions to the base game's campaign. Speaking of which, the game features an ever-increasing number of campaigns, varying in length and difficulty. The first campaign (in my opinion, the best) features you, the player, trying to conquer the games fictional planet of Neter. In which, you'll face numerous ofher factions on a large map, with enemies varying from tanks to ships to planes to submarines, and even spacecraft, all of whih hwere designed by the community.
The building/ designing aspects of the game realy are nailed. Construction, once you know the system, is quick and easy, and has few limitations. The sheer number of blocks to choose from in the build menu is also astounding, with both more available on the workshop, and more planned for future updates.
The multiplayer aspect of the game is also excellent fun, having seen a bit of tlc recently, bringing greater stability, and better support for more players. In multiplayer, you can pretty much do anything you could in singleplayer, including building/ designing craft, playing through any of the campaigns, using mods, and several of ter gamemodes.
There are a few additions and changes I would like to ee implemented into the game, although I'm sure these will arrive at some point in the form of a mod or an update anyway:
-AI; While the AI has seen some improvements, there are a few errors and bugs here and there that still need ironing out.
-More blocks, namely 8m blocks (beams, slopes, or otherwise): there are several situations where I have felt that an 8m block would be welcome, such as when blending a curve to a straight line, i.e at the bow of a ship. Also, larger or customisable propellers: the game currently features 1x1 and 3x3 propeller blocks, but they are either out of place or simply inadequate on many sedigns.
In conclusion, Fron the Depths is a fantastic game with it's  foundations solid enough for it to become even better with time. If you're looking for a game that's very origional in it's design and how it plays, or are simply a fan of sandbox games or games where you like to blow stuff up, I cannot recommend this game enough, especially considering the price... If I had to score it, i'd give it about a 9/10, due to, mainly, bugs.
P.S. If anyone gets past the tutorials and still doesnt have a clue, just pm me and i'll try and help you... After all, the community is part of the fun of this game.

As someone who's played the two games that came before, I was happy to see the kickstarter. Some continuation on the story and maybe even a conclusion. I've been with the game since the kickstarter and the developers haven't disappointed. Regular updates and lots of fine tuning. Although they have chosen for an episodic release, I rather play the game in one go so I've waited until all 5 books were released.
The game itself is a worthy successor to the story and offers some nice plot twists. Choices you make actually make an impact on the story and for some of the choices you'll hit yourself in the head later on in the game, even though at the time you thought you made the right call or thinking wouldn't have any repercussions. I'm sure there's a lot of content I haven't even seen yet.
There's a pretty decent introduction to the story included in the game, but to grasp the full story you really should play (or watch a let's play) of the earlier games. There are quite a lot of references in the game that are only appreciated if you have played the earlier games.
The story is mostly linear with only a few puzzles that require you to wander around and find the right things to do. This is a plus in my case as I love to enjoy the story and not have too many distractions of pointlessly running around until I find the one thing that the developer hoped you'd logically find in order to solve the puzzle. I think a pretty nice balance is found here. The pause introduced in order to solve the puzzle allows you to appreciate the story more once it continues.
The graphics are great and the only downside I'd think of would be that there could be more expressions on the faces of the characters during conversations.

Update: The game is very linear. Mercury Steam did some work on the metroidvania elements, but they feel very simplistic when the general level design lacks the organic and interconnective feeling in the previous games.
They implmented fall damage into the game to create some tension in platforming, but it also makes the linearity even more obvious that the developer wants you to play in the way they want you to play.
And there's performance issue which is very bizarre. It seems the game has two framerate caps: 30 and 60. When your PC can reach a framerate above 60 on a certain setting, it gives you 60 FPS. When it's between 30 and 60, the game locks at 30 FPS. It is literally a very odd port choice
Framerate cap aside, the game doesn't run very well. During some cutscenes and special effects, you will see some severe framerate drops. The game's graphics is not top notch. Such performance is kinda unacceptable.
First impression:
2D graphic looks pretty good. The music is very nice and dramatic. The environment is dark and fit the Castlevania universe that I'm familiar with. Also the game runs well. Some players reported crash issues, but honestly, my first start of the game was problem free.
And here's the cons: The combat feels a bit sluggish and inresponsive. Just like its console counterpart, every hit animation feels powerful yet slow. It works well in 3D environment that requires you to think before attack. I'm not sure that is the case in 2D. The responsive and reflex based Castlevania combat in previous 2D titles like Symphony of Night is not here in my judgement.

The original text was published on Kanobu on 25.02.2014
I don’t know if a secret contest is taking place among the slasher game developers for the most over-the-top prologue*; but if there is one, then Lords of Shadow 2 is a shoe-in for the grand prize. First game of the series reboot by MercurySteam has greeted you with a slow gothic fantasy. This time the game gets right into the action. The protagonist is Dracula himself. He uses his own blood as a whip. His castle is under attack by an army of thousands. This army has a giant humanoid robot. The stakes are high, rivalries are thousands-of-years-old, prophecies are dark, and angels are fallen. And then there’s the usual removal of all those nice abilities which used to allow you to perform a complete massacre on poor grunts of the army which was attacking you.
The combat system looks exactly like the one of its predecessor: accentuated counter-attacks and two bars of special energy used to break blocks and heal. Both kinds of magic now have unique weapons, but controls are still the same. What stands out is a free-floating camera as opposed to static angles from the first game. A lot of delightful improvements to what already worked perfectly before aren’t the biggest surprise. The game looks back at the series’ legacy and remembers where the second part of metroidvania term came from. The world is a holistic labyrinth with inaccessible high passages and grates standing in your way. This promise of big and small secrets is the foundation for everything else here. The story progression path goes in big stretches only occasionally offering to come back to the earlier places. You could replay levels in the first game to access locked upgrades once you’ve acquired the required ability, but you also had to go through the repetition of story scenes and routes weren’t particularly interesting.
The second installment simply blends the secrets in the world as a part of a bigger picture. The scenery is grotesque most of the time and is occasionally filled with details for you to look at for some time. Half of the locations are in the future, of course, so it adds up to a final result of a truly bizarre over-stylized collage.
The wild outlook in accompanied by an equally wild script. It defies logic in favor of having more and more bizarre characters and spectacular action scenes. If there’s a fight on a moving train it’ll end with a crash, explosions and acrobatics. You can’t just kill the giant boss — you have to rip out its heart. It is completely normal for the protagonist to ride a giant gas bottle because he needed a new entrance in the building. The headcount of unlucky enemies of Dracula is in a thousands range. Relentless postmodern carnival wouldn’t give you a break, so at some point you just can’t be surprised by anything. Raisa Volkova, the daughter of Satan? Sounds completely normal!
Lords of Shadow 2 wants to go further than its predecessor so desperately and tries so much new stuff, that sometimes it ends with stuff that is just too cringeworthy. Clumsy stealth sections simply don’t hold up to the pace of the game and are irritating rather than entertaining.
Still, you get transformations into blood mist and rat pack out of this torture. Two more instruments for world-exploring toolset. You can see in it the reminiscence of what Symphony of the Night did to Rondo of Blood. The story of the series also goes in circles on the moebius band of time-travelling nonsense. The game may pass a self-parody for the long franchise with a few dozens of titles in it. And that may be a good thing sometimes.

I am prepared to give this game a recommendation, however one glaringly bad issue has sprung up that prevents me from recommending it at full price. However I'll get to that afterwards.
Let's get one thing straight, I do enjoy Anno 2205. The big complaints from people seem to be that it departs too far from the typical Anno formula, however I'm perfectly fine with that! I'd rather we get big changes than see the exact same game with a new coat of paint every few years *cough*2070*cough*. The game does lack the same freeform gameplay of the previous Anno's, this time focusing on 9 pre-determined sectors that you can switch to at any time (assuming you've unlocked them). So no more settling islands and exploring the world. Is it a little disappointing? Sure. But being able to get right into the game without too much hassle does help.
I don't want to spend too long talking about how I feel about the game as whole. Many of my thoughts are shared with other people, excluding the fact that I enjoy the more efficiency based gameplay over resource management. The big thing I've noticed however is game saving.
This game does use UPlay. And thankfully it doesn't seem to rely on it too heavily. Or so I thought.
Anno 2205 does NOT have manual save functionality. It is entirely reliant on UPlay Cloud Saving. I was however unaware of the save failing after my Internet went down as I was closing the game. I started up the game today to find over 4 hours of work had vanished.
So the question is, do I recommend this game? Yes, but ONLY if you have a stable internet connection AND you have enough room on your hard-drive for the game saves. Otherwise you will lose progress seemingly without warning.
SCORE: 7/10
TL;DR: This game is in my opinion a worthy successor to Anno 2070, however its issues with saving and very linear gameplay prevent it from getting a higher score. Wait until it goes on sale.

TL;DR: Don't buy this now. Wait for sales / additional expansion(s) to play this game. There's no MP, so you won't lose any fun.
The game LOOKS gorgeous, but compared to previous installation (Anno 2070), there's so many elements that have been cut down from this game, such as:
- Skirmish, Multiplayer mode. You can only play Campaign.
- Massive command ARK that you can personalize & store items.
- Events
- Army. There's no army production or military buildings that you can build. Battle has been seperated into its own mission, away from the base building. And you can only use ships (not even submarines!). And you are stuck with 3 types of ship that you can upgrade (stats only, no visual difference).
- AI Opponent. In any map, you're playing by yourself! There's no opponent AI, only some static trader AI.
- Random map. You will be playing on the same map on all playthroughs, 3 different map for each region type (Temperate, Arctic, Lunar)
- Progression. You'll only unlock some achievement and some MINOR cosmetics for your command ship & corporate logo. That's all. Unlike Anno 2070, where you can customize your Ark, get some rare components for stats upgrade in an island, etc. You will have nothing to do once you can build company HQ except for one-time achievements (in Anno 2070 you can continue playing to get some rare components)
- Manual resource management. All items produced in a regions is calculated into a total automatically, unlike in Anno 2070 where you have to carefully adjust your trade routes and amounts.
- No component research. You can't make some upgrade to boost your production / reduce maintenance of buildings in an island like Anno 2070.
Then there's some part that annoys me:
- The company HQ doesn't provide any benefits at all, but will need an insanely high maintenance (Credit, Power, Worker).
- Building location for docks are fixed, as well as locations for mountain / coastal buildings.
- Building modules for your buildings require special resource that can only be earned from missions / special map project. Really problematic in early game, but not at late game. And different for Temperate, Arctic, and Lunar regions.
- Resources are shown in net rate, not amount. I can have surplus of +1 of Android (late-game resource) and 400 of it in storage, but I can only sell / transfer it in rate, not amount.
- Amount of credit that you can hold is limited, based on your company level.
- You will jump a lot between maps to adjust your production rate. It's very repititive and brainless, BORING!
- Sector projects are almost only for getting achievement; once you're in late game, their bonuses are small compared to what you can make by yourself. Oh, and the ornamental projects are purely for some ornaments, not even a steady income.
- Every new game will be the same. Same story, same maps, etc. It will only differ by the game settings that you picked.
- There are some rival companies, but only for preventing you from buying additional regions. Once your level is above them, you can buy the regions they hold. Only that. No economy sabotage or any of the activitied that the AI used to do back in Anno 2070.
But, there are some parts that I like:
- Resource are counted in rate, so it's much easier to control resource production, especially one requiring many other resources. And it makes transfer to multiple regions much easier.
- All special buildings for increasing population level as well as warehouses doesn't have radius, but instead provide a constant amount. This adds flexibility to building placement, as well as some realism where I have to build multiple of them in a small, dense population area.
- Uniqueness of each region type. In arctic, you can only build resident places near factories, and in Lunar you need shield around everything.
Summary:
Clearly, Ubi wants much larger player base (= MOAR MONEY), and thus this game is streamlined as **** to almost pure pile of ****. There's no depth at all, no sense of progression, almost no online features, no opponents to challenge my company, trading with AI is almost useless, no military buildings, bland army, and some units are clearly reskin of unit models of Anno 2070.
Perhaps, Ubi is cutting down all those elements so they can charge them for additional $$ as DLCs (or expansions. Ubi & EA name DLC as Expansion, as the term 'DLC' has such a bad rep because of them)

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is a good game.  In fact, I'd call it very good if it weren't for a few glaring flaws.  Critically, this game floundered since the media focused on what the game did wrong rather than what it did right.  This game has many extremely memorable moments.  The battle with medusa and the battle with the toy maker immediately come to mind.  However, for a short amount of time,  the game throws some bad stealth mechanics at you.  There isn't much to say about them, the stealth is barebones and feels very out of place in the story, outside of a single instance where it seemed logical.  Luckily, their presence is more like a puzzle in the game than an actual mechanic.  You won't spend much time stealthing around.
Now, on to what this game got right:
Combat is A+.  It's up there with the best action games imo: God of War, Devil May Cry, etc.  It's more comparable to DmC: Devil May Cry all the way down to the weapon swapping mechanic.  It feels smooth, responsive, and impactful.
The graphics are fantastic.  The art team did a wonderful job in this game and the engine devs did a great job focusing on the most important aspects of the engine for this game.  The modern city looks great and manages to feel victorian while also looking modern, and Dracula's castle is absolutely gorgeous.  The game also runs like a dream (originally played on a gtx 780 with plenty of power to spare).
The story is...well it's nothing to brag about.  The premise is interesting, and the beginning isn't too bad, but some cringy dialogue and a painfullly bad ending ruin it.
In the end, I recommend this game.  The good outweighs the bad by a long shot.  Critically speaking, it's a heavily underrated game.  It's hard to accurately express what makes the good parts feel so much better than the bad.
If you are interested in this game, download the demo.  It's a good representation of what you'll do in this game 80%-90% of the time (minus the exploration).

I think I need to add this to the "games that most people hated which I actually enjoyed" list. Admittedly, I'm biased because I really dig Castlevania, enjoyed the first Lords of Shadow and Mirror of Fate, and am a sucker for the idea of playing as Dracula himself. But even at its most frustrating moments, Lords of Shadow 2 isn't nearly as bad as Edge Magazine (which gave it a 4/10) or any of the other mainstream reviews would have you believe.
Bloodsucking awesome stuff:
+ I feel like combat's speedier and more responsive than it was in the first Lords of Shadow, and there's less reliance on quicktime events. This might have to do with the fact that I'm just more experienced with the combat system after playing through the first game and Mirror of Fate, but I had a lot of fun beating up some of the bosses, which leads me to the next point...
+ The boss battles (with the exception of the finale) are grand as hell! You've got some classic mainstays in there, like Death and Medusa, whose inclusion instantly make this game seem "more Castlevania" than its prequel.
+ On that note, the first Lords of Shadow got criticism from many people who felt it was Castlevania in name only (though in a surprising twist, I've noticed that the first game is now retroactively considered great in the wake of the poor reception the second got). This isn't the case here - from the getgo, when you start out as Dracula in your castle sipping a glass of blood, Symphony of the Night references start popping up everywhere. These plus the haunted atmosphere and the inclusion of Alucard just make the game *FEEL* more like a proper entry in the series.
+ Lords of Shadow 2 is beautifully presented, and like its predecessor, has some of my favorite menus ever in a video game. (I'm just a sucker for any menu that resembles an old torn book and has little hand-drawn animations showing your available attacks.) The music feels like it's from the long-lost Castlevania movie that got stuck in development hell, and the environments are amazing...at least for the flashback sections of the game.
Not so bloodsuckingly awesome
+ The game has two worlds, Zelda-style - a flashback castle that sort of exists in Dracula's mind (or in another dimension, it's never really explained) and a modern setting. And while the castle is gorgeous, the modern levels are laboratories, deserted hospitals and dirty streets that resemble Gotham City in the Arkham games at their best but are just forgettable at their worst.
+ With the strange duo world thing comes the plot, which I actually enjoyed for the majority of the game, even though there's one big twist near the end that is really the most comic book thing ever, and I don't mean that in a good way. But the ending is very weak. Let's just say that the final boss battle doesn't exactly hit the heights of previous fights, let alone the epic clash of Gabriel Belmont versus Satan from the first game, and even though there's a big redemption story that builds up for Dracula over the course of 30-some hours, the whole thing concludes like a wet fart in the night. Also...Victor Belmont, what a waste.
+ Unlike Lords of Shadow 1, this sequel's a Metroidvania. This is good in theory, but on the negative side, enemies are still damage sinks, which interrupts the joy of exploration, and the shackles of the level-based structure of the first game are still there. Many times you can only traverse areas in a VERY SPECIFIC WAY that the game wants you to take - ie, even though Drac gets a double jump, he can't jump over this crappy little ledge to get the collectible on the other side even though you can CLEARLY see he should be able to reach it. No, you have to take the long route around and use your mist form to pass through a gate (and the mist form can only be used in a few key places too) because the game's been programmed that way. Mirror of Fate had this issue as well, but it wasn't as noticeable because that game was 2.5D. In a 3D environment, it's very obvious.
+ Tying into this element of restrictiveness, the stealth sections that got slammed by every reviewer ARE quite annoying. If you dunno what these are - there are a few enemies, like some huge armor-plated guards and Pan's brother, who can kill Drac in two shots, even though in every cutscene the Prince of Darkness easily demolishes much bigger foes. The only reason Drac is vulnerable to these guys is because the designers needed an excuse to make the players complete so-so puzzles where you need to change to rat form or cling to walls to sneak by them. It's kind of a ham-fisted way to switch up gameplay, but luckily it's only about 5% of the game.
Lords of Shadow 2 got massacred upon release, but I'm glad to see it's at least getting positive reviews on Steam two years later. I still liked it enough to go out of my way to find every collectible, which is rare for me. It's biggest flaw is that it has the restrictive design of a PS2 game, but was released in 2014, a year which also saw innovative titles like Shadow of Mordor which introduced fresh gameplay mechanics. In a nutshell: Microsoft Office Excel 2205, AKA Spreadsheet Simulator
If you're a fan of the Anno franchise like I am, I'd say skip over this entry, or if you can't resist the temptation, buy it when it gets a price cut and is on sale.
The way the game is handled is
different from any other Anno game so far. Strategy is not a thing in this game, you can just throw down buildings randomly and happily chuck along. Your citizens need food? Place a rice farm in an spot and they're instantly supplied. Are they thirsty? Find a coastal slot and throw down a water bottle whatever. It's simple and it's unappealing, half of the time I'm just waiting for numbers to go up.
Oh right, there's combat too, I guess.
See, the game is split into "sectors", some of which are Crisis Sectors. These are the only points of the game where you will get
excitement. You can just ram on through everything, spamming abilities to get yourself out of the danger and then do the objective.
Speaking of sectors, one of the selling points for me was that 2205 was supposed to be "5 times larger" than it's predecessors. Well, it technically is much larger than any other Anno game, but in the wrong way.
As stated earlier, the game is split into sectors. These sectors will
be the same, no matter what. The temperate sectors are the same, the arctic sectors are the same, the crisis sectors are the same, and - surprise, surprise - the lunar sectors are the exact ♥♥♥♥ing same.
"Lunar sectors, you say?"
Oh yeah, you go to space. It's more of a novelty thing. You build your cities in craters on the moon and have to make shield generators to protect from meteor showers, it's nothing exciting.
"Shield generators? Are you saying we build cities with a TWIST?!"
Oh no no, it's not as exciting as it sounds. In fact, it's more of a hinderence than anything.
In the arctic sectors, your citizens need heat, so you need to place your housings next to factories and mines and such. This becomes an
annoyance when you're trying to get the neccesary amount of citizens to advance, seeing as they cant even be a single inch outside of the heat radius of their pinky toes might freeze to death or something.
Still, the game is enjoyable for an hour or two, I'll give it that. But don't expect this to be worth the 60€ you're cashing out for it.
Long story short, I would not recommend buying Anno 2205, I regret pre-ordering the Gold Edition and I don't want anyone else to make the same mistake as I did.
Rating: 1/10.
-Kian
EDIT: Felt like pointing out that I did leave out quite a few things (unintentionally) like the lack of multiplayer and such. The other reviews probably do a better job at explaining everything anyway, this was just made as a rant review to vent my disappointment.

The game starts with a very retro cinematic, it shows you that yo grill gets shot, and to keep her alive you connect her to the speedometer of you car. You have to maintain speed to keep her alive.

Go to slow, and her heart's stops, go to fast and her heart overloads.

The game is a endless runner, but unlike most you have full control over your character (in the style of a racing game), most games would have you move between columns. Not here, here you have full controll.

The controls are simple, W for gas, S for reverse, Space for Drift, and Shift for turbo. One thing I really like about this is that you can use turbo for however long you want, there is no limit. But while using turbo the car is harder to turn. It adds a nice level of depth to a otherwise brainless game.

Every once and awhile you will come across giant helicopters that try to kill you. This is nice because without it the game is kinda easy.

But it might be a good thing, this is not a game that needs a lot of strategy. It’s the kind of game that makes you melt into your chair and forget about all of your problems.

One reason for that is it’s amazing soundtrack, it’s very retro and basey, using synths and other “Vaperwave” sounds. Something also amazing about it is that it’s all made by individual creators that have these songs in real albums. Buy the soundtrack on steam, it’s pretty fantastic.

One cool thing about the game is that the tempo of the music is directly tied to your speed, so the faster you go the more tense the song gets.

Moving through the amazing landscapes while listening to the music will leave you in a almost trance like state

This game is also really visually pleasing, It’s a eyegasm that will leave your spectacles sticky.
It’s using a very retro wave graphical style, it’s like a mix of gta vice city and tron.

So if you have a little bit of leftover money sitting in your steam wallet, you should give this a try. You won’t be disappointed.

= = = INITIAL IMPRESSION = = =
Currently, the best word to describe this game is using the word "solid".
Not good, not bad, not awesome and not horrible. Just solid.
Its an ok game for the price.
As it is, its an ok game i can recommend to those who thirst for build-up strategy games, as the genre isnt saturated by any means.
If it was, i think the game would be overlooked and not stand out in any way.
Doesnt even really have a unique aspect that sets itself apart.
As the market is now, thats fine, as delivering what we already know is already more than we currently have.
Searching for build-up strategy games, especially with combat as part of the gameplay, you have not many choices.
= = = GAMEPLAY AND CONTENT = = =
You will be busy for easily 10 hours.
Thats a careful estimate, as you will probably play for longer to get everything out.
But, considering that the game in each of its systems is only scratching the surface, it could easily be that you think you are done after 2 hours, or even 10 minutes.
There is NO meta gameplay or overlaying system that could give a feeling of depth and purpose to be found.
Meta gameplay examples: Diplomacy with factions, trading and relations with factions, a goal you globally work towards like a worldmap or campaign map, research or other abilities, local policies customizing your kingdom or a connection between all of your islands where you can share resources and the like (Sim City 4 style).
Any of that could give the player a feeling of not only working in a micro level of gameplay, but a meso level connecting each small thing you achieve together with other aspects.
As it is, you select a randomly generated map, but very limited as there are no different biomes, no mountains, rivers or hills.
You then start building and take care of basic needs.
The production lines are never "complicated", nor deep.
Wood is directly ready to be used, no sawmill or similar. Stone aswell.
The maximum complexity of a production chain will be getting wheat off a field and directly into the bakery to get bread. Mills are only giving a buff to surrounding fields (you get 15 food instead of 13).
This wouldnt be a problem, since games like Northgard show that a game in the build-up genre dont need to be complicated and have large production lines to gain depth in gameplay.
But Northgard, which i really recommend to each interested in a good build-up strategy game, achieves depth with connecting each system together and keeping you busy.
I never feel this way in Kingdoms and Castles.
The game consists of 3 modes, peaceful, giving you enough freedom to build how you want, easy, which is normal mode where you get attacked sometimes and so on and hard where you get attacked more often and winter is more harsh.
No multiplayer, although it would benefit from it and thats an understatement.
It has barely customization, you can name your city/kingdom, and choose a banner. Thats it.
Even the rooftops of your buildings dont have chooseable colours, so they stay violett by default.
Which is far from nice looking in my opinion.
Maps are quite small, enemies consist of 3 types, number of different buildings is ok and i never felt it was too less, especially since buildings overlap graphically so each city looks unique even though you place the same buildings all the time (no different skins for regular buildings like houses).
= = = TECHNICAL SIDE = = =
The visual design does the job, no opinion from me as its up to personal taste and you can see, whether you like it, in the video or on screenshots.
What i want to mention though, is that its visual presentation has nice details, such as clouds, giving the game a really nice touch.
Clouds are visible from afar, but whenever you get with the camera at a point where they would block your vision, they fall apart in a nice looking effect.
I think thats a really nice idea to give a immersive visual impression without creating gameplay problems.
It still seems to have issues though.
Playing on my PC with a GTX970 Stryx, FX8370e CPU and 8GB Ram i started with around 140-160 fps. Going on on the same map i then reached around 48fps, although i only had about 600 people in my city running around, and by far not built enough to justify such a drop (screenshot on my profile).
I heard from others, and it seems achievements indicate that this is true, that they had around 2-3k people in their cities.
Leaving the game alone for an hour with my stable running city (which i did when i was young with Simcity to see what happens), the game somehow managed to drop to 13 fps although nothing changed.
Closing and restarting the game pushed it back up to 48-57 fps.
Still a big drop considering i barely had any people, but it tells me that there is a problem on the technical side of the game.
Also there will be bugs, for example people starved to death although they had a fully stocked up granary, bakery, corn fields and a market directly next to their houses.
They somehow couldnt stock up their foodsupply.
I suspect there is a pathfinding issue, as there is a somewhat similar issue regarding the harvest of fields.
Placing a granary directly next to fields leads peasants to bring the harvested corn directly there to store it, as when winter comes all that is left on the field will disappear.
That means they have to go about 3 times from field to the granary to bring all the corn there.
Even though the granary is directly next to the fields, they never managed to get all the corn.
Cant tell why.
The advisor tells me to place the granary closer, which isnt possible, except maybe theres a way to build the granary OVER the fields (there is not).
Apart from that the game runs fine, no crashes to report.
= = = RESUMEÉ = = =
A solid game, for all who are fans of the genre, get it.
As the price is well set for what you get.
Its by far not perfect, and far from awesome. But its also as far from being bad. Again, its solid.
A good portion of building, in a relaxing way, no need to react fast.
Just playing and doing what you want, building your little Kingdom and take care of everything.
Difficulty felt hard enough, but variety is a big problem with the game, as enemies are too few, complexity is too low and depth isnt really in each system.
It keeps you busy, for an unknown time.
Maybe you will hit the 2 hour mark and be done with it, congrats you can refund then.
Could also happen you will spend 10, 20 or even 40 hours with it.
Depends on how deep you jump into it and how often the randomness can get you into replaying. Maybe theres this thing that gets you hooked.
Or maybe its missing, keeping you from playing.
= = = FINAL THOUGHT = = =
That they take what they have here as a basis, and expand it A LOT.
I even believe, that if they were to put a mode in where you play against an AI on your level (building a kingdom by itself and dealing with the same stuff as the player), or even have an Multiplayer mode where a player takes that role, it could be a must have for this price. Its like a really dumbed down Stronghold, where the Swine sends yet again 20 archers and 10 spearmen to run against your walls with over 300 crossbow soldiers waiting.
Its fun enough, but soon you want to get into skirmish and challenge the AI and a friend, do a compstomp or whatever.
As the basic gameplay loop will let you hit a wall where replayability is out the window.
So i hope they fix that.
= = = MY ADVISE = = =
If you didnt already, head over and take a look at Northgard.
It has a somewhat similar basis, but deeper systems, more unique experiences each game, enough randomness without being bad, a multiplayer and currently 4 clans to choose from, all with a different playstyle.
All that while looking really good and being fun with new and fresh ideas.
If you are into the genre, its def. a must-have.
You have questions, feel free to ask.

* No-spoilers review: *
The game's Books One through Four are nothing if not spectacular and spin the story's threads in a very skilled and logical and thought-provoking manner. I couldn't recommend them more.
And then comes Book Five. Which I can only describe as: WTF?
First of all, it's not a Book like the others, it's an overblown ending sequence, with very brief interactive intermissions. It's so obviously rushed, that I immediately catch myself excusing the creators for some simple reason - I don't know, running out of money? out of studio time? personal issues? - the likes of which tend to plague Kickstarter-born, drawn-out projects - and I start thinking, "well, all right, it was probably either a rushed Book Five or no Book Five". But then again I slap myself mentally a little. After all, I did pay for five books of an interactive story. and instead I got four interactive books and one blatantly rushed epilogue. Mixed feelings abound.
Oh, and if it were a nice, wrapping-it-all, climactic epilogue, I may not have whined as I am. But whine I shall.
* Spoilers from here on. *
First of all... Saga. Previously a doodling toddler, known to have some connection to April. A reincarnation? A kindred soul? Aaactually, no, rather a rebellious songliner (what?) who prefers songs to drawings now (because?) and she's actually traveled a countless myriad worlds, that's what she does, playing life on cheat mode and apparently being a professional prophecy-fulfiller. WHAT? Oh never mind, we'll never know. And who is this Rose, whom old Saga mentions when talking about flying teacups and dragonflies, wasn't it Queenie the Chinese-ish old lady who did those? Mind you, I love throwaway expositions and  cliffhanger endings, but not instead of a proper, logical, consistent wrap-up.
Then... Kian's future. Saga steps in, saves the day, actually saves several decades, making Kian the Bloodless King with herself by his side. Roll credits, "And The Adventure Continues"! Aaactually, no, we're seeing Kian as the king, and then Saga as an old crone, and worlds after the Merge, and... Wait, wait, the time to do a cute, perversely counter-climactic cliffhanger is over, why do we have SEVERAL of them?
Next... Undreaming takes center stage. It's the most horrible, destructive force! Let's set it free. Book Four mentioned the Nightmare as being the necessary, unavoidable dark side of the Dreaming, very specifically NOT the same as Undreaming, which just cancels out everything. And yet here we go, Undreaming has an Undreamer and is needed to Balance? What?
And next... The Machine. On the Arcadia side, it was built by Westhouse to power the spear to unleash the Undreaming, all right, but how come a very similar machine was built on the Stark side at the same time? Sure, there's a nice "worlds mirrored" vibe here, but it's never explained nor even hinted at. Brian only names Helena a "tool", hardly a mere insult, rather a direct reference to her being a pawn in his game - but wasn't he, like, unable to get to Stark in any way, let alone manipulate people there? Also, does Eingana "collect dream energy" (for whatever purpose and whatever that is), or "influence people's dreams to reshape reality"? Those are two very different concepts, and yet they're mixed up in the same dialogue.
Finally... It was all about choices so far. We got to decide people's lives or deaths, we got to watch the Balance icon shift this way or another... And in the end, Zoe simply calls Helena "insane" and prefers to help destroy Eingana, without a single thought that maybe, just maybe, "rebooting the world, without disease, without violence" might actually be a GOOD thing, if possible? No moral dilemmas, no free will versus wise control?
All this looks as if the storywriter for the previous four Books got fired, and a new one was brought in for the last Book, and he/she did as good a job as they could after being given only 10 minutes to acquaint themselves with the whole story so far.
Book Five belongs in a different game, in a different reality. A damn shame. The first four Books are truly magical, enthralling and a true pleasure to play - but Book Five just deserves a rewrite.

After playing The longest journey, Dreamfall and Dreamfall chapters I have made up my mind on this game. Although I generally do not recommend it, there are plenty of good parts and it's a decent story.
However, be aware that it's highly advised you play TLJ and Dreamfall before playing Dreamfall chapters.
PROS
-----------
- Decent and (sometimes too) expansive story.
- Probably the only game out there whose single story was told over 3 games and over 15 years to tell.
- Voice acting is pretty good and the characters are interesting.
- SOME good jokes.
- Crow.
CONS
-------------
- In the end, choices don't seem to matter much and don't affect the main story.
- Good number of lose ends left unexplained. The devs seem perfectly fine with that and acknowledging the fact that stuff needs to be explained. For example one of the most mysterious characters tells that he/she will explain everything but the player never gets to hear any of it. With Book 5 being very very likely the last entry for The longest journey series, they could've used this to tell and explain everything. Yet, they choose to end the game like they did. With even more questions...That's fine with some people I guess, but not for me.  If I wanted to guess, then I wouldn't need to even listen to the story.
- Devs did a poor job at reminding everyone about the story so far. Sure we have a recap now,  but it's far from perfect (and doesn't recap TLJ). A lot of times you will need to remember stuff from 1999 and 2006 to fully get what's going on.
- Some attempts at humor are cringe-worthy. Especially the sex related jokes.
- Book 5 has no gameplay. You just walk and talk, with a wild puzzle here and there. This would be fine, plenty of games have only that and they're pretty good. However, since choices don't matter much and Dreamfall: TLJ had simple combat mechanics, it feels like shame not placing them in (especially since you control a strong warrior character).
- Some characters seem very bland and one-dimensional. Also there are times when characters say something that doesn't really seem in line with their persona (sometimes for joke purposes)
The game has  a lot of merits I guess and a very good basis for storytelling. However, the execution could've been done a lot better and the bad sides really stand out and sometimes overshadow everything else. Dev's expectation that we remember most of the story so far didn't help the story telling aspect at all.

The cutscenes are a bit long. There isn't much I can say without spoiling it. I've never played The Longest Journey, so I may have missed out on some references, but the story stands on its own, for the most part. Well-thought-out and genuinely interesting and often funny. The gameplay is minimal, but not obnoxiously stupid, i.e. no pointless flash events. I'd like more games to use these kinds of mechanics rather than the idiocy that telltale games force on the player.
I complained about some of the story elements on social media and one of the devs chased me down to clarify it - I haven't seen someone care this much before, really happy about that, especially since it's a pretty high-profile title. Get it, play it, enjoy.

As much as I would agree with people that this game is stripped down to its bare concept, I must say that it is a very clever and innovative one. However, if you have a group of at least 3 friends, this is a fun and entertaining game to play, especially if you’re creative enough to play around with the limited objects it provides.
Once again, I would love to see updates to this game, because as it is, the concept has not been fully explored. Anyone could think of new and interesting things to add to this game, as a quick example, a block which gravity applies to, which can be pushed around and dropped off edges to land on players to kill them, but once again, this is down to the developers implementing these into the game.
I can fully understand that an online multiplayer mode should not be based on port forwarding, and should include a lobby, but people do need to understand that this is a very difficult goal to achieve and even requires money to be put into it, which may be what’s holding this game back.
I have a lot of respect for this game and its concept, and can only suggest that everyone give it a fair chance, instead of spending minimal time in the single player mode and whining for your money back. This game is an underrated gem. Not sure where the bad reviews are coming from. Most of the game takes place in an interconnected castle that will remind players of the metroidvania games. The combat is simple and satisfying and rewards variety and good timing. The boss battles are epic, and each one is unique and requires the player to learn a specific strategy. Sound design, music, graphics and presentation are all fantastic. Stealth sections provide a change of pace and though they are not as fun as the exploration and combat portions of the gameplay, they are few and far between.  Happy I decided to pick this up despite the abysmal reviews.... If you are fan of the first Lords of Shadow then you absolutely must play this game. If you haven't played the Lords of Shadow series, definitely pick up the first as it is also a classic IMO. The series gets a lot of hate from Castlevania fanboys, and whilst it is definitely true that it deviates from many of the series tropes, I don't consider it a bad thing at all.  A lot of care and devotion was poured into this series and it's a shame it has not gotten the positive reception that it deserves.
Bottom line is if you are a fan of 3d action/adventure games you need to play this game.

All in all I'd consider this a very good game, an 8 out of 10.

Due to all the mixed reviews, and removal of things like multiplayer, changes in gameplay...and so on, I was unsure if I would enjoy Annoy 2205 as much as I thought I would. Turns out after installing it I blasted through till morning and yeah. It was good.
One of the major complaints I see is that 2205 is dumbed down. I disagree. While at first it might seem simpler, it's not. A lot of people say that the change in surplus/shortage is a change from previous cames, but I also diasgree there. You were always producing a set amount over time, consuming a set amount over time with other buildings, needing a set amount over time to sustain your population's satisfaction. The only change here is you get to atually see the production numbers, you don't have to go to the wiki to figure out what you will produce x units of whatever over y minutes.
The game starts to become fairly complex fairly quickly, if you're growing your company. Once you get transfer routes, you're going to need to start shipping biome specific items to other biomes in order to continue growing. To support that, you're going to need a healthy population, requring more shipping lanes...and so on. Finding a balance to grow your population steadily without endagering your bottom line is the main component of this game. And I'm happy to say that it delivers a challenge.
If you want Anno 2070 Part 2, this is not the game for you. 2205 took some risks in changing up the formula, and I think it maintains itself as a very good management/simulation game. Sure, there might not be multiplayer, but if I want multiplayer Anno, I can go play 2070 or 1404. This is not the game I play for that. This is the game I play for a streamlined management experience

Anno 1404 was a magical game. The setting was perfect for me. I love history, and that game scratched every itch I had. Everything made sense: Of course your pioneers needed fish. Of course they needed meat, coffee, wine and tools. The production chains made sense, I understood them. You need cows to produce meat. You need iron and wood to produce tools.
That is why Anno 2070 did not manage to suck me into it. That is one of the reasons Anno 2205 fails. Do you need nano ceramics and cobalt to produce construct-o-bots? I have no idea.
What I truly loved about the previous Anno games was this:
If you had joined a game after 20 hours, everything would seem like complete chaos. Fleets of ships going in all directions carrying tons of different goods to a dozen islands. But for the player, every little thing made sense. Because they had built everything from scratch. Every boat, every building, everything. That was the real beauty of it. The best learning curve I have ever witnessed in a game.
It was challenging. You had to keep trying getting the perfect balance in your production chains. You had the option to taxate the population and selling surplus goods. You had to fight for the best islands.
Now, they have stripped most of it out. Every warehouse is in prebuilt locations. The ships are just generated, making no sense. You cannot set taxes, you dont need to fix production chains as they tell you exactly what you need to do, and you cannot sell goods! So what do you do when you are low on cash? Its quite simple, actually: You just leave the game with a positive income, and let time take care of it.
That was the point when I realised how poor this game was: When I could leave the game on for several hours, and when I opened it again, the ONLY thing that had happened was a big bank account. In Anno 1404, that would have been a suicide. Pirates would attack. Other players would steal the best islands, they would invade you. The production chain was guaranteed to be a little off-balance, so after some hours your citizens would have left your town. Because they would run out of bread, meat and books. And I understood them. I would leave too.
Would I leave due to a lack of neuro implants? I dont know. Probably not.
This is not strategy, its barely administration. Bring back the excellent gameplay of 1404, and make a Anno 1800 or 720bc. Until then, I will keep beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Leif Jorgensen.
PS: If you havent played Anno 1404, do it. Its the pinnacle of the series in my opinion, and it has aged quite well.

The game starts with a very retro cinematic, it shows you that yo grill gets shot, and to keep her alive you connect her to the speedometer of you car. You have to maintain speed to keep her alive.

Go to slow, and her heart's stops, go to fast and her heart overloads.

The game is a endless runner, but unlike most you have full control over your character (in the style of a racing game), most games would have you move between columns. Not here, here you have full controll.

The controls are simple, W for gas, S for reverse, Space for Drift, and Shift for turbo. One thing I really like about this is that you can use turbo for however long you want, there is no limit. But while using turbo the car is harder to turn. It adds a nice level of depth to a otherwise brainless game.

Every once and awhile you will come across giant helicopters that try to kill you. This is nice because without it the game is kinda easy.

But it might be a good thing, this is not a game that needs a lot of strategy. It’s the kind of game that makes you melt into your chair and forget about all of your problems.

One reason for that is it’s amazing soundtrack, it’s very retro and basey, using synths and other “Vaperwave” sounds. Something also amazing about it is that it’s all made by individual creators that have these songs in real albums. Buy the soundtrack on steam, it’s pretty fantastic.

One cool thing about the game is that the tempo of the music is directly tied to your speed, so the faster you go the more tense the song gets.

Moving through the amazing landscapes while listening to the music will leave you in a almost trance like state

This game is also really visually pleasing, It’s a eyegasm that will leave your spectacles sticky.
It’s using a very retro wave graphical style, it’s like a mix of gta vice city and tron.

So if you have a little bit of leftover money sitting in your steam wallet, you should give this a try. You won’t be disappointed.

There's potential here, but it's hidden underneath irritating controls and laggy menus.

I decided to buy this game just from sheer curiosity at a random Steam sale they made, celebrating the completion of all the five books I think or something along those lines, and man, it was so worth it.
At first I was totally at loss, I was like, what in God's name is going on. The story I felt I was missing something, and yes I totally did, I was totally oblivous to the fact there were two other games before Dreamfall Chapters, even though this was in the game description I read too fast...however, having the summer sales in front of me, I just grabbed them and started playing them, that's how cool I found these games.
Never having played these series, you eventually get more and more bits as story goes on, and you begin to understand the context, however, to my horror, I realized I actually spoiled myself several important things that happened in the previous games, that should I have played them, would have gone "Aha..." with a knowing smirk, instead I was at a loss, and then I realized I was with the whole story of The Longest Journey in front of me, shucks!
If you have not played the others, don't you worry, you will get to love and understand what is happening just fine in these games, but perhaps, with less insight and complementary details of whole story. Should you go and buy the other 2 games first before playing these? Well that will depend, I'm still playing the first, and I like it, but the first game is a 1999 game, so gameplay inclusions (such as the little journal interface that tells you what are your objectives and such) & graphically-wise it *might* not be suitable for you, it is up to your tastes.
It is sort of weird at first and at a loss, but I found it quite enjoyable, really enjoyable. Quite...original in a sort of way, if you ask me. Certainly, there could be improvements here and there, and if you can't help but try to find out every single  flaws that might and is, and concentrate on them like you can in ANY game really, you will ruin yourself the game of course and won't like it. People can sometimes find anything to rant at if they want, however, if you sit back and relax, this game, I can assure, is an entertaining experience.
The Story takes place in four dimensions principally, one futuristic (hovering robots & stuff), one archaic (magic, knights, etc.), dream-state, and a location in between time and space. I really don't want to go on much about what this is all about, because part of the treat of this game is to progressively discover it by yourself, but this has stories that take good advantage of their varied tematics and manage to blend them well.
The voice-acting is really good, the voice tones adequate to their characters, and the dialogue is pretty funny, specially if you have a twisted/dark humor. Gotta love Mira.
This is actually something that I found out, that if you have not played the other games, you will be probably at a loss at first like me, like "what is this, and what does it does?", but somehow, it was obvious enough to get it after the very first intro level, and after that you will be learning new tricks. Sometimes the puzzles can be pretty tricky because you expect to find everything in the environment, and you forget to check your inventory. Sometimes it will ask you to remember past experiences you had while interacting with the characters and the like to resolve a problem you might be facing, one involving a certain robot had me laughing in disbelief, thinking, "Oh my, had I not talked to it for kicks and giggles before it would have never occured to me, and I can't believe this was the true purpose of it all along". Sometimes things are just plain hidden (sometimes well too hidden) or are just plain, and you'll have to sort of just go around searching what is the only thing you can "target" that you had not noticed before or such, and that is a little meh, but you find the forgiveness in your heart for the devs.
While you are setup in different areas, it might slightly feel at first that you have a lot to explore and that you'll find scurvy rich pirate treasure if you look hard enough, but no. I mean, you'll certainly find an interesting reference or something funny here and there, but in truth I felt it was pretty linear with a touch of an open-world illusion, but of course, you have to remember you are in a playable bedtime story and it is easy to forget it.
I must confess that what has given me most thrills in this game, is the very moment where you are expected to make a decision. You are offered to see what the rest of the people has chosen the most, but I advise out of it, you'll get biased for sure. But it is not having to take the decision that gave me goosebumps, but what comes inmediately next. "The Balance has shifted", somehow everytime that happened I had an ominous feeling, like I had sealed my fate for good, and had me eager to see what would happen now. The little versions of it, with the "!" symbol at first were not as dreadful in my head, but I soon learnt to rethink that. Everytime it pops, I went "Oh my...", sometimes you don't expect what you answered to have an effect, not always it does, and not always you'll know that its going to be, so play true to yourself.
The Arcadia world (the magical, archaic one) made me feel like I was playing Dragon Age: Origins, if you have played it, then you know what to expect graphically. Meaning, a beautiful world available for you to gaze at (unless you start to hyperventilate if things aren't in 4k and such), *however*, you will perhaps encounter here and there little small things that could use improvement or don't show properly, but that won't ruin your experience at all, specially in the Book 1 and 2. An accurate name for this game would be: "
"
I'm not saying it's bad, I enjoy it so far. I just want you to know what you are getting into. :-)

It was fun at first then and especially if you want to get all 3 skulls on every level you have to do them over and over in oder to get everything to come together perfectly, its like a stressfull puzzle.

Though the campaign can be finished in about 3 hours or so, this game is ridiculously fun.
At first I thought it would turn out rather boring and slow-paced but hell, wasn't I wrong.
Crush your Enemies isn't as it says, a 'glory-days-RTS' since it shares so few similarities with the genre as it was in the early 00s, but it does show its creativity as a standalone game.
Pros:
-Tile-based one-screen seems obvious enough for turn-based strategy but for real time it's something new. You're always watching what the enemies are doing and this plays a huge part in the tactics section. Welcoming change.
-The gameplay is frenetical: decisions must be made constantly. How many guys do I need to keep the units income flowing? Since the number of units in a single tile controls the speed of everything they do, separating them to micro-manage is key.
-Strategy and tactics are both indeed required; managing shield bearers, archers and mages is rewarding as well as deciding 'build' orders, which go vastly different from map to map.
-Graphically it's very solid. Everything feels crunchy and well animated.
-Musically decent, fitting with the theme.
Cons:
-As a mobile port, controls are fully moused and may not come out as intended.
-Little troop variety. Units are very specialized but alternatives are missing. I was expecting giants, catapults, cavalry, women, pigs, but none of that is present, only warriors, archers, shield bearers, scouts and mages, apart from map-specific gods.
-Campaign is way too short. No alternative such as conquer the world campaigns or anything randomly-based other than skirmishes. Sense of accomplishment is rather halted in this.
-Items are weird. They're interesting to use and provide a lot of strategic value, but nearly half of the missions ask you to win without using items. This is counter intuitive as the only campaign resource you collect other than 'stars' is beer, which is used to buy items, which mostly just stay there.
-No upgrades whatsoever.
Overall 7.5/10, good fun and very enjoyable but kinda lacking. Get it on sale.

This poor excuse for a Half-Life mod does everything contrary to what its store page description says:
"Intense action" - Hardly. The most intense part of this mod is watching a random person in a dark, broken down elevator get eaten by a Barnacle.
"Set in Half-Life universe" - I have a hard time believing that as well. This doesn't fit into the Half-Life canon whatsoever. Why are creatures from Xen roaming this boat BEFORE your character finds the "artefact" (this mod is full of typos as well) that opens the portal to Xen? Furthermore, why are you on this boat in the first place? Why is there a military presence on this boat? Why was the Ninalanth in the boss fight flying around in a fixed pose with a Barnacle tongue? So many unanswered questions...
"High quality soundtrack" - I found the soundtrack to be extremely annoying. I tried turning the mp3 volume all the way down in the settings, but my ears were still violated by repetitive synthesizer beats.
"Spirit of Half-Life technology to enhance visuals" - Spirit of Half-Life technology? What does that even mean? The visuals were by no means enhanced; rather, they were exactly the same as they were in the original Half-Life.
"High definition models" - It actually DOES ship with what the original Half-life defined as "high definition", but it really wasn't HD.
Overall, I'd have to say my most recent bowel movement was A) more intense B) more true to Half-Life's canon C) of a better quality soundtrack D) more visually impressive and F) more HD than this mod.

I'd love to give this game a thumbs up but unfortunately I think there's still way too many bugs to be able to state that the game is good enough.
List of noticable bugs:
-Can't interact with objects such as desks or even the potato peeler. (until you reload)(happens about two or three times every in-game day, very common bug personally and needs to be fixed)
-Can't pick up items. (until you relog)(just as common as the one above, may be the same bug)
-Lockdown starts after afternoon rollcall when I left and rejoined the game during the period, despite being at rollcall and having the green tick in the top right.
-NPC hits me instantly again after already being hit, which I'm pretty sure shouldn't really happen (no time at all in between hits, boom boom, not boom, boom).
-"Knocked out" sound effect plays when the game thinks the player/NPC has been knocked out when it really hasn't, just at low health. Not that big of a bug.
-Doors requiring keys sometime open more than once while walking through it in a straight line.
-Player models don't show their "knocked out" pose, lying on the floor, on occasion.
-"Knocked out" animation restarts after coming out of desks, menus etc.
Those are the main ones I've encountered so far, excluding the multiplayer bugs/problems that are probably more annoying than any of the ones I've mentioned or could've mentioned. Most of the bugs in singleplayer aren't that bad, except for the first few which are *really* annoying. I've been backtracked or had to start over several times because of them.
Personally I hope the team adds more features to the main game as time goes on. DLCs are ok, but new features and more ways to escape or new ways to interact with the prison would be really awesome. Maybe make the guard/control room actually operable or other objects or devices that could be used. The staff who just randomly walk around doing nothing could have more purpose than spouting out goofy lines every once in a while.
Despite that I still enjoy the new features, graphics and escape routes of the game! It just needs a lot of improvement is some places, especially multiplayer. I haven't tried it myself but from a couple of reviews I've seen it looks pretty bad.

Castlevania LoS2 Is what I would define as bad oatmeal. Strong elements of several kinds without a smoot transition is what makes the experience feel forced, or what may force you to have harsh feelings about the game. (Like I did)
Merging strong storytelling with exploration using cutscenes is a big no in the experience category. When you find a new area or get past or to a boss or story area, you get a cutscene that either  shows you everything you want to find on your own, or tells you a story that moves you from the area before you can finish exploring. Other games manage this type of merge by using character narration or slowing the walk speed.
Strong combat elements with excessive backtracking: Having to down half a dozen enemies who are tiered to what part of the main story you are on just because you are looking for something is what I hate most about the game. The lack of loot and a equipment system makes me lose the edge for excessive combat, but in addition to that, almost every enemy has a ranged attack that has huge hitboxes that they are all too happy to use deciding you would like to skip the battle. Most battles near the endgame or after you gained a new traversal ability are begun with a groan because you've been shot off a ledge to the point where you do want to fight just so you can enjoy the game. The mastery system ends way too early to entice excessive battling and credits are easy to get provided you dpend them properly upgrading skills you'll most likely use.
The open world element is trashed by an isolated map system and the same looking load elevators and hatches. Find things in this game is met with repeatedly going the wrong way and passing points where you cannot backtrack through the area after you jumped down. The areas are intertwined somewhat and only one or two pllaces have this problem, but that tied with the block the area rests in being behind one of like 5 blue elevator doors makes the experience irritating and repetitive.
But after you swallow those strong flavors and seperate them by improvising, you can stop to appreaciate the art and fluidity of the combat and the thought they put into hiding the upgrades. And then when all that is getting good... The game is over. It's metroid all over again. Get the screw attack, Find stuff, kill the last guy. I just hope there is a secret boss or something.
The alucard dlc is honestly why I bought the game. For some reason, everything dracula backwards is in seems to get more polish than the game itself... for some reason, that's still true. Alucard has proper last gen hair animation, a shiny coat, skin that is also pale but not sickening to look at, skills that are practical, a sword and movelist that probably drove the fans crazy, and one of the coolest ideas for a puzzle element ever. It doesn't break pace ever, and it makes you feel like you're a strong character. Instead of being dracula where you never even got to beat one of the guards that caused you so much trouble without taking over their body and dropping their gun.
It's one of those games that gets better when you play it. The start is slow, and the search is tedius, but after you play through it, you realize it is really a fantastic idea made into a just okay game. Where in my opinion, Lament of innocence probably takes the cake for a castlevania game, and alucard still takes the cake for the coolest vampire. Dracula should have stayed dead... Could have been a way better game.

In short: it's officially not Early Access, but it really is. Despite this, I have hope and reccomend it. For further info, read below...
Very much so a work in progress, Kingdoms & Castles is another one of the dozens of games that while not officially used by the Early Access format in order to show players a particular game early and allow for indie devs funding to continue the game, this is very much what the game is. As for my thoughts, it is something that I never thought I wanted, yet am both surprised an happy with what I found. Very much like the mobile games Clash of Clans and other such titles, the game simply takes that formula and removes the long wait times, providing a faster and more enjoyable expirience. But what really made this game stand out to me was the level od detail that goes into every single citizen. Much like Civilization, you number of citizens matter. But unlike civilization, these villagers are distinct, with names and skills, the latter of which grows as they work on particular tasks, improving efficiency as they age and yes, eventually die. The game creates something interesting and fun enough while not being too generic to be annoyingly bland and boring. The game does stand out at least somewhat and is much more than worth the meager 9.99USD I payed. At about 6 hours of playtime as of the writing of this review, I have acquired some insight on the game and here is a truly great piece of advice for anyone starting the game for the first time; play about an hour or two of the game mode where there are no enemis attacking you to understand how the game works, and you will be much better off than I was. As for content, it is rather light at the moment, but updates are inbound, so hopefully this game does get legitimate support over time to add more content and not end up like so many other games like this that crash and burn. As for whether to buy it or not, I will say that this game is a bit of a gamble. There are so many games like this that are never truly completed, and this one may very well suffer the same fate. But, I have hope for this game, as the base version still has enough substance to stand on it's own, and with that amount of work put in by the development team, with the first update already not just in production, but the details already concretely established withing a few short days of release is a good sign that this game will not grind to a halt, and will (hopefully) continue to evolve and grow. Besides, as far as gambles go, 9.99 is not much compared to some official early access pricepoints of 19.99USD or even 29.99USD in some cases. Kingdoms and Castles is a game that I think will eat up quite a few hours of my life, and entertain me for quite some time. In fact, I think I'll go play it right now. You should too.
