What you see there is rather a simple mod for Half-Life 1. It consist of a very short simple level where you travel from one end of ship to the another and then backtrack to the beggining, while being encountered by the enemies placed here and there with no pressure on you. Once done with it, you will be transported to the boss level, where you have to fight a rather easy boss, from who you just need to run away and shoot.
Now, the quality of said mod. What it looks like to me is that it was one of those small mods that amateur modders would make, quitly post on moddiing forum and then get some feedback from it. It's short, it has some strange looking things, it puts you in linear path, giving you random new models and music, which probably were taken from somewhere else. With some stuff not making much of sense. Hell, the boss looks a lot like it was done using the tricks in level editor, looking more like a hack job. It even makes me nostalgic about times when I was part of Russian Serious Sam modding forum, where no one could truly make new elements or edit old ones, and just were abusing whatever level editor would allow them.
Yet this one was taken much futher, being few years old, it suddenly surfaced on the front page of Steam, probably managing to get pass the Greenlight, and gained a lot of attention, having presentation of more promising mod that what it actually is. As a result it gave people a sheer dissapointed and is being viewed negatively.
While if this would come out quietly on the forums or workshop, it would have gotten mostly positive responses, for it's still enjoyable. So I guess as a small mod, I can recommend it for bored half-lifers.
It all surely brings a lot of question about reasons why Steam Greenlight exist when stuff like this can easily get past it. And the reason why the "mods" section in Steam exist, when there is now a workshop in most games. But then again, Valve didn't implent Steam Workshop to any of Half-Life games, so I can see why this thing had to appear on the front page. Which brings us to question why it wasn't implented to HL series...
Funny thing, it's the only mod on Steam for Half-Life 1 that it still downloable through Steam.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is the follow up to Orcs Must Die 1, and is a third person tower defence game, developed by Robot Entertainment.  The game was released on PC July 2012.
The main difference with Orcs Must Die 2 is the addition of co-op gameplay. Everything else is virtually the same. You play either as a War Mage or sorceress in the story mode. You have to defend at one or more rifts which open at the start of the level. Each level has a varying amount of waves of enemies continuously spawning in order to reach said rift. Your aim is to stop them by building traps whilst also using your own character to kill them as well. Before each level you choose your load out of traps that you want to use. You start out by only being able to take 4 or 5, but work your way up to being able to take 10 traps on a stage with you.  Before jumping into each level too, you can upgrade your traps to do more damage, have a lower cool down time, or some other ability such as slowing the enemy if they are hit by it for example.  You'll notice from the very beginning that there are a few traps that you'll always want to take with you, such as the slowing trap - but included in your loadout, is your characters weapon, so you have to choose carefully.
You are given an infinite amount of time to build your traps at the start of each level, and you are also given a healthy amount of time between waves to allow you to build more. You are granted extra coins after each wave, and for killing enemies, and you use these coins to purchase more traps. Whilst you can also place traps when enemies are spawning, this isn't always a good idea as your main focus should be on killing enemies then.  A large portion of this game is actually you spamming your left mouse button using your main weapon, whilst you aren't able to destroy everything with this weapon; it is more used as filler for your time as most of the damage will come from the traps.  There is a huge variety of traps as well, and you probably won't even use them all even by the end of the game, leaving you plenty of chances to experiment.
The graphics in Orcs Must Die 2 are really nice. They are in the cartoon style that many of us really enjoy, but they aren't so childish that they can't portray the maturity of the title. There are some really nice special effects, such as the lava and ice traps, they all look marvellous. Everything is perfectly animated too, whilst a lot of the enemies are copy/pasted, that is to be expected from a game of this type.
Orcs Must Die 2 has a very catchy sound track too; the song is played constantly and it will be driven into your head and you'll be whistling it without realising it. Other than the soundtrack, the rest of the game's audio is brilliant too. The game is narrated in the cut scenes by the male character; it would have been nice to get voice acting on the female though.
This game has varying levels of difficulty, the regular easy, medium and hard mode. You only unlock hard mode after you have beaten the game. There is one other form of difficulty, and that is endless mode. This will pit you against an endless stream of enemies, meaning you have to constantly upgrade your traps and the enemies will not stop until they either kill you or destroy your rift. This mode will really test your metal but is extremely fun to play in. Most players should really be playing this game on the Medium skill level, the easy mode is too easy and will not really offer any challenge to any tower defence veteran.
All of the levels in Orcs Must Die 2 are so well designed; I cannot find any faults with them at all. The early stages of the game are a tutorial stage really, allowing you to test out your traps to work out how they are best used, so the levels are pretty simple, but once you reach the end levels, you'll really be putting your trap building skills to the test, as you have to defend multiple rifts from multiple entry points of enemies. Some of the bigger levels offer a bit of support in getting around quickly in the form of teleporters, these will teleport you to the other side of the map once stepping in them.
I have been playing Orcs Must Die 2 for almost thirty hours, this is because there is absolutely tons of content in this game, not only is the single player story mode eight hours of gameplay, you also have the added replay ability of playing the story again as the other hero (with different skills and abilities), and then you also can replay the whole game again on co-op which adds a whole another level of content as the enemies are all scaled up to match you and your friend - and finally, we have the endless mode, this is the part of the game that I have spent the majority of my time and I am absolutely hooked on it. As you play the story mode, once you reach the final waves of a level, you'll often feel like you wish you could carry on and see how far you get, you can do that in endless mode; you just keep building traps, and facing more and more enemies as they just keep coming. This mode alone has given me about fifteen hours of gameplay.
Orcs Must Die 2 can be played on all resolutions. I played on 4k with everything on max settings and was able to get 60 FPS constantly. I did however have a few crashes, this mainly happened when you minimize the game too many times, and it gives you a message something regarding DirectX. Although this was annoying, I only had it when minimizing and not whilst in the midst of gameplay. The game can be played with a controller, but as it has elements of aiming with a crosshairs, the game is highly recommended to be played with a keyboard/mouse - it just works so much better on them.
This game is an absolute must play for any tower defence fan, if you had any sort of enjoyment out of the first, you'll get more of the same out of this, and the added edition of co-op makes it even more appealing to a wider audience. Not to mention the hours and hours of content on offer in this game. The regular price tag of £10, 99 is fairly marked and should be considered a must play for me.

Long awaited conclusion to The Longest Journey saga.

If you only read one line of this review, this is the important part. This isn't a "fun" game; this is an experience.
For reference I played The Longest Journey for the first time only within the last couple years. It was excellent. Then I played Dreamfall, and it too was excellent. Maybe it was because I don't have rosy nostolgia of TLJ that I was actually more drawn into Dreamfall. TLJ was perhaps excecuted better, with Dreamfall having lousy and unnecessary combat, and the Kian parts seemed tacked on and didn't make much sense to me. But Zoe and her story made her as much a real person as any fictional character has ever been to me. So, having just finished chapter 5 I feel I can finally review Dreamfall Chapters.
Before weighing good and bad I want to say this. If you want an action game, this isn't it. There are cutscenes and sections that are just conversations, some of them reasonably long. This game is in so many ways, a story. An epic one at that. And one thats not even about winning. Your decisions really affect things. Bad things will happen.
The Bad
- I don't have the newest computer so i wasn't able to run the game at its highest graphic quality. The only reason this is bad is the graphics look sooo good. Its the first game I actually thought about upgrading my computer just so i could push the graphics up.
- There are some graphical glitches. The odd torn texture, animation stutter. Nothing game breaking.
- The time between chapters was painful. But its all out now so if you're just picking it up now you're gold.
The Good
- What you do really matters. What you do in each chapter not only affects that chapter, or even the next chapter, but everything that comes after.
- The story is so good. You will laugh, you will cry. Characters that fell a little flat in Dreamfall like Kian are fleshed out.
- The graphics really are amazing
- You will care. Barring everything else, like the best kind of book, you will care. The whole series, TLJ, Dreamfall, and Chapters are so well done when it comes to story.
In the first line of this review I stated this isn't a game, this is an experience. And it is. If you take into account TLJ, Dreamfall and chapters as a whole, probably the best gaming experience I've ever had. I can only hope that they make The Longest Journey Home to complete the journey.

I really would liked to appreciate this game. Unfortunately, it's plagued with technical issues and I found the story got on my nerves at times.
Graphically, Dreamfall Chapters is absolutely gorgeous, the character models, the environment, it's pretty amazing. Unfortunately, even with v-sync enabled, the character models tore all over the place, making it extremely irritating to my eyes and spoiling its beauty. Also, performance was a bit of an issue. I would have expected this game to perform more consistently that it did. Sometimes, I'd have sudden low FPS indoors for no reason. But since it's just walking around, it's not a major issue.
I noticed a bunch of annoyances, some probably bugs, others due to bad design. Character models going through one another because they're too close. My character's head getting stuck in weird angles and staying that way unless I changed areas or reloaded a save. The gamepad and the kb+m control can't be used at the same time, meaning that if I decide to use my mouse to do something, suddenly, my gamepad analog buttons won't get the character moving. Another major error in design is those bloody stupid maps. They create nice beautiful cities and make you run around them while only giving us maps located in the city that you have to find if you get lost. For Europolis, it made no sense. You've got futuristic communicators but no integrated mapping technology? It caused me to get lost trying to figure out where to go.  And on top of their poor implementation, the maps were terrible at helping you find your way. Puzzles were also barely there and you sometimes had to scour the city to find one stupid item.
I have to give the dev credit for its choice-consequences system though. It was crafted beautifully and you had to think carefully which option to pick. Unlike Telltale's joke system that changes nothing in the story, there are major consequences to your actions. I just wish the story would have been as inspired as that system. It worked best when it focused on what made this series great, fantasy, conspiracy, etc... Instead, the devs seemed more interested in pushing a political agenda regarding race, sexual orientation and gender. The writing gave us your typical mustache twirling villains and not the funny kind. No greys in this story, no sir. It ended up feeling extremely hamfisted. They even mislead you into thinking you could build a romance with one character only to rob that away just so they can make make a point about homosexuality and how it should be accepted. No♥♥♥♥♥♥ it should but giving a fake choice that gave me false hope really annoyed me. It gets even worse in the later chapters where those villains end up become a farce. Their motives are never properly explained so they're evil just because. They were unintentionally comical. The story seemed crafted to make points about inclusivity rather than tell a tale of adventure through fascinating worlds.

At the time of writing this review, I have put fifty hours into Starbound. I can safely say that those fifty hours have been some of the most fun experiences I've had in gaming.
If you want to get straight to the point and just see pros and cons see below, if you want to have my full review, go to the bottom.
Pros:
-Satisfying Combat
-Procedural Generation for -everything- works great and I feel is implemented extremely well.
-Multiplayer is hectic, fun, and a great experience.
-The "collectathon" elements rarely feel grindy (save for maybe those stupid action figure things) and add depth overall.
-There are small details and mechanics you won't notice your first time playing.
-Building is fun and there are many blocks and decorations to make use of.
-SHEER DEPTH.
Cons
-Story missions can feel either unfair or too easy at times.
-Controls can feel slightly wonky.
-RNG can get you sometimes when it comes to drops. (I don't really see this as grinding, but I have had to go back and refight a boss once or twice if I missed out on something. If you are familiar at all with Terraria, this game's boss "grinding" is a lot easier to swallow.)
That is my very skin deep observations of Starbound.
Now for the real review.
One of my friends got me a Steam Gift Card for my birthday, and I decide to make use of it by buying this game. I had been following it since earlier in its development, but never took the plunge. I already had fallen in love with Terraria, and like most of the population of the planet, Minecraft. Just having the baseline understanding of those games let me hop right into Starbound feeling prepared.
Shortly after I got it, around 9 of my friends also bought it because they thought it looked so fun. Then there we were, a bunch of circus freaks, gorilla rebels out of an orwellian novel, medieval robots, cowboy starfolk, and feral flowers ready to take on the universe. Our opening hours were spent shooting birds out of the skies with bows made of the timber we scavenged, and many, many, deaths due to hunger. We made our way to what can best be described as a stargate. Blah blah blah exposition. Then boom, we found it. A GUN.
The minute we found our first gun (and the knowledge it didn't need ammo) we were ecstatic. It was a crappy pistol that probably only does 1 damage against the things we would fight later on, but that's not the point. If you only take one thing away from this review, it would be that:
Starbound has one of the most rewarding exploration and loot systems in perhaps all of the genre.
Nothing beats finding a rare weapon, or an enormous vein of ore in this game. You will stop looking at the progression system in this game as a grind, but rather as a GET GEARED TO THE TEETH SO I CAN GO SHOOT STUFF RIGHT IN THE MOUTH system. I highly value this as playing games like Terraria make the first 10-15 hours very boring due to just how tedious it all is, while Starbound makes it your most fun time in the game. (I might add it's one of the few games I look forward to playing from the beginning.)
As great as the game is, there are a few flaws. My first one is that at times I would feel as if I was either under or over-geared for a story mission. I could either finish it in 5+ minutes or it would take me a party of four and multiple tries. (and an embarrasing amount of time.) New players may also find the controls to be weird, I don't really have a proposal as to how they could fix this, which is why I won't fault them that much. I'd say the biggest gripe I have is the RNG. Most of us know the feeling: "Please... please... and it's a common." Sometimes this game feels like you're opening a Star Wars Battlefront 2 Lootbox looking for Darth Vader. You and I both know that you're not getting Darth Vader.
All in all, just take the plunge. It's only 15 dollars for a pretty great experience, and if you don't wanna spend that much, wait until it goes on sale. The fun goes up x10 if you have friends, so keep that in mind. Thanks for reading this review, and I do hope you'll give this gem a go.

Missions are few and far between (or hard to complet as soon as you get it); upgrading the ship feels amasing once it's done and you have all the fully upgraded crafting stations for the first time, but there's not much to it after that; there's almost no reason to build a hub world as once you leave the system if you don't leave a tel point you'll likely never see it again; if you wait till you have good gear to fight bosses most are push overs; combat is repedative after a short while and over all feels unfair at times do to lag; if you intent to test out every race, don't bother. Final Throughts: I really loved this game for the first few hours of exploring, building, and crafting, but once I did all that there wasn't really much to do after that. Having a crew does basiclly nothing as the AI is a moron and the only ones that have any sense of a role on your ship is: the medic, chief, and Qurter Master. Everyone else ether does nothing unless with you or just expand your fuel (equaly as useful as nothing). The modding community will help you get just a few extra hours more, but it just doesn't do enough to make me want to come back and play for hours more on desalent planets with the only things to do is explore, kill, build, and do an occaonal mission if you're lucky. Castlevania Lords of Shadow 2
A wasted opportunity
Mercury Steam had the chance to close his Castlevania trilogy in a high note, with a golden lock, but instead, all it accomplishes is a terrible failure. I have not reviewed a game in a while but I really need to let out some steam. Lords of Shadow was a great game, a good incarnation of the Castlevania series and the first one to actually manage to pull a good game in 3D. With it's combat mechanics, it's boss fights and a story that I find quite interesting. The first Belmont turns out to be the one transforming into Dracula and the greater evil is Satan. Bravo!
Mirror of Fate was a good game, just that. It had a good story, the first time that the Belmont (Vampire Hunters) went on for Dracula's head and how Alucard came to be. Pretty original all around. But it can't compare of course with the first game. And then it came the trilogy closure. Lords of Shadow two. The first game to actually put you in the role of Dracula and in the present. At glance, it's an idea worth exploring, a finale worth telling; to know what happens to Gabriel Belmont now as Dracula and to see if Satan returns. Will Dracula find redemption? At least I know the game won't. The combat mechanics are the same as Lords of Shadow, but now instead of light and shadow magic you have a Void Sword (light) and Chaos Claws (Shadow). Not one change in the mechanics aside from that. If it ain't broke, why fix it?
But oh! Mercury Steam tried to step up the game with the world and the map. What a big mistake. The map, instead of being presented as the first game, in which you were advancing from place to place and you could revisit them whenever you wanted and relive the boss fights; now it's just a conglomerate mess. It deviates itself into a sort of open world with a map room every now and then in some locations that help you fast travel from place to place, but it is hard to keep track of where have you been and where you need to go to get all the upgrades. The map is divided in two: the city and the castle. What you may say? We are in the present day right? Yes! We are, but on that later.
The city is just dull. All grey, wherever you turn. Generic places, streets, alleys; only for a few landmarks where you fight bosses or big group of enemies. The presentation of the place is lame, it does not encourage the player to explore. The castle has some epic scenarios and places that vary from each other, one time you are on an underground city and another you are exploring a hall; and that's a good thing but unfortunately that is all. The enemies are generic as hell. The demon spawns are so generic and there are so few types of them that you feel like you are battling the same enemies all the game. It is another story for the castle, but nevertheless, there are not so many different types of enemies.
And here come the bosses. I don't know where to start. Let's see...
There are many bosses on this game and their design is great, but just two of them managed to wake my emotion battling them. The rest of them felt kind of cheap. Also, there aren't any or at least few mechanics whatsoever to kill them. You literally (aside some exceptions) can blast your way through them with brute force. What thing that was a big letdown was the final battle. I was expecting an epic clash and what I received was a boss battle that felt forced and a killing scene that couldn't be more lame, LAME with capital letters, do you hear me mercury steam?
Now, onto the point where you are Dracula, the prince of darkness, the dragon, the... Wait... Do I need to hide from this guys because I can't fight them? Do I need to turn myself into rats because of the fear to be killed by them? Am I not the Dragon? A force of darkness to be reckoned with? The one who vanquished Satan?
Let that sink in. There are some parts of the game that put you up against some body guards of Satan and you can't fight them, you need to sneak past them transforming into rats or mist; I get it, Dracula can use those skills and I know that he is weakened by his long sleep but there is no part in the game that we face them directly in combat; but oh the final boss? Yeah sure bring it on! I am certain that after that fight, Dracula still needs to sneak from those bodyguards. So in a few words: you never really feel like the dragon.
And now, for the final part of this review and my conclusion: the story, if that thing can be called that. The story is just a convoluted mess. Mercury Steam clearly had no idea on how to develop the story and how to end it. The premise is a fantastic one: you are now Dracula and you are about to confront the lord of hell, Satan himself with acolytes around the city paving his way; also, there is something within his mind, dreams (I really don't know what was it) that draws you back to the castle, and when you are there you discover that a corrupted blood, a dark entity is trying to keep Dracula there for all eternity. The story, as I said before, is developed in the present day at Castlevania City and in the Castle. You travel from one another by portals around the world or when a vision comes to play or Trevor appears and guides you to the castle.
So this was the ending of the trilogy, of Mercury Steam take on the franchise and what did they do with it? They blow it off. The story is weak, doesn't give a closure and nothing great happens. Dracula sets to stop Satan but ends in a very weak tone for this part and it is never explained why there was dark blood in the castle possessing the minions of Dracula, also it is never explained why you travel back to the castle.
In conclusion: this game is mediocre. All of it. The combat is the same as the first entry but you as a player don't need to develop it to conquer the game, there is no need for it. The map, the map is a mess. The bosses don't have any essence to them (in a story way) and have no mechanics whatsoever, just two or three of them. The premise of the story was amazing! It could have been taking through a glorious path and end on an epic note, but instead you get a story that feels dull and no closure at all.
Don't play this game if you haven't. Just stay with Lords of Shadow 1 and Mirror of Fate. This is a waste of your time.

The Anno series has been around since 1998 as an intricate business simulation and city building game.  It is similar to the Settlers series and the old Sierra City Building games in that on top of the city building elements, you have to develop a balanced economy to ensure that goods and services are available for its citizens.  If you compare this series to a game like SimCity, Cities XL, and City Life, the focus is less on the individuality of the buildings.  Instead, it is solely on the ecoomics of the town.  While the city feels more alive, the one downside of these games is that unless you can develop a sound strategy for trading, your city will always be stunted and never grow.
Specifically on Anno 2205, the most recent in the series, it is very much a refined experience.  Compared to the freemium game, the game has no microtransactions and you do not have to wait for buildings to be built.  Compared to the previous game in the series, Anno 2070, this game is definitely more accessible.  Rare resources are not has impossible to find as you can win them in simple combat missions or fetch quests.  The basic economy, which has less granular information and no tutorials, is at least easier to understand.  With trading between cities (one of the biggest strengths IMO), your cities feel important.  I constantly find myself going between the different maps in the game to build up my economy so that I have more money for other cities.  Oh yea, your balanced check book is based on the combined value of all of your cities.
Overall, I recommend this game for anyone who like city simulation games like Settlers, Caesar series, SimCity, City Life, and Cities: Skyline.
Pros:
-Graphics
-Music
-Performance
-Quest System
-Combat Minigame
-Generally Fun Experience
-City Networks that actually make sense
Cons:
-Less Granular Information
-Season Pass

I figured I'd help those that are thinking about this purchase and have no idea what to choose based on mixed reviews.
The game is gorgeous for one and its hard to pass up a game even if not great when it looks better than every city builder in existence.
I have not played a lot at all but started out and could immediately tell how different this was.
Whether or not you would enjoy this game determines what previous Anno camp youre from or if you've never played an Anno game before.
New comers would probably love the game because there is nothing to compare this to except Simcity or Skylines in most cases.  I've played previous Anno's and have both city games and this is what Sim City should have looked like graphically.
Now, as for my previous Anno experience: I came from the camp that never played Anno all the way through because I get tired of managing EVERYTHING.  It becomes really tedious and a very difficult balancing act to enjoy.  I also didn't like that resources ran out, meaning at some point the game was going to end even on continuous to make people happy....Or I'm missing something that would allow iron, coal etc to exist forever.  On top of that, other islands eventually become unhappy if one side is prospering in new food/technology etc.
I learned that while a great game, that level of micro managing makes playing like a full time job and things can go really south if you lose track.
I know some people love that about Anno and that is mostly why they dislike this game.  Its much easier to get started, not as complex planning is needed right off the bat, it is much more forgiving and changes have been made to remove a large portion of micro managing.  When I say a large portion, consider any previous Anno series game is entirely micromanaging comparatively....so I welcome the break.
So ultimately it comes down to what you liked about the previous Anno's or if this is the first time you've run into an Anno game.
If you like micromanaging everything to the T and enjoy tedious planning, then the previous Anno's are for you.
If you like a slightly more casual gameplay that escalates in a controllable manner without feeling like a second job and like to spend the time watching things grow instead of checking your inventories regularly, boat schedules/transfer rates, trial and error etc, and are looking for something a little more involved than Sim City or Skylines, this is probably going to be a Good - Great game for you.
I hope this helps to clarify some of the mystery.  I haven't played long enough to go into full details but it is really hard to get a reading for this game from some of the reviews...especially ones that say "this game is crap, refund" or "not like anno, the others were so much better" without the discussion of what the difference really is or which camp they're coming from.

A fun RTS that doesn't take itself too seriously. Punishing campaign difficulty and online multiplayer modes help build a long lifespan for our barbarian friends. While it won't replace your Starcraft or Total War, it'll complement them nicely when you want a more lighthearted change of pace.
Take an old school real-time strategy game, replace the units with angry Scottish barbarians who like to drink, swear and fight, and add a hearty supply of good beer. Welcome to Crush Your Enemies.
Crush Your Enemies has a fairly simple premise: Take everything you love about real-time strategy games like Starcraft or Command & Conquer, and distill it all down to a compact experience focusing more on action rather than planning.
Crush Your Enemies looks and feels like an overlooked gem of the MS-DOS era — its charming pixelated sprites and rudimentary UI hark back to the dawn of real-time strategy titles, and the gameplay is very easy to pick up and run with; no hours wasted learning typical RTS mechanics like diplomacy or tech trees here.
Each mission in Crush Your Enemies uses a common three star (or in this case, three skull) system, with every mission having three progressively more difficult objectives to achieve. Skulls unlock more villages ripe for plundering, and each conquered village yields beer after every successful mission.
Beer acts as the currency of the land; it can be spent on buying additional items, such as damage-boosting potions or explosive bombs, which can be brought into every future mission.
While starting out simple, Crush Your Enemies soon starts to offer a challenge with their objectives. Goals such as completing a level within two minutes or with a minimum remaining barbarian count often end up surprisingly tricky to achieve, with most levels requiring multiple retries for those seeking perfect marks.
While Crush Your Enemies is at heart a real-time strategy game, it’d be more accurate to call it tactical. With the removal of common RTS mechanics such as scouting for enemies, developing bases, or improving tech, the focus of the gameplay shifts towards more immediate decision making.
The entire battlefield is visible with no fog of war, and fits squarely on-screen, so you’ll always have a clear idea about what’s happening around you. The game even lets you soak in the map before gameplay starts, waiting for you to be ready, so you’ll have plenty of time to plan out how you’ll tackle each level.
You’ll start with one or more groups of basic barbarians who can be directed around the battlefield, which is divided into orange friendly turf, green enemy turf, and unclaimed territory. Moving through owned terrain is instant, but moving onto unowned turf means your barbarians will work to claim that land before they’re able to move forward.
Most maps have buildings scattered throughout which offer various tactical advantages to your savage little buddies — defense posts from which to fire upon approaching enemies, huts for breeding additional troops, or training buildings for swapping to a different troop type. Barbarians will change profession depending on where they’re sent; sending them to huts switches them to simpleton laborers, who (when not breeding) can claim land or fetch resources much faster than their combat counterparts, but they’re more vulnerable in a fight.
Barbarians can swap roles at any time simply by moving them to the relevant building, and later missions will definitely test your ability to juggle different roles at once.
Combat in Crush Your Enemies has a slight rock-paper-scissors flavor. Warriors will easily roll over a bunch of simpletons, but archers will stop them in their tracks, pinning and stunning them under a hail of arrows. However, bring a troop of taunting shield bearers, and they’ll reflect those arrows right back. As you unlock more roles, combat gets progressively more complex, and it can be surprisingly difficult to build and maneuver strong, balanced barbarian packs.
In the second single-player campaign, resource harvesting mechanics appear: building and repairing structures requires wood, and breeding expends food. This leads to a massive spike in difficulty as you struggle to continually revisit trees and farms for resources as well as breeding barbarians, expanding territory, and fighting off a well-supplied enemy.
While the first campaign gets difficult towards the end, especially if you’re aiming for three skulling all missions, the second campaign is far more brutal, with new unit types and items to handle, on top of the new fetching and management of resources.
While the game has its frustrating moments — missing an objective due to one more death than necessary, or the final enemy troops suiciding to your warriors moments before you’ve captured the last building you need — Crush Your Enemies does feel enjoyable to play. Daft humor and playful items, such as an inflatable dummy barbarian, keep the game firmly rooted as a wisecracking game for fun.

Being a big fan of the RTS genre I was interested in seeing what Crush Your Enemies would be like. The game takes the traditional RTS game and streamlines it into a game that just requires clicking on units and telling them where to go. While people who require a lot of strategy in their games may not like it, I think Crush Your Enemies is a really interesting take on the genre.
In most RTS games you need to gather resources which you use to construct buildings and create new units. Crush Your Enemies has next to no resources with the only resource in most levels being the number of troops that you have. The levels that do have some additional resources are so straightforward that people that hate this aspect of RTS games will have no problem with it. People who like the resource gathering/base building aspects of RTS games (like myself) may be a little disappointed at first but I adjusted to the game and I didn't mind the streamlining of the resource gathering/base building.
The combat has also been streamlined with only five different types of units. Each type of unit has their own strengths and weaknesses which you need to take advantage of to beat your opponent. While the game has streamlined a lot of mechanics, there is still quite a bit of strategy in the combat. The game plays like a game of tug of war as you slowly take over the map from your opponent.
I had a lot of fun with Crush Your Enemies. The single player campaign takes around six hours to complete and you can play the game a lot more if you get into the multiplayer.
There is a lot to like about Crush Your Enemies but the one thing that I didn't really care for was the story. I personally didn't find it to be very funny. The story uses a lot of fake swearing and just seems kind of immature at times. This does fit the theme of the game though and some people will really enjoy it. I personally didn't really care for it though.
If you insist on deep strategy in your RTS games, Crush Your Enemies may not be for you. If you are looking for an interesting take on the genre though I think you should enjoy Crush Your Enemies. The game may even appeal to people that don't usually care for the genre.

Consider me skeptical of games that proclaim that they will take you back to the glory days of a genre. I read this far too often. An all too common result is an itch that remains unscratched and a subpar game in and of itself. I believe that some developers think that as long as they use retro-styled graphics it will suffice. When I discovered that the opening words of Crush Your Enemies synopsis I was pessimistic. It reads ‘Go back to the awesome glory days of Real-Time Strategy games’. Further, it proclaims that it ‘has everything you love about the genre.’ This is a hard sales pitch. Thankfully, I needn’t have been. Vile Monarch have nailed it in their first game since their free to play insult simulator title, Oh…Sir!
Crush Your Enemies is a genuine throwback to the real-time strategy genre. It certainly offers everything that RTS fans love – planning, unit variety, resource management, territory control and most significantly on the fly strategy. These are all important components when considering the whole. All of them have been carefully considered
The gameplay is addictive. The game takes place in rounds and you are given a number of various challenges – three on each level.  These challenges are fairly generic of the genre but they’ve become that way because they work. You’re going to see a lot of ‘crush the enemy in X time,’ ‘survive X time,’ ‘take control of the enemy’s territory’ type challenges. They give each round a purpose. You have to complete the most basic challenge to advance to the game. What I enjoyed most were the survival rounds because they offered two times for you to beat but also a conquer their territory challenge.
You begin each round with a small amount of units. Generally these are your foot soldiers or peasants. You need to consider how you will build your army. This is achieved through your housing building which will add units to your army as long as you have at least one person at home. The more people you have at home the faster units will develop. You can have a maximum of fifty units at any one time.
You have specialist buildings at your disposal that will give you different tools. For example, you can transform your standard units into warriors and archers by simply taking them to those allotted buildings. However, you cannot mix troops (e.g. archers and warriors may not be on the same tile). Be careful, however, as if you move your specialist troops onto a home unit they will transform into standard units. This tripped me up a couple of times.
Rounds are only a few minutes long at most making the game ideal for those who are time poor. However, I would also say that the shortness of the rounds is an overall advantage of the game itself. There is simply no time for the game to become boring and overly tedious. It allows players who do plan on completing the game to jump from round to round quickly.
Inventory management starts off small but does become a game changer later on. It’s up to the player to determine how each item is best utilized. That’s a great strength of the game. Almost every important thing in the game comes down to the player’s decision.
The game controls extremely well. I only have one small criticism. I would like to see a minor improvement on pathing. The player, to a significant degree, controls the paths that their units take. However, it isn’t always accurate. Given that the majority of rounds are a race against the clock a slight deviation can have future consequences. It’s not something that happened frequently enough for it to be a large concern but it did happen.
Those looking for a story to tie the game together are in for a treat. The decision to work with a barbarian setting and atmosphere is what makes the game for me. It could have so very easily been just a generic game. However, the comedic touch to the narration is fantastic. This generally takes place between levels but can and does occur during levels. The in-round narrative generally takes place before the rounds begin but there are occasional humor filled pop ups informing you of unlocked events and features.
Graphically, I really enjoyed the retro look to the game. The colors are bright and sharp. It’s a case of Red Vs Blue. The maps have been well designed and are, by and large, clear. It achieves what it needs to do without being overtly spectacular. The utilization of the color palette is in keeping with the setting and the classic feel. The sound, on the other hand, is definitely a little generic. The music is thumping
I did run into a weird glitch where the game wouldn’t allow me to pick a unit and move it. I’m not sure of the reason why this glitch occurred only that it did a couple of times. Exiting the game and reloading fixed the error.
Finally, a word of warning on the humor. It is potty mouthed, sexual and not going to appeal to everybody. You do have the choice of skipping the dialogue. Therefore it may not be a game that you’d allow younger games to play. Then again, there is far worse stuff on television that many children do watch.
Crush Your Enemies is super addictive thanks in large part to a wonderful presentation. Those who demand to see innovation in every game that they play may feel disappointed. However, it doesn’t need to reinvent the wheel. This is an easy recommendation for both fans of real-time strategy games and the casuals out there. It’s a game that has something for everybody. I honestly don’t foresee many people not liking this one.

Alfred the Great and Uno!
Through your own deduction you'll understand that it makes more sense to launch an act of treachery only after a player fends off such a maneuver or better yet fails to.  If you play your cards right you can spam these cards in a way that you may in Uno.
Random or Strategic?
There's no such thing as an optimal deck, because there are so many ways to counteract different decks.  To the extent that in a table of four there's a good chance that a player will have the cure for your strategy insofar as much if they do decide to hobble you it's nearly impossible to combat their hands.
The Dane Law!
The introduction of Vikings is a welcome dynamic.  It is a fun kind of foreboding to stare down a horde or better yet direct them against your enemies.  There is a countdown component to a Danish landing that is offset by player aggression and accelerated by currying favor with the barbarians abroad.  You may spend cards in order to have better odds of directing their assaults.  The Danish invaders provide a strikingly realistic RNG offering.
Expeditions Easier than Defense?
It may feel strange, but the designers decided to build this card game in a way that lends itself to balance.  It would be more realistic for it to be easier to defend your own lands rather than going on the offensive.  Especially in regards to your vassals and farmers having a vested interest in their lords success would be easier to rally against an invader.  However, I believe that although this is flipped it lends itself to being a more dynamic game for it.  It's be likely that everyone would turtle and allow their opponent to crash against their towers before a third player launches their own assault.
Conclusion
I'd say it's worth several tries, but I wouldn't download it unless it was free and you love the middle ages.  It entertained me for a long while; just don't expect there to be that many people playing the game with you.

At the time of writing this review, I have put fifty hours into Starbound. I can safely say that those fifty hours have been some of the most fun experiences I've had in gaming.
If you want to get straight to the point and just see pros and cons see below, if you want to have my full review, go to the bottom.
Pros:
-Satisfying Combat
-Procedural Generation for -everything- works great and I feel is implemented extremely well.
-Multiplayer is hectic, fun, and a great experience.
-The "collectathon" elements rarely feel grindy (save for maybe those stupid action figure things) and add depth overall.
-There are small details and mechanics you won't notice your first time playing.
-Building is fun and there are many blocks and decorations to make use of.
-SHEER DEPTH.
Cons
-Story missions can feel either unfair or too easy at times.
-Controls can feel slightly wonky.
-RNG can get you sometimes when it comes to drops. (I don't really see this as grinding, but I have had to go back and refight a boss once or twice if I missed out on something. If you are familiar at all with Terraria, this game's boss "grinding" is a lot easier to swallow.)
That is my very skin deep observations of Starbound.
Now for the real review.
One of my friends got me a Steam Gift Card for my birthday, and I decide to make use of it by buying this game. I had been following it since earlier in its development, but never took the plunge. I already had fallen in love with Terraria, and like most of the population of the planet, Minecraft. Just having the baseline understanding of those games let me hop right into Starbound feeling prepared.
Shortly after I got it, around 9 of my friends also bought it because they thought it looked so fun. Then there we were, a bunch of circus freaks, gorilla rebels out of an orwellian novel, medieval robots, cowboy starfolk, and feral flowers ready to take on the universe. Our opening hours were spent shooting birds out of the skies with bows made of the timber we scavenged, and many, many, deaths due to hunger. We made our way to what can best be described as a stargate. Blah blah blah exposition. Then boom, we found it. A GUN.
The minute we found our first gun (and the knowledge it didn't need ammo) we were ecstatic. It was a crappy pistol that probably only does 1 damage against the things we would fight later on, but that's not the point. If you only take one thing away from this review, it would be that:
Starbound has one of the most rewarding exploration and loot systems in perhaps all of the genre.
Nothing beats finding a rare weapon, or an enormous vein of ore in this game. You will stop looking at the progression system in this game as a grind, but rather as a GET GEARED TO THE TEETH SO I CAN GO SHOOT STUFF RIGHT IN THE MOUTH system. I highly value this as playing games like Terraria make the first 10-15 hours very boring due to just how tedious it all is, while Starbound makes it your most fun time in the game. (I might add it's one of the few games I look forward to playing from the beginning.)
As great as the game is, there are a few flaws. My first one is that at times I would feel as if I was either under or over-geared for a story mission. I could either finish it in 5+ minutes or it would take me a party of four and multiple tries. (and an embarrasing amount of time.) New players may also find the controls to be weird, I don't really have a proposal as to how they could fix this, which is why I won't fault them that much. I'd say the biggest gripe I have is the RNG. Most of us know the feeling: "Please... please... and it's a common." Sometimes this game feels like you're opening a Star Wars Battlefront 2 Lootbox looking for Darth Vader. You and I both know that you're not getting Darth Vader.
All in all, just take the plunge. It's only 15 dollars for a pretty great experience, and if you don't wanna spend that much, wait until it goes on sale. The fun goes up x10 if you have friends, so keep that in mind. Thanks for reading this review, and I do hope you'll give this gem a go.

Absolutely amazing.
Very hard to learn.
Quick story:
Doing the practical engine repair tutorial:
I had just finished setting up my engine, a lot of exhaust piping, pumping water out of the lower decks, etc.  Finally got ship-shape.  Made it out to the first waypoint. Alright cool.  I see some sort of dots on the horizon, figure it might be some kind of tutorial structures like buoys.
Turns out they were pirate ships. Game warned me and notified how I can fire the missiles. I set it to AI control, seemed to work but there were too many pirates.
Took a HUGE beating. port side was sagging on one side, taking on too much water. The engine below-deck had taken on water and could no longer propel me, I used the last of the momentum to orient starboard side towards the enemy.
While the ship was firing missiles at the enemies I took it upon myself and swam towards the enemy ships. They had no small-arms weapons and could not stop me. After destroying the engines and weapons on the enemys main ship I swam back to my own vessel. below deck completely flooded, so many hull breaches. port side was just metal framework, shredded wood spread across all decks and some machinery on fire . Now that things were calm, I took to repairing the vessel.
Took me 25 minutes, the game has an automatic repair function that will replace blocks if you have resource units (don't worry it's not complicated in this regard at all) and I re-worked the water pumps and reconnected crankshafts up.  Finally, the ship was back in commission, albeit with some scorch marks on the top and port side hull.
Armed with the knowledge that I should only engage one enemy at a time from a way longer distance (I was originally trying to battle like old 1600's vessels when I had long range missiles) I took to taking out the enemies methodically. Totally owned the tutorial with some patience and quick engineering.
TL;DR:  If just the tutorial can give me such an emergent ship-captain experience, I can't even fathom how great the campaign will be (Which is already out, just haven't touched it yet). I barely know what I'm doing.
I will say this: If you have the patience to play other crafty/inventive type games (eg: Space Engineers or even infinifactory/besieged sort of) you will take to this from the get-go. There's a lot more to learn but if you're patient and don't try to rush through this game, you will find one of the most engaging and satisfying ship-combat simulations out there.
I will say there's some negatives. For one, the graphics could use some work. I think simplifying the models, or removing the cell shading (or toning it down) could help get rid of some of the clutter.  The menu graphics have this "Blah simulator 2016" look, the light blue bubbly design. Could be reworked to a much simpler design, maybe like how Beseiged does their GUI menus.
Summary:
Buy this if my first few paragraphs drew you in. I'm the most mindless gamer and I was able to enjoy this and overcome the learning curve. Loving this game.

I really would liked to appreciate this game. Unfortunately, it's plagued with technical issues and I found the story got on my nerves at times.
Graphically, Dreamfall Chapters is absolutely gorgeous, the character models, the environment, it's pretty amazing. Unfortunately, even with v-sync enabled, the character models tore all over the place, making it extremely irritating to my eyes and spoiling its beauty. Also, performance was a bit of an issue. I would have expected this game to perform more consistently that it did. Sometimes, I'd have sudden low FPS indoors for no reason. But since it's just walking around, it's not a major issue.
I noticed a bunch of annoyances, some probably bugs, others due to bad design. Character models going through one another because they're too close. My character's head getting stuck in weird angles and staying that way unless I changed areas or reloaded a save. The gamepad and the kb+m control can't be used at the same time, meaning that if I decide to use my mouse to do something, suddenly, my gamepad analog buttons won't get the character moving. Another major error in design is those bloody stupid maps. They create nice beautiful cities and make you run around them while only giving us maps located in the city that you have to find if you get lost. For Europolis, it made no sense. You've got futuristic communicators but no integrated mapping technology? It caused me to get lost trying to figure out where to go.  And on top of their poor implementation, the maps were terrible at helping you find your way. Puzzles were also barely there and you sometimes had to scour the city to find one stupid item.
I have to give the dev credit for its choice-consequences system though. It was crafted beautifully and you had to think carefully which option to pick. Unlike Telltale's joke system that changes nothing in the story, there are major consequences to your actions. I just wish the story would have been as inspired as that system. It worked best when it focused on what made this series great, fantasy, conspiracy, etc... Instead, the devs seemed more interested in pushing a political agenda regarding race, sexual orientation and gender. The writing gave us your typical mustache twirling villains and not the funny kind. No greys in this story, no sir. It ended up feeling extremely hamfisted. They even mislead you into thinking you could build a romance with one character only to rob that away just so they can make make a point about homosexuality and how it should be accepted. No♥♥♥♥♥♥ it should but giving a fake choice that gave me false hope really annoyed me. It gets even worse in the later chapters where those villains end up become a farce. Their motives are never properly explained so they're evil just because. They were unintentionally comical. The story seemed crafted to make points about inclusivity rather than tell a tale of adventure through fascinating worlds.
With such technical issues, a poorly thought out design and a disappointing plot, I can't in good conscience recommend Dreamfall Chapters. And I won't be backing further games from Red Thread Games. What a let down!

You should play at least Dreamfall, its prequel, in order to get what's happening in the story, as DF Chapters won't bother too much to explain what's going on to newcomers of this franchise. There are story recaps within the game, sure, but I don't think they contain nearly enough information for someone who doesn't know anything about this series. Also, you'd be missing on some of the greatest adventure games ever by not playing the first two games - especially the first one, in my opinion -, so you should definitely play them!
You might say that this is an issue with the game itself, the fact that it relies on its prequels too much to tell its own story, but I don't mind it too much as it does a fantastic job in delivering a long awaited (10 years!) and all-around great epilogue for all fans. A bit of a shame that we don't know the fate of ALL the characters in the game by the end, but I guess I'll take what I can get.
I'm so happy that after more than 15 years this series is finally over - and with such a good send-off, too! I hope that you too, like me, will get a bit teary eyed at the end when you think back on all the adventures that happened in all these games. It's been truly an amazing ride.
I know that the developers said that it'll be difficult to see another one of these games in the future, so I'm writing this review partly because of it: I'd really like to have more, so I'm sharing the love. Please buy these games, they're really good I swear!

Plots and characters this great are just unheard of in video gaming. Dreamfall and Dreamfall Chapters stand far above every other plot-focused game I've encountered, and Chapters itself is mindblowing, heartbreakingly beautiful stuff.
It does a phenomenal job of drawing you into each character's head, and each 'you affect the world!' choice presents a thought-provoking dilemma of moral greys, and lend enough dialogue/scene variance to add definite replay value.
The dialogue is just unsurpassed, worth playing for alone. In fact, it would be worth listening to if it were just a radio play over a blank screen.
There are too many great scenes to list, inventive and compelling world-building, and relatable personalities all pleasingly playing off each other. I particularly love Kian's randomly too-thoughtful over-specified deadpan descriptions of mundane items, so perfect for his thoughtful-but-blunt character. These are often satisfyingly subtle, but are also unabashedly used as the basis for numerous silly throwaway jokes.
It builds up one of the most enjoyable game worlds to simply exist within and soak up. I played much longer than necessary, looping around, admiring the scenery. The graphics are incredible; it looks gorgeous, and in terms of quality/polish, Chapters is a very well refined experience, with far fewer rough corners than its predecessors, although not entirely without small problems here and there.
It's still technically an 'adventure game', and has several moments of frustration due to unintuitive item/event 'puzzle'-solving. These are thankfully infrequent and self-contained, and all brute-forceable, in that I never had to look up a solution online (unlike some parts of the original Dreamfall). I personally think that the characters and dialogue are of such surpassing quality, they more than justify putting up with a few minor gameplay gripes. Having said that, the story does have some incredibly odd, discordant moments and weirdly dark elements. I'm not saying the story or the overall experience is without flaws, but I am willing to overlook almost anything for more scenes with these characters.
In terms of recommending this game, anyone who is tired of lacklustre/token writing in games
play it, and everyone else should make the effort. Having said that, it's still tricky to recommend it to people, somehow. The odd thing is, I played Dreamfall and fell into this franchise entirely by accident, and while I wish more people could do the same and appreciate it, I understand why they don't.
And, DFC is an adult story with adult themes and language. Plus, DFC is very much part 2 of 2. I don't think it's a good starting point, I think Dreamfall: The Longest Journey is essential to play first.
I hope Red Thread might create a graphically updated re-release of the original Dreamfall, as its graphics haven't aged well, but all the audio and most area scenery could be re-used.

Shortly: (trying no to tell any spoilers and and I didn't play the DLC: Revelations)
Basically, the game is a sequel for the original Castlevania: Lords of Shadow and the Castlevania: Mirror of Fate games, and it continues the story of Dracula (Gabriel Belmont) thousand years after the events of those 2 games.
The game is staged on a modern era, where Satan is once again trying to destroy the world of men with the help of his Acolytes.
Unlike in the original LoS game, this time the game is a openworld game, however you can only travel to new areas AFTER you've aquired a certain powerup to access them. And like in all openworld games, this one also has fast-travel system, but its pretty primitive.
There are 2 different worlds that you can travel, the modern era where the Satan's forcers brings havoc and the Dracula's Castle where the Dracula's own blood is trying to trap you.
Graphics are decent, sounds and voice actings are doreable. The battle system is slightly better than it was in the original LoS, but at the same time it feels a little bit watered down from what it was.
The overall story is a cliche, because you can easily predict that what's about to happen. However, it is interesting enough to see it through. The ending itself however was a disappointment for me, because there's no conclusion, but that's just my opinion.
Pros:
+ Battle and upgrade systems
+ Boss encounters (though the last boss was disappointment)
+ Lots of different enemies
+ Lots of collectables for those interested
+ Over 20 hours of gameplay if you collect every collectable like I did
Cons:
- Disappointing last boss
- Awful Fast-travel system (though you only need it when you're searching for collectables)
- Lots of annoying enemies at the end
- Bad ending (there's no conclusion in my opinion but then again I didn't play the revelations DLC)
- The Shop's location is bad, because getting some of the collectables requires a certain item that can only be bought from the shop, so you need to visit it a lot
- Kleido's Challenges offer no reward except a few Steam achievements
- Few un-skippable cutscenes and events such as the slow paced transition between the modern era - Dracula's Castle
Do I recommend ?:
If you're interested to see what happens to the Dracula after the events of Lords of Shadow and Mirror of Fate, then this might interest you. But if you haven't played those 2 games before, don't care about the story and are only interested for the action, then don't bother.

It's games like this that really make me wish Steam has 3 recommendation buttons: thumbs up / thumbs down / apathetic shrug. Because LOS 2 is far from the great game the first one was, but also isn't totally crap - I'd say it's about 60/40 on the quality divide.
If you played LOS 1 you'll recall it finished with a gob smacking reveal - that had me extremely curious as to how the developers would follow up on this audacious twist. As it turns out - not particularly well. It's a beat em up platformer just like the first, but in this case the camera is moveable - which makes a big, and unwelcome, difference as it is slightly too far out to see the action, and also gets obscured by the ridiculous amount of special effects that happen with EVERY attack.
The game begins back in ye olde days with Dracula's castle being attacked by a giant robot that looks like a building. At first I was like WTF  is that?? because it looks utterly stupid - until I remembered the Titans from LOS 1: those majestic towering elemental creatures that were so impressive. Well, this is one of those - except it's been put through the moronometer, and come out with totally dumb design. Technically impressive for sure, but so NOT Castlevania!
If you hated the liberties the first game took with the series design - you'll be frothing at the mouth over this one....and I'd probably best not mention it gets even worse when the game jumps back to the present day, because those bits will  likely cause your brain to explode in disgust. They annoyed me, and I wasn't bothered by LOS 1's changes.
In the modern day bits you begin by traipsing through a pharmaceutical warehouse, beating up crates and plastic barrels - but not the enemies because you are too weedy after starving yourself of blood for hundreds of years. Yet there's a cutscene where Dracula gleefully murders a family of three - kid included - to regain some of his strength, and to show you how EVIL he has become...err, okay ...not really selling it so far (mainly due to Robert Carlylse's utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥performance), but whatevs!
Anyway, because you've become a total wimp  the first enemies you face have an enforced stealth aspect, which is pretty basic - and by the way, said enemies are big dudes in demonic armour with a gun bigger than you are.......Wot tha fudge?
Eventually you get through these dull encounters, and get sucked back into ye olde times - which thankfully are (a) much more enjoyable, and (b) less crap stylistically, though the first boss you face in this world isn't the greatest to look at. Duff them up, explore a bit more, and then...it's back to the crappy warehouse, traipse thru that some more, and it's back to ye olde world. The games a YOYO!!! Ye olde world =good, modern day=big bag'o'shito
Back in yon days of lore there's a bit with these creepy snake headed girls that's very....creepy, as they skitter about, and contort themselves in a fashion that really won't be doing their spine any favours. They're genuinely disturbing, yet at the same time it's such a pity the whole game seems incapable of maintaining the menace they exude.
The boss battle that precedes this bit has an awfully written cutscene, that's very japanese (even though the devs are spanish...) With an overtly sexual demonic villainess who laughs like a demented walrus, and then says you make her wet....yeeeessss, ok then. The bizarrest thing about all this - the first game had Hideo Kojima involved and wasn't this bad, this time around he was nowhere near this game and it's even more Hideo Kojimaesque than Hideo Kojima.
And, well, that's as far as I've got so far : that's an awful lot of crappy aspects for the first 3 or 4 hours of a game. There's still some enjoyment to be had with it, but it's a shadow of LOS's greatness and a horrendous treatment of Castlevania.
On the plus side - Patrick Stewart is much less awful this time around, so there's that. So, here goes - time to push the 'meh' recommend button, oh wait - there isn't one.

Is Anno 2205 the classic Anno experience? No.
Is it a bad thing? No.
I have been playing Anno since ANNO 1602 and I can say that my experience with the latest release has been an enjoyment rollercoaster. Many of the old mechanics have been removed or changed and admittedly I was mad at first. But as I took the time to play the game the new or changed mechanics started to make some semblance of sense. The first thing that caught my attention was the initial lack of farms you can attach to plantations. But as you played the game you unlock rare materials that you use to build additional farm modules to the plantation, increasing its productivity past 100% and making it more cost effective than building a second plantation. It around this time I realized that Anno 2205 is focused more on space management and economy, and I enjoy it. The game might seem dumb in the temperate zone where there are no restrictions on where you can build and space is relatively plentiful, but when you go to the Tundra and the Moon, the game gets interesting.
In these locations you are limited to where you can build. Not in the traditional sense where you are limited by land, but also by heat in the Tundra and shielding on the Moon. Your factories, in the Tundra, give off heat which your residence need, otherwise they will not inhabit the building. In place of the traditional method of building your cities in huge blocks and production complexes separately, you need to figure out how to build your production and shelter together in order to maximize the amount of people you can host. And on the Moon is changes again. You need to shield all your buildings from space debris. Now you have the issue of building and powering these awkwardly shaped shield generators to protect your buildings. Not only do you have to worry about shielding your building on the Moon, you have to fund all the production on the Moon and OMFG is it expensive.
To afford building and upkeep on the moon you need to expand your taxable population in the Temperate zone, and they consume a lot of material. If they are not happy they will not pay as much. Now you have to pay for shipping from the Tundra for the population’s demands which costs money. And having a positive income can be difficult at times, let alone a high positive income. So to build on the Moon you need to wait until you have enough tangible wealth to actually build. So why not kill some time with combat missions? Set your economy to a surplus and take a half an hour clearing out a hostile zone. You gain experience to unlock new ships and get rare materials to upgrade your factories. If you want to play the military missions on a harder difficulty for more rewards you are strongly recommended to increase your fleet’s level, which costs money. I am constantly moving between locations expanding and optimizing my economy trying to get to the next phase of the game. I feel like there is a lot going on for this game and it is quite possible that if all the old mechanics were in place with the new mechanics, the game would be too slow and no one would want to grind on a single player game.
What can the game do to improve? Bring back the shipyard. It is pleasant that the ships are “free” in the game, but there should be the option to build the ships used for trade and combat. If you could build transport ships, trade would be easier. It becomes a huge expense for your economy to pay 200c for every 20 stack of product shipped between the temperate and tundra zone. It costs 3000c for every 20 stack for the transport to and from the Moon! Giving the player the option to use their own ships to move as much product as possible on a single route should be brought back into the game. As far as Military ships, this can solve several problems at once. First in makes the ships you lose more valuable since you had to pay for those ships to be built in the first place. Secondly, it makes the rare material slower to gain and more valuable since you need to pay for the ships to get the material. After a few visits to the hostile zone I have maxed out my rare materials, and I could do it because it did not cost me more than a few upgrades to win the engagements.
The Co-op and Multiplayer needs to come back. Ubisoft, this function has been a part of the game series forever and you need to stop cutting corners. Additionally, the cost is too high. If everything that was in the season pass DLC was in the game at Launch, then it would be worth $50; at launch. Recommending this game to another person, I highly suggest waiting until there is a handsome discount on the game. If you can pick up the game and season pass for $20, pounce on it. It is not a bad game contrary to community’s attacks on it. It needs some free add-ons and hot fixes, but it is visually beautiful and still a fun game to play despite the change in game mechanics.

I can't recommend this game. Or maybe I can? I don't know yet, but I bet by the time I post this crap, I'll have made up my mind.
Either way, this game has a lot, and I do mean A LOT, of issues. I'm gonna do here what I did with SimCity 4 vs Cities Skylines. COMPARE THE LIVIN' SHÏT OUTTA THIS STUFF!
First off, let's look at building stuff. 2205 DEFINITELY has improved over 2070 on that point. I liked 2070 fo' sho', but göddämnit, building cities in it was a freakin' chore! Just trying to plan out the whole "making room for more police stations end-game" crap was focking infuriating. Now, with 2205, you have a LOT more freedom about where and how you place these sorta buildings. Now, you can move buildings around (don't ask me how they thought this made sense in-game-wise...) so accidentally miss-placing something is no longer a rage-inducing mistake.
Next up, let's look at the whole "citizens and upgrades" thing. This, unlike point #1, is not a pure upgrade (no pun intended). Granted, it's become an extreme lot easier and more fluid to attract new citizens to your city, as the amount of people a house holds is directly connected to the general satisfaction level of that type of citizen. These numbers aren't necessarily correct, but here's an example formula: your level 2 citizens have a satisfaction level of 50%, which means all level 2 residences holds up to 50% of their maximum capacity of citizens.
You can also "promote" (i.e. upgrade) new residences just a moment after they've been built, unlike in 2070 where you had to wait almost a minute or more before you could upgrade them after you established a new housing block. So that's nice. What ISN'T nice, however, is the fact that it's now almost IMPOSSIBLE to keep your citizens well-fed and hydrated while expanding your city. Every new house you build is another strain on your rice fields and desa-whatever plants, and every citizen you attract is a fraction less surplus of food and water.
This wouldn't be an issue in 2070, since IRONICALLY, the ISLANDS WERE A LOT BIGGER IN 2070, BLUE BYTE! Focking retärd devs needs to learn what "five times bigger" really means. Idiots, the lot of 'em.
Anyway, on to issue #3! And this is a direct DOWNGRADE from 2070, imo. The islands. When you start out, you're restricted to the choice of ONLY THREE DIFFERENT ISLAND REGIONS. That's right, no more slight-but-still-refreshing randomly generated islands. From here on out, it's STRICTLY pre-rendered and pre-built islands for you to settle! Now THAT, if anything, is what would've been a HUMONGOUS deal-breaker for me, if those cünts at Ubisoft had told us this before release.
I mean, okay, the islands you DO get to choose from are interesting, with the chiefly intriguing one (so far) being Walbruck Basin (seen in screenshots as the place with the dams). It's cool. And I like being able to actually perform quests in the game which ACTUALLY GIVES A USEFUL REWARD. Because most quests don't even give you a remotely useful or even NOTICEABLE reward. Money? "GEE, THANKS UNCLE NIC! IT'S NOT LIKE I'M GENERATING THOUSANDS OF CREDITS EVERY MINUTE, AND HAVE A COMPLETELY ARBITRARY, BÜLLSHÏT CAP AT A MEAGER 1M CREDS!"
Moving on. Thing #4. The economy. I like the new stream-lined system, I really do, and actually, there's no "but" here either. The system is no longer based on having 8,000 depots near your rice fields so that you can have a constant focking flow of rice into your warehouse like in 2070. Now, it's based on a new tertiary resource called "logistics", and this dear kids is what I REALLY liked: You no longer have to build depots! HOORAY!!!
Seriously though, ANYONE who played 2070 for more than 30 minutes remembers the EXTREME displeasure of having to CONSTANTLY establish motherfocking 20 BILLIONS depots on an island, just to keep the infrastructure running smoothly. It was a CHORE. Now, you build transport terminals instead. And what really tickles my economical strategy strings here is that if you position one JUUUUUUST right, you suddenly make it worth more than THREE of them placed in shïtty locations.
Again, these things work like the whole citizen satisfaction thing. Actually, no. Not really. The closer a transport terminal is to an industry building, the less of a strain is put on the logistics resource from that building. So planning is important. Goodie goodie! Me likey!
Last but not least, #5: Politics. 2070 had a really cool political niche. I liked it a LOT. It made you feel very involved in what happened in the game. The senate/council votes, the Nordamark Conflict, it all made for a very "global" feel of the game. And the fact that no one made a huge impact made it even more involving. You had the sense, even if you were only ever playing it in SP, that you were part of a whole WORLD of players.
But that's completely missing from 2205. There are no votes that makes ANY kinda sense any more, and "events" are nowhere to be found either.
On the plus-side, you're now free to create your own corporation instead of being restricted to just the EI or GT like in 2070. So that's... actually no, it's not nice at all. It's actually a very dull and restricting experience, considering the vast dichotomy between EI and GT in 2070. They had completely different playstyles, whether you played industrial-economical, domestic focus, or even just militaristically. Now, your playstyle is blended into a gray goo of generic "Do what you want, game doesn't care" style. It detracts a LOT from the game.
So I guess, in closing, 2205 is not much like 2070. Actually, it's nothing like 2070. If you're new to the Anno series, and 2205 is the first to tickle your fancy, go for it! Maybe. Actually, don't. I regret spending a massive 60€ on this game by pre-ordering it, so I won't recommend it yet. But once it's dropped in price, then yeah. Go for it! ...maybe. 5.1/10

Shortly. I like changes made from 2070 to 2205. Citybuilding - less micro, more macro. Combat in separate sectors. Combat mission are not hard, but I prefer it this way. This is city builder, not war game. There are only a few combat missions, but I assume, there will be more coming in the future.
