Definitely worth a download, and it's great with a couple friends. But, the cards are lame-looking, and could use a re-design. Definitely one I'll keep playing onward.

It's really good. I don't like how there's only very few cards, but as a medieval strategy game that isn't CK2, it's really really good. It's not Pay-2-Play or Pay-2-Win at all; this may change in the future, but for right now the only thing you can buy is physical copies of the game (as in a real life board game).
I think with a little more expansion and a little less-cliche (for example, the "king" card is a bit cliche), Ortus Regni could be a real contender for a truly great game from an independent developer.
Game of Thrones: The Card Game.

There is a printed rulebook, available via link in-app, contrary to reviewers who don't know how to read that say otherwise. However, as far as I can tell, they're woefully inaccurate. From the very beginning the game and manual both present the victory conditions quite simply: Be the last man standing, and you lose either by losing all your land or running out of cards in your deck. Yet, this information is apparently wrong, or at least out of date. I was starting to like this game, until I got out of the tutorials and into actual play and the game ended in a loss multiple times despite never entering any of the loss positions, and with a simple defeat message which fails to explain how or why this is happening and yet simultaneously covers the entire screen so there's no way to even review the boardstate to try and root out the cause.
I will still begrudgingly reccomend this game because, for one thing, it's completely free, and for another, it has some fairly interesting design elements. It's possible that you'll pick up on whatever it is that I've missed. It might be easier to just play Ortus regni via Tabletop Simulator, to be honest, though you can't do that with AI.

This game came out of nowhere. It's got a pleasant aesthetic, it's simple, the UI is really clean, and it's really fun to watch your minions... ahem... citizens build stuff for you. It's one of those city builders that shows your buildings being created, step by step.
You might look at the screenshots and or videos and think "Wow, this looks like Godus, I wonder how similar it is..." Thankfully, it's very different from Godus. For starters, it was released finished, not in some Early Access state of limbo. So, while it might share a similar aesthetic to Godus, it already knows what it wants to be, and it does the city builder genre justice by being fun and working well.
I would say the future looks bright for this title. It's priced right, at only $10, and has already started gaining a pretty good following. If the devs keep at it, while the hype is hot, I can only see good things in the future. I've also read that the devs are planning to add future content for free, so that's always a good sign.
Honestly, if you like city builders, you're probably going to like this one. For me, it was a no brainer. It's cheap, well made, and those UIs... they're really simple! One of the biggest problems I have with games of this genre is that I lose interest in them due to convoluted mechanics and unpleasant menu systems. This game will not confuse you with its menus and mechanics. Want to build something? Have the resources? Do it, it's simple, it's straight forward, and it works.
No, you shouldn't buy it, you should actually close Steam, turn off your computer, and go play outside. Seriously, what's wrong with you!?!!?!? :P
Steam has a 2 hour return policy. You'll probably know within 10 minutes, whether you like the game or not. Thanks to that clean UI and straight forward mechanics, you can get your little town up and running within the first 10 minutes.
I certainly recommend this game.

Here's the bottom-line: if you've played The Longest Journey and its sequel, Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, then you had might as well play this and see how it all ends. Also, Crow is back and he's as delightful as ever.
Book 5 is released and it ties up virtually all the loose ends from a story roughly 17 years in the making. The ending is satisfying. If you're like me, and grew up playing The Longest Journey, then you gotta play this game to see how it all ends. No need to read further; hop to it (or wait until the game is on sale).
Anyway, the game isn't great. But it has great moments. The earlier episodes are repetitive and a slog. Still, they lay the groundwork for some fantastic set pieces and epic moments in Episodes 4 and 5.
A lot of your choices end up being non-choices; no real impact on the ending. Still, they add a lot of flavor, and they do a good job of making you pay attention to details of whether something is a good idea to pursue or not.
The animation and environments of the game leave a lot to be desired. The characters move clunkily, unbelievably.  And the environments, while cool at first, are boring after you've ran through the same areas over and over for four episodes on various errands. Finally, though, episodes 4 and 5 introduce some new environments that are gorgeous to look at, and, thankfully, they don't overstay their welcome.
As an adventure game, Dreamfall: Chapters is consistently underwhelming and simple-minded. No, I don't miss the obtuse puzzles of TLJ, but I wish there was some more depth to the gameplay. I can't help but feel like the episodic nature of the game only hurt it in the end; but I suppose there was no other way of financing this project.
But let's be real: you're not going to play it because you're expecting an adventure game with memorable puzzles that make you feel like a genius.
You're going to play it because Ragnar Tornquist created a captivating world populated by relatable characters that you care about.
And you're going to enjoy it.

This was a truly amazing, fitting, and deeply satisfying end to a saga that has lasted over a decade - and began even before that. A pair of wonderfully realised worlds, filled with colourful and well-written characters, voiced by incredibly talented actors and actresses, played out to a deep and thought-provoking script, wrapped up in quite possibly the worst game engine on the market today.
Yeesh. To say this had "performance issues" would be like saying the sun is a "bit warm" - the engine choked and groaned under its own weight, often crippling itself in the process, and suffering from janky animations, poor facial expressions, missing audio effects and other not-so-niceties to boot.
It's a shame that, even after the switch to Unity 5, the game still runs so poorly as it can, at times, really drag the whole experience down --- and what an experience it was! Not many games, or dev studios, or writers, can bring a satisfying resolution to so many loose ends and plot threads, but I can happily say Ragnar Tørnquist and Red Thread Games on the whole have succeeded. Not every question was answered, but the majority were and the ending was touching, and sweet, and satisfying, and brought up a few more questions :P Well worth playing, just make sure you've got the Mother Of All Rigs in order to bruteforce through lousy coding on a lousier engine. Was it worth a decade wait, a Kickstarter, and then episodic cliffhangers that dragged over nearly 2 years.....?
eeeeeeghhhhhhh... maybe. It was a mighty fine experience regardless :)

EDIT 2/21/15: Steam Workshop support is up and running for sinlge player mode (to be changed to multiplayer once Valve fixed the Steam-wide Workshop issues).
I installed and tested my first Virtual Desktop way back in 1998. It came with a new Gateway PC and, while it was an interesting concept, there was nothing about it that made me fell like it was any better than just clicking on my desktop icons. Since then, I've tried several more, with the same results: install, play around a bit, say "meh," uninstall. But....this. This...this should be called Addictive Anarchy Arcade. It's ridiculous how often I boot this thing up to walk around a virtual space to play a game, rather than just clicking the link in Steam.
For an alpha, it's incredibly stable. I've not had it crash once, and it runs much smoother than I had expected, given the age of my computer and the fact that it's a shell that runs other media from within.  The only issues I've noted so far is that it can't play mp3 files (which is probably a proprietary thing), and it's not playing sounds to videos linked from your hard drive, but this is currently being worked on. Another slight issue is that it can take up to two days for newly added games in your Steam account to show up; however, this is an alpha build, and it's something the developer is addressing.
That said, there is
goodness here. Obviously, you can use AA to build your own arcade, by very easily linking a variety of cabinets to your Steam Library. There's more though. You can place listening stations (or CDs on tables) or movies on the walls that, when linked to Youtube, any visitors to your arcade can come and watch or listen to. The game (because, at times, it really does feel more like a sandbox game than a virtual desktop) will even synchronize whatever movie you're watching so that you all see it at the same time. That's right: Anarchy Arcade can be multiplayer, allowing others to visit your arcade, and vice-versa.
Placing items and cabinets can be a bit clunky, but the variety is already pretty large, and there is
Workshop support
. New items and buildings (where you can build your arcade) are opened up as you place new items, earning points and reaching goals. It's a clever game-like concept and, while I'd have rather had everything opened at once, it did keep me coming back. Additionally, any content created for Source-engine games (Half-Life series, Portal, Counter strike, et al) can be imported here. Want to create an arcade using your favorite DOTA map? Do it!
The fact that this is free is just the gravy on this already delicious chocolate cake; once you play around, it becomes clear that this is a quality program from someone who clearly loves gaming and who is skilled at programming. The developer is dedicated, frequently on the forums, and open to suggestions: all bonuses to an already pretty great experience. Oh, and did I mention it has Oculus VR support?
Recommended? Absolutely. And at this price, what have you got to lose? Try it out, and get building: I want to check out YOUR arcade!

+ Multiple ways to earn rare resources t (Trading, mission/quests, and combat)
+ Build and manage cities in 3 different areas at the same time or focus on one, from temperate climate, artic, and lunar. Still your choice on what you want to focus on

+ Each areas of the world requires different strategy for settlement placement i.e placing near factories to stay warm in the artics, having to build under shield generators on moon to avoid space debris
+ Hopeful for additional content and release for the game to make it much better than it is which is a base game atm

This is a tough game to boil down to a simple Yes/No recommendation.  It's not full Civ.  I wouldn't even call it Civ Light.  So what is it?  Imagine you took all of the hexes that weren't cities out of a Civ map. Then convert those cities to planets and change the background from surface map to a star field.  Now, eliminate all of the units from the map except for one.  On your turn you may move this one unit (which is actually composed of multiple starships) from the planet it is on to an adjacent planet for a "crew exhaustion" cost. Once it arrives you will engage in one of a handful of templated battles: destroy the enemy fleet, survive for 5 turns, escort a ship to a warp point, prevent an enemy ship from reaching a warp point, capture the resource point, and so on.  You'll see exactly what you are running up against in the mission preparation screen.  When you succeed in the mission you will receive between 1-4 "influence" with that planet.  Once you've reach a full 4 influence, the planet aligns with you and becomes part of your empire.  You'll typically have enough "exhaustion points" to engage in at least two missions per turn.
The missions themselves are turned based tactical battles.  You can upgrade your existing starships with features like torpedoes, improved long range lasers, short range weapons, deployable fighter ships, stealth cloaking, and more.  The more features you load on a ship the slower it gets, so you'll also be pumping points into your engines to keep your range up.  You'll eventually want to purchase additional ships, but don't go overboard because not every mission will allow you to bring your full fleet.  Once the mission begins you'll find yourself on a new hex field cluttered with planets and asteroids that block movement and weapons, "Narrow Passages" are gaps that toggle open and shut between some asteroid sections. There are also warp fields randomly littered around the mission area, and random is truly the word because if you move into one you will be warped to the location of another random warp field.  This can be really frustrating, as you have no control over where you come out, and you can sometimes step on one when not paying attention to your ships pathing.  Each ship will have a set number of movement points and may take one action per turn, whether that is firing a torpedo (which is a special type of timed weapon), shooting directly at an enemy, engaging a cloaking field, or detecting cloaked ships.  Battles quickly become repetitious as you maneuver behind a ship, fire, and move away.
Planets you have influence with you may modify.  You can add more cities to improve their population and production. You may build improvements which increase production of certain commodities: science, energy, metal, and so on.  Planets within your empire can have Wonders constructed which provide unique advantages.
This probably sounds very similar to Civ, and it is.  However, in Civ, especially on harder difficulty levels, you can easily improve a city into weakness.  You have to carefully balance your improvements, purchases, science, and so on.  In Starships you would need to make an effort to build your way into weakness.  On the contrary, the game seems built to provide unbalanced advantages to you.  Unlike Civ where you can only reach higher tiers on tech tree after fulfilling a set number of base technologies, in Starships you are free to Min/Max the techs.  Want to quickly annihlate your opponents? Spend all of your science points on upgrading torpedos and outfit your ships with multiple torpedos.  Each mission will be a breeze.
You declare victory in the game in one of four ways: Population (over 50% of the total galactic population is yours), Domination (last player standing), Science (have three Lvl 6 techs), and Wonder (control 9 wonders).  Population is definitely the easiest of the conditions to meet.  Once you win, you're done.  There is no "Just one more turn" option.
Starships lacks the depth of a full Civ game, intentionally so.  So where does this game fit in your game library? Steam often has sales for Civ V that discount the game to $5, so I can't recommend Starships at full price with a straight face. On sale for a few bucks, though, and Starships might have a niche spot.  You can play a campaign in just a few hours without spending too much thought on it. Have a long conference call that you need to be on? Starships in the background would be a fine distraction.  It doesn't replace full Civ, but it also won't keep you up until the wee hours of the morning.

You can grind a town to a complete halt, get down to 5 villagers, but nothing will happen. As long as you have one hovel, the 5 people left will equalize to medium happiness, prompting you to build more houses to get more villagers. You won't be able to get any more because you lack beds, but none of the villagers will die of starvation, they just won't. As long as they have medium happiness (which they maintain due to the low population), they will not starve, even if there are no open food production buildings. You can blow up the last house, but they stil won't starve. Now they just want a house. I waited for something like 30 minutes trying to get rid of these last few straggelers in a dead, raided town, but they stayed no matter what I did. I like that the game is this nice ride of lulls and highs of tension, but if there is no way to really fall bellow where you started, it feels a little cheapened.
Overall I like the game a lot. The visuals are great, charming and easy to read. I sorta wish you could draw roads, but other than that there isn't much I dislike. I think the population system and happiness system both need to be altered somehow to allow for some sort of fail state, even if it's fairly easy to avoid.
Edit: Just realized this is a feature, you cannot die unless you play on Vinter difficulty. This pretty much nulliffies my point, but in that case I would just like to have it be more clear, or have an option to have fail states on any difficulty

That’s it, then.
Dreamfall Chapters: Book Five – Redux has the unenviable task of not only wrapping up its own plot, but offering a proper conclusion to the original Dreamfall, released back in 2006. That’s a heavy task in and of itself; both games are companion pieces to The Longest Journey, a mammoth tale of twin worlds and the people who can move between them. That initial story was begun much further back, in 1999, and has threads of its own woven into Chapter’s narrative. What all of this means is that, at least for now, a story that took more than fifteen years in the telling has finally drawn to a close.
It’s a lot of narrative to conclude. And while Ragnar Tørnquist’s trio of games has sometimes come under fire for mechanical failings, there’s rarely been much complaint about the encyclopaedic lore and deep intertwining plot lines. These tales are a clear labour of love, all brilliantly sobering, self-deprecating, tragic and immersive. They're about a futuristic dystopia under the ever watchful eye of a Big Brother with ill intentions and a magical world at war with religious zealots determined to wipe magic out completely. So, yeah, there’s a lot of ground to cover, and Redux does struggle to bring closure to it all. There are still some questions unanswered, while others seem rushed through, thrown in during a static corridor of exposition leading to the big villain reveal some of us figured out in 2006 (and, to be fair, even the game pokes fun at itself for giving this away too early). There’s a lot of weight on the shoulders of Redux, so credit where credit is due: its knees might wobble now and then, but they never buckle.
Screen time is roughly split between the two protagonists, who mainly stick to their respective worlds to tidy away their efforts. Kian returns to his résistance army, which is under different shades of disaster depending on some of the running choices you’ve made thus far in the adventure. Zoe, on the other hand, finds herself returning to Stark in a way she couldn’t have expected. While Kian’s left to pick up the pieces of his shattered comrades, Zoe’s trying to piece together her origins.
That description sounds vague, doesn’t it? Some of that is because I’m graciously tiptoeing around spoilers, but some of it is also because a lot of what you'll experience depends on those pesky choices you’ve made. Sometimes, they kind of matter. Kian’s shattered group is tragically splintered regardless of what you’ve done, but people you’ve grown close to and come to rely on are either alive or dead based purely on your actions. You have that soul-destroying sucker punch at the end of the fourth book to deal with, for instance. On the other end of the spectrum, everything you’ve come to believe about Zoe’s adventure is turned on its head in a second, forcing you in an instant to re-evaluate everything you’ve done thus far and to ask yourself if any of it really mattered, or if any of it was real at all.

Now that all 5 books (aka episodes) are released, I can safely say that this is a satisfactory conclusion to The Longest Journey.
It is also a game that is strewn with winks to the previous games and with various pop culture references.
I was blithesome as the game answered various questions that had been floating around for years, but I was also mirthful for those that were left unanswered.
Love great stories and adventures? Get the trilogy (The Longest Journey, Dreamfall: The Longest Journey and Dreamfall Chapters)

Dreamfall Chapters is a decent finale to The Longest Journey and Dreamfall. I have first played the saga more than 10 years ago, and it offers everything good an adventure series is able to offer - perfected story, believable characters and complex puzzles. The third game is mostly no exception to this, though I'll expand it later. Definitely buy the game and support Red Thread Games, at least for what they and Ragnar Tørnquist had to accomplish in order to complete the series.
As for the setting, you'll visit both Stark and Arcadia at about the same rate and recognize Marcuria from the previous games. There's a high variety of beautiful locations you'll have a chance to visit, ranging from the already mentioned city you'll visit the most, various cyberpunk locations in Propast, and of course some stunning places in neither of the two worlds. In some locations I almost didn't want to leave, admiring how well had they been made.
The music fits quite well, like in the previous games. You'll recognize tunes from Dreamfall, and
appears more than once.
You'll meet characters you already know from previous games, like Roper Klacks, Brian Westhouse, of course Zoë and Kian, Reza, Helena, and also - April. All characters have a developing personality througout the game, and you'll be able to progress your relationship via the choices.
As for the decisions and choices, I was surprised a lot how even at first sight minor choices influence the development of the story, and how largely it may deviate. However, you'll probably at least once think how you messed everything up, same as I did.
The feature not present as much as I would like though, are the traditional adventure puzzles. The previous games contained the right amount of puzzles in them, TLJ even being considered in some locations as hardcore. Although Dreamfall Chapters arguably contains puzzles and even some well-made ones, it varies noticeably between the books, some being only mostly story-related, and the amount of puzzles generally decreases over the chapters.
Though the episodic format has been discussed and considered a lot during and prior to the development of the game, I think it doesn't hurt over all, and is barely noticeable if you play the game now. Each book contains close and related unit of story, and takes about 3-4 hours. The last book is vastly different to all the previous ones in that it explains more questions than it raises, something not seen previously in the saga at all.
Now I find it amazing that it seems like the whole story has been thought up almost 20 years ago, and now it all wraps up perfectly in the last game. Until the last chapter, you'll be constantly puzzled and seeking explanaions, and then shocked at how the things reveal at the end.
All in all, I've enjoyed playing this game since the release of the first book, despite the fact it makes me think of it more like of an interactive movie, not as bad as Minecraft: Story Mode, but it seems the good old adventure times are yet to be revived. Nevertheless, what the game lacks in puzzles, it gains in story progression and decisions.

This game runs like a slide show on the specifications it lists.  It is a Unity based game, and since I have had a good experience with DreamCarRacing 3D, another Unity based driving game, I thought it would be worth a try.
I found the car control was just bad all around.  The steering has this delayed feel, and the cars handle in some very strange ways, like rolling over on thier side when trying to climb a steep grade.  The handling is very unpredictable, one bump may be huge, but the car absorbs it no problem, the next bump may be smaller and looks smoother, but hitting it sends the car bouncing off the course.
The main interest I had in this game was the included track builder/editor that looked pretty good and the workshop listed some nice looking player made tracks.
I have been playing DreamCarRacing 3D (another Unity based car game) for over a year, and it runs and drives about 10x better than this game.  DCR3D only short coming in my opinion is the track creator is very primitive, limited to dropping checkpoint flags while you drive a car, with no way to edit them once placed, and now way to set the number of laps in a course you create this way. DCR3D does allow you to create custom maps using Unity, but you are still stuck with using the primitive checkpoint flags to mark a course that can be timed.
I was hopeful D Series Off Road would be a better game for creating tracks and racing, but after trying the awful driving out, I could see not reason to invest any time into the track builder.
Maybe if you have a good gaming rig, it will run better for you, but if you go by the advertised specs, this is a real dog.

Update 10-11-2016
Ubisoft responded to the community, and as of today the Frontiers DLC will be included to anyone who owns the Season Pass. I had purchased the "Gold" Edition, so that means I received the DLC for free now as well. As a result, I will be reversing my recommendation back to the original review.
*****************************
Update 10-06-2016
For a while, this was recommended by just a sliver. Each new DLC had added promise to what the game could have been. However, with the release of Frontiers and the total lack of respect to those that had supported the game, I can confidently say that I no longer recommend this title.
I got my money's worth in playtime, so I don't regret having bought this entry into the Anno series. I bought the edition that should have had all DLC included, but apparently that  was not enough. Unless they change that, I will no longer be purchasing anything from Ubisoft.
*****************************
I am a fan of the Anno series because I like the complexity. You cannot just slap some buildings down and hope to succeed. You need to micromanage your production lines, plan out your cities, and if a major restructuring is needed, you're going to have to work at it.
So, why recommend this Anno when there are better games in the series out there? Plain and simple, this is a good introduction to the series.
if you will. For example:
Not all of the changes are bad however, and some I feel do add to the gameplay.
I left combat and multiplayer out, because I am unsure how I feel about combat being moved off map. I certainly miss harassing my competitions trade, but without a means to directly confront an opponent on the map in the first place, not really sure how to respond to that.
Multiplayer not being present yet is not really a bad thing either. I miss it, don't get me wrong. However, with the game as it is with what I'll assume is features coming in DLC, it would in effect be bad. So, wishing for a badly implemented feature is no better than not having it at all.
If you're a hardcore Anno fan like me, the game is a mixed blessing. It will certainly draw in new players to the series. I'd expect them to be hungry for more, and then seek out titles like 2070 or any of the ones from the Age of Sail. On the other hand, I feel this entry is still lacking in what makes the series truly special.
Expect to see updates to this review as the DLC comes out. Until all the DLC is said and done, I'll be playing this game here and there. I do not necessarily regret my purchase, because I think there is a lot of potential here.

All in all I liked the game, I just think they could add a LOT more to it. I like the streamlined interface, mostly all buildings have a module system. Fantastic! I think the graphics are amazing! So far from what I've played of the campaign it's intense and fun. Also, I enjoyed the little conflict zones that you play to get mats for building upgrades. I think that's a nice touch and helps break up the tedium of managing your city.
What I don't like is sometimes pertinent info that you need isn't there. Take for example anno 2070. At a glance all I had to do was check my warehouse and I would know exactly what I had in there. I don't know if I'm mising it or not but all I have now is a production sheet that shows me what % im over or under producing. When you're the type of person that doesn't like to overproduce and make sure your city is constantly in balance like I am, lacking those numbers drives me nuts.
The one thing that I thought was absolutely amazing was being able to fill up my ARC and be able to take it with me to whatever map I wanted to play and have those mats there for me. That's completely gone now and was something that Immediately I noticed and didn't like. The campaign was fun in 2070 but what had me invest over 1000+ hours was the ability to start up a randomly generated map on a whim, take my ARC in and go.
Bottom line as it stands I do like the game and would reccomend this game to people. I think that people are going to get bored pretty quick with just a campaign to play.

A massive step back for Anno; playable but in no way worth the price tag.
Major cutbacks:
- Military REMOVED from the game; there are combat missions but your cities and trade routes will never be attacked. You have no shipyards, ships are provided for free for combat missions and transport ships just cost upkeep. No ships or vehicles present in cities except for cosmetic doodads that do nothing.
- Huge shift in focus; you'll spend a majority of your time doing missions that are as terrible as ever, fast forwarding the game while your command ship (The only controllable ship outside of combat) does the same gather flotsam/lifeboat/buttplugs missions from anno2070
- Factions are island specific: no option for where and when you pursue them. Arctic, moon, temperate all have seperate people and production chains but they aren't interesting anymore; since military is cut there are no alternate ships available, and:
- Island variety is gone; different islands (There are only 3 of each type in the game BUY THE DLC FOR MORE!) have different layouts and mining/fishing spots, but there are no fertilities, no finite resources like ore/gold, they just keep going. Did i mention every map is a single island and you just swap between them? To top this off all factories require population to work so having different islands serve different purposes is no longer a thing; they are ALL cities now.
- Extremely casual resource management. The game looks like a proper game, but oozes IOS gameplay: basic buildings are built like normal but they require special resources for upgrades that make them more efficient; resources you can get by doing the stupid combat missions, regular missions or buy at a ridiculous price. Instead of producing goods that go in your warehouse, the game's economy operates on the Cities XL formula: Each building produces X amount of tokens and consumes Y amount of other tokens; There's no storage and goods aren't collected by warehouses anymore.
- Modules/equipment/research removed. A major part of anno2070 was the academies; producing and distributing equipment for increasing finite resources on an island or giving an island certain bonusses.
I've got more complaints and no space. It's CitiesXL now, might as well get that instead since it's cheaper and has curved roads.

OutDrive is a relaxing game that is great to play in the background while you talk to friends. The retro landscape and music is nice, and it's easy to be lulled into a calm space.
That being said, this game is very repetitive. Once you've played for 7 minutes, you've played the entire game. The track you drive on is one big loop, and nothing every changes. If you crash, it is very easy to start going again before you fail (where you clearly should), so there is virtually no challenge to this game. This game offers very rudimentary car physics, and it's easy to spin out from tapping the edge of the map or going from 0 to 60 in a way that just feels off. In my opinion one of the best voxel-based game out there.
Especially when you want to get a bit crazy.
o You can build pretty much everything you imagine, Tanks, Hovercrafts, Planes, Spacecrafts, and all kind of buildings and so on. Land, Space, Air, Water and Underwater are the locations you can make crafts for.
o The design feels very natural, every design decission you make could have benefits or consequences. Every block you place is there for a reason and changes the behavior of your craft.
Say you build a ship, that can be destroyed very easily. Then you upgrade your armor, so it wont take as much damage. But higher armor increases your ship costs, weight, speed and other types of damage like emp do now more damage.
Dasign is the best part of the game, and it goes deep, really deep, so deep that this the biggest turn off for casual gamers. It took me literally more than 20 hours to undestand how to build a ship, I looked alot of youtube, forums, reddit to get into the game. So this was quite an afford, and I´m still not "there", loaded a hovercraft from steam workshop - and literally dont understand how it works, even after 500hours of playing. And even though this sounds bad - it´s not.
Thats the point, you can experiment a lot in this game, you start simple, try diffrent things, and in order to check if you understand it, I tend to build minimalistic design to capture the idea of something. Then I move on to the next chapter of block and so on.
After you understand some of the game mechanics, you can design really naturally, and everything you want or imagine.
You want a laser-drone-swarm ? do it. You want a super-big-laser-satellite as defense? Yeah why not. You want that thing out of the Movie you saw? ok.
Weaponsystems go deep to, you can make the any type damage you like. If you want explosions, you get them. I like to make my oponnents look like cheese, shooting thru them so they have more holes then cheese could have. You can build all type of missiles you want. Actually every type of weapon is not "modable" but consists out of mods, thats why there are so many diffrent ways you can build and use them.
I would recommend this game to everyone who likes designing crafts.
Some parts of feel a bit undone and it´s not the most graphic intense game.
But it´s the closest thing to this thing you imagined it can do when you played with lego.

"The Dark Souls of ..."
It's like after this game people felt the need to compare it to any and all future games. There is a very good reason for this: the original Dark Souls does so many things right and borrows and builds upon so many genres that it can be difficult to describe it succinctly. It's an action-RPG that requires precise movement and twitch reaction. It's a metroidvania-type game where the world is interconnected and varied: encouraging you to make it just a little bit further the next time so that you can unlock that short cut or find that hidden area. It has traditional RPG leveling mechanics and stat requirements that helps make every play through feel different due to the ten starting classes to choose from and the large quantity of equipment and spells to find. The story-telling is completely hands off and for the player to discover; you can make your way through the game speaking to less than three characters and enjoy the somber silence that comes with that.
By far though, and what will most likely have the longest lasting impact from this game: the "multiplayer." Demon's Souls and Dark Souls introduced a Co-op and Invasion type system that I had not seen prior to these games. Players are able to leave messages to one another: ostensibly to provide insight as to what will gank you in the corner coming up. This isn't always the case though and often times you will find numerous messages encouraging you to head directly into the traps. Further, whenever you are in human form in the game you can be invaded by other players. Fortunately, at the same time you are able to summon yet more players to assist you. Nearly all of the Covenants that can be found in the game are built around the multiplayer system. That all of the multiplayer aspects of the game are opt-in is what makes this game so unique. You can take it or leave it: it's up to you.
As you can tell from the hundreds of hours I poured into the game I can probably gush about it for pages on end. To summarize: there is a reason that so many people compare this game to any and all future games. Although the Dark Souls sequels have built upon and improved a lot of what the first one did I still suggest playing the original to see where it all began. Make sure you install dsfix though as the PC version isn't the best port.

I've been playing Starbound on and off since the early stages of the game. What I've experienced over that time span is as follows.
(Early Stages)
What I Enjoyed:
1.) Exploration was rewarding albeit dangerous during early stages of game. UI was sometimes cumbersome but otherwise useful
2.) Combat was simple, charming, and could quickly become challenging if you took a wrong step (Very Terraria esque w/ non-boss mobs)
3.) Exploring the infinite planets solo or with friends was a blast, reminiscent of my first time playing Minecraft but with the charming 2D sidescroller that I've come to love
4.) Modding community active and healthy (albeit still getting on it's feet)
5.) In game music simple and beautiful. Love ability to find instruments and play songs yourself. Often found myself sitting still in safe area to just listen to it
6.) Very low hardware/sytem requirements, very accessible to the casual gamer
Issues I had:
1.) Multiplayer was somewhat a chore to get to work smoothly, often dealt with desync or random disconnects due to script errors or random bugs (no mods installed when issues arised)
2.) Combat could be buggy or outright cheap at times
3.) Story was very....very short and basic. Felt like more of a sidequest/fetch fest
4.) Replayability was kinda lackluster after exploring the same biomes/planet types after a while. Required mods to freshen it up
5.) Mod community was still getting on its feet with many issues of multi mod compatibility and installation issues
6.) NPCs were fun but had very little impact on gameplay aside from stores, story quests, and random dialogue
(Current State of Game)
1.) Exploration is still extremely fun and has immensely improved with recent updates. Vehicles, player made structures, new and improved biomes/random structures, and overall depth of game VASTLY improved. Mechs and ship travel more in depth and plays larger role vs. Galactic Bus Service + mobile base from earlier stages
2.) Combat more varied while still retaining original charm minus many issues it faced before (getting stuck from monster knockback, instahits, issues with invulnerability or lack thereof after getting hit)
3.) Story added to and much more in depth. Entertaining and healthy amount of lore for those who care WITHOUT shoving it in your face
4.) Modding community booming with many established mod devs and can easily add hours upon hours of gameplay
5.) MULTIPLAYER GREATLY IMPROVED along with ease of access
6.) NPCs now offer quests and have a much larger impact on gameplay and making the game feel more "alive and populated"
6.) Music still fantastic and music addons to game create huge selection
Issues that I still have:
1.) End game can quickly become stale without installing mods to add to your game (think endgame Terraria if you're not into speedrunning boss fights or farming events for that one f****** item)
2.) High end gear basically eliminates any challenge in combat due to enemy difficulty being directly linked to area/planet you're on (once you're past a certain point in the game, all enemies basically become cannon fodder with little challenge)
3.) No difficulty scaling outside of story progression and planetary danger levels
4.) PvP extremely basic and relies heavily on level of gear vs. skill
OVERALL:
Starbound was and still is an excellent 2D sidescroller sandbox explorer that holds many many hours of gameplay. It contains a vibrant and fairly tame community that invests heavily into the game. The developers are actively engaged in the product and seem genuinely invested in the community as well. Any major issues I have with the game are mostly stylistic opinions that can be easily remedied with either mods, a fresh start character, or a brief hiatus from the game.

Dreamfall Chapters is the complete opposite: it doesn't merely crank out the happy ending that fans clamored for; it presents a thorough, multithreaded series of conclusions that expertly merge Dreamfall's dark maturity with the first game's sense of wonder and magic. Skip forward some years, and key members of the development team launches a kickstarter for Dreamfall Chapters: The Longest Journey, meant to finish the story started in the first Dreamfall game. Released in an episodic format over a couple of years, the fifth and final episode became available just three days ago! And my, was it worth the wait!
The game continues where it left off, and immediately gives conclusion to one of the biggest cliffhangers from the previous game. Starting with that, the game takes you on a rollercoaster ride of adventure and emotions!
Music, graphics, gameplay, etc. ... everything is top notch, and it all adds to the stories that are told throughout the game. Characters, both playable and non playable, are multilayered(possibly with the sole exception of a certain commander) and feel like living people. The environments are beautifully crafted and highly detailed, with nothing left to chance. Everything adds up to create a unique experience I have yet to see anywhere else!
The game is a perfect mix of fantasy and science fiction(as is the series as a whole), and if you enjoy GREAT stories, then this game is for you! You can jump right into Dreamfall Chapters, but I do highly recommend playing the whole series from the beginning.

I'm writing two versions for the review - if you are new to Anno, keep reading, if you are not new to it, scroll down a little. Or read them all, whichever you prefer.
Anno games are more of a tycoon game; an economy simulator rather than a city builder. So if you are expecting a city builder to kill your time with, Anno isn't for you, and I recommend checking Cities: Skylines instead. But if you are still reading, that means you are interested and I'll do my best to help you decide.
There is no multiplayer. However, that shouldn't be a deciding factor for your purchase, not for this game at least. Multiplayer has never been a strong point of the series. Anno 2070 features co-op in addition to competetive mode, maybe 5% of my total playtime is in co-op multiplayer. However I gave up on it as you cannot speed the game up in multiplayer. The bread and butter of any Anno game is continuous play; which is intertwined to the base campaign now, and I like it quite a lot.
Game focuses around building a population, and supplying them with their needs. As they get satisfied, you'll have an opportunity to upgrade their residences, which opens new building options, and unlocks new production chains. Production chains get very complex as you progress, and requires several buildings to keep the efficiency at 100%. You have a nice little panel which tells you exactly how much you are producing and consuming (or sending/trading).
There are 3 types of environment; lush, arctic, and lunar. Lush is maybe the easiest, with no additional mechanics. Arctic and lunar has different mechanics. Arctic for example, residences can only be built around a heat source - your production buildings so to speak. This makes Arctic map different from Lush, a lot. Every environment has their own set of buildings, and in order to proceed in the game, you'll have to transfer resources between your regions. It's very easy to set those routes up though. You'll swap between these regions, and play every map at the same time so to speak. credit income from one map affects you globally - only resources are localized.
There are 9 maps as far as I can tell, and you start on one lush, then grab an arctic, and then grab a lunar region. You can purchase the other regions though. Every one of them looks gorgeous, and I didn't really miss a random map generator - because as I've said before, bread and butter of Anno games is continuous play, and when you start a game, you'll keep playing it. Being able to also play on 8 different maps - that's even more butter for the bread so to speak.
Aside from the resources, there are 4 things that you need to manage; power, workforce, logistics, and credit balance. At first it may seem easy to do so, however as your city grows, the distance to your warehouse increases, and production buildings will have higher logistics requirement. Soon, you'll have to build transport depots to increase your logistics capability; however these depots require power and maintenance of them is rather high. After a while you may find yourself in situations where you are trying to get a balance between power, logistics and maintenance. Aside from these, there are special, rare materials which you get by doing mini-missions and combat missions.
Mini-missions are non-mandatory, optional stuff that you can do in order to get more of the rare materials. Combat is on separate maps, so you don't have to worry about them if that's not your thing. However, I found myself quite enjoying the combat maps from time to time. You have a separate military ranking, and as you gain levels, your fleets gets bigger & better. Each map has one primary goal, and up to three secondary goals, and you get a lot of power-ups & pick-ups on your way to deal with the threats in the mission. Your rewards are rare materials which you require in order to upgrade your buildings - and these upgrades are very powerful.
Graphics are very nice, however I feel that the game could use more optimization. I also feel that there may be a memory leak, as after 2+ hours of playtime, the framerate starts going down. I have an average PC, and usually sit around 40-60 FPS on medium settings, but it starts dipping down after a while. Music is as always, very good. Relaxing, soothing. The UI could use some help though - I'm not sure if I can - but being able to pin some stuff on the screen would eliminate a few mouse clicks.
Overall, I highly recommend this game if you like economy simulators / tycoon games, with a little touch of city building. If you are interested, but would like to wait for a sale, it is understandable, it's not a cheap game afterall, You may want to check Anno 2070 meanwhile, however this game has big differences to Anno 2070, just keep that in mind. Have a nice day!
I see a lot of reviews, comments, and discussions saying that this game is dumbed-down, and is easy. I beg the differ. All the changes I've seen are primarily aimed to please the people who enjoy continuous play a lot. I'm someone who plays Anno just because of the continuous play, and I'll take Anno 2070 as a base while trying to explain the changes.
No multiplayer - I believe it was the most underused feature of Anno 2070, and that's why they got rid of it. Anno has never been a good RTS either. It was the right decision in my opinion. I tried to play it, but I gave up on it as you cannot increase the game speed in multiplayer (naturally) - and at most 5% of my playtime is in multiplayer.
No storages/warehouses - To me, primary aim of these two buildings was to provide logistics drones to your facilities. Now, we have something called Logistics, and it makes the game harder actually. There is a building that increases your logistics capacity, but it doesn't come cheap. And as the distance to your warehouse / depot increases, the logistics maintenance also increases, so you cannot just put cheap storages everywhere to cover the map and then build as you like. There are no aerial drones to make your job easy either.
No random maps - I am STILL playing the very same map that I've started months ago in my continous play in Anno 2070. To be honest, looking at the same thing for a rather long while gets a bit boring. In 2205, the main campaign is actually a beefed up continuous play, and you can swap between your maps with a short loading time. You can establish routes between your regions - as opposed to establishing routes between your islands, to develop them even further. What I'm trying to say is, now at least I get to look at 3 (9) different maps, the main difference is that we all will be looking at the same maps. But personally I'm fine with it, since they are hand-crafted, they are gorgeous to look at.
Infinite resources - Well, Anno 2070 also had infinite resources. You either researched or traded special warehouse modules, and applied those on an island to regain some resources. It was tiresome in continuous play, checking every trader, doing research, etc... and doing this for every island that you owned, and every resource that you needed... Now it's infinite, and I'm glad they've changed it. It was one of the most irritating aspects of previous Anno titles.
No factions - No, there are factions. It's not what we had before though. As the game has 3 different environments, you also get to play 3 different factions in essence. Arctic for example, you can only build residences with access to a head source - a production building so to speak. That alone makes arctic play out differently than what you've got used to before. Not to mention that every "faction" has different production lines.

Great game for the price. I recceived a coupon after badge creation and ended up being deeply discounted. Most smaller games like this, I simply tend to write off as shovelware. I keep coming back to play The Collider for it's sheer simplicity, challenege and overall fun.
Who is this game for? It's primarily best for those who want to develop better hand-eye coordination, with speed and complexity increasing as the game rolls along. It's a good fit for those who want to test the accuracy of their mouse and it's settings for FPSs and the like. Those who get off on  high scores and perfection in beating a game would beneift from this game. Lastly, whomever has had a fleeting thought of what it would be like to be a particle in a massive collider shuld try it. The concept is great and it's the imagination the developers had that puts it to good form.
Soundtrack is simple, consisting of two songs, on the main menu and in-game. It's great and effective, adding tension at the correct times. Who knew speed could considered within the horror genre?
My only caveat is that the acheivements are glitched and the developers have no intention of fixing them, ever. The awards unlock after exiting the game and sometimes do not register, especially when going for the Perfect Score acheivements. Not a major issue, but it will annoy the acheivement hunterts out there.
Overall, The Collider is worth your time, especially when on sale or if you're lucky and get a coupon like I did.

The game continues the story from Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth, where the original colonists of the planet have advanced down three possible paths. You get to choose one of the same three paths in Beyond Earth in this game as well, only in space this time with spaceships. This affects the cosmetics on your ships as well as a few other things. You are also able to choose from a variety of different leaders which give a unique starting bonus. One of these bonuses that I love is the one that gives you a second starting ship, since you only start with one.
After you choose your starting conditions and possible victory conditions (there are many ranging from population, to even domination.), you then jump into the game. It's quite easy to win even on hard difficulties. The player takes their ship to a neutral planet in an attempt to make the planet join their side. After a few missions (that you have to pass), they join you, but don't think you can just go and take it with no competition. Your ship/ships have limited movements, so choose which planets you want to take wisely. Other civilizations will try to compete against you for the neutral planets until there are basically none left, leaving only one way to expand. Domination. Or you could just win a different type of victory by then and have the game end, it's quite possible.
Combat is quite easy, as long as you don't throw all of your ships into the grinder to get shredded apart. Your ship can use a variety of different methods for combat such as hangars, long range weapons, short range weapons, and other utility items such as a cloaking device or a scanner. The problem is that if you have enough supplies to upgrade your ships to be overpowered, then you will be unstoppable. Resources are quite easy to get too, so that means overpowered ships are as well. So you could just win the game with one ship if you really wanted to, instead of making a ton of ships. Do this by getting a max level hangar and spitting out little fighters to wreck your enemies.
There is also diplomacy in this game, so feel free to explore that option as well. You can befriend others and team up to take down another, or force others to give you resources or ship upgrades. Last but not least I will mention this: each planet has upgrades that you can do to increase resource production, population, etc. Most planets also have great wonders you can build that give (sometimes overpowered) upgrades to your ships depending on your playstyle. Some upgrades could be useless to you if you don't want to use a certain thing.
Basically, if you aren't a fan of easy games I'd avoid this, but I still enjoyed my experience with it. I'd give it a 5/10.

If you're expecting an In-depth game of intrigue, war and complex resource management, prepare to be disappointed. This game is diet Sid Meier’s.  It has the resources you expect from playing Beyond Earth and even ties into the game nicely giving you the ability to continue your political chess match into the stars after you have conquered the land. All the Alliances and wars you had follow you.  I think that’s cool.  Just don’t expect the same amount of subtly and finesse in this game as there was in Beyond Earth.  This game is almost casual in its approach to strategy.  Each time you go to a planet you are given a scenario and if you complete it, you get a reward and you gain some influence over that world.  Do enough for them or just loiter around long enough and they will join your team. GO TEAM! There is research but it’s purchased with points.  There are buildings but they are also just purchased with points.  You can grow your colonies on the planets you control but… you guessed it. Purchased with points.  There is strategy involved but it takes no patience or time to play this game, especially on easy.  One thing that I do find annoying is that there is no load function in game.  You can save all day long but you have to exit to the main menu to load.  But that’s just a minor inconvenience, really.  The main reason this is an issue is that, like all of Sid Meier’s games, this one can be quit unforgiving especially in the beginning.  If you don’t make the right decisions earlier on, prepare to be left behind by the AI and hopelessly out gunned.
All in all though, this game is a decent time sink and easy to pick up if nothing else.  It can be a little unforgiving but it’s easily to lean and if you manage to spawn in a good location, you can beat this game in an evening then play a new game as someone else tomorrow.

While I really like the theme of the game, it has many design issues.
Firstly, the tutorial is quite possibly the most poorly written tutorial I have ever seen. I do not aim to exaggerate here, it is actually that bad.
The game is based around very many different mechanics. While this can be a good thing when executed properly, the developers have shown their lack of experience here by struggling to represent as many historically-accurate mechanics as possible without giving much thought to their impact on the learning curve or player strategies. This creates a ridiculous amount of complexity but not much depth. Imagine a game where you play as a person but had to constantly keep telling them to breathe, which leg to put forward when walking, etc. This is the sort of issues we are talking about here - throwing in excessive mechanics does not necessarily make the game any more rewarding or enjoyable. This, combined with the atrocious tutorial, make the game impossible to play.
The game puts so much power in the hands of random chance that playing well is almost pointless. Fate cards, viking dice, etc. do nothing but exacerbate the already problematic amount of random chance that is inherent to games that involve drawing random cards. As a result, winning and losing a match is almost entirely dependent on chance and not on player skill.
The card design, although great for setting a theme, is very poor from a UI perspective. There is absolutely no information on cards unless you choose to zoom in on them, and there isn't even so much as an indication to what kind of card something is just by holding it. Even then, you will be met with around three or so different effects for each card, depending on the situation you're using it in. This is somewhat remedied by the absurdly limited amount of cards available in the game, which is a problem in itself, but it could be fixed much more easily with some redesigning.
All in all, this game feels like it was designed by someone who played Dominion, felt that it was not historically accurate enough, and thought that they could create a better game despite having no game design knowledge or experience.
Let me close by saying what I did like:
Drawing a card at the end of the turn and not at the beginning of the turn is great. It means that while your opponent is making their move you have time to evaluate your strategy, instead of having to rethink your turn as soon as you draw a card because it completely changes your options. I would like to see more card games do this.

While I dig the move from Micromanagement to Macromanagement, this has been really oversimplified.
1) You do not need trade networks in between islands
2) You do not need to connect your recourses/manufacturing to warehouses
3) Productions times are instant as in all factories ect will produce the commodity directly into the island cluster pool
4) Trade between island cluster pools is done by automated trade routes that do not require anything (even ships)
5) Combat has been removed from city developments ect, and it is now done ONLY in combat areas.
6) You must do combat areas to get recourses for building building modules
7) You do not make your own combat units, instead you are provided with units for free.
I do like some new mechanisms however, such as dynamic viewing of required and oversaturated goods.

Parts of the game feel really phoned in, and the combat isn't really clicking for me.  Lack of multiplayer is kind of a killer.  singleplayer campaign structure has been improved consiterably.
That said, I still recommend it but not at current prices, wait for a deal.
It's an interesting new approach to the series, parts of it work and parts don't.  The multi-region interplay is pretty good, even the abstracted logistics became a net positive for me.  The combat has been entirely seperated from the main part of the game and sequestered into side missions.
The game is in dire need of more content in general, what's here is a good starting point, but I'd really like to see it evolve like 2070's content did, with the monthly events and all that kind of stuff.

If I was to sum up Dreamfall Chapters in one word it would be inconsistent.  Everything from writing, to acting to graphics and performance has an inconsistency to it.
Coming into the game I knew there would be some areas that I wouldn't understand as I stopped playing both The Longest Journey and Dreamfall when getting to Marcuria, this didn't really hurt the experience until right at the end where I had to read other peoples opinions to understand the closing scene of the game.
Zoe is a joy to play in this game.  She is well realised and is blessed with great writing and acting.  A couple of plot points in Book 3 feel sluggish for her but in Book 4 she has almost all of the best moments of the game.  Book 5 struggles to round all of her story up and feels like a missed opportunity.
Kian has the majority of the weakest moments in the game, with weaker writing and acting, a lack of consistent characterisation and too much tedious hidden object fetching.  The supporting cast of Arcadia suffer from poor acting and writing, and Arcadia itself struggles with being a realised setting with too much anachronistic humour to undermine to plot it wants to host.
Saga is a good character looking for a good story.  A fantastically built character that never fits into the story of the game, and then clumsily interjected into the deeper story of TLJ.  The rest of the supporting cast are wooden with a few exceptions (Bip, Nela, Shitbot), with the bad guys suffering from poor acting and nonsensical motivations, with a cringe worthy Anthony and Cleopatra situation becoming laughable in the final book.
Outside of the story the character models can vary from outstanding (Zoe, Saga (and family), Crow, Witches) to poor (Reza, Anna and most of the human Arcadia cast, anything to do with The Eye, Baruti).  Animation suffers throughout the game, with cutscenes frequently showing characters rotating on the spot and puppet like lip movements.  A few moments shine through in Book 4 but animation holds this game back in a big way.  Sound design is expressive and has a musical score that is well placed, fitting and emotional.
Performance is another huge problem.  I've played the game on a good rig (i7 2600K, GTX 680) with constant frame rate issues even on the lower settings.  I eventually had to play the game on medium and was around 40ish frames, but having to deal with a lot of tearing.  I also have access to a more powerful machine (i7 4820K, GTX 980) which struggled to keep 60 frames on high, let alone ultra.  The game is not bad looking, but it doesn't feel like it should tax systems anywhere near as heavily as it does, especially when it comes to lighting which causes huge framerate drops.
I wouldn't recommend the game unless you want to wrap up TLJ saga, but the final Book is disappointing and the ending not satisfying.  The animation and graphics performance problems also detract from the storytelling, but the weakest aspect is the poor and sometimes unnecessary light puzzle elements the game has.  If you have not played Life is Strange, consider playing that instead.

Anno 2205 contains all of the elements from previous Anno titles, improved upon and streamlined, whilst cutting out some of the annoying micro-management pains, and problems with giving the player the right information at the right time.  You still get the piecing together of the familiar production chain to make better stuff, to make better stuff, etc. all in aid of attracting higher taxed citizens to fund your off-world colonies.  It is still as complex as Anno 2070, but the interface provides the information you care about in such a way that it feels less frustrating trying to balance and juggle all of these things.  In Anno 2070 I almost never felt on top of the balancing act, but in Anno 2205 I very much feel this way... some of the time... then it all tips again (because I've started a new colony on the Moon, or built on a new island in the Arctic), and I need to re-balance the scales again.
It is a thoroughly enjoyable and satisfying, (not to mention beautiful), city building, planning, and resource management game suitable for players new to the series as well as veterans, however it does need a few hours invested into it to unlock all of the complexities and can seem very simplified at first glance.
Those giving it a bad review after just a couple of hours have quite clearly not spent enough time with the game to find out that YES, it does include storage, and YES it does include modular production plants, farms, power, mining etc. amongst all the other familiar systems from Anno 2070, for example. They are just hidden away under a couple of hours of gameplay in order to not completely overwhelm new players to the series... and personally I think this is a really great implementation of how to do a tutorial of sorts within the game itself whilst actually playing.
There are 3 different climates within Anno 2205, Temperate, Arctic, and the Moon.  Each climate is split into 3 zones, giving 9 total zones where it's possible to build cities/colonies, (your first in each climate is free, and you can purchase the others later on for huge sums of hard cash to add end-game longevity).  On first starting the game, you get to pick one of the Temperate zones by reviewing each different map, consisting of multiple islands and one special monument option for each.  I chose the zone which could get the electric dam monuments as I know how power generation in Anno can be a real killer of your profits (and it turns out this was a very wise choice!).
You are essentially walked through your journey by the familiar mission layout on the upper-left corner of the screen.  This contains all the information you need about your main task, and sub-tasks, without shoving a tutorial in your face if you want to just get on with your own thing.  I really love this and I think it is a good and smooth experience for familiar Anno players, as well as newbies.
It turns out that the Temperate zone tends to be your profitable zone early-game, and you need it to fund Arctic and Moon zones which sap all your cash until much later in development.
Now this is the point where I believe a lot of the negative reviews are coming from... it appears after the first couple of hours that there is over simplification to this version of Anno.  There doesn't appear to be storage, there doesn't appear to multiple add-ons to farms and production facilities to boost production etc. there doesn't appear to be island trading, (all islands in the same zone partially share resources), and there doesn't appear to be any fleet or combat!  At face value within the first hour or two, it seems like these things are gone... OH HOW WRONG FIRST IMPRESSIONS CAN BE!!
As soon as you start diving into the next few hours of this game, you soon start seeing all of these complexities showing up in their vastly more streamlined implementations.  The game turns into a mixture of familiar Anno, SimCity, and Command and Conquer, but every element fits perfectly into this strange cocktail.
Firstly, the resource counter only shows + or - numbers for production and demand.  This is a simplified view, yes, however a brief hover of the mouse over each resource shows the total in storage, and although we had to build more storage containers in Anno 2070, you soon realise how utterly pointless it is storing these goods... and all you really care about is producing just enough to meet your citizens' demands without overproducing so much that you're wasting maintenance money.  I really love this, and it takes the player's mindset away from meaninglessly hoarding tons and tons of resources to fine-management of your production chains.
Then you unlock the combat missions.  Basically you get told there is a crisis somewhere on the globe, you pick which difficulty you'd like to play the mission on, then you load into a totally new zone (map) where you sail around with your fleet blowing the living daylights out of any enemy that so much as gets in your way.  This combat feels very trivial at first, and it is.  You can lure enemies into mines, ambush them on their patrol paths, plan your route of attack to reach their weak points etc.  However, once you start doing these missions later on the harder difficulties, it actually does get quite a bit more challenging and you need to use all of these tactics to your advantage.  The other thing to note is that you soon realise clearing the entire map of enemies is a bit of a waste of time.  You end up taking all 3 sub-missions at the very start of the map, as well as turning on the elusively hidden feature to show all the resource buildings on the minimap (this should be shown by default imo).  These are your real objectives, as they are your source of the rare resources which you desperately need in the city building part of the game.
These rare resources are then taken out of the combat missions when you succeed and are used to upgrade your factories and production buildings!  I had first built several farms and power plants around thinking "This is way over simplified" and then upon doing this first mission and seeing how the modules worked I suddenly had a eureka moment where it all made sense suddenly! (and I immediately had to use the awesome new "move building" feature ;) haha).
Trading doesn't need to happen within the same zone/map in Anno 2205, (they share all resources and workforce automatically).  Trading starts to happen shortly after you colonise the Arctic in another zone and this is where your inter-dependencies come into play.  You will need to produce some goods in the Temperate zones to send to Arctic or Moon zones, and all variations therein.  This is necessary to increase the happiness of your populations to get them to upgrade to the next level (and then want even more difficult to obtain goods).
The trading happens much more fluidly than in Anno 2070 by having the player simply choose a trade good, the start and end of the route, and how much to send.  Simple but effective, and less annoying micromanagement.  Again, all the info is shown in one place easy to see and modify without deleting trade routes and worrying about boats being shot by pirates (*looks at Anno 2070*).
My overall verdict is very positive on this game.  The first couple of hours felt a little lacking, but it soon unlocked its full potential and now I'm off fending for myself, trying to balance my colonies against my main settlement, and looking forward to unlocking new zones to build in fresh, as well as work towards getting all of the monuments going.  Anno 2205 is a very cool and sleek new addition to the Anno series.

As with many of you, I have many fond memories about the previous two games in this saga, so I really tried to like this game.
But what have appealed to me the most in the previous games in the series are notably absent in Dreamfall Chapters: the characters.
This series felt so good because it had such strong, yet very believable characters like April and Zoe, who looked so different from typical super heroines of other games at that time.
We could easily relate to them because they were just ordinary people, like us, at the begining of their journey. Both of the games allowed us plenty of time to familiarize with the characters, and showed us many little details about their personal lives, like going to school, hanging out with a boyfriend, and etc before revealing to us how their fate would change all that in an instant, which made it much more believable and astonishing at the same time.
However, with Dreamfall Chapters everything has changed.
Now all the important characters start with a big mission from the start, and as the story picks up the pace, there's no time to spend on those mundane little details which are, however, crucial in making them really believable.
It feels especially bad for Kian, who had limited appearances in the previous game but has been given much bigger role in Dreamfall Chapters, though without sufficient details to make him feel as familiar to us as Zoe or April in the previous games.
And his story almost feels like the writer couldn't decide what to do with him, as his personality seems to fluctuate from one moment to another. In the previous game, he made various comments about how hot magical womens look in Marcuria, or saying that how deep an impression he had when he met April for the first time.
Even in an earlier episode of Dreamfall Chapters, he looked to be such a guy who has led an abstinent lifestyle his whole life and he just begins to open up his eyes to the other sex, when he  awkwardly allows himself to be warmed up to Enu, for instance.
But only a moment later, he just declares he's a gay so he doesn't feel anything about women at all.
Earlier on, he said he doesn't drink at all, and later remarked that beer was not so bad. And in the final episode, he's going about commenting how he can't stand a Northern wine brand compared to ones at home, as if he was some kind of a somelier himself.
At the beginning, he was presented as a serious, or even a blunt kind of a person, which is quite understandable considering his supposed background. But too many times, his character is abused to fill mandatory share of witty remarks which players might expect from an adventure game. But unfortunately, this series isn't The Monkey Island, and him not Guybrush Threepwood (or April Ryan, for that matter, as she had quite a few hilarious lines in TLJ).
It's very unfortunate that we have such a fluctuating and underdeveloped character as one of the main protagonist in this game, as he deprives us much time we could spend enjoying more familiar characters, like Zoe or even Crow, and he's not alone in that regard because they have introduced many other new characters in Dreamfall Chapters, who feel even more shallow and underdeveloped than the character of Kian.
Enu, for example, seemed she could become one of the more memorable characters in the series, but her potential completely wasted as the story moves on. The same can be said of the most other characters as well, as Dreamfall Chapters is filled with such cheap stereo types, like a girl who have a crush with the one who saved her, or a caricature of Hitler, for instance.
Even those intriguing characters from the previous games turned into cardboard villains in Dreamfall Chapters, like Brian Westhouse suddenly starting to play a Sith Lord impersonation (and with that signature 'bad guy' mask, and force choke ability), or Helena Chang becoming a typical 'mad scientist' we've already seen gazillion times in movies or other games.
A few characters which could have been memorable, like Shitbot, Bip, or even Mira are quickly swept aside after their brief appearances, probably to make rooms for what developers thought to be more important, like some out of place political agenda, for instance.
You will keep hearing extremely exaggerated and obviously ridiculous racial hate speeches from a caricature character of Hitler all through the game, until thankfully he burns himself out in the last episode.
And a cold blooded warrior in a semi-Medieval fantasy world suddenly reveals his most liberal mind for the one who wanted to kill so badly, once the target of his revenge begins a long tirade about how it is to live as a sexual minority.
Probably to emphasize the importance of social diversity, people in a magical world of Marcuria show more ethnic diversity than that of modern European countries, but somehow they can't stand to live with those have blue skins. It makes them even more unbelievable as their Japanese, German, or many such contemporary regional names, as the developers decided to name them after Kickstarter backers, apparently.
Granted, the plot of Dreamfall Chapters is quite complex compared to others, as it involves travelling across the multiverse and even shaping the reality itself by dreaming. But without strong characters to move the story going, and without sufficient attention to details, it simply feels like a cheap sci-fi comic from an artist with too big an ambition, and not enough skill to realize it. (And perhaps, the notably bad quality of animations and, in some cases, that of graphical effects have contributed much to that feeling.)
Understandably, the high points in Dreamfall Chapters, at least for me, were those moments when I could get a glimpse of old, familiar characters like Crow, April, or even Wonkers.
Thinking about those beloved characters made me realize that, however may I have been disappointed in Dreamfall Chapters, it's probably because I had such high hopes for the sequel of such a great series - a series which had so many memorable moments which haven't faded a bit, even with the disaster of this game.
And it also reminded me that how hard they must have worked to create those games, and even in the times of financial difficulties, how they remembered the promise they made, to continue and conclude the story of April and Zoe someday. And actually kept their words.
For that, I really feel grateful for all who have been involved in making of this series. Even though I'm utterly disappointed what it became in the end, I'm now fully aware all my fond memories of the series wouldn't have existed without their efforts.
I suppose I'll play TLJ and DF again someday, when the bad taste DFC has left me fades away. And then, I'll probably stop playing at what I believe to be the emotional climax of the series, which was the moment when Zoe meets Faith in TLJ: Dreamfall. And when the credit rolls, I'll try to pretend I didn't know how the story ends and Zoe and April had so much interesting journey left in them beyonds that big cliff hanger.
