The game was alright overall, but it's a poor man's Arkham game. The story of the main game was interesting and the art style is fantastic, but the gameplay and combat system actually got quite annoying near the end, when trying to get all the collectables.
Part of the problem is the level design which is a non-obvious corridor, where areas are separated by a multitude of sluice-gates, elevators, decontamination rooms, etc. It's constant delaying and unnecessary gratuituous animations which get boring rather quick. It takes a very long time to navigate between areas and respawning mobs often prevent you from leaving before you dealt with them, even though you have nothing else to gain from killing them. Once I got the final secret collectible, it took me something like 20 minutes to get to the area where you trigger the final boss encoounter.
Unlike the Arkham games where collecting additional content is enjoyable and adds to the experience, the design of the levels actually takes enjoyment away. I would recommend doing a story driven run and avoiding backtracking for collectables and challenges.
The music is OK on it's own, but doesn't fill inspired as much as the art style and often doesn't really fit the environemt or add much to the game.
The PC port is pretty bad. You pretty much need a controller, as all the button prompts are laid out for a 360 pad. It's much worse than the first game which you could play with KB/Mouse perfectly fine. The game runs well and stable, but it's absolutely impossible to tab out. You need to trigger an automatic save, which often happens between areas, but isn't reliable, and quit the game.
Lastly, something that bugged me personally. You frequently either fight or partner up with humnoid characters. They have about 3 phrases each on average and will keep shouting them non-stop. Gets seriously annoying.

The Collider is an exhilerating Indie title in which you navigate through a tunnel at an increasing speed while trying to make it through the same type of obstacle -- the infamous rotating vertical disc with a hole in it. Spooky.
If you played Rayman 3: Hoodlum Havoc and partook in the Missile Command minigame, this should feel familiar to you. You're essentially guiding a camera through a series of conveniently placed rotating discs with holes in them. The holes differ in size and shape, which I find to be challenging yet rewarding. As time progresses, the speed at which you're zooming by increases exponentially with each interval (every time the counter reaches 100, to be exact). If you're appreciative of pretty colors, you're in for quite the treat here -- there are a
of them.
The soundtrack in the game is an upbeat electronic motivator. It makes the entire experience a bit more exciting, though it does get old as you continue playing. Hearing the same song over and over again typically doesn't bode well if it doesn't resonate with its listener, surprisingly enough. Still, though -- it's a tune I certainly wanted to dance to at one point.
If you're looking for a euphoric graphical experience, you've come to the wrong place. You can see for yourself in the screenshots provided on the game's store page.
The only indication that you're finished with the game would have to be the achievements. I'm not too keen on my champion status (the game includes a leaderboard), and as such, the game is finished for me once I've acquired all of the achievements available for me to earn.
The only issue I've found within the game is that at a certain point, your crosshair is simply too large. I often found myself struggling to see where the hole was because of it. It's easily remedied by proper peripheral vision, though.
Definitely worth the price. I bought it while it was on sale for a few cents, I'd advise you to do the same.
Oh, and don't blink.

Basically they did a lot of things.. um, not wrong, but poorly, but for what it is, and that's pretty unique nowadays, I still recommend it. I love playing city builder and simulation games. My review is totally biased because of that. I also don't write reviews very often so I'll try to keep this short but I'll probably fail
My view on this game: It feels like a megablox-style cousin to Banished, which I love both for and in spite of all its flaws.
You start by choosing a randomly generated map, then placing your castle keep, off of which you build roads. You can only build your other buildings within proximity to these roads, and you can only place buildings when you have enough materials to build them. There is no 'place it now, pause it until you can afford it' like in Banished. You cannot pre-plan your city in-game.
Your castle keep has 3 'advisors'. Agricultural, Social (or something like that), and MIlitary. The first two don't really tell you anything your UI can't tell you. 'Your people are starving! We need more food!" and "If we make the villagers happier, we can raise our taxes!". I was expecting the advisors to be a little more tutorial-like, especially since there's a setting to turn them off. BUT the final advisor, the military one...she is actually useful for foreshadowing of attacks.
Because I play games like this often, I roughly knew what I was doing in terms of what I needed to  build and stuff. But I admit I was not prepared for the attacks or illnesses, and suffered for it. If you are a complete newbie to city building games, this may be a little frustrating at first due to its lack of hand holding.
But since it's so new, it has a very quick 'endgame', so it is easy to start over and try again and see if you can get ballistae built before the first dragon appears, or a wall or two up with archers before vikings come by sea.
The only reason i'm not still playing it right now is because I got to year 62 on my first city in one sitting and need a break!
SUMMARY:
Pros - Fun graphics, appropriate challenge balance, logical villager pathing (unlike Banished), amusing name generator (I've been following a villager named Fearjoey for about 20 years now since I know which farm he works at), active developers, and clear promise for the future of the game. I feel that the price of $9.99 is fully appropriate for what the game is right now.
Cons - no tutorial for new players, a few non-game-breaking bugs (to be expected), no way to pin a certain villager's info to the screen if you want to follow them around (but that's probably just my years of RollerCoaster Tycoon and now Banished talking), and MOST IMPORTANTLY no way to pre-plan the city.
Overall I'd recommend getting it if you like these kinds of games! It's already very well done and it can only get better from here. I think it has a lot of replayability and I look forward to losing 19 more villagers to plague when my hospital only needs 4 more wood transported to finish construction.

First things first, I LOVE the art design of the whole game, they're really masters when it comes to imaging how Dracula Castle would look like, sound its also very good, music its good, visually its ok too.
Now for a Castlevania game it lacks a lot from other games, including handheld versions (GBA/NDS). Game lacks collectibles, gear to improve you status, weapons, etc
Gameplay its ok but having so many attack combos can be too overwhelming, most of the time you'll use only use 2 or 3 combos for the whip and sword, I barely used the shadow claws (except when required by the game). It might be my bad memory but I found myself checking too many times how to make that cool looking combo I just unlocked and not so much time using it cause you can beat the game without it.
Controls are fine but a few times they can get very frustrating, camera its also a bit frustrating since there is no way to lock your attacks to an enemy and the game will try to "auto aim" your attacks to the closest enemy but always the one you don't mean to attack.
Collectibles are a bit boring, scrolls that try to complete the story and tell you parts of it that are not currently happening in game. You (Dracula) feel like the less powerful Dracula from the saga and the stealth sections of the game make no sense for a Castlevania game.
Overall its a good game, not so much a good Castlevania. Definitely an improvement over the first LoS.
I'll only recommend it if you don't mind a short game with almost no replay value and very little exploration like in past Castlevania games and you are a "true" Castlevania Fan

This was my most anticipated game of 2014 and it lived up to everything I expected and more. Castlevania games have always been good gameplay wise and I've been playing them since the originals on the NES. While the others Castlevanias games were great in there own right, Lords of Shadow is the first in the series to actually attempt and succeed at providing a cohesive narrative about your characters journey and motivations outside of a simple I'm a Belmont and it's my destiny kind of thing which is what the older titles relied on.
As for the game itself it delivered on just about all aspects graphics are amazing, the composer Oscar, Araujo provided an excellent soundtrack. The game is a good length and challenging enough it's also open ended so you can backtrack to previous areas unlock new abilities and upgrades you may have missed initially. Combat is on point, there are a few different weapons you can use and you can level them up to unlock new moves and abilities so it never gets old.
But most of all I enjoyed watching Gabriel Belmont's journey and how he struggles with being an immortal. Who at this point in time wishes for nothing more but to find a means to end his own life. Due to the lost of loved ones over the span of centuries and the turn of events that has made him the Lord of Shadow he never really wanted to be.

Very cool, quite fun. I'm glad that they're still improving it, as there are a few minor issues here and there. I find this to be superior to the usual comparisons due to the art style, the theme, the pacing, and the overall variation. The gameplay may become a little repetitive over time, but there's enough diversity if you know where to look for it. The sense of progression isn't as satisfying as other games, however. Because there's no sense of starting up from nowhere, attaching yourself to your first building, etc. Starbound may not feel as homely as games like Terraria or Minecraft.
There's barely any grind, all of the grind ends pretty quickly at the beginning of the game. You'll be getting lots of rare ore quickly even on survival mode. There's no creative mode, but the casual mode accentuates how easy the game can be so much that you'll probably feel like you're almost in a creative mode. I haven't taken my time to build anything complex, but I believe I'll build a base sometime in the future.
I haven't had many encounters on the biggest multiplayer server I found. There are few servers, and the majority of them are empty. There's no built-in server list, so you'll have to look for servers on the internet. From what I noticed, multiplayer is extremely unstable now, and there are even instances of people getting their character files corrupt (the server I played on has a client that backs your characters up before you play in case that happens). There's no mechanism against griefers, so modders had to circumvent it by making a way of claiming and backing up worlds in a specific server. Thankfully, mods function properly with servers.
It's a good-quality game, but I believe there's a long way to go for this to remain interesting after a long time. Sadly, Terraria is more popular, and I guess the multiplayer for them is better as well. I still plan on sticking with this game and checking on it whenever it updates — they do update regularly. If you enjoy this type of game and Terraria doesn't seem your style, I'd recommend Starbound, most definitely.

One of the great things about this game is it's diverse cast of characters who are all fleshed out and charming (or hateable) This is what got me to play the game. One of the games protagonists (they are three, just like D:TLJ) is Kian, in book 3 it's revealed he's gay. This is important to me as a Pansexual Woman. Very rarely do games give you Queer protsgonists unless it's a dating sim or RPG with LIs. It's normally something you opt into. You cannot opt in Kian's gayness. A straight gamer cannot deny Kian is gay no matter how hard they try. (For some of you this may be a detractor  but this is my steam review, write your own if you're that homophobic) Should the player want to, you can get close to Lihko (voice wonderfully by Dave Fennoy) The relationship between these two can build from distrust and hatred to grudging respect to admiration and friends. I did. I was interested to see where Kian and Lihko's relationship would go. Lihko reveals he's gay in chapter 4 and we leave Kian and Lihko trusting and caring about eachother deeply.
There was the undeniable undercurrent of romantic interest. I was exicted. Even with big name games like Dragon Age and Fallout 4 it's still very rare to see Same gender romances in games.
Lets talk about Anna, Anna is brought into chapter 2 as a sort of love interest for Kian, obviously this cannot happen. He's gay. He states this quite a few times (earlier on subltly, later on more obviously) Anna is revealed to be more in love with the idea of Kian than anything else. But you can kiss her. Three times. (one is forced on you which, ugh)
So what of Lihko? Kian's actual love interest? Well I got him (and Enu!) in chapter 5 alive and well. So, Kian goes to talk to Lihko and...bro-zones him. Yes all that romantic buildup and it ends in queerbaiting.
Never thought I'd be queerbaiting by two canonically gay characters but. Here we are.
Then Lihko ♥♥♥♥s off 3 hours only returning in the end and epilogue but you get to spent time with the unlikable Anna, even though Lihko is more trusted and a bigger character.
Dreamfall Chapters fails at the last hurdle as a choice based game, just like Life is Strange and every TellTale game before it makes your choices meaningless?
Save Falk Friedman's life? You get a throwaway line. Break up with Reza? He's there for you anyway. Avoid releasing too much information to your therapist? Doesn't matter. Keep Anna at an arms length? She still won't take a hint. Keep Lihko and Enu alive? They are they sure, but Anna replaces Lihko's role regardless.♥♥♥♥♥♥Enu off bigtime? She'll still tearfully hug you goodbye. Pursue your relationship with Lihko? Not even a chaste kiss.

As I was just entering my first year in College, and working my first job as a barista; I began to develop a deep sense of searching. Searching for deeper meaning, and adventure. During this transition I found Dreamfall The Longest Journey, and fell in love with everything, the music, the imagery, the story, it all captivated me and even felt like a symbolic dialogue to my life's journey. I can't express enough how life changing this game was. Naturally, I became a supporter of Dreamfall Chapters.
I was so passionate about this series, that I dropped $135 of support through Kickstarter, during a very challenging time in my life. I had left my dead end job, was in my second year of marriage, just had a baby girl named Faith, and was buried in debt. I literally maxed my last credit card out on this Kickstarter campaign. Now, this may sound foolish to many: it even sounds foolish to me. However, this was about more than getting an amazing game or buying groceries next week. This was about changing the entertainment industry. This was about encouraging the creation of beautiful art, and deep ideas for the mainstream. I always felt there was a vast void of quality games (or quality anything). Quality games seek to be story tellers, they seek to be teachers, they seek to inspire a person to pursue their created destiny. When you leave a Dreamfall experience, you come out on the other end changed. So to me, this was joining a movement, and taking a leap of faith that there is something better ahead.
I can gladly say my story has ended well. I was able to pay for my groceries that week and ended up on a new career course that has taken me to new fantastic heights. So here I am a little more than 3 years later, in a beautiful home on an acre of land in one of the wealthiest cities in my state, and a second daughter named Hope. Now, to play this masterpiece all the way through.
Thank you, Red Thread "For not underestimating your audience"

I wrote a review a while back, saying this game was alright, and to only buy it if you had a G27, or any other simulation grade wheel. Now, this new update changes it, and now, buy it if you really like off road racing with trucks.
First off, this game went through a massive overhaul to DX11, so that is a nice thing to see. Updates to support Mac and Linux came through, and several other bugs were ironed out. However, there are still bugs in this game. I will explain them a little more going through this.
New tracks were added, old ones overhauled to reflect new objects in the game, and new vehicles came out. Along side the Stadium Super Truck (SST), Pro4 and Pro2 trucks, ProLite Karts, and AWD Hatchback, there is a 4WD Monster Truck, known as the Ruckus, and a 4WD Crawler. Another bug is that I can't find old skins that were in the previous version of the game. Something else that needs to be changed.
More camera options also came out for this game, not only allowing you to be in first person view, and Following camera view, there's also a rotate camera, drone camera, and a Larry Camera, for walking and stuff. As Larry, you can wash things, which is pretty neato, but the way he holds it looks a bit...suggestive. Viewmodel placement in the next update would be nice.
Lastly, and I've been holding out for this, track creation! This is by far my favorite part of the update. It is somewhat similar to the track creator for Mx Vs Atv Unleashed, but somethings that need to be added is an Undo button, which the developer said he will add in sometime. When saving a level, the game freezed for me. Probably because I have this game not on my boot drive, and my OS drive, where the track files are kept (probably?), is full, and I can't continue on. A option to select a folder to store track files would be nice, or just default it to the Documents Folder, which you can move to a separate drive.
To add, Steam Workshop integration is also here, allowing you to share and download tracks with others in the community, and Multiplayer, however, with the amount of people who play this game, I don't see that coming into effect yet.
A pretty good game, all coming from 1 person. This is a cool little project that he/she is doing, and by buying the game, can continue that dream, making this game look good on their resume, and hopefully land their dream job at a large company, or build up their own company.
7/10 Amazing game, but some features still need to come and bugs need to be ironed out.

Amazing.
This game makes you feel like you're actually in an off-road trophy truck. I'm not kidding, the force feedback is amazing. Of course, if you don't have a FFB wheel, it's not entirely the same, but do not pass up this amazing game.
Sure, there is no AI. There is no multiplayer (which I will explain more later on), but just the single player experience alone is enough for me to pour plenty of hours into this game.
Many people in the community hub and even the reviews have complained about graphics.
Graphics, in my opinion, do not make or break a game for me. Do they make a game look better? Sure. Do they hinder my gaming experience? No. Maybe it's just me, but when I play a video game it's usually not one thing that can make it or break it for me. I'll use GTA V for an example: I love the graphics in that game. The sunsets are beautiful. But that's not the whole game. The game has so many other features that it's almost overwhelming. So, back to my point, graphics should not ruin an entire game for somebody. It might be because I grew up with old Nintendos in the house, but I've never seen graphics as a problem. And to be honest, the graphics in this game do not look all that bad; to me they look pretty professional.
I can't wait for people to start raging on me for saying that graphics don't matter.
Questions:
I have a few questions I would like to be answered, if possible.
Will there actually be any multiplayer or AI implemented into the game at some point in the future? I understand if not; like I said, still an amazing game. Even local multiplayer, or just some simple AI in the game would be nice. If not; no problem. I understand Devotid Media is a one-dev team (or so I've seen, correct me if I'm wrong), and it would be quite the amount of work to have to put into the game to implement these features.
Another question: will there be more vehicles? The current fleet is awesome on it's own, and I'm sure modding in new models is/will be a possibility, but developer-made vehicles are well-tested and professional.
An amazing simulator that I will be replaying plenty of times. Also, huge props to the developer (whose name I cannot recall) for making a game of this size and quality. Sorry for the wall of text, but this is a game I will be playing over, and over, and over.

Started off by watching a bunch of tutorials online, which helped immensely in the long run, and started making random crap, just to mess around.  Then I started the campaign, and I had no idea what I was doing, so I started spawning in several planes to make an Air Force, which then failed me miserably.  I then decided to make ships that could carry way too many resources than necessary, and had missiles and AA guns on it only, and that was my main battleship for the longest time.  I appropriately named it the Scavenger, and moved on to make another air fleet, consisting of several vintage WWII aircraft.
After a long and decisive battle with a Deepwater Guard Airship, I ended up losing all my planes, and I had to retreat to my slow♥♥♥♥♥Scavenger, which I was attempting to transport to the Warzone.  At the time, I never undershoot what it meant to pull all my forces out of play, so I would idiotically wait onboard the scavenger, till it finally reached the Gantry I had captured in the previous battle, and there the airship flew, too high for me to hijack, which was my tactic for the longest time, and still is.  After accumulating more air forces and retrofitting P-51s with laser guided missiles, I engaged the airship.
After what seemed like a few minutes, the airship fell to the ocean, and I hijacked it and destroyed every last component on the damn airship.  I scrapped the ship and used the reassures to make a tall spotting tower, which aided me in discovering where I actually was on the map.
After numerous engagements, I set my sight on what I thought was a military land installation, and I attacked with everything I had.  Long story short, I lost almost all my P-51s (which all crashed into the ground on their own, because I assume the AIs got drunk) to find out it was just a fishing village.  Go figure.
After many more days of planning and attacking, I finally beat the Deepwater Guard (after making a carrier and War Ship), and decided to make the best and safest headquarters for my nation.  It took me forever, but I was satisfyingly awesome to walk around the halls of my very own Capitol in the end, with the flags of my nation flying proudly overhead,
Long story short, this game has almost infinite possibilities when it comes to just doing whatever the hell you want.  I haven't even scratched the surface of it all yet, and it's exciting to figure out how to make new things, like lasers (which I actually don't know how to make yet), or even CRAM Cannons (Because Advanced Cannons are life).  I would definitely recommend this to anyone willing to learn how to play it, because it does have a huge learning curve, but that's not entirely bad, in fact, it's pretty much a part of life.  So consider this game to be a fun, yet important life lesson.
I would play this for as long as I could, if life altogether would allow me to.

+The visuals are amazing, and perfectly 80s. I kept slowing down just to watch a section of terrain roll past, and the opening cinematic had a great 80s-noire feel to it. I half expected the car to ask me if I was a bad enough dude to save the girlfriend.

-There is literally nothing to do in this game but drive. The only obstacles are turns and jumps, and because of how terrible the controls and handling are these obstacles will usually end the game.
-The car handles like a brick on crisco. While holding forward it shimmies left and right for no reason, even on straightaways. While drifting (the only other control in the game) the tires' friction spikes and drops randomly, meaning you need to mash left and right to avoid slamming into a wall.
- Touching a wall at all is like running headfirst into a tree. There's no grinding around a curve, you just get slammed to a stop and, usually, turned around. At one point my car flipped on its side, and the game decided that was my new road. I was only able to drive straight up into the air until the meter dropped and the game ended.
- There's no validation on the randomly-generated road. A jump can spawn that fires you directly into the wall, at which point you get to choose whether you hit the barricade and lose or take the jump and lose.
The game is, unfortunately, not fun. It looks and sounds awesome, but the gameplay designer seriously dropped the ball here. I understand it wasn't meant to be a game, just an "aesthetic concept", but the bugs and shoddy controls ruin the experience completely.

Anno 2205 brings a lot of change to the Anno franchise. Unfortunately not all of them have been thought through.
Let me start with some good changes: The economy system has been changed. Inside a "sector" the need of establishing trade routes has been removed. Power, build force and resources are automatically transferred between different islands. However the concept of trade routes is not gone entirely. It has been shifted to the "world view", where you can exchange needed resources between sectors.
Also, thanks to the fact that the game now displays resource and goods output per building and also per sector, it has become a lot easier to create such routes.
A lot of reviews claim that the system of "storage" on an island/sector is gone. This is not true. Overproduction is still being sent to the warehouse, and you can still monitor it by hovering your mouse over the goods item in the sector overview (found in the lower left corner of your Hud in sector view). It will still fullfill the needs of your residents if the sector output drops to the negative. However, if you have negative output and build new production lines to fullfill that need, it will increase resident satisfaction instantly, instead of slowly charging up like in the previous games.
What is gone from the game is the ability to load overproduction onto your ship at will (you still do this for missions). I am also still searching for a per sector breakdowm of my inhabitants and, more importantly, free living space. This, among other function the Anno regular might be used to, seems to be either removed or tied to one of those final monument structures that I have yet to reach.
[edit] ScoobyDoomyDoom mentioned in a comment that you can find your population statistics hidden behind the little "people" button next to the minimap.[/edit]
[edit] I have encountered a very annoying bug with the public needs buildings and the "move structure" feature. Whenever I move resident buildings in order to optimize public needs output, to reduce the amount of required public structures, the game will calculate the new layout wrong and assign needs deficits when there is actually a huge overproduction. Strangely enough, this bug will sometimes fix itself by closing the game and restarting the map. It is quite annoying however to have 150.000 Investors move out because of a lack of mobility even after creating a +27 surplus around them, with sufficient road connections. Especially when this means your income suddenly takes a death plunge.[/edit]
Different sectors
Right now there exist 3: Temperate, arcitc and lunar. Arctic and lunar have special requirements to their building sceme, and Lunar buildings cost an arm and a leg to build, but other than that they mostly add some visual difference rather than gameplay ones. Your population in temperate regions mostly provides the money for your exploits in the other two sectors, so you go back once in a while to up population. Meanwhile population in the other two sectors is only important to increase your spaceport level (to be able to transport goods back to your home region).
Modules
This is probably the best addition yet. For every production building you can make meaningful adjustments in order to increase productivity or reduce maintainance. Not only that, but in different sectors different modules make more sense. Rule of thumb: upgrading a farm is cheaper and puts less strain on your energy/income than building a second farm. It also takes up less space. And for those mountain and shore spots it is absolutely neccesary in order to get the best out of them.
Now to the absolute negative... combat.
I am not sure what to say about it, so here a brief description: Instead of waging war with concurring factions in your own sector the game has a set of crisis sectors where you can duke it out with a preset fleet of ships that can be upgraded and will be expanded as your population grows. The gameplay seems like a simple Dawn of War 2 Clone, with varying but similar objectives. So far so boring for someone who came to Anno after playing RTS for years.
The AI is horrible. Ships patrol in preset sectors, you get too close they stick to you like glue until you run away far enough. The games trickle down to "kill those five ships, retreat, repair, kill those four ships, retreat, repair" while finding the best route to your objective. In order to increase the difficulty the amount of ships in the sector is simply raised, to the point where you are tiptoeing trough a minefield on hardes settings. Tedious, but not in the slightest challenging.
Variation? No. There are three or four scenarios for each region, and they will start repeating soon. by repeating I mean very same map with opponents in the very same spot. The only reason to do this is to get rare materials that can be used to upgrade your buildings. It could have been a smartphone app. Woud have had more replay value than the app they actually released, if not by much.
Compared to the excellent combat system in 1404 and the still very god combat system in 2070 this is a joke, and a direct insult to my intelligence.
The crowning touches is that the only online activity in this game are council votings and trading on the online market.
If Ubisoft wants a positve review they will need to address:
The combat system, best you throw it out and do it anew.
Ship building, I want to build my fleet myself. And I like my fleets big.
Multiplayer, and by that I mean both coop and competetive
[edit] According to Ubisoft, multiplayer is to follow soon(tm). There is no information yet on how exactly this is to work, though.[/edit]
If you want to pull Anno out of the garbage before the playerbase vanishes you better get those done. Not neccesarily quickly, but in a well polished and professional manner. Playable. Enjoyable.
[edit] Minoes claimed that if you were looking for a singleplayer economy building game and did not care about the military part, you could safely buy the game. I felt that I had to put up a clarification for people like him: Yes, the economy part is done well. No it does not make the game a safe deal.
The problem is the replay value. The average player will be hitting the last technologies after 15 hours of gameplay. Adding the sector projects you gain roughly 20 hours of progressive gameplay. Half of that if you build up a strong economy from the start and do not take up as much time waiting to unlock sectors from other corporations.
After that there is pretty much nothing to do other than prettying up your settlement or perfecting your goods chains. The 9 sectors currently ingame are pre made with pre made main and side missions and repetetive mini-quests. This might be great for casual players and people going for the perfect pretty city. But even that only became interesting in the prequels because the random islands and their different properties spiced things up.
Okay, 10 to 20 hours sounds promising to some, but in the prequels you spent the same amount of time on your average random map, with always changing challenges and opportunities (some which you could pick, some which the map predefined), with a singleplayer campaign and single missions still on top of that. And (I know I am repeating myself) multiplayer support to play together or against each other.[/edit]

A cash in on the franchise one more time.
Awful story that has ruined the heart of Castlevania as a game franchise. Decent graphics and responsive gameplay, but heavily mired by a flawed combat system. Still perhaps worth getting if on sale for the mindless smash enemies combat. Great voice acting from the main actors, but less should have been put in to the voice acting and instead spent on developing a real story that respects the franchise mythology. Big thumbs up, the scourge of modern games, QTE's, can be disabled permanently.
Awful to put it simply, it's a train wreck. Castevania is at its heart a conquer the castle and kill Dracula game, this "re-origin" story series has just wrecked that with taking away everything that is Castlevania in exchange for trying to dramatise the backstory of Dracula to make him a tragic hero; with an overwhelming judeo-christian mythology shoehorned in to dominate the mythological aspects whereas previously the series was only very loosely tied to any particular mythology. The whole story was just 'Ugh, it's the devil is the bad guy story, how original...push that religion on us even more'.We are meant to believe the city is built on the ruins of Castlevania (dont even get me started on that nuke effect taht was shown large enough it would have destroyed several ENTIRE EUROPEAN COUNTRIES), and the devils kids would use that spot to try bringing about their dad's return...ofcourse. Use the site your ancient enemy is at his most powerful as your base of operations.....yep, perfect sense.
Major plot holes exist *spoiler* e.g. Zobek could have read Drac's mind to discover his deception unless he lost his memories, but Zobek couldnt realise that his lieutenant had been replaced by Alucard by, oh I dont know...reading his thoughts....yeah, sure. I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
The deal with Castlevania itself is never really clarified, is the castle real and split off from the modern era dimension, or just a figment of Drac's fragmented mind....Major problems arise with the story regardless of which it is.
The story is jsut a cavalcade of bad ideas.
Tight controls that function decently for getting around and in combat. Probably the aspect of the game that is most positive. The grappling aspects are a disappointment, see that you can only use fixed grapple points to get around, instead of simply making anything that is like a ledge able to be hung from, and the game is loaded with invisible walls which is hugely disappointing for exploration. The game is heavily walled in and you will find that you are limited to very selective above street level areas, and street level, if you want to go explore over the rooftops of the city like some real badass vampire god, forget it, go buy a copy of Batman arkham city, a game which did city exploration properly.
The combat is broken down into mobs using 3 types of attacks: range, melee blockable, and melee/range unblockable.
You have 3 weapons, a whip, sword adn claws. All with varying utility, the whip is a mid range weapon that is usable for building up 'focus' which when you hit 100% then attacking enemies will cause them to drop little gems that can be absorbed for magic power for your sword or claws, this only works with the whip though so you will spend a lot of time using it. Void sword burns magic and leeches life on hit, while the claws also burn magic but deal high damage and destroying shields and armour. The shields and armour♥♥♥♥♥♥was a terrible implementation, mobs can stand there blocking forever if you dont destroy the shield or armour, forcing you to use the real core combat mechanic, "timed counters" where you hit L2 at the right time in their swing to block an attack and stun them for a second and smash away, this builds huge focus so you can get your claws powered up to break the shields, alternateively you can somersault over attacking monsters and smack them in the back, whatever works. Unfortunately unless you are good at it, you are ♥♥♥♥ed, having spent significant time playing dark souls it was♥♥♥♥♥♥easy to time compared to parries in DS, but often if you are using the void sword or claws the actual enemy attacks get obscured by the flashy animations of the glowing weapons that you dont see them, this is a♥♥♥♥♥♥implementation really forcing play where you dont really engage upclose with magic weapons you mainly use a couple of specific moves then go back to the whip.
There is though a mechanic of "unblockable attacks", which is a huge flaw in the combat and you are forced to dodge, these attacks are indicated, but seems like lazy design, especially when you come to the bosses who their attacks are pretty much all unblockables or range attacks other than usually 1 blockable melee attack, this menas you can spend boss fights frustrated and magic starved as the range attacks keep you away, and the unblockables are chained so often the fight is 30 seconds of dodging and waiting to get one block and some melee attacks, absorb some magic and hit them a couple times for reasonable damage as the whip does ♥♥♥♥ all. In this way the game lends itself to securing really only a couple of the actual skills for the sword and claws to 'gg no re' your way through the game, namely: Whirlwind for the Void Sword, and Flame Claws for the Chaos Claws. Both expensive to use but when you see them in action it's pretty much a no brainer to use them. You may simply discover the other method which is boss cheese and basically forces you to pop relics such as ensnared demon then go crazy with the inifnite magic while timer counts down (spam those flame claw attacks, for real, ~300 damage per hit on everything), then when it runs out pop the dragon emblem and finish the boss off, takes about 30secs per boss fight, even on PoD difficulty and is almost zero effort (you may have to use the void sword to freeze bosses to spam them hard with the claws).
Skipping combat and bypassing trash is often impossible, as pretty much every enemy has some sort of range attack intended to knock you off a hang point if you try to grapple away. Some monsters (the wraith type guys at the end msotly) have ridiculous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t attacks that you cannot do anythign to avoid and hit extremelyhard, as noted, the wraiths, tey have a lightning attack that will hit you from 50 metres away, is practically instant hit and dodging it not really possible as by the time you see it, it is hitting you, and there is no way to defend against it other than popping the sword or claws shield magic. As these creatures fight in packs of 4-6 generally, you can imagine, Drac at max HP has about 300 hp, and lightning hit's for 40 each time....6 of them will kill you in about 3 secs, faster than you can close the distance to get to them sometimes....
Also, finally, the camera is terrible, even with "combat assisted", it is awful and seems like it tries to blind spot enemies, and the trash monster scripts seem they are intent on getting behind the camera when they can to hit you in the back. This because truly frstrating when their seems to be no 'free camera' even when assist is off and the camera constantly tries to centre in ways that make no sense and you often spend as much time trying to correct the camera so you can see wtf is happening as actually paying attention.
Revelations has good puzzles, but disappointingly cruel end boss fight due to endless unblockable attacks and mechanics that dont work with the camera (teleporting behind and unblockable charge).
Is the game worth buying? Not at full price, it seems like an effort to just milk some more money out of the Castlevania fans who are holding on to hope that each release will be the next Symphony of the Night. Something which the LoD series just hasnt been anything near, ultimately this game is completely forgettable.

To preface: I came into this game off the expectations of the first Lords of Shadow, which I found to be one of the most worthwhile plays of the generation, marred only by the disconnect between cut-scene plot and loading screen plot (the former I chose to ignore for the much greater depth and intrigue of the latter). The way the last game ended, the trailer involving the castle siege, the unique universe and artistic style the game takes place in; how could they go wrong?
And at first, it seemed like they'd made another great game (just like the first, which also came out to muted-to-mediocre reception but would prove to be a stellar experience). Even beyond the introduction sequence, with the lackluster stealth, linearity and meagerness of the city, it stilled promised to be much more, at least to me.
For as long as I could, I held onto the concept that, at worst, it could be a poorly executed great concept; it kept sliding further and further away from that great concept ideal, to be expected of something coming from such a high plateu with too much expectation; a fault of my own if anything.
What was dreadful about this game, however, was not its inability to match the former game's great expectations: it was unbelievably poor direction the plot lurches towards the mid-to-end of the game. In almost complete contrast to Lords of Shadow, which started off slow, picked up speed and took off into orbit: this game started off in orbit, slowed down and instead of just falling to the ground, somehow fell into a wormhole that took it straight into the jaws of a black hole where it went full-on Event Horizon.
Give this game a massive miss; play the first and imagine what could have been, don't make the mistake that I did and assume the reviews were just a repeat of the first on release, of fans of Castlevania of old and this game just didn't live up to their rose-tinted rememberance of easiers times, and those who refused to do anything but accuse it of being a God of War clone, when it was so much more.
In short, this game represents a tragedy in what could have been, of which I am saddened to have been a part of.

After sinking 5 hours into the game immediatly after buying it, I can honestly say that this game has a insane amount of potential to become one of my favorites. With that said thoug the game so far does have is fair share of issues (though some of them are might just be my opinion)
1. The game early on run's like a dream, but once you get above 150 peasants the game starts to stutter (Though I don't believe its a problem on my end seeing as my pc will run much more graphically intense games just fine) The stutter doesnt reach any unplayable state in any regard, but it does become really distracting close to 300 citizens
2. The Viking attacks seem Overpowered (at least to me) in the sense that the archer towers arent accurate enough to consitently kill the smaller groups (especially later on when your forced to fight 6 or 7 at a time), and the ballista is only really useful when fighting the ogres or the dragons that'll pop up from time to time. Now the accuracy problem with archers can be solved with sheer numbers, but the amount of damage a single viking froup can do if they enter your city is ridiculous. The fires they start (instatly, might I add) can destroy massive parts of the city in mere seconds if you don't have enough peasants nearby to fight the flames. If there was a slight pause for the vikings at a building before it was set ablaze it would help not only give the archer towers a chance to kill them, but the vikings also wouldn't destroy massive swaths of city in one attack.
3. I don't know if this is just me being the casual I am, but city gates don't seem to stop vikings at all. (Though this might be an issue of a peasant opening the gate as they try to get to another area)
The issues I've noticed might all be symptoms of me being bad at games, so take my complaints with a grain of salt.
This game is well worth the 10 bucks and I'd personally say thats its easily worth twice that, especially now that I've heard the dev's are planning on continuing to add free content on top of this already great, though kind of low on stuff as of now, city builder.

I see why this product has mixed reviews.
The game itself is meh.
The graphics are great and all the animations are very true to the 80's era.
The soundtrack itself was worth playing for an hour or so as well since I'm heavily into the 80's retro synth genre.
Unfortunately if your car so much as slows down too much or bumps into a wall or obstacle, this wonderful music gets interrupted with a very VHS style sound glitch(this is intentional as a design element, mind you).
This wouldn't be that bad if you could maybe turn it off but you can't. At first it's kinda funny because it reminds you of when VHS tapes(if you're old enough to remember them) would lose tracking and make the audio slur for a moment. The novelty of this wears of very quickly when wanting to just listen to the music, though.
The controls are somewhat slippery and while they're not that hard to pick up, there seems to be no real option for recovery whenever you make a hard crash. This game would be a poor effort at a stand-alone game.
Frankly, it's a pretty poor effort at a mini-game spinoff of a stand-alone spinoff of a good game (Beyond Earth and Civilization V, respectively).
The real problem that I have with this game isn't the stripped-down options, the modest graphics, the periodically-uncotrollable game volume (I'm serious - have your hand on the volume when you win or you'll lose hearing), or the clunky and insipid AI.  No, none of these broke the game for me.  What broke the game is that when you capture an enemy capital you suddenly control the entire enemy empire.  Ta da!  It's like a game show bonus round worth more points than all of the previous game show rounds, making them a complete waste of time.
HOWEVER, if you really enjoy Civilization: Beyond Earth, Starships does have some really neat unlockable content for that game.  The new goodies are two new maps and two new customization options each for starting ships, settler attributes, and cargo when you start a new Beyond Earth game.  That alone was kind of a consolation prize as I worked through the achievements for Starships.
There's a catch, though.  These games, although running through Steam, do not track each other's achievements through steam and require a 2k account (free, linked on the title page of Starships and Beyond Earth) for the games to "talk to each other."  That is not at all clear and I only discovered it later as I tried to figure out how to get the Beyond Earth save achievement for Starships.  The achivements are not awarded retroactively - I had all of the Beyond Earth achievements before I linked the games through 2k and so had no unlockables for Starships.  Frustrating.
Unless you're a fan of Beyond Earth, pass on this one.

This is the worst game to bears Sid Meier's name.
"Surely it's not that bad" You say.
I'm afraid it is.
In the build up to the release of the game there was little doubt that it was going to be a less involved game to play then the typical Sid Meier fare, more Ace Patrol then Civilization 5. When developers were discussing the game, that was pretty clear and I have no qualms with that.
In fact I was quite happy with the idea of a strategy game designed so I could play over an evening after work.
Initial impressions are poor. The game launching in a tiny window and into a bare, personality-less main menu that could have been ripped from any sci-fi title (it reminded me of the Sword of the Stars 2 menu). I sought out the settings menu and within that I found volume controls and "Windowed Full Screen mode".
I'm sorry what?
I know the game was being made for tablet as well, but this is Firaxis. I asked another friend playing it "Am I missing a settings menu somewhere?" bemusedly. "Nope" He replied "It really is that sparse"
Oh well. Not a great first impression, but not necessarily the end of the world. I setup a game.
Setup lets you pick a faction and a leader. Each faction gets the same leaders, with slightly rejigged artwork. Which comes across as a bit lazy. The factions have a unique bonus with the leaders adding an additional bonus of their own. I was a little bemused at what the various bonuses meant as I only knew about one aspect of the game (crew morale) from previews nothing else made a lot of sense and there was nothing to explain the benefits of a choice, no tooltips, nothing.
The lack of tooltips persists throughout, with a general lack of accessible information.
I setup my game, stabbing blindly in the dark at things that sounded useful
The galactic playing field looks alright and I wait for the useful tutorial to kick in and explain things to me over my first few turns. I get nothing. I understand there's an info button to click but I don't understand why there's a lack of tutorial and I fumble around the first few turns getting to grips with the games systems.
As the game is all about moving a fleet around space bringing disparate planets into a federation you'd expect load out/designing of the ships to be one of the most involved aspects of the game. Instead, you're presented with a list of things to click away at to upgrade or downgrade (removing components nets you some resources back to spend elsewhere) different aspects of each ship.
My fleet consisted of three ships throughout the course of the game, starting as corvette's, ending as battleships through upgrades and the games automatic ship classification. All 3 focused on speed, one was paticularly tough and loaded with close range weaponry. One was less tough, also had close range weaponry and could cloak. One had longer range weapons. The limitation to what you can actually do with ships meant all of them had max speed, and were stupidly tough by about mid way through. But this simple setup felt game breaking. I could defeat any mission or enemy fleet, outside of the missions where you have to defend an outpost that can only survive two hits with fast enemies that just head straight for it.
The empire building aspect of the game is no more involved. "Click this to make numbers go up, because numbers" about sums up this aspect of the game. There's no interesting trade off between balancing metal, food or energy. Get lots of whatever you can, click stuff to have more stuff.
I actually beat my game accidentally. I was working my way from planet to planet, building one ludcriously over powered wonder after another because why not, then a conquered a planet which also had a wonder and triggered the wonder victory.
Well victory nets you a much more rewarding end then it does in Beyond Earth at least. You get 10 seconds of video which is better then a text box. But does it really matter when the rest of the game is so unengaging?
Overall, it's an ok game to have on a tablet, nothing stand out, even where there isn't much competition. But on the PC there's tons. Weird Worlds in Infinite space did something similar but better years ago and it's Early Access sequel likely will to. There is no reason to buy this game for the PC, and very little for a tablet.

This is a great, streamlined strategy game with a heavy focus on -- surprise, surprise -- building a fleet of starships and improving their stats. You improve the ships by spending resources and you get the resources by exerting "influence" over planets (basically, you conquer them). You can buy influence or gain influence by either completing a mission at the planet or by giving your crew shore leave there. Shore leave basically serves as an "end turn" button on the main strategy map and allows your crew to rest and recover, so you can move again next turn from planet to planet, improving them (by building cities, improvements, or wonders) and gaining influence.
Aside from the main strategy map, you'll also be conducting an awful lot of combat missions on a more detailed battle map. You'll fire torpedoes, which you can detonate at will after the first turn when an enemy is nearby (or you think it's nearby), or perform scans, or simply shoot an enemy vessel with your ships' weapons. Asteroids little the 2D battle arena that provide some cover for your vessels as you manoeuvre into an advantageous position. The best thing? These battles, while numerous, move very quickly, so you'll never get bored.
You can win the game through a variety of means, though the most common one is the "population" victory, where you control 51% of the galaxy. The end isn't particularly exciting: you'll get a dialogue box that essentially tells you, "You win!", followed by a short and rather nondescript video. But the game is fun! Yes, it's nowhere near as complex and involved like any of the Civilization games, but it isn't supposed to be. This is Sid Meier's Starships, not Sid Meier's Galactic Empires. It's streamlined and simple without being simplistic. You'll be doing all the standard 4X things: exploring, expanding, exploiting, and exterminating, but at such a brisk pace you can easily finish a full game in a couple of hours or less.
If you expect this to be the next big Sid Meier game that will devour your life for months if not years on end, you'll be disappointed. (And incidentally, congratulations on having so much spare time on hand!) If instead you're looking for a quick, fun turn-based strategy game with lots of fairly interesting options and brisk combat, then Sid Meier's Starships is worth your time and money. I thoroughly recommend this.

I took a chance with this game back in the day. Saw a youtuber play it and I thought it was a pretty dope game. Back then it was only on the Xbox 360, and I forked out cash and played it there. Was a blast then. Still is. I don't think back then there were zombie survival games that centred on building a community. Either that or I didn't know of any. So this whole build a small thriving community and looking after their needs and such drew me in. And boy, it got me hooked. It's a simple game at its core, you pick a character, you go out and do a few things. One, you can advance the main storyline which, should you finish, ends the playthrough. Or two, go out and scavenge. This involves visiting households and buildings as well as general areas and checking out what's in it. Could be ammunition, could be food. Could be supplies. Third, you go out and do the side missions. These can range from rescuing survivors to helping hunt down zombies.
Speaking of zombies, there are a few types to spice it up. Big ones, small shrieking ones, fast strong ones. All have different traits so you have to be prepared to face them lest you lose the fight AND your survivor. Yes, permadeath is present. The game lets you control most of the people in your camp, so there's no 'main character', save for the core few. And when your controlled character dies, you lose him or her and get pushed to control the next available one. This forces you to be extra careful with your choices.
You also have to take care of your homebase. Stock up on supplies, ammunition, set up traps. You can upgrade it with facilities like a toilet to improve hygiene and reduce disease and such. Building these upgrades require components, which you go out and scavenge. Pretty simple premise, but it can get tricky to balance all these needs whilst going out on missions. You have to prioritise.
So, combat then. Ranged, or melee? Ammunition is limited, and you can carry, with your medicine and melee weapon, probably 90 or 120 on a full load with a backpack. This will go down quickly if you engage too many enemies. So you're off to using melee then. The melee system is heavily dependent on the stamina system, which means you can't keep swinging your katana then expect to have energy to sprint away. You have to time it right, then finish them off with an execution. Along with the degradation system of weapons, sometimes its wise to just run away.
So, what of this game? I like it. Not as much as I used to, but its a pretty fun game if you like a zombie game with base building and supply management. Almost everything you can use degrades and most of the time can only be repaired and not make a new copy of. This is especially true of vehicles. Get it if you don't mind the slightly dated graphics and slightly clunky combat.

Well, looking at all of these other reviews, I'm not going to complain about the quality of the port. I used a fanmade patch, and an Xbox 360 controller, and that worked fine, at least, when comparing it to the PS3 version. It was a basic problem with an easy fix. On to the meat of my experience.
I'd characterize Dark Souls as an RPG in the same way I would Monster Hunter, where even ideal equipment won't save a player who doesn't use the right technique, and like Monster Hunter, I regularly find myself saying "Oh, my God." and "Are you joking?"
First, let's talk about the harmless stuff. Graphically, the game aims more to impress with its scale than it does with miniscule details. For every mile-long vista of traversable territory, there's a mouth that seems to be stitched shut. At the very least, the game isn't particularly visually confusing, outside of its combat. The music, or what little there is of it, is pretty well done. It usually plays only during boss battles, so most of the time, the only ambience to hear is the white noise of the surroundings.
The game world feels open, yet structured. The paths to objectives (that is, main quest objectives) are not immediately explained but are still fairly obvious. Experienced players will know where to look for shortcuts in certain areas, and the tedium of backtracking is reduced toward the middle of the game, when the player earns the ability to warp between some discovered locations.
"Artificial Difficulty." It's a buzzwordy term, but it needs to be addressed. Dark Souls is fine when it gives the player a fair challenge. Unfortunately, it doesn't usually give the player a fair challenge, and there are some things that simply cannot be adapted to, even after getting knocked on your♥♥♥♥♥a few times. Enemies who alter their trajectory mid-jump, bosses that constantly use their most overpowered abilities, attacks with hitboxes not accurately represented by the visuals, and the list goes on. It's not insurmountable, but it often seems like blind luck, and it makes the easier parts of the game a breeze by comparison. I probably spent more time in the Four Kings boss battle than I spent in Sen's Fortress.
My main problem with this game is the lack of consistency in the controls. Sometimes I press a button, and nothing happens. Other times, the game will remember something I pressed a full 3 seconds ago, and try to play catch up, even if I don't want the action to go through anymore. I don't think I've ever encountered a game as selectively amnesiac as this one. Now, I can withstand laggy control, as long it's consistent, but when it aggressively slingshots back and forth between responsive and unresponsive, that's where it stops being fun. Especially in a game like this, where a fraction of a second can mean the difference between winning a fight, and walking for five minutes to even attempt to try again, inconsistent control equals regular frustration.
The multiplayer ranges from decent, to kind of bad. It depends on who you fight, where you fight, and how bad the connection is. When it doesn't all line up perfectly, it's an incoherent mess with balancing issues, lag which makes the already iffy disparity between action and visuals even worse, and often involuntary participation. I suppose allowing forceful invasions is one way to keep the multiplayer going strong, but goddamn, can it be annoying.
When it does work, it's a very emotional and intense experience. There's a lot of freedom, evidenced by the variety of techniques I've used and seen others use, although it's on this point that I stress the major discrepancy between the PvP and PvE. The player versus environment experience is most definitely RPG. You know where to find specific threats, and you know what their weaknesses are. That's kind of what every RPG is. However, in PvP, there's an element of unpredictability. It's not just about memorizing enemy patterns, because your enemy won't have a pattern. It's a different sort of game altogether, certainly with more emphasis on "action", which probably better defines the gameplay style as a whole.
The conclusion I can draw about Dark Souls' single player is that it's designed to be abrasive, but not in a way that feels particularly entertaining. After clearing the initial hurdle of cheap deaths, it becomes apparent that most of the challenge is based solely in memorization, and it stops feeling rewarding from that point on. It will be decent for two playthroughs, which alone is well worth the price tag (despite its problems, it's still a meaty game), but once it gets stale, the enjoyment will start to come almost exclusively from multiplayer. As of writing this, the community is still somewhat active. If you can deal with bad connections and occasional balance issues, you can tack on extra hours to what is already an engaging, if deeply flawed, action RPG.

This game is kind of a mixed bag with me, so I'll just list the pros and cons.
The gameplay is quite a bit improved from the first game; camera is no longer locked, climbing is easier, items are actually useful this time, and there's items dedicated to helping you uncover secrets. I'm also quite fond of the openness, allowing you to go back at virtually any time to explore, collect items, etc.
Visually, the game is beautiful, and there's plenty of areas in the game that are simply stunning. Found myself taking in the view more than once.
The mastery system rewards using different skills to enhance your weapons' power. Each of Dracula's weapons have their own specific use, similar to the first game, but are more than just enchanting your whip with magic this time around, giving you entirely different movesets for each weapon. Also you get to drink your enemies' blood.
The music of the first game was good, but it lacked any sort of memorability. The music in Lords of Shadow 2 is much better, although you'll hear a lot of the same tracks over and over. Somewhat of a hit and miss here, but a majority of the music is good enough that this is more of a pro than a con.
There was a lot of nothing in between the major events of the first game; the pacing was just kinda crap, in all honesty. There always seems to be something going on in LoS 2, it's easier to feel like you're actually doing something rather than roaming through some ruins without much of a goal, which was a major problem throughout the first third of the first game.
I was completely incapable of feeling any sort of sympathy for Gabriel in the first game. He was a cardboard cutout of a character devoid of most emotion. In this one, however, he's a little more interesting simply because he is fairly PO'ed. Also he's the dark lord, he has a reputation to live up to. Thankfully, he does.
As previously mentioned in the Graphics, the game is beautiful. The environment is also essential for this as well; for the areas that they created, the world is detailed and interesting. Areas are distinguishable from other places, and the concept of building a city on the ruined foundations of Dracula's castle is, honestly, quite interesting. It creates a distinctive gothic-type city that still seems reminiscent of Dracula's castle pre-ruin when you have opportunities to overlook the city.
While the story blows (more on that later), it does have some intriguing lore to find, some of which indicating that the people of Castlevania City are fully aware that monsters and magic are a thing. It's definitely a turn from the original Castlevania games and other games such as Vampire: The Masquerade- Bloodlines where hiding the supernatural from the world was of the utmost importance. In Lords of Shadow 2, I find it intriguing that they accept, and are even fascinated by, the fact that there used to be werewolves, vampires, and even the siege against Dracula are merely documented as history and treated as such. Their history is as natural to them as our own is to us. This is certainly something I'd love to see expanded on in future games- maybe not Lords of Shadow, but other franchises where the supernatural is merely embraced as a part of history rather than hidden from the world for safety.
You can add the title, give the characters the names, and everything else, but it still doesn't make it a Castlevania game. Let alone it's horridly out of place with half of the game taking place in a modern day city. To be perfectly honest, it feels more like Darksiders than Castlevania due to the themes throughout the game. The heart and spirit of the series is completely absent from Lords of Shadow, hence I only ever refer to it as Lords of Shadow.
I find it ironic that they rebooted Castlevania with an intended focus on story, and then ended up dropping the ball. The first game had an okay, albeit not-very-original story with Satan having Necron Syndrome and popping up literally out of nowhere at the end. Mirror of Fate was an atrocity of a game and explained jack squat. Similar problems are in LoS 2- Gabriel often finds himself back in what appears to be either the past of his memories of his castle. Honestly have no idea because it's
. His memories/past/whatever-the-fudge-is-going-on also has zero relevance to what's going on, aside from getting back his powers because reasons. There's also some Resident Evil bullcrap going on where the citizens are mutated by some demonic virus; this is so out of place it hurts. Everything else is fairly easy to follow, and there's some interesting things that do happen throughout the game, but it's nothing to write home about. Story is honestly not a good reason to play this game, and if it's what you're looking for, turn the other way.
Found a door? Guess what? You're going to have to pull a switch to open it. He's only a superhuman Prince of Darkness, godforbid he opens a metal door on his own. There's a lot of this crap that just slows the game down needlessly, especially since it takes
for said doors to open. This game was made in 2014, this is rather inexcusable.
There's a guard/perfect guard mechanic in the game, which is quite useful. Unfortunately, roughly 50% of the time, the enemies perform an unblockable attack, which renders guarding a lot less useful than you'd like it to be. Also there's plenty of times where I simply wanted to get somewhere and didn't want to fight. Going places often involve climbing. Guess what?
often forcing you to fight enemies when you don't want to. This is often infuriating when you merely want to explore for upgrades and other hidden items.
Okay, I get that he's weak and whatnot at the beginning, but this just seems so unnecessary. Especially since the stealth segment with Agreus is absolutely infuriating.
Every now and then, characters may "say something" without sound- basically the sound file for the line they're supposed to say doesn't play (no subtitles either, which is even more aggravating). I've had other instances where the objective was the last objective I just did, and wasn't up to date. Worst of all, I've had it crash on me for no reason once.
While the story is laughable, the stealth is pointless, and bugs are afoot, the game is actually quite fun. I do not recommend it at full price; wait for a Steam sale to get it because $40 is a bit much for some of the frustrations of the game. Gameplay-wise, it's pretty good, despite the annoying gameplay oversights. Worth getting if you're interested in, or at least play the demo first to know if you'd like it.

As a Castlevania fan (and I mean all of them), I recommend this game sincerely to fans of the series, gothic atmospheres, vampire and other mythical lore and fast-paced action games.
I've played this game before on a different system, but I needed it again for the PC. That's how much I love it.
The negatives about this game often are about the stealth parts and the modern day sequences. I also find those less appealing, but it makes me appreciate the castle sequences even better. The environments are beautiful and open for exploration. Once you've got the majority of your abilities the exploration becomes the best part of the game, for me at least.
Some people say the story is so so, but I love the amount of effort they put in the lore. A lot of the story is hidden in the pages of the bestiary and abilities. Accompanied by amazing artwork and good music (though, earlier Castlevania's had better music), it makes it a atmospheric experience of storytelling.
My opinion might be influenced by my love for the series, but I can still recommend this game just for the amazing leveldesign, atmosphere, awesome bossbattles and rich mythological lore.

This game seems really fun so far. As a player of Anno 2070 I can say it obviously does some things differently, but I don't think it's bad at all.
First off, this game is gorgeous, although that has little to no factor in this review, that is just worht noting for those who are interested and didn't notice that. The game looks great.
People are complaining about having specific nodes where you can build things, but that's only the case for some resources, it's just like in Anno 2070 where you could only build mines in designated mining spots, it's no different from that, except now instead of just having mines, you have mines and some awautic facilities! It's really no different in that aspect, I think people are just forgetting that this is a differnt game, although the previous Anno games had a large sea element this one doesn't so much, and I think that's okay. Would I like to have more freedom with where I place my buildings in terms of both mines and aquatic facilities? Sure, but I don't think it's really a big deal, it works just like the mines did in Anno 2070 and I enjoyed that game a great deal and am still doing so in this game, not in spite of it by any means.
You still have the same sort of layouts you had in Anno 2070 where you have one factory with components branching off of it, except this time they are optional (but recommended as they are better in every way to building a whole new factory). People are saying it's been dumbed down, where if anything I think it's been made slightly more difficult in some aspects. In terms of your factories, sure you aren't required to lay them out quite like you used to be, but now if you want to be the most efficient you can be, you'll have to strategies with how you want to expand your factories with the various components. Now this may not completely be the case, as there only really seems to be one worthwhile component so far that I've seen, which is the one that increases productivity at the cost of higher maintanence. As the others don't really offer much that I could see myself needing, but perhaps they will be more important later on in the game, as I am still fairly early in.
The theme is really cool to me, I love sci-fi and general space stuff, the idea of building a colony on the moon is just really cool to me, so that's a plus in my book.
There are some aspects I don't really like, such as the fact that there are no more randomly generated maps. One cool thing about 2070 wa that I could open up a new map and I would have to deal with what the game threw at me in terms of resources, where they were on islands and the relative size of the islands for factory placements and all that. However in that game it was fairly shallow and not too random as you could expect a large variety of things, it was still kinda fun. However the game does look very nice, which I feel is due in part to the fact that they don't have to worry about randomization of the worlds.
I've also noticed that trading doesn't seem to be as big a thign so far. I did notice that there was a way to trade from my soon to be arctic colony to my temperate one, although I haven't actually done that yet. Either way, in general trading just isn't as big a thing because you have now more interconnected colonies as opposed to the disconnected island colony of 2070. I'm not quite sure whether that's good or bad. The trade routes in the past did kinda seem unnescessary, although they were kinda fun to play arounf with, so I'm a little on the fence about this, but I think overall it's not a big deal.
tl;dr:
I think the game is good, all the complaints I've really seen so far aren't really making any good points and it seems to be just as complex a game is the series has ever been and seems to still be a good and true member of the Anno series. I look forward to many many more hours playing this game.

Don't let the bad reviews on here turn you off, Anno 2055 is a great game, it's just not a great Anno.
If you want to micromanage resources, build stockpiles, set up local trade routes or have nigh infinite quantities of depth on a single map, this game will diappoint you. If you've always hated having your transporters do♥♥♥♥♥♥you don't want them to and get annoyed looking at the same biome for hours on end, this is you Anno. Sure, the production chains are not as complex any more, but building the factories themselves has, with the new module system, become a whole lot more interesting. The different map regions (Temperate, Arctic and Lunar, with more to come, apparently) would be games of their own if they were not dependent upon each other for specific resources. The whole setting is very interesting, though the villain does feel, well, a little too "for the evulz" villiany and not well thought out, but Anno was never exactly Mass Effect to begin with. The one thing that actually really, really, really bothered me is that you apparently can no longer name colonies and ships.
So yeah, if you've always wanted to get into Anno but thought it was too complicated, give this one a try, and then later you might go and buy the previous one, or stick with this one. Either way, you'll be thoroughly entertained for a long, long time with this.

There may be a lot of negative reviews for this game, but for the right people, this game really hits it.
If you've ever wanted just the turn-based tactical combat without the baggage of empire management, this is the game to get. If you've ever set up a Civ5 game on a huge epic pangaea with only elimination victory type, you might want to try Starships using epic + impossible + domination-only setup. You get the fun battles with much less empire management baggage and with much less possibility for lopsided technological mismatch.
And if you want turn-based combat in the form of starships in space, this may well be the only modern take in existence because I haven't managed to find any other. Most other 4X games have gone real-time with combat and they come with massive empire management and ship design overhead.
Here are a sample of things I liked compared to other tactical (mostly RPG) games:
- You can reconfigure your party instantly with little to no resource loss, promoting build diversity. You can refit your fleet into any spec to suit the next battle and respec it back. In most other tactics game, you're locked into particular builds accompanied by long grinding process which you have to repeat if you switch builds.
- The game gets going fast with minimal build-up time. Within 2-3 battles, you're already progressing up to considerable strategic options (e.g. cannons, fighters, new ship). In most other tactics games, you'd have to grind around for dozens of missions to gather resources and gain EXP.
- The galactic screen is essentially a very good mission chooser screen. Most other tactics games offer very little choice with regard to choosing missions. (e.g. limited to open sidequests, random battles that interrupt your travel, etc.) In Starships, you can look at your borders and choose a mission based on the other empire's strength and your crew fatigue. Mission types on non-federated planets are quite varied.
- Planetary Wonders are a really nice way to differentiate the strengths of each player in the game in a way that's halfway between randomized and controlled, and also in a way that you can't plan for from before the game starts the way you could with Civ5 leader traits or world wonders.
- No random chance to miss. (looking at you XCOM) Cover reduces damage instead of chance to hit.
The only real complaint I have for this game is the lack of multiplayer, although ultimately its addition would probably be no more than what multiplayer was in XCOM which didn't really do much.
Another possible complaint is that the AI is not terribly difficult, but I find that it only really has problems when you start using special tactics (like invisible torpedoes). In an open brawl, I find that the AI is quite competent with finding odd line of sight that I can't fire back to and are pretty good at finding a way to shoot your engines. The Impossible difficulty should be good for the vast majority of average players.
I like what the game has to offer in its current (and probably final) state and wholeheartedly recommend it for fans of turn-based tactical space games.
