Here is my review of OutDrive: (Do note, that if you are somewhat offended or think my review is wrong in any way, try not to get triggered by it, and tell me why in the comment area)
The game has a good concept, being set in an "Aesthetic" synthwave 80's era, I do genuinely think that the concept of this game is great! Although that being said, it should be noted that everything inside it can become repetitive. As a quote-on-quote fan of the synthwave style of music, I do like the setting of the game as a whole
As I mentioned earlier, I do like the synthwave genre of music with songs such as "Decay" by HOME and their other song "Resonance" I do find however, that the soundtrack is a bit repetitive and sounds god awful when it slows down (More on that later) I also find that (In my opinion) that the music is to fast to be classed as synthwave, but I suppose that it's due to the fact that it's a driving game. I do wish they had implemented music from HOME and others into the game, but again, that's my opinion
Eh... They are not the best in the world, I don't know if it's because its coded in Unity (A personal displeasure to me and doesn't say as far as I know on the store page), if it's because it's a driving game, or if I am terrible at driving games. The idea of this game is to keep your girlfriend(I assume?) alive by driving your car, you also have to keep the icon in the blue area (Or the safe zone or whatever) or it can go into the red zones by either; over heating, or going to slow, to stop this, you have to either slow down, or speed up. That is essentially what you have to do, also, did I mention that you can also make the icon go into the low red by hitting something, no? Me neither! as far as I know, it doesn't mention that anywhere at all and I didn't know that, until I lost the game because of that, bare in mind, that the physics of the game itself and the driving mechanics are VERY wonky, and don't really work with a keyboard and would be best played with something like an Xbox controller or a Steam Machine or Steam Link, then again it might just be me. To me also, it's counter intuative to have it so that the icon goes into the low red when you hit a wall when the mechanics are god awful, well that's in my opinion.
Overall, I don't personally recommend this game, it's not suited for PC, but would be better as some sort of indie game on console's, but overall, I like the style, not so much the game its self. But don't let my opinon deter you from this game. Oh and also, while you're reading this review, you might want to get this game on sale, for it's low price at the start, I wouldn't say it's worth it (I got it for 49 pence, bet you can tell where I come from now ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°))

Since using the Lordvessel in the previous
game you completed and avoiding your
evil double's dark fate of plunging reality
into darkness, you find yourself in a retro
1980s world, leaving a nightclub with her,
Summer-Rain, or an analogue of her in this
neon reality.
The soundtrack floods overhead as color
accents the world, immersing you fully as
you remember what it is to relax properly,
to love again as she smiles and takes you
by the hand into the smoky streets of
1985. Suddenly, men from this timeline
pull up with guns, mistaking you for their
target. They open fire.
Now you find yourself in the game, stuck
within the confines of the world. Simple
and easy to maneuver with a beautiful
retro-synth soundtrack permeating every
corner, the rules and gameplay of this
world are dead simple - if the car stops,
Summer-Rain's heart stops too.
So you drive. Onward and forever. There is
no true payoff to the game, the world in
itself, the only gain of this strange, ideal
world you wanted was the chance to be
with Summer-Rain again. But every time
you stall or are hindered, the game brings
up the game over screen, but instead of
yourself, you see none other than the
second of the Trinity of Hollywood, your
enemy Shadow of Doubt.
You reload into the world once again,
Summer-Rain breathing hard as you level
out your speed while trying to maintain a
cruising speed while the world demands
more of you to keep Summer-Rain's heart
beating consistently. After what feels like
an eternity of constant speed, stalling,
death and rebirth, Shadow of Doubt
appears in the backseat as you respawn.
Doubt announces,
as you blink a bit to make sure he is really
there. You maintain speed once again as
you feel the car gaining, and Summer-Rain
quietly easing into the seat for the drive.
Shadow of Doubt adjusts his glasses
before interrupting you with an arched
eyebrow and a smirk.
You wince as you pass a lap completion and
the demand for constant speed gets higher
you hiss the
retort through gritted teeth.
Shadow of Doubt leans back and checks his
fingers, looking bored.
You glance back at Doubt,
who gestures for you to focus on the neon
landscape ahead.
You ask, surprised by
your own concern at the fate of the leader
of this band of enemies.
You question Shadow of Doubt, who
sees this version of Summer-Rain looking out
into the window, quiet and morose.
Shadow of Doubt begins, looking a lot more
serious now.
You realize with the newfound emotions on
display from Shadow of Doubt, that this land
of the 1980s is his own reality.
You panic
slightly as a large helicopter veers across the
horizon into view, here to stop you as the
world did not expect you to survive this long
and prolong Summer-Rain's life.
You nod, looking
at the helicopter and tensing to adapt to its
attack pattern.
Doubt looks at the helicopter,
to his Summer-Rain and then to you.
The helicopter unleashes a torrent of bullets,
trying to veer you off course and stall the
precious speed keeping Summer-Rain alive.
Summer-Rain
closes her eyes shut as Shadow of Doubt puts
his hand on both you and her shoulders.
You shout, incredulous.
You look back to the helicopter as it readies
a volley of rockets towards the car. You look
back to both Shadow of Doubt and this version
of Summer-Rain, who is already phasing out,
about to be reborn again for the next round.
You look at the Lordvessel in your pocket as
it glows faintly, and the rockets are unleashed
upon the car, closing in fast. You feel the warm
glow of reality bending, while Shadow of Doubt
awaits for the world to respawn him and the
love of your lives. In an instant, you are gone,
and Shadow of Doubt closes his eyes.

I really recommend this game to people whether they want to take it seriously or just to have fun:
At first the game felt and was not at all finished as well as the controls being very awkward but fortunately due to several updates this game was really brought to life - The controls became easier as i played, which was a lot considering how addictive i myself found this game, I also know that some people would not enjoy this game as much and i can also see why people who played the old game dont enjoy it but i enjoyed the old game and still gave this one a chance, thus is why i can write such a positive review. I believe they put a lot of time and effort into this game to make it as enjoyable as possible since every level there are new things to craft new hard ways to escape and a real challenge for each prison. I no longer find that i am grinding as much as in the old game either and it helps when there are secret areas with stuff over some of the prisons. Its multiplayer still has very minor bugs but nothing that should affect the main fun and escape, fortunately multiplayer has some unique areas to help you escape. Transport prisons were interesting but i thought at first that they were a bad part but as i played through them i realised they are fantastic and provide loads of fun. Most people i doubt would care about customisation items but i believe adds something interesting to the game as you unlock them as you play and as they help you make hilarious characters. The only downside is the keys, i like how it encourages you to escape each prison in every different way possible but it means it is way to easy to unlock each prison, this also means if you want to play versus after one prison you might start being given prisons that u dont want to do versus on meaning you would have to wait and do that prison first.
Overall i think its brilliant how they have combined singleplayer and multiplayer without changing the prisons while keeping it just as much as a challenge, adding transport prisons to add some variety and so if you dont have much time you can do one quickly. It is very well made and definetly worth looking into getting if you are interested

Very cool, quite fun. I'm glad that they're still improving it, as there are a few minor issues here and there. I find this to be superior to the usual comparisons due to the art style, the theme, the pacing, and the overall variation. The gameplay may become a little repetitive over time, but there's enough diversity if you know where to look for it. The sense of progression isn't as satisfying as other games, however. Because there's no sense of starting up from nowhere, attaching yourself to your first building, etc. Starbound may not feel as homely as games like Terraria or Minecraft.
There's barely any grind, all of the grind ends pretty quickly at the beginning of the game. You'll be getting lots of rare ore quickly even on survival mode. There's no creative mode, but the casual mode accentuates how easy the game can be so much that you'll probably feel like you're almost in a creative mode. I haven't taken my time to build anything complex, but I believe I'll build a base sometime in the future.
I haven't had many encounters on the biggest multiplayer server I found. There are few servers, and the majority of them are empty. There's no built-in server list, so you'll have to look for servers on the internet. From what I noticed, multiplayer is extremely unstable now, and there are even instances of people getting their character files corrupt (the server I played on has a client that backs your characters up before you play in case that happens). There's no mechanism against griefers, so modders had to circumvent it by making a way of claiming and backing up worlds in a specific server. Thankfully, mods function properly with servers.
It's a good-quality game, but I believe there's a long way to go for this to remain interesting after a long time. Sadly, Terraria is more popular, and I guess the multiplayer for them is better as well. I still plan on sticking with this game and checking on it whenever it updates — they do update regularly. If you enjoy this type of game and Terraria doesn't seem your style, I'd recommend Starbound, most definitely.

While not quite what I'd wanted after the first game in the series (and Mirror of Fate,) this is a good place for a semi-closing chapter.  Without any spoilers, a lot has happened since Gabriel Belmont originally set out to kill the Lords of Shadow and Do Good Things.  And this is a worthy addition to that story.  But what we see here is literally centuries after everything that happens in the other two games, and that gap feels kinda weird.  I suppose it's all explained via flashbacks and things, but even still.
Lords of Shadow 2 improves on anything the first game did that needed improving, while not messing with 95% of the things about that game that worked great already.  And it THANKFULLY brings back one continuous world that you can explore as you see fit.  Physically walking back to an area with a new power to get a thing you saw but couldn't reach makes sense; selecting an earlier chapter from a menu in the first game, and running into characters and even bosses that are already DEAD... not so much.
That said, the tone of the two games is much different.  This one doesn't ride on Hope so much.  Some might like the darker story, but personally I thought that it was a little somber and depressing at times.  It was all well told, and Robert Carlyle and Patrick Stewart knocked their roles out of the park, but I think that the darker universe just kinda took a toll on things.  We'll be visiting different environments, but gone are the sunny paths, baked desert-scapes, and clear skied mountain fortresses of the first game.  Here you get plenty of variety, with stormy locales, night cityscapes, fiery caverns, frozen mountainsides... but you'll never be doing anything during the day.  That's understandable, as Story Reasons require you to get everything done in one night.  And hell, Castlevania games usually all happen indoors, in one night, IN Dracula's Castle, so I can't fault it too much for grim, darkness.
Powers work better in this game than the first.  Alternate weapons/magic/sub-weapons, all that stuff is great.  In the first game, I found myself doing everything with the whip, and never bothering to use my daggers, fairies, or dark crystal.  I used Holy Water to deal with BS waves that got boring, but when I used sub weapons or items here, it was all strategic and useful.  Especially in the Kleidos Challenges.
Kleidos Challenges are unlockable (and thankfully optional) challenges that put you in a circular area with various enemies.  And there are three objectives, different to each challenge.  You might get, say, don't break any shields, don't use the Void Sword, and don't recover health by any means during the fight.  There's always the same 4th objective: do all three in the same run.  I did more than half of these before I got annoyed, and then just stopped.  For the super-hardcore, this is your kind of thing.
Collectables are EVERYWHERE!  Kinda literally.  I've found 3 or 4 things in the SAME ROOM, sometimes I needed different powers for each... and sometimes when you find the first collectable, it's actually only half-way down a secret path, and going just a little farther will find you a hand-hold to climb or sneak or do something to get to another.  I liked that, using one power-up as a distraction so you'll think you've got it and miss out on the next one.
Speaking of those collectible powerups, the come from two major things: Pain Boxes and Piles of Sacrifice.  The Pain Box is a box with a mouth that cuts or stabs your wrist when you stick your hand in, but then you get a Health, Void, or Chaos shard to raise your HP or Void or Chaos magics!  The Pile of Sacrifice is a little statue of a dude with a big curved sword over his shoulder, and you slice your wrist on it, bleed a LOT into the bowl beneath it, and then the bowl gives you either a capacity upgrade for 5 of your 6 relics or a Kleidos Nail, to get them Kleidos Challenges unlocked.  Don't worry if hunting for all this sounds annoying: you can pick up or shop for Dodo Eggs, and using one will mark the nearest collectible on your map.  It was fun for me hunting these down, though I did Dodo around... 15 of the game's nearly 200, just because I was at the end and wanted to get everything before I hit the last area.
Some people say that the bosses here aren't as good as the first game.  True, for the most part, but at the same time not true.  They're very different.  The first game's bosses were huge and awesome, but had some HIGHLY scripted ways to beat them, and most ended in a series of Quick Timing Events.  Here it's more a real fight, relying on your gameplay skills.  QTEs have been dialed back A LOT from the first game.  Lords of Shadow 1 must have something like 800% as many as this one does.
So I'll conclude here saying that this is a solid game with a cool story, and voice acting from two guys who do very good work.  Definitely, without question worth a buy on sale, and honestly even worth a buy at normal price if you're into Castlevania stuff.  But as a caveat, you might want to get the first game and Mirror of Fate HD first, as this is one epic overarching story, and though they do a pretty good recap at the beginning here, you want to be attached to the characters and the world first.  It makes this much more powerful.
Here's hoping they make the intended third and final game, and round everything out as incredibly as I hope.

It usually happens I find myself torn between a diamond in the rough and problematic technical or some other aspect of the game, but with Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 it's somewhat different. Time to see if I can put into somewhat coherent paragraph or two as to why that's the case.
Let's start off by saying I was one of the people who enjoyed the original Lords of Shadow for what it was – not necessarily a creatively original masterpiece, but a game of astounding production values, competent writing and tight narrative punctuated by stellar voice work and lastly, and perhaps most importantly, it was a very meaty game which lead to some even saying it was too long for its own good. Fast forward to sequel and you can see it basically falters in each of these categories.
Interestingly enough game seems to swing between two polar opposites with its visuals because on one hand you have this classic Castlevania look comprised of foreboding yet mystical gothic castle to romp through, as well as its assorted menagerie of beasties to but heads with and solve painfully few puzzles compared to the first game, but on the other you have to contend with extremely bland modern-day warehouses and science laboratories ad nauseam alongside some fairly uninspired enemies ranging from more classical demons and Satanists to, what really should've been more interesting that ended up, futuristic soldiers and cybernetic abominations roaming the streets. But honestly, it's this weird disjointed narrative that undoes the game the most in my mind because you can clearly tell there was meant to be more there instead of just going from A to B and meandering in-between retreading locations with nothing but brief radio contacts from time to time. And lastly – game is simply short compared to the first one and that probably ties into my previous point. Rumors abound regarding game's troubled development were apparently well founded.
That's not to say game is bad because, as you will have most likely noticed despite my continued rambling on regarding its negatives, this is marked as a positive review overall. It's still Lords of Shadow and if you liked the original you'll probably like this considering you can overlook its weak story. Gameplay feels familiar and skippable QTEs are god-sent, both of which are points in game's favor for me, not to mention combat and item system was expanded and enemy variety despite their designs actually means you'll end up facing quite a bit of different behaviors. Story establishes the mood very early on as one of Dracula's somber and more resigned journey, one profoundly personal despite all other events that unfold over the course of the game. Had it been properly fleshed out and Robert Carlyle's more subdued performance given time to develop, occasional hamfisted melodrama notwithstanding, it would've been a much, much better final product. I also heard some nay saying about mandatory stealth sections in the game to which I say it's about time to drop hand-holding. Barring for one section involving leaves and crazed Satyr these were a welcome diversion for me and fitting considering MC's condition story-wise.
One last caveat I feel should be posted is that playing the original game and Mirror of Fate is recommended before tackling the sequel.

This game was terrible, don't let the old school Half-Life graphics fool you. This game looks like it could have been made by a third grader, with poor level design and writing slapped onto the Half-Life gldsrc engine. In fact, the first time I saw an NPC, I thought that the game had no voices, only subtitles, because the programmer made a basic coding error that caused the voice not to play after a certain number of sounds had been played.
The first thing I noticed about this game is that there was obviously no proofreading of any of the lines and subtitles, with comical errors like, "it has escape i think it cose escape of other monsters", many of which are so rediculous, they sound like bad Japanese translations on an NES game.
The game claims to provide a backstory to Half-Life, however, the developer clearly did no research, as it explains things that are already explained, like, "What are the aliens?" and provies their own explanation, unfaithful to the Half-Life story. Also, there's really very little of this, mostly consiting of one conversation that almost explains the alien overlord. This game seems like it was written by a 10 year old.
The developer rushes the progression of the game, giving you half the arsenal within the first map. It tries to teach you how to use weapons through poorly designed puzzle gates, which are jokingly obvious to returning players, and completely impossible for new players to figure out.
To add insult to injury, the levels are confusing and poorly laid out, I got lost in the first level of the game, and found that a door previously in the level was opened for no apparent reason, most likely because of a map trigger farther along in the map. Most players could go past this part and never realize the door could be opened.
Also, it breaks basic first person shooter conventions. I found out that the reason I couldn't procede was because I needed to go to a door I thought I couldn't open, because the game does not use the E key to open doors, although it still makes the handle jiggle sound when you try to open one, probably because the developer was to lazy to take it out. Instead, you open doors by walking against them. For any past Half-Life player, or almost any FPS this is completely unintuitive, lazy, and confusing.
In short, don't waste your hard-drive space because you think this is a charming nod, or interesting new take on classic Half-Life like Black Mesa was. This is a poorly made joke of a game, falling way below the standards of the Half-Life series. There is no reason to get this game, and I am thankful that the game was free, I would be furious over spending even a penny on this piece of garbage. Go play Black Mesa instead, it's actually good.

Admittedly I'm quite a casual gamer, and have never played the Anno series until 2070, of which I only spent less than 200 hours on; as thus, I'm only comparing this game to Anno 2070.
Tl;dr: a mild Yes. And before anything else: Uplay was not an issue.
--------CON--------
Admittedly, aspects of this game are indeed a bit too simple. There is no longer a need to control Ecobalance (of which I actually found to be the most fun) or manage your production chains as much; instead of having to check your stocks and add storage to see how much resources your growing islands need, you look at a tab integrated into the UI and do simple arithmetics to see how many more production chains do you need. Also quite a large disappointment is the fact that I can't now manage to sell stuff to NPC's by building my own boats or wage wars by building my own airplanes; micromanaging your own transportation route was so much fun, and the lack of that ability is indeed disappointing.
Overall, this means that there is less to do to manage your enterprise. You sort of just keep on plopping down stuff, check spreadsheet, make sure your balance is high and keep on plopping down stuff. Anno 2070 for me was plopping down stuff constantly as well, but aside from the plot efficiency managing, you also had to think a bit more about how to organize your transportation routes and so forth.
--------MEH--------
Crisis sectors are the only real places of combat. Although this means that at least you don't have to worry about your islands being ruined, they didn't need to have taken out normal ship-building as well...
Quests... eh, they're sort of like the previous game. You pick up stuff, you find stuff, you hand it to the quest giver and get some resources or cash. Playing on standard, this often gives you a lot of rare resources, of which sometimes you may not need, but having is better than not having I guess.
Personally, I'm ok with having no coast buildings other than the slot ones. However, I would've liked to control where I placed my own port... the slots they give often requires you to place extra long roads to connect, and with the fact that you can't build warehouses to control your transportation this forces you to tie everything into the same road network; production layouts that was closed on the outside like in 2070 now requires extra roads to connect and nothing on the interior other than expanding your building.
--------PRO--------
As much as people say gameplay over graphics, the graphics is ABSOLUTELY WUNDERBAR. Like, certainly the most beautiful city-building game out there at the moment. The temperate region is ok, but the chilly arctic and the foreign moon just completely blew me away... and I was running on low with reduced resolution, as a Macbook Pro isn't exactly designed for gaming. The visual attention to details as well as the small audio blips, like from the last game, really adds the sense of immersion in this game, to the point where when I get my desktop back I'm going to just have a monitor dedicated to only run the game in postcard mode and turn on the day-night cycle.
Although the plot is fairly weak, the game was never about plot; bits and pieces of carry-over from 2070 gives a good feeling, seeing humanity recover from the great disaster that set the stage for 2070.
--------ENDING WORDS--------
Once again, I never played previous Anno games other than 2070. Even compared to 2070, this game is a fairly simple game that, indeed, doesn't have that much depth. This certainly makes the game less challenging; however, I personally enjoy the less amount of things to think and worry about, as I want to play a game to relax and have a good time. With its clear UI, simplified mechanics and the stunning graphics, I can definitely recommend this game. Maybe not so much grabbing it right now, but when it's on sale some times later I'd say that this game is definitely worth it.

The interface is intuitive, and if you've played heavier games like this, you'll pick it up quickly. The graphics are bright, colorful, and fun. The city's aesthetic really comes together well as you continue to expand, and you feel like you've built a small kingdom as you continue to grow.
All in all, the game is well-executed, pretty relaxing, and all around a lot of fun!

I played and finished this game from BOOK 1 to 5 and purchased this few day after the BOOK 4 was released. But unfortunately the number of hours doesn't show up because my machines got rebooted while somehow retains the previous save games (maybe because of the cloud save, idk for sure). Still you can trust my review. As 18.06.2016, there is a discount for this game. Grab it, buy the previous games if you haven't and enjoy the best, non-mainstream adventure story in gaming.
Mostly people complain and give bad reviews here because they:
1. Only play BOOK 1 and are disappointed on the bad graphics, boring story, and glitch
2. Don't speak english
3. Never play TLJ series before
4. Want an adventure games like The Longest Journey
At least when BOOK 4 was released, the technical and/or stability issue hardly exist. Non-english speakers may have to wait a bit for their native language to be used though. This game more similar to Dreamfall than The Longest Journey while adding some new mechanics and left out the bad ones. It works! So I commend them for doing this, no matter what the nostalgia fans will say.
Overview:
Book 1 will slowly reintroduce the characters and the situation they are having. Book 2 will allow you to explore more the world while seeing the struggle the characters. Book 3 will have the characters facing the consequence of their choices and the decision and problems start to affect them personally. Book 4 will put your characters in the middle of conflict. Book 5 will answer your questions.
Story:
I am actually glad that I play Book 1 - 4 without waiting in between because combined, the story has an appropriate pacing and character development. There seems a lot of contents that are left out of development but the story is presented beautifully and complete from Book 1 to 5. The choices and consequence are interesting and contributes well to the story. It doesn't feel like a jump from Dreamfall: TLJ  in terms of story but it still overwhelming on the first 2 hours as they throw the lore at you. But the story will walk you through it gradually. The lore is also very refreshing as they put some references of tales from other cultures and not something similar to D&D with something overly-used like the Orcs, Elves or medieval european heavy armored knights. For new players, I highly recommend playing this game after finishing The longest Journey and Dreamfall.
Graphics:
The design is cartoonish. I like it. The atmosphere is so lively in open air. And calm in private rooms. The lighting and colours are so beautiful. Literally wallpapers worthy at every scene. The face texture is also great and adds emotion to characters. The monster and non humans look absolutely great and unique. I use ASUS G75V gaming laptop. I set the resolution to 1600x1024 and the whole settings to medium and I get a smooth gaming experience while the beauty remains. This is why I like cartoon design. Not only timeless but it doesn't depend on the quality of the settings to look good.
Music/Soundeffects:
It is so amazing.... It adds so much to the story. Combined with its graphics, it creates a great atmosphere and experiences at a great effect to the story at the right moment. The volume is really well set and not overwhelming. The choice of indie soundstracks are cool too. And finally, Ingvild Hasund - Rush is back!
Dialogues/Voice acting:
PERFECT. Truly a trademark of TLJ series. The gem of the game.
Gameplay:
You will spend most of time running around the area to reach the goals. The speed of run is quite slow if you compare to popular action games. But it makes sense because the character you are playing are mostly in public and live their everyday life. So it is just weird if the sprinting around asking questions and frantically searching for stuffs and clues. Speaking of which, the game will rarely help you to find these. You have to rely on your common sense (aka understanding of the game concept/mechanics) and interact with the things around. That is immersive. But you may feel frustrated especially when you are used to the slow jogging. Most of puzzles are quite lame and easy to solve
Verdict: 8/10
As a TLJ fan, I think this game is just a little less than perfect due to mediocre puzzles and some minor inaccuracies. Dreamfall Chapters is immersive, beautiful, lore-heavy, story-gripping, adventure games. All fans should play this game when they are able.

Warning: This not a review but a personal thought about the game.  If you are looking for a review go check what other good people wrote :-)
It was 7 or 8 years ago, I bought a (long gone now) PC Gaming Magazine called PC Master.  In it, there was a game called Dreamfall : The Longest Journey.   "The long awaited continuation to the Longest Journey" it said.  I started playing it and that was it.  I fell in love with the protagonists.  Fell in love with the story.  But the second game ended and I was full of questions.  And then nothing.
Years passed.  I finished school, I nearly finished my studies. My father died.  Life continued.
And then I heard about a kickstarter campaign to create a third game to the series.  That was one of my happiest days of my life.  It reminded me of a simpler time.
And today, at long last I finished the story of this game.  One chapter of my life closed.  But the story has not ended.  My life continues and this game reminded me that every decision I take, adds up to who I am.  And to where I am going.
Thank you Red Thread Games for creating an awesome finale to the series. Thank you.

OutDrive is a time-based, retro driving game where you must maintain a relatively constant speed in order to keep your girlfriend alive. During the introductory scene, you face off with three unknown assailants with terrible aim, who miss you entirely and strike your girlfriend in the chest. With instructions given from your on-dash computer, you install a makeshift terminal to her heart and drive off into the sunset. End scene.
With that being the whole plot of OutDrive, we're left with little else to go by. Now, I can get past a subpar story if the game is well made, but the key, untold aspects of who we are, who those people were and why I can perform heart surgery on a whim are just the beginning. OutDrive is truly a dull, pointless game to play.
With no key binding options available, pushing play will start the game immediately, without any formal instructions or direction, nor any prompts telling you what the controls are. You're left with ten seconds to figure it out before you lose and have to restart. Now, restarting isn't a big deal since there is little purpose to starting in the first place; however, once you begin cruising along, your mission is to maintain your high rate of speed to keep your nameless girlfriend alive, keeping the engine running between "too slow" and "too fast". Driving too slow will kill your girlfriend, driving too fast, in theory, would do the same, but it doesn't. You can hammer down the throttle and suffer no consequences, despite what the game tells you.
Driving in OutDrive is cumbersome and feels unnaturally stiff and heavy. Your car flip-flops between feeling like go-kart and a truck with no power steering; hitting curbs or boundaries will cause your heart meter to fade drastically and often send your car flying in a seemingly random direction [if you're lucky you'll crash in the tunnels and clip through the terrain].
After some practice, I was able to control the car appropriately, but after mastering the controls, there wasn't much else do to. The game states the track "never ends", which to date nobody can prove otherwise, removing a satisfying ending from the mix; so you're left wandering aimlessly down the track, dodging other vehicles, jumping ramps and taking sharp turns and hoping you run into some fun along the way.
On the store page it hints at something interesting at the eight minute mark, stating: "P.S. Try to hold out for 8 minutes...", which, once you get there, becomes a major disappointment. A neon helicopter descends from the sky, firing mini guns and rockets, creating the first and only burst of energy the game could muster. However, after 30 seconds the helicopter randomly explodes, leaving just you and your thoughts alone until the next eight minute marker and its inevitable return.
The longest I drove was around the 36:00 minute mark before realizing I was just wasting time, expecting entertainment and adventure from a game that has none. As the realization set in and I started to think of everything else I could be doing with my time, I crashed into a wall, died and shut it off. OutDrive does just what it says: it drives you out of the game.



Overall, OutDrive is a hollow, shell of what a game really could be; with boring backgrounds, clunky steering, no purpose and no story, OutDrive is nothing more than an 80s mix tape that you listen to while smashing the space button until your fingers hurt.

8.5/10
Overview: Third Person Action Adventure
The Good
+ The setting is a mixture of a modern city in ruins and Draculas old castle. Both settings provide a nice contrast with each other and are fun to explore
+ The first major difference from the original is the ability to control the camera as opposed to having a fixed camera in the first game.
+ The second major change is all the levels are interconnected with each other. This provides for a much more immersive and seamless experience with gameplay.
+ Combat is more refined than the original and just as fun. You have light magic that does less damage but heals you whenever you damage an enemy and chaos magic that does significantly more damage but is slower and has less range. Effectively dodging and switching between your magic meters is fun and engaging. If you played the first game, the combat should offer little surprise to you. One key difference is by using attacks over and over again you can increase your mastery of a certain weapons making them stronger.
+ Boss battles have always been a highlight for this series and this game is no exception. Bosses are unique, well designed and will require you to use all your techniques in battle to defeat them.
+ the game has plenty of collectables scattered throughout the world
+ The game features 16 optional challenges to further extend your game time. Each challenge has a series of objectives that has to be completed in order to complete the challenge.
+ option to disable quicktime events
The Average
The story is not awful but it didn't really do much either. It doesn't help that most of the dialogue spoken by the villains is bad.
This game has some REALLY annoying enemies that will test your patience
The Bad
For some odd reason the developers decided to include stealth sections in the game. I like stealth games and I like it when developers try to mix up the gameplay but this was just a bad effort. The stealth sections feel very out of place and are not always clear in what you have to do making for some really frustrating trial and error. It also feels very odd that you play a badass destroying most enemies in your path only to reach a section in the level where you have to avoid enemies.
Conclusion
This game fixed two of my biggest gripes from the first game. The fact that the levels are interconnected and the ability to actually control the camera make for a much better gameplay experience despite the awful stealth sections. I was a bit baffled that reviewers panned this game pretty badly as I think this game improves the first game in many ways. If you enjoyed the first game then there is no reason why you shouldn't love this game as well, unless of course the modern day setting doesn't appeal to you.

First Review uptade:
Short Version: Management games don't have to be about isolation. Isolated maps, isolated game modes or missions. Anno 2205 is about continuous gameplay, development, integration and blending of systems. Elegant game design is the core here. Its like previous games of the series where cake ingredients and this edition finally mixed and taken then together to the oven.
Long Version:
Anno 2205 mix in a very interesting way the concept of endless mode and campaing of most city builders. The improvements and streamlining of user interface and gameplay are notable and really make the game more enjoyable to play than previous titles in the series.
The use of more than one "biome" really put more emphasis on interconnecting the economies of different regions and the little changes in gameplay between this biomes are a nice little change of mood.
Battles still feel like a inadequade guest in Anno games, but at least this time they are more well constrained to a side mission structure, making them easier to ignore if you like or more like a small lite action romp to briefly easy your mind.
A big notable change to gameplay is the fact that now you can change the position of previously placed structures. At first this seem like a way to make placemant mistakes less of a nuisance, but on long term has few interesting repercussions on gameplay. For once, previously planning placement of everything on the map is much less important, but at same time you have much more room for constante tinkering and optimization city of layouts. A feel that, for the proposed structure of continuous gameplay and multiple cities, this is a welcome change.
A nice first impression from this strategy/builder. It is familiar but not afraid to change core aspects of the genre design and I think mostly well succeded in doing so. If any impression changes in the long term gameplay I'll update the review again.

After reading the many negative reviews from people who played it for less than an hour -- some were even from people who played for 30 minutes -- then reading the reasons for the negativity, I just want to warn you guys about the accuracy of some of the claims. I've played all the annos and loved them. I purposely did not read the reviews until I got it for myself and played for 6 hours. I already know a lot of the bad reviews would solely be over the fact that you have to use uplay. Lo and behold, I got it right.
--First, I want to say, give the game about 5 hours of gameplay. That's about how long it takes to really feel the game as a whole and see what it can bring and if you like what it's bringing--
I'm going to talk about the game first. When I just started, I felt like the game was a bit "fast" in terms of progression and I was breezing through it. I wasn't forced to micromanage right away like the older annos. Now am I saying that the game is easy like the others claim it to be? No, not at all. For those who never played any anno series, I think starting with this one would be best because the game starts off easily enough. However, I think they designed it this way so that you can reach the point of the game where you now have to be aware of your resources and if leveling up your people into higher tier shiny buildings can cause you to not have adequate resources for your regions/cities. It pretty much wants you to get to the meat of the game fast. But once you get to that point, you have to take your time.  Also, unlike the other anno series where you have to check your cities on the other islands constantly, this time around, you just need to simply  go back and forth from the temperate region, the arctic, and finally, the moon. Once you hit the arctic region, that's when the fun starts.
Again, you must be willing to invest more than 2 hours to really experience what the game is capable of (although, as I've mentioned earlier, I really recommend 5). When you start having colonies in the arctic region, you must ensure they have enough heat sources which they can get from the factories you plop down *they have a heat radius*. From there, you must make sure that your other region is trading enough of what they need (and vice versa). It's more streamlined/trade flow than the other annos.
The moon is my current challenge because it's very expensive to colonize. You also have to make sure that you have the protective shield around your colony so they don't get smashed into smitherins by them asteroids.
Aesthetic wise, the game is gorgeous. Very beautiful and I just love going in postcard mode, just looking around my settlements. The only issue I have with this is it might need a bit more optimization. My desktop can run skyrim with all the heavy mods in ultra setting with no issues. But I get drops of FPS here and there with this game. Not so bad though and not often. But I feel it will be a bit of an issue later on when I have more things congregated in one spot.
Bugs? Currently no bugs for me.
Interface? I love the interface on this one. That one they optimized well.
Battle system? I never liked that part on any of my annos because I always felt them lacking. However, I liked what they did on this one very much. You now have to have fuel in order to do certain things with your vessels (like, repair) but at the same time, you can salvage around for the "special" abilities as I call em. You can get them from enemies you sunk or just floating around. This revamp made battling enjoyable for me.
I'm not saying the negative reviews don't deserve to be heard. But, generally, with games like these, it's best to eye the ones that invested a big chunk of time before putting a negative reviews. Reviews such as, "ugh, uplay! Bad GAME", or "NO MP?! WELL F-- THIS GAME! TIS HORRIBLE!", isn't exactly something to go by. Sadly, it repels other gamers from getting the game and they end up missing out on a game they have the potential of investing a lot of time and enjoyment in.
Again,I've played the other annos. I actually like this game a lot. I read some inaccuracies on a bit of negative reviews which made me realize they obviously did not invest a couple hours at least in the game. It's not water downed. It's a bit different from the previous anno but it brings it's own flavor of difficulties with it.
That's about it. I don't want to invest too much time on other's reviews than the actual game itself in my review. I hope I pointed certain things out enough that it will encourage you to make your own decisions. Luckily steam has a refund policy so you always have that option.
PS: Do not listen to those who said even on youtube it has a negative review. No. Most of them are quite positive (I know because I've been watching a lot of em' before  I bought the game). Also, there's a lot of fair reviews about the game and I saw it was a pretty consistent B+ average. (A lot of the ratings I've seen so far were averaging 8).

Purchased on sale for $4.00 US.  I must stay I this is the best deal I have gotten on Steam.
The game at this point is still in early access but there is a lot to do.  I you enjoy designing and building as I do then this game is a no brainer even at $20.00 US.  I like that there really is no unit balance.  There are weapon balances, and counters but bigger is better as long as your ship/sub/flying thing does not have a weakness.  It is fun to kill large craft with a small one when you know the weakness but it is frustrating to have your large craft destroyed by a flying squirrel as well.
I enjoy playing the game in the state that it is in currently where you can build a fleet and attack an enemy fleet either in testing or in campaign.  I have tried out multiplayer a little with a friend and it is fun to play but needs some polish is some areas.
My biggest dislikes at this point are that when switching views from first person to map to a fleet view the ship selection keys are not the same and sometimes a selected ship will not be selected in the next view.  This can be frustrating expecially for a new player that expects these things to be seamless.
My second dislike is that in order to save processor time some ships are "out of area" which in itself is a good idea but I don't like how it is handled in combat.  In my experience, you start with one ship and over time get access to more ships or as ships are distroyed a different one comes on line.  From a balance, standpoint it makes it so that bigger is better.  You cannot have multiple small ships take on a big ship and if I have a huge fleet against 3 ships I have to fight them 1 on 1 which is not how it should be.
The game is under heavy active development so be warned.  If you make a ship today, it may not work at the next update due to game changes in development.  I understand and don't mind learning the new things as they come but if you don't like change you will not like this phase of development in this game.  Example, Campaign resources went to 0.  Ship AI changed and all player created ships would not attack correctly in this last update.

To be perfectly honest, if you want more Lords of Shadow, you're better off replaying the first game.
I feel this one really missed the mark, and after reading about the internal struggles of the development team and their near-constant battle with their director, I can say I'm not really surprised.
Lords of Shadow 2 is, in every way, inferior to its predecessor. Graphically, it fails to impress. Mechanically, it feels sloppy. The combat is frustrating and choppy and, while LoS1 had its fair share of controller-throwing platforming segments, LoS2 doesn't even justify its own such moments with an equal helping of fun, satisfying ones. I have only put a couple hours into the game so far, and already I'm mad at it. I cannot comment on the overall story yet, but the beginning feels rushed and strange, and I have to feel bad for Patrick Stewart being forced to deliver such a petty script as Zobek. The writing is childish and uninspired, and the semi-animated lore sequence explaining the Belmont lineage is utterly boring.
But you know, I could forgive all of that if the game didn't so completely miss its own point. At no time during play did I ever FEEL like Dracula, who is supposed to be an absolute powerhouse, combining strength, speed, and magical abilities to devastate ranks upon ranks of foes. The most basic of enemies can take a monumental beating from any of your weapons, and can even attack straight through your combos to strike you. One minor strike from an enemy, however, will interrupt your combo and send you flying, which makes your stature feel pitiful, even if you aren't taking significant damage from those attacks. These problems are only magnified and exacerbated when, after the tutorial sequence, the story fast-forwards some centuries and resets all of Gabriel's powers, requiring you to slowly unlock them, one by one.
Other games have successfully portrayed their protagonists as extremely powerful beings without robbing the game of its core challenge. A great case in point is Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine. Lords of Shadow 2, however, takes the legendary Dracula and nerfs him into the ground, and then poops all over him with bad gameplay mechanics.
I'll say it again: if you want more LoS, play the first game again, because you'll enjoy it a whole lot more.

If you enjoyed the first game this one is even better, spoken as one of the many who openly hate other attempts at 3d Castlevania titles, playing as Dracula for once was a welconme twist to the normal gameplay.

Solid, smooth fighting mechanic is not sufficient in my opinion to carry the whole wieght of this game. I'll start with the good elements of the game, then follow up with what went wrong with it:
Pros:
-Smooth fighting style and movement
-All three weapons are unique and special in thier own way with robust upgrading tree for each.
-Atmospheric scenes and amazing Castle design are enough to leave you at awe at some moments.
-Some great and well designed boss fights scattered throughout the game.
-Collectables scattered throughout the game encourage you to explore many areas and backtrack.
Cons:
-Absolutly shallow and unnecessary "stealth" mechanic slapped on multiple parts of the game.
-The city doesn't leave a memorable moment. Its colorless and many times make you feel like you want to run through it as quick as possible.
-Particle effects of attacking/blocking leave you blind to where the enemies hits will come from midcombat.
-Blocking is ineffective when you are swarmed my multiple enemies. leaving you vulnerable to consecutive hits after your first block.
-Many boss fights feel scripted, with no way for you to beat bosses unless you do it the way the game wants you to.
-The story is such a drag, with characters coming and going with no backstories to them.

I enjoyed State of Decay. It feels like there is a lot more going on under the hood than what you see with the naked eye. Perhaps it's simply because of my play style, but I felt like there was definitely a difficulty ramping which made things frustrating by the end.
Sure, it's fun to find new and inventive ways to kill zombies, but by the end of the story, I was definitely feeling like they were just throwing waves of things at me until I died. It really shines early in the game, when you are gathering resources, striking out into the world and trying to see what you can find. There's nothing quite like the tension of hiding in a house which you know is not fully cleared, only to discover that a horde of zombies has rolled up outside. Do I lay low in this room and hope for the best? Do I try to stealthily clear the place and hope I don't catch their attention?
The system for resource management also feels nice, with upgrades to keep things feeling fresh, and then finally a chance to create your very own outpost and supply it to keep people from being zombie snacks.
All in all it excelled at making you feel like a survivor, even if it was lacking some of the grit and horror that many franchises have brought to the now heavily populated genre.

I enjoy playing the game in the state that it is in currently where you can build a fleet and attack an enemy fleet either in testing or in campaign.  I have tried out multiplayer a little with a friend and it is fun to play but needs some polish is some areas.
My biggest dislikes at this point are that when switching views from first person to map to a fleet view the ship selection keys are not the same and sometimes a selected ship will not be selected in the next view.  This can be frustrating expecially for a new player that expects these things to be seamless.
My second dislike is that in order to save processor time some ships are "out of area" which in itself is a good idea but I don't like how it is handled in combat.  In my experience, you start with one ship and over time get access to more ships or as ships are distroyed a different one comes on line.  From a balance, standpoint it makes it so that bigger is better.  You cannot have multiple small ships take on a big ship and if I have a huge fleet against 3 ships I have to fight them 1 on 1 which is not how it should be.
The game is under heavy active development so be warned.  If you make a ship today, it may not work at the next update due to game changes in development.  I understand and don't mind learning the new things as they come but if you don't like change you will not like this phase of development in this game.  Example, Campaign resources went to 0. This is a great game.  It has a connection with Sid Meier's Beyond Earth.  I've never played Beyond Earth.  I bought Starships because everything I read reminded me of the best parts of SM Railroads and Civ Revolution, in terms of presentation and style.  The play is split between tactical turn-based combat with a handful of ships and empire management.  All aspects of the game are simpler to carry out than in a full-fledged 4x game.  But this is not a 'casual game' any more than Advance Wars or Master of Orion were casual games.  The game has elements in common with both of those icons of pc gaming.  More on that later.
Shipbuilding is quick, easy, and elegant.  A simple table shows your ships and their abilities (of which there are eight or ten).  Just click on the box to upgrade X ability for Y ship.  It's one of those panels that could be dull and lifeless.  It isn't because the UI is friendly and well-made.  The combat is so streamlined and straightforward, I can look at those boxes and see in my mind the maneuvers and tactics I can pursue.
Is combat too fast and easy?  I suppose it depends on difficulty level.  This is one of those games that wants you to not just win, but to win without getting hit.  To win with style.  You can destroy every enemy ship, but if all your own fleet goes limping back to the shipyard with gaping holes, you will fall behind the building curve.
I mentioned Advance Wars above, an very simple tactics game that involved zero luck in combat:  No such thing as a miss or a fumble, and no damage roll.  All the values are fixed.  Starships is like that.  Combat among the asteroids is a game of cat-and-mouse, and it's fun!  It's actual strategy.  When the enemy ship moves right up behind your ship with its plasma cannons, you know you're dead before the weapon animation plays.  Now, there are elements of luck - a warp point (teleportation square) could drop you exactly where you do (or don't) want to be; you could end your move near a cloaked ship and see it too late to do anything about it; a severe hit could cripple your engines.  Things like that.  But all attacks hit always, and with fixed damage, unless modifiers zero out the damage completely, such as firing through too many asteroid fields or from too far away.
On the imperial side, the game's diplomacy and construction takes just the right amount of time.  Enough to engage you but not enough to drag you through tiresome clicks and endless notifications.  Strategic turns end when you grant the crew shore leave (almost like dividing the treasure in SM Pirates).  Empire management is quick and easy, and it all makes sense.  I feel compelled to repeat that:  It all makes sense.  No arbitrary or clumsy features at all.  And the possibilities are legion.  You can have a couple of uber ships or several lesser ones.  There is a lot to experiment with.  Empire and fleet mirror each other in a sense - each has to fit the other's strengths.
The other empire leaders and admirals have just enough artwork and personality to give you the sense that the galaxy is alive and populated.  Dialogue lasts just the right amount of time - not very long.  You can examine the shps you will be fighting, and you really should to avoid nasty surprises.
Really, SM Starships is a computerized board game, just at the border of a full-blown pc strategy game but not going over the line.  It is clearly a game, not a sim of anything or an attempt to capture the whole universe in a gigabyte.
Many games offer a thousand paths to victory, all of them dull.  It's hard to put a finger on what it is that makes a slew of possible strategy all sound appealing, but Starships succeeds in that, with bright colors and bright ideas.  I feel in charge of all my fleet and empire's doings, with no compromises just to make the game or the dev's  happy.  It's about me.  Or you.  SM Starships is good stuff.

Starbound is a game that features a ton of different mechanics and items, weapons, etc. After playing it a while, I really enjoyed my time there, but man, there are a lot of flaws. As with many people that write reviews, I just wish there was a 'neutral' option for the recommendation choice. I'd only use it for this one, however.
Anyway, here's the premise of Starbound (Spoilers Ahead)
[spoilers] Starbound starts off in an alternate universe where several different races coexist with one another. These races include the Humans, the Apex, the Floran, the Avians, the Hylotls (or however it's spelled), the Glitch, and the Novakids. These races can be played as your character, however you want them to be like. The Terran Protectorate is an organization founded to keep the peace across the galaxy, and your character starts off as a graduating member of the Protectorate. Everything seems fine and dandy when all of a sudden: the Ruin, a being bent on mass galactical destruction, destroys the entire Earth and forces the player to evacuate on a beaten-down ship, which is where the official game starts, as the player now has to survive with limited resources and a ship that can barely function. [/spoilers]
One of my biggest gripes with this game is the Main Questline. It could have been so much more in-depth, (more spoilers) [spoilers] but it's literally "Go here, scan things relating to an alien race, come back and do a quest dungeon"[/spoilers]. I would have enjoyed it I could get to know the characters better, listen to what their story is, but my wish was not granted. Sure, they aren't soulless machines (those are the Glitch), but you don't know a lot about them, either.
Do not get me wrong, it's a good game, but it's not at all
. I just hope the devs make some kind of a DLC to crunch out more story, so some people enjoy the game better.

This game improves upon everything they did in first game.  No more fixed camera, and there's a decent arsenal of subweapon to experiment with.  They way you level up weapons and techniques encourages variety in combat.  Unlike the first game the Light and Dark magic forms have their own weapons.  Void Sword and Chaos Claws once leveled up can be used long enough so you can experiment with them instead of just using them when you know you the extra health or damage.  Also since the game is open world it's much easier to backtrack and find secrets you may have missed on your first time through.  That was the biggest pain about LoS1 since you have replay an entire stage.  Though at least the chapters were divided up into multiple areas.
Hard to understand all the hate for this game, but I get why it's not for mostt.  The story whacky, and the events that bridge the two games have their own 3DS game (which was ported to console and PC).  Kind of depressing since the summary they give in the beginning of this game is really interesting.  Almost wish that Mirror of Fate would've been Lords of Shadow 2, then make this game Lords of Shadow 3.  My biggest complaint about the story is how they treated Victor Belmont.  I assume he's suppose to be Richter, but given that you meet him and 20 minutes later he sacrifices himself, I can see why they changed his name.  Really wish there was more of him in the game.
Environments in the present day segments are pretty dull.  No real variations in it, just greyed out industrial areas.  The other parts of the set Castlevania's past feel alive.  Definitely feels like the devs had fun making those areas.  On the other hand, maybe it's some sort of commentary from the devs saying that building and architechture in the present day are boring compared to ancient castles.
Enemy designs also don't feel very varied either.  Boss design is on point though aside from the final boss.  *SPOILER WARNING* Final boss is Satan inside Alucard's body.  I was hoping for something a little more unique.  And since you only see Alucard for the last little section of the game (though technically he is there for the entire game disguised as the Zobek's second in command) it's disappointing that he's only there for that last little bit.
Speaking of Alucard.  his DLC is solid too.  It has actual cinemas unlike how the DLC for LoS1 was handled.  He doesn't have new weapons for the magic modes, but the DLC is just long enough you don't notice it.  The only disappointing thing about the DLC is Alucard doesn't have any attacks for his Bat Swarm or Spectral Wolf abilities in combat or with magic.  Would've been a nice touch.  Oh yeah, the actor that plays Rob Stark from Game of Thrones does his voice if you're wondering why he sounds familiar.

Kingdoms and Castles is an excellent sim game, in the vein of the old Caesar strategy games.  The pixel art is adorable, and the music and sound fits the game perfectly.  It is an economic sim - there are enemies, but gathering lumber on the first play through is harder than any combat I've dealt with.  I would highly recommend this game to anyone interested in economic sims or building games.

While this game does not have many structures to build, and a few bugs, I had a large amount of fun while playing. This game uses the features it has extremely well and provides a significant challenge once the viking raids and dragons become more common. It is like Banished but I find this game to be better due to its better designed UI and art style. It also helps that the dev team has a discord serer set up so they can easily hear community feedback and learn of bugs quickly. Something that stuck out to me was when a player reported a bug he was having with the main menu and the devs responded to him almost instantly. This tells me that the devs are trying to make this game into the best it can be and i look forward to seeing what they add in the future.

(Please do not be put off by the amount of time I have poured into this game on Steam; I have braved Lordrans challenges when Windows Live was still a thing)
Prepare To...
...fall in love with a game series that has left its mark on the video-game-landscape of today like nothing else has.
Do not make the mistake of reducing Dark Souls to only the challenge it presents.
It does not do the game as a whole justice.
Dark Souls is a masterpiece because of its world design and the way it tells a story.
Most areas tie neatly into each other, creating an interconnected world where the magic lies in the presentation and the attention to detail - not in an inflated empty vastness. Being able to look around the kingdom of Lordran, recognising certain landmarks and thus being able to trace every step of the route you have taken so far - this feels much more rewarding than just running off in one direction for miles and miles without reaching the edge of the map.
The world of Dark Souls feels coherent and believable, giving a certain weight to your journey through its forests, valleys, dungeons and castles, from up above to down below.
And the environmental storytelling in this game is, in my opinion, still unparalleled today. The exposition is minimal and Dark Souls does nothing to force its story onto the player. You can finish the game, not knowing a thing about Lordran, its past and the role you have played in the last 40-50ish hours. Or you can dive into the abyss that is the Dark Souls Lore, talking to NPCs, reading item descriptions, keeping your eyes open for the little details in the environment. Trying to piece together all the lore bits and pieces is a challenge all in itself. But it adds to the feeling that you are part of the events that are taking place, that you are part of the history of the wonderfully intimidating world From Software has created.
Dark Souls is not perfect. It is rough around the edges, but honestly - truly great games have never been perfect.

One of the most compelling and incredible games I've ever played. The graphics are amazing--I found myself enjoying just wandering around Propast. Each scene is ginormous and detailed. Having watched Marcuria develop from the first TLJ and Dreamfall: TLJ, I must say they've perfected it's design in Chapters. It was the perfect little fairytale town. The story takes it's time unfolding, and that's fine. You don't want to get in a hurry to finish, because then you have to find something else to do. And there is NO combat or stealth gameplay, much to my relief. Glad the developers decided to kill that idea after the disastrous Dreamfall: TLJ.
Take heed: Anyone who tells you that you don't need to play The Longest Journey or the sequel Dreamfall: The Longest Journey is fully and completely LYING to you. If you are playing Chapters and haven't played the other two, stop what you're doing now and go back to the beginning of the trilogy. These are an absolute must if you want to fully understand and appreciate what's going on and pick up on the nuances.
A word of warning, the task of completing the first two games in the trilogy is a bit of a drag (just my opinion). The storylines are fantastic, but it's the gameplay that will make you go grrr. The first one, The Longest Journey, was released in 1999 and the graphics, well...they were cutting edge for the turn of the century, but having played it for the first time in 2016, I was woefully underwhelmed. The storyline is fantastic, though, and you'll find you can easily overlook the ancient technology. And then the second one, Dreamfall TLJ, well...while the storyline of the second one is just as rich and deep as the rest of them, it contains elements of combat and stealth (hiding from beasties and what-nots) that I did not care for AT ALL. I'm a purist when it comes to adventure games. I like to relax and appreciate the environment and storyline--if I wanted action I would go play an arcade game. I don't know how the developers slept at night after giving us the frustrating combat/stealth garbage that went with Dreamfall. Even people who enjoy that kind of thing found it bad, sluggish, and just overall poorly designed. One good thing (and the only good thing) about it is there's an autosave feature just before a fight, and you don't run out of lives so you can die as many times as it takes to get it, and you will, eventually. If I could do it, you most certainly can. But anyway, like I said, in order to appreciate Chapters, you gotta get through the first two games. So I recommend you get an XBox 360 controller for Windows (about $20 if you want brand new), because that's the only way you're going to get through Dreamfall:TLJ without tearing your hair out.
Enjoy your trip down the rabbit hole, and don't forget to come up for air.

While the store page lists the many features this game has to offer following its predecessor, they are simply not sufficient to do justice and present an acceptable game. Red Faction 2 is a sequel but instead of being superior it manages to be inferior in almost every aspect.
While the Geo-Mod has been revamped it actually offers fewer possibilities for experimenting and is ultimately a letdown during the story mode. Instead of controlling a miner joining forces with the rebellion we control one of the 6-member squad that wishes to take revenge against their former leader. Sopot is the chancellor of a military state known as The Commonwealth and he eliminates thousands of soldiers that all became enhanced through stolen nanotechnology. He fears they may take over one day so he quickly eliminates them - but not quickly enough for our protagonists to escape.
The red planet has been replaced with planet Earth. For me one of the key elements of Red Faction's atmosphere was Mars where the journey was taking place. Regardless of how many more weapons, items and controllable vehicles the sequel has to offer its atmosphere cannot match that of the first game. And while Volition and THQ managed to get voice actors such as Lance Henriksen and Jason Statham they are not enough to change our mind.
These former squad members are all professionals; enhanced by nanotechnology so you essentially control a super soldier called Alias. The combat is much, much faster (in fact, too fast) and you notice you keep dying but not due to the game being difficult but because your health packs are automatically used once your health bar reaches zero. Essentially, due to this mechanics you'll check your health bar less frequently. The story is clichéd, there's a twist here and there, some boss battles and some (very nice) pre-rendered cutscenes but all in vain.
I think it's a matter of even versus odd - the 2nd is exactly as Armageddon was to Guerrilla: a letdown.

While the gameplay is fun, the way that the menus and tutorials are written leaves me wondering who this game was made for. "Hamming keys"? "Rage quitting"? One of the tutorial quizzes asked whether a certain mission was "Too hard" or "Too easy". "Too hard" was counted as a wrong answer, with the admonishment of "nonsense" when clicked. The mission took me something like 5 tries to get it right, because the missiles wouldn't fly where I pointed them to. That's an acceptable bug in an alpha, but what's unacceptable is being told it isn't a problem at all. It leaves me unimpressed and not very hopeful that the final product will be any good.
Beyond that, the options for gameplay are pretty limited, and again I have little to no hope for improvement in this area given the attitude of the developers, ie "if you don't like it, you're wrong." The gameplay options are
1. Creative mode, where you can build anything you want with zero challenge and infinite resources. Bo-ring.
2. Adventure mode, where you have resource limitations that force you to build using your head, but also are quickly overrun by waves of enemies that will quickly destroy you, even when the damage is set to 10%
3. Campaign mode, which would seem promising: You start out with a large base that is both an excellent resource gatherer and has good defenses. But as soon as a battle begins (which cannot be canceled, despite there being an option for it--it is greyed out with no hint as to what enables it) your home base, and any ships you might have, turn into green rectangle outlines and are useless. You can't even stand on them and your little robot sinks. Selecting to end the battle automatically destroys your ships as "casualties", and then you have nothing.
This game has a LOT of areas where it desperately needs improvements and bugfixes, but the die-hard fanbase seems bent on insisting that there's nothing wrong with it, at all, ever, and the devs seem to agree. Don't count on this game being worth your money.
As a postscript, I've noticed that a lot of reviewers for this game have mentioned that the learning curve is too steep. I'm not going to discount or invalidate their opinions on the matter, since I'm sure the plurality of such reviews is indicative that there is a subset of gamers for which this game's mechanics will not be in the slightest bit intuitive. I, however, have extensive experience with some of the more finicky mods in Minecraft such as IndustrialCraft and Forestry, and therefore have that background in hooking up blocks correctly. The only hitch I ran into was learning that exhaust pipes are not omnidirectional and have to be oriented a certain way in order to attach. That said, despite fully understanding the building mechanics, and seeing a lot of potential for this game, I once again must say that I have no faith that this potential will be lived up to. Not only have I seen this attitude in the game's writing, the authors of positive reviews, and commenters on negative views, this review, despite being written out with great thought and care, is being marked as "not helpful", by who I can only assume are those die-hard fans feeling salty that anyone might say anything critical about a game they like. This is what is killing gaming.

This game is awesome. I don't think there is any other game out there where you can design a cannon that can punch through the armour of a warship, then add a fuze that makes the shell explode inside the target ship for lots of damage, then mount that cannon on a turret on an airship, aircraft, or just a regular old cruiser. Then design a gatling gun to take out aircraft, build a laser system to shoot down incoming missiles, and then switch gears and build a submarine that launches torpedos loaded with EMP charges that zap through metal armour to take out the electronics controlling turrets and weapons, or the ship itself.
The best part is that everything is built out of blocks that interact with each other so that the effect of the damage on subsystems can be interesting as well e.g. if an explosion takes out a chunk of your engine, the effect varies whether it manages to break the crankshaft in two, takes out exhaust piping, etc.
This game requires a lot of patience though, the learning curve is steep. My very first ship would flip over the moment it hit the water. That said if you like building and designing it is well worth it. 233 hours in and still having a lot of fun with this game. I think that stands for itself.
P.S. There are some really useful guides on the various systems in the game on the official forum, I suggest taking a look once you've gotten your feet wet. Looking at designs there was a great way to get inspiration for hull shapes and weapon systems as well. Also, if you're like me, I suggest looking at some of the engine collections on the Steam workshop, there are some well made and optimized engines e.g. KuramaFox's unified engine raft. I like to pick a pre-made design that suits my needs (high-efficiency, high-power, or small size?) for my ships on so I can focus on other things, like fine tuning cannons or designing torpedoes or a laser system. OTOH you might find that you enjoy building and tuning engines ...there's a lot of content in this game.
Lastly, it helps to start small. Try building small boats and airships and work your way up from there.

I'm a great fan of the Anno series, but my recommendation is as follows:
Do not buy at this time.  Wait for a significant discount.
Pros
Graphics are, as always, extremely beautiful
Cons (in order of impact from my perspective)
*  (Added later)  My new worst con is that the epilepsy warning lasts literally 30 seconds and you can't escape out of it.  You have to wait every time!!!
*  The change in battle mechanics is just too much for me.  Having a dedicated zone with no risk in your home sectors is no fun.
*  There is no sandbox game capability - it's all campaign only.
*  You can't trade energy from map to map, so I have +1000 energy in one map because it's special project is actually energy generation, and am starved in the next, but can't utilize my surplus.  (Edit:  You end up being able to very deep in the advancement chain)
*  Islands are in no way 5 times larger as was stated - they might be larger, but the buildable space is actually pretty small.
*  Zoom capability - you can't zoom out much and I feel too close to the map.
* Control-Number assignment doesn't work.  You can't assign 1 to your command ship which is actually quite disrupting.
* Other comments have mentioned the change in logistics, storage etc, and I actually prefer the old way.  Everything seems too dumbed down to me and it potentially removes game play hours.  I can see myself getting bored much more quickly since it already seems like a simplified (and disappointing) grind.
My hope is these things will be addressed in patches or free updates, but for now, I'd wait if I were you.

This game is gorgeous, filled with lots of fun, action, and intrigue. Ultimately it is a city builder, but it also has a lot of naval combat and more from what I can tell so far. You start as a fledgling corporation of your design. Slowly you build your way up, gain connections, and explore the vast areas of the planet and the moon! No longer do you have to balance climate and factory output like in its predecessor. Instead just keep a balanced checkbook, build, explore, and destroy. There are tons of sub missions inside sub missions and a ton of achievements to unlock. Did I mention how beautiful this game is? The attention to detail is exquisite to say the least. There are no save game states like before, now it is an automated feature, kind of like in an MMORPG. You make a corp., and work within that game state. If you want to make a new game, you start a new corporation. So the missions, achievements, and different gameplays, are all a part of the same ongoing campaign. I am not sure how deep the game is at the moment, but from what I can surmise and from the previous Anno titles you can rest assured that the game will be a joy to play, over and over again. If you are a fan of Anno titles, or like building sites, exploring, and blowing stuff up, then this game is for you!
