TL;DR : The game's scope is smaller than I expected. The combat is passable with a few fatal flaws. There's almost too much sh*t going on at once, making your fellow survivors seem incompetent. You become the ONLY survivor capable of making any change.
Combat: I initially liked it. It felt right, except when I started to get into it, the flaws became apparent. First is that your hits feel weak. You can hit a zombie multiple times and they don't go down. 4-5 hits into one zombie at times? Come on.
The next issue is that when you knock a zombie onto the ground, you have to press a special button in order to finish them off in one hit. That's fine, but if you attack normally near them, your survivor will just lock onto that downed zombie and chop at him uselessly. It can take many, many hits just to kill a downed zombie that way. That, while annoying, isn't the issue. If another zombie walks up to you while you're spazzing out on the downed zombie, they can just ignore your hits on that downded zombie and f*ck up your day. So you can end up in a situation where your survivor is fighting a group of 3 and is struggling hard.
The last thing about combat is that some of the skills that you learn are useless, while others are very useful. So you have 'beginer's trap' skills that are completely useless. Great.
Oh and heavy weapons are sh*t. They're too slow to be useful and they don't seem to hit any harder. Other than occasionally knocking zombies to the ground.
The scope : It's small. I looked at the map initially and I thought to myself " Cool, when I'm done looting all this stuff I'll be able to move on. I mean, this sh*t's all finite anyway." Nope. That's all you get. You have one map and it never gets bigger. I'm not expecting Grand Theft Auto levels of grandure, but come on. The size of the playable area is pathetic.
The missions that pop up onto the map are too numerous. It becomes stressful and overwhelming because chances are you're trying to do your own sh*t. Thinking about the base and what you might need at the time and oh look, there's about five f*cking people who need your help. It wouldn't be so bad if there were a timer attached to each of the missions that you could SEE. There already is an invisible timer, so it's a f*cking guessing game how long you can ignore it a given mission. Generally they're pretty generous, but regardless I would like a time frame and just less bullsh*t to deal with.
The last thing is the AI. By and large they're good. Sometimes though they become catatonic for absolutely no reason. They're being attacked by two zombies and you're right behind them. They'll crouch down, cover their heads and scream like a b*tch. No reason. Then seconds later they're start swinging into a group of five zombies. Great.
Oh and time passes ingame while you're not playing it. They don't explain that at all. It's just a thing. Enjoy watching your hard earned resources p*ssed away by time!

I absolutely loved the first game in this series I was literally dumbfounded at how much I loved it. Unfortunately this can't be said for this one. The fighting system didn't feel anywhere near as fluid as the first game, the environments were no where near as atmospheric and the story felt rushed and fractured. The curse of the sequel!

- Graphics :
Very very good. Few glitches here & there. Still wondering why Dracul would have a shadow but no reflection (because they're kind of the same thing...). But a very nice and polished game graphically speaking. Artistic direction is... you know, quite nice. The environment are less numerous than in the previous game considering we really have two sets : the castle & the modern town, but both are cool to explore (yes, even the modern world).
- Sound & Musics :
Voice acting is yet again very good, musics are kind of below the quality of the first game's ones.
- Gameplay :
A bit better than the first game : it's still the same thinking but with more variety (you got a whip, your fists & a sword this time), the moves are really fun to launch and there's more strategy this time. The boss fights have also improved.... 'xcept the last one...
- Storytelling :
So, it's the conclusion, and all in all it's not that bad but there's one thing that totally ruined it for me : the ending. The last battle & the ending following that is one of the worst I've seen. Last battle : too easy and not at all making you feel involved in it. And the ending was totally rushed, it just sucks. This whole ending was completely rushed.
- Length :
Half the time you'll need to complete the first LoS, this game is much shorter (partly due to the fact that it's much easier)
CONCLUSION :
IT'S NOT A BAD GAME. You need to remember that. BUT:  it's lacking a lot in the storytelling (especially nearing the end) & in environment. I still recommend it because the whole experience isn't a bad one... not just the epic game everyone was expecting.....

Lords of Shadow 2 is a great game when it wants to be but unfortunately it's marred by misguided forced stealth sequences and a story that goes nowhere until the tail end of the adventure. The modern setting looks more like a faux Resident Evil than it does Castlevania and the game only really shines when it will occasionally go back to its familiar Gothic locale.
It's not all bad though, the combat is really great and even by the end you'll still be pumping points into it to unlock new combos. It's also a very gorgeous game and is a fantastic PC port.
Lords of Shadow 2 is a disappointment more than anything. The series had amazing potential after the underrated Lords of Shadow in 2010 but it's all been squandered here with head scratching design choices and plot that just plods along until it feels like pushing forward. This is a game only for those who have put their time in with the two games before it and really want to experience the ending of the trilogy.

This mod is a fairly well constructed mod but it falls short on multiple areas.
Before I get to those points let me discuss what it does well:
1: Remodels nearly all weapons
2: Nice setpiece of the boat
3: Challenging, this game actually is HARD. I played it on normal and I barely survived the mod with about 14% health left.
Now that I discussed how this mod is good let me discuss how it falls short:
1: Little to no story. Seriously the most story you get is from the title screen. Everything else is either hidden away or non existant.
2: Very short. If you are a skilled player of Half-Life you can probably breeze through this mod in about 20 min or less. The boat is the ONLY level.
3: Boss fight is lackluster. Just circle-strafe the motionless (And by motionless I mean it has no animations except the grabber tongue.) Nilanth trying to get you like a Grabber and unload all of your bullets into it. Done.
4: The flying enemies glitch into the sky when you kill them. Maybe this was a problem with the original HL as I have only played up till Lamba Labs.
5: Box puzzle with the elevator could have been a bit more obvious as most people don't know you can grab sliding objects with their USE key. I sure didn't and that's the first time I have seen that in action and boy does it not want to go into the spot you want it to.
Overall if you wanted a quick mod to breeze through mindlessly then go for it. Otherwise just don't bother as it is just lackluster.

Reviewing Dark Souls...
How do I even review Dark Souls?  It is one of the most notorious games in recent history.
Well I'll make a few points that I would have liked to know when I started this game:
#1. Go to the Dark Souls Nexus and download the graphical mod called DSfix.  Do it. That mod is practically mandatory for the PC version of this game. It is the only way to play the game at high resolutions, among other things. It makes everything shiny and beautiful.  I'd also recommend browsing a few of the other mods there... especially texture and graphical upgrades.
#2. The difficulty this game is notorious for is... a complicated thing.  It is difficult because it does NOT tell you how to do things, but once you learn how to do them, it becomes more... moderate. It is never entirely easy, but the game doesn't tend to randomise things, so you can learn this game as you would a formula or equation. But expect to have a hard time the first time.   THAT SAID... if you play New Game Plus, it does change a few things up and makes the game more difficult.
#3. It isn't too difficult to get 100% achievement on this game, but you'll need to do a few NG+ playthroughs. Probably the last achievement you'll be able to get is the one for collecting all the boss weapons. That is because there are three of them that require Sif's soul... which means you need to get at least that far (and to Anor Londo) on your third playthrough.
#4. There is cooperative multiplayer. Helpy people in blue. There is also competitive... i.e. invaders in red.  There are certain level limitations in place on both, BUT the higher your level, the more difficulty you'll have in finding anyone who can do co-op with you, while invaders can be below your level. Also you can switch all this off if you like. It'll also remove those messages you find lying around... the ones that can be helpful, trolling, or just lewd.
#5. Beware the Anor Londo Archers.  I've found two reliable ways of dealing with them:  Either be invisible and silent (there are rings or Sorceries for that)... OR have a huge bow of your own (either the same bow they use or Gough's Bow from the DLC area). Any other approach to the two will be frought with peril and possibly one of the most difficult areas of the game. Best of luck...
... The rest, I'll leave for potential players to figure out on their own... or read one of the wikis.
Make no mistake though... it is a fun game once you get the hang of it.   And beautiful too if you're playing with DSfix.

I think people were expecting a lot more from this game than what this game really is. It's just a little twiddle exploring one of Sid Meier's ideas. I can beat an "epic" difficult campaign in a matter of hours - my 26 hours as of this review has already put me through multiple campaigns. And in XCOM or Civilizations, I'd normally be maybe halfway through. And it's a spinoff of the Civilization Beyond Earth games - which are okay in their own right but thankfully the real Civilization games are still being actively developed.
- Graphics? What graphics. They get the job done, though, and the engine's fairly optimized (Not completely stable, but optimized) so even paper PCs will run it well. And there's no finnagling with the UI, for the most part.
- The ships are interesting at first until you understand just how simple they are. It's easy to learn, easy to pick up, and easy to exploit - perhaps too easy.
- Combat is really simple - if you don't splurge on turn-based strategy games it might even be interesting, intriguing. There are a few options available to you - long-range laser sniper, hive mind swarmer with fighters, or close range facepuncher with plasma cannons. But compared to a game like XCOM, which has many small intricacies and almost nothing is certain (everything is certain in Starships, believe me, the only random action in a fight is whatever the AI does), Starships really does fade in comparison. You always know what's going to happen, and it happens the same way every time. It really hurts the replayability when you know the same thing that happened last campaign will probably happen again, even on the harder difficulties.
- I consider the difference between tactics and strategy as follows: Tactics is being able to whoop someone's♥♥♥♥♥ whereas strategy is putting yourself in a great position to whoop someone's♥♥♥♥♥ That being said I think while the strategy level is just as simple as setting up your ships, the actions you take in the galaxy have a direct and tangible effect on the battlefields. For instance, you can't really be a great carrier swarmer without having Tight Squeeze, Hyperlaunch and Dual Command wonders built and AI modules researched to make the fighters worth something instead of just bait. You can't cover your ships in plasma cannons, engines and shields without having the planets to produce your energy, or which specialize in building said equipment for cheap. So the benefits to good strategy are there. But, like almost everything else, it's just really simple.
It's difficult for me to recommend this game, it really is, because of what people will want and how simple this game is. I'm half-convinced that the main target platform for this game is the mobile platform - this would probably be a great mobile game, and it's just so underwhelming for a PC.
But for what it is, it's a nice little gem to me, worth a few dozen hours. In the end I won't try to dissuade you from buying it, particularly if it's on sale. Even though feedback is bad, I want a bigger, badder, more complex version of this game that we can really sink our teeth into. Something that can stand proudly by Civ and XCOM. Even if it does have to sprout off Beyond Earth.

Here's how to have the most possible fun with Anno 2505:
Step 1) Quit the game
Step 2) Launch Anno 2070
Step 3) Play that instead
Because this simplified and featureless excuse for a game, and I use that word cautiously because it seems like everything from the previous Anno games that could be considered gameplay has gone, is not deserving of your time or money.

I feel like a minority when giving a positive review, I think other people are being to irrational on the gameplay experience. It doesn't play like the previous annos but for me thats not a bad thing, I like what they have done here, it's refreshing.
The pros:
-Amazing aesthetically, the graphics are really nice, the character models/animations and even voice acting is much more improved.
-Regions of settlements - this is really refreshing and nice to build up and start fresh with new visual styles, new conditions depending on the climate in that area and trading depedancies between regions really give them personality (Artic region costs a bomb but is essential for other regions to develop).
-The campaign flows much better, in previous annos you would have mission that you would load in and out of to complete objectives, this anno feels much more seemless, a persistant long term goal that lasts throughout the game.
-The combat - in previous annos it never felt like a core pillar of the game, while still being completely optional this one it treats it as a seperate experience, which does infact remove from the risk of getting your hard built settlement blown up (I kinda liked that in the old ones), but it does mean that they got to focus on the combat elements in a completely fresh way that actually makes it more engaging. You have a ships that you can unlock via leveling up your corp level (through population and other bits and bobs), you earn experience via doing the combat missions and this experience can level up your boats, each boat has a key role to play which brings quite a bit of interesting strategy to the table, on top of that you now have abilities which you can use to call in reinforcements, nuke, stun, repair, shield and send out a wave to push the enemy back. Overall this is much better than previous annos as you won't need to wait until the 20 hour+ mark before you have any fun with the military side of things.
-Modules on factories are quite refreshing, allowing you to customise your settlements focus, it means I don't have to keep spamming tea farms down and finding much more real estate for additional buildings, if you are negative in a particular resource, find the building and simply place a production module to tip you over the edge back into positive readings.
The cons:
-No multiplayer, I think people have expressed this enough already that this was a weird design choice when the previous annos where so popular for it (It increased the longevity of the game considerably).
-Not enough information is easily exposed, in previous annos you had how much of each resource displayed in your depots, in this one you simply have a positive of negative number and as long as you keep it at 0 or above, then everything is gravy.
-Everything feels a bit too simple in regards to raw RTS traits, they have removed the hard numbers in areas and streamlined it so you know exactly what to do and when, although this isn't really a con, compared to old anno games it can make it feel 'dumbed down' saying that I kind of prefer it in someways as it means I can focus on getting that space elevator up and progress with a lot more flow.
-Slots, this one is mentioned a lot by other reviewers but my opinion of them is quite indiferent, in anno 2070 you had slots for mines, slots for river modules and slots for dams, in this one they have extended it to bridges (Which are large), to your depot that settles on new island and to structures that would work similar to fishing ports... I don't really get how this makes for a negative experience other than restricting customisation in regards to building (Which doesn't account for much with these few structures).
Overall, maybe give it some time and see what blue byte does with future patches/DLC, if you are looking for a traditional anno game then this may disappoint you, but if you are looking for a casual city builder with combat elements to distract you then this one will keep you entertained for 30hours +

Don't let the (sometimes-deserved) anti-Ubi hype keep you from this very, very fun experience. It will hook you. If you liked any of the previous Anno games (or Dawn of Discovery, as it was pointlessly renamed in the U.S.) then you will love this, and please help send the message that we don't want horrid bloated flash Anno games (*cough* Anno Online *cough*) but rather, lovely and original titles like this one.

It can literally be finished within 10 to 20 minutes. I thought the other reviewers were being hyperbolic, but it's the truth.
It is, in essence, a simple fan map that was made to establish the origins of the sample used in Gordon Freeman's test chamber... which appears to be some random cargo ship that's filled with Xen creatures. Worth a look? Maybe if you're studying level design and want an example of good intentions with sub-adequate execution. Or maybe to pick apart in Hammer to see how to create a bullet-sponge creature with a barnacle as its means of attack. That is, if you get nostalgic about the amount of custom maps for HL1 that used to come out, good, bad or otherwise.

I have to agree with the large amount of others here on this mod. I was actually very interested upon seeing this on the front page, but then I saw the original release date and it made me wonder why I never heard of it. I still wanted to play. Its "difficulty" is mainly cheap enemy placement and level design. For example, the moment you start, a head crab jumps right at you, and you can BARELY see it in the opening cutscene because you are too focused on everything else like the friggin ship, Machine gun on the helicopter, zombies, aliens, etc. There are just enough health kits to get you by(If only enought to keep your health under 100), and honestly its still cheap because they fill ten health per kit and enemies can do large amounts of damage. And while I commend the limited ammo feature in the start, its barely utilized to its full potential later on.
You have enough ammo to get you by, as long as you don't use the worthless machine gun here (Except the Grenade Launcher), the magnum and crossbow only have one magazine and are both dumbed down in damage, so that previous knowledge of those weapons being useful? Gone. Then there is the soldiers you encounter, the first one is behind a door that can bug out and flip out in mid air (check my profile for a pic, I am not joking), where he has supplies that YOU MUST GRAB, if you don't, the door shuts later and you can't access the supplies for future use. Then there is the soldiers you duke out against up above who take a ludicrous amount of damage compared to the HECU troops back in HL1 and love spamming grenades and grenade launchers.
I must give the dev credit though, the AI is smart enough to throw a grenade down the pit you came up from if you run away, but they spam them so its quite ridiculous. Then there is that infamous scientist who DOES have a voice actor who reads the lines EXACT WORD FOR WORD, but sometimes the game bugs out and only plays a few clips or none. Then the final boss, which I did not think was too bad, but jeez. Remember all those supplies and battery pick ups you saved up? Well thats all gone; the modder did not even properly program for you to keep your weapons, ammo and suit life, which is sorta sad to be honest because you are on the last level at this point.
An event to how you lost everything would have justified it, but as it stands its pretty lazy how its handled. FYI, no stretegy to the boss, just run and gun. Like good ol Doom. Just don't get caught or you have 2 seconds to escape. After that, its over. And yes, it will crash back to the desk top after the credits. For a Steam release, its a bit underwhelming. If the modder has difficulties with certain aspects, he should have gotten help, end of story.

There is something oddly compelling about this game....
Despite the fact that I have died time and time again in the Adventure mode, and despite the fact that the game has an extremely steep learning curve (though, if you have played Minecraft Mods like Buildcraft, it's not really as bad as it appears on the surface), this is a surprisingly engaging game, possibly because of the promise of what you CAN do if you persevere.
Like Dwarf Fortress, losing is 'fun', and each iteration takes you slightly nearer to survival as you learn your way through the components you are using, your knowledge of how to assemble and use the equipment available is the key to your survival.
Looks-wise the game is reminiscent of games like Minecraft or Starmade, the GUI is basic, and can be fiddly at times, it works ok, but probably needs (and will probably get) a polish in the future.
There ARE glitches, the AI can have the occasional strange mood, and I can understand how the level of complexity can be offputting, engines are easy, but some of the weapon stuff is pretty complex, I've yet to manage a working anti-missile laser, but I'll get there.
If you're the sort of person who doesn't mind losing frequently, and who doesn't mind having a wiki open in their browser whilst playing, this is a fun, challenging game with a massive amount of scope. Even the tutorials try to kill you and you know what? That's oddly refreshing.

UPDATE POST-BOOK 5.
Book 5 was, sadly, a disappointment. There was no "game" to the last chapter--mostly, the game element involved moving your character from point A or point B, with the occasional pixel-hunt thrown in for good measure.  There were so many long cut scenes with long dialogue explanations (also known as exposition) I started playing solitaire on my phone.  The various plot elements never really came together. It's like the various story threads got away from them, and they tried to wrap it up as best they could, but they bit off more than they could chew.  The character's movements were quite limited, and sometimes the need to search the screen for the "hot point" made me nauseous due to the rotating perspective.  This game just had too many characters and too much plot.  The whole tower/dream/etc. stuff never made any sense whatsoever.  Ambitious game, but it does not measure up to TLJ.
Review of parts 1-4; *mild spoilers* (thematic, not plot or puzzle).
I liked it...until it became about the Nazis.
One of the things I loved about the Longest Journey series was its originality and unpredictability.  The stories were compelling, with interesting characters and good puzzles.  This game has some great visuals, and it's certainly a fun world to wander around in.  Some of the characters are boring/two-dimensional, though (Kian, I'm talking to you), and there isn't much to do besides find & fetch puzzles and wander around talking to people.
It's the story I have a big problem with, however. How many games, TV shows, and movies have to be about Nazi Germany and the Holocaust? Doctor Who does it practically every season (exterminate!), Star Trek has done it (you will be assimilated), and pretty much every sci fi show has done it. I play these games to be transported, not massively bummed out and reminded (yet again!) of the deaths of 6 million Jewish people.  It's utterly disapponting.  I get it, it's important for people to learn the lessons of history, but this is like smashing people in the face with a history book (simply turning Jews into "magicals" does not conceal the heavy-handed message).  It isn't original, or even interesting.  It's supposed to be a game, not a history lesson.

Kingdoms and Castles is a simple but fun city building game. You build your little city starting from your main castle, make sure everyone has enough to eat, try to keep your growing population happy in order to attract more migrants, and build your defenses to fend off attacks by dragons and viking hordes. All of this is rendered in an art style that is both cute and easy to read. The game is quite intuitive to play, the mechanics are easy to learn, the graphics are charming, and as a whole it offers a relaxing and well-polished experience.
On the downside, the game doesn't offer much in the way of an actual challenge and the content is rather limited. Unlike some of the more complex entries in this genre, Kingdoms and Castles doesn't do much to sustain endless hours of play while you try to create the perfect city. So I really enjoy this game. Yes it does have some issues and is far from perfect but is a great time waster.

The first time I played Red Faction II was around 2004. I'm not sure when exacly, but I know that something made me mad and I haven't really finished it since then. Now that I own it here, on Steam, I managed to play it to the end - now I know the reasons.
I'm big fan of the first Red Faction game. It's one of best games I ever played in both single and multi player. I played it probably for more than hundreds hours and it wouldn't surprise me if I will install it to wash off the taste of it's sequel. To keep it short: it's nothing like first Red Faction game, it can't be called even a good game.
First of all, what the hell happened to Geo-Mod!? You can no longer makes yourselfs a tunnel, a hole, or anything else, in a wall and make some kind of shortcut. There are almost no random damage on the walls or floors - you can't destroy almost anything in Red Faction II. There are some statues that aren't destructable when shoot, so it's a huge let down. And while we are at Geo-Mod, I felt like idiot playing this game. There are only few times when you NEED to destroy something and no, you can't to find out it yourself. There will be always hole on the wall or somewhere else saying "hey you, look, there is a path here, destroy a wall here and see how fun it is". That's not what I would ever see in sequel of the great game, the game from times when there were so many interesting ideas and devs weren't affraid on making them come to life.
Another big "boo" for Red Faction II is lack of the multiplayer option. There are bots only. They did great in the first game and even NOW (yes, in the 2017) there are active players enjoying first Red Faction with others. Why skip it in sequel? Sure, there are some interesting options, you can follow progress and stats for every game mode and all but there comes one question - FOR WHAT REASON? I don't think anyone would want to brag about making beating bots. Sure, you can, but it's just boring.
There comes the third one, next "are you kidding me?" thing. Spawn of the enemies. There are moments in the game when they will SPAWN behind the barricade on the middle of map, there are moments when you will turn around and somebody will shoot your back - yes, looks like enemy spawned when you wasn't looking, lol. And the most annoying, at least for me, was the moment when you needed to kill some snipers and just when I gotten rid of all of them boom, here comes another wave from HIDDEN ON THE SAME PLACES, STAYING AT THE SAME POSITIONS. Sure, it's really old game looking at the date when it first come out, but I don't remember this kind of stuff in previous Red Faction game.
If you are fan of the Red Faction first game, then don't even bother to play this one. I mean, it's not made with only bad stuff. The graphics are something that you would expect in the game from 2003 year, same about the music, videos and such. There is really interesting arsenal of weapons and two-wielding was somehow rare in games, so Red Faction II did it great. Maybe the game itself isn't really long (it took me around 3 hears to finish it) but there are also bonuses like concept arts, which are unlocked if you play the game on all difficulty levels, earlier mentioned "multiplayer" with bots. Play it only when you don't mind all of the negative stuff and if you just looking for some short shooter - which finished once, can be forgotten forever...

Hello people, I am writing this review because I am seeing a lot of negativity, which personally does not make sense to me. This game has a lot to offer, even though there are some let-downs.
If you are expecting Anno 2070 with a Moon expansion and a fresh coat of graphics, you will be dissapointed. I am reviewing this game as a stand-alone, without comparing it to previous titles. Also, I have previously only played 2070, so it is up to you to judge my credibility. Here we go:
- Great Visuals
- Long-term Gameplay
- Continuos Gameplay
- Various Difficulty Setting
- Price ($$)
- Combat
- Unengaging Campaign
- Hardware Guzzler
- No Manual Save
You create your own Corporation. You answer to yourself and only yourself. You are guided by the World Council, but ultimately what you do is UP TO YOU.
As you progress, your Corporation levels up, and competes with the other NPC Corporations. Eventually you can surpass them and buy their land (sector) for your own use. In the mean time, represenatives from various Corporations will offer projects to help you develop different benefits, such as improved logistics.
While it is true that there is no separate "Sandbox" mode, the main game IS the sandbox. Yes, there is story behind it, in the form of quests/tasks you have to complete in order to progress your population and advance to the next tiers. Whether you breeze through the story and start over afterwards, or spend a whole calendar year in the same game, is entirely up to you. Also as far as building your city, as long as you are connected to islands (Temperate Zone) via huge New York style bridges, or have a Warehouse on an island (Arctic), you are free to build your Residential Areas and Factories WHEREVER they can fit. The only exception to that are the mines and the water resources (Energy, fish etc), which are restricted to specific locations, but that is not necessarily bad. It makes management of space more simple.
As you advance your civilization you can expand to two more regions. Here is a summary of all regions you will eventually have access to (in order of progression):
This is where you will spend most of your time, because it is where your population is most dense and this region has the most resources. The region has a warm climate and a series of islands you can connect via the long bridges, mentioned above.
As you progress, eventually you will need resources/goods you cannot acquire from the Temerate Region and you will need to expand to the Arctic. Much like the Teperate Region, the Arctic has a seres of islands that you can expand to with the use of warehouses.
The moon is the final frontier in Anno 2205. Much like the Arctic, the moon has resources you cannot obtain anywhere else. The region has a series of craters that you gain control of through warehouses, like in the Arctic.
IMPORTANT:
Have you ever wondered why we never went back to the moon? (Humans) Well, one answer could be... Because it is VERY EXPENSIVE. If you go to the Moon too early, or as soon as you are able to, your people will experience an event that would make the term "Great Depression" sound like "Oh, it's no big deal". Develop your economy and then go to the moon. Or don't, and then it will be rough for a while, until you eventually have the means to balance it all out.
Each zone: Temperate, Arctic, and Moon, has three regions (maps). Once you get your initial region you will need to buy the rest from other Corporations if you wish to exapnd further.
Two more zones are in the works. Check the DLC section on Steam or the main game website.
One problem however, is that while the campaign can teach you how to advance your civilization, it doesn't really do much to keep your interest in the setting of the game. Yes, you are supposed to advance your civilization, but you know that from the nature of Anno. The campaign does not reinforce your motivation to play what the game is all about.
Once you control multiple regions, say one in the Temperate Zone, and one in the Arctic, as long as you develop the space port of each, you can set up a trade route for resources between the two zones. You can also set how much resource to trade. Eventually you will also gain access to the World Market (Space Station), where you can buy and sell resources.
While the focus of this game is city building and civilization development, there is some combat involved. After all, as you expand you need to defend your interests from extremists. Combat is in the form of missions. Some you need to eventually complete in order to progress, however, as far as when you do that, it is again, up to you. Other combat missions are completely optional, but can reward you with rare resources. NOTE: Some reviews say that those "annoying missions" are the only way to get rare resources. NOT TRUE. Each sector has an NPC Trade Port that sells rare resources for credits. Combat is the easiest way to aquire those resources, but if you have a stable tax rate, you can get said resources without firing a single shell.
That being said, if you want to build a massive fleet and reign supreme, play an actual strategy game. The combat here gets very repetitive at a pont and you have very little (if any) freedom of choice. It is a good way, to break the monotony of managing your cities, but don't expect an adrenaline rush.
The game looks amazing. The level of detail is definitely some of the best I've seen in a long time. If you go to postcard view (camera mode) you can really see your creation come to life.
There is one downside though. If you consider your PC a gas station, Anno 2205 is either a Big Rig, a Hummer, or their demon love child. The game eats your GPU processing power, like a kid in candy land. The maximum setting is ULTRA. I play on HIGH, and still get occasional chop.
My Rig:
Alienware 18, Intel i7 2.80 GHz. 16 GB RAM, 2x Nvidia GeForce GTX 860M (2 GB each) SLI Enabled. OS: Windows 7 Home Premium 64 bit
- - - - Additionally:
While I get why some would want to build an empire together with friends, the game is built in a way that you don't have to. Players still can influence the prices in the World Market and vote in the World Council.
This game relies entirely on Uplay Sync to save your progess. You CAN save if offline, but either way you have no control over the saves, aside from exiting Anno 2205 every now and then.
Written after 20+ hours of Gameplay
Overall good game, but falls short in some areas. I give an 8/10 score, because I personally enjoy it, but can understand if others may not as much.
I've also never had issues with Uplay and this time was no exception. Note: Sometimes Steam messes up the Uplay lancher installation. If you don't already have Uplay, I suggest getting it from the Uplay website and THEN installing games.
I Recommend this game to both Anno veterans, and newcomers. Veterans, please give this game a change. You may like it. And if you don't like it you can always play 2070 :). It is not the end of the world.
That being said,
. The game is too expensive right now, and not offering enough to make up for it.
This is my first ever review. Please provide feedback.
See you soon, friends.

[spoilers] Starbound starts off in an alternate universe where several different races coexist with one another. These races include the Humans, the Apex, the Floran, the Avians, the Hylotls (or however it's spelled), the Glitch, and the Novakids. These races can be played as your character, however you want them to be like. The Terran Protectorate is an organization founded to keep the peace across the galaxy, and your character starts off as a graduating member of the Protectorate. Everything seems fine and dandy when all of a sudden: the Ruin, a being bent on mass galactical destruction, destroys the entire Earth and forces the player to evacuate on a beaten-down ship, which is where the official game starts, as the player now has to survive with limited resources and a ship that can barely function. [/spoilers]
One of my biggest gripes with this game is the Main Questline. I would have enjoyed it I could get to know the characters better, listen to what their story is, but my wish was not granted. Sure, they aren't soulless machines (those are the Glitch), but you don't know a lot about them, either.
Do not get me wrong, it's a good game, but it's not at all

This is a very, VERY good game!  Take note that this is a review from a gamer that ACTUALLY read all the memorials, did not skip a scene, took the time to look at statutes, arts and building structural designs, and all the back stories in every description. I also take this game as it is, instead of relating it back to any other Castlevania, such as Symphony of The Night or the first LoS.
10/10 would recommend this game, and here's why:
Pros
1) The story is amazing.  As I dig deeper into the story, I feel I can relate to some of the characters, know why they did what they did, and that is important! Some may argue that the ending is dull, I personally think that it is fitting.  Reading the memorials help me understand how the modern era portrays the world and history.
2) Voice acting is phenomenal.  They not only fit the characters, they brought out the emotions of their characters and made the story more colorful.
3) The soundtrack is amazing as well.
4) The city and castle designs are amazing.  While it is set in a modern world close to ours, it also retain some original castle structures that makes sense to remain there.  The castle is, well, Dracula's castle, and it is beautiful.  The texture of the stone/wooden floors, ceilings, and walls are so detailed that they are worth admiring, one could feel that this is not a simple copy-and-paste world.  I actually took time to look at statutes from different angles, just to admire them.  The world is interconnected, different routes to a place is possible.
5) Game's free-camera-control is great, and the combat is fluid.
6) I love it when in Dracula's rat form.  While some will argue it's necessity (Dracula too powerful to be a rat), it gives me a different view of the city.  What amazes me is that despite everything being bigger, the texture of the world is still amazing (floor tiles, walls and cables)!  So what he turns into a rat? He's a ♥♥♥♥ing Dracula!
7) The most controversial part of the game: Argreus.  I like the stealth part in his maze.  Again, many people would argue that since Dracula is so powerful why the sneaking and the one-shot-kill? Ever heard of Pan's Labyrinth? Well, Argreus IS Pan's brother, so it makes sense that a maze like that would be his world, and the one-shot-kill is justified.  That is why we have to make it past the maze to a higher ground where it is not a maze to fight him.  Savvy?
Cons
1) The stealth system is flawed.  While bat swarm works on certain enemies (only on the red armored marine if I recall correctly), most of the time when you use it sneaking up on an enemy, it just draws attention to every enemy in the vicinity to focus on you (once you use it, they know where you are).
2) Despite having so many different skills, as the game progresses, skills will become less useful.  Some enemies are so aggressive that you just don't have time to use different attacks without being knocked down first.  I ended up using basic attacks in most of the situation.
Overall, this is a great game.  You will be missing out if you rely your decision to buy this game on unprofessional critic's opinions about this game.  Hell, reviewing a game ain't even close to my profession, but after seeing some negative reviews of this game, and after personally playing it, I feel compelled to write something to justify the unjust.  After all, it's really about whether you had fun or not about a game, right?

If you've ever played Swarm Simulator, you owe it to yourself to give this a try. It's has a very similar playstyle but with 5 "tiers" of resources to keep track of.
Comrades are larvae; spend them to make workers (drones), which produce a raw income (potatoes, land, ore, ammo, medicine, basically 5 different versions of "meat"). Combine multiples of those workers to purchase a bigger building that will then spawn those workers regularly (much like a nest makes queens, which make drones that farm meat, or in this case potatoes). Further down the line, you will need land to purchase the high-tier potato buildings, and you will need ore/ammo to purchase high-tier land buildings, and so on. Once you've reached a certain number of workers, typically a multiple of 10, you gain an unlock that will either provide you with extra comrades/sec or outright boost the potential of that unit/building.
Additionally, there are "achievements" in the form of medals, which grant a substantial amount of science for each unlock you obtain. Science is used as a currency to purchase permanent upgrades, as well as massive temporary boosts, whether it be a clicking boost or an autonomous worker boost. Science can also be earned daily in the form of 15 capsules; clicking on any of the resource generating buttons will eventually grant you up to 3 crates for a particular tier, and when added up together can net you as much as 60 science just for checking in daily for a few minutes. Also once you have unlocked them early on in the game, each tier of resource has a science-generating building that finishes every 6 hours, netting you a decent portion of science at the expense of manual collection.
The biggest difference here is the speed you acquire comrades (larvae) and the lack of a nexus, but there is a similar function called "experiments" that more or less justifies the lack of a nexus, as they allow you to use science you've acquired to boost yourself to unconceivable levels in mere minutes. There is "prestiging" in a sense, as once you upgrade one of your science-generating buildings (say a colony for example in the potato tier) it costs an increasing amount of max-tier buildings (so it would first cost 3 hives, then 9, 27, 81, 243 etc) as well as resets every other building to 0, INCLUDING your base potatoes. As far as twinning/cloning goes, there isn't any unfortunately, but that's because the comrade (larvae) generation is much more tame and realistic.
And oh yeah, no stupid territory mechanic that you mostly ignore after your first prestige anyways. Good riddance to Roach XXXIV

Should You Buy Kingdoms and Castles? I have made a short video to help you decide that:
Pros:
- The price is right
- Developers are very active in updating and transparent with their community
- There are already FREE future DLC's planned
- 3 different game modes: Easy, Normal, and Hard
- I have put in 20+ hours of fun(played it before it was on Steam) and still want to play it  lots more
- The music is quite good and relaxing
Either:
- The art style is very simplistic and(I think) cute
Cons:
- I have still encountered a few new bugs after every game update but nothing has been game breaking
- The advisors in the game are a bit underwhelming and not useful after the first 5 minutes or so - in fact the notification "!" can be a bit annoying when there's nothing important to learn
- On normal mode, the viking attacks can sometimes be frustratingly close together and not allowing you time to recover from the previous attack, but there is always peaceful mode if it becomes too much for you
Overall I have had a lot of fun with this game(around 20 hours played including time outside of Steam) and the price is so low that, if you enjoy simulation and city building games, you will surely get your money's worth of fun out of it. Hope this helps!
Edit: Adding Q/A here from comments:
Q: Is it hard to keep a working economy or does the city run itself like in many other builders once you have the basics down?
A: It runs itself in the sense that you don't have to click on each civilian and tell them what to do - jobs are taken care of automatically once you build the thing that needs workers. However, sometimes you may have the need to close or open the building if you already have enough of that material or you want your people to focus on something else instead. So, in a sense it runs itself but you still have to balance how many foresters you want, how many quarries, blacksmiths, farmers, etc.
Q: Are there goals in the game or is it just build a big a city as possible?
A: It is an open sandbox game so the goals are what you make for yourself. If you need more structure than that then you'll probably get bored fast. But for me, I like to make goals such as - can I actually be  successful enough to build my entire city within castle walls? Can I get my defenses up high enough that I'll be able to have minimal damages when invaded? Can I build an army big enough that I can send my general in and conquer their armies and constantly have bonus happiness from winning battles? Can I expand my kingdom enough to encompass the entire land that is provided to me? Can I have a really happy kingdom while taxing them to the max? So far I have not achieved any of those completely so I am still working towards them.
Q: Are there multiple ways to build a city or will every game take the same course?
A: You can build your city however you want - but there will always be things you need such as wood, stone, and food. You can make the layout however you want as well, and if you don't feel like building churches you don't have to build churches, it will make your citizens unhappy but you can choose to try and make up that deficit with something else.
Q: How many options are there for aesthetics individualiziation of your city?
A: It is a visually simplistic game which I touched on that may be either a pro or con for people depending on personal taste. Every building has one design.

Edit: My feeling of the game remains unchanged as time goes on. I understand why die-hard fans of Anno may be disappointed, but the game is still very fun in its own way.
I've found Anno 2205 to be extremely enjoyable. I've sunk about 5 hours in it today and I loved every minute of it.
Compared to Anno 2070, I feel that the gameplay experience is a lot smoother. It's always extremely clear what kind of material you need. The buildings' area of operation are much less restrictive. While a house can be out of range, now the community buildings are considered a resource in themselves. This enables the player to be more creative with his cities without being punished too harshly because of building placement. In my humble opinion, this is a huge positive change.
To the people that say that trading has been removed from the game... It's still there, but now you don't micro-manage the most inconsequential trade routes with boats. Now you just have to keep an eye on how resources flows between your colonies and make sure your production can handle the demand. It's an important change considering you are not trading between islands but between different maps completely.
Talking about the colonies... Having three biomes with completely different play-styles is really fun. Switching between each one adds variety to the game. And they are pretty.
The campaign integration is, in my opinion, very well done so far. Maybe it won't work for everyone, but I think it's a good way of making the world feel real. Honestly, I could hardly bother doing the Anno 2070 campaign because I found it tedious. Here, it feels like a suggestion. "Hey, by the way, I know you're busy but could you help us not dying pretty please kthx? Or just keep doing your thing, whatever." While the Lunar terrorists are a bit unbelievable, at least they are menacing villains with a really cool leader.
It's too early for me to give a verdict or talk about the re-playability. However, based on my experience so far, I am very pleased with my purchase.
TLDR; I really liked Anno 2070, but I feel that Anno 2205 is a better game so far.

Possibly one of the best space-exploration games ever, Starbound has an extremely fun base game, and is endlessly replayable, with constant updates, a huge modding community, a seemingly endless universe, and more.
The gameplay itself is amazing. You explore planets and more recently, some of the stuff between them, in search of loot, other people, and things to kill. Speaking of killing, combat is extremely fun with different types of weapons, with different elements, different stats, different secondary skills, and a metric f***ton of things to kill- And guess what? IT'S ALL RANDOMLY GENERATED! Exploration is a ton of fun with randomly generated worlds, ships you can go to, different "anomalies" throughout space, and tons of different ways to explore all of them! Already you have infinite ways you can play and i haven't even gotten to mods yet.
Graphics are great for a sprite-based 2D sidescroller. Lighting is realistic, especially with the help of some mods. Items you hold will usually cast shadows when they hit block. Flashlights are a good example, and you get one at the start of the game. Spritework is amazing. The artists have managed to pack a lot of details into fairly small blocks. Enemy and humanoid sprites are big enough to fit some decent detail, whilst not abandoning the artstyle of the rest of the game completely. Animations are amazing.
Now, i'm not sure what to talk about here other than mods. MODS. MODS! Minor changes, major changes, weapons, armor, costumes, ships, races, interfaces, some completely original ideas and MEMES! Memes. That's all you need to know. Memes. Now go play this game. Better than anything else you'll get in this genre.

So having played this a few years back, after finishing Terraria, I enjoyed what I played but felt it didn't deliver the same experience for a variety of reasons. Several years later (like a week ago) I gave starbound another go, and my feelings haven't changed.
Combat: 5/10
The combat in Starbound is, at best, serviceable. Beyond weapon types, no weapon felt particularly memorable, none felt like they had personality and many felt same-ish. Many times I would just stick with the same weapons, as the advantages of new weapons were scant. Fighting itself can be awkward, with an energy meter limiting or often crippling your ranged weapons, and melee weapons often being better but subjecting you to more damage due to no invinciblity frames, which can be problematic, especially in the final boss. Still, there are enjoyable moments when jumping in to the frey, but generally combat is tedious, awkward, and frustrating.
Exploration: 7/10
Probably the biggest point of starbound is its unlimited planets. While starbound does offer more volume to explore than Terraria, Terraria's one planet is chock-full of more worthwhile materials and other goodies. The possibilities of what you can find on a planet is also a bit of a double-edged sword, as if you intend on gunning through the main quest first, you'll likely hit a point where you'll have to explore several similar planets looking for your objective, sometimes needing to find two+ towns since one did not contain the right or right amount of objects.
Planets themselves are varied from each other, though it doesn't take long to run into the same structures on the same planet types. As stated above, weapons have a greater variety then Terraria, but less distinguishably severely weakens incentive to spend a long time exploring. That, and ways to explore, as well as mobility in general, feel limited compared to Terraria.
Plus, creating a new world in Terraria is faster and more effective then going to a new world in Starbound, even if you cut out grinding for fuel.
Music: 4/10
Starbound's music is particularly emotional, but incredibly destracting and often not very fitting. The somber music isn't particularly soothing when my starchild is being buried in slime and starving; instead, all it does is draw the image of her tombstone, as she dies alone and unknown, buried on some random planet, no one to discover or remember her. Needless to say, Terraria's more laid-back or kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack (for exploring or fighting a boss respectively) are much better.
Story: 6/10
The main quest is serviceable, with tons of extra details in the codexes. Obviously it's better than Terraria's non-existant story, but it's still fairly mundane.
Graphics: 9/10
The sprites feel nice and detailed, having quite the variety when it comes to npcs. The backgrounds are pleasing to the eye, Npcs are fairly recognizeable from one another, and items are usually distinct. Weapons suffer from having minute difference unless they're high-grade, in which they tend to have unique and interesting sprites.
Overall: 7/10 stand-alone, 6/10 compared to Terraria. Despite my somewhat harsh score, I still enjoyed this game and found it worth the purchase. If you're looking at either this or Terraria, I'd have to urge you toward Terraria; if you're just eyeing this or both, I say grab starbound, it's star-bound to be worth the investment.

Lords of Shadow 2 is a very good, but not quite a great game. It has some flaws, but it has fun gameplay and a rich atmosphere. It's mostly a character action game with some open world elements.
Firstly, the good stuff. Most of the time playing this game you will be either in combat with enemies, or exploring the world. Combat is very fun and engaging, albeit not the deepest of the genre. It can't rival the likes of Platinum's work, but still creates a fun system that keeps you wanting more. It has a nice rhythm to it as it requires you to always keep an eye on enemies and properly timing blocking to keep your combo up, which is crucial for the "Focus" system. This system is also what gives you the power needed to use two of the three main weapons. These two weapons also have special effects, such as freezing enemies or burning away their armour, but break your Focus. It creates this flow to combat that feels very fluid and back-and-forth, meaning you can't get lazy and just endlessly wail on enemies without opposition, especially on higher difficulties. The different weapons also feel distinct from each other outside of their special effects. They each have different range, speed, and power, and there are plenty of combos in each weapon that all have a use in different combat situations, which are unlocked in an RPG style experience system.
The aesthetic of the game is also great. Everything has a dark and intricate look to it, with stunning Gothic architecture and really interesting world and boss design. The soundtrack is also fantastic, with a sweeping orchestral sound that fits the melodramatic and dark feel of the game. This makes simply being in the game world and moving around it a lot of fun. It does a good job of helping you soak in the atmosphere, both in and out of combat. The kinaesthetics too, are fantastic. The weapons all have a very satisfying feel to them. A sense of power and impact, but also vibrancy. They leave trails colour that arc around in the air as you swing your weapons, or explosions when they hit enemies. Some of the more powerful moves are especially impressive in how they surround you in a storm of whirling lights that destroys everything in the area.
The structure of the game world is pretty interesting as well, and quite unique for the genre. Unlike the first game in the Lords of Shadow series, this game is set in two moderately sized open-world areas. It is somewhat inspired by the traditional Castlevania style of level design, but isn't really the focus of the gameplay here. Yet it still manages to achieve this feeling of place to the game world. You can explore around the worlds seamlessly, without any loading screens, and many areas are connected, and sometimes loop around on each other. This also aids the sense of atmosphere to the game, and gives the game much better pacing than the first as well. Here, you're not thrown back to the main menu to sit through a long loading screen every fifteen minutes. It's nowhere near as dense and maze-like as the older Castlevania games, or something like Dark Souls, but for what it brings to the type of game it is, it's a great addition.
There are also some areas of the game which are clearly lacking, though they are not anywhere near significant enough to ruin the experience.
Firstly, there are the much lamented stealth sections. These are pretty bad, but not game-breakingly so. They feel half-baked and somewhat forced in to the game, by taking away your ability to fight while entering a stealth section. The mechanics of the stealth sections are also shallow, and it’s not exactly clear when you are detected or not. When you are, although it's not an instant failure, it might as well be, given that you will be attacked by enemies that can kill you in two hits or so, even with all the health upgrades. But even so, these sections are relatively rare. They make up only what is probably 5% or less of the actual main story. On top of that they are all incredibly short and easy. All they require you to do most of the time is sneak to the other side of a small room. Usually that involves nothing more than distracting one enemy, or possessing another. Additionally, once a stealth section has been cleared, you will never have to do it again if you return to the same area.
Another problem is the story. It's a confused mess of underutilised characters and poorly explained plot devices. This game was set up as a big finale to the Lords of Shadow story, and unfortunately it mostly fails at that. There are a lot of characters in the game which don't get as much time as they need to really make the impact they could. They often appear only as bosses, given a short introduction and forgotten immediately after. While the boss fights themselves are fun, from a story perspective they feel like they are being given the short straw. There are also some elements of the story that are fairly crucial to the plot which aren't explained well at all. For example the Mirror of Fate, from the game of the same name, also plays a prominent role in this game, but its significance isn't explained here, and its role seems unrelated to the game it was introduced in. But despite this, there are a few good moments. A conversation or two that hit on some interesting points, although they are never explored as they could be, still bring out some good character moments. Even so, the story isn't a huge part of the game. It can be mostly ignored, and it's not as if the series had a particularly great story to begin with. The best part of the story was mostly the tone and feeling of it, which in both the previous games and this one, are mostly achieved through the aesthetics.
So overall, Lords of Shadow 2 is a pretty good game. Far from perfect, but certainly undeserving of the baffling critical mauling it got. If you were a fan of the previous Lords of Shadow game(s), then this should be right up your alley as well. It's far from the best game in the world, but much like its predecessors, it is a flawed gem.
As a side note, I recommend that if you have played the first game, but not Mirror of Fate, you should also play that before this one. The stories are quite closely connected, and as previously mentioned, this game expects you to be familiar with it. Although it’s not as good as LoS2, MoF is short and can be beaten in a day if you focus on only the main story.

The game is more than just a simple time waster.
What it is, essentially, is a sandbox-puzzle game.
You play a prisoner and your objective is to escape, naturally. You are given a prison with diggable floors, breakable walls, cuttable fences, explorable furnace ducts (classic), disguises you can use, and collectible items which include:
Weapons (Of varying quality)
Tools (Of graduating quality)
Items of value (for using as bribes to other inmates or as valuables to make money from quests)
It has a simple money system. Do "quests" and make some money. Use that money to buy items from other prisoners to craft the items you use. Sometimes you won't always get the same items, so your escape method must adapt to what's available.
You also have a "job" system. This can be a way you can get materials, or even gain access to areas as part of your escape strategy. Even getting a job can be tricky if someone already has the one you want, and you must now strategize in how to make them lose the job so you can apply (assuming you have the right skill prerequisites).
In the mean-time, as you're getting your items, building up your stats (required for crafting certain items, surviving combat, and other things depending on how you're trying to get out will decide what is important), you'll need to hide your materials and progress from the guards and possibly other inmates so they don't take things from you or blow your plan to heck, ALL while making sure you stick enough to the prison routine to avoid raising "heat" levels and attracting attention to yourself.
Now, add in the fact that this is multiplayer, and suddenly you can now craft some very VERY interesting plans of escape.
There is plenty to do for only $25, and there is likely more to come. It's a GREAT value if you like exploring, sandbox, or simple "puzzle" solving. Lots of room to experiment and try different things, and with the COMPETITIVE multiplayer, you can have some really funny and great moments trying to figure out what your friend is doing and screw them over as you make your own escape XD
Full recommendation. Would buy again.

A super simplified 4x game. It is incredibly shallow but it had enough decisions involved for me to enjoy it as sort of a mindless time waster. I beat it once on normal and never looked back. I wouldn't pay more than a deep sale price for it (66%+).
You get to take over planets, research tech, build a fleet, and fight other empires, but everything is very simple to the point of feeling limited.
You only get one fleet - yes that's right, one fleet total. The entirety of your combat and conquering happens with that one fleet. You have a "fleet fatigue" counter which means you have to manage your turn to be as efficient as possible with your fleet.
Research techs have different names but come down to 9 categories that just "level up", rather than some kind of tree with decisions to make about similar space drives with different advantages or anything like that.
There are "wonder" type things that provide bonuses. Planets can have very simple buildings built to improve them.
Combat is turn based with a hex grid, and you get to make decisions on how you outfit your fleet (weapons/shields/etc take up space and add weight which require stronger weapons to move farther per turn).
Overall I felt like the decision making was fun and I especially enjoyed outfitting my fleet and planning out my turn movements. But it also was so simple that by the time I beat a game it felt like I'd seen everything I needed to see. I have 5.5 hours playtime total, but I did spend a couple scrapped games figuring things out so that's basically 1.5 games.
I'd recommend the game if you want a fun simple 4x that's almost mindless, or you like 4x but find them too complex with too much stuff to manage, or you want a simple intro to the genre (although Endless Space is a better intro imo). Be aware that you might not find much replayability value. If you're looking for anything like Civ or Orion, don't bother.

So having played this a few years back, after finishing Terraria, I enjoyed what I played but felt it didn't deliver the same experience for a variety of reasons. Several years later (like a week ago) I gave starbound another go, and my feelings haven't changed.
Combat: 5/10
The combat in Starbound is, at best, serviceable. Beyond weapon types, no weapon felt particularly memorable, none felt like they had personality and many felt same-ish. Many times I would just stick with the same weapons, as the advantages of new weapons were scant. Fighting itself can be awkward, with an energy meter limiting or often crippling your ranged weapons, and melee weapons often being better but subjecting you to more damage due to no invinciblity frames, which can be problematic, especially in the final boss. Still, there are enjoyable moments when jumping in to the frey, but generally combat is tedious, awkward, and frustrating.
Exploration: 7/10
Probably the biggest point of starbound is its unlimited planets. While starbound does offer more volume to explore than Terraria, Terraria's one planet is chock-full of more worthwhile materials and other goodies. The possibilities of what you can find on a planet is also a bit of a double-edged sword, as if you intend on gunning through the main quest first, you'll likely hit a point where you'll have to explore several similar planets looking for your objective, sometimes needing to find two+ towns since one did not contain the right or right amount of objects.
Planets themselves are varied from each other, though it doesn't take long to run into the same structures on the same planet types. As stated above, weapons have a greater variety then Terraria, but less distinguishably severely weakens incentive to spend a long time exploring. That, and ways to explore, as well as mobility in general, feel limited compared to Terraria.
Plus, creating a new world in Terraria is faster and more effective then going to a new world in Starbound, even if you cut out grinding for fuel.
Music: 4/10
Starbound's music is particularly emotional, but incredibly destracting and often not very fitting. The somber music isn't particularly soothing when my starchild is being buried in slime and starving; instead, all it does is draw the image of her tombstone, as she dies alone and unknown, buried on some random planet, no one to discover or remember her. Needless to say, Terraria's more laid-back or kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack (for exploring or fighting a boss respectively) are much better.
Story: 6/10
The main quest is serviceable, with tons of extra details in the codexes. Obviously it's better than Terraria's non-existant story, but it's still fairly mundane.
Graphics: 9/10
The sprites feel nice and detailed, having quite the variety when it comes to npcs. The backgrounds are pleasing to the eye, Npcs are fairly recognizeable from one another, and items are usually distinct. Weapons suffer from having minute difference unless they're high-grade, in which they tend to have unique and interesting sprites.
Overall: 7/10 stand-alone, 6/10 compared to Terraria. Despite my somewhat harsh score, I still enjoyed this game and found it worth the purchase. If you're looking at either this or Terraria, I'd have to urge you toward Terraria; if you're just eyeing this or both, I say grab starbound, it's star-bound to be worth the investment.

What a botched sequel this truly is. I loved Lords of Shadow. It had some issues, but was incredibly enjoyable, from the variety of settings to the classic monsters Gabriel did battle with.
I'd read that this one was very slow to get going, but that once it did, it was solid. That disappointed me in and of itself, but it also made me wait for a sale to buy it. Finally a good one came along, and I bought the game, looking forward to get back into the world and see what had become of Gabriel since we'd last met.
Because I'd read the reviews already, I was willing to sludge through the awful stealth sections where you have to turn into a rat to accomplish a variety of goals. And yes, they were terrible. But what was also very annoying was a constant sense of "where do I go" and "what am I supposed to do now?" A lot of time was spent backtracking or wandering all over the map looking for the next goal. There were areas that I couldn't get to simply because I wasn't SUPPOSED to get to them yet, even though I could see things I wanted just beyond simple things like rocks that Dracula should've easily been able to leap over and obtain.
Not this Dracula. So that took me right out of the immersion. But OK, I can overlook it if the game itself is good.
It's just the opposite of the first LoS to me. That one was excellent with a few flaws. This one is generally bad with a few bright spots, none of which make up for the game as a whole.
The voice acting, aside from Dracula, is absolutely terrible, especially the "extras" you fight who constantly shout out the same lines over and over. The monsters in this one are poorly designed as well, and even the humans look bizarre. Garbriel's head often seems way too small for his giant body, for instance.
Some of the fights were OK, but the vast majority just came down to relentless button mashing mixed with evasion. You can learn all the "cool moves" you want, but you really don't need them. Just mash that X and Y, and you'll get through most of the fights. Boss battles are typical of the problem with so many of these types of games today: big, giant, lumbering beasts or creatures that you have to climb or hit a glowing portion on, blah, blah, blah. Nothing exciting, nothing very interesting.
The only thing that kept me going in this was really wanting to see a resolution to Dracula's story. Quite frankly, I wanted to see him become Gabriel again. But about 3/4 of the way in, I realized that, despite what some of the reviews said, this game was not getting much better. I was revisiting the same places over and over again, and who wants to walk Dracula around science labs in a game like this? Drab, boring science labs is where you spend much of the game, not the gothic settings of the first.

A few notes about this review: I'm yet to play the prequel to this game as of the time this review was written, and as such, will not be comparing this title to Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 1.
Gameplay:
The game is very reminiscent of open-world  hack and slash classics such as Devil May Cry and Bayonetta. The mechanics are well varied and properly executed, and at its' very beginning, launches the player into action.
The boss fights are bloody, epic, and memorable. Little was spared in terms of length and difficulty when encountering various bosses, who are well varied and endowed. Prepare to die a few times in your quest to make progress.
Note that duie to the nature of the story (see section below) , repetitive gameplay is necessitated for one to unlock Dracula's potential abilities as the story progresses. This is executed in a repetitive manner, and as such, incurs a considerable challenge at the early stages of the game. However, as an indirect consequence, later sections are very rewarding as your new abilities are fully utilized in making progress. Prepare for a challenge.
The stealth system and mechanics used are not ideal and are out of balance. A being such as dracula shouldn't be reduced to a powerless imp in the stealth sections, which can be confusing and often convoluted.
Graphics:
Excellent, judging bu its' requirements and visuals. They are well balanced and properly executed. Details are clear and vivid, and so are the vast, open world environments. Character forms are well refined and so are their spectral abilities.
Story line:
All in all, dependin gon your background, its' taste may differ to you. I've read previous reviews from people who played the games' prequel and most were not pleased.
in my opinion, I found the fusion of both the present and the past (through the use of the Wolf Medallion) a bit unique in that you can switch to either timeline and progress at your own rate. In a manner, this further enhances the open world experience. As a drawback, this can make the game very repetitive since the environments are consrained to one transitional area, a chemical company. This also incurs a drawback to the overall quality of Dracula's retelling as a legendary vampire who must be trapped to a moden themed factory for extended periods of gameplay time as a requirement to progressing in the game. This repetitive nature may not bode well for all players.
Overall rating:
The production quality is superb, and so is the gameplay. Comes highly recommended.
My personal rating is 7.5/10.

I recommend the game on the basis of it being an ANNO game.  Here are some of the pros and cons I could think of.
Pros:  Graphics are amazing but will melt your computer if you dont have a beefy GPU or CPU.
Pros:  Artwork is very nicely rendered, all in all, its a very pretty game and full of eye candy.
Pros:  Its a bit easier to understand demands of your citizens, gives statistics on how much each industry produces instead of running to a WIKI like in Anno 2070 to figure out what you need to build and how much of it.
Cons: Maps are prefab, beautiful, but prefab, no random element like in 2070.
Cons: I feel as if the game has been EXTREMELY dumbed down.  Instead of supply chains (seeing transports on the streets) ferrying goods to and from it just instantly does it and shows the animation of stuff being moved about.
Cons: No multiplayer and I have to honestly say, after playing it I highly doubt there ever will be multiplayer in a game like this, it has changed that much between 2070 and 2205.
Cons: Maps feel extremely small but is a new engine, you can definately tell they skimped in a lot of areas probably due to engine stability and perfomance issues.
Edit:
I decided to add some additional details in regards to my opinion of dumbing down of the game.  What I mean by this is we were originally accustomed to the previous Anno games where you have to setup up trade routes etc to get the supplies to the manufactor and the end product to the citizens.  In 2205 this is not the case but rather deciding on how you are going to build the city, theres alot more city planning in this game than the previous Anno game.
In 2070:  Buildings and building layouts were static, no upgrades other than enhancements you loaded into your warehouse, global effects, or ARK upgrades.
In 2205:  Theres still a global effect through voting at your ARK *Space Station*.  However, as far as buildings go, most of your production buildings do instantly provide the product, however they are far from static in layout.
Building Upgrades:  Each building that produces a product (electricity, water etc) has so many upgrade slots to enchance production, running costs, workforce costs etc.  So cramming abunch of veggie farms in one location, not wise.  Not only does it cost more in power, maitenence and workforce to run x2 said farms its better to bulldoze one, upgrade the other to exceed the production of the lost farm for a cheaper, more efficient cost.
Building upgrades require rare resources which you cant really obtain from the map, you must buy them from the exchange or do combat missions to get them.  Scour the combat map, theres plenty of extra stuff you can get besides the end mission results.

I've played the hell out of 2070, and I'm very much enjoying 2205.  People posting reviews about the lack of 'depth' are mostly referring to the fact that you no longer have to download an external spreadsheet or calculator program to figure out how much of what you need to satisfy a given population.  You can, for the first time, use in-game feedback to figure out whether or not you're making enough widgets for your folks.  Further, while its true that the building of fiels is gone, the building of modules provides the same tetris gameplay with dramatically increased effect.  The alt-tab savings alone are astonishing.  If you combine that with the fact that your main population centers require more different goods than ever before, and the fact that you have 3 totally seperate production areas (as opposed to 2 in 2070 and 1404), the depth has by any reasonable measure increased.
Many of the reviews have also not finished the intro/campaign portion and hit the wall that is large-scale lunar construction.  It's bloody expensive to build things on the moon, and doing so requires massive expansion of your primary settlement, which in trun requires expansion of your production base and so on. You will be constantly expanding your population and production in a very fun version of the red queen's race, just as it should be.  U-play is also a non-issue for me, worked perfetly first time and continues to do so.
TL:DR Buy this game.  Unless your favorite parts of Anno games past is the parts you spent alt-tabbing

If you enjoy building games like me, this game is gem in the rough.  It has similar vehicle design to Empyrion, but much more detailed. Submarines, surface ships, aircraft, spaceships, land vehicles and forts can all participate in the same battle.
Pros:
- Sky's the limit in design possibilities.
- Lots of combat.
- Repair bots function automatically.  No need to repair/replace damaged blocks by hand.
- Thousands of designs on the Steam Workshop.
Cons:
- Some counter-intuitive physics at times.  (For example, ships use bouyancy rather than displacement)
- Incredibly steep learning curve.
- Maximum of 50,000 blocks per battle.
- The UI is difficult to navigate and controls are somewhat clunky.

Dieses "Spiel" ist ein 3D Desktop, der eine oder mehrere Wohnungen simuliert, in denen man sich frei bewegen kann, und Gegenstände aufstellt, die dann als Startpunkte für Programme aller Art dienen.
Dadurch ist es möglich, Spiele, Programme und Medien auf natürliche Art und Weise zu gruppieren, ihnen Titelbilder, Cover und Trailer zuzuordnen, und sie dann auf einfachste Art und Weise zu starten.
Während man sich auf einem Desktop mit der Maus bewegt, geschieht das hier durch Bewegen durch die Wohnräume.
Letztendlich ist das Erstellen der Oberfläche aber zeitaufwändig, da jedes Objekt sorgfältig plaziert und eingerichtet werden muß. Das ist der einzige nachteil, den ich sehen kann, da auch Befehle zum kopieren fehlen, um z.B. in eine "neue Wohnung" umzuziehen.
Wer aber grundsätzlich Ordnug in seine Sammlungen bringen möchte, und Spiele starten will, ob sie nun von Steam, UPlay, GOG oder woandersher kommen, ist hier Bestens aufgehoben. Endlich Ordnung, alle Sammlungen in einer Ecke/Raum, etc.
Auch wenn man verschiedenste Emulatoren nutzt, vereinfacht das den Aufruf und die Sortierung der Spiele ungemein, da alle auf die gleiche Art und Weise gestartet werden. Grade diese Objekte können denkbar einfach eingerichtet werden.
Sogar Medien/Serien lassen sich in einem Objekt gruppieren, und starten.
Wer Zeit hat, und den Aufwand als ein Spiel betrachtet, der ist mit diesem Desktopersatz gut bedient.
