Original review:
This review is for Books 1 - 4, as that is what has been released at this time. No spoilers.
If you've played The Longest Journey and Dreamfall and enjoyed the story, this is a must play. The gameplay is closer to a refined Dreamfall than it is to TLJ, but it's less buggy and without the combat. There are some "adventure" segments with puzzle solving, and a lot of exploring and talking. Lots of great returning characters and familiar locations, along with some new ones too. The artistic direction is pretty incredible, being able to see Marcuria in full 3D is a delight.
A new feature to the series is the introduction of decisions that affect the story. I have currently only played through the four books once, so I'm not sure how "worth it" it is to play again and see different paths, but it's in interesting addition. Decisions can for example effect which location you end up spending some time at, or which ally accompanies you on a mission. I could take or leave this feature, but some may feel strongly about it one way or another.
I am loving the story. Eager to see what happens in the concluding chapter.

My first impression is... likely to be my last impression.
This does not at all feel like it was designed to be a standalone game -- but as DLC. If that's wrong, and it was always meant to be a proper sequel, then its the dictionary definition of over-reaching. The first prison has something like 20 inmates, just as many guards, and two stories worth of prison for the player to familiarize themselves with. Couple that with cluttered visual designs that fail to clearly communicate what a given room is meant to be, and a train wreck of UI implementations that solve challenges by chucking everything plus the kitchen sink at the player's head... (sans regard for whether prison inmates are likely to have been given detailed maps of the prison's ventilation systems when they were admitted)
...And what you've got is a developer trying to address the biggest loudest complaints of its player base from the first game: 1.) without realizing that it's player base is NOT composed of GAME DEVELOPERS and therefore: 2.) sacrificing any notion of tutorialization via gameplay arch by: 3.) overwhelming new players with an excess of mechanics; way-too-big, asymetric starting levels; onscreen clutter; and about thirty-too-many NPCs in the first prison.
Rather than focus on escape, I spent day one seeing how these systems - old and new - work in the sequel. My first mission was to get a manicure kit for a prisoner. Neither flavor text nor UI communicated to me that this was an item that had to be crafted from its base components. Meanwhile the crafting menu, having two dozen entries on just one of its five pages, set me spending my first minutes in the game mousing over them one by one to see if SOMETHING in this clunky UI would give me a clue as to what it expected of me.
As I collected the items needed, the on-screen mission log, with its great big bloody check boxes, failed to tick any of those boxes as I gathered the items; Leaving some of my audience (livestream) reasonably presuming that there was a "quest-version" of the item that I had to find somewhere in the prison before I could craft the manicure kit. There isn't. It's just half-done UI implementation.
I never found the nail polish needed to craft the kit, but in the meanwhile I took a quest to bring J-Bomb (or some such fellow) a tub of talcum powder. I found it, brought it to him, pressed 'E,' saw J-Bomb's stats displayed, ticked over to the 'Gift' tab and gave the talcum powder to him. He happily accepted! And then walked away without giving me a dime. Using the gift tab to deliver the quest item did not count as mission completion, I wasn't rewarded, but at least J-Bomb's itchy red areas would improve?
Summarily, what we have here is DLC for The Escapists, meant to be played by enthusiasts who are still enjoying the original game. There's no introductory game arch in this sequel because it expects the player will be coming to it on the heels of finishing the original. The first levels are too big, over-populated, and non-instructional, because players buying DLC don't want or need to start from scratch -- they want expansion on the game they're already familiar with. Makes sense.
The only problem is that someone decided it would be way more lucrative to sell a sequel to the massively popular original than to merely release DLC for a title that few have bothered thinking about in the past two years. Which also makes sense.
Sadly, what we get is a game that not only assumes, but in its present state outright demands, that its players be returning from having played the original... and recently. Team 17 hasn't planned for newcomers or short memories.
Strictly speaking, I'm not a newcomer. Having played The Escapists back when it launched, this sequel reads like an over-reaction to playerbase complaints featuring expansion for expansion's sake. They've gone around spackling in every hole and crack that someone pointed out to them with whatever game device happened to be handy at the time. Um... here's an onscreen mini-map. Why? Dunno. Does that make it better? How about stacked levels, each with ventilation systems, plus the underground? That's 5 unique depths to use level one! Is that too much? How about a dedicated crafting menu with descriptions listing sixty-some items, and no more trading for recipes? Is that an improvement or the opposite?
In their eagerness to please, Team 17 seems to have tried to address everyone's complaints all at once. And by getting rid of what Joey and Davey and Mary each individually disliked, they've accidentally plastered over all the thoughtful game design that made the first title enjoyable. Leaving a game that was once simple enough to explain itself by way of playing it, now complicated beyond comprehensibility by the developer's fevered explanations.
To be clear, I'm not saying that The Escapists 2 is hard. I'm saying it's illegible. If you narrow your attention to simply trying to escape each prison, and block out the excess of static noise presented by the design choices, cluttered spaces, and excessive UI, you'll surely progress.
I simply found that after a half-hour's play, I couldn't be bothered to.

So having played this a few years back, after finishing Terraria, I enjoyed what I played but felt it didn't deliver the same experience for a variety of reasons. Several years later (like a week ago) I gave starbound another go, and my feelings haven't changed.
Combat: 5/10
The combat in Starbound is, at best, serviceable. Beyond weapon types, no weapon felt particularly memorable, none felt like they had personality and many felt same-ish. Many times I would just stick with the same weapons, as the advantages of new weapons were scant. Fighting itself can be awkward, with an energy meter limiting or often crippling your ranged weapons, and melee weapons often being better but subjecting you to more damage due to no invinciblity frames, which can be problematic, especially in the final boss. Still, there are enjoyable moments when jumping in to the frey, but generally combat is tedious, awkward, and frustrating.
Exploration: 7/10
Probably the biggest point of starbound is its unlimited planets. While starbound does offer more volume to explore than Terraria, Terraria's one planet is chock-full of more worthwhile materials and other goodies. The possibilities of what you can find on a planet is also a bit of a double-edged sword, as if you intend on gunning through the main quest first, you'll likely hit a point where you'll have to explore several similar planets looking for your objective, sometimes needing to find two+ towns since one did not contain the right or right amount of objects.
Planets themselves are varied from each other, though it doesn't take long to run into the same structures on the same planet types. As stated above, weapons have a greater variety then Terraria, but less distinguishably severely weakens incentive to spend a long time exploring. That, and ways to explore, as well as mobility in general, feel limited compared to Terraria.
Plus, creating a new world in Terraria is faster and more effective then going to a new world in Starbound, even if you cut out grinding for fuel.
Music: 4/10
Starbound's music is particularly emotional, but incredibly destracting and often not very fitting. The somber music isn't particularly soothing when my starchild is being buried in slime and starving; instead, all it does is draw the image of her tombstone, as she dies alone and unknown, buried on some random planet, no one to discover or remember her. Needless to say, Terraria's more laid-back or kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack (for exploring or fighting a boss respectively) are much better.
Story: 6/10
The main quest is serviceable, with tons of extra details in the codexes. Obviously it's better than Terraria's non-existant story, but it's still fairly mundane.
Graphics: 9/10
The sprites feel nice and detailed, having quite the variety when it comes to npcs. The backgrounds are pleasing to the eye, Npcs are fairly recognizeable from one another, and items are usually distinct. Weapons suffer from having minute difference unless they're high-grade, in which they tend to have unique and interesting sprites.
Overall: 7/10 stand-alone, 6/10 compared to Terraria. Despite my somewhat harsh score, I still enjoyed this game and found it worth the purchase. If you're looking at either this or Terraria, I'd have to urge you toward Terraria; if you're just eyeing this or both, I say grab starbound, it's star-bound to be worth the investment.

Something to keep in mind, I do not believe I have found all the content in this game. There may be machanics or items I don't yet have, but I feel I have experienced enough of Starbound to express my feelings about it.
-It's like Terraria, with a dash of Stardew Valley, and a pretty big spoonfull of MMO grinding.
-Making little colonies is fun.
-Combat is simple and kinda dull. 90% of the time you'll be backtracking with a ranged weapon, which will probably be a bow.
-It's missing the little details that help Terraria stay fresh. Playstyle customization is limited.
-The mech is cool, but it's a shame you can't use it effectiely anywhere but space. I'd love to take it down to mine and explore, but it would just run outta power. The mech parts (and components to build the parts) are all RNG drops, so they're a pain to get.
-Optimization issues. Lag spikes most notably. Mobs kind phase around in responce to damage sometimes and weather effects can drop the framerate.
-Bad story. I've only glanced at the story, but it's already tossing red flags my way. That may be unfair, but I usually hate the type of narratives Starbound is setting up.
-Useless morph ball mode. We could have had something cool and useful, like a grappling hook in that ability slot. Instead, we have a morph ball mode that feels like it's only there for the reference.
Starbound is still not bad. I couldn't see myself playing it with my friends though.

Starbound is a calm, open world, 2D sidescrolling, open world game. It is a game that you can play whenever you happen to feel the need or have a quick 15 minutes to kill. In case you get tired of the FPSs, MMOs, or you're just bored, Starbound's gameplay is casual and calming. The sound track is absolutely no waste as it submerges you into the worlds you happen upon and discover; well done Mr. Schweitzer. The game might be worth getting just to listen to the various songs and sounds. The art style is more simplistic, utilizing pixel art to an incredible effect. The sights and art that can be acquired or found make the experience blissful and highly appealing to say the least. Many parallels have been drawn Terraria, or other less popular, but similarly styled games. Starbound includes a far greater variety than any other game of the genre by far. The game has beautiful graphics, a stunning sound track, and has more than plenty to do. There is only one down side I would point out: Once the story line is complete and you have fully upgraded your ship, maxed out your armor, and discovered all the different main variation type planets, the game slows and losses momentum if you happen to lack a creative mind set. This stage of the game is not quickly acquirable though, taking a solid 50-60 hours of game play to come close. I would absolutely rate Starbound 5 stars and high recommend for anyone with patience and a nack for civilization building, adventure, or side scrolling gameplay. Would also highly recommend headphones; I cannot do proper justice to the soundtrack in this reveiw.

Anno 2205 has taken a different direction than its predecessors, and I think that decision was needed to keep the series great. However the game feels lacking in terms of randomized challenges. This is its biggest flaw in my opinion.
As a player I want to feel a sense of adventure, and that requires randomness at some level. This game doesn't provide much of that, even on the hardest difficulty. It is as challenging as previous Anno games if played on a high difficulty, which was a concern I had before launch. But it can certainly be easy for all newcomers to the series too. But what is completely lacking is the randomness of discovering an unforeseen problem and dealing with it. That is such a necessity in gaming. Natural disasters and rival corporations provided this previously, and I would be fine if they took one out, but not both. To me, this game without randomness is like food without salt. Sure, the food is fantastic, but I don't want to keep eating it. It will get old much more quickly than it should, and it won't have the replayability that I need.
Pros (in order of strength):
The graphics
Multi-session gameplay
Accessability for newcomers
Management of a city's resources
Music
Cons:
Lack of features (randomness)
Combat
Lack of compelling goals
Story (Campaign)
Linear Gameplay
The thing I love most about this game is the multi-session gameplay. It works so well and so easily -- it's something I always wanted in Anno. I can't praise this design enough. I will easily put 100 hours into my corporation, and I think I could spend 100 more on optimization, solely because of this feature. The modular buildings make the gameplay much more strategic than previous Anno games, although more could be done to make this aspect of gameplay more valuable. Furthermore, and perhaps most importantly, this is a true Anno game. It retains much of the feelings I had for the previous games. It is complex, strategic, beautiful, and addictive. It would definitely be the best Anno game in the series if the criticisms I have listed were resolved in some fashion.
Specifically combat I want to mention because this seems to be a mixed bag. Personally I love the new combat system... if it were a tech demo of the new combat system. As a finished product it feels very incomplete. It reminds me of the RTS games I love, like Sins of a Solar Empire or Age of Empires. But there's no variety -- no randomness that I spoke of above. I played it once at each difficulty setting and that's all I'd care to do for now. I love that you have abilities to use now to help your ships in combat (1404 and 2070 had this concept but it is better implemented here). I just wish there were more of a point to it beyond grinding for resources and xp.
Many reviews I have read are unfair and go beyond the scope of critising this game. I have had trouble with Uplay when I played 2070 around 2 years ago. It stopped me from playing the game completely for a long period of time. But, that experience in no way affected my decision to buy this game. Uplay has been perfect so far with 2205. Lack of multiplayer may be a criticism for the direction of the series, but it is not a valid criticism of this game. I have used multiplayer in 2070, and it was fun, but it would not work the same way in 2205 if it had it. A different concept for multiplayer would have to be established for this game, and I'm guessing that is why they chose not to include the feature. I would also argue that no feature is dumbed down in this game. They simply took out tedious micromanaging that I can't believe anyone would consider a strength of the past games.
When it comes down to price, I don't see how this game is worth $60 or $80. I payed $80 and I'm glad I did, but for a lot of people it may not seem worth it. $30-40 is the price I would value it at.
The conclusion: I would bet that most people would enjoy 2070 more, but if they added some much needed features, this game (or its sequel) will definitely be the best of the series. For now, it remains on par with 1404 and 2070.

Firstly, I will say I have been with the Anno franchise since 1602 and have played every single Anno since. Anyone who is a fan of the franchise should know that each game has changed considerably with each iteration whether it be the use of community centres, what resources you will need and where, what sort of factions you will build... 2205 is just the same. Whilst I agree mildly with some reviews which says certain features have been removed for no reason like having a warehouse with goods in that you can trade for profit and not knowing how many of each production building you will need for optimum output, once you put some time into the game you realise that it's very much an Anno game at the core.
I am at the point in the game where you first start to colonise the moon which was 5 hours of casual play. When I first started the game I was a bit worried. It didn't seem like it had the same production managment that you did previous. I loved optimising farm space and working in little tight production trees which use as little space as possible and once you start on the later goods you realise that it's still there in the module system. I'm loving modules and figuring out how much space I need to optimise the production factory to maximum. It's just done in a different way.
As for rare materials, I remember that 1701 did a similar thing with resources like Jade? And lets not forget licences from 2070. You get them from completing quests, you don't have to do the combat minigame.
As for the combat minigame, I agree there needs to be more maps. But I feel that maps will be added to the game as it moves along and I don't think that's a bad thing. It's keeps interest. I like the combat as it gets rid of a bit of monotony, though the people do start bugging you about completing and then suddenly another will be available.
When reading reviews bear in mind the amount of time the person has played they game as like any Anno game it's a nice relaxing start that suddenly becomes too much to bear. And whilst I believe I'm a player that will figure these problems out quite easy (Watching youtubers play this game is rage inducing.) I'm still not worried about longevity.
If you must. Give it time, wait for people to get over the rage of how easy 1 hour of gameplay is and then come back and see if opinions change.

A pretty hard game to review, since so much has been changed to Anno since the last game. The one thing they did away with was the stockpile, as other reviews said. I actually quite enjoy this to be honest. I previously experienced this style of gameplay in Grand Ages: Rome, and I thought it was an improvement, as it meant "resources" would flow instantly, instead of having to wait for an individual unit to travel from island to island, and it gave me a firm grasp on where production was having problems along the supply chain, instead of having to figure out that Factory X is only producing at 80% because it doesn't have enough input.
This will probably get a ton of hate, but I never liked having to deal with trade ships in Anno. It ususaly meant that I had to either constantly decide how much a ship would take off of one island to keep the balance between the two, or I would just build dedicated resource islands whose sole purpose was outputting the maximum ammount of resources or goods to the main island.
I've read in reviews that people complain that the city building aspect is gone, and I have to ask, was there ever really one in the first place? Place houses around a city center and level them up with goods and buildings was probably all the depth Anno had in the first place, and that's all still in this game. Labor actually matters this time around however. You need to have enough people to run your buildings or production lags behind.
All in all, I do feel like this is a huge departure from the previous Anno games, and that always creates hate. Remember the rage when Civ 5 first came out? The lack of unit stacking turned Civ into a board game it was said. Well, I think that same kind of hate is being applied here.
So personally, I find that there are changes I like, changes I dislike, but I find the ones I like outweigh the ones I dislike.

I really enjoyed this game. I played 1st one as well so I was interested in how the story ends especially because of amazing outro. The story of previous game was amazing with a lot of plot twists. However, in case of this game, it was shorter and narrower. Anyway, I still enjoyed it and I really loved the ending. If I would play it as a standalone game I would be still satisfied, but I also understand those who are disappointed especially when they are comparing it to the first game.
When it comes to gameplay - play this game with controller!!! (I played with X-box controller and I can only recommend it). There was like only one mini game when I switched to mouse for a faster and smoother aiming. Otherwise this game is really difficult to play with keyboard, especially because hints are given in X-box controller binding (for example "Press [insert green circle with A letter] to continue").
Combat system was amazing compared to the previous game. Camera was also improved. Those two things let you really enjoy all the fights, especially those with bosses. On the other hand, difficulty was decreased (at least this is my impression) compared to the previous game. And not only during fights. I also found climbing passages much easier. Yes, they were smoother, more intuitive and much less painful than in previous game, but on the other hand, I felt like I am just moving stick in one of the 4 directions and Gabriel is auto-piloting himself through those catch points on the wall. If those passages are replaced with cinematics of Gabriel climbing some wall, I would not see any difference and that is a bit disappointing for me.
When it comes to stealth passages, I see a lot of people did not like them. Honestly, I expected those passages will be very often and very boring after reading some reviews, but I found them quite interesting and there were actually only few in the game.
Another thing I would like to mention are puzzles. I really liked puzzles in the first game and this was probably the biggest disappointment for me, because there were only few puzzles and difficulty of all of them was like difficulty of puzzles in pre-school kid magazines.
And last thing I would like to talk about are graphics. They are really amazing. Especially castle is truly master piece. However, it is looking quite the same all the time. During playing the first game, player is going through various environments. Each one looks different. Each one got different colour scheme. Each one got unique textures. Environments in first game are truly amazing and I still remember a lot of amazing sceneries from there. But with this game everything is dark and quite the same. Only colourful place I can remember was one garden passage within the castle (I will not say more details to not spoil it). Details are still really amazing, but everything is so dark and similar, that you will stop sense them.
I guess this is mainly because the game is open-world like and not level system like in previous game so environment have to be "one solid connected piece". In the first game all what was needed was simple introduction "and in this level Gabriel went to some other place far away from previous one" and environment could change drastically. In this game it has to fit all together, because there is no space for long distance travelling.
Well, to sum it up - I was satisfied with this game. If I would not play the first one I would probably enjoy it much more. The truth is, that the first game set really high standards and they were overcome only in a very few cases. For the most of them, they were below those from the first game. Still, I would give this game something about 70-80%.

Well, this was quite a waste of potential. Dracula vs Satan in the fantastic/futuristic modern day setting among the apocalypse - sounds exciting. Plays boring.
First LoS was a really boring game, but at least the story was coherit, the art style was beautiful and it, while borrowed, truly *tried*. It felt like it was trying to be a good an exciting game. Usually it wasn't. But it's the thought that counts.
Mirror of Fate was surprisingly fantastic, falling slightly flat from what people expect from the 2D Castlevania, but a fun mix of classic games in the series with gameplay elements of LoS.
LoS 2 tries to improve. It looks better technologically, tries to rebalance some things in a good way, makes camera mostly good, removes the linear level progress in favor of the open world and makes soundtrack especially nice. And then adds forced stealth sections. And boring bland looking levels. And "secrets" which usually feel like pointless stuff. And incoherit storytelling without any conflict you can feel (but it's there, honest!).
This feels like Blood Omen 2 recreated in LoS universe. Except Blood Omen 2 was still a pretty okay game with some excitement and Kain, while this game just... is. LoS 1 was boring, this game just exists. It's just there. And you can play it. But you really shouldn't.

You establish sets of a small group of people, and start with a basic town. The leaders, workers, and such are chosen by you (loosely). When you say so, a group of scouts is sent to explore the rest of the world. As you grow, more in-depth technologies, concepts,  and ideas are thrown in. There could be a government run business, build housing, stores and such. Afterwards, the game goes into a mode similar to BEYOND EARTH, and your civ decides to settle a new planet, whether out of prosperity and a want to expand, or a chance to start a new life from Great Mistakes. Some of the planets you choose may be inhabited, some may have lower intelligence life forms, and some may have a mix of lower and higher intellignece life forms. The higher ones are actual alien civilizations, true NPCs. The planet may have one alien NPC civ, or multiple ones with their own culture. After that, you expand further, have interplanetary wars, alliances, and maybe even go across the galaxy. Some civs may even "absorb" each other into one bigger civ. The chance of having one civ from one planet in the corner of a galxay rule about 100 different galxies is there, just near impossible. I challenge you to design such a game.

Call me Ishmael. Some years ago - never mind how long precisely - having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen, and regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people's hats off - then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and ball. With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself upon his sword; I quietly take to the ship. There is nothing surprising in this. If they but knew it, almost all men in their degree, some time or other, cherish very nearly the same feelings towards the ocean with me.

There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs - commerce surrounds it with her surf. Right and left, the streets take you waterward. Its extreme down-town is the battery, where that noble mole is washed by waves, and cooled by breezes, which a few hours previous were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.

Circumambulate the city of a dreamy Sabbath afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip, and from thence, by Whitehall northward. What do you see? - Posted like silent sentinels all around the town, stand thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries. Some leaning against the spiles; some seated upon the pier-heads; some looking over the bulwarks of ships from China; some high aloft in the rigging, as if striving to get a still better seaward peep. But these are all landsmen; of week days pent up in lath and plaster - tied to counters, nailed to benches, clinched to desks. How then is this? Are the green fields gone? What do they here?

But look! here come more crowds, pacing straight for the water, and seemingly bound for a dive. Strange! Nothing will content them but the extremest limit of the land; loitering under the shady lee of yonder warehouses will not suffice. No. They must get just as nigh the water as they possibly can without falling in. And there they stand - miles of them - leagues. Inlanders all, they come from lanes and alleys, streets and avenues, - north, east, south, and west. Yet here they all unite. Tell me, does the magnetic virtue of the needles of the compasses of all those ships attract them thither?

Once more. Say, you are in the country; in some high land of lakes. Take almost any path you please, and ten to one it carries you down in a dale, and leaves you there by a pool in the stream. There is magic in it. Let the most absent- minded of men be plunged in his deepest reveries - stand that man on his legs, set his feet a-going, and he will infallibly lead you to water, if water there be in all that region. Should you ever be athirst in the great American desert, try this experiment, if your caravan happen to be supplied with a metaphysical professor. Yes, as every one knows, meditation and water are wedded for ever.

But here is an artist. He desires to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting bit of romantic landscape in all the valley of the Saco. What is the chief element he employs? There stand his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as if a hermit and a crucifix were within; and here sleeps his meadow, and there sleep his cattle; and up from yonder cottage goes a sleepy smoke. Deep into distant woodlands winds a mazy way, reaching to overlapping spurs of mountains bathed in their hill-side blue. But though the picture lies thus tranced, and though this pine-tree shakes down its sighs like leaves upon this shepherd's head, yet all were vain, unless the shepherd's eye were fixed upon the magic stream before him.

Updating this review...
Pros:
- Player feedback is asked for and listened to
- They're adding player mods that are deemed good into the game, accelerating the development by letting YOU participate in it.
- Customizability^4
- Actively developed
- Coop / vs with people you invite
- Great tutorials
Cons: Some graphics things:
- No graphic transitions between land, water and vehicles. You know... Eye candy that pretends to be physics.
- Inventory is just text, no fancy images (icons)
- I'd like to see some permanent effects on the terrain if/when I crash a flying fortress into it. (EDIT: Turns out the code for terrain damage already exists, but it's turned off. Dev response was about new components taking priority. Can't blame.).
Don't get scared off by "hard to learn" reviews. Your in-game failures don't make you angry because there are no serious consequences. And if you DO get angry, you get to know the reason and the solution for it. There's no grinding for days to get what you want. Your progress is not limited by the hours you put into the game. This also means that if you don't progress at all, the game won't punish you.
For example, I went into designer mode, built my boat, spawned some enemy ships, got obliterated in seconds, sunk my character to the bottom of the sea and spawned some planes and submarines of a third fraction to destroy the one that killed my ship. I could respawn my ship at any time but I enjoyed watching their combat with camera detached from my character! There are A LOT of other designs you can watch do battle. Or spawn them as your own and reverse-engineer some things :D
You can also go and do different story missions and scenarios. You can set the difficulty EXACTLY the way you want it. Ever bothered you that enemies on "hard" do more damage than you with the same weapons? You can tone that down or even turn the odds in your favor. You think that salvaging enemies is unfair? Make vehicles worth less or no resources when destroyed. Etc.
The game is Alpha. Might get more expensive upon release. It doesn't have a demo version so I waited for it to come on a big discount. Bought it on 80% off and I have a great time with it. Worth the full price. Might buy it again if I convince a friend to play it someday.

If you have an OCD personality that loves to figure out how complicated systems work, this game will entertain you for weeks.
For the amount of money this game costs, there is incredible depth to the game system design that most games do not approach including games with tens of millions of dollars of development budget.
This is made by a small indie developer that deserves and has earned my patronage, and imo deserves yours as well.
Pros:
*Vehicle design lab lets you build and test your designs against a library of enemies I have collected so I can see how various defensive/offensive systems work
*Very complex weapon systems that allow you to fine tune almost any aspect of behavior
*Layers of offensive and defensive systems, not every weapon works in every situation and likewise not every defensive system will save you from every weapon
*Physics based so if you are building a ship, sub, aircraft or spacecraft you have to balance your mass, deal with drag surfaces, pitch, roll, and yaw, and figure out how to balance power requirements, propulsion, and attitude thrust
*Some cool sci-fi ish things like lasers, ion cannon, warp drives, rail guns
*Customizeable AI behaviors so you can turn them on or off to suit your needs, make a few drones and set them on auto while you manage your feel or build something new
*Supply resources that can be set in global or local mode - you can choose if you want to make your game harder by have resources localized so you cant just insta build a huge asset far from your supply lines without bringing those supplies there - you have to protect your supply assets
*Watching 60 VLS missles, cannons, lasers, and all manner of weaponry firing simultaneously is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic
*Much more
Cons:
*Small team so development takes time, I personally think with more resources this game, which is already worth far more than is being charged for it, could be truly amazing
*Multiplayer is limited to a few people where one person hosts the server and is pretty jankyu right now in campaign mode, lots of save corruption and at times the players get de-synched from the server and really wierd♥♥♥♥♥♥happens - if these guys can fix the multiplayer though omg badass

The developer goes out of their way to explain that it's "not a game, but an aesthetic concept". Ok, I get that. OutDrive hits a lot of marks - compelling artstyle, pretty great music and it runs well to boot, but in the end it actually is a game in the sense that you need to control a car and keep it between a number limiting factors, namely the road edges and the upper and lower speed limits. Sadly, this part just isn't fun. Devs, if you want me to hear (and potentially buy) your music and you choose to package it in the form of a game, then you'll need to make the game component compelling as well, especially since I'm forced to actively play the game in order to hear the music.

To start with I could not work out how to move the car at enough speed to last more than 10 seconds but once I realised I needed to rebind the Boost key from SHIFT to another key I found this game entertaining.
The car handling is not smooth as it likes to fling itself about a bit but once I got the hang of using the booster to keep it under control I found myself enjoying its unique handling experience.

There seems to be a lot of negative reviews out for this game today about half a day after release. I would like to share mine.
I’m not really a fan of Anno games, but I do like city building / resource management games. I have played Anno 2070 for 265hours, finished all the hardest missions, and filling all the islands with endgame building monuments and modules for all 3 factions.
I’ve been in Anno 2205 for about 3 hours. Much has been changed in this game. Resources are less modular and simplified, there is much less of needing to use your command ship to ship fixed amount of resource, most are done automatically. Your residence generate income, create workers supply, factories create more advance building materials to make next tier of buildings, and uses electricity and workers as maintenance. You build electricity modules to power all buildings, it simply cost income to maintain. Maintaining this 3 core resources seems to be the core of the resource management system, with much more advance building material in the late game.
In 2070, quest offered by npc are limitless. In 2205 there seems to be less quest offered, at least in early game, but they are much longer in chain, with the first quest resulting in being able to rebuild a dam offering lots of power resource. There are 3 regions to play in, each with multiple sectors, temperate, artic and lunar. Each sector has its own long line of projects to complete. The early intro quest extends to the late game from the start, guiding you in your entire game progression.
The combat in the game has been change. Instead of being in the sector where you build building, you join standalone missions and complete military missions with your fleet of warships. There are alot of variety in the different ships at your disposal. Modular upgrades that you can buy and place in your ship for extra bonus in various attributes from the previous game has been removed. Instead, each ships have multiple abilities, missile barrage, emp etc. Ships has utility abilities like repair and shield. This cost either limited uses or fuel, which is also limited. This can be replenished by fuel lying around the map or powerups that you can pick up with your ship to replenish ability use or fuel. By finishing assignments and missions, you gain military experience where you can permanently upgrade your military ships attributes or gain new ones. You also earn new rare resource iridium and graphene that can be used to upgrade your HQ or your factory with additional modules that boost productivity or becomes less taxing on worker use or power usage.
Multiplayer has been removed, this game no longer has pvp support, though I wasn’t really interested in the pvp element of the previous game.
One huge impressive element in this game is the graphics. The islands and water in the game looks beautiful. The amount of artistic work placed in the futuristic theme is huge. All ships and buildings looks extremely high tech. Factories all have their unique looks from different regions. The military missions are much more explosive with the much more Arcady style of gameplay, with improvements in the fx effects etc. Large bridges extend and connects islands in the temperate region. Beautiful glaciers and artic mountains cover the artic region. Each sector also seems to be larger than in the previous games. All Sectors in different regions, including the lunar ones are all connected via the global map, which is where you can see the progress of other npc owned areas and also set up global trading routes from one sector to another.
Overall I have enjoyed the game experience so far, and if you’re looking for a relaxing casual single player only game of city building mixed with military ship gameplay enhanced with gorgeous looks, I would recommend this game to you. (Will probably update this review as I play longer)
EDIT: Been playing this for much more longer and game definitely has much more challenge.

EDIT: 1.4m+ population, this game is awesome.

The game fails in execution as it suffers from asymmetric difficulty between beginning and end.
Now that may sound like virtually every game ever but the goldy locks zone in the middle is short-lived at best and non-existent at worst for this game.  Game starts off with a modicum of difficulty but it's pseudodifficulty in the form of RNG more than actual skill as the AI is dull and repetitive. The only solace comes in the form of wonders which apply unique upgrades but these do nothing to change the calculus of battle.

Red Faction 2 has issues but is worth playing anyway.
There is no multiplayer (except vs bots) but then again even if it did by this point nobody would be playing it. There isn't as much destructible terrain as in either Red Faction 1 or Red Faction Guerilla but there doesn't neccesarily need to be. The story is a bit boring and more than a bit predictable but truly amazing stories in shooters are a rarity.
As for what the game does right the weapons for the most part are very varied and feel decently well balanced. There are some weapon balance issues, the grenade launcher pretty much beats every other explosive weapon in the game in terms of efficiency and the sniper rifle is extremly powerful for how much ammo drops for it, but they aren't massive problems. The game has regenerating health but it is slow and mostly there so you are never in an unwinnable situation. Most of your healing will be done with medkits which you can carry 3 of with you that are used automatically when you would die. The campaigns vehicle sections also aren't the worst thing ever being playable but not fantastic.
Overall the key is to not go into Red Faction 2 expecting the greatest shooter of all time or some completely destructible environment. If you go in expecting a decent old school style shooter you will probably enjoy yourself. If you need a score i would say this game is a 7/10.

First, let me get this out of the way:
I am a big Castlevania fan. I got into the series during the GBA days (for the record I was about thirteen when Circle of the Moon came out). I played it, I played Harmony of Dissonance, Aria of Sorrow, both the DS Castlevania games, and yes... I wish they'd go back to those... but that doesn't mean this is a bad game.
The voice acting is good, the combat is fun and engaging, the level design is interesting (especially the bits in Dracula's castle), and it has some of the most imaginative bosses I've seen (the Toymaker is a special favorite).
... it just doesn't play like a Castlevania game.
Its neat to play as Dracula, its neat to have to fight as a vampire and use vampiric powers, and damn if I didn't let out a laugh when I saw what happened to that Chupacabra ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ from the first game.
... but it feels more like God of War.
Its by no means a bad game! I had fun with it! The giant robot fight at the beginning was lovably nuts and the fight against Death was really intense and actually almost killed me more than a few times.
... but it just doesn't feel like a Castlevania game.
So, go into it not thinking of it as a Castlevania game. Think of it as a game where you play an ancient vampire who was awoken to fight off invaders to his realm and who has to learn to act and fight in a modern day world and regain his powers after his long slumber.
Its great, its a hell of a lot of fun. Its just... not really a 'Castlevania' game.

I would say I recommend this product if you enjoyed the first game, but by itself...a 60/40 chance like/dislike it. While I have not played the Handheld Mirror of Fate, I did play the First Lords of Shadow (which, seemed more like different series than Castlevania at all).
Story-wise it seems to be true to the "Lore" its built more or less. I think it might have the weird notion of putting lore in there you might not really interact with, nor I think it was as compelling as First one in that regard. The story does have at least one twist near the end, but seemed ye can probably guess fair bit of it. Nonetheless, conceptually still pretty cool at least, and castle bits I'd say were the more interesting of it all. Funnily enough, taking to a modern-futuresque setting seems like what the series did before its reboot...
Gameplay wise, its similar to the first, but with too many enemies that have Guard-breaker attacks. Quite a bit of depth with lot of the moves you can use, including fun glitches which you can find at a give GameFaq's site for more details on. Unlike the more mission/level selection screen of the first, they instead wanted to opt for little "exploration" like the more hack & slash ones did. Albeit not as focused on it, making getting collectables/powers-ups far more tedious than the first LoS. In addition to that, there's a lot of "Waiting" with exploration, that I felt really bogged down the game. As well that most of the exploration isn't till near the end game, making the likelyhood you'll do so that much more unlikely.
Lastly, yes, there is Stealth, and its alright. It's moreso just very short puzzles of sorts. It makes sense in the begining from a story perspective, but after that seemed uneeded, they were mostly not that fun unfortunately (I'm on generally ok with Stealth gameplay in games).
I understand this isn't really a in-depth review, but I figure the ones top-voted already do the game better on details. I just want to try and give my thoughts now while they were fresh.

I had a much better time with this than I expected. The early reviews for the game made it sound like it was terrible, but it really wasn't that bad. However, that's not to say it isn't without its flaws.
The highlight of the game is probably its combat. You get three different weapons this time around instead of just magical powerups for the whip like in the original LOS: A light magic sword, dark magic gauntlets, and the whip returns as the default weapon. Each has their own style and role in combat; the sword can heal you when you do damage, the gauntlets do more damage than the other two overall and can also break enemy blocking, and the whip has good crowd control skills and has more range overall. Each weapon also has a fleshed out skill/move set tree that you can unlock with experience points. Gabriel controls more or less the same as he did in LOS with a couple tweaks, like a free moving camera.
For the overall main plot the game is shorter than the original Lords of Shadow, but it has much more in the way of secret items and challenge modes. The game is also much less linear than the original, with a semi-open world map that you can freely roam when not in a specific mission. The voice work is high quality, with much of the cast of the original returning (Patrick Stewart FTW) along with some new cast members who give a great performance as well. The game itself also looks great with very detailed and unique locals, characters, and monsters.
The biggest let down of the game is probably the forced stealth sections. They slow down what is normally a relatively fast paced game to a crawl, and don't work out well with how the game controls. They also don't really make sense in the context of the game, you are supposed to be this powerful being and yet these power armored lackeys can utterly destroy you if they see you. Thankfully there aren't many of these sections, and the rest of the game definitely makes up for it.
Overall I'd say the game is pretty good and is definitely worthwhile if you've played the other Lords of Shadow games.

Robot1: BaBaBa Ba Ba, Robot2: Ba BaBa BaBa Ba

Okay, so first off, after about 17 hours of gameplay I can say I have finished the main story line and therefore believe I am ready to truly talk about the game itself.
Here is the pros and cons:
Pros:
+ lovely asthetics, everything looks and feels very well made.
+ very well made music track
+ the new map system is very nice, and while you will have to load between changing to the different maps, you can often check up on other things such as trade routes.
+ the mechanics have been "streamlined" a bit more. Instead of having only a number with the amount of goods in storage and a small arrow to mark if it is increasing or decreasing, they now show you much you actually get "overflowing". And you can see how much you have in storage by hovering over the resource.
+ the UI is a lot sleeker now and hides a lot better everything, but at the same time gives you much information by a few button clicks. Wanna check how much goods is made/used up? One click. Also more emphazism on the different hot keys (a to promote, c to copy a building, d to destroy, m to move)
+ the modular system is absolutely wonderful and gives new depth. You no longer "have to" put down all those farm bits for 100% working condition, but if you spend more place you can get up to 300-800% effectivity at the maintenence of 150-500%. It gives you new reason to attempt to build up a perfect system where everything fits a'la tetris.
+ some smart small things, such as capability to press on a specificed sea or mountian spot and simply build what you want like that.
Cons:
- the old trade system where you could use say one ship to transport six different kinds of things are completely gone. Whilst the new one is good I still wished we could somehow upgrade and make our transports bigger for having different kinds of material on same transport.
- crisis zones are only really there since they choosed not to have war in your sectors, and that would be hard with war on nine different fronts, and the only us for them is to get rare materials, which you can later get with a project. Also they quickly become a chore.
- the content amount maybe feels a bit to small. Yes there is nine projects you can do plus increase your military rank to new heights, but it quickly becomes the same old grind.
- no multiplayer, in any form except for the world market that interacts with all players, also the Council.
- as of right now, no random true sandbox maps. The nine maps are the ones you get.
While yes Anno 2205 has deviated a lot and as many people say they have not followed the true spirit of the Anno games, I absolutely still love this. It is a fresh breath of air, giving us a new onlook from the old games. Anno 2205 is no clone, copy or retexture of any of the old games, as it is truly new mechanics. Do I say these mechanics are good? Well not always, but they are really all not that bad as some people would like you to believe. And the thing is the things we've lost to this Anno game is due to something we've all be screaming that we wanted, the multi-map system. For example the old trade system, setting them up in nine different sectors? Count me out. If you thought it could be complicated with one map and the old trade system, try nine with the old one. Also multiplayer (which we might see in the future?) I have to ask how they would implement it. Maybe through players having same company? Well the maps are now saved on your computer and there is very little usage of the internet and cloud. Most likely it would lag and in need of hosting from a certain computer. As the chosen computer probably would have to send information about all the different maps. And since there is nine maps right now only you cannot have another company.
So yea, I believe they done everything right to take the Anno series in a new direction, which I am interested to see how it will be because I believe, the multi-map system is here to stay, and that is for a long long loooooooong time.

Greetings fellow gamers.
My History with Anno Franchise:  I have played all of the Anno games since the very first one. I loved every game to the bone, playing more than 500 hours each. I loved the intricate system in which you guessed the consumption of your citizens the trade that you could create, and all of those good things the game had.
•	As various posters wrote, I check and found that indeed there are stockpiles. What I find lacking is the ability to do something with said stockpile. ATM (I am already established in the Luna zone) I don’t know what to do with my excess, I cannot sell it to an NPC, or let my warehouse sell the items.
•	More mechanics have appeared, Artic zone compels you to build housing within range of factories, which produce heat. If you do not build the houses within range of heat sources, they will not function at all. This is cool, because it tends to make you fashion towns based on your factories, instead of the usual clump of housing. Luna, on the other hand, needs to have all of the buildings protected with shield generators to “avoid radiation and meteor strikes”. I find this part super cool.
•	As more your progress your resources take a new spin, mainly you cash turns out to be a rather important item. Factories start to cost 45000 credits, which can be a hefty sum. Heck even housing costs. This makes money way more important than in previous anno games which focused on the goods produced. I still prefer the old approach.
The game is indeed oversimplified, as it was stated on videos by the company. But hell, I never expected the game to be dumbed down.
At first glance the first new feature is the fact that the people who work in the city, now indeed work, which is a cool addition, your population now means something else besides taxes. But that’s it. I haven’t found a way to increase or lower tax rates, and now I need to have everything in the island connected with a road. I remember my storehouses connected with the farms and that was it.
Production was completely destroyed. You now have buildings which state how much amount of something they produced, (which is cool, but takes away from the tinkering of preview Anno games). So you know exactly how much of a given building you need to get resource “A”. There are NO STOCKPILES, so if you have surplus of a resource it won’t get stored, therefore you cannot sell that resource and trade with NPCs. You may upgrade production buildings with different stuff, such as more production of said resource, less worker/energy/supply maintenance, of course all of these upgrades cost “special materials” which are acquired by doing quests, and/or fighting the warzone maps, I have only experienced one shortage of a product because I rushed in on a quest. Finally resources have been tampered with, rivers are gone, and in with the “coast slots” just a cosmetic change in my opinion.
Fleets are gone, and this surely pisses me off. I’d love building boats, and acquiring defenses for my towns. I remembered popping my first transports creating connections between my islands, well that is gone, the only “trade” in existence now is between the different “zones” (more of that ahead). If Zone A produces more than 5 of “x” you can trade that to zone B. Continuing with fleets, you now have “warzones” or whatever they are called, in which you are provided with an amount of ships and you have to complete a certain target (capture a point, destroy X objective, and so forth). You only interact with your ship by purchasing upgrades for the different models you are given. Fielding a fleet by manufacturing the goods, gathering the cash, and building a shipyard? Yeap, that is all gone. You cannot create controls to you ships, you can select all of them with the TAB key.
There is no save icon, or option. I had my brain going nuts about, it Today I hope the save is still there cause in the end I left my “corporation” by leaving the whole game.
You got zones now, which are basically the different areas in which you produce different goods. Ala European/Arabic Island from Anno 1404, or Eco-Tycoon/Tech/underwater Island from anno 2070. Thing is they are on a whole different map. WTF? You now have Temperate, Artic, and Luna. So if you need product X produced at Artic on temperate, you go to the “world map” if artic has surplus of said product you select it and create a route to temperate. DONE, no real boast involved no nothing just a few clicks.
I truly cannot find the challenging layer from other Anno games in this one. It is completely simplified, and not in a good way.
Factions are gone. No more Ecos or tycoons. Which blows for me, but then again they did announce it on the trailers. Still there are “factions” AKA good guys vs bad guys.
Combat is simplified, yeap, there is not even that rock/papper/sicsors thing from the lastone. You now have various boats, which surely have those capabilities, but since you never really build up your forces you just horde the enemy slightly smaller horde. After the skirmish you heal up with the “fuel” dropped by the enemy. Rinse and repeat.
UI is amazing and up to day standards, sleek transparent and cool looking. Graphics are mind-blowing, but I sometimes get stutters I run the game with 16gb a SSD drive and a 290x graphic card. The water physics are cool and everything about the visuals is amazing. There are some in game videos with subpar animations (the people look like they were brought from 2003).
I could not find any skirmish modes, or some way to play multiplayer, I shall be updating this review with more hours played though.
•	Game is beautiful. And the views are amazing, from the dazzling buildings to the waves in the sea.
•	UI is amazing, sleek, minimalistic, and very modern
•	I’d say this game would be OK for someone entering the anno series, it is a very, very simplified version of original Annos,  this of course is a Con for those of us already engaged with the series.
•	You now know how much stuff is produced from each building
•	No trade, just a simplified version between zones
•	No storage just positive and negative outputs.
•	Since you now know how much is produced, for those experienced Anno players, the difficulty depth was taken away
•	No ships, you make do with what you are given. You can upgrade your boats but that’s it.
•	To those knowledgeable with other Annos, you will find this game too simplistic, and should avoid it. Stick with the other older versions.
Hope this was valuable for you.
Will try to keep playing to get to know the game better.

Somehow this game is even LESS like Castlevania than Lords of Shadow 1.
It's like Mercury Stream's objective was to cram in as many aspects from OTHER successful games as possible, hoping that by emulating them that they'd make a blockbuster. This game took a lot of chances by drastically distancing themselves from the traditional Castlevania formula and judging by the abysmal metacritic score, things didn't pan out for this game as the devs had hoped.
Dracula endures stealth segments like metal gear solid and at times transforms into a rat to covertly delve into enemy ground, very much like the morph ball from Metroid Prime. Also instead of a level select book like in the prequel we now have a psuedo open world to explore, like SotN. Beating up enemies is a 1:1 conversion from the previous game and the rockclimbing simulation aspect was reigned in just slightly.
I have a few gripes about this game. Though the overhead map in the corner ensured I'd not be lost for very long, I still managed to get stuck in several rooms scratching my head hoplessly trying to figure out what to do or pick up to continue. Eventually I'd stumble upon whichever asanine detail of the room I had missed in my multiple examinations.
This game's biggest shortcoming is the plot. The writers had an outline of what they wanted to have the main character do and feel, and while they try to explain his motivation the game just feels full of holes.
This game is like a delicious recipie with some fresh ingredients, but the chef forgot to stir the pot as it was cooking so now the meal separated. Rather than blend together into one satisfying experience we have competing facets of gameplay (flavors) that seem to detract from one another.
I heard mercury stream had a lot of problems. Maybe if the people running the company paid their employees and stopped enforcing their asanine and uninspired ideas over the people who had experience making games then this game would have been better recieved.
As it is only TWO people on my ~200 friend list have bought your game and BOTH dropped it more than halfway through.
Despite all this game's shortcomings it has plenty to offer and overall I enjoyed playing it.

While I originally enjoyed my experience with the game, while also getting it at a good price, I find the choice of the developers distasteful. They left the game a bit of a buggy mess, and pretty much dropped all support for it after they released the YOSE version of the game, which also has a few extra bells and whistles that this version of the game does not have. This forces any loyal players to have to buy the game again in order to get those bells and whistles. Anyway, on to the game:
You start off on a camping trip to the forest of a small town with a buddy of yours, when suddenly the zombies come. Fighting them off, you decide to find out what happened, as you had been away from the civilized world for some time. You meet others, and find out that whatever this thing was, it was widespread. The whole town had been infected, only leaving small groups of survivors. I will say no more to prevent story spoilers.
The main gameplay aspect of this game is probably the base building. You start off with a little base but could move it to a more suitable location, of which there are many. From wherever your base is, your main goal is to pretty much go through the story as you upgrade your base, kill zombies for XP to level up and to gain new abilities, and get supplies to upgrade your base. I know it might sound a bit boring but it can be pretty fun. Especially at night, when it gets even spookier. Not to mention there are special zombies, that can mess you up real good. This makes clearing out buildings full of zombies even more challenging, and if you're easily frightened then you'll be in for a bad time as well.
One honorable mention is the cars. They're very fun to drive in my opinion, especially when mowing down a horde of zombies with a truck. Just keep an eye on the cars durability. You don't want to lose the survivor you're playing as (you can choose to switch between survivors - useful for when your main survivor is killed or injured.)

your primary objective is to survive, of course, but beyond that it’s about building and sustaining a community. Which means keeping everyone fed and housed, stocked up with ammo and medication, and building materials to expand. It’s your choice how you go about it, and what kind of leader you become: though you’ll need to switch characters when one is too tired or hurt (or dead) to continue, you’ll generally have a small core group under your control, and a handful of AI allies to join you on missions. Not that two heads are always better than one on stealth missions, though it pays off when you’re unexpectedly ambushed.
It’s a game that affords you a rare degree of freedom, and as such you’ll sometimes find yourself paralyzed by choice. Do you lure zombies out of a house you’re planning to ransack, or smash the window and lob a Molotov through? And when you find a rucksack, do you risk the long trek back to base while encumbered, or break it open for less valuable rewards?
It can be tough going at times, and any misjudgments are harshly punished. That’s no criticism, because

Overall I enjoy the game quite a bit, but it is certainly lacking in a few categories.  Its basically two completely separate games in one: one world map in which you navigate to different worlds and choose to enter the battles, then the battle map where you spend about 80-90% of the game in spaceship combat against pirates, marauders, and your enemy empires when you inevitably go to war with them.
All in all, it is a simple game that may not be terribly fulfilling, but is entertaining and relatively quick compared to other Sid Meiers installments.
My biggest complaint is the bugged diplomacy system.  Diplomacy basically consists of "Hello, let's leave each other alone...Oh, I'm attacking you now.  Now we are at war permanently."
This is OK with me, except the AI players can form these BS alliances.  It actually merges the two empires into one.  Since the easiest victory objective of the game is to control 50% of the population of the map, this completely turns the tide of the game.  I was just playing a very pleasent game when, suddenly and with no warning, All 5 opposing empires allied on one turn, easily giving them the required population to abruptly end my game.  I restarted a few actions before that to see if a slighly different action would change the trigger, but NOPE, they all banner under the strongest AI player and that is the end of the game.  Nothing to do about it, except perhaps operate a weak, crappy empire to not threaten them in the first place.  The AI players didn't even like each other!
Great to pass a few hours but the price is a little steap for what you get, I'd wait until it goes in the sale.

An interesting idea, badly crippled by a lack of (sorry, Sid), Interesting Decision.
-There are three weapons to put on your ships (four if you count fighter bays), but one of them is clearly better than any of the others.
-You can have a lot of little ships or a couple big ones, but aiming for the middle of the road is clearly better. (you can only fire once per turn, so big ships get outnumbered and surrounded. Hulls have a fairly high cost just to start, so in the part of the game where your money is still limited, it's better spent on improving your existing ships than getting more flimsy money-sinks)
-You can upgrade your tech, but all upgrades are flat percent increases of one stat, so the decision is entirely binary. 'Do i have enough science points to upgrade a thing my ships use. If yes, do it." There's no depth, complexity, or strategy.
-There are eight 'leaders', but honestly i would have liked a 'choose random' button because they have no personality (they all speak in a different accent, whoo) and are only differentiated by each having a small, unique advantage.
-The AI barely understands how to play its own tactical battles; but if it understood optimal play then an endless slapfight between identical assault cruisers wouldn't be interesting either. I guess I do have to give it credit for making Gallente Style the key to galactic domination, though.
-Game modes that aren't conquest continue far past the point where one player (you) is obviously going to win. Game modes that are conquest can be brutally cheesed by sniping homeworlds (which flips their entire empire over to you)
Think about it if you ever see it on a tablet app store for $3, otherwise, avoid.
The gameplay is (relative to other Sid Meier's games) too simplistic and the game is too short with no option to continue after a victory.

Brace yourself, hipster Nac Mac Feegle is once again going to attempt to confound popular opinion with a wordy, over-stuffed review.
Red Faction 2 is a great game. It isn't deep, it isn't an industry leader, but it is a fun game. I know this because I had it on my gamecube back around 2004, completed it, and always remember it as an underrated shooter.
What does it get wrong?
Well, they will tell you it is shallow, predictable, a bit bland and a big departure from what made the original game so good.
What does it get right?
Well how about I answer this question with a bit more depth:
I want to make it clear that I played the first Red Faction, and I really enjoyed it. I loved the gameplay, setting, and also the little 'glass house' side game. I didn't feel any sense of disappointment, however, when I played this sequel.
The game starts with you acting on behalf of a corrupt dictator (looked a bit like one S Hussein) as part of his elite counter-goodperson squad, sieging a base of revolutionaries. The mission introduces you to fellow cybernatically augmented comrades, destructable environments, a great assault rifle/grenade launcher weapon, and sets you up for a campaign of twists, thrills and spills.
The very next mission has you and your turncoat comrades storming the central government tower of the dictator, blasting chunks out of his gigantic stone bust, flying through the streets shooting fools from a gunship gunnery seat, and getting right into the nitty gritty of joining the Red Faction.
Missions are varied. Weapons are also varied and generally well balanced. Pacing is good and tight, maps are thoughtfully conceived and often showcase the wide range of vehicles one can make use of. The graphics and gameplay may be getting outdated these days - how could they not? - but the fun of the game shines through yet. Incidentally, the console version had multiplayer with good bot AI and some great scenarios, something that was golddust on the often PG rated gamecube system.
I don't know why people didn't like this game, even if it didn't blow my mind in the same way Halo or Metroid Prime did, I really enjoyed the storyline - in the later stages of the game the levels get really good indeed - and I actually thought some of the weapons were pretenders to iconic status, the relatively vintage AK-like assault rifle, the aforementioned super assault rifle, the blocky shotgun and dual weilded submachine guns were all really great.
I think you can get a raft of shooters that may be better, but this shooter deserves to be played if only because of the hours that went into producing it, the genuinely wide range of things they developers got right, and the unfair blasting it has routinely suffered from critics.

First off and foremost I'll name the good things about this game: If you like games to challenge your friends to play, this is a decent one. It's cheap, starts off slow but gets going and has pleasent music paired with pretty colors. Gameplay is simple: get through the holes without crashing. There is a weekly tournament held for retry coins that you can also earn in-game. It's not Pay2Win. I've never played a game quite like this and I must say it's nice to take a break from shooters, RTS and open world sandbox style games. Basically, it's a good way to waste an hour or two.
With that said, why do I not recommend The Collider? Well at the risk of sounding like a broken record: "Basically, it's a good way to waste an hour or two." There is no replay value whatsoever. The highest speed you can start at is 1300 even if you get up to 1400 speed. After you reach your peak there isn't really a good reason to keep playing. There are no "levels" in the traditional sense. The color of the track changes as the speed increases but thats it. There are no characters, no story, no other game modes to play - NOTHING. You could challenge yourself to get all the Achievements but, they do not unlock. AT ALL. EVER! I've seen other people have this problem since at least November of 2014 and people still are having this problem now in April of 2015. I'd say any chance of a fix is long gone by now. I would only suggest buying this game if you have a coupon for it as a way to increase your steam rank. Otherwise it's not even worth the $2.99 asking price.
EXTRA COMMENTS: I have no clue how fast we are going. 1300 MPH? 1300 KPH? 1300 Light-years per hour? In my personal opinion I'd rather spend $2.99 on a pack of gum. I'd get more use out of the gum than this game. Thank goodness for that 90% off coupon, only cost me 30 cents.

I appreciate this is "Early Access" but the entire thing needs a major design update. So far the use of the Source Engine doesn't have the features it needs and includes a lot that you don't. It's a direct HL2 engine port with very few changes, so you still get the Flashlight and Sprint options from that game, but nothing like the Havok engine's ability to move objects around in the air for free placement. You can't resize objects and some must be fixed to a wall when you really want to just "drop" them onto another object.
The lack of basic object choices (1 chair, 1 couch, no variations) and inability to change even the wall colours and open/close doors show extremely limited interaction with the map and level design is badly implemented so far.
1st level (Apartment) you can't see out of the window and have two closed doord you can't get past.
The 2nd level (Orchard House) is better but you have a nice-looking outdoor area that you can't get access to get a better view of your house.
The 3rd level (Party Cabin) doesn't even have a front door and there is an open-plan toilet and shower with a balcony view over the large bay windows. It's a good job you can't interact with those objects or the neighbours can see you naked!
Hopefully the next few updates with include a lot of miscellanous items to populate the cloak rooms and kitchens with interactive toys, and a major clean-up of the interface for each object type.
The entire "unlockables" seems to be geared towards spy-ware of your netflicks, youtube and social media accounts. It has good potential and is worth a little play for a free interface you can show-off to your friends.

You mostly play this game as Kian or Zoe from Dreamfall: The Longest Journey (as you can see on the game's cover left is Kian and right is Zoe).
This game is all about story, search for something, a little bit thinking, and some decision making that affect how the story goes.
Tips:
If you want to fully understand the story you should play The Longest Journey and Dreamfall:  The Longest Journey first.

What I like:
This game has a fantastic story and pretty good graphics/dialog/atmosphere. Choices that you make affect the story and it's really well made. There hasn't been a game recently that sucked me in and made me want to keep playing as much as this one.
What I don't like:
Some of the puzzles are hard or frustrating. Some you have to walk around aimlessly looking for "something" until you stumble upon something you can pick up. Then comes finding where to use it...
Overall, this game is definitely worth buying for the story and the experience as a whole. I don't mind shift-tabbing to look at a walkthrough every now and then to get to the next cutscene or choice. Because of this, i'll give it an 8.5/10 until the last book comes out.

Recommended for anyone who enjoyed The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: The Longest Journey.
This game is divided into multiple books (episodes), none of which reset the chapter counter.  I was confused by this at first.  It makes more sense to think of the game as a volume of books with continuing chapters (book 1 is chapters 1-3, book 2 is chapters 3-5, that kind of thing).
With that said, give it until at least book 3 (chapter 6-7).  I wish books 1-2 were a bit more palatable.  The foul language and tense personal relationships just ground a bit on me because, in a game full of decisions, I had little control over them except at a high level.  Oh well.  I got past it.  Chapter 3 is where it took off.  Some of the early decisions can have big ramifications, but the thing is, you can only guess at their ramifications.  There is no combat.  The tension that combat might usually serve is replaced by decisions that you can only make once (unless you reload prior to the decision and do it again).
The music is setting appropriate, the scripting is clever (Enu is great, as is the best bird in gaming, Crow) and taps into events in previous Longest Journey games, the voice acting is clear and fleshes out the characters (again, props to Enu and Crow), and despite a bug now and then (as of this writing, 3-20-2016), I would recommend this game.  21 hours in and I'm through book 4 and waiting for book 5!  If I was faster at some of the puzzles, a playthrough would have been a couple hours shorter.
