We published an article about this. Here's a bit more than half of the article.
"[...] Normal prisons are completely different from transport prisons. You could literally spend an eternity in a normal prison and never escape. In normal prisons, all that matters is that you follow the daily routine in which you go to meals, do work for your prison job, work out, go to roll call, and so on, all the while trying to sneak in little bits of time here and there to begin hatching an escape plan and carrying it out. You get half a star in increased security for each player that misses each part of the routine—reaching upwards of a total of two stars if an entire four-player group misses a single part of the routine—up to five stars. The security level will drop a certain amount each day until it reaches zero again. You really want to keep this down, as reaching a higher level of security could lead to the thwarting of any attempts at escape before you even begin to attempt to escape.
Because of the way that the system works, your entire prison life is a balance of trying to get the resources you need in the smallest bits of free time that you can while diverting suspicion from yourself. To the developers’ credit, there is a lot of nuance involved in this. So long as you visit the location in which the current routine event is occurring, you can spend the entirety of that event’s time doing whatever you want. You don’t have to eat lunch, as long as you go to the cafeteria, but you might want to, as previous efforts might have left you low on stamina.
However, it’s not always as simple as scheming in free time. There are a few prerequisites to any escape attempt. The majority of your attempts will require tools, which you will need resources for. There are several ways to acquire these resources; you can steal them from another prisoner’s desk, find them in other desks that are scattered throughout the prison, beat up prisoners and prison guards and take what they have on them, buy them from other prisoners that have a high opinion of you, or, in some prisons, get them from visitations. Because each and every one of these options is completely random, with desks and prisoners that sell items restocking with random resources each day, it can sometimes feel as if even the most carefully calculated plans could take forever. For example, deciding to dig your way out of the prison could take hours, as you simply might not come across the amount of files and sheets of metal that you need to produce the number of high-tier shovels that you need to get out.
It’s also not as simple as just having the resources. You also have to actively increase your stats, primarily your Intelligence. Your Intelligence level determines what you can craft, with new recipes unlocking every 10 points until 70 points. You can also increase Strength and Fitness, which could help with combat, but they’re not quite as crucial as Intelligence is. Early on, you will really want to spend your blocks of Free Time increasing your Intelligence, so that the recipes you need are simply available to you. You will also want to take a careful look at each of the recipes that are unlocked, as different prisons have slightly different sets of recipes.
[...]
The most interesting nuance by far, however, is that of restrictions that are placed on your escape attempts in multiplayer. This is the reason that Central Perks 2.0 took a total of eight hours for us to complete. Both [my co-op partner] and I had ample opportunities to escape—on our own. Both of us had obtained the resources to disguise ourselves and simply walk out the front door, but it wouldn’t allow that. We needed a way out that would allow both of us to escape. To clarify, the game doesn’t simply require everyone to have the resources to escape in a particular way; some methods of escape simply aren’t possible with multiple players. This level of detail significantly adds to the multiplayer experience, even if it also adds to the amount of time that it takes to escape.
That being said, these nuances make one of The Escapists 2’s most glaring flaws that much more painful to report. You see, a lot of the game’s logic simply makes no sense, which makes escape attempts far more trial and error in nature than they should be. Lighters and wads of putty that you use to create molds of keys aren’t contraband, but somehow paper mache, which is primarily used to make fake vent covers, and sheets of metal are. There are metal detectors placed around later prisons, limiting your escape plans somewhat, but they don’t just detect metal; they could detect your contraband paper mache if you walk through one with it on your person. Medics and other employees will never call the guards on you; they simply don’t care what you’re up to, even if you’ve broken into their offices.
However, the biggest offense is a complete lack of logic in the way that guard towers work. If you’re outside and you so much as put a spoon to the ground while it’s in your hand, they will open fire on you for digging, no matter where you are at. If you enter guards’ quarters from outside, even if you have a complete guard uniform and a fake key, they will open fire on you. Somehow, if you break ground on the way out of a tunnel and enter the parking lot, where civilians’ cars are, they pay you no mind. This logic is frustrating at best and is an affront to the level of detail put into the game’s other systems.
The game’s multiplayer systems are also flawed in nature. We always test multiplayer modes from across the office, with our computers hard-wired to the same network and placed but a few feet away from each other. Even in such conditions, the amount of lag that we experienced bordered on the absurd, with various characters often simply teleporting around.
That’s not to mention the bizarre manner in which saving is currently handled for multiplayer. At launch, the characters of clients simply didn’t save; they lost their stat progress and all of their items. Now, it saves to the cell. You see, when you connect to the game, you are assigned a player number of sorts. That player number is tied to a cell. Every time players connect, they are assigned player numbers, and thus cells, in the order in which they join. When they leave, their progress is saved to the cell and, if someone else joins, they take over their progress. In order to keep your progress, you have to join the same game in the same order every time you play. I can’t even begin to understand why it was set up like that, but the very fact that the game does save progress now is a testament to the fact that Mouldy Toof is working on improving the multiplayer components of the game.
Despite these issues, I have had and am continuing to have a lot of fun with The Escapists 2. It’s a game of careful balance, of constantly being aware of what’s going on around you. The addition of multiplayer, particularly the cooperative mode rather than the competitive one, improves the core formula greatly and augments the way that you have to think about your escape plans. There are a few key issues involving the game’s logic, its netcode, and the way that saving is handled in multiplayer, but they don’t ultimately drag down the game’s wonderfully nuanced experience. If you haven’t yet, I would definitely recommend picking the game up."

So after 5+ hours of playing I am going to post my review. Rather than posting a review after less time than it takes to complete the first mission and declaring this "Not My Anno" like many reviewers who havent played since Anno was a faux-historical game.
2205 Is clearly an evolution of the franchise It takes a lot of what worked with 2070 and expands on it while scalng back some of what did not. Production is a lot easier to manage. City building can be done with an eye towards style rather than trying to maximize a social buildings footprint. Instead of the strange magic that people within a certain radius suddenly have their social needs met, the roads play a part now from what ive seen, better road planning can maximize the area of effect of buildings to an extent.
For those who claim the "challenge" is gone after playing 45 minutes have not progressed to the Artic map yet where the return of the dreaded sphere of infunence actually makes sense in the form of "heat". Certain buildings will give off a heat radius that is needed for housing which makes the city planning more of a challenge. I can only imagine the moon at this point.
The game runs bug free so far for me, it looks gorgeous and is easy to pick up and play even if you are not a vet without dumbing it down.
A lot of reviews are claiming its been dumbed down, but it is fact simply better optimized to remove a lot of the nitpicky micromanaging that got so tedious late in the game. Instead its streamlined, it still requires you to pay attention but it is possible to play and plan a successful settlement without resorting to yield calculators and placement charts which always took me personally out of the game and made previous Annos a chore late in the game.
This review is admittedly only about 5-6 hours of playtime but I wanted to give it a fair try before posting.

EDIT: After coming to the conclusion of the story, I would say that the "streamlining" which feels like it enhances the gameplay in the start becomes excessive by the end, making this game incredibly boring for replay value. Did not ever hit any environmental disasters, which were a hallmark of ANNO 2070's replay value.
The main "streamline" that alters the game from 2070 is that resources are managed as a surplus/deficit counter instead of actual supply/demand. What this means is that it's much easier to see whether you need to produce more of a certain good, but surprisingly this makes the game less fun: it is too easy to balance the deficit for a good, and then when you're running a deficit of that good again it's obvious, so there is no real supply chain breakdown ever, and that was half the fun of ANNO 2070.
The combat is lacking, and seems to have degraded from 2070, where your options for combat involved planes and nukes, in addition to boats. Combat now feels very arcadey, with powerups and roaming groups of enemies. It is just not the same as 2070, where the military aspects were very engaging and intertwined with the city-building.
TL;DR
Anno 2070 is better, buy that instead.

This is a fun game.  I am running it on a 960 GTX and Windows 10.  No compatibility issues - I had 1 crash in the 33 hours I was playing it.
On to the review:
I completed the game in 33 hours, however, at 15 hours I accidentally deleted my saved game - Start New Game is right next to Continue, and both are activated with the space bar.  So I basically finished it right in line with with the expected ~20 hours.  I had all but two of the original game achievements (the DLC achievements are listed even if you don't have them), and I had two characters fully maxed (Cardio, Fighting, Specialized weapon, etc)  and 2 others that were about 75%.  I spent a lot of time doing side missions, and building up two different settlements.
The game starts out right in the middle of the action...black screen fades in to your friend grappling with a zombie.  You bludgeon it and then try to figure out what's going on.  Heading to a ranger station, you find out that while you've been camping and out of cell phone range, the zombie apocalypse has happened.  After checking for survivors and supplies, you end up having to head down the mountain to the town where a woman is broadcasting on a CB.  From here, the game becomes one of resource management - ammo, medicine, fuel, and building supplies.
Zombies are pretty slow and uncoordinated, so they aren't much of a threat when there is just one or two.  But they can take a lot of damage until you can destroy the head so if you aren't careful you can find yourself surrounded.  Headshots are one-shot kills on them, but ammo is very scarce until you start tracking down sources or trading for it.  Early on, you'll find that stealth is a better option as you go to houses and other buildings to scavenge for supplies.  As you clear buildings, you have the option to setup outposts where you can resupply and use as a source for medicine, fuel, or whatever is found there.  As the story progresses, you'll come across special zombies that reflect what they were before they died such as a zombie in police swat gear.
As you scavenge for supplies to reinforce this first settlement, a few other story lines emerge with their own missions. As you build trust with other survivors, they're willing to share more and better supplies with you from guns to vehicles. Apart from the various mission trees, there is a set of recurring missions to rescue an ally/find a missing person, hunt down a particular zombie that's terrorizing the area, investigate signs of other survivors, clean out an infested building, defend a perimeter while it's scavenged or reinforced, helping a survivor that's gotten too angry or scared, or complete a trade with another group of survivors like ammo for food.
In your settlement you can build up facilities like a medical bay, a workshop, library, kitchen, sleeping quarters, a dojo, and so on.  Each of these will serve a specific purpose, plus several of them have special things they can do.  If you have  a kitchen, you can prepare a big meal to boost your people's vitality..  A watchtower can spend time clearing out wandering zombies with a sniper rifle.  A workshop can repair your vehicles or make other useful items such as weapon suppressors, IEDs, and so on.  A library works in combination with these to offer more choices - with a food storage area and a library, you can research and experiment in creating biodiesel as a fuel source.

I'm recommending this game, but a fair bit of this review will be negative, but this doesn't come from vitriol, only from wanting to see the game in a better state. I'll start with the things I dislike.
First and foremost,
, while I applaud the idea of creating maps by hand and having instance bosses, the instances are boring and repetitive and feel like chores, they're way too long and get boring real quick, I wish they were just scrapped or made entirely optional to be honest. For a game all about exploring and crafting, I wish the progression system was as hands off as possible.
could get a lot better, it can create some good-looking maps, but most of the times it creates ugly planets full of holes that look real blocky, there's also the common dirt towers that pop up here and there. I hope that in the future it can create some smooth looking planets with intended cave entrances that lead somewhere.
, some look nice, some are real generic, most of them are real hostile and bother the hell out of you, some big monsters that you'd suppose some of the bigger monsters are a bit slower, but nah they're still pretty damn fast. And yeah, before I forget, they also get pretty repetitive, you visit multiple planets and find the exact same monster, without any difference in color, size or behavior.
, if I didn't make this clear enough yet, there's a fair amount of repetition, repetitive enemies, biomes, dungeons, weapons, planets. I don't think I need to explain why this is a bad thing.
, while I understand Mechs are a newer feature, it can't be understated how much better they could be. They're slow and cumbersome, they're ok in combat against land creatures, but real weak against the space monsters. They excel in no particular area so far, except maybe combat, but even so there's very limited applications to it, you have to drop it and walk slowly all the way to wherever you need it, since you can't call it in while in the planet. In the future maybe separate mechs in function: Combat, mining or transportation, maybe even have a utility mech that serves as a walking storage unit, with lights and that serves as a sentry.(Note that I have used only two mechs so far, one was the very first one, the other one was from a mod, which would fit among the stronger mechs in the game)
, you have to open the dedicated host then open the game and connect to yourself, which might impede slower PCs of playing Online.
Well, now for the good part(which I have less to talk about really):
houses is pretty fun, there's enough furniture and interaction with some of them to make whatever house you're making a bit more like a place, you can even have a NPC live there, which is pretty neat.
The game
pretty good, all things considered, which makes that point about the map generation not being good sting that bit more.
Some
look pretty nice and colorful.
Generally the
is nice and peaceful, pretty nice for exploring and chilling.
I might have forgotten something, but that's pretty much it. Since Starbound changes every so often, if you're reading this review too much into the future, it's possible multiple of the things I complained about changed, for the good or for the bad.

Ah yes, From the Depths, this is an interesting little sand box game that is hard to describe. Remember when you were a kid (or maybe right now?) and you would make spaceships and other stuff out of lego, and then have them fight? Well that is a very basic way to describe this game.
Now lets just clear this out of the way, this game has a steep learning curve (some would describe it as a cliff), and the in game tutorials are not the greatest, however, the community, both on youtube and on the forums have some fairly comprehensive guides on the various aspects of the game.
As for the gameplay, there are three main parts, you have the vehicle designer which in its basic form is a sandbox where you design and test your own vehicles and can spawn in any of the vehicles already in game. There is a basic "story mode", which mostly just acts as a simple tutorial as well as a set of challenge missions. Finally you have the campaigns; in the campaigns you put the vehicles that you have designed to the test in a quasi real time strategy game with resource and army management.
In the main campaign you do battle against the various AI factions (8 in total) of the world of "Neter", these factions range from the ramshackle wooden designs of the Deep Water Guard, and their eternal foes, the Onyx Watch with their floating castles mixed with Age of Sail Galleons. In the Steel Striders you have more conventional warships that would be familiar to a World War Two buff alongside futuristic destroyers and battleships. For some truly unique designs, there are the "alien" Scarlet Dawn, and the tribal Grey Talons with their imposing airships. Of course the most unique in my opinion are the White Flayers, a group of religious fanatics whose ships seemed to have been designed in the wastelands of the Mad Max franchise.
There are other worlds as well, including one meant for a World War II Axis vs Allies campaign.
As for the vehicles that you can build, they come in a few different flavours; you can create a wide range of naval craft, along with helocopters (very complex to do however), airplanes, low orbit space craft, land vehicles, and if you are so inclined, you can also make stationary buildings.
While the game is in Early Access, it is complete enough that you are only really limited by your imagination (and your ability to actually make said imagination work) as well the game recieves frequent updates. Of course, if you purchase the game, you do have to be prepared for updates that may change how the game plays, or messes with your carefully designed vehicles (the much needed engine rework was a good example of this). However, the games developer is pretty good at making it so that any changes are fairly backwards compatible so as to avoid completely breaking designs.
So yeah, get out there, make a raft that can barely float, and then before you know it, you will find yourself conquering the world.
*Edit* I forgot to mention that the controls in this game are awkward to get used to, standard WASD to move the camera/character, but the vehicle controls use other keys such as UJHK, which would probably make the game awkward for some people, particularly left handed individuals. However, the controls can be rebinded in the launcher, though I have not attempted to do so, as a result I am not sure how well the game responds to this.

I'll start this off by saying that none of what I'm about to list is a deal breaker and I still highly reccommend it over most of what's on the store pages at any given moment, and it is far more worthy than a fair amount of triple-A games. That said, it has its glaring flaws, which I urge you to read.
While bugginess and crashing have never really seemed to be an issue for me in the time since release (I purchased this game on day one), it all ran fairly smoothly. As I'm unqualified as an armless gibbon with half its skull caved in when it comes to coding and bug diagnosing, I can't point out what might be the cause of this problem, but don't let that turn you off. If it's not already fixed by the time you're reading this review it hopefully will be shortly since it is the major thing piledriving the reviews into the ground with the force of a hippo being pushed from the back of a cargo plane.
Gameplay-wise, it's very reminiscent of the original with most of the annoyances ironed out, for example, you no longer have to find a piece of paper lying around that has to attest to the usefulness of an electrified baton before you can actually craft it. Unfortunately, a new niggle pops up like a meerkat in a beet patch in Siberia--incredibly out of place and baffling. The very few blueprints you don't know how to craft (Fairly simple things) are no longer able to be crafted without the blueprint, which the game very helpfully does not explain the method by which you obtain them. No longer are you able to intuit the melting of chocolate in a cup until your feeble prisoner mind finds a blueprint showing them that lighters are hot and chocolate melts.
The major fix that I will happily praise until my vocal chords give out is the fact that your stats no longer bleed over time like they're hemophilic rose garden workers, removing a majority of the grind involved in raising your intelligence. While this does make things slightly easier, the added minigames and increased fatigue balance it out rather nicely.
One "feature" that nearly broke the game for me was the lack of a hard save system, instead opting for an autosave system that fires off like a man with parkinson's trying to quicksave, as well as an exitsave system that ensures if you're screwed over by one of the more irritating mechanics you'll be stuck there forever with no recourse. I have fond memories of beating down a guard with a bar of soap in a sock (which of course alerted every single person in the compound despite the guard being alone in a room without cameras) and taking her key to make a mold, at which time the medic came racing into the building with the speed of the Flash hopped up on cocaine and grabbed the body before I could put the key back. While guards will not immediately finger you for the theft, the 99% heat I took for beating up a solitary guard in an empty room with nobody around meant that I was beaten to death during the ensuing lockdown with my plastic key, weapon, and imperative crafting materials in my inventory, and, thanks to the lack of hardsaves and inability to load, I was set back to square one and frankly ♥♥♥♥ that.
I speculate that the lack of a save/load system is thanks to the multiplayer focus this time around, as there is no "play offline" mode, only a "local" mode that still has you online. While some may call this a more "realistic" approach, realism should take a back seat to fun. If you're looking for realism, play a Call of Duty game or one of the billion wilderness survival games out there.
All-in-all, the game is worth your time, but it does have its problems. It gets a tentative recommendation from me, but be sure all of the above is not an issue for you.

OutDrive is simply "all style, no substance". The synthwave aesthetic, graphics and music make the game look promising from the trailer, however, those are probably the only redeeming qualities it has. Going fast isn't a requirement either - driving at a snails pace while maintaining the arrow is also completely acceptable. There are pretty much no limitations or any actual challenge besides that, and on top of that there's only a few pieces of scenery put together into an endless track, most of which you see within about 15 minutes of playing. All of that mixed together with unresponsive menus, slow loading times, weird controls and handling make it hard to recommend it as a game. So I love this game. Here's why.
Streamlining:
This game is actually quite easy to play! A lot of people are comparing this game to Anno 2070 (for some reason, like every ANNO game is the same. Which they aren't) but it is it's own game.
My favorite streamlined feature is that of the "sectors". There are three, the temperate, the arctic, and the moon. Each one is it's own map, instead of everything being on one map, which demanded micromanagement on an insane scale and was for the most hardcore of players.
Trading:
No more ships!
I hated those ships and setting up the trade routes. Trading is now just a simple thing in the strategic map where you decide what and how many of each product you want to move to what sectors. Setting up the ships before was such a pain. I know I'm in danger of sounding like I don't like certain complicated mechanics in games, but it's not like that. I just hate trade routes, I felt they added an annoyance to the previous games.
Ship Combat:
Ship combat is no longer waged on close to your cities. They are not waged on separate maps designed specifically for fights, which are actually kind of fun.  Your unit have a mix of abilities and types, with special powers that need to be recharged or found on the map to be used. No longer can the enemy come along and mess up your TRADE ROUTES with sabotage. They are also optional. For certain parts of the story, a combat mission can be used to proceed, but so can a second option. I take the combat route though for the upgrade resources.
Visual:
Probably the part I love about this new entry. It's beautiful. Like really beautiful. All 2 sectors look amazing. The buildings look amazing. The water (as always) looks amazing. And my personal favorite, the MOON. It looks amazing if you haven't guessed. My favorite touch is the traffic in your cities though, because I very much enjoyed watching in my arctic sector with everyone bundled up and all kinds of snow vehicles and the like. And then on my moon sector, people on jet backs and moon buggies. Lots of attention to detail.
I haven't played enough to offer much more yet, but it's worth buying. Make your own opinion.

I've played for over 9 hours now and while I would not consider myself a powerplayer in previous anno games, I HAVE been playing the Anno series since Anno 1503. I have seen a whole lot of < 3.0 hour playtime reviews and I felt compelled to leave my own thoughts after playing nearly nonstop since launch.
A number of things have changed since 2070 but I think that on the whole it's for the better. That's not to say that I dont think they couldn't improve some things.
-Random maps are gone which is really sad and is one of my only gripes at this time. More than anything This needs to come back or give us a map editor so that we can make more variations. 3 variations of each of the 3 climate types is really not enough.
-They've added a Move Building button which I've seen a lot of people complain about but I absolutely love. It was annoying as hell to need to tear down my carefully contructed factory complex just to move the entire thing over 1 tile. To be fair, there should be some small cost at least, but its hardly the end of the world.
-Combat mission maps are where all of the combat takes place in 2205 as opposed to having to defend your islands in 2070 and earlier games. Another FPS that could easily be called a CoD clone in many regards but a well executed one at that.  Now granted,  when this game has to compete with other F2P games like Warface, Ghost Recon Phantoms, Blacklight Retribution (to name a few from my library) it doesnt really stand out too well from the pack in most of its game modes.  That's not to say the game is bad, quite the contrary actually.  I thoroughly enjoyed Soldier Front 2.  The graphics are definitely good enough to get a passing grade, the maps are good, and everything feels as it should in an FPS.  But for the longest time for me there wasnt really anything to set this game apart from the countless other shooters I could play.  Then I found Hero mode.  To my knowledge this is still the only game (or at least the only F2P game) with this mode or anything similar to it.  Hero mode  imo is to Soldier Front 2 as "Zombies" is to Call of Duty.  Hero mode is so much fun and what truly sets this game apart from ANY other FPS I've ever played and it alone makes the download worthwhile.  a mix between a MOBA and a FPS is such a good idea that I am truly surprised no one thought of it sooner.  Hero mode is something I definitely want to play more of and is quite honestly the only reason I keep SF2 in my library.  While developer Dragonfly may not have revolutionized the shooter as we know it much like Halo or Call of Duty both did in their own regards,  Soldier Front 2 definitely breaks some new ground that is worth investing some time into with Hero mode.

The Collider places you inside of a particle accelerator that shoots you to incredibly fast speeds. The object of the game is to get as far along as you can before crashing. As you move along at dizzying speeds, you collect coins while avoiding obstacles. The coins can be used to revive you when you crash (which will be very often) up to three times in a round, which ends up being very helpful once you get farther along in the accelerator. There is a nice variety of obstacles, but I sometimes wish there were more.
The sound is okay, but not something I would want to listen to for long. Luckily, there is a mute button, so this isn't a problem. You can just rock out to whatever you want, while improving your reflex skills.
There's not much to The Collider, but it's definitely worth picking up if you like racing games. It's also nice for achievement hunters, since it only take a little bit of time to unlock them all. Be sure to get it while it's on sale, for that's when you'll be happiest with your purchase.

Aiming is far more sophisticated than in it's predecessor Contract Wars, so simply point and shoot isn't going to work unless you are face to face with an opponent.
The benefit of this game being on steam is that PunkBuster is used as well as Hired Ops' own safety measures, which I believe should eliminate most attempts to hack or cheat.
One of the downsides of the game, although similar to Contract Wars, is the fact a starting player you can only play Bay5, but once you level up a bit, Team Eliination becomes available, as well as other maps.
Anyone who has played Contract Wars will recognize the basic layout of the maps, but they have been redone completely for Hired Ops. The 3 maps I've played so far, Bay5, Evac and Site are very reminiscent of Contract Wars, but are still different, so you still have to get used to the updated layouts.
Overall it's quite a fascinating game, which offers a new challenge for seasoned players, but once you get the hang of aiming, the rest comes naturally..

Did you play "The Longest Journey" yet?
DId you then play "Dreamfall: The Longest Journey?"
If not, go play those two games first or the story won't make much sense to you.
If you played those two games and did not like them, well then you should stay away from this one because it is a sequel.
This game picks up a little while after the end of "Dreamfall: The Longest Journey" which I will not spoil for those who haven't played it.  Let's just say it was a surprise to me when I played it.  You are still tasked with saving the world (or two worlds, depending how you look at it) and someone is still using people's dreams for evil purposes.  But in this game, you get to make choices along the way that change the way the story plays out.  There are several branching paths you might follow, but each choice is permanent!  Some changes are small, others have big impacts on the events around you.  It is a little bit like a "choose your own adventure" story in that sense.
Bottom line:
this game is a bit different from its predecessors.  In some ways it is better, in other ways I personally prefer one of the other two in teh series.  Do you like adventure games?  Do you like some suspense - rarely knowing how your choices will play out in the long run?  Do you like solving puzzles with seemingly random (and sometimes borderline insane) item combinations?  Do you want to be a super-hero who can walk in and out of other people's dreams?  If you said yes to those questions AND you enjoyed the first two games in this series, then you need to play this game.  I'm not sure what they're charging for it these days but I got it on sale.  Totally worth $15 or $20 I think.

The mod features around thirty minutes of gameplay (Source: My playthrough on hard difficulty) with cheap deaths and fairly stock assets for the most part, with the only "new?" weapons being the replacement for the pistol and the replacement for the magnum (the magnum replacemant seemed to have a broken or extremely short animation) with the rest being the exact same.
The enemies are also the exact same ones from Half-Life with the exception of some reskin work, and I THINK the zomop4 guys were new, but I'm not entirely certain. Also, the guy in the coat as seen in one of the screenshots may be a new model, but once again I'm not certain.
The music is okay, but extremely loud with no option to really make it quiet. (I know the MP3 slider made it a little more quiet, but not by a significant amount) It also features no new voice acting, not even for the guy in the coat.
The written dialogue in the game is mostly in broken English and most likely wasn't read through for mistakes, as the little written dialogue within the game is littered with errors and mistakes.
Overall it felt like a very weak experience which could have been a lot more, and to me felt like an experiment in mapping and design compared to a new experience within the Half-Life universe. I'd only be able to recommend this if you were bored and REALLY enjoyed Half-Life, and if you want to laugh at some of the moments within this short experience.

This game is absolutely insane!  I love a good racing game every once in a while, and this one is definitely great.  If you've ever wanted to feel like the driver in an action movie, this is the game for you.
So the main gimmick of this game is the power meter, which increases as you do things such as jumps and drafting.  With it you can set off power plays that are scattered around the track.  The power plays can do things such as opening up a shortcut, blowing up a bus so that the person ahead of you crashes and you can overtake them, or even major route changes to the track.  For example, on one track, setting off a route change will cause the roof of a warehouse to collapse, creating a ramp that you use to jump onto a huge aircraft carrier, which starts to sink so everyone has to dodge the jets that are slowly sliding off of it.  The power plays are absolutely amazing and the main reason I recommend checking this game out.
So far I've only played on the campaign mode, which is set up like a TV show.  While this may sound it a bit weird, it really works in context, and the cutscenes showing off the track in the next episode get you pumped to try them out.  Playing the stages in the episodes will give you credits depending on how well you did, and the more credits you get the more cars you unlock.  There's also several different gameplay modes, from your standard race, to an elimination mode where last place blows up every few seconds, and even a time trial mode where power plays trigger ahead of you and you have to dodge them.  The game also supports LAN and even Split Screen gameplay, though from what I can tell the Online mode is dead.
I have also heard of issues with save files corrupting, and I'm being careful and backing up my save data in case this happens to me, but until i get further in the game I don't really have much to say about it other than be careful.
All in all, pick this game up if you're a fan of racing games and explosive environments.  I'd say this is worth the asking price of $20, but it can go on sale for around $5, so you may want to wait.
Edit:  I managed to fun into the save bug.  Basically during one the the ep. 6 races i got a message saying the autosave failed and that saving would be suspended.  I tried overwritting the save with a backup but I just got the same message when it tried to save again.  What fixed it for me was just leaving the corrupted save file alone and playing till the first race of ep 7.  Hopefully I don't run into this again.

So I've played this game a few times now and I have a love-hate relationship with it.
Things I love:
1. It's relatively easy to learn how to play
2. The controls are straight forward
3. It's a quest like, planet upgrade system based, sci-fi starship combat game
4. You can customise your ships with a range of weapons and/or defenses
5. Turn-based tactical combat
Things I hate:
1. Ship upgrades have absolutely the bare minimum of information attached to them.  Want to know how much damage an extra point of "lasers" will do on your ship - sorry, that's just too much information for you to handle, so no.  Want to know how much damage a point of shields can handle - "you want to know the truth? well you can't handle the truth!"
Shield upgrade information says "damaged shields regenerate each turn", but during combat you have no idea what the strengths of the shields are or  by how much they've been damaged.
The truth is that there is about as much information on things like shield strength and weapon strengths that they may as well have said that this weapon upgrade will improve your firepower by three bananas and a pineapple and that would still have been more information than you're currently given!
2. The tech tree is very simplistic, and every time you buy a tech, every other tech goes up in cost - there's of course no information that this is going to happen or by how much, because information is a dangerous thing in the wrong hands!
3. Ship combat - well, suffice to say that I have found the path to victory is fighters - upgrade them to the max and equip a couple of fighters on each ship - by tech level 6, they're deadly and you can literally spam them out in sufficient quantities to overwhelm your foes without ever really risking your capital ships to any damage.  Of course YMMV...
4. Wonders...they range from meh to OMGWTFBBQ!  And the great/sad news is they all cost similar amounts.  So if you're lucky enough to get the "two actions" wonder early on - congrats, you've probably just won the space race!
5. The diplomatic options are so underwhelming, it's like some kids from kindergarden got together to try and form the UN and then realised that politics is just way too complicated for them and decided to go back to just playing cops & robbers.
6. No multiplayer options :(
Overall I rate this game about 6 out of 10 for the style more than the substance.  If you're looking for something deep, this isn't the game for you.

It's hard to give a review for this game.
I'm a big fan of previous Anno games, and I've spent a lot of time with Anno 2070, doing little side missions, replaying the main content, continuous games... I never did multiplayer, admittedly, because I'm not a huge fan of acknowledging other people even exist, let alone let them invade my game.
I reccommend this game... with some stipulations. This is a great game, but it seems Anno fans will have to give it a little time before it gets really great. The complexity is still there, and don't let anyone tell you different. They just haven't played it long enough.
Here's my pros and cons list.
PROS:
+This game is BEAUTIFUL. I mean, absolutely astounding. I played on both low and ultra graphics, and I must say it is spectacular on all counts, little details are so satisfying I don't mind ignoring gameplay for a few moments just to watch the little people move around in the buildings.
+The characters are intriguing. For a city building game, anyway. I'm visiting new areas and I'm seeing people who, admittedly, are cliches. The Lunar faction bad guy might a well wear a Darth Vader costume, and "Mysterious Woman" is a strange way to hold emissary to the big space station. But I enjoy their presence for the most part, even if they like repeating the same phrases in heavily accented English.
+Accessible, easy to understand gameplay. The moment you begin, you jump right into the game. I was expecting a tutorial of some sort, but it's streamlined easily into the entire system, a rather fantastic setup. I don't mind the lack of other game options, for now, but I'm also not far into the game. There IS that little bothery feeling that the story will end and I'll be left bored, or have to start over to play more.
+Interface. Besides being beautiful, clean, and simple, you get to see exactly what the load balances for your economy are. This means you know exactly what you need to balance the lines, and admittedly, this change might make previous Anno game players feel like it's TOO simple now. Before, you just had to sort of guess: or look up schematics online for high-efficiency building layouts.
CONS:
(This one is no longer valid, as of 10 hours playing the game. It got complicated pretty fast.)
-It DOES feel like baby's first city builder. It's simplified, no doubt, and the added interface telling you exactly what you need only makes it easier. Eventually the difficulty ramps up once you colonize new lands and have to balance your needs, but your workforce doesn't seem as demanding, and without any sort of trade ships and storage, it remains a simple act of adding more weight to one side in order to balance things. Only rarely have I really messed up and had to do damage control.
-No multiplayer. As I've said, I don't do multiplayer. But I've seen a large number of people complain about it, and seeing how there's only one game mode, I can see why the value should exist. There should be SOME other option to enjoy, instead of this on-the-rails experience.
-Lack of Lore. In my opinion, this world is very interesting. I like seeing all the little details, and I like hearing a vague idea of how the factions work and fit together. But I want more story, I want to know what it was like 100 years ago, or how exactly my new implants are changing the population of my people.
TL;DR Anno 2205 is a really beautifully constructed koi pond. It's great to look at, maybe even jump into, but if you're looking for depth and power, you won't find it. Everything you see is right on the surface, and jumping in only gets you wet and wishing there were more.
Nonetheless, I give it a thumbs up because... while it's just a kiddie pool, it's a pretty damn fun kiddie pool. But then again, I'm a pretty casual player, so I don't mind the simplicity. If you don't mind a simple, good-looking game, I suggest you jump right in and splash around. But do it somewhere else, there's no multiplayer.
EDIT: I'll update this once I've gotten about 12 hours, as per Shynx's suggestion.
UPDATE: I tried to wait the full 12 hours, but I'll stick with 10.

I don't usually write reviews, but I spent countless hours both playing and watching streams of Anno 2070 and wanted to give my first impressions. I found this game to be simplified, but not in a way that was unpleasant. For example, there is a new window which tells you how much you are consuming and producing of each good; this makes it so much easier to balance production chains. Additionally, the move tool is awesome given that I like to rebuild things.
Overall, based on my 4 hours in the campaign, I would recommend this, especially if you are on the fence because it is published by Ubisoft. BlueByte did an excellent job with this game and I am enjoying it so far. It's both simpl er and more complex than 2070 (haven't played the other games, so can't comment on that). Running one city is pretty easy, but moving up the chain and expanding to having multiple cities is a more interesting thing. Definitely worth a look at least and I am excited to see what else they do in the future.
Things that are different:
1) Multiple "theaters" in the form of Temperate, Artic and Lunar biomes which each have their own gimmicks. Artic bases are built around factories in order to protect warmth which results in sprawling collections of hamlets while lunar bases are built under forcefields to protect from meteorites. I am not sure on this, but it looks like you can "buy" theaters from other corporations once you are ranked higher (read more citizens, supply chains etc). Not quite sure what this does yet, but it looks like you can you have quite a number of theaters going at once and not just one of each type.
2) No manual trade routes for ships in each theater, all goods / energy in a theater is instantly traded by a fleet of ships which grows as you do, but which you do not control. Instead, you form trade routes between theaters as there are specific items only produced in each one which are demanded by employees in other areas. Some people will not like this, but I think it works due to the fact that you are in multiple theaters at once. Having to run trade routes manually would cause a lot of lag I think. Also, having a centralized store of goods in each theater makes it easier to expand and develop islands. Trade between theaters is handled by a space port, which you need to build / expand in each theater. This means that you need to actually build in each area and can't just "load an ark" with everything you need. Credit balance is global as well, so you definitely want a big positive balance before building expensive stuff in the artic for example. All in all, I don't miss the setting of routes that much.
3) Combat, at least in the campaign, is removed from the central gameplay by making it an optional side mission which rewards you with resources you can use to build modules. Combat puts you in command of a few ships with abilities which you can power up from drops in the map. Ships can be upgraded over time, but the upgrades are linear per ship.
4) Modules: this is the big one. In 2070, you built these massive collections of fields in the hopes that you built enough for the demands you needed. Fields had to be attached to each farm. Here, farms run on their own, but you can add modules in exchange for resources. The modules do different thing such as boost productivity (more productivity than you would get with another farm at the same resource cost), reduce workers needed to maintain the place or lower energy consumption. Modules in each theater use different special resources. I have found that the way to go, at least so far, is to build a farm and then build up modules before building a new farm. This lets you save space.
5) Mountain sites: you can build any resource gathering field on any appropriate (mountain / water) site.
6) Move tool: oh god yes. You can move any factory, farm or building (even between islands) for a nominal fee / free (I forget which). This is amazing. In the campaign, I built up my first island with people and production, but ran out of room. I upgraded my production facilities with modules in a random fashion and then moved all the population to another island (I demolished the buildings). Then I moved my existing farms and factories to something that both worked and was visually pleasing without a massive loss of resources. Coupled with a central storage of goods in each theater, you can easily rebuild islands whereas it would have been prohibitively time consuming in 2070. This encourages you to expand organically.
7) Graphics are very, very pretty. It's not Crysis, but it all feels real enough to let you get lost in the game.
8) Production balance window: This is actually a massive thing and can't believe I put it this low. You have a window (small one which you can see by hitting 'v') which shows you all your goods. It shows you the production and consumption. This was need in 2070 as you often had massive surplus or massive shortages. Now that you have modules, you can slowly increase your capacity so you keep pace with what is really needed. This makes it a lot easier for people to get into building cities I think. That isn't to say that you lose all complexity though, now that you work in different theaters, you need to produce goods for your own theater as well as others. It becomes a game of balancing things in a region and then figuring out what is needed elsewhere. The system plays together nicely and prevents newer people from dying instantly due to lack of consumer electronics or whatever.

10 Hours in so far. Like it.
It is a change from Anno 2070, for sure, but I am overall liking this game. The naval combat mission are a nice change of apce from base maximizing.
There is still storage like before, but this time the obvious number is the amount that that particular material is increasing or decreasing, not the amount in storage.
There are resources that your building consume to maintain population or to create other resources, but there are also building materials that you use to build other buildings. There are a few resources that only cannot be created by a building. They are given quite freely from the naval missions and even once through Uplay Rewards.
There is no multiplayer. There is no sandbox mode. Just campaign. The maps are huge and you can have multiple maps.
The building and management aspect of the game is still my favorite aspect, even if it has seen an overall simplification. In my opinion, that simplification was much needed polish to game mechanics that took too long to gleam valuable info from or to perform, such as resource balancing and moving buildings.
I love the new modular building upgrade system. One of the best additions so far.
I am also digging the regions and the trade between them.
So far I have not seen any real threat the AI factions pose. I just see them as a type of leaderboard.
Not a single bug, although the game got a little bit laggy after 10 hours non-stop.
I waited for this game for months, and even bit the bullet when the Beta was stolen out from under us. Yeah, Uplay is a sad reality, but I didnt have any problems with it (the download was kinda slow though even on 100Mbps).
Overall, I am not dissapointed, although 60 bucks is a big pill to swallow for nearly any game. If you are undecisive, I would hope to see this on a winter sale or maybe cross your fingers for a free update or two. If all else fails, you can bet on DLC in the future to flesh out this game more.

This is my favorite game in the Red Faction series outside of the fact it didn't have multiplayer. The storyline was fun, the story didn't have overused tropes, the humor could have been better (especially with Shrike) and the boss fights were challenging. The weapons had multiple abilities that made a meaningful impact on gameplay and the way you approached enemies. The enemies also felt alive in this game, as they weren't just AI roaming around in scripted paths and events. They would have conversations, make lewd comments to eachother, talk♥♥♥♥♥♥about you when you were fighting them, and it just made the game a lot more enjoyable. Overall, the game has a really industrial/cyberpunk theme to it and a pretty appropriate soundtrack.
As far as the multiplayer went, it was fun playing this game in splitscreen when I owned it on the Playstation 2. The only downside to this game is that it's a port from a console version and it doesn't include all of the maps that were in the console version for the multiplayer. I believe the Xbox version had more maps than the Playstation 2 version. The AI in the multiplayer, especially if you were just playing alone just to kill time, was fun. They were challenging and not just mindless bots running around. It almost felt like an arena shooter. The gamemodes are pretty fun as well, CTF, Bagman, Deathmatch, etc etc.
I would recommend this game solely so people could see the pinnacle of this game series, not the attempts made to resurrect the game years later with Guerilla and Armageddon.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is an awesome game and the classic example of what's wrong with Metacritic. A 58 out of 100 seems awfully low for a game that plays so well, that I'm baffled by the hatred it gets from critics. Or, perhaps, the way Metacritic aggregates review scores is the problem? A single negative review can make that score right there plummet and provide extreme misinformation on an otherwise great game!
Lords of Shadow 2 does a few things quite well. First, it removes the stupid locked camera. Second, it has easy to learn combos that the game outright encourages you to use via the "mastery" system. Third, it has far more gothic scenery and themes that pay a deep homage to Castlevania in general. Fourth, the graphics are absolutely beautiful yet they run at 60 frames per second. Fifth, the bosses are incredible. Sixth, there's a ton of secrets and for the most part you are encouraged to explore at your leisure between objectives. Those are the six key aspects I can think of, besides the music, voiceacting, and controls being stellar as well. The story can be confusing, but it's the most tragic tale of Dracula I've ever seen in my life, and that is awesome in itself! Have you ever found yourself rooting for Dracula in all of the Castlevania games? Well, you WILL in this game!
The most criticized aspect of this game is that it "doesnt know what it wants to be", on critic reviews. I'm sorry, but there is such a thing as "gameplay variety". Consistency is nice, but this game isn't trying to be 100% like God of War, and offers decent stealth segments which aren't awful. Some of these segments are even a little clever, but they could be better. In fact, the game IS consistent for the most part, offering lots of platforming, action, exploration, secrets, and grand vistas. So why is that the worst part of the game? Is it really too linear? Does it really change too often too fast with the gameplay? Is it not trying hard enough to be Metroidvania style? These questions don't matter. The classic Castlevania games were by far more linear than this game, except the often criticized Simon's Quest entry. There are things wrong with Lords of Shadow 2 as well, but does it really warrant a FIFTY EIGHT OUT OF ONE HUNDRED Metascore?!
So, I highly reccomend this game. I like it much more than Lords of Shadow, in fact!

After I was highly disapointed by the console port of Lords of Shadows 1 I must say I really like this game. It got a 58 Metacritics score, but since I'm a sucker for Metroidvania and God of War-like games I gave it a try.
And boy am I glad I gave it a chance. I have to admit the game needs some time to get you. The first two hours are kind of lame (The fight against the angelic robot and the boring sneaking part). But after the tutorial and the first visit to the science facility the game unfolds its beauty.
The artdesign is fabulous, overall graphics, shadows and lightning are fantastic. Even more important, the controls are smooth even for a non gamepad-player like me. Combat is challenging throughout the game. After unlocking more and more combat options the normal fights as well as the boss fights are immensely fun to play (The whole toymaker part is a lesson in gamedesign for other devs). You can adjust the camera by mouse so there are no more fixed angles and even jumping is fun again. No more QTE, thank you for that dear devs.
The game is kind of an open world game, you can constantly roam your castle and the modern world and unlock secret after secret while advancing through the game.
The speakers and the music are nearly over the top. The speakers are so good and the music fits so fantasticly well it's scary.
And last but not least this game is dark, no emo vampire he's the kind of vampire I want to watch in movies or play as in a game.
My rating would be a 86 (edited), it's one of the best games of this kind I ever played.
So give it a try and don't let yourself get fooled by the not so brilliant beginning.

If you're looking for a puzzle heavy point-and-click adventure game, then this one might not be for you. While there are certainly puzzles that need to be solved, much of the game is more like a click-through story with branching dialogue than a cryptic head scratcher. But it's a very, VERY good story.
This is really a game about choices, and the consequences that result. It can be pretty harrowing.
I made choices in book 2 that have killed some people in book 4, and I'm certain that more people will die as I continue to struggle to save 2 worlds; the futuristic 'Stark' (our Earth in the near-ish future), and Arcadia, a fantasy world experiencing what may be the end times.
The characters are brilliant, the dialogue is absolutely top-notch, and the world building is fantastic, although I think it is definitely a sequel which demands some familiarity with its predecessors.
Dreamfall Chapters is the sequel to Dreamfall (2005) and the Longest Journey (1998), and I recommend both of them. The Longest Journey is where the story begins, is diabolically difficult in places, and is the only point-and-click game I’ve ever played through twice. Dreamfall is a less well realised point-and-click / action hybrid, but is still highly enjoyable, and has a great story to it (and that ending!)
That Chapters has been built by a core team of maybe a dozen people is really impressive. You’ll probably notice that some of the graphics lack the kind of polish that a AAA title would boast, but like most of the people playing this game you probably won’t care.

I remember when I was a kid playing games like Pole Position and some other great arcade and Nintendo racing games, some of which I can't remember the names of anymore. During the SNES years, it was Top Gear. Anyway, I remember my dad commenting a time or two about how it bothered him that in these racing games, you have this background that you're heading to, but never seem to actuly get to. The background never tessellates. I remember, at like 10 years old, explaining to my dad that the point of the game was the race, not to actuly "get anywhere," and the background was just an esthetic choice by the artists that had nothing to do with the game's core mechanics. My pops agreed with this, but said it would be cool if you could get to the mysterious city looming in the far background. This struck me as strangely magical thinking for a guy who rarely played video games, who usually spent his days with invoices, groceries, dishwasher repairs, and other boring adult stuff I still don't care about, and probably that is why the idea of "getting to the background" stuck in my head for many years. And I'm not the only one, apparently. Games like Grand Theft Auto 5 represent the full experience of the long drive that actuly gets you to the background. Magic. I thought about that a lot after activating Trevor in GTA5, and the game makes you take that LONG drive from the background into the part of the game you were just in on Franklin. Epic. Thought provoking. But one of those thoughts is, In this rush to make these hyper-advanced sandbox games that let us do all these things we dreamed of doing in less-interactive games for years, have we ignored the simpler, more pure and patient pleasures offered us by older games, have we neglected updating that simple experience in favor of games that really just have TOO much going on in them sometimes? Enter the new generation of "retro" games, with new graphics and sound, but with more pure game-play elements than the standard "do whatever you want and get a trophy for everything" style that the console industry churns out by the billions these days. Out Drive is one of those games. There is no where to "get to," once you're there you just win. But the GAME itself is driving, just DRIVING. Driving with a sense of urgency, not to get anywhere in the game, but to GET somewhere inside yourself. Plumb the depths of your skills. There is no real plot, you just HAVE. TO. DRIVE. You're already where you're getting to. Just. Drive.

Tl:DR: It looks great, sounds great, but is held back by mechanical weakness.
Story:
Outdrive is a game about driving (unsuprisingly). The story outlines a nameless man who gets in trouble with some other nameless men, leading to the first mans girl getting shot and now the only thing he can do to save her is hook her heart up to the engine and keep on driving so she can keep on living. Essentially, the story is very week and should not really be bothered with.
Sound:
The music in this game is fantastic, no other way to put it. It really helps bring out the neon 80's aesthetic and doesn't get old too fast. The sound effects are serviceable but are nothing special and the acceleration effect can become irritating after awhile.
Graphics:
Another thing the game does well is visually present itself. It looks great and the color scheme is perfect for the atmosphere the devs were shooting for. As a side note the launcher itself could have a few more presets. Even though it's a unity game it would be nice to have 8x AA without forcing vsync on as well.
Controls:
The controls in OutDrive aren't terrible but they don't necessarily feel good. The steering feels rigid and the drifting can be quite fiddly at times, which many times ends up with you smashing into the invisible barriers alongside the road.
Gameplay:
This is my major gripe with this game. Now, first let me clarify that I understand that the devs were not trying to develop a "game" persay, more of an "experiment" or "aesthetic concept" as the description puts it. That being said, that doesn't excuse OutDrive from having a mechanic that really irritates me and that really is a shame because funnily enough, it's one of the only mechanics in the game. The mechanic in question is the fact that you have to balance out your speed so that your girls heart (which is hooked up to the motor) doesn't overheat or get damaged. On paper this sounds like an excellent idea and I can kind of see where they were going with it. However it means that you can never buildup speed and you must constantly slow down to make sure that your girl doesn't die and end the game. There is also almost no obstacles anywhere and even cornering is ridculously easy due to the slow speed you are forced to move at. This one gripe could be easily be fixed by either eliminating this mechanic all together or just creating a seperate mode where you could drive as fast as you like (hoping the devs add this in the future!).
Conclusion:
I'm going to recommend this even though I don't beleive it's worth the full $3 CAD. For 99 cents I'd pick it up, but anything more and you're bound to be disappointed, as there's only one mode and it gets tiring very quickly. Thanks for reading, and if the devs see this I hope they take my criticism into consideration as I'll be happy to update my review as the game gets updated.

So since people like to compare this with Terraria, I'll do the same thing.
Terraria has very well designed and interactive boss fights that you'll need to farm items for in order to get the best advantage and highest chance in succeding the game. The bosses in Terraria are the main focus of the game and is extremely combat oriented, whereas Starbound, yes, has interactive boss fights, but are quite inferior to Terraria boss fight mechanics and you wont really need to pre prepare with flasks etc. The combat in Starbound is quite interesting in comparison to other games such as Terraria - each weapon can have a unique 'modifier' to the weapon giving them a right click attack (Terraria has actually implemented a weapon with a right click button in a recent update) which drains energy upon use. Starbound weapons such as guns and magic actually drain this resource instead of making you go through the hassle of collecting ammunitions. Overall, there is alot more and interesting weapons in Terraria than what there is in Starbound and the bosses are the main focus, and so of course are much more engaging.
The review doesn't end here, though.
Starbound has a much better building and mining system than Terraria does - instead of using the typical 'upgrade your tools' niche, Starbound has a tool called the Matter Manipulator, which allows you to dig underground, cut trees, place blocks (both background blocks and physical blocks) etc. It can be upgraded with an item to increase the tile range and the geometry of the tiles cut at a time etc. It can be quite tedious to get used to at first as you need to hold shift if you want to place a singular block, otherwise it'll place or destroy 4 blocks at a time. In this case, Starbound wins.
Starbound has a storymode, unlike Terraria, which makes you keep track of what you need to do in order to progress, in addition to a quest log where you can keep track of both your main story line quest and the side quests. These quests consist of fetching quests, kill quests, delivery quests, exploration quests and so on and so on. Terraria doesn't have quests, except from the fishing ones which in my opinion are extremely boring and tedious. Starbound wins again.
Terraria has thousands of items and allows players to choose between classes (the typical mage, warrior, ranger and summoner cliche), giving each class very different, distinct features that makes you feel really special. As far as I'm aware, Starbound does too but the Terraria class system is much more defined and polished.
Both games have great modding communities, so you can never get bored! The possibilities are endless!
I'll set this out straight right now, because I know this is a topic that confused alot of people with Starbound and it was holding me back from getting the game for a long time - YES, STARBOUND HAS MULTIPLAYER.
I've really only scratched the surface, as I don't have time to write a full blown review and have little time in Starbound, but believe me when I say this - Both games are within the top 5 best games I've ever played, I honestly love both of them and I have over 1700 hours split between two of my accounts on Terraria and I'm looking to do the same with Starbound.
I have to say though, on Starbound I feel overwhelmed by things to do and it's burnt me out a little, so I've just not played at all recently - I'm personally going to get back into Starbound soon and figure out what the hell is going on ;D
If you want combat, start with Terraria.
If you want RPG, start with Starbound.
In the end, get both games!

I'm recommending this game, but a fair bit of this review will be negative, but this doesn't come from vitriol, only from wanting to see the game in a better state. I'll start with the things I dislike.
First and foremost,
, while I applaud the idea of creating maps by hand and having instance bosses, the instances are boring and repetitive and feel like chores, they're way too long and get boring real quick, I wish they were just scrapped or made entirely optional to be honest. For a game all about exploring and crafting, I wish the progression system was as hands off as possible.
could get a lot better, it can create some good-looking maps, but most of the times it creates ugly planets full of holes that look real blocky, there's also the common dirt towers that pop up here and there. I hope that in the future it can create some smooth looking planets with intended cave entrances that lead somewhere.
, some look nice, some are real generic, most of them are real hostile and bother the hell out of you, some big monsters that you'd suppose some of the bigger monsters are a bit slower, but nah they're still pretty damn fast. And yeah, before I forget, they also get pretty repetitive, you visit multiple planets and find the exact same monster, without any difference in color, size or behavior.
, if I didn't make this clear enough yet, there's a fair amount of repetition, repetitive enemies, biomes, dungeons, weapons, planets. I don't think I need to explain why this is a bad thing.
, while I understand Mechs are a newer feature, it can't be understated how much better they could be. They're slow and cumbersome, they're ok in combat against land creatures, but real weak against the space monsters. They excel in no particular area so far, except maybe combat, but even so there's very limited applications to it, you have to drop it and walk slowly all the way to wherever you need it, since you can't call it in while in the planet. In the future maybe separate mechs in function: Combat, mining or transportation, maybe even have a utility mech that serves as a walking storage unit, with lights and that serves as a sentry.(Note that I have used only two mechs so far, one was the very first one, the other one was from a mod, which would fit among the stronger mechs in the game)
, you have to open the dedicated host then open the game and connect to yourself, which might impede slower PCs of playing Online.
Well, now for the good part(which I have less to talk about really):
houses is pretty fun, there's enough furniture and interaction with some of them to make whatever house you're making a bit more like a place, you can even have a NPC live there, which is pretty neat.
The game
pretty good, all things considered, which makes that point about the map generation not being good sting that bit more.
Some
look pretty nice and colorful.
Generally the
is nice and peaceful, pretty nice for exploring and chilling.
I might have forgotten something, but that's pretty much it. Since Starbound changes every so often, if you're reading this review too much into the future, it's possible multiple of the things I complained about changed, for the good or for the bad.

I am a huge fan of the old Castlevania games. I've played through Castlevania Lords of Shadow and Castlevania Lords of Shadow: Mirror of Fate, both were good, but I found myself enjoying Castlevania Lords of Shadow 2 the most. The best way to describe it is that it plays a lot more like a Castlevania game than the 2 previous games. Definitely worth checking out. I was thoroughly impressed with this game.

A great Castlevania game and a great sequel to the first Lords of Shadow. Even outside of its own series, this game is worth a recommendation, as it can easily appeal to you if you've enjoyed games with similar gameplay like Devil May Cry or God of War.
While some aspects like the stealth puzzles or the metroidvania-esque level design may be divisive, the game features a uniquely satisfying, visceral combat system with finely-tuned fights and excellent controls. The game's difficulty modes are well balanced with a good challenge waiting for you on the higher two settings. The presentation is fantastic—all the graphics, music, sound effects, and amazing gothic-styled vistas mesh together perfectly to create a haunting and memorable atmosphere. The length of the game is equally impressive for a game in this genre, easily clocking in at over 20 hours just to finish the story.

According to Steam I've sunk 16.8 hours into this game from beginning to end, and two of that was on the last boss, because jeez, what a pain!
If you were a fan of Lords Of Shadow 1 then the next entry should definitely satisfy your jonesing for another foray as Gabriel Belmont.
The story is decent, it's not an amazing articulate and in depth thriller, but it is serviceable for the game that it is, and honestly, as far as Castlevania games go, it is probably the best story.  (People really seem to love the 'plots' of Castlevania games without understanding that the story is generally pretty weak.)
Gameplay-wise, big improvement over LoS1.  The camera isn't locked, the environments are open for fighting and the "background" doesn't obstruct the combat the way it did in LoS1.
The platforming is guided, there aren't a lot of fall down and die challenges, if you can make a leap, you'll make a leap, and there's a lot less guesswork than there was in the first one since the camera now sits behind Gabriel not a mile away from him while you judge a gap.
The pace does get disrupted in several moments with these bizarre stealth pieces that, as you approach the end of the game, will have you wondering how it is you still aren't powerful enough to sneak around enemies you should be able to kill.  If you've been playing about 45 minutes of combat, then expect to spend the next 45 dealing with sneaking.  There are a couple of scenes that will definitely test the frustration durability of your controller as well.
The game allows backtracking, but it isn't as crucial as it was in LoS1.  I remember in LoS1 NEEDING to go back and get some more upgrades because combat was such a pain.  In this I tended to find enough health upgrades, power upgrades etc. along the way if I kept my eyes open for side passes, that I did not backtrack at all.
I didn't backtrack because it is a giant pain in the♥♥♥♥♥  The environments are HUGE, there is a quick travel system but it goes to like 4 waypoints in massive areas in the city or in the castle, so it doesn't exactly put you right where you want to be.  I thought about it said "nope" and never backtracked, aside from hitting up a shop.
You may also get locked into certain fights and you can't back out of them to go back and farm health potions, so you're screwed.  Let's just say I spent so long fighting the last boss starting with a shred of health and zero void sword power that I had to learn how to fight and counter him effectively.  I'm probably pretty much unbeatable now thanks to my own lack of preparation going in to the end game.
Despite some of the flaws, fun game.
So...
Get this if:
You love the atmosphere / plot of the Castlevania games and aren't so linear in your thinking that "ZOMGZ ITS NOT CASTLEVANIA IF ITS NOT 2D!"  Or if you were ever a fan of the Legacy of Kain games, because there hasn't been a better "bad♥♥♥♥♥vampire platformer" since the last ones of those were made.
Avoid it if:
You need complicated platforming, not the hand holding kind, or if you're the kind of person who will put a game down if the pace of it gets disrupted.  Because this game definitely upsets its own pace several times during a playthrough, and then it just sits on your computer never getting played.
When in doubt:
Steam sale!

Red Faction II is the sequel that fans of the Red Faction franchise would rather forget. Decent graphics for the time, trouble free gameplay (no crashes & full 1080p), multiple environments (some levels are completed on foot, others in planes, others in tanks, others in power armor), and great voice acting (Jason Statham!).
So what are the drawbacks?
Red Faction II contains little or nothing that made the first Red Faction game a classic. The game is linear as hell. So was the first game, you might say; but even within the levels, there often were multiple ways to progress. Not so in Red Faction II. What about Geomod and destructible terrain? Well, that's still here, kind of. There's plenty of stuff that is destructible. But instead of unlocking different routes, Geomod's role is reduced to the only path. One level begins with Alias in an alley with both ends blocked off. There's no way to progress forward. Oh, wait, shoot those barrels. Boom! The wall explodes and (realistically) crumbles, opening a hole to walk through. There's your Geomod.
Also missing is the Everyman character. Parker (Red Faction), Alec Mason (Red Faction Guerrilla), and Darius Mason (Red Faction Armageddon) were all ordinary joes called upon to be heroes. In Red Faction II, we play as a Nano-agumented super soldier who is already special. The plot might look fine on paper – super soldiers attempt to overthrow a despot – but the execution isn't even up B-movie standards (maybe C-movie standards). And while the voice acting is good, there's no emotional attachment with Alias (your character), even when he is betrayed and has to fight an entirely new enemy about half-way through the game.
Red Faction II is also short for a fps. A complete run-through clocked in around 5 hours. The enemies are generic and repetitive (even the “zombies” of later levels present little challenge). If you're good at getting head-shots, you'll be able to coast through this one. The boss battles do present a decent challenge; the final boss is insanely hard / old school at first. Then I realized his pattern (from which he never deviates), and beat him in 90 seconds. There was one boss that had a charged electrical field for protection; if he got too close, and you became electrocuted, all of your controls become inverted (left is right, down is up). That was fun and a great challenge.
But one unique and fun boss isn't enough to save a game, and unfortunately Red Faction II has little else of interest. Skip it unless you can get it REALLY cheap.
Of note: If battling bots is something you like, you might be interested in Red Faction II's highly customizeable Bot-Match mode. There are quite a few maps and a great variety of weapons.
