This is truly wonderful.
I won't discuss the story in details. The only thing that really matters is that this is an adventure made with an incredible amount of love and care. Awesome, tragic, deep. Very consistent. All that's left is Book Five, which is, well, coming soon.
EDIT: Book Five is out right now, and, well -- although some story lines were wrapped, let's say, really quickly and in case of the few -- without proper explanation as of how and why, the main story line and an epilogue are massive tear-squeezers.
Graphical and sound design are executed very thorough. This is a very solid work, with the teeny-tiny exception of voicing for some characters, especially Reza. Voice volume levels are also tend to differ from chapter to chapter, but I can live with that.
As for technical realization, well -- as a Linux gamer, I'm quite used to all sorts of glitches. Fortunately, they are mostly visual, due to use of some shaders which are not available in *nix-version of Unity. Lack of optimization also shows, for I'm struggling at Arcadia with medium graphic settings set, on a rig running 2-gig GTX750Ti b\w AMD quad-core and 32 Gbytes of RAM. Propast, on the other way, runs super-smoothly. Dunno what I'm doing wrong, to be honest.
Nevertheless, ported version is, well, okay. It's stable, it's not crashing. And Linux is my personal choice, so I guess most people won't encounter these issues which I've mentioned.
To summarize: yes, this, in my opinion, is a good game. It does not feature complex puzzles. Sometimes it suffers from technical issues. But I do recommend it, for it's a game made with unbelievable amount of love & attention to details of the story (which is pretty much what you'd want from an adventure/quest), memorable characters -- and let's not forget great soundtrack.
So yeah, don't be a greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and buy this one already. We almost drove everything to hell once, with pirating The Longest Journey and everything. Let's not make the same mistake again.

Well. I've got to tell you that my expectations jumped real high when I saw a new Half-Life game in the Store. Turns out it's actually a Greenlighted mod. "Oh well, it's free and it's a mod for one of my favorite games, why wouldn't I try it?".
40 mb downloaded later I was in the main menu of this thing. I pressed that magic "New game" button.
The game starts and I see a poorly-made cinematic of a camera (that seemed controlled by a player with shaky hands) flying over a ship, to a point where there's a helicopter landed.
You know, I seriously expected this to have something like that 30 epic minutes of running around in the original HL. I expected some backstory. When I saw the helicopter I thought "Hey, maybe I spawn in there". Nope, nope and nope. After the cinematic the game makes you spawn in front of the helicopter, like if you had been teleported, with no story or anything like that. Those 30 minutes in the original game made you get used to the controls. Here you don't have a single second, since as soon as you're given control of your character, a headcrab attacks you.
I opened my way through the headcrab and all the zombies that were in the area in less than a minute. Comparison time again: Battles in HL were long and difficult at first because you only had a pistol and a crowbar. You were given more guns gradually and you had time to get used to every single one. As well as the enemies, they all didn't appear in the same level, within the same 10 minutes.
Here 5 minutes after I started I had a gun, a rifle and a crowbar. I killed all the zombies without spending a single bullet because inside of the helicopter there was a mounted machine-gun. The kind of machine gun that you only get to see like 10 hours in in the HL campaign. The kind of machine gun that won't run of ammo, deals a lot of damage and literally makes you feel like an overpowered turret. The kind of machine gun that here I used to make my first encounter with the enemies last less than 30 seconds.
I run towards and find a shotgun. Then two new enemies appear (new as in the first time they appeared in the mod). With one of them I find the alien bugs that you can throw and use as bio weapons.
To get to the next part I had to solve a jumping puzzle! A jumping puzzle 10 minutes after I had started playing. Of course that new players would have no idea of how to move boxes. I only figured it out minutes after running around aimlessly, feeling like an idiot. So you're supposed to drag a box, jump from the stairs (jumping from the stairs is extremely hard, as usual) and crouch to get on top of the box, then jump even further to get on top of a container and keep on moving. How the hell is a newbie supposed to know that?
There are cringe-worthy moments as well. The dev put a newspaper-like page that can be found in the floor, kind of advertising himself. On it you can read "Interview with Andrii Vintsevych. This guy is a ♥♥♥♥ing genius. You should learn how to do maps like this guy, ok?". On the outfit of the corpse you find when the mod starts you can read "L337". And there are the un-forgivable typos you'll come across while trying to play this. Seriously, at some moments it makes you worry about the mental sanity of the people you're talking with. I'll quote some: "I think it cose escape of other monsters" and "It has escape". And in the credits it says "Spacial thanks". Yes. Spacial. What you just read.
I don't want to make this review much longer. You could read reviews by other people and see the same I want to tell you; I highly recommend you doing so. This is a short mod for one of the best games ever made that won't even reach the knees of HL. But of course, maybe you don't believe all of the people who are giving it negative reviews and may want to try it for yourself. It's free (if you own Half-Life) and you don't lose nothing. I'm just saying that I didn't like it and I wouldn't recommend it to anybody.

Combat is pretty stale too, as it is shoehorned in with battle arenas that are forced with each stage of your space program.  Take your fleet, navigate the given arena, kill ships, and loot things in the water to call in artillary or EMP.  I miss having all the factions present on the map and having to defend my settlements when the time came.  That aspect is no longer present.  On top of it, it all feels incredibly linear as to your settlement's direction.  There's no harbor design, many buildings go where the slot on the map is, and goods and storage are so streamlined the game basically plays itself.
The game is fun, but very very stale in the complexity department and I feel I won't return for a new game after one is completed, because the experience will largely be the same events in the same order.  I want to enjoy this game, and the theme is amazing, and it's gorgeous to look at, but there's no substance here, not for $60 at least.  Wait till it gets cheaper, or maybe changes with patches or DLC.

I've played all of the Anno games before, and I have hundreds of hours on them. I have played on the hardest difficulty from when I started this game up for the first time.
Anno 2205 differs alot from the other Anno games and many of the mechanics are more streamlined and dumbed down. Infinite resources, no random maps, no multiplayer, no AI to battle on the maps where you build your cities and no warehouses or town halls.
The Anno feel is still here though, managing your supplies and juggling betwen regions instead of islands and send materials back and forth betwen your different cities. Trading is now instant and you don't need boats to do it, instead it will cost X ammount of cash to maintain each trading route.
For anyone new to the Anno series this is probably the best game to start on, and for the veterans it is still a polished and bug free game. Just keep in mind that alot has been changed, so that it wont come as a surprise.
Difficulty is really easy, even though I'm playing on the hardest difficulty. Generating resources and income is as basic as it get's in a city sim and I've had no problems getting the resource I need. Planning your cities ahead isn't that big of a deal any more since you can freely move buildings around and since you have no warehouses, building a logic road system isn't an issue any more.
They've changed how the industrial buildings work by adding the ability to upgrade them with modules which costs resources you cannot obtain other then by doing missions. This does add a sense of missions actually being worthwile. But I have so far not ran out of said resource and I always have a surplus of them.
Battles are now confined to areas where there are no city building. You will get a fleet and a mission on a map that you need to complete to get the rewards, which consists of rare resources to upgrade your factories. You can upgrade said fleet if you have the cash and experience needed, and it feels like a nice edition. This does mean that there will be no combat where you build your cities though, so no defense what so ever is needed in your cities or on your trade routes.
You will spend most of your time on three areas; Temperate, artic and the moon, each being more expensive to build on and each having it's own resources that all of your cities will consume. Going between them isn't an issue for me, but if you don't have a good computer the loading time is probably really laggy and long.
All in all it's a polished city builder with some really basic trading elements. And it would be a great game if the price was lower. Considering all of the things they removed from previous games, like multiplayer, I can't see how the price is acceptable. As I keep playing I just get this feeling that an DLC will be released sooner rather then later that will add a bunch of the stuff that feels like it's missing now, and we the players shouldn't accept this buisness model.
TL;DR
Get the game on a sale, there are more content rich city sims out there that are alot cheaper then this one. This feels like a set-up for DLCs,
Imagine Civ Beyond Earth, SimCity, and C&C naval combat had beautifully well presented baby; and this baby sucked your life away one hour at a time...

Orcs Must Die 2 is a tower defense type game in which you play one of two characters (male/female) in order to top the Orcish hoard from getting to their destination (of which there are sometimes multiple points to protect.)  To assist you there are numerous upgrades for your character, minions, and traps that are unlocked as you progress.  You get an action bar where you can put a set number of these things and then start the level.  Using some of these things (like minions and traps) costs coins.  Coins are independent of each level (they don't carry over so don't be shy about spending them.)  You get more as the level progresses and there are other items you can unlock that increase coin drops.
For me, survival mode was the most fun.  Still haven't made it to wave 30 of any level yet though (it's hard!)  Essentially it's progressively harder and harder waves until you're finally overwhelmed (or make it to that legendary 30th level.)
The fun factor is through the roof on this one and I highly recommend picking it up!

Congo:
~~~~~
It is pitch black and you are stranded in the middle of the Congolese jungle. You keep hearing noises coming from the bush and the foliage is cracking everywhere you look around. All you have going for you is a torch in one hand and a machete in the other hand!
Congo is an action/survival game where you can play by yourself, but it’s primary aim to play on a co-op basis with up to 3 of your mates. You will be able to play in two type of mods; defence or objective. The defence mod currently has 8 different locations and the aim is to make sure you do not lose your radio transmitter and to stay alive as long as you can. For the objective mod, well I guess you can figure this one out. Whatever you prefer to play, you will have to explore the jungle to find additional weapons, gizmos and tools either in crates or on the ground. You will always start with your machete but crates will get you access to revolvers, machines and submachine guns, shotgun, carabines and of course a limited amount of ammunition. Just a little tip for you, make sure you collect as many knives as you can. You will be pinned down to the ground by one of these demons and the only way to kill them went they are on top of you is to use a knife. Gps, flares (which scare the demons), fuel can, cutters and revive syringes (you can’t revive yourself, so this is only if you play as a party) are pretty much your gizmos and tools.
The A.I. is actually very good, demons (Congolese Apes) will sneak around, move away if you flash them with light or use a flare on the ground and attack you at a prominent time for them. The atmosphere is genuinely scary and I really like the fog of war type of setup where you only see clearly around your character(s) which amplify the fear aspect of the game.
From the controls point of view and combat system, they are easy to use but I must admit that I would like to see an easy way to use items in the inventory. The graphics are good and polished.
Congo is an early access game and show great potential, worth giving it a go!
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Scary atmosphere
-	Great A.I.
-	Polished graphics
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Items in the inventory should be friendlier to use
-	No trading cards
7.5/10

I don't normally post reviews. But I sort of felt this was needed.
With Red Faction II, I went in blind, expecting some continuation of the story from Red Faction. What I got was a mess.
Red Faction is a great game, with an interesting story and characters that, whilst somewhat wooden, are still decent and have their uses, dealing with a corrupt corporation that is using it's workers as test subjects for horrific experiments, so with Red Faction II, I expected something similar, maybe playing as a member of the Red Faction or Earth Defence Force, getting rid of remnants of the Ultor Corporation or whatever.
Instead you're playing as a super soldier on (what I assume is) Earth, to bring down the leader of The Commonwealth, a previously unnamed political organisation, and getting your hands on or destroying some sort of Nano technology that is loosely connected to the first game, and even saying loosely is a stretch, aside from the name, there is basically no connection to the rest of the Red Faction series.
Calling the characters wooden would be an insult to trees. I found myself unable to actually care about any of them, even the guy I was playing as, and once I was rid of the BBEG known as Sopot or something like that, I found myself with a new BBEG, my... old commander... who's reason for this was "hurr durr we need more nano soldiers because war reasons". Basically imagine a dumbed down and uninteresting version of Sundowner from MGR and you're pretty close to the mark.
Then he gets stabbed in the back by one of the guys who originally helped him stab you in the back after he branded you an enemy of the Commonwealth for... reasons, I suppose? It's never actually cleared up aside from "You were helping the Red Faction" which is something we were all doing.
Then it's all wrapped up in some sort of 1990's TV Series "Where are they now?" segment, which would have been funny if it wasn't for the fact they were 100% dead serious with this.
I also managed to complete the whole game in about two hours. So go figure.
TL;DR: What the ♥♥♥♥ Volition? Seriously, what the ♥♥♥♥?

I've been a very big fan of any decision making game. Life is Strange, Heavy Rain, etc. I even loved how your choices throughout the Dragon Age series effects the future games in a way. But I feel this game takes it to a whole new level. In many choice based games you end up feeling that the final decision makes all the choices in between fell pointless. So not to spoil the game, I will leave out the name, but one has a final decision of saving one or sacrificing that one to save everyone else, and despite the toughness of the decision, you may or may not feel like being nice to everyone else, or mean, or accusatory, was completely trivial since they're just dead.
However, in Dreamfall, you feel like every decision will not only effect you, but a person you care about too. And the effect of some decisions will make you think "Did I just trade a good friend's life for a good friend's life?" Rather than choosing a lesser of two evils, you feel you need to pick between two equally bad decisions that can put people in jeopardy. You end up feeling like if you reload and change your decision, you might hurt someone else just as badly. So rather than a traditional "choice based" game it in turn seems to be more of a "punishment for your actions" most of the time. Even ordering the lunch in episode one seemed to have more of a consequence and visible change in the relationship between your character and other characters, even though you look at it and think "ordering lunch is such a trivial decision, why did they add it?" But it has a lasting effect. I'd compare this to watering your plant in Life is Strange, correct me if I'm wrong please, but that action seemed to be pointless. I don't remember in my few playthroughs of that having an actual effect, other than the plant sprouting, but I could be wrong.
Now I understand the premise of those other games I mentioned, listed and left out, are different, but I just feel like this is a game where you feel like every decision actually has a lasting effect. Not just on the lives of others, but relationships too. Sometimes you feel like "I'm making progress with this character, he/she is starting to like me" but unfortunate circumstances rip them out of your character's life. And other decisions you made that didn't seem like the; lets call it a line of cause and effect, I'll refer to it as a line, so think of it like a string, it doesn't seem like that line of decision making would matter with other lines, but suddenly, those lines intertwined and start having an effect on one another.
The game makes you realize something that's not just true in some games, but is true in everyday life, things you say and do, no matter how trivial it may seem, mayeffect the people around you, not always physically, but how they look at you or your relationship with them, whether a friendship or otherwise.
Now as for the game's premise. I played the first two games as well, and despite everyone's *****ing and moaning about the second game in the series, I've enjoyed the whole series and world. I feel since the first game, it's gotten deeper with more of a depiction of social issues but in the past and present. And that makes it feel that much more realistic. I never could've imagined just how interesting a story about "dreaming" could be until I found these games. The rivalry of "science and faith" that is ever so present in modern culture. The "crusades" that are talked about and in motion in the final game. And a very "1984" type feel to it at times. The list could continue for the points of the game that could relate to history or the present, but some of those would spoil, so I won't continue.
I know that people were upset with the structure of the second game, "the story" was not good enough, "not the same gameplay style" I've seen somewhere about it. I think that one may refer to it not being point and click. Yes, it's too bad that now you have to use TWO HANDS to play a game. Partially. However I thought it was a great lead in to this game. And you have to realize, the first was made in 1999, the second in 2006 (correct me if either years are wrong) as technology advances, the game does too or it could get left behind. I hope everyone one who plays the game judges the whole series rather than individual parts, as I think it's a masterpiece when played. I highly recommend this game for anyone who likes story, choices and some puzzles to be predominant in a game.

This game can be safely thought of as a super-lite form of civ.  You are expanding your federation and competing with other similar organizations.  Expansion is done by completing quests for nearby planets, which will grant you up to 4 points of influence (at which point the planet joins your federation).  Quests vary slighly through the usual escort, exterminate, etc, but in the end they all feel the same.
Content is very limited, and a single play through can be completed in two hours or less.  I paid $8 for this game during a sale, yet I still don't really feel I've gotten my money's worth.  There are too many other options for turn-based tactical combat out there that are done far better; avoid this one.

Do the whole thing again, this time, do a little better.
And when you finally feel like you've gotten somewhere, you have to build planes, submarines and spacecraft.
Serilously: This is a lot of fun. You're building vehicles (be it boat, plane, submarine or spacecraft), and completing story missions and campaigns. The story missions are a bit tutorial-ish, and rather fun (although difficult). In the campaigns, you wage a dynamic war against other factions, competing for resources and building ever larger craft.
If you like building and testing things, this is the game for you!
Pros:
- Fun building
- Fun gun building (Missiles, cannons, grenade launchers, lasers, all built part-by-part from constituent blocks)
- Already lots of campaign content (37 tutorials, about 8 different story mission categories each containing about 5 missions)
Cons:
- Complicated, lots of things to learn
- UI requires some getting used to, but is efficient enough (Lots of key controls)

Essentially this plays like a scaled down and simplified version of Star Wars: Empire at War.
The differences are:
* Factions. There are a few different factions as apposed to EaW's two
* You can chose between three main races and a few different leaders each with different abilities
* Only one fleet. Each ship is highly customizable.
* The fleet has a few action points which regulates how much it can do in one turn
* buying planetary upgrades, research or fleet upgrades can be done anytime in your turn, except when in battle
* Turned based. The game is essentially turn based, both in the overview and in the space battles.
* There are no ground battles.
* A game can be completed in relatively short order.
* More control on research
In essence, a game can be finished in a few hours. It is interesting enough to keep you playing until the end. it should have a decent replayability value based on choice of starting race and leader.

I'll start this review by saying that OutDrive is at best a glorified flash game.If this ''product'' would have been released in the 1980's,it would have been a decent experience but it was released on Steam in 2016.
Default controls for keyboard are WASD for directions,SHIFT for speed boost and SPACE for drifting.
If you jump into the game without reading something about it beforehand,you might be confused.The game fails to explain exactly what the objective is.Apparently you need to save the girl by driving fast.If you are driving too slow,her heart will stop.If you are driving too fast,it will hurt her.Sounds simple enough..and it is.After 5 minutes you will be bored to death.The music isn't particularly good for you to keep playing..and you can simply listen to it online and do something else in the meantime.Only one map that never ends and after awhile,seems to repeat itself.No obstacles,weird car physics and an attack helicopter that spawns and shoots you even if you are in a tunnel but misses every single shot all the time.
The retro style graphics look decent and the world around the car is certainly more interesting than the gameplay.

I can't recommend this game for a few reasons.First of all,it has a pricetag.There are literally thousands of free games out there that are better than this.Second of all,there are literally thousands of similar/better retro music tracks out there that don't require you to play a boring car game.

Not a lot of games can produce a truly heart-rushing scare once you've played Alien : Isolation - but Congo is gnarly good at it !
Congo is primarily a top-down action title where the camera slightly pitches up to show a dark and uninviting expanse as you thread carefully in half-steps, and to great effect. The tension is immediate, the danger, even when yet manifested, instantly palpable. You barely see as far as where your modest torch - probably your best friend early in the game - will generously shed light on. Not of a lot of games offer a distinct advantage in wielding a gun over a 2-handed-firearm, as you can still hold the handmade 360-degrees beacon to spot foes (relatively) early on. And let me add that you start with just a big knife.
The enemy is intelligent, powerful, stealthy. Most of the time 1st contact starts with the sound of the enemy carefully brushing the vegetation, and still you have to rely on you best aurality to pinpoint exactly where the threat is approaching from. It knows how and when to attack, when to retreat for a renewed or flanked offensive, and it uses the element of surprise and teamwork to stalk and hit the invader - you, who is in the end of the day only trying to haul out of this sinister place of a jungle by night.
Congo is a game about pure survival from a place where every second takes a toll on your nerves, and a place where rushing blindly and pseudo-merrily will put your stride to an abrupt and violent end.  A game still in development despite its "as is" robustness, but already showing great promise and a rather terrifying presence not often approached or executed as deftly.

This game is incredibly entertaining.
The graphics are nothing spectacular and this game have several bugs (such as zombies are sometimes able to rush through doors without breaking it), even with the bugs I still found myself playing often. There are no "Main Characters", you start off as Marcus but you are quickly able to play as other survivors in your base. If one of the survivors die, they are gone forever you don't get a "game over" you simply play as one of the remaining survivors. That being said each survivor has his/her own traits, skills, and levels. The more you use the survivors the more they level up, if you play only as one survivor and he/she dies you will have a harder time playing as the other low level survivors (if you didn't level them up). You get to build up your base and you are even able to relocate to other bases. Getting all the materials to build and level up your base can be grinding but well worth it. There are a variety of buildings you can create in your base. Watchtowers (to snipe zombies), Garden(to grow crops), Library (to research advanced buildings) and a variety of other buildings.
This game is a fun game to play to just kill some time, the bugs are a slight Inconvenience but nothing game breaking.

This review is for Early Access (EA) and may change over the development cycle of this game.  Hired Ops (HO) is a first-person shooter and sequal to Contract Wars (2013) which has 48 million players worldwide.
HO is based on the Russian 2028 lore you may be familar with after the announcement of  Absolut Soft's sister company, Battle State Games' Escape from Tarkov. HO takes place after you have escaped from Tarkov and move onto a global mission.  As such, the maps are based on different locations around the globe.
The gameplay is a fps run and gun styled game similar to CoD and BF games. The current game modes include deathmatch, team death match, and target designation (similar to bomb defusal in CS). I like the gunplay of the game and the modes while simple are the most popular in most fps games.
The game ran fast but seemed to lock my frames at 144 which is what my monitor is defaulted to support. While the weapons look good, the textures overall need improvement as do the character models. The graphics overall lack fidelity and look dated. For a browser game designed for handheld devices, the game would look well but for PC with HD monitors and high end graphics cards the graphics are lacking. Hopefully this will change as the game is polished.
There is also a field of view (fov) issue obscuring the picture when moved above the default of 60 (a max of 90). I managed to keep mine at 75 without too much noticeable problems, but people who get motion sickness should avoid this title until this issue is resolved. There is also an issue with blurring of the weapon while moving. This may be intentional but I for one do not like it because it is distracting.
HO is in early access and as with any EA game you can expect game breaking issues, lag and rubber-banding, a small community, as well as changes as the game is patched and content is added. I believe this game has a lot of potential but it will take time and the game is nowhere near release.
If you want to help shape the developement of this game or simply want to back the game, then invest now and have fun with it. In its current condition you can have fun with it, especially when playing with a group of friends. If however you are expecting a finished game then stay away until the game is fully released. There is no guarantee the game will develope into what you expect it to.

This game is excellent. The story is very emotive, very smart, it really does feel like your decisions have weight. I felt like it was such a weighty cliff hanger at the end of this game, very bittersweet, sad but hopeful. As a person who was not familiar with the previous games, I sort of just jumped in, based on some videos about it and other reviews. I have to say, I was not disappointed. Sometimes, there were parts, especially during book 1 & 2 where I had to think about things on some puzzles, or how to interact with an item or how I was suppose to use said item, but it's not impossible things. The vents was very tricky and I admit, I had to seek out help during that part, but I did not want to read hints on other parts of the game. I really did want to be surprised by the results. I came to the conclusion that there are a few choices which are better than others, but like most things, there's really no wrong answer. Life by its nature is reactive, it's fluid, it's changing, and this game does a great job of capturing how tough it is to know which is the right path, and is there truly a right path, rather than simply things you get caught up in sometimes? I like how this game truly makes you think about things, it's not the average cookie-cutter adventure/RPG, but it's not morbid, it's strange I'll give you that, but in a wonderful way really.
I do think this game would be better served by allowing you to save different formats, instead of it rewriting over your saves. I don't honestly know why some games choose to do that, but that is always a little annoying for those of us who need to see different sides of a game, who want to get different perspectives (and perspective, isn't that mostly what life is about anyway?). But, it's still probably a minor point. I have to say that, I would have prefered some of the buildings to be a tad more interactive, just being able to go inside more places instead of only being allowed in certain areas, but I realize this was fan-backed, so I have to say in that respect, much was accomplished from that and the development team seemed to make good use of what was provided. It's a game I'm proud to say I wanted to finish, and I'm still thinking about Saga, and Zoe.
I really thought that showing Saga grow from a baby to a child to a teen was really clever, it gave me a strange sense of ...wonder I guess, development did a really good job of making that baby look so very realistic, baby fat and chubby cheeks, and I loved that locket, it was so touching to see that scene, and I really felt for Saga's dad (even if he placed those wards in the first place, I'm sure he had his reasons, even if they were misguided). I loved how authenic Saga's dad's accent was, I swear he was from Dublin, who knows maybe that voice actor was haha.
And correct me if I'm wrong, but didn't Stephanie Leonidas play Zoe? I only know because I've seen mirror mask like 20 times, so you get to pick up things when you hear someone enough, anyway, it does sound like her, but not fully sure if it is. In fact, so many of the voice actors sound really authenicly UKish, you even threw in some Cockney sounding rustic gents, in the Mercuria village, like some of the farmers saying "I'm really lookin' forward to this years fes-teee-val, I could really hear that rustic charm, it really made me laugh. I'm from America, though I have a few UK friends, but I've never been to any of the isles, but you get to know a thing or two about voices once you've heard an accent enough. Like how the people from London tend to say "innit", the cockney people tend to put extra S's on everything and they generally reflect a more laid back way, like people in the south in American do, though we tend to not say "we be over there", now we might say reckon, which is strange the similarities there.
Anyway, sorry...nerd alert I like language and and literature. Anyway, I've played alot of games where the voice acting just did not sound believable, but it's really awesome in this game, closest one was perhaps Bard's Tale (but then again Cary Elwes is Welsh I believe, kind of surprised I didn't hear his voice in this, wouldn't he have also made a great Doctor therapist, wink, wink). I do like how there's different sounding nationalities, and all the languages seem hodge-podge, like some of the curses are mashed together, you saw this in Blade Runner (movie/short story), though there were quite a few Indian sounding people as well, but it really gave the future a more wider scope. Isn't it ironic in the story though, that everyone doesn't seem to make a big deal about langauge or race, in the future, it's when Kian is in his world, where people start discriminating against magicals (book 4, especially the end, reminded me of the Nazi concentration camps, to be honest... Ge'en was very believable, and I did not expect the admin of the camp to look like that, very unassuming, but isn't that how it is sometimes? Scary.
I'm hoping in book 5 we'll find out what happened to Bip, he became very endearing, I almost felt bad about not telling him the truth about his parents, even though I know the game is usually ran a certain way, if I think about it psychologically, he needed to prepare himself for that death camp; it might have helped him to put up a smarter fight, though in the end he's still a boy, not superman. I really felt for his character, and I really didn't feel guilty about knowing that woman into the pit, it was quite enjoyable really, she was really sadistic, and the joke between Kian and Leiko was funny, though it makes me wonder, if you go solo ...I do wonder, does she just point the gun at Kian, and if so how would you distract her? That's part of the joy to getting more than one perspective in a game. I'll really enjoy another play through, but I'm not sure if I should wait, and maybe part 5 will come out in a few months, if that's the case I can probably wait then, but I would like to alter a few of my decisions on a next run through, since I'm fairly aware which choices are the worse ones. There are a few parts where it's simply personal choice, like about either torturing that solider or not doing it, in one instance Enu will like you, in another Leiko will dislike you (but you can redeem with him later). In this respect, it is in a similar vain as many of the Tell-tale games, however...I'll choice fantasy and sci-fi anyday over zombie/horror, perhaps because I'm more a dream than a realist, but people can display many sides sometimes, just depends on which you do/enjoy the most? I really recommend this game, especially to a buff of either genre, and I do enjoy my share of thriller titles, but I'd rather be thought-provoked, than just adrenalined all the time, I will admit Yaga's house was scary as hell though, and that really creepy feeling you get when you hear that voice (yikes), but it was only in one part of the game, so it's not like my adrenaline was high the whole time. I sort of like that, when it's used as a rare effect, but not in everything. I mean, once you get jump scared 20 times it sort of looses it's rush, and you're still getting anxiety which is not so good on the stress meter you know. A good story can win over game play, but it all matters. This game felt like just the right balace to make it immersive, in fact when you first see the sprawling city, it's easy to just be in wonder at the sheer size of it, it really felt like another world.

The only other Castlevania game I played to completion prior to this one was C:SotN, widely regarded as the best Castlevania in the series. Without knowing until after I finished this Lords of Shadow series follows an alternate timeline from the others in that series, and without playing Lords of Shadow 1, I enjoyed it a lot. The game catches you up to the story of Lords of Shadow well, and I enjoyed the plot and flow of the game.
Gameplay (fighting) is pretty hack-slash with comboing using the whip, or sword/chaos claws but is quite simple. I've read people compare it to God of War, but having not played that series I wouldn't know. I wasn't expecting anything amazing in combat but I did find it fun to play despite not a huge variation in enemies. At least most of the enemies weren't annoying, but I did dread getting into fights. There was a fair bit of platforming, some stealth missions which I hated, and some nice simple puzzle-solving. There as good flow and variation during the story to keep it fresh.
Exploration in this game is pretty lacking. Missions/the story is pretty linear/guided, and unless you wanted to upgrade your weapons/skills (not necessary if you played on an easier difficulty like me, I just wanted to play this game casually) there was no point in re-visiting areas. You can access 'new areas' in levels with upgraded abilities later in the game, but there's really no point unlike in Castlevania:SotN because you won't be getting new weapons/skills/etc. doing so. Don't expect some Skyrim/TES bonuses from going off the beaten path
Visually, this game is pretty good. Nice background scenery, the castle looks beautiful. The modern city is kind of 'meh', but I did appreciate how the game looked. Some of the audio tracks are great too, but you will run into a lot of the same music.
Overall, I had fun with the game and enjoyed it for what it was. I admitedly got frustrated with some parts of the game and would just quit playing 10 minutes in if I couldn't advance through the story fast enough to do other stuff but my yearning for knowing what happened in this game kept me coming back. I won't be playing it beyond the story mode and doing a NG+ mode or anything like that. Buy it on sale for 10-15 dollars but I wouldn't pay full price for it.

One of my favorite action-adventure games; but be careful, this game has a different tone than the first Lords of Shadow and also, it has big plot holes and some gameplay flaws.
The combat is very similar to the first Lords of Shadow, but improved.
The puzzles are easier but most of them are more related to the game than the puzzles of the first Lords of Shadow ( now many puzzles involves using the abilities of Dracula instead of moving pieces in a board).
This game also have camera control with the right stick instead of the predefined camera of the first game.
Another noticeable change is that now there are exploration in the game, it's really a 3D Metroidvania game, where you unlock new areas while getting new powers.
About the tone, LoS 2 has an atmosphere much darker than the first one, basically you explore two worlds:  one is very similar to the first game(but darker), and the other one at the beginning may look like an arkham city less appealing, but most of the game it's more like the first Darksiders atmosphere.
The story also remind me Darksiders and a little bit of Hellboy.
The bad parts: there are some stealth sections that feels out of place and there are not very fun, the first hour of two of the game(after the prolog) are not very good, Dracula doesn't look like a vampire(but you can buy a skin :) ), and the game has some annoying on-screen suggestions (fortunately, they can be deactivated in the menu).
Even when these shortcomings most of the game is great.

I actually enjoyed this game more than Lords of Shadow 1. I felt that the story was more engaging and the gameplay was more fun. There were a lot fewer gimmicky moments than the first game as well. Some of the gimmicks really got frustrating. My only complaint is what everyone else complains about: the stealth sections, particularly the Agreus cat and mouse game. I eventually made it, but not without a good amount of cursing. All in all, I really liked the game.

Let me say this straight and simple: If you are going to buy this game, you are going to buy this game because of the incredible ease it takes to obtain all the achievements. It takes most about 20-60 minutes to do this, and even still many people have difficulty getting the achievements validated. Look to the forums if you have problems, the solutions are there.
The reason why I put this as thumbs down is because there is a free (and much better) game that is like this one on Kongregate. It is called Accelerator, here's the link
.
The main differences between this one that you are paying money for and the free one are the sounds, visual, and a few game play differences. Accelerator has a much better sound system, but no music. It doesn't need it. It ends up giving a much better atmosphere than Collider without the music. Also complimenting the atmosphere are the visuals. There are no drastic colour changes besides the square tunnels being blue. This gives the game a more stream lined sense, and helps the progression without accidentally crashing.
While this isn't a problem in Collider because of the reviving function, Accelerator doesn't have that. it is much more harder because of this and you feel like you have actually achieved something. What Accelerator does have is a difficulty setting, and this changes one thing mainly, the level design. Harder difficulty levels will result in tight corners and diverging paths, which when you are going fast, become really difficult to traverse. It just adds to the feel of satisfaction when you get that impossible badge for reaching a speed of 1000.
All in all, my basic gripe was paying for this. Yes it is cheap, yes it gave me a perfect achievement thing, but in all honesty, why play this when Accelerator on Kongregate is free and so much better?

This is the age we live in. The rip-off games (erhm-- "inspired games" I mean) are released before the actual game.
Aside from the drama, here's my quick review:
GRAPHICS:
Graphics are nice. 80s synth "inspired" art is cool. The palm trees and sun models are pretty nice, but some of the more "original" models, such as the rows of cars and jumps... not so much. For me, the frame rate can be a bit choppy. I would have expected a simple unity game to run a little nicer on my PC.
SOUND:
The sound is a major component of this game. The original synthwave tracks are nice to listen to. I would have liked for there to be a sound test present. It's unfortunate that maintaining a consistent speed in the car is difficult, as it fluctuates the track's pitch and tempo as your girl nears death, which happens often. The engine roars and screeching breaks are barely audible for me, but I don't know that I care whether they're loud or not-- I'm here for the music (and not much else, unfortunately).
CONTROL:
Bleh. Doesn't auto-configure for either my Xbox Controller or generic Bluetooth controller (NES30 PRO). The steering is too loose using the keyboard. Drifting takes a little practice. W (or Up), for acceleration, is a really tired setup for steering a car in a video game, one that was proven to be a miserable gaming experience time and time again in the past 30 years of gaming. I would have prefered for a seperate acceleration, and a seperate turbo speed button.
STORY/REPLAYABILITY
The games intro is decent, and the story is short, sweet, to the point, and gives the player inspiration to get into the game. Unfortunately, the only further plot development we receive is a GIRL IS DEAD screen when a game over is reached. A little further development after x amount of minutes of driving would have been nice. Perhaps individual levels for each soundtrack or artist in the game? With only randomly generated tracks and no further plot development, there's little reason to play this game longer than 15 minutes or so. In fact, I think I've spent more time writing up my opinions on the game rather than actually playing it.
VALUE:
I don't think I'd reccommend satiating your curiousity by paying the $3 asking price to try this title. You could however pick this title up in a bundle as I did, and feel a little bit better about having paid for this game at all.
OVERALL:
OutDrive has a few standout moments in the introduction, plot, and thumping synthwave soundtrack that are left unenforced by a lack of fun, driven gameplay. As an "experience," as the author of this game wishes to be judged, OutDrive is a middling, uninspired 80s racer, one that has been done better before-- and surely will be again in the future.

It could have been a game if it had a little more thought put into some form of goals.
And if it's supposed to be a relaxing aesthetic experience, it should be easier to stay on the road.
At least I got it for free on a Gleam giveaway.

I have never written a review before, nor ever felt the need to write a review.  However, with the launch of Anno 2205, that changed.  I know this is a way for the developers to read about what players think about their game, so I would like to put my opinion out there.  This review is not hating on Anno, however, it highlights differences between this one and previous ones.
Now, I'm sure people are going to challenge my opinion because I have less than two hours in the game(as of launch day).  However, I own almost every other Anno to date, either virtually or hard copy, so I think I have a pretty good knowledge base when it comes to city building, micromanaging, and fully enjoying an Anno game.
On a good note, the game runs beautifully on Ultra High graphics.  The textures look astounding, from buildings to oceans to mountains.  Anno 2205 is a more casual, new user friendly game compared to other Anno's(1404,1701, 2070), which I assume because the developers want the game to target a wider audience.  However, Anno 2205 feels like a dumbed down version of previous Anno's.
What do I mean by that? The challenge of "building a city" is gone in this Anno.  Instead, you are building a corporation to fight for resources and land in temperate, artic, and lunar zones.  Yes, there is still building of houses, managing of energy and money but many of the tasks which made Anno stand out are gone.
-The concept of storage is gone(edit: changed per say), same with overproduction and underproduction.  In previous Anno's, you had to balance amounts of materials you obtained, otherwise you would end up with a surplus or a deficit of material.  If you mined too much or too little, there were repercussions.  Also, This Anno has removed non-renewable resources all together. For example, I can mine coal out of a mine until the end of time, whilst in previous Anno games, you'd eventually run out of coal on one island and need to switch to another.
-Anno 2205 limits the user to where they can build on land zones. For example, You want to build a algae farm(which is built on the coastline). It must be placed on a spot which gets highlighted for the user when they try to build the algae farm.  You cannot choose where the building is placed on the coast like you could in previous Anno's.  In simple terms, Freebuild has been limited.
-This may be the biggest one for me.  No Skirmish or Multiplayer.  For $80, I do not want to play a campaign only.  I enjoyed having the ability to create a randomly generated world to play on.  It keeps the game interesting, as you don't ever see the same map twice.  The Ability to add or delete AI's, and make the game as challenging as the user liked.  Being able to spend hundreds of hours with friends building and cooperating. That is what defined Anno as my favorite city builder of all time.  Without these features, the game will become boring very fast for many players because no one likes repetitive things.
Now, I will be updating this review as I keep playing the game, as I have only played a short amount of time into the game.  If other modes to play are released in the future as well, this review will drastically change.  However, until updates happen and changes to the game occur, I will have trouble enjoying this Anno like I enjoyed the rest of them.
Edit 11/3/15(answers to comments, cleared up some things):
Just some random answers:
"For example, I can mine coal out of a mine until the end of time, whilst in previous Anno games, you'd eventually run out of coal on one island and need to switch to another." Well that was also removed in 2070, so you can't really comment on that
-The player would have to build something(or buy it from traders) to obtain more coal on the island, which means you had to plan ahead for when you ran out.  And it added a miniscule amount of coal compared to what the island started with.
"You cannot choose where the building is placed on the coast like you could in previous Anno's. In simple terms, Freebuild has been limited." - I'm not really sure what you mean by this but it's not like you could place buildings where ever the ♥♥♥♥ you wanted in old Annos. Coastal buildings especially only went in certain places.
-Coastal Buildings can only be placed in designated "slots" now. There are no beaches to fill full of fisheries etc. like in Anno 2070.  So I guess you could say its like Anno 2070 crab fishing now, where there were designated areas only for crab fishing.
"There was no challenge in anno 2070 either when it comes to managing production and overproduction. All you had to do is look it up online. So in essence I see no problem with removing a bit of tedium of looking up something online."
-I guess I never looked it up online, but by taking it out it still simplified the game too much, at least in my opinion.  And I will be playing this game all today to see what else I can say about it.

UPDATED REVIEW.
Recommendation: YES, but at a lower price due to replayability concerns.
(Changed from NO from previous DAY ONE review)
First of all, thanks to all the commenters... You've really amazing people. ;)
Anyway, short form: Not quite the Anno you know. A lot of the core aspects are present: resource and production chain management, income balancing through satisfying population needs, laying out roads and your city, and the complexity of not having all resources at one location. Caveat is that the scale of the game has become a bit grander that it takes time to manage your chains because instead of managing different islands you now manage different maps you have to jump in and out of. The maps are limited in selection, and without multiplayer replayability is pretty low.
Is this an Anno game? Yes, in it's own way.
Long form...
The story is also you guide to "winning" the game and also your basic tutorial. Playing the game for the first time, you will be thankful how the story progresses and asks you to do tasks sequentially based on what kind of resource chain should go up next. If you already know what you're doing, you can safely ignore the story content and it will actually automatically progress as you build your chains on your own. One quirk is that you may get intrrupted by the story as it automatically progresses along with you.
Resource collection and production chains remains pretty much the same, except you no longer directly deal with invetory counts. Yes, storage does exist. But, it's not really there because you need to keep watch. The new UI now presents data in a meaningful way and goes completely out of the way when you don't need it and is easy to access when you want to see them. Also, you only see if you surplus, deficit, or not. If you want to see how much is stored in your map, you will have to over over the good's icon in the UI. With the invetory system stripped away of it's essential fuctions, you no longer have the ability to transfer quantities of goods between spaces. They simply exist in the background automatically stored and consumed by your production chains, and citizens. The only goods you actually see and need to care about are goods that you use to build and upgrade your buildings. They are presented at the top of the screen, only displaying relevant goods based on your map.
Trading is stripped converted from the easy drop and sell to the new surplus trading. You sell the surplus flow your sector creates, oh and it costs some amount to "transport" these goods magically to the world market. Each good you want to sell will have to have it's own trade route, instead of maybe a a ship that can be filled in with goods of different kinds for a cheaper transport. Oh, and you cannot sell to the world market if you are offline. And, you cannot sell to the other AIs in the game, but you can buy from them! I tried trading, but unless you are selling higher tier items, your trading lines are just going to bankrupt you as they don't really provide any profit, if at all.
Remember when I said you now manage maps instead of islands? Yeah, you are presented with a global map, prefilled with pre-created maps. No, no random maps. Bummer. No big deal, the maps given present their own challenges and puzzles in their own way. I'm just a bit worried about replayability when you get tired of playing the same maps. (What's that? there might be a map pack DLC? Colour me excited). You are given 4 map types, the Temperate map, Acrtic maps, Lunar map, and the Crisis map. The first three are your build your city and production chain maps, while the crisis map is an optional map where you control your military ships to attack enemies, gain non-renewable resources, and earn some more credits. They are completely optional, but they do grant some nice incentives if you play them.
Combat. I'm not exactly a fan of combat in my Anno games. Separating it on a different map makes the game a bit more accessible and relaxing. I did play a good amount of combat in the Crisis maps, they were entertaining but after a couple fo plays they just gave me the same maps and missions. I suspect if you play them more they might give you more variety? But, that speculation on my part. I don't bother much with the combat. Actually, I only played them to gather resources used in upgrading buildings, like iridium, and graphene.
Overall, this game still feels familiar if you've played Anno before. What's new is that this is a whole different beast on it's own. Once you grasp the game further, you'll understand that this new Anno tries to be a whole new game on it's own while building from the foundations that it's predecessors have built. That's a good thing. However, due to the limited map selection, and pretty linear story (which is more like your progression guide) I am highly concerned about the replayability of this game. I understand you can play this a higher difficuluty, but that only goes so far.
Without Multiplayer or random maps, I doubt this game will go far enough for me to sink in as much time as I did playing the previous Anno games. As much as I hate to bring up the topic, but an Anno game just has to be replayble. At it's current price, it just feels like it's overpriced for what it gives you.
If you want to play this game, I'd recommend waiting for it to hit a lower price. You won't be missing out as much not being able to play Anno 2205 right away.
P.S. I have a season pass, so I'll be receiving future DLC automcatically. Depending on what DLC comes out, this recommendation may change. As of now, it stands where it is. I don't see myself updating this review even with more time I invest into the game and learning more about it.

I still remember it. 3 years ago. 4th September. I was about to date one of the most bomb girl you ever saw. And guess what? What I was doing instead of doing what I was suppose to do? Well, I believe you got it right. Since this is review of State of Decay and I mentioned it just now for the first time, your answer is State of Decay.
Alright, enough of sentiment, let's get into the game. Story starts out pretty weak, again with lot of questions and as usual you are just ordinary citizen of small US town and after a while zombie-killing machine. The whole story itself is really not that important, at least wasn't for me, it's about enjoying that zombie rampage, enjoying RPG elements and just trying to survive.
Really good thing is, that you can die, your friends can die, people in your house can die but you will take the control of somebody else and you'll continue. That's really awesome. Way more better if it was just "you die, game over" cliche. AI is really really weak. No matter if it's zombies or survivors, it's both really low. Survivors are absolutely not independent. It's not like I do mind taking care of somebody else, but thing is that they can't take care of themselves and that's it.
Getting supplies, scavenging town, building rooms in your house, upgrading your house,, building new spots and making area secure is one of my most favorite elements out of this game. Audio is not really strong side of State of Decay and visuals are not that good either, but there's no reason to turn away from it.
Game will last you estimated 12 +- hours and price point is fair. You can extend that time period by buying two DLCs which are basically worth buying. I will make more in-depth reviews on both on their respective Store Page. So now just few sentences.
- This DLC does not carry any story, it's just basically let you do infinite survival. You're unlocking different heroes and try to survive as long as possible. Hordes are spawning fast, and supplies going away fast too. When you run out of everything you'll use your RV to get out. And to be honest that's it. Get it for 2,49€ in sale.
- You are in control of Greyhound One unit on your way to rescue scientists. New map, new characters and new weaponry. It'll extend your gaming experience by 3-4 hours. Linear but still fun. Again, get it in sale and you're good.
Get both for achievements.
To sum it up, pretty nice zombie survival game for good money, pretty enjoyable and you can play it even second time and still enjoy it. Easy achievements and killing hordes is fun. Weak AI and audio but you can live with that. Most definitely worth the shot.

Red Faction II is a sequel of Red Faction by Volition Inc. While the first game has you starting as a simple miner caught up in the rebellion and you end up being the best soldier capable of defeating even mercenaries, this one has you playing as Alias, one of the few nano-tech enhanced soldiers left in the world, joining Red Faction against the authoritarian regime of Sopot and his elite guards. The story felt very derivative and rather lame, compared to the "fish out of water (that turned out to be a shark)" story of the first. This time, you're simply better than anybody else, and everybody knows it. You're the demo guy, while others in your squad are scout, sniper, heavy weapons, vehicles, and commander.
Graphics are good for the time, and Red Faction has a feature called "Geomod" which allows certain walls or terrain features to be destroyed, creating alternative avenues of approach. However, what's destructible and what's not are not obvious and you don't have indefinitely amount of ammo for experimentation. in the single player you will sometimes have to create exits with the explosives.
Based on tech of the time, poly count is relatively low, but tolerable. Texture was state of art back then and merely tolerable now. The fun part is the gun play, but this is an old-school shooter... no lean, no cover and blind shoot, no tagging, What you see and aim in the crosshair is what you get. And you get to carry bazillion weapons... single or double pistol, machine pistol, and later, nanotech pistol (single hand means you can throw grenades, doubled gun can't use grenades). Then you get to shotgun (dual barrel, one with regular buckshot, other with incendiary) SMG, assault rifle, assault rifle with grenade launcher, LMG, rocket, grenade launcher, sniper rifle, railgun, and other fancy weapons. There's also grenade, incendiary grenade, and satchel charges.
You will also sometimes get to play with vehicles, such as aerial gunner (man the turret!), submarine fighter (launch torpedoes), tank (main and coax guns), as well as armored suit with rockets and twin gatlings, just to break up the monotony of shoot, shoot, and shoot.
There are occasionally severe lack of hints, as you are given NO IDEA on where to go, but if you explore a little, there's probably a door you need to open, or a hole you need to make bigger, or a wall you need to jump over, and such. And to encourage you to go on your way, an infinite number of enemies will spawn to "encourage" you to move along and since your ammo is limited, you should move along, albeit this was never explained anywhere.
On easy level your health resets to 100% between stages, so that makes the game quite a bit easier. Furthermore, your health autoheals if you stay out of combat for about 10 seconds. You can have up to 3 health kits on you, and they will auto-heal you when your health gets too low. Obviously that means you should not get hit that often, lest you run out of them! Fortunately, they often can be found on dead soldiers (just run over them to collect). It's only later that there are certain enemies that don't leave loot.
All in all, RF2 is an also ran. In making the protagonist a super-soldier, it also lost most of the charm of "fumbling your way around" of the first RF game. Not to mention the plot is virtually cliche. Basically, you do the heavy lifting, someone else reap the benefits, and then there's the... surprise! :)
I managed to finish it in a couple hours, and I'm not a speed-run guy. It's just very short in single player. I imagine there can be more fun in MP, but being this old, MP lobby's long dead. It's kinda fun for historical purposes, and it's cheap, but you'd probably be better off with a modern RF, like RF: Guerilla or such.

Pros:
+ Excellent weapon variety
+ Satisfying gunplay (sometimes)
Cons:
- Numerous on-rail segments
- Graphics and voice acting from 2003
- Lackluster "geomod" gameplay [1]
- Unskippable cutscenes immediately after checkpoints
- Annoying boss fights (bullet sponges)
- Uninspired story that only makes sense if you're on drugs
- Uninspired level design that ranges from dull (offices) to confusing (sewers)
- No challenge on medium difficulty [2]
- Extremely short at 3 hours (this might be a good thing)
[1] The GeoMod technology is the cornerstone of Red Faction. Red Faction: Guerilla is considered the best of the series because of how far they took it. This game, not so much. There is no destroyable terrain, only a handful of walls that almost always need to be destroyed to progress. There was no strategy element to it as enemies always know where you are and there is no debris to take cover behind.
[2] I can count the number of times I died to normal enemies on one hand. The other deaths come from annoying suicide drones that inexplicably hang out in the sewers, or bullet sponge bosses who are a war of attrition rather than skill.

With that being said, the game is truly great when things work well. The gunplay is good, the movement system is... well, decent. Its a bit grindy for my taste, but im sure thats perfect for some people. I've noticed that the stat cards aren't accurate, so you do need to try out all the guns to see how they perform; though you'll run into the grinding issue because of this. You get (on average) 500-1000 credits/match, assuming you do well, which as an American is quite easy.
You start with 100k credits, allowing you to get some of the better guns up to tier 3, like the MPX.
Onto balance: The MPX is broken. At close range, it hipfires far too well, and with the accuracy issues, you don't even notice the innacuracy. The ACR is simply godlike on any non-sniperfest map.
And for maps... well... Meh. They're decent. A few are long ranged, leading to longer and more skillful matches, but those are completely unplayable unless you have a DMR and scope, which you don't when you first start.
All in all: Wait for it. The playercounts are too low, the game is unbalanced, and im not even going to talk about the optimization (or lackthereof).

Fun initially, and with really nice presentation and graphics, but it is incredibly formulaic.  Just keep on searching the same "desks" over and over until you have enough duct tape to build a shovel then dig out.  You have to show up for rollcall/breakfast etc, but all you need to do is go to the location then you can immediately leave again - e.g. for meal times/exercise/shower/rollcall you walk into the room then walk out again immediately and get back to digging your tunnel without any consequences.
Each prison is largely the same (apart from the odd "puzzle" one like the train) - there is not much variety and it gets boring fairly quickly. I like Dreamfall Chapters, but will you enjoy Dreamfall Chapters?
Some things to consider:
This is the third game in a series that started with The Longest Journey (2000) and continued in Dreamfall: The Longest Journey (2006).  The Longest Journey is a wonderful point-and-click adventure game classic: if you like adventure games and haven’t played it yet I highly suggest you do so.  Dreamfall (there’s no way around it) just isn’t as good.  This is not to say that it’s unplayable or that I didn’t enjoy it at all, but as a stand-alone game I wouldn’t whole-heartedly recommend it.
In order to really appreciate Chapters you don’t need to have played TLJ, but, unfortunately, I really think you do need to play the original Dreamfall first.  Among other things, Dreamfall ends on a cliffhanger and Chapters more-or-less picks up where it left off.
Chapters takes places in a rich game world revealed and developed over the course of the series.  This applies both to Stark, a vaguely cyberpunk version of our world set in the near future, and Arcadia, a fantasy world that’s the flipside of the coin—where magic rules rather than technology.
I think the legacy of TLJ and Dreamfall is both a blessing and a curse for the creators of Chapters.  As I said, they started off with a storied, well-developed setting; but, at the same time, Chapters needed to continue Dreamfall’s story—a story that had arrived at a critical moment where sinister forces are on the verge (we’re talking like seconds) of upsetting the balance/taking over the world/ripping everything apart.  Marcuria, the city we visit in Arcadia, is under military occupation and the invaders (who have their own interesting culture) want to stamp out magic and replace it with their steampunk technology (and the purpose of some of these machines is very suspect).  Meanwhile, in Stark, an entertainment device called the Dream Machine has become ubiquitous and people are using it to escape the troubles of reality and spend more and more time in a virtual dream world.  From the very beginning one feels that a dramatic climax is imminent.
Chapters is a story rich game (and it’s an interesting story), but sometimes story rich means gameplay poor.  The episodes where you have control over the main character and get to move around solving puzzles are unevenly interspersed between long conversations and cut scenes.  This is, to some extent, made up for by the fact that you’re sometimes given a chance to make choices which will affect what happens later in the game (Chapters sort of beats you over the head with “This choice will matter!” although there’s an option to turn those messages off).
So all-in-all, I think you’ll risk being lost or not invested enough in the characters if you play Chapters without playing Dreamfall and there are parts where the game is light on interactivity and heavy on dialogue and exposition, but the story is an interesting one and in other places gameplay and story are balanced enough to satisfy.

While it may not be a technological marvel at all times, Dreamfall Chapters continues the tradition of great writing, superb atmosphere and memorable characters that the series is known for. Can't wait to see how the story ends!

It is a shame that Steam only offers a binary choice for recommending a game, which means that it's not possible to distinguish between "a bit on the boring side" and "completely unplayable trash". This game is more on that former side. On a scale from 0 to 10 (where 0 is absolutely horrendous unplayable utterly broken, and 10 is one of the best and most enjoyable games I have played in my life), I would give this a 4. Because it falls just a bit under that "completely average" line, I have to give it a negative vote.
The major problem I have with this game is that the tasks and puzzles are simplistic, even trivial, and completely unimaginative and outright lazy. It's like no effort whatsoever was put into them, and they were slapped onto the game with no thought or inspiration or effort put into them.
What is worse, it seems that no playtesting whatsoever was done on some of the puzzles because, while trivial and unimaginative, some of them can still make you run around for an hour and just not find what you are looking for, for the simple reason that the game literally gives you zero hints of where you have to go or what you have to do. For example, one of the tasks is finding an NPC who is normally at a vending cart, but is not there anymore. No hints whatsoever are given where exactly you should be looking. You can run around the city for hours, looking in every single corner and every single place, and the NPC will be nowhere to be found. Then you look at an online guide and it turns out that you had to check a box behind the vending cart, which contains some receipt, and by taking the receipt that NPC suddenly appears at a location somewhere else in the city... a location you probably checked three times already. The NPC now just magically appears there after you take the receipt. That box is inconspicuous, and unless you happen to stumble across it by chance, chances are that you are going to miss it and waste hours in a wild goose chase. And the "solution" is completely nonsensical. (It may have a semblance of sense in terms of storytelling, but as a puzzle it's nonsensical, trivial, needlessly hard with no actual rewarding challenge, and just bad. It's simply a question of whether you happen to check that one box or not.)
And that's just one example.
The story is also trying really hard to be deep and immersive, but ends up being quite shallow, slow-paced (which isn't helped by the wild goose chase "puzzles" you have to "solve") and a bit boring.
At points I was tempted to just stop playing the game altogether (especially on that "puzzle" I described above). I don't find this game all that interesting. The story advances too slowly, and the "puzzles" are too trivial, lazy and uninteresting. There is no thought put into them at all.
That being said, it's not a horrible game. That's why I'm giving it a 4 out of 10, rather than somehing less.

A truly captivating story driven game that beautifully immerses the player into the lives of Kian and Zoe.
It starts off slow, running seemingly useless and boring errands, running from one side of the city to the other BUT it gets better.  It builds the foundations of each character so that the player gets a true understanding of what each character resembles. Reading the other reviews, I see that this alone caused many players to lose all hope in the game and give up after only just beginning Book 1. That's their loss.
Dreamfall chapters accomplishes something that many games cannot, to make unqiue, likeable characters. Sounds easy but it is rarely achieved. The choice factor in this game DOES MATTER. Sometimes its something silly, other times it can be the difference between your favourite character surviving or dying. It also strongly matters to the relationships between characters in the game which will further impact how the characters will interact with each other. Will they assist one another or choose not to. That is based on the players dialogue decisions.
Being such a long game, averaging around 20-30 hours for the first 4 Books it really draws out and explores everything that it can, without it seeming like a bland and boring story. The pace is just right.
SUMMARY
This is a beautiful adventure game with gorgeous visuals, logical and likeable characters, a stunning choice of music and a choice-consequence system that can advertently effect the future. Dreamfall Chapters clearly demonstrates that story driven games can still be masterpieces in todays gaming world.

GAME REVIEW TIME:
Okay, so, I'm sure you all know, or at least some of you know, how passionate I am about Darksiders 2.
That game, was a brilliant masterpiece of a creation. I must'v played through it at least 5 times.
Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 COMPLETELY matched up with it. I WOULD say it beat it, but I hold Darksiders 2 near and dear to my heart, I couldn't betray it like that.
Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is a GREAT Action/adventure game, with tons of different enemies, with different attack patterns, it forces you to adapt to your situation really quick, and I think that's what we need more in games.
I'm going to be comparing CLOS2 (castlevania: lords of shadow 2) To Darksiders 2, since it has a small bit of similarities. The problem with Darksiders 2, was that they threw the same enemy at you constantly, and it made the game a bit boring, not to mention memorizing all their attack patterns, and making the game a breeze. Not much of a challenge, in hindsight.
CASTLEVANIA THREW THAT OUT THE ♥♥♥♥ING WINDOW.
MOTHER ♥♥♥♥ING♥♥♥♥♥♥TONS OF DIFFERENT ENEMIES LEFT AND RIGHT EVERYWHERE
Everywhere you went there was a different enemy, and it really brings out that sense of impending doom thing they have going for it.
Like, 'oh i'll just go over here and grab tha-wait... no... no i won't. it's scary over there'
Granted, if you're skilled enough, you can defeat the enemies no problem, and grab whatever the hell you want, but that's not the point. The point I'm trying to make is, you never know what's going to be behind that corner, so it really makes you stop and think about your situation. Do I have enough health in case a huge ♥♥♥♥♥ shows up? Do I have enough healing items in case I get ♥♥♥♥ed over? THAT'S what makes the game fun, exciting, and fresh. It just throws new♥♥♥♥♥♥at you, it keeps it FRESH.
And the weapons you get, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ Your main weapon is called the "shadow whip" and it's basically, a whip that Dracula (main character) can summon whenever he wants, as it's made out of his own blood. The lore about the weapon says that people who get hit by it says it feels like "A thousand fangs piercing every inch of your body." Also, it hardens on impact... That's why it's able to hit people, and not just splooge all over the place.
Your secondary, or heavy weapon, is called the "chaos claws" These deal... MASSIVE amounts of damage, but they can't be used for long, as they require a chaos charge. you get a Chaos charge by absorbing blood orbs from enemies.
Your third weapon is called the "Void Sword" This is the same as the Chaos claws, except it doesn't hit as hard, AND with every blow you land, you get health back. So, basically, if you've played Darksiders 2, it's basically health steal.
And the Graphics... The Graphics, and the lighting technique are AMAZING. Everywhere you go is beautiful scenery, be it the modern city or Dracula's castle. The Characters models are amazing, as well. The art they chose for Dracula, and alucard, and all the other people you come in contact with is BRILLIANT.
And the best god damn part of this whole game? YOU DON'T EVEN NEED TO KNOW THE STORY! CLOS2 is technically part of the story that Castlevania was portraying in their earlier days of 2d sidescroller, but it doesn't match up with it.
It's almost a different timeline.
You know what? ♥♥♥♥ it. Castlevania beat Darksiders 2 in my list of all time favourites.
You had a good run Darksiders 2...
Seriously though, go buy this game. It's ♥♥♥♥ing great.

At first, I was a bit miffed by the fact that this game becomes anachronistic (
, Gabriel in the future), but the story ties it together nicely and it fits together with the in-game lore.
The game itself is played out across two worlds (the "mission" world and Gabriel's Castle). Both worlds are free-roam and you can backtrack as needed to explore or to get items previously missed.
Pros:
- Option in menu to turn off QTEs. This made the first game really annoying with the constant QTE prompts; now it's optional.

Cons:
