- Lots of backtracking (re-exploring and getting items from areas already explored).
- Modern setting sometimes feels un-Castlevania like.

Allow me to add to the chorus that says "The Metacritic Score is a lie."
This was a good game. Though it differs from the first. It is by that measure that I think its best compared.
+Graphical Presentation+
The first game had your character crossing an elaborate, Lord of the Rings like world with plenty of variety and set pieces. It was absolutely beautiful.
None of that beauty comes close to be realized here. Instead, what you get is an atmosphere...
...THAT ACTUALLY FEELS LIKE CASTLEVANIA!
There are many reviewers who will cry at the fact that the last game was prettier, but here, you are in a dark, moody castle with full control of your camera and dammit I just couldn't help but love how it actually felt like you were involved in a dark tale of vampires and demons, unlike the first. So between this and the first, its an apples to oranges comparision. In the end, the graphical presentation gives you that SoTN feel that the first game was missing (the sexy mountaintops of LoS1 be darned).
+Story (Spoiler Free)+
The first game was about losing faith. The second game is about redemption. Obviously. What else is new? What's important here is characterization and voice acting delivery. To which it does an absolutely fantastic job of delivering. Though, in my view, its story is not as heavy as the first, given that every single chapter in LoS1 had Captain Picarde himself explaining what the heck is going on in detail. We really could've used that narration to explain some of the strange stuff having in this castle-city. Like what the heck is a castle doing here in the first place? That was a head-trip, but hey, its Dracula; his castle be constantly respawning I guess.
So here's what I recommend you do before jumping in here: 1) Play the first game first (or read its cliff-notes). 2) Play Mirror of Fate (or read its cliff-notes) . They frequently make references to the first game and the hand-held tie-in so if you skip these steps then expect a confusing plot.
Given that I didn't skip these steps, I found LoS2 to make for a pretty good story. Certainly has more heart than most games these days. It's like a DMC that you can take seriously.
+Gameplay+
Here is the one place where I can say without a doubt that it delivers better than the first game. You see, LoS2 is easier than the first, for all the RIGHT reasons.
The first had some Nintendo-hard bulls*** issues holding it back that have been fixed. For one, you have more options given the three weapons to choose from. The lame Light and Dark Magic system is replaced by an Ice Weapon and Fire Weapon.  In the first game, you only switched to Light to heal on occasion and that was it, as you were constantly struggling to fill up the focus meter to fuel your heals. Dark magic was never used. It was nothing more than an unimportant DPS buff.
Here, the replacements to the old magic honestly feels different enough for you to want to mix it up, what with the fire ability being able to break enemy shields and blocking (in addition to doing more DPS), and the ice sword having some mean crowd control abilities (in addition to healing you). Filling up the focus meter is much faster and easier so you can continue to fuel these things without fear, and with the camera in your control, you just won't feel as frustrated as before.
The side items and powers are must more useful as well, and a power you get later on adds a whole new dimension to to your defensive options. Overall, I'd say LoS1 comes no where CLOSE to being a steller action game in the gameplay department. It was servicable and that was it. Here, we actually have a system that's as fun as God of War.  YOU FEEL LIKE YOU'RE GOD-DAMNED DRACULA, AND NO ONE CAN F*** WITH YOU! You ARE the final boss of over 30 games, and nothing can stop you, only slow you down.
Hell yeah.
About the only thing relatively weak are the stealth sections, which make sense only at the start of the game...how is it that you're a threat to Satan, but these red guys can blow your♥♥♥♥♥away doing 9999 damage per shot? I need Captain Picarde to explain. Fortunately, such sections are mercifully short and easy.
There are also fewer puzzles than the first game. But who cares?
+Overall+
Overall I give this game a 7.9/10. Its not the greatest thing since Bayonetta but taken as a whole, the Lord of Shadows series offers the best story in the action game genre today...taken as a whole.  View Lord of Shadows 1 and 2 as one really long epic and you're pretty much doing it right. When the dust clears, you'll likely give this game a worthy playthrough on New Game + and have fun with it as well.

Very cool idea, very boring execution.
This feels like it was supposed to be "Civ in space." In reality, it's not even close. This isn't even Civ lite. The idea is cool. Instead of cities, you have planets. You send your eponymous starships on missions to help the residents of various planets in order to win them over to your side.
The glaring problems:
You get one fleet. The game is built around only having one fleet, so it kinda works. Just doesn't make any sense. Why would a space-faring civilization artificially limit themselves to a single fleet of eight warships? If this game didn't have Sid Meier's name on it, I wouldn't mention this. If it wasn't obviously meant to be viewed as "Civ in space," I wouldn't mention it. Want Civ in space? Go play the "Final Frontier" mod from Civ 4's Beyond the Sword expansion.
Diplomacy is stupid. It's a ridiculously stripped-down version of the Diplomacy mechanics from Civ. You're always either at war or have a peace treaty with every other federation. If you're not at war, you can't move onto one of their planets. You must first declare war (using the diplomacy menue), then the move will be allowed. Here's the stupid part. Try this:
1. Declare war.
2. Conquer one planet belonging to enemy faction.
3. Move to second planet belonging to same enemy.
4. Accept bribe.
5. War is over. "Enemy" will not attack you on their turn.
6. Repeat.
Battle AI is stupid. Enemy ships tend to stay in groups of at least two ships, making them very susceptible to torpedo attacks. Even if this wasn't the case, the AI hardly ever uses torpedos or stealth, making your opponents boringly easy to dominate.
Conquest is the entire game. There are apparently other victory conditions but I can't see why you'd pursue them, since this is a game about spaceships fighting each other for control of planets.
Battle tactics quickly become about filling the map with as many torpedos as possible to make sure you take out enemy ships without having to get lucky. You could certainly swarm the enemy with fighters instead, or pump the crap out of your plasma cannons and stealth units, getting in close for the kill. The point is: any "tactic" you choose simply works. The AI provides no challenge whatsoever.
I'll admit that some of these things might be the result of me only playing on "Normal" difficulty. I'm going to go try it again on hard but I'm not hopeful that I will meet a much greater challenge or that I won't be able to loop a war with one opposing faction at a time.
TL;DR
After playing Doom 3 or Colonial Marines, go back and play Wolf3d or Catacomb Abyss. Starships feels like a 1991 PC game that should by now have 4 sequels, each one a bit more complicated than the last (like Civilization). In reality, it just feels undeveloped. Not unpolished or incomplete; just featureless and bland.
It feels like unfinished product.
The game got quite repetitive after only about an hour. There's nothing really compelling here to make this game worth much to me.

Sid Meier's Starships isn't a bad game, but it isn't a particularly good game either.  It certainly isn't worth the $15 asking price.  The gameplay is incredibly shallow, and although the missions appear to be randomized, each game feels more or less the same because there are only a few types of missions.  Faction and leader choice don't make much of a difference which further harms replayability.  Games can be completed within as little as one hour, and I don't think many people will feel compelled to play through the game more than a couple of times.
There is very little ship customization--all you can do is add new ships and increase stats.  Missions are so basic that strategy is almost non-existent.  The AI is horrible; I once watched an AI controlled ship fire a torpedo into a planet in a vain effort to hit one of my ships that was behind it.  Although given how little depth there is to the game, I don't know what could be reasonably expected of the AI.  You can use asteroids for cover (which can be bypassed by certain upgrades and torpedoes), and there are warps placed around the map.  Ships entering a warp are randomly sent to another warp; strategy is somewhat limited because of this.
Starships is a streamlined mobile game and it shows.  In addition to the lack of depth, it is not well optimized for PC.  The fullscreen option is weird and the game won't cover the task bar (you need to set the taskbar to auto hide in order to get real fullscreen).  Some of the text is also very hard to read, and there are no options for graphics settings.
I got Starships in a bundle and I don't regret playing it, but don't go out of your way to buy it or spend much on it.

When I first played this game, I wondered why it received such low reviews.  Now I know.  While the basic game mechanics are really a lot of fun, the late game combat gets so tedious and boring that I dread when enemies attack me.  Sure, I know I can beat them, after a 45 minute battle of them running away while I chase them down, one by one.
This game would've been better with a 3 or 4 ship maximum (currently 8).  Also, combat turns are slow and tedious.  Movement and attacks are about half as fast as they should be.  When you get an extra movement action and want to spend it on using the impulse action twice (move 1 extra space), there is no hot key, so you have to click the icon, select a location, click the icon, select a location.  It may not seem like much, but when chasing down enemies, and you've got a full fleet of 8 ships and something like 10 fighter ships (or whatever the max is), it adds a minute or two to every turn.
The animations for attacks are also really slow.  It's supposed to be a laser, but you have to watch it for ups of 5 seconds as it travels through space and hits the enemy ship.
The combat seemed like it was going to be fun, but it just burns my brain at this point.  I'm scared that the enemy will attack me, cause it'll be soooo boring.
If they would fix that, I'd highly recommend this game.

In the long line of Sid Meier sticking his name into game titles comes "Sid Meier's Starships," a hexigrid turn based galactic strategy in the vein of Civilization. The twist here is there are planets to join your galactic federation and turn based starship battles with your armada against an opponents.  Building your armada and competing in battles is by far the most fun of the game. I'd say it is the real game and everything else is just fluff. You can buy vessels, then upgrade engines, shields, armor, lasers, cannons, torpedoes, scanners, stealth and fighters.
The world is never enough and the universe is yours to conquer, purify or unify. There are several victory states such as domination, population, building wonders or scoring the top tier of a few science fields. While its nice to have all these ways to win, it feels like the game is geared toward conquering the galaxy. There's an entire space battle system in place and its silly to overlook it and play diplomatic. The only real way to ensure that I'll have a science or wonder victory is to make that the only type of victory allowed.
Battles take place on a hexigrid map, which in a way is illogical since space has a Z axis, but whatever. You can make use of heavy asteroids, planets and moons as cover. In a way its laughable that planets are as wide as four vessels. Smaller asteroids give less cover, but you're still prone to attack, but take less damage.
If a vessel is hiding behind cover, you can fire a limited amount of torpedoes that will breach cover. The only catch is you need to detonate the torpedo one turn later, so that gives your foes a chance to move. You get to see your torpedo fly and then push the button to make it explode. Its a great dynamic to have. Even when I'm out of range, I'm firing torpedoes just to do something. Torpedoes are limited to the number you have upgraded on that star ship.
Each ship gets a turn with a movement and an action in either order. During an action it depends what the vessel has upgraded. You can attack, impulse an extra move space, cloak hide, scan for cloaked vessels and release ships. If you chose to move, you can attack as you move you move between two cover points, but I never felt a need to get that complicated. Releasing ships adds a small cluster of fighters with long range movement, little health and no shields.
Vessels have shields, so if your weapon's attack power is less than the shield, its ineffective. Once shields are down, then you can do some big damage. The armor rating amounts to hit points. The more upgrades you have to a ship, the slower it moves, so you'll need to upgrade engines. Then there's stealth that conceals a ship unless an enemy is near it and upgraded scanners will compensate for finding stealth enemies. Its a good dichotomy.
Other notable features on a map include anomalies that when you fly into them, you appear out of a different one. Its good for speeding things along if there's one ship left, but your comrades are across the map. Even if you pop out in a random location, its still closer and a chance to flank enemies.
Battles have a victory condition, a map condition and a card. Most of the time you earn victory by annihilating the opposition. Other times its defend an outpost, escort a vessel to an outpost, guard warp gates, destroy a single vessel or get a ship of yours into a warp gate. The maps feel generated and the map conditions are things like enemy torpedoes are undetectable, more asteroids, less asteroids, shields are less effective. It adds some diversity to the battles. Then there are the cards which feel forgotten about. You get one or so cards during each battle and its a gamble when you use them. I wish I could say more, but in seven hours of playing, I never made use of them beyond a curiosity.
The idea of the game is that your entire armada flies from planet to planet. After these battles win or lose, you keep all your ships, but you need to repair them for the damage that they've taken. So a major loss requires you to repair everything. Well if your armada wrecks the armada of a competitor that leaves that same competitor open for more attacks on the same turn. Blood thirsty players like myself will keep pushing through, but to prevent the entire universal conquest on a single turn, your crew's efficiency goes down with each battle. Once its as low as it gets, you're forced to take a shore leave and end your turn.
Like a lot of these hexigrid games, you're competing and aligning with other competitors. You start the game by visiting planets, gaining their support which seems rather easy. Just win a battle and you're halfway there! Take a shore leave on a planet that you have 50% devotion with and you can gain an extra 25%. Some planets end up contested where four competitors can have a stake in it.
Once you've taken quarter of a planet you can spend food to plant cities; I'm sure that's how it works. Cities increase workers I guess. I was never too sure. The game just told me to build cities, so I did.
From there there are upgrades to a planet. Upgrades cost metal and give you more resources across various types that never felt of any consequence. Other planet upgrades include planetary defense craft, giving you a home field advantage with an extra vessel if an enemy ever attacks. Constructing a warp gate can bring your fleet to a planet under attack.
Spend science points on technology upgrades that will boost armada stats by 25% of a single category. Plenty of planets will reward you with a technology of your choosing. Even if you are about to enter a battle with someone, you can negotiate and they will give you technology or food to leave the planet. If you agree, that's some sort of a peace treaty right there. Other times if you have a 95% chance of winning, the game lets you have the planet without a fight.
It feels like I managed the bare minimum of micromanagement and got away with it. Rather than clicking on each planet to build this or that, I just clicked on one and upgraded until I was broke. There is an information icon to click on that will advise you what you should do, but it should just be on the screen without me having to click something. Perhaps a hide button would be better for players that want to play it their own way. Even with no guide and little to no tutorials I still managed to get through it.
When you start a new game, you select map size, up to six opponents, difficulty and victories. Enormous still felt small, but I suppose on normal took me four hours to conquer the galaxy while easy took only three. Easy mode is laughable. My first time playing, none of my vessels were ever damaged, let alone destroyed. Its a good way to get your feet wet, but about an hour in, there was no challenge. Normal felt like a good challenge, but there are still two difficulties.
You have a selection between twenty-four characters, eight within each of the three motivations for supremacy, harmony and purity. Each one has their own stat boost. One character has a 25% better this or that. Sometimes less cost, other times more of whatever. Some start with an extra vessel.
I feel less stress and more joy playing this game than I do with Civilization games. Those other games feel like there's always a cold war and you need to prepare before the invaders come, while I feel like here I have my destiny in my own hands. I'm smart enough to win battles even when the game tells me that I have a 25% chance of winning. Its also a small game. When other publisher and developer are 4 GB large, this one fits on a CD at 650 MB. Must be all that blank space rather than terrain.

It's essentially a mobile game ported to PC and an offshoot of Civilization:Beyond Earth. From the settings, over the game setup down to the entire gameplay concept the game feels very light in terms of substance. You control a fleet and send it around the map to take over planets via tactical combat. You develop planets and do research. There is diplomacy, a market system and different victory conditions.
You may now think:
Unfortunately, since it's a mobile port, the game lacks in all mentioned aspects.
The AI in tactical combat is not very clever and can be easily outmaneuvered, leading to repetitive combat making it, due to the lack of auto-combat, appearing like a chore after a while since scenarios differ very little. This cannot be offset at any time by the fact that you can customize your ships even though even that feels a little bland as it's more or less pushing weapons and speed to the maximum of level of 8 for each ship. Your ships also do not get destroyed per se but only suffer from repairable damage and based on random chance may also level up.
Planet development is based on four resources (metal, food, research and cash). Each resource has a resort function, food allows you to spam cities which in return allow higher production of all resources, metal allows you to build a select few different buildings up to an amount of 8. Research allows you to tech certain aspects of your ship up to a level of 6 while cash is solely used to upgrade different modules of your ships whereas ship class is almost meaningless as each ship has exact the same amount and type of modules.
The diplomacy system is as deep as billboard and the market system at some point a pain to use due to static and low exchange rates.
Even though overall gameplay can be further tweaked through selection of affinities, victory types, difficulty level, map size and number of opponents I find its replayability degrading quickly. You are in fact better off playing a better space combat sim or just BE(RT).
Overall the game can be quickly summarized and in terms of essentially being a mobile game: its gameplay depth and replayability is far lower than say Fallout Shelter is and that one, despite also being a different genre, is free.
I don't expect much depth from a low-budget PC game but there are better choices for 14.99 €. I suggest not to buy it outside special sales events at a maximum of 7.49 €. If you are a hardcore TBS player I would skip it really unless you really feel the need to unlock those traits for BE(RT).
Firaxis can do better but this game is really not adding anything positive to the genre, at least not on PC.

Congo is a promising looking early access game. It's a top-down adventure/horror co-op survival game. You (and your "friends") find yourself in the middle of a jungle at night, with bloodthirsty, gorilla looking demons, lurking and growling in the shadows. There is no health bars or anything, if you get jumped, your done ... so get a couple friends, that can resurrect you, if needed, and get the party started!
There are 3 kind of ammo you gather in the jungle and quite a few weapons to use it with -  there are no names, but you can recognize your standard AK-47 , SMG, pistol and shotgun. Some weapons you can use with one hand, while holding your torch, other weapons have a flashlight on them. When you open a weapon box, the weapons kinda fly out of it, sometimes to an unreachable place, sometimes right into the hands of your friends, so be positioned and ready to snatch them fast ;) You always have your trusty machete with you from the start, in case that you prefer some hand to hand combat - it chops down demons quite effectively. There are some other goodies spread around the map as well - the revive "needle", a compass ( I have not found a map yet) to somewhat help you with orientation. The pliers and fuel canisters you need for the mission are also randomly scattered around. While carrying the canister, you're defenseless and die in one hit ( or well one "jump up" ), so co-op is highly recommended to ease the situation, as dropping the canister to pull out your weapon sometimes cannot be done fast enough!
The game uses Unreal engine, the graphics are OK, nothing special, but get the job done. The dense vegetation sometimes get in the way of your overhead camera, so using the road is always better. The lighting effects from the torch and the flashlight are reasonable.
I've only encountered one type of enemy so far - the bloodthirsty gorilla demons, that are not always the brightest, but definitely can be sneaky and keep you on your toes. The fighting / shooting mechanics / animations could be better, but it's not terrible in any stretch of the imagination, and get the job done. There is no music, and frankly I haven't noticed the need for it - the crickets in the background and the subtle growling from the demons, are atmospheric enough ;) The sounds effects are reasonable as well, nothing special and nothing to complain about.
All in all, even in this early access the game is working as expected and is an enjoyable experience (especially in co-op :p)
TL:DR you can check my solo gameplay video and get an overview of the game, (co-op videos will be coming soon™)

Having had a single and multiplayer experience, I'd have to say that Innocent Devils have managed to create a game that definitely requires team work, communication and organisation! Single player is like playing Permadeath, so it is ill advised, although MIGHT suggest room for some AI? Even one...

Some "Early Access" issues are present. THE GREAT
If you own Half Life already (Which you do, because you are a GOOD boy who bought Half Life when it came out) then this mod is free and doesn't cost you anything.
THE UGLY
This was based off the Half Life engine. That is fine. Using the same enemies, weapons and skins is less so. I would have liked to see a little more change with the weapons, the enemies, or even the skins. Sadly, most of these are just copy and pasted. The only encounter with a friend in this game is a scientist who claims to know what you want, opens a crate which contains a medkit and presses a button which allows you access to the next level. While this may have been a nice idea on paper, glitchy AI prevent you from moving too quickly, which disrupts the flow. You can open this crate and push the button faster than he can, making him redundant. And when he talks, he talks in text form. No problems here, except it is unpunctuated and misspelled. This is lazy. And then the boss. The Nihilanth plus a barnacle is NOT a good boss idea. The boss fight is a cheap idea. It scatters your weapons around the (Small) arena, drops a snark in with you and has a whole lot of ammo in a metal container which provides no escape route when cornered. And after beating him, a black screen and the entire game crashing sours the experience.

I do not enjoy saying that this mod is bad. I've actually had a bit of fun with it, but framerate issues and a lack of direction just makes this experience not worthwhile. Sure, it's only two levels and it's free, so there's not too much to complain about, but it feels like a waste of potential. And that really is a shame. Red Faction 2 is a significant step down from the first game for several reasons, though it is an enjoyable FPS on it's own. I bought the Red Faction bundle during the steam sale and I decided to play the first two again before I replayed Guerilla and then got stuck into Armageddon. Playing it right after the first game definitely highlighted the drop in quality for me.
My feelings for this game are as mixed as the reviews it's had so far, so I'll list the pro's and con's and let you decide for yourself.
PROS:
- Fun gameplay, the main reason I decided to recommend it. Once you get into the game, it is an undeniably fun sci-fi FPS.
- Dual-wielding pistols, machine pistols and nano-machine pistols was a nice touch, although you never actually do that until you get the NMP near the end of the game, or in multiplayer.
- Ammo animations. Instead of just a number counting down as you fire, there are bullets/grenades rapidly sliding down next to the number, and back up when you reload. Although this does not affect the gameplay in any way, it does look cool.
- Bot matches. If you don't have anybody to verse in multiplayer, you can start bot matches with up to four enemy bots in a variety of new locations. The kicker is that you can create your own four unique bots, with their own names and which bodies they have, and after each match each bot gets a few points for you to use upgrading its accuracy, toughness, speed and damage, so that each bot match is slightly more difficult than then one before. This isn't really noticeable until you've played about ten or so bot matches and then create new bots only to realise how weak they are in comparison. This does help you get better at multiplayer matches.
- Rail Driver. Instead of showing a heat-signature outline with the RD scope, you get pulsing concentric circles, representing the enemy heartbeat. While it's actually more difficult to use these to find the enemy than large orange outlines, I really love the idea behind it, so this is a pro for me.
- MOLOV. The commander of your squad, Molov is voiced by none other than Lance Henrikson, who does a fantastic job and is a truly commanding personality.
- SHRIKE. The mad pilot of your squad, Shrike is voiced by Jason Statham, and I'm pretty sure he enjoyed voicing Shrike. It's just a shame that Shrike didn't have a larger role.
CONS:
- The biggest con is definitely the almost total lack of geomod destruction that made the first game so original and so fun. You can destroy certain walls in certain parts of the game, but most buildings and all of the scenery is otherwise indestructible.
- REPTA. The heavy-weapons member of your squad, Repta is at least as annoying as Rico from Killzone, with the same irritating 'macho' voice.
- TANGIER. The stealth soldier of your squad, Tangier's only purpose in the game seems to be flirtatious dialogue with a breathy voice. This isn't a con because it's sexist, but because it's really, really annoying.
- Short campaign. This campaign is definitely shorter than the first game. It took me 9 1/2 hours to play the first Red Faction and less than 9 to play the second. That may seem like a really small difference, but it was only that long because of the following two things:
- Game divided into missions without the auto-save feature of the first game. If you reach a hard part of the game, you cannot save just before hand, and if you die than you will have to replay the entire level again to reach that point. On hard difficulty and in areas without medkits, this can be frequent. This extends the playtime considerably. What makes this doubly annoying is:
- Unskippable cutscenes. That's right, you cannot skip the cutscenes. Normally I enjoy watching the cutscenes, but when you're watching them for the fourth time and they do nothing more than show you the area and a bunch of soldiers waiting, it gets aggravating. With 11 missions, divided into numerous levels, almost all with their own cutscene about half a minute long, this becomes so frustrating that I have quit the game a few times because I couldn't stand to watch the same clip one more time. Playing the game on Hard mode, where you can expect to die about ten times in most of the boss fights, this has meant that I was stuck on one boss for several days. In total I have spent at least half an hour watching the same cutscenes over and over, and the same again for having to replay the same levels because I died near the end, which I consider to be a rather dishonest way of adding to the runtime of the game. These would be much less of a problem if they had also been in the first game, which they weren't, which just makes their inclusion baffling. On Normal difficulty, this game takes 6-7 hours, and on easy it takes 4-5. It takes longer if you (as I did) spend a while on each level trying to ferret out the hidden bonus objectives.
All in all, it's a game worth playing, although more frustrating on Hard than the first one was on Impossible difficulty, with the most annoying parts of it only coming into play on Hard. A significant step down from the first game.

Ouch. What a disappointment. This is not only a downgrade compared to the first game, but it's a radically different kind of game whatsoever. Not that I have a problem with something different, but when the first game was already quite original and interesting, sacrificing that in the name of dumb, macho straightforward action with a laughable storyline and unappealing characters. The level design ranges from frustratingly confusing to infuriatingly linear "Call of Duty" style, complete with piles of rubble conveniently blocking the paths you can't follow. What's worse is that the game boats is Geomod feature, but makes poor use of it -- you can never know when you're allowed to blast your way through a door or wall, or just patiently look for another way around it. And really, when you have rockets and grenades that can punch massive holes in regular walls, not being able to walk through a simple locked door is pretty insulting.
If there is something that could salvage this game is the weapons, which are pretty nice and diverse, but weapons alone don't make a good game. The bad level design and arbitrary variations of difficulty along the way work against the fun constantly. But what utterly killed the experience are the unskippable cutscenes. Now, the first Red Faction also had those, but you could save the game anytime and anywhere, so you could conveniently save after one of those. But here, you're not allowed to save manually, and you can only restart between level transitions; and some of them have some extremely long and boring cutscenes at the immediate start, especially the tough boss battles. I have no problem with a tough boss, but when I'm forced to idly stare at the screen for 20-30 seconds to watch a cutscene I have already watched, and which adds no information at all about the game, that drives me nuts.
Overall, it's a huge wasted potential: it's not very fun, it's very ugly and boring to look at, and it doesn't follow the original game at all. If you really expected something to carry on the experience of Red Faction, abandon all hope.

I loved the hell out of the first Lords of Shadow, and I enjoyed this game as well. However, it's not without its share of problems.
First and foremost, there's the setting. I didn't mind the fact that a significant portion of the game was set in the near future, but the open nature of the environments (both the castle and the city) seemed to sap the creative element from their design. Yes, it's cool that all of it links together, but that feeling of exploring strange new landscapes with all their weird quirks has been completely sacrificed. I get that it works with the plot, but I feel like the game would have benefited from having a level structure like the first.
Speaking of plot, there's the second problem. The story in LoS2 doesn't stack up to the first game at all, opting to go with a campier plot more reminscent of other Castlevania games than the original Lords of Shadow. While this isn't inherently a bad thing (I love Castlevania as a series, cheese and all), there's a massive plot hole introduced at the beginning of the game that is never resolved. Dracula was defeated at the end of Mirror of Fate, but apparently rose up again at some point between that game and this one. This is entirely glossed over in the main narrative and only offhandedly mentioned in Alucard's lore entry. I might be expecting too much out of the story of a Castlevania game, but it bothers me nonetheless given the detail and work put into the first game.
Then there's the stealth sections. Oh god, the stealth sections. For the most part it's not too bad; there is one enemy type that requires you to go around instead of confronting directly. These sections are mostly just mild hiccups in the pacing (which also isn't quite as good as the first game), but the final one is absolutely one of the worst segments I've had the displeasure of playing through. Not only is this segment immensly frustrating, but you battle the thing you were sneaking around immediately afterwards; no new weapon, no new powers, no upgrades whatsoever. You just fight it straight away, essentially rendering all the work you just did completely pointless.
Fortunately, it's not all bad. The combat is a ton of fun, giving you three different weapons with distinct features and fighting styles. It also looks fantastic; though I disparaged the nature of the new environments earlier, I can't deny the level of detail put into the city and Dracula's castle. The creatures and characters all look great too, from the detailed facial animations of the humanoids to Satan's grotesque abominations. Voice acting is solid; the actors did a good job delivering the lukewarm script in a believable way.
All in all, Lords of Shadow 2 is a solid action game with a few flaws. Go into it expecting more of a Devil May Cry experience than a Lords of Shadow 1 experience and I think you'll be able to derive more enjoyment from it that way.

I... lack the words to describe this game, mainly because I don't even understand what it's trying to be.
If you wish to enjoy this game... de-attach yourself from the first Lords of Shadow entirely. Picture this as a fan-made sequel. Mirror of Fate is not even worth describing, mind you, as it's essentially the same confusing thing as this one, but forced to play as a side-scroller, limited to 2 directions.
I'd really like to be able to speak to the lead developers for this one. Lords of Shadow 2 abandons the soul of Lords of Shadow, just like Mirror of Fate did, and ends up becoming a clusterfudge of bent, choppy lore, combined with teasingly sexy graphics, expanded (though... intriguingly empty and uninteresting) mechanics, and bucketloads of loopholes, empty holes and nonsensical progression (gameplay-wise) and evolution (lore-wise). Since the moment you start to walk the streets as a worn-out Dracula, you realize this game had potential for greatness, but it fell short. A few minutes later, you notice the progression of events lacks sense, and it feels (and probably is) it's due to content being taken out. The game shows you, at all times, that the devs couldn't make up their minds on what they wanted to do with the darn sequels - and Mirror of Fate shows it even better than this one.
All I can say to describe what I feel is that this game is a sequel to Mirror of Fate and Mirror of Fate only. Lords of Shadow 2 and Mirror of Fate are two games that I find unworthy of being called "sequels" to Castlevania: Lords of Shadow. They are a disgrace and, sadly, a huge disappointment. So much potential gone to waste.

The stealth sections are very annoying, as most would say. Quite disposable, and shouldn't have been part of the game. More focus on puzzles would have been appreciated, instead.
Another big complaint is the city over the castle... the apocalyptic castle/moderncity is rather unique, and imho, still beautiful. At some parts it feels a little like the modern parts of the city desecrate the castle, but I think that's intentional, too.
COMPLAINTS:
You cannot play this without a controller. None of the keys are coreographed properly for quicktime, skill use or anything else (X, Y, A, B on EVERYTHING) You can re-map the keys and go through it (mostly) fine... with one, notable and game-shattering problem: navigating the skills menu. Unless it gives you a pop-up, you just can't, and that's a deal-breaker for PC support.

Oh my gosh, this game is so cool! This was one of the first games I played on my own Xbox 360, and I got pretty far in it. Playing it now, I was able to not only relive memories, but remember why I loved this game so much. It's so good, and it feels good playing it.
You drive in races and learn to master your car, building up a meter by drifting and drafting and such. You can then use this meter to create destruction in an effort to destroy your rivals and take the lead. You can also use this ability to create shortcuts and alternate routes for yourself. Not only is it satisfying taking down a bunch of rivals in the course, but it also makes being ahead the most intense and nerve wracking thing; you would have drivers behind you who want your position, and can take it at any time by force if you're not careful.
The whole thing is set like a tv show, with "episodes" featuring several events each. This adds to a feeling of you being an action hero or movie star; the whole thing made me feel like a badass. I've said it to friends before and I'll say it on this review; this game is amazing!
No steam achievements, but there are in-game ones which add decals to your car, which I think is a clever addition. It feels like battle scars or what you would see on the uniform of a seasoned veteran; your progress is literal and visual.
Graphics wise, I think it looks pretty cool considering this was 2010. Some people have a problem with the frames not being 60 FPS, but I think it just makes it feel even more movie-like with the way that it is! The soundtrack is also incredible as well, and I think it's dynamic to events on the track as well.
All in all, Split/Second is an absolute blast to play. Worth the full price for sure!

Starbound is a beautiful game, in terms of its visual quality, music and general philosophy.
It borrows a lot of elements from Terraria as well as a thing or two from Stardew Valley, but
not in a way where it feels like workmanlike mimicry; it takes these elements and enriches them
with its own narrative and style.
It's hard to talk about Starbound without drawing obvious comparisons with Terraria, as that is no
doubt the biggest influence at play here. So, rather than talking about how those two games are similar, it's worth mentioning what Starbound does differently and how it is effective on its own merits.
Starbound takes the basic skeletal structure of a 2d Crafting/Survival game and leans more towards a competently told story along with some excellent world-building, which blatant time and effort went into. As a young graduate of the Terrene Protectorate, a peacekeeping authority of harmony and unity, the character you play is plunged into a desperate escape due to a terrifying threat which consumes planet earth in the blink of an eye. Without giving away too many plot details, the main story focuses on how the protagonist overcomes a world-consuming beast named 'The Ruin'. And although its by-the-numbers in terms of its plot and exposition, the main quest is designed in a way which forces exploration upon the player, which gives the game many great opportunities to show off its splendid wonders and dynamic cultures.
Base-Building and Farming are highly enjoyable. There are a vast array of resources available and blueprints for different interior designs are dotted out across the universe for you to find. The most impressive thing about the exploration in Starbound is that you have your own ship. The navigation system on the ship shows an expansive map of different solar systems, all with their own planets, ships, astral anomalies and so forth, which are randomly generated and fully explorable. The level of detail and sheer volume of content really makes you feel like this game is bursting through its seams with activity and purpose. The fact that you have your own ship, traversing the galaxy, makes it all seem believable.
There are a few negatives, but in the grand scheme of things, they're fairly inconsequential.
The mech suit upgrades were fairly hard to come by, and this subsequently made the side-quests
related to your mech a bit choppy, as some quests were fairly difficult without decent suit upgrades. The act of trying to hire crew members for your ship is monotonous. You have to find random colonies and do tedious side quests until one of them offers to work for you. It feels unrefined and arbitrary, but the small inconvenience of it makes having a diverse, multi-race crew who all hold different beliefs and have different roles aboard your ship makes the tedium worthwhile.
Overall, there isn't really much more to say about Starbound. The animation and look of it is fantastic, the music is wonderfully composed and its streamlined main quest along with the many procedural side-quests are a welcome addition. The boss fights are well thought out and challenging (The Big Ape fight being a particular stand out moment), and to top it all off, 11.99 isn't a bad price at all. I've already got just over 50 hours out of this (at the time of this review) and I feel there is still much to do. Starbound should be an essential buy for any Terraria fans out there, and I'd wager that a lot of Stardew Valley fans would also get quite a lot out of this.

Congo is a top-down Co-op Action horror survival game where you have to complete objectives while fending-off hordes of "demons".
Along the way you will need to gather resources such as weapons, ammunition, revive kits, compasses, maps ? and so on and so forth.
If you ignore the boxes of resources you'll quickly find yourself either dead from a severe case of lack of bullets or that you can not proceed because you forgot to pick up a pair of pliers or a canister of gas.
From my time with the game i can tell you its much more fun with friends then in single player (just make sure your friends can shoot straight...)
So, the best recipe is to gather a few mates grab a pizza and have a go at it.
The boxes containing resources are randomly generated adding a bit of replay value... so you will not know where to get X tool or Y weapon.
The "something is coming" feeling is well felt mostly because of the sound-work, the tropical white-noise plus the vegetation displacement sound effects are done very well and relay the intended message to the player.
The graphics are decent for a game of this price, delivering on what it's suppose to while being nothing special. The animations are "off" if you ask me but i hope this aspect gets some attention during the early access stage.
There are no checkpoints which i found, so if you mess-up and die you get punished for it and have to begin from the start of the mission. I detest the current hand-holding trend so this is a big plus for me.
The camera did play a few tricks on me but considering this is early access i expect this to be resolved by launch. Camera can always be tricky in these top-down games....not my favorite.
I do hope they add more levels, more objectives and a much larger variety of enemies to fight, the monkeys do get boring after a short while.
In my opinion it looks decent for a Early Access Tittle, much better then many others that come along asking much higher prices.
I did not run into any game-breaking bugs, just a slight pop-in here and a slight stutter there.
I did not play a ton of the game so take all information given here with a grain of salt and as always judge for yourselves if this tittle is worth your time and money.

Rating: 6/10
Overview: Run and Gun First Person Shooter
The Good:
+ The game has a lot of weapon variety, most weapons have a primary and secondary function
+ The game has a lot of gameplay variety. Some levels feature traditional FPS gameplay, other levels have you riding a vehicle blowing things up.
+ Short game, this is good because you want it to end quickly.
The Average:
The level design is all over the place. It ranges from boring, uninspired to sometimes confusing.
The game has a lot of level destruction which is really cool except the game doesn't do a good job of telling you which walls can be destroyed and which can't. Only certain walls/objects can be destroyed which sometimes makes for a frustrating experience. Whenever I got stuck in a level I began to blindly fire rockets/grenades at all the walls around me in the hopes that one would get destroyed and reveal a path. It's a cool feature but one that wasn't executed as well as it should have been mostly because of the technological limits at the time.
Graphically it looks worse in some areas than the first game.
The Bad
- The story, characters and dialogue are bland, boring and very forgettable. It was hard to like any of the characters, the story made no sense and I couldn't care less about what was going on, I just wanted it to end.
- The first game takes place on mars and featured some varied and unique environments which made this game all the more disappointing when it takes place on earth and most of the levels feature bland office spaces or large empty areas filled with bullet sponge enemies.

- Unskipable cut scenes especially placed before frustrating boss battles. The game is pretty easy (on medium settings) but the bosses are basically bullet sponges.
- Lack of quick save/quick load
- Terrible 360 default controls: Either I experienced a bug or the person who did the default controller controls was tripping out on acid. Pushing the right joystick left made me walk forward, right joystick up made me walk backwards, etc. nothing made sense. Stick to keyboard and mouse.
Conclusion:
Aren't sequels suppose to be better? This game takes a large step backwards. After the first Red Faction game the series had real potential to be really good. The first Red Faction reminded me of Half Life in its linear level design and pacing, this game reminds me of quick cash in and a poorly made one at that.

The Longest Journey and its sequel Dreamfall are some of my favorite games.  Dreamfall Chapters continues the rich lore and storyworld first established in its predecessors and strives to provide that same level of storycraft and immersion.
That said, I am not sure if a newbie to the franchise would get much out of Chapters.  So much of it, including the characters and settings, are direct continuations of Dreamfall (and The Longest Journey) that I don't think it would be very "new user friendly".
Also, I would say it is more helpful to think of this as an interactive story or comic book on par with Telltale Game's offerings rather than a full-on video game.  In that sense, Chapters is a good successor to the point and click adventure, but it is much different than most other games today.  People looking for continuous action, open world exploration, or a handholding tutorial will be disappointed greatly as the game does one thing--narrative--and it does it well, often at the sake of other game play features.
The graphics are also somewhat dated, but still quite nice.  The people look a little plastic, but the voice acting makes up for that and then some.
So, all and all, I would definitely recommend Dreamfall Chapters, with the cavet that you should plan on playing The Longest Journey and Dreamfall as well or you will miss out big time.  I hope that Chapters is successful and inspires more entries in the franchise, as this is a very unique world that bears much more exploration.

Years ago, I played Dreamfall: The longest Journey on a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ PC without much experience with PC games, and loved it, even though I barely remember the story. So I had to buy this game for nostalgia reasons. Again, I love it.
The story and the really well developt characters alone makes it worthwhile and fun. The puzzles are good, there's even some tiny form of stealth in there. I expected some sort of combat like in "The Longest Journey", but even without that it is really fun to play.
I really liked the choices, too, so far. Not all choices have big influences on the story, and because I've seen with a lot of these "your choices matter"-games, I don't expect the ending to be completely different and influenced by everything you decided. But the NPCs give you the feeling the choices matter. Mostly it's relationships that depend on what you do, and seemingly also some lives. Also, not every choice is obvious and you'll only notice later that you actually made that choice, which is a great touch. And sometimes your choices don't matter at all, just like in real life :)
I have some negative points, but those shouldn't keep you from playing this game:
* The first two hours or so in the first book start off a bit slow. You run around a lot, you talk a lot, you don't really get to do that much. From a story-perspective, it makes sense, but it's very linear.
* It is sometimes buggy, though I know the devs are working on it. Most bugs I've encountered fixed themselves after restarting the game.
* The puzzles are linear. I would have loved to have two or three different possibilities to approach most puzzles. the levels are also quite linear, there's not much exploring to be done - which I would have loved to see in such a rich and well-developed world as this.
EDIT: Oh yes, and there's a lot of swearing and genital-jokes in there! Fits the settings perfectly ;)

Hard to recommend to players new to the Dreamfall/Longest Journey universe but it might still be worth a crack to them.
The story may have started off a little slow in the early chapters but I actually appreciated the pacing. Beautiful environments created although it does cause my craptop to work real hard. In the most recent fourth chapter the story has really gone places and I have to compliment the writing overall, it's quite something.
Clearly inspired by recent Telltale games with branching decisions but I've been impressed with how well these have actually meaninfully impacted the story. Voice acting is top notch, if unfortunately minor character voice actors cropping up too regularly (not enough variation).
Overall I love the mash of fantasy with dystopian science fiction and story full of compassion for other people.

(tl;dr at the bottom)
Hired Ops (Originally Contract Wars 2.0 Standalone) is an online first person shooter game based on the free to play game, "Contract Wars." This is strictly a multiplayer game, meaning that there is no campaign and no bots (although there is a storyline behind the fighting) While most of the maps and weapons are just ports from the original game, Hired Ops did introduce some significant changes.
First and foremost, Hired Ops is an HD remake of Contract Wars. The lighting and textures have been significantly improved, along with a few collision meshes.
Second, you no longer have to complete a W-Task to unlock attachments for your weapons. For those of you who are unfamiliar with the term, a W-Task was a feature in the main game that requred you to complete a task (often difficult)  with a certain weapon to unlock attachments for said gun, such as 70 longshot kills or in the most difficult case, 100 triple kills (That one took me months to complete. It sucked.) W-Tasks are still present in Hired Ops, but their difficulty is significantly toned down and they reward you with experience points instead of weapon attachments. That being said, weapon customization leaves something to be desired, as there are not nearly as many attachment options here as there are in Contract Wars.
Last but not least, Hired Ops has introduced some significant gameplay changes that set it apart from the original game. You are now given the ability to sprint, a feature that was not included in the original Contract Wars game. They have also added a new killstreak reward that allows you to call in a missile strike on a certain target (not to be confused with the mortar strike) And finally, the VIP loadout has been revamped to give you a better chance of survival should you be the lucky winner.

In most action/adventures games (God of War, Batman: Arkham series) there is a nice mixture of combat, exploration, puzzle solving, and traversal (climbing, swimming, grappling, etc.) What I wanted from Lord of Shadow 2 was 50% combat and 50% everything else. What I got was basically 15% combat with a TON of emphasis on uninspried puzzles, boring traversal, and some rather obvious exploraiton. There were many, many times in the game when I would walk down a hallway and wish I would be jumped by a bad guy just so I could use my weapons.
In the end, I still played and enjoyed it. But I wished for a lot more combat and a lot less of everything else.

Overview: I recommend this game because it has a surprising amount of strategic and tactical depth yet is simple to pick up. Steam's returns policy makes it well-worth trying out and returning if you don't like it.
I am not a huge 4X fan; but I enjoy Starships because while it provides a light introduction to the genre it also, IMO, provides a satisfying degree of strategy at the map level and tactics at the system levels of the game. Some people don't like the game because they claim it lacks depth, but I believe they haven't tried to play on tough enough difficulty levels. One of the things I've noticed about several 4X games is that there are a lot of turns where you don't do anything, you simply press the End Turn button and let things develop. There is NONE of that in Starships; every move and action count.
The game requires you to balance your ship capabilities with your play style. Do you like to use lasers at long distance? Or do you build ships and armor and Plasma cannons to mix it up in close? Fighters and Torpedoes can be cannon fodder and simple barriers to your opponents movement or, properly built, can be decisive scouts and salvo weapons that can devastate your enemies. The hex grid at the system combat level makes it look like a board game, but that is a refreshing change IMO.
Balancing resources appears simple, but at higher difficulty, you have to build the right improvements on the proper planets to get maximum resource benefits. You should also connect your planets with Warp Nexus' to allow movement with no morale point penalties.
Strategically, you can assault your opponent's planets to take Wonders away or deprive them of resources; or you can drive accross their empire, cutting off their fleet and allowing you to defeat the AI in detail.
In all, this is a simple introduction to the 4X genre, and on the Mac, where options are a bit limited, it is a good start.

I love this game!
I always had a thing for naval combat, and this game delivers that in spades. You can take to the skies, the sea, under the sea, in space, and even on land now. However, there are a few things that concern me.
The part that hooked me the most is the building. It's not some Minecraft or Space Engineers clone, no. Building has all sorts of customisable elements that allow for endless creativity. While there are simple one click placement weapons and things, the game's true power comes alive with the various customisable cannons, missiles, and even engines. Every cannon, missile, engine, etc. have multiple components that determines how it functions and what it can be used for. Even the ammo is customisable.
Even in its early access state, the game has balance in it's own way; in order to have a big gun you need a big ship, there is just no way around that. Some issues exist, like under-powered torpedoes. But in the end, how you build will determine how you emerge from combat.
Combat is perhaps, either a weakness or a strength of the game: Combat is decided by your skill in the build designer, not your skill on the battlefield. Combat is resolved almost exclusively through AI control with very limited tactical input. Boarding and capturing ships, while possible, is made nearly impossible for most parts of the game. Many ships have multiple AI cores (destroy these captures it) hidden across the ship, then buried beneath umpteen layers of armor. Still, the combat is satisfying with well though out victory mechanics.
Probably what concerns me the most is the developer's focus in making the game. Every new patch brings new balance fixes and parts, which is all very good. But, each patch also brings out new world maps, all of them incomplete. Even the most complete of the worlds has parts of it that say "to be written". So it seems to me that the devs keep making new stuff without finishing what they already have. This makes me question whether the main world will ever be completed at all.
The campaign also gets tedious once your on a roll. Essentially you battle enemies in a map tile to gain control of it, then repeat for the next, and the next, and the next, until you reach the enemy base. Then repeat again.
However, when things get tedious, I just build something new; his is firs and foremost a building game. Then take my new ship (or submarine, plane, fort, tank, airship, or spaceship) back in there for a fresh new change in the mode of battle.

OutDrive is almost a great experience (ALMOST). The aesthetic is of course top tier and the music is great as always new age synth. In this respect it feels like FarCry: Blood Dragon mixed with the movie Drive and that is a stylistic match made in heaven. These music and visuals are both pretty solid qualities of the game but unfortunately what supports these aspects are nowhere near as impressive.
You simply drive in OutDrive, it's a procedurally generated driving game in which you just have to keep moving within a certain speed range or else you fail. Sometimes there's some random events that happen but that literally just consists of either brief oncoming traffic or an attack helicopter that tries to shoot you. These are handled pretty well for the most part and I don't mind a game in which you just drive but there is a real lack of content here, even for a game that's £2.
There are no online leader boards or particular diversity to each playthrough. Despite technically driving through a unique path each time, it barely feels any different and having only a couple of short random events just leaves me slightly unsatisfied.
However there are two major problems with the game that render the rest unimportant. The game performs horrendously, this will likely be one of the most demanding indie games you play. It's surprising how good of a rig you will need in order to run this game at 60FPS, it even struggles to maintain 30FPS on a PC that can run most big releases on mid-low settings. Another problem in terms of optimization is crashes, I've had this game crash 4 times on me completely out of nowhere and I've heard similar complaints from other Steam users.
The second major problem would be the controls, the car just doesn't handle well at all. It feels rigid and clunky, I fail to see how such a key aspect of a driving game was made so poorly. While it's possible to overcome the bad car handling to an extent, you'll never feel as though it plays the way it should.
I really wanted to like this game and from a visual and audio standpoint I absolutely do. I even think many tracks from the OST will be ones I'll listen to outside of the game. But a lack of diversity, lack of real content, lack of optimization and lack of decent controls stop me from being able to recommend this game. Don't bother with the game at all, even if you see it for free just don't get it.
Scores:
Audio & music : 8/10
Visuals: 8/10
Gameplay: 3/10
Optimisation & performance: 2/10
Value (at full price): 5/10
Final verdict: 4/10 AVOID COMPLETELY!!!

Red Faction II (henceforth referred to as RF2) is a disappointing sequel to the original Red Faction (RF1), which I felt was easily one of the best story-driven first person shooters I played from 1994 until 2007 or so. (I think RF1 still ranks favourably with the likes of Strife and Half-Life.) Here's are the key areas in which RF 1 and 2 differ in terms of quality:
RF1 features a captivating, Total Recall-inspired plot, memorable locations, and destructible environments. (Developer Volition coined that feature 'GeoMod Technology'). It's PC port was augmented with a very fun online multiplayer mode.
RF2 has a decent sense of plot, but to be honest, I didn't care for it until I was on the verge of beating the game for the first time. Something in the second half of the game caused the plot to 'click' with me in the sense that I started to give a damn about the story. In fact, I felt motivated to replay the game to better understand the story and characters that I previously found dull and unworthy of my attention. For that reason, I actually enjoyed replaying the game more than the experience of taking it in as a new experience. RF2's plot is merely serviceable, whereas RF1's plot is interesting enough to keep you playing to see what happens next.
RF2's gameplay is mostly fine. The limited extent to which you can create improvised stairs, entrances, and tunnels by blowing up concrete and terrain is one of RF1's major highlights. Unfortunately, this 'GeoMod' feature is so limited in the sequel that it's virtually non-existent. I found far more instances where 'GeoMod' technology could be actualized in multiplayer maps than in the single player campaign. The fact that RF2's solo campaign is far more linear than RF1's* does nothing to offset this disappointing discrepancy, and the fact that RF2 features no online or even LAN capabilities makes the multiplayer mode a tremendous disappointment. Playing RF2's multiplayer mode against bots is no substitute for playing it with real people.
RF2 is one of the first games I can remember playing that features regenerating health, but it features a hybrid system that combines traditional FPS health management with Halo-esque health regeneration. To its credit, RF2's plot legitimizes the fact that the character you play has the capability to heal. Because healing occurs at a far slower pace than in Halo and the tons of clones it spawned, taking damage in battle does not feel inconsequential unless you make a contrived effort to stall the game by holding your ground after a battle.
I give RF2 a score approximating 5.5 out of 10, which might be a tad generous. It's not a horrible game, but it's not worth going out of one's way to acquire. Give it a try if you invested in the Red Faction bundle, which is worth getting for RF1 and RF: Guerilla (and maybe RF: Armageddon).
* = Some of RF2's vehicle-based sections literally play like rail shooters. In contrast, RF1 gives players the freedom to fully explore their environments while operating vehicles.

This game diverges from the setting, characters, and ideological premise of the original Red Faction, without adding any improvements in appearance or gameplay mechanics. The characters are severely underdeveloped (worse than the original RF), and most of what happens in the story occurs for no explicit or implicit reason. Some parts are needlessly difficult, others pointlessly easy. The boss fight with Quill was pleasantly atmospheric, but that's all I've got as far as positive criticism goes. Please don't waste your time on this game like I did. It's bad. Go replay Mass Effect, because unlike RF2 it's a legitimate contribution to the scifi FPS genre.

Many years ago I had played the demo version of this game on Playstation 2, which included most of the second level. Having played the first game on the same console, I had a higher expectation of this one.
The game feels and looks basically the same as the console version. There are a few subtle good things worth mentioning upfront. It would have been one of the first games to move towards some proper dual-wielded weapons- in which left-click fires one and right-click fires the other. It has an interesting way of introducing each (admittedly bland) character upon your first encounter with them. It has fancy animations on the edge of the screen when putting on your nightvision goggles (rather than just instantaneously switching like most games) or getting into a "Battle Armour"- unlike most games of the time, in which the player was simply in a vehicle right after pressing the button to enter it. One weapon- the NICW- even has a digital ammo count on the side of it, reminiscent of the Assault Rifle from the original game.
Unlike the PC version of the original, this includes a Bot Match mode against AI-controlled players- something which was in the console version of the original. This is a typical Quake-style deathmatch which strangely has a different HUD- and the weapons behave differently. For example, the Rail Driver in single-player has 3 rounds and a reload between each. In Bot Matches, this same weapon has 6 rounds and only requires a reload after firing all 6...
The story is almost cringeworthy at times. It goes on a semi-political bent and basically has all the characters betray you shortly after first meeting them. It has almost no connection whatsoever to the story of the original game. It reuses some music assets from the first game in Bot Matches- some of the techno-style tracks from the first game, some of which are quite impressive.
The game is basically linear and very poorly designed in some parts. The sewer level's beginning is one of the better examples of this. Everything is maze-like and you'll probably just get through it guessing where to go- having to shoot at the same constantly respawning enemies along the way. Once you're at the end of the level, you probably won't be able to think about the map design in your head. Trying to understand the maps... your thoughts will be about as murky as the sewer water.
The game's difficulty is also really inconsistent. You will find some shockingly easy parts and then run into a boss battle with an enemy possessing a ridiculous amount of health and respawning minions to assist them. Boss battles should have been toned down, standard gameplay should have toughened up. You can't leave a vehicle that you have entered unless you are in a certain area. You can't skip cut-scenes- prepare to rewatch the same one before a boss battle several times if you die in it. The game includes a fairly rudimentary health regeneration- where you essentially have one small health bar and you automatically use a health kit once that health bar runs out. You don't manually use your health kits- nor does it take time to use them. You will finish it in 3-4 hours (maybe less) if you don't die much through it.
As many other reviewers have stated, this is something of a downgrade on the first game. For something from a professional studio- Volition- it is almost unforgiveable. I think most players will find this game to be extremely generic and short- a 5/10 at best. Spend your money on the first game instead.

I've been a fan of The Longest Journey since I came across Dreamfall: The Longest Journey and it left me in a state of emptiness after I finished it, like the feeling you get after you finish a book. I found out about The Longest Journey and played it as well and ever since, The Longest Journey and Dreamfall are one of my favorites games of all time. When I learned they would be making a sequel to my favorite games I was so happy but frustrated that I would have to wait so long, but it was worth the waiting! If you're into fantasy, cyberpunk, adventure and story this game will have you come back to it's universe
over and over again to meet some of the best told and designed characters in amazingly made two different worlds.
Previously, I recommended this game to my friends but I told them they should play the previous games before this one to understand the story and love it, but as I progressed, I saw that this game alone has so much to offer even if you don't know much about the universe the story keeps introducing new characters and shows how the old ones changed as the worlds kept changing. So, even if you haven't played the other games I totally recommend it and I believe it's worth your money.
If you've played the previous games I doubt I need to say more because this game takes the story where it left off.
The game has one of the best stories I've ever heard, read or seen and it NEVER lost its magic for me, I was never bored in any part of the game, there was always something else to be curious about something else to explore and understand and try to figure out. The moment you start your Journey, you should be ready to be surprised by anything because this universe is anything but boring. I enjoyed every single moment of it. Exploring the world in Dreamfall: Chapters was especially amazing because of the improved graphics. Every place you wander will have it's own magic with their own colors and a theme unique to them. The game has a fantasy side to it but not in a universe that is filled with Elves and Orcs or Angels and Demons. It introduces so many races with their unique cultures, designs and stories. They beautifully fit in the games universe and they shape it into what it is. The cyberpunk side of the game doesn't look as unique as it's fantasy side, but it brings humans from different cultures together and you will be seeing how they blend in the futuristic world of TLJ. The voice acting is great dialogues are not dull and if you take your time to interact with objects around yourself the protagonist will comment on the objects and Zoë tends to have interesting things to say about pretty much everything. I like her style. Her voice actress is different from the previous game but she does a great job as well. And as I said the story is amazing but I loved how it pulled me in and at some point I was so mad at something that happened I decided harshly and the consequences were so awful it made me feel horrible. So, yes the decisions you make, so far, have great effects, makes you consider the tiniest things over and over again. I hope the fifth book will live up to my expectations and my decisions will affect how the game ends. I loved "Lords of Shadow" and the intermediary sequel, "Mirror of Fate", but I heard a lot of bad news about this game before it came out on Steam. There was a letter from someone in the development team that talked about how the production was disjointed, some bad reviews, etc. There was no way I was going to pass on it though.
The player returns again to the role of Gabriel Belmont, who is now Dracula. Following a tutorial level that takes place in his castle, the game is divided between two major environments, both of which are "free to explore". The first is the city of Castlevania in the 2040s or 2050s (mostly modern, but with some nice cyberpunk and gothic touches), while the other is Dracula's castle of antiquity (which has been destroyed in the modern day, but still exists as an extradimensional realm; I don't believe it is in Dracula's mind).
Unlike the fixed camera angles of "Lords of Shadow", this game features a true 3rd person over-the-shoulder camera. It is well executed, and allows the player to really drink in the beautiful visuals that drip ambience. I personally preferred the castle to the modern levels, though.
Combat still consists of basic attacks, combos, dodging, special weapons, and special powers. I have to admit that most of the fights were a bit dry for me. Most enemies require a single special tactic to defeat, and I frequently found myself looking for ways to bypass them (and there aren't enough ways in the game to do so). The designs are interesting, but fighting even common enemies frequently took as long as a boss fight; that was annoying.
The boss battles are a lot of fun, mixing again a good amount of combat, quick-time elements, cinematics, and great music. Unfortunately the game suffers from boring boss battle environments; like the first game, it's usually just a sort of open arena (though the music, in my opinion, imparts the sense of swinging around to avoid attacks and other epic thoughts.)
The voice acting and story are still excellent. Robert Carlyle and Patrick Stewart really have to carry most of it, and they do great jobs. The game takes some time to defeat, though all the events occur in a single night (this is undoubtedly longer for Gabriel/Dracula, since half of the game involves him traveling to his other-dimensional castle).
The music in this game is AMAZING. It's probably my favorite video game score, and possibly my favorite of both video games and movies. To say that composer Óscar Araujo accomplished something amazing would be an understatement.
Despite so many similarities, this game didn't feel the same as the first "Lords of Shadow", so I can't say this one is either better or worse. There are some weak points in the gameplay (such as some enemies that Dracula is NEVER able to defeat in combat, regardless of how powerful you become), but this is balanced by some truly amazing scenes as well (the train battle comes to mind).
In some way it is more "Castlevania" than the first game, and less so in other ways.
Ultimately, I would recommend highly it to Castlevania fans as well as fantasy action fans. It's a shame that this game will be the last in the series (to my understanding). Mercury Steam and the designers did a great job of creating a Castlevania series that represents Western concepts and artistic values over the Japanese anime style that the original games devolved into.

Awak­ened after cen­turies of sleep, Gabriel Bel­mont joins his for­mer men­tor in an attempt to reclaim his pow­ers and defeat Satan and his acolytes in this final chap­ter in the Lords of Shadow series.
The game tran­si­tions between present time and medieval times, just before Dracula’s cas­tle was ruined. Dur­ing these tran­si­tions, Gabriel must not only fight Satan’s Acolytes, but he must also bat­tle his inner self in order to be able to regain his strength.
Lords of Shadow 2, like its pre­de­ces­sor, is an action-adventure hack n’slash game, but unlike pre­vi­ous install­ments it has some inter­est­ing game­play inno­va­tions, such as var­i­ous puz­zle ele­ments and stealth-like sec­tions. The new addi­tions, espe­cially the stealth ele­ments, tend to hin­der the pro­gres­sion of the story though and being totally scripted does not seem to add any­thing spe­cial to the whole gam­ing expe­ri­ence. There are no alter­nate routes, there is only one way… Despite this fact how­ever, the pres­ence of var­i­ous col­lectibles and upgrades which can be found through­out the map of the game make explo­ration quite a reward­ing experience.
