UPDATE
This review is for those who are already familiar with the Anno series. This isn't my first language, but I did bother to write this all up to give a warning for anyone who hasn't already preorded it. This is NOT a clear "BUY IT!", but merely a description of how things have changed, sometimes quite radically, which can be a huge turn-off for those who expect the same gameplay like in all the Anno games before.
Short and superficial summary:
Limitless ressources. No free harbor building - everything is now confined to slots, just like mines and quarries. Decent graphics. Surprisingly bug free as of now. Small-ish individual map sizes. Less inflexible production complexes but predefined amounts of input/outpot, more individual tinkering and upgrading of buildings with modules. Combat is optional and plays out on separate maps. Also: NO AI BOTS!
I have always been a great fan of the Anno series. Even the fact that the 2 recent games can only be played with Uplay didn't exactly bother me, so no negative review just because of that. I want to exclusive talk about the gameplay experience I had in the first few hours of playing Anno 2205.
Just as stated by the publisher, there have been radical changes to the game as we know it. Certain elements that every game up to this point contained, that provided a coherent structure to the series and were an integral part of the overall gameplay are now gone or replaced by new means production layouts and ressource management.
The first big change: No more storage limits and heavily reduced penalties for low stockpiles. All ressources except a very few building materials are part of a flow dynamic. Overproduction is ok, perfect satisfaction is great (as it means that your production runs efficient), underproduction has an instant impact - although not as heavy like in the rest of the series - and should be avoided. Your civil society won't crumble anymore just because your CEOs are low on service robots... they get mildly annoyed (depending on the amount of underproduction) and tax rates are reduced.
All buildings either provide or need several of new "ressources" in different combinations: Money (for maintenance and building in the first place), energy, construction components (different types of them, just like wood, bricks etc.) and the new "workforce" (which is basically your population that gets substracted for every new production building). Additionaly, theres logistics, which is used just like workforce, but is provided by what was known as the basic warehouses, which are now dumbed down to simple area-of-effect logistics centers without any (real) physical interaction of drones and production buildings, although this isn't really a bad thing. (Warehouse spam in 2070 because drones aren't fast enough with picking up wares was a minor flaw, which the developers have solved quite nifty)
Furthermore, all non-renewable ressources are gone. You get a certain amount of building slots per map - just like in Anno 2070 - but instead of riverside buildings you can now utilize seaside slots. Yes: SLOTS. No more free building of customized harbor areas. The only limitation to ressource exploitation is the amount of slots for mining and coastal extraction.
These changes radically simplify the game (HUGE EDIT HERE: in some areas). It feels more like a puzzle: Build this, stress a ressource, build production building for said ressource, something else is now in low supply, build another thing. It is sometimes more unnerving than a challenge, but that's just my personal opinion.
EDIT: I said in my original post that I assume the rest of the game will be quite like the first zone (temperate island). After some additional hours spent with this game, I have to partially correct my statement. The core dynamic of flow-based ressource management doesn't change, but that is no surprise. What does indeed change is the way settlement has to be laid out: Arctic regions recquire placement of houses close to industrial buildings since they need to be heated by thermal "power" which is provided in a small radius.
A similar amount of rethinking is needed on the lunar colonies, where shields against meteors have to be built.
All three (types of) settlements have to be connected by trade routes, since a zone needs a ressource that it can't produce itself - similar to the different islands of the game's predecessors. Trade routes don't come cheap, especially for space routes. This changes the focus of the game more on efficiency management and less precise ressource storage management. As radical as this change is, it does offer a refreshing innovation to the series. This new approach is reflected in the way that production buildings are built. Individual (industrial) buildings can be upgraded via two types of connected modules (each recquiring a special ressource, but I'll get later to that in the combat section) that improve the output or reduce demand on energy, workforce or logistics.
Less inflexible production complexes that should be closely packed together and basically only work efficiently within a confined ratio of buildings, more precise tinkering with input and output.
Now to a completely different subject: Combat and AI interaction
If you don't want to fight, you don't have to. Since you are now mostly alone on your map/zone, there aren't any direct competitors that try to snatch important islands. The other coorporations have their own zones which you can buy for a hefty amount of credits. Your own assets - islands, buildings, trade routes - aren't in any way endangered. Military conflicts are played on separate maps with ships you don't even have to build. As I said, these conflicts are optional. They can provide you with additional special ressources (graphene, irridium, oil) that are needed for upgrade modules. Each conflict map offers a primary goal, mostly just destroying a target. Additionally there a optional targets, which mostly play out the same: Destroy something and then collect stuff, or just collect stuff (and destroy something on the way there).
As open-minded as I want to be concerning the gameplay changes, this is my biggest issues with the game. I really like the threat of disrupted trade routes or blockades and the additional ressource management, logistic planning and spending that went into a considerable defence/attack force. As demanding as the overall efficiency management may be, this dumbed down combat puts it all kinda in perspective - at least for more competitive players like me, but there are certainly quite some players who will welcome this change.
As stated in the summary, the graphics are fine, but not overwhelming. I have a decent, albeit older rig that can run the game on high settings, althoug after starting on the moon (the third zone) my FPS and the simspeed tend to drop sometimes. Since I'm not focusing much on graphics in such games, this is all I can honestly tell.
To my surprise, I haven't encountered any bugs and I'm still waiting for my first crash-to-desktop. I had now problems starting or running this game, but maybe I'm just lucky.
To come to an end: I still can not wholeheartedly recommend buying this game. There are a lot of refreshing changes, demanding new approaches to certain problems - which I really like. Parts of the game are so simplified that long time players of the series may regret putting their money into this.
And to address some critique from the comments: I am very well aware that 30mins playing Anno2205 won't provide any deep insight into every feature the game has to offer, but some core features/flaws can be accessed in this time frame. I don't need to spend 20-60 hours to write a qualified review on the most basic features. Nevertheless I greatly appreciate any constructive criticism.

Moves can be strung together into crevasse-crossing combos, launching you across maps in joyous ways. The game looks great, and runs amazingly for the entities on-screen, which is a necessity in a precise game such as this.
That being said, there is one glaring issue. There are quite a few areas, especially in the Volcano Entrace, where it's difficult to find your way or figure out what to do. Players, without the intuitive sense of direction that the level design should give, will throw themselves at obstacles, hoping to survive. There are also a lot of areas in which the objective is impossible to understand without first failing. This becomes annoying in sections with lots of enemies, where health is at a premium and death restarts you far, far away.
Overall, this is a great addition to the series and one I intend to replay many times.
P.S. I bet Brad Borne could make a hell of a Sonic game if he tried.

Lord Mayor developed by John McCann and published by Bottlenose Bits, LLC. is a casual city building puzzle game. The object of the game is to deliver upon the goals that are set at the beginning of each level. Although it appears to be designed simply the amount of strategy and understanding of each of the building types is significant.
Gameplay consists of a playing grid-like playing board. Each level has its own grid. You can place one building in each vector. Each building type has a price in terms of monetary and resources required to build. Each round gives you a deadline to meet the requirements of each level. For example, the tutorial expects you to reach a population of 1000 with 5 happiness, 5 prosperity and 5 culture. Each building type has a different value. Failure occurs when either happiness, prosperity or culture hit rock bottom.
There are more better developed games on Steam that attempt to do the same thing. However, at the price point you're looking at a rock solid title gameplay wise. Therefore, when you factor in the value proposition - cost when compared to entertainment - the game is fairly priced. In fact, I would argue that the game is a bargain if you are into the genre.
Such is the complexity of the different buildings and their individual values that I found it easier to play organizing a spreadsheet for the game. With a spreadsheet you will have a better idea of what buildings you need to build in order to accomplish each of the tasks that you are set at the beginning of each level.
It's always a little disappointing when developer/publishers release a game onto Steam and disappear into the oblivion. As of writing there are a total of five discussion threads on the game's board. None of them have received any official response. Several of them require attention. Certainly this may only be a $2 game but that doesn't excuse you from caring for your community. Consequently, I am more than a little disappointed that the developers appear to be absent and may have deserted their game.
Lord Mayor is yet to be Steamified. It is a single-player game that lacks trading cards and Steam achievements. It also does not utilize the Steam leaderboard system. This is something that I would utilize in order to create a sense of competitiveness among the players. It'd be nice to be able to compare time played and in game days required to achieve the goals of each level. As a result I am disappointed the game is lacking in utilizing Steam to the best of its potential.
Although I am disappointed in the absentee developer/publisher and the lack of Steamification if you are a fan of the genre the you can't ask for much more at this price point. Therefore, I somewhat reluctantly recommend this product. If the developers were to respond to their customers and potential player base, achievements and trading cards were added and leaderboards considered I would certainly recommend Lord Mayor a lot more firmly.

Split/Second is a unique racing game. It's HEAVILY Arcade, so if you're looking for anything remotely realistic, veer clear. There basically 2 types of cars in this game: those that take a lot of punishment and those that are fast and drift around corners. The game's career mode is split into 12 episodes, presented like TV episodes (just a very quick narration of "this time on" followed by some explosions. Speaking of explosions: This is the meat of the game. You will be racing against 7 opponents, blowing them up, while not getting blown up yourself. But this is no combat racer. You don't have any weapons, apart from your "power play" bar. You can have 3 different bars and you fill them up by drifting or drafting. Once a bar is full it can be activated at certain moments to either activate a shortcut or one of the many booby traps on a track, which consist of exploding vehicles, giant cranes, rocks, exploding barrels dropped by helicopters and so forth. Some can only be activated once, others as often as you like. This simply requires an opponent ahead of you and you timing correctly when to press the button and hoping to catch them in the detonation or blast wave. You will have to learn the tracks and their respective booby traps to be effective, since each and every one works differently. This is also where heavier vehicles have an advantage, since a blast wave doesn't knock them out as easily.
The game also offers various "landscaping" options for each track. Once you fill 3 bars of your powerplay, it turns orange and you can cause major destruction, which results in the track being changed. Very effective if an enemy is right in front of you and gets crushed by a ship or whatever. This makes the tracks even more interesting and volatile.
Apart from that there are a few different modes like Elimination (last place after x seconds is out), time trial (with explosions), Big Rig (pass trucks that bombard you with exploding barrels) and Heli Attack (evade missiles from a helicopter). Can't remember if there are any more, apart from the Elite Race at the end of each episode that you need to finish in 3rd at least I think to continue on.
Each race awards you with points to unlock new vehicles. The better you place, the more points you get (not repeatable, but you can replay every race as often as you want to get 1st place if you so desire). They also unlock the next Elite Race, so technically you either don't have to do all the races or you don't have to finish 1st. Apart from that each episode contains a bonus race if you wreck enough enemies throughout that episode (repeatable in races).
It's pretty much the only game that offers this gameplay as far as I know, at least the only one with halfway decent graphics even by today's standards. Also runs perfectly fine under Windows 10, just the sound is weirdly subdued for whatever reason. Can't remember if this had been the case when I played it years ago.

Gameplay-wise, it’s a point-and-click interactive movie thing with shallow and predictable characters. Think 3D visual novel, complete with writing that would only appeal to 13-year-olds, but without the frustrating story flags that end up killing you and all your loved ones because you made the wrong choice somewhere back in the second chapter. There are very few ways to really screw up in this game. It has very few puzzles (if you could call them that), and they mostly consist of finding and combining items or putting things in the right order. On the positive side, it still manages to make me curious about how things are going to play out, and there’s a little value in replaying the game to see how your choices influence what happens to individual characters (they generally make no difference in the grand scheme of things). The voice acting is quite good.
I give it a 3.5/5 there. Entertaining, but far from a masterpiece.
Where things really start to crumble though is the technical side. I’m not going to beat around the bush here, this thing’s a MESS and it tends to absolutely ruin the immersion. Graphically, the game looks comparable to titles released in 2006, only with slightly higher texture resolution, a lot of post processing, awful lighting, beginner mistakes (depth/alpha testing failure and z-fighting for instance), distance popping, broken shaders, and rigid, almost robotic character animations that are not timed or positioned correctly most of the time. But it needs a very high-end CPU and gigabytes of RAM to pull this off at acceptable framerates. And even if you have lots of RAM, at some point (roughly 4 GB), performance just falls off a cliff as the garbage collector struggles to deal with all the memory fragmentation because someone thought they didn’t have to care about memory management with a game written using .NET. Nothing could be further from the truth. This seems to happen with a lot of Unity-based titles, so future gamedevs take note—GC’d languages are not a silver bullet. VSync is dysfunctional (probably due the unstable framerate; didn’t attempt to pin down the cause), mouse grabbing does not work properly (cursor leaves the window if you move it too quickly). The list goes on and on. In two hours of gameplay, I hit the “Report Bug” button about a dozen times (as of version 4.1.1). It’s frustrating, to say the least.
I still give it 2/5 points here because at least it hasn’t crashed so far, so it’s not totally unplayable.
Overall, I don’t think I can recommend this game as it is. I might have reconsidered if the developers had fixed some of the major technical flaws (instead of just the symptoms, like Propast completely wrecking performance in earlier versions), but apparently that is either not very high up on their list of priorities, or they simply lack the expertise to do so.

Having played through the game entirely with THREE different friends, I can now say that I think this game is the current standard for the tower-defense/fps hybrid genre.  The interface (extremely important in this genre) is very good, the gameplay is smooth, the characters are funny and interesting, and the story even makes enough sense to pay attention.  I highly recommend it over other td hybrids such as Deathtrap or Sanctum, though those games have some merit as well.
The game's main problem is that in order to unlock all of the traps and empower them properly, you have to play the game through many times, or endure boring grinds.   Because you can refund your trap decisions at any time for free, this seems like a pointless mechanic which amounts to a pile of bookkeeping every time you wish to change strategies.  Skulls should come at a rate several times what they drop at in the game, because the game should be (and is for the most part) about your strategy and choices of traps per level, not what trap perks you happened to have unlocked at any given moment.  This is especially true since, with a little annoying click-through processing, you can rearrange your trap features anyway.

OutDrive is almost a great experience (ALMOST). The aesthetic is of course top tier and the music is great as always new age synth. In this respect it feels like FarCry: Blood Dragon mixed with the movie Drive and that is a stylistic match made in heaven. These music and visuals are both pretty solid qualities of the game but unfortunately what supports these aspects are nowhere near as impressive.
You simply drive in OutDrive, it's a procedurally generated driving game in which you just have to keep moving within a certain speed range or else you fail. Sometimes there's some random events that happen but that literally just consists of either brief oncoming traffic or an attack helicopter that tries to shoot you. These are handled pretty well for the most part and I don't mind a game in which you just drive but there is a real lack of content here, even for a game that's £2.
There are no online leader boards or particular diversity to each playthrough. Despite technically driving through a unique path each time, it barely feels any different and having only a couple of short random events just leaves me slightly unsatisfied.
However there are two major problems with the game that render the rest unimportant. The game performs horrendously, this will likely be one of the most demanding indie games you play. It's surprising how good of a rig you will need in order to run this game at 60FPS, it even struggles to maintain 30FPS on a PC that can run most big releases on mid-low settings. Another problem in terms of optimization is crashes, I've had this game crash 4 times on me completely out of nowhere and I've heard similar complaints from other Steam users.
The second major problem would be the controls, the car just doesn't handle well at all. It feels rigid and clunky, I fail to see how such a key aspect of a driving game was made so poorly. While it's possible to overcome the bad car handling to an extent, you'll never feel as though it plays the way it should.
I really wanted to like this game and from a visual and audio standpoint I absolutely do. I even think many tracks from the OST will be ones I'll listen to outside of the game. But a lack of diversity, lack of real content, lack of optimization and lack of decent controls stop me from being able to recommend this game. Don't bother with the game at all, even if you see it for free just don't get it.
Scores:
Audio & music : 8/10
Visuals: 8/10
Gameplay: 3/10
Optimisation & performance: 2/10
Value (at full price): 5/10
Final verdict: 4/10 AVOID COMPLETELY!!!

On first glance, it feels like Rad Racer from NES.  A game from my childhood.  I booted it up and saw that eerie little window that shows up before you open a game asking me for my graphic preferences.  I then am able to access the game.....no....no dear god, NO!!!!! "Made with Unity personal edition".
Well, the story's simple even though the text goes off screen, and no matter the resolution, the relatively quick scrolling text vanishes on the left and right sides of the screen.  Basically, you end up in a gunfight while on a date with your girlfriend.  During the gunfight, your girlfriend gets fatally wounded.  In order to spend more time in her last moments of life, you hook her up to the car's engine to act as her life support.  After that, the game begins.  The goal of the game is about survival.  Go too slow, the girl dies.  Go too fast, the engine overheats, the girl dies.  The controls feel awkward and the game needs polishing.
Although everything I've said so far is negative, there is good news.  The graphics look good and the music sounds sweet.....until you overheat or go too slow, to where it sounds like distorted garbage.
This game is on the right track to being something decent in unity, but it needs a lot of polishing before it can be something good.  $3 is not justified here.  Not yet, at least.

While they are both quite different, they do have their similarities, wiht some things better than another. While Terraria is more of an rpg where bosses fill the entire screen, many many totally random things and massive amounts of combat, Starbound has more of a personality. Bosses for instance mostly take place in an enclosed room and it doesn't have as much content as terraria. Though everything seems to be carefully crafted to make even random stuff fit into the game. The story really isn't anything special, the missions themselves are sometimes quite fun, the real thing you should go for is to kinda make your own adventure, enjoy the beautiful, peaceful atmosphere and build comfy houses. Combat is also quite fun, not too over-the-top as in terraria, but really fun, in a more strategic manner. And with workshop support and lots of mods you won't get bored anytime soon. Definetely recommended.

Split/Second is a game developed by Black Isle Studios and surprisingly published by Disney Interactive Studios
Split/Second is, hands down, my favorite racing game ever and one of the few racing games I actually I enjoy playing! This is a great game that any racing fan should play at least once and is also a great entry game for those wishing to check out the genre
You are a contestant on the new explosive racing show Split/Second. During the course of the season you will have to compete in races to advance to the next episode. Finishing higher in events will get you more points and will allow you to progress further in the season. Each episode is capped off by an Elite Race, a race around the track against Split/Second's best drivers. Beat each episode to win the season championship
The gameplay is extremely simple. You race around a track, drift around the corners and use power-ups to destroy your opponants. You attain energy through drifts, drafts, and air-time. Once you have enough, you can activate power-plays on the track, which usually involve destroying parts of the track to crush your rivals. Filling up your energy all the way will allow you activate the biggest power plays on the track and will also allow you to change the track's route. Racing hard while effectively using your power plays are essential if you want to win the season championship.
In addition to the races, there are also several other types of events. The first one is Elimination. It's similar to the race, but there aren't any set laps. Instead, a there is a timer that counts down. When the timer reaches zero, the last place car is eliminated from the race
The second event is the Air Strike, where a helicopter shoots missles at you and you have to dodge the missle waves in order to gain points. The longer you last, the harder the waves become to dodge
A variant of the Air Strike event is Air Revenge, which is kind of like a boss fight. Instead of getting points for dodging missles, you get power-play energy in addition to the energy you get from drifts and jumps. You can then use the energy to reflect the missiles back at the helicopter
The final event is by far my favorite: Survival. Here, semis are driving around a track while dropping bombs in front of you in order to kill you. As you stay alive and pass these trucks, you gain points. Passing several trucks in a row without dying will increase your score multiplyer. Get the highest score to win the event
Split/Second's graphics are pretty standard. It looks okay, there are also some glitches and hitbox issues that, while not game-breaking, can lead to outburts of rage over what the heck just happened. It is a shame that the game is capped to 30 FPS which for me personally in a racing game, you need the 60 FPS. Thankfully, there is a mod that unlocks the 60 FPS as well as adding a slow motion option which is cool
Split/Second is a very simplistic but very addictive game. Although it is a shame that the game's multiplayer has been shut down by Disney quite a number of years ago, the game is still fun to play on you're own or with a friend through split screen
People who are fans of racing games or are interested in racing games should definitely try this game out!
The driving takes a bit to get used to, but it is a lot of fun! Split screen support for 2 player makes it amazing. If only it could do 4 players...

Quick summary:  save your money.
I'm highly polarized on this game so far (through book 3).  I really appreciate the episodic installments as an idea but don't believe the creators have hit their stride just yet (the pacing is slow and at times the material is trivial).  In general, I'm not a point-n-click fan but this story is rather epic and I love that.  Is the story enough tho?  The answer is no.  The game-play is laborious.  I almost feel as if it would be better without the puzzles as the pacing is rather slow and with the puzzles added in I feel like I'm lagging behind.  This is a negative impact on enjoyment obviously.  Perhaps it has more to do with the fact that I prefer RPG's but this game is not satisfying for me.  And this is where I'm polarized; I love the ever-evolving story but hate playing through it.  Cycling through the past two games (via walkthroughs) did add an appreciation for the entire story arc and helped to draw me in.  But this is a case where the amazing writing is overshadowed by the Gumby game mechanics.  I feel that perhaps just leaving this one as a QTE game would benefit it as less time would be spent on slow environmental interactions and more time on the part I love.  In fact I'm wondering if they should even bother with the pretense of a game on this one and instead simply allow the audience to click through the chapters like a DVD book.
I hate to say it, as I really want to support this team, but this one is probably best experienced through walkthroughs with the current going rate of $30 USD.  Knock that price down to half and it's still better through walkthroughs. If you think of the Civ Series "Beyond Earth" as the "meat and potatoes' of Sid Meier's 4X games, you can think of Starships as the "snack food" equivalent. Most people have had a beef with this Sid Meier spinoff game because it doesn't look or feel like any of his similar 4X games. This one is built for speed and playability, but still has depth if you want to go deeper on the building and resource explotation aspects. Most fans of the regular Sid Meier games who expect something like it in Starships aren't going to find it here. However, if  you take the game for what it is, a 4X lite game where you can jump in and finish a game in under a half-hour when you just want to jump in but don't want to play something that's going to suck you in for hours, it's quite satisfying.  It does have some downsides, the integration to Beyond Earth is kind of a throw away feature that seems like a a good idea never brought to fruition. In any case, I would still give this one ups if you want a "Sid Meier's Light" game in your collection you can play with a non-gamer cousin.
Just not good, not worth the money.

I paid nothing for this. It was a giveaway thing. As such the following will be written from that perspective.
Outdrive is a game that is almost not a game. It has some loose narrative in that your girlfriend gets shot and you must 'out drive' the the 'bad dudes' in order to save her and presumably get her to a hospital, if such a thing even exists in the retro neon dystopia of the far flung future. The juxtaposition here is that there is no hospital. For what seems a procedurally generated track, the actual game is really just an endurance run with a timer.
You must use boost to keep the car at speed designated by the blue bar directly behind the car. Go to fast or go to slow. She dies.
Now, the music in this game is actually quite decent. Its mindless and very relaxing. The tempo decreases and gets distorted when your car is not going at speed. Which is a bit disappointing for relaxing aspect of it but its no matter really.
I had a hell of time trying to get a gamepad to actually do anything worth while. Trying two 3rd party programs as well as just setting the key bindings in the setup utility. I eventually settled on just WASD'ing my way through it. I'm no stickler for peoples preferred control method but certain genres beg a specific control scheme. Either way WASD works well enough for this task.
The car physics are extremely suspect as well. A gentle tap on the wall will send you spinning and usually end up facing the other way. It seems once the car leaves the ground it weighs less than a piece of paper. At one point I started driving sideways on the invisible boundary of the track and a helicopter knocked me off and I was able to drive out of bounds a short while until I was blasted into the sky and juggled for a bit until my girlfriend died.
All in all, for free I can't complain. The music is good and WASD isn't totally the worst thing ever for an arcade driver. However, I would never recommend this should you have to pay for it.

This is foremost a team management challenge in an open world, resource gathering survival game in a Zombie infested land. I can’t express how much this game makes me care and how upsetting it can be to play, every event matters - a lost survivor can never be regained from a reload. This game is not zombie-braindead as many other games with this them are – it is rather deep in strategy once you learn about all the options that are possible and it forces you to prioritize between missions that will not stick around forever. You constantly will think: that if I do this… then what will the consequence be.
It was so gut revolting and chocking to see the groups most influential survivor Dante torn to pieces by a Juggernaut and much later to see your next in line most influential survivor Maya get her throat torn away by a Feral. It is moment like this that can turn your economic situation back a lot if you do not have other character high in influence because it takes some time to build up this games most important resource that is so easy to waste on things that did not matter.
So, the advice I can give after playing this game for 16 hours is to have no favorite survivor in the group because you will probably lose him or her. Be ready to find and develop the next survivors to step up to fill the gaps of the fallen ones. But darn what I miss every single one I have lost so far.
Pros:  Everything will break or die, everyone will get tired and hungry, not just zombies, all resources you gather will eventually run out.
Cons: Game do not support high-res monitors well  on +1080p it will just scales the graphics to so that it looks pixelated. It is not nice art styled graphics so it looks outdated already. There are bugs, mostly graphical glitches, everywhere you look but fortunately none that will make the game unplayable

I discovered Fancy Pants for the first time when I was ten years old, ever since the games have always been fun to play. The visuals, one of my favourite thing about the whole Fancy Pants series are the visuals, backgrounds can be sometimes abstract and sometimes there's a whole story going on that you can follow as you play throught the stage. The volcano level does this very well because it's all about telleportation and moving from one background to another.
My only complaint about this game: When beating the final boss a text appears on the screen saying TO BE CONTINUED! There better be an update soon Brad!! :(  No part 2 that'll be an entirely seperate game pls..
Anyway, that was the best I could review this game. I'm usually more articulate than this, this is my first ever review on a game and it's 23:50 so gimme a break. Byeee :))

Purchased on a whim to get a few hours of gameplay with a friend I was dissapointed when the multiplayer didn't work properly for me ( this was a personal issue, and no-one else seems to get it, so don't worry ) I decided to try the AI campaigns out, just for a gander, and From The Depths quickly became in my list of most played games, at 300+ hours and still rapidly rising the challenge this game presents is formidablle for even the best of players, all the while being perfectly capable of overcoming it.
There is a massive customizability in each ship, tank or whatever you create. I shouldn't realise say 'customize' as you get no set pieces, you get blocks, 1 meter, 2 meter or even 4 meter sloped glass blocks against Explosive Reactive Armor. Each has benefits that are detailed. They aren't simply placed on an 'armor' preset number, each block handles the fire it takes differently, being deflection, completely stopping a shell / missile all the way to being ethereal.
The customization comes in the form of the weapons you use. There are currently four weapon types:
CRAM Cannons: These are your artillery-type cannons. Although perfectly spammable by your choice, these cannons are commonly used as slow-firing but incredibly powerful area of effect devastators. And will more than easily create an explosion capable of tearing vessels in half.
Advanced Cannons: These more modern-esc cannons are used as either Anti-Missile, or just Anti-Everything, you can set them up to destroy shields, penetrate armor and burst molten copper into a vessel, EMP areas or flat out blow things up. These can be gatling guns or massive 300mm + Destroyer cannons completely at your personal discretion.
Missiles: Great for getting past shields these again, very extensive weapons can be used in a variety of ways, be it super-fast Anti-Air or Massive anti-capital torpedoes.
Lasers: Never really delved into these personally, but they haven't been left out the by the developer, this weapon system can do serious damage and are just as useful as the others.
Speaking of developers you can see just how active and knowledgable the developer is in the scene of creating games by looking at the From The Depths forum, where you can see updates, suggestions ( Which are not negletected) , other players builds from typical modern-like creations to vehicle representations of the Kraken.
All in all a VERY diverse game about blowing things up and creating what's on your mind.
After 3000+ hours in Minecraft 'cause I'm a scrub I thought I'd never want to build anything again, From The Depths taught me other-wise.

(DISCLAIMER: Objectively, as a game, Castlevania LoS 2 is a good, overall,  game that has some flaws. However, as a follow up to Castlevania LoS, it is terribly disappointing. My recommendation is based on the game itself, not my disappointment as  a sequel to the original.)
Let's start with the GOOD. The combat has been refined in a very nice way and thusly feels a bit more responsive. As in the last game, with the points/experience that you receive from defeating enemies, you can use that to buy additional moves for your weapons, but this time, you have the addition of the chaos claws and void sword AND they have their own moveset on top of the same function as shadow and light magic respectively. Thusly, giving you many combo possibilities. Dodging is smooth, although I would have preferred a roll like the original, or the turning into smoke like Laura in the original game as well. I'm glad for the addition of the free rotating camera that was lacking in the first game.
Platforming has also been improved and is much smoother than before.
The graphics, very,very nice. However, it seems a bit of a waste since the most of the environments are dank, dark and very similar; unlike the original game where there was a lush forests, autumn ruins, icy castles, dark dungeons, crazy grand canyonesque platforming. Just wasted potential overall, but a great graphics engine nonetheless.
Now for the BAD: STEALTH, man oh man, this game never needed stealth to begin with so I don't know why it's even here. Not that I mind stealth, it's just done very, very poorly in this game. The stealth sections were very tedious and boring. It was repetitive and not necessary to the game.
Speaking of not necessary, the section where you have to hide from Pan's brother so you don't get one-shotted....ridiculous! You're freaking Dracula, the prince of freaking darkness. Satan is even scared of you in the game, yet, you have to hide from this guy? Again, since this was a stealth portion, it was terrible and necessary.
The modern setting, I'll admit that I was excited to check out a modern setting in LoS, but honestly, it felt so out of place, especially the robots and commandos in exo suits. The sections you get to go back to the castle felt much more appropriate and epic.
The story, the story this time around, lacked a sense of urgency and purpose. This is probably partly due to that you're now Dracula and you don't care weather thousands of people live or die. I through most of the game, it felt as if I was just trudging along just getting through the game, instead of feeling like I'm making real progress. The story lacked any real revelations, twists or turns, like the original had. It was very one track and lacked anything with real substance. There is no internal struggle like in the first game, any real tragedy with character investment, the story felt like it had a beginning and an end but missing pieces in the middle, not necessarily plot holes, but more so they needed to add elements to make it really interesting.
Overall, the game is ok with some flaws. I did have fun with the combat, especially in the intro of the game, but after that, it felt like it was all downhill from there; lack luster story, repetitive environments, terribly implemented stealth. Sadly,  Castlevania LoS 2 just couldn’t meet the standards set by the first. As a huge fan of this series, I'm hugely disappointed. As a gamer, it's a “not bad” game.
7/10

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is an action-adventure game, the sequel to the 2010 game Castlevania: Lords of Shadow, and the 34th installment in the Castlevania franchise (37th if one includes the 3 Pachislot games). The game was developed by MercurySteam and published by Konami. It was released late February 2014 in both North America and Europe and on March 2014 in Australia. A Japanese release was released on September 4, 2014. A downloadable chapter has also been released in March from the same year.
Gameplay
As in the previous game, the player controls Gabriel Belmont, now known as Dracula, as he fights through an open world. During the game's opening sequence the player is able to control Dracula while he still possesses all his powers as well as all of his weapons. Dracula's main weapon is his Shadow Whip, a weapon that is comparable to the Combat Cross from the original Lords of Shadow. Replacing the magic system from the previous game are the Void Sword and the Chaos Claws. The Void Sword can replenish Dracula's health when used while the Chaos Claws can be used to break through enemy defenses and deliver powerful attacks. The story mode in Lords of Shadow 2 has been stated to be far longer than the previous one. The game is mainly an open world allowing the player to choose what route to take. Lords of Shadow 2 features a movable camera, something that was not available in its predecessor.

One of the best interpretations of Dracula's castle, marred by a clumsy early game and the occasional design choice of dubious quality. The characters are enjoyable, the boss fights are true highlights, and the combat remains the meat of the game. We finally get to explore Dracula's castle in a modern 3D environment that does it justice, there are too many instances where a new area makes you pause just to admire the scenery. It is like the level designers took the concept art (which always looks so much better) and then implemented it literally, and somehow made it even better. I like the anti-hero that Gabriel became, even if they fumbled a bit in justifying how he got to that point.
The original LoS had puzzle sections which some players did not care for. LoS2 eliminates those in favor of "stealth action" puzzles, which even fewer people cared for. Whoops. There's about three or four of those sections in the game, and they're really not as big of a deal as they're made out to be, but they do remain pretty funky standouts. The biggest error LoS2 makes, which I haven't really seen mentioned anywhere, is being a wildly lavish game that was hamstrung by console design. There aren't any loading screens, but there are enough terminal areas where things are being loaded in the background that it's painfully obvious what's going on. At least there are no chupacabra levels.
It's clear the designer's hearts were in the castle levels. The modern era is "fine", but really lacks anything interesting. And monsters shouldn't have guns, they break your concentration meter easily and are barely telegraphed.

I've played The Longest Journey, Dreamfall: The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: Chapters 1-4 and I'm highly anticipating book 5.
The story is rich and the characters well acted, well rounded and interesting.  If you haven't played The Longest Journey or Dreamfall: TLJ then I highly suggest you do.  These games are well deserved of their status.  The story is original and engrossing, and something I'd never seen before.  The first and second game are quite different in mechanics.  In the second you are able to fight and there are things you can't miss.  In the first pick up everything even if you've placed it somewhere, as you may need it in the future.
Dreamfall Chapters is incredible.  The graphics are a wonderful improvement, the story is still amazing and the characters are what those who have played the first two games have come to love.  The worlds are in peril and I'm still not sure what role Zoe plays in everything but her story is intriguing.  While the first and the second didn't have much choice, the third takes your choices into account and molds the story in regards to your choices.
I reccommend playing the first two before you embark on your journey into Dreamfall:Chapters. If you don't, you'll have a lot of questions and you'll be missing out on the wonders of Arcadia and Stark you've missed by opting out on TLJ and Dreamfall TLJ.

(No spoilers)
Narratively this is a real joy to play. There are not many games like this out there.
One minute you're saving people from nightmares, the next you're arguing with your loved one about the dishes.
The story is rich and complex.
It was recently updated to the Unity 5 engine, and it looks beautiful.
The developers have created excellent aesthetics that fit the stories well.
An important thing to know is: it's a kind of interactive story, with puzzles,
and choices - that actually matter in this game. So don't expect 'traditional' gameplay.
Also, if you're stuck, try out every option possible, literally. Examine everything!
A few points of criticism:
- The solution to some puzzles require very specific ways to use the UI.
(E.g. at one point I accidentally apprehended the wrong person because I didn't know what a symbol meant.)
- The animations could be better. It's sad because everything else looks fine.
- Quite a few objects could use proper collision meshes. It's a detail but walking through objects breaks immersion.
(E.g. in the Pandemonium the robots on the wall have no collision at all.)
All in all, one of my favourite games. Wholeheartedly recommended!

is a simple, quick, fun little strategy game. Don't go into this game expecting a 40-hour campaign and hours of careful planning, because that's not what this game is made for.
feels and plays like a very casual game-in fact, everything from the UI to the simplistic controls and systems screams that this game was built for a tablet or phone rather than a full blown PC. This isn't exactly a bad thing as the UI is clean and easy to navigate, with oversized text and icons.
Combat is on a 2d hex grid, with various objects(asteroids, planets, etc.) either blocking vision and fire, or reducing the damage dealt when firing through them. Positioning, shields, and weapon types all factor in as well, giving just enough depth to combat to keep it from getting too stale.
There's not really any alien species, just different flavors of humans. All the ships have similar looks and feel, though you can upgrade their weapons and systems in anyway you want, which is neat. I'd have liked more variety but what you get is servicable.You can only have one 'fleet' on the campaign map though, which is a bit annoying.
Really my biggest gripe with this game is in the achievements, as you need
(or at least a save game from it) to perfect it.
Final Verdict:
Decent buy, especially on sale. Scratches that strategy itch without needing 40+ free hours.

When Volition released the first Red Faction-game back in 2001, it created quite a stir because of the Geo-Mod Engine. Suddenly gamers could mould the game environment with rockets and grenades; for example, shoot holes in walls and walk through those holes; things we don’t think are particularly exciting these days.
Released only one year after the first game, Red Faction II (2002), is surprisingly bad in almost every category. Most obvious is the edgy graphics and the somewhat short campaign. The story has its flaws as you can imagine. To be honest it is quite bad and you never really get to know the characters very well. I don’t know who wrote the script, but a sexual innuendo like:
“Hey Alias, let’s get wet ...” - is pretty dumb coming from a female character in a sub.
I had no trouble at all playing this PC-version on my Windows 8 OS. Everything worked very well. I experienced no crashes or any problems at all. (I played the STEAM-version of the game).
POSITIVE:
+ Voice actors Lance Henriksen and Jason Statham are fun to listen to.
+ Some memorable moments.
+ Easy to play and get a hang of.
NEGATIVE:
- Bad graphics.
- Bad character control (especially the menu system).
- Boring plot.
I would only recommend this game to people who want to find out what happens in the Red Faction-universe.

Super Fancy Pants adventure is slightly tough to recommend but I'm going to give it the thumbs up anyway and here's why:
Movement in this game is fun, much like all of the others in the series Super Fancy Pants adventure has incredibly tight, fluid controls that give you a myriad of fun ways to travel through levels and make you feel cool, it's super fun to pull off a backflip then land on an enemy grind on your magic ink pen and then roll down a hill. The aesthetic is also really quite nice I like the hand drawn style that it has but this might not be for everyone. The basic game levels are really easy especially if you're somewhat experienced with platformers, but the bonus challenge stages that get you new pants and hats can actually be quite hard and require you to have a good grasp of the game's mechanics in order to complete them. My biggest gripe with this game is that it's short, really short, you wind up having a great time with it and then suddenly it's over and I felt a little cheated, I think that for the amount of playtime you're going to get out of it the price is a little steep. Surprisingly engaging game, good for longer sessions and as a break from other, more sofisticated titles. Sensation of speed is taking you over quite early and it holds onto you for a whole duration of the game.
As far as mechanics go, game is very simple - you just manouever with your mouse to avoid hitting the obstacles while velocity increases. No clicking or keys involved. Just a movement, that's what this game is all about after all. And it's really engaging.
Graphics and sound are very minimalistic and raw - if you liked aesthetics of TRON movies, you will feel right at home with this one.
All in all, I like this game very much.

I'd say the replay value is abysmal but it's actually absent.
There's literally like a dozen (or maybe less?) of obstacles that pop up in front of you every now and then. I mean, I'm sorry, I meant to say that this game is "procedurally generated".
The only other thing that's supposed to add an edge to the gameplay is the coins, which are pointless. You can only use them to buy continues, and since you can get the "perfect/clean" playthrough achievements in 30 minutes anyway, you don't really need the coins and they're merely a distraction.
Verdict:
Possibly the most forgettable game I've ever played on Steam.
But, for those of you who need to bump up that 100% achievements count, sure why not, go nuts.

I absolutely adore this game and the sheer freedom of design it gives to the player. You can build practically anything. Realistic warships, flying castles, sea monster submarines, laser-spewing hovercraft, the list goes on for ages.
With that said, it's not perfect. The controls are difficult to learn at best, with two options of a mouse-based control scheme that's easy to use but can make building difficult at times, and a keyboard-based scheme that is vastly superior to the mouse-based scheme for building, but much harder to learn and use. The learning curve is very harsh as well, considering just how much stuff there is to build with and how complex building effectively can get.
Pros/Cons:
Pros:
-Allows an unreal degree of design freedom
-Great fun once you get the hang of it
-The build mode has a lot of useful features like mirroring and the ability to copy and paste subobjects (turrets/rotating parts).
-Absurd skill ceiling, you will never stop learning clever tricks or new methods
-Updates fairly frequently
-Combat is hilariously destructive, in some cases with weapons blasting entire chunks of enemy vehicles off
-Vehicles can be fitted with customizable AI that allow the ship to be controlled automatically
Cons:
-Battles can cause massive drops in performance if the fight is big enough (huge vehicles/lots of vehicles).
-Difficult to get the hang of.
-Difficult, period. Enemy vehicles WILL give you trouble when you start out.
Overall, it's a very good game and can be a lot of fun once you get the hang of it, but the difficulty and learning curve are pretty intense. Highly recommended for anyone that enjoys designing their own vehicles, as this game allows you to do precisely that.

While the initial learning curve might be really steep, this game has a surprising amount to offer. The realistic physics make solving problems with your designs interesting and realistic and you can spend dozens of hours trying to make the perfect ship or plane, or whatever you can imagine. Be warned though the initial learning curve is steep - if you're somebody who likes making things in games like Kerbal Space Program and such then you'll love this.

From the Depths is a voxel based vehicular combat game, in which you create your own weapons of war and pit them against AI.
Currently, there are three campaigns. Neter, Dangerous Waters, and Glao. In Neter and Glao you can make your own ships and are competing with AI factions to win territory. Dangerous Waters however is a World War 2 based campaign in which you can spawn in ready-made vessels based on WW2 designs. Dangerous Waters is completely community run, from what I know. Neter and Dangerous Waters are very large, where Glao is geared toward newer players and is far smaller. Personally, I prefer Neter over all of them.
The real meat of the game is the vehicle construction. Any form of vessel you can think of, you can make. Boat, submarine, plane, spaceship, a flying death chicken... the list continues. All* weapons are custom made by you, the player. Configured to perform whatever task you wish. Anything from lasers to missiles to the humble cannon can be employed to bring swift death to your enemies. The newest addition to the weapon roster is the Particle Cannon, in which anything on the recieving end can be penetrated, smashed, shocked or exploded. Not particularly in that order.
*There is a class of weapon called "Simple Weapons" which are basic single block cannons and lasers. They are cheap, spammable, and suck. Don't use them.
The combat is a combination between how much damage you can deal, and how much damage you can take. Big ships are going to be large targets, literally and figuratively. The AI usually goes after the larger ships first. There are counters to every weapon, aside from the Particle Cannon. Cannons are easily countered by shields. Missiles are countered by the various anti-missile systems and anything underwater. And Lasers are countered by the water (partially), and by deployable smoke. Usually, you will want to hook up the majority of your weapons to AI, as a robot will always be better than a human brain... That usually just leaves navigation to you, however that can also be plugged into the AI.
There is an indevelopment Story Mode in which you take part in several of the factions. They serve as a bit of a tutorial, I find. Although, there is an official interactive tutorial going over all the features of the game.
Adventure Mode is a recent addition that I have not explored much into. It revolves around scavenging other ships that you find on the open sea in order to not be scavenged yourself. I think...
Multiplayer is available. I myself have only participated in the cooperative campaign mode of Neter with some friends, however I believe there is a PvP mode. Unsure if it is a competion to see who can construct the best ship in the shortest time, or if it is just a brawl between ships you have made previously against other players' ships.
Overall, FtD is a fantastic game. The freedom given by the contruction system is wonderful, and the combat is really fun. Except when you get absolutely pounded by ships far above what you were planning on fighting... Looking at you White Flayers.

When people say a game is hard, most people usually think,
(Don't take that as inspiration . . .)
This game isn't hard. It's much higher.
Whenever I play a game, or, ya know, do actual thinking work in real life, I can always see the most difficult part first.
Starting. (As in the act of starting.)
And there's too much work to start out. Vehicles aren't in play yet there's nothing telling you how to put it in play, two different top-down screens to control units (or something like that), EXTREMELY cluttered UI, and lack of polish. . . . That turned into a cons list. Oh well.
If that didn't make you want to look away from this for quite a while, then keep reading.
Mostly just the building UI. Whenever you want to build, you always have to have a block selected. But this will get in the way. FIX: Use keyboard controls. But that's not a complete fix; you must always have something selected. This just makes it stay the same size. This would be less of a problem if the art style was changed. Yeah, I like it, but it's just terrible for building. If you don't know what I mean, you can look at the screenshots.
I actually went through all the tutorials. Some were great; interactive, able to make what you want, teaching you. Some were just manuals. Some were links to Steam manuals (I'm not joking on that. Seriously). Some were step-by-step building tutorials that taught you how to build something . . . if you paid attention . . . kinda. That means that they were just bad. The tutorials didn't really do anything, so YouTube guides were the answer. . . . They didn't help that much.
I feel like this can be related to a Mount & Blade game. Starting out is still the hardest part. Once you have enough resources or large enough fleet (or army in this metaphor), it's a lot easier to actually do things.
The game has a lot of potential. It's just that it needs polish, a lowering of difficulty, an art style change (or tweak) for building mode, and more polish. I don't really mind difficult games. But this difficulty (at least for starting out, the most important part) is so absurd. Even when the difficulty was as low as it could go.

This is the sequel to the original South Korean F2P MMOFPS which had an insane amount of skill requirement and map familiarity. Every minor to major update made players rethink their playstyles, which weapons they should use, and had a very dedicated community alongside and because of it. It wasn't a very content-heavy, graphically impressive, or technically advanced game. In fact, it was a poor man's CS 1.6 clone, but it was still extremely good because of it. It barely had seasonal costumes added to keep it fresh and the maps were few but familiar which kept the fact that new maps took years to get more tolerable as each was designed so well that every game felt different from the rest.
The sequel remains faithful to the series by retaining the original maps, gameplay types, and weapon advantages while adding modern staples like ironsights, sprinting, and newer gameplay modes like survival, endless team deathmatches, and sniper duels. It still doesn't get content updates fast enough, but that doesn't really matter to the community that enjoys this game.
I personally love this game for staying true to the original's vision and retaining the same flavor that was unlike other FPS's from that time and to this day.
Play this game, if you don't like it then move on, you'll find greener albeit different pastures. If you do, congratulations and I'll see you on the battlefield, soldier.

Dreamfall Chapters is a game that can be apreciated for what it sets out to do. It was successfully funded on Kickstarter, and it is clear that the team at Red Thread Games is passionate about the Dreamfall franchise. This however, does not change the fact that Chapters (atleast in it's current state) is a bad game.
So what exactly do i mean by this? Well to start off with, the game runs like crap, and without the graphics to back its poor performance. Despite the game having recently been upgraded from Unity version 4.x to 5.2.3, I still struggle to maintain 60 FPS on my current rig(i7 2600K/GTX 780sc).
But what about the game itself? Well. To be fair. It's also very weak. Chapters LOVES to waste your time. It contains tons of illogical puzzles, and pixel hunt-like item scavenging. And when you aren't walking around a large level looking for pointless items, you're likely walking from point A to point B, just to be sent back to A again. Overall the game manages to drag out what could've been a nicely paced 2 hour per episode experince, into a tedious 5 hour walkathon, with very little exposition.
As such, I really cannot recommend Dreamfall Chapters, as it is simply a bad game. I will however recommend the previous title in the series, known simply as Dreamfall, as it is arguably a much better game.

The game has definate replay-value and I'm looking forward after the final chapter is released to replay it and make different choices.
If you love story-rich games, this one is a definate yes for you. For others who'd like to try out story-rich adventure games, this is a good place to begin.
Hope you enjoy!

I've really enjoyed this game so far, having completed the four episodes currently released. While Dreamfall Chapters is very much a slow-boil of a story, I also enjoy the amount of time I got to spend in the locales, just soaking in the lushly designed ambience. This is a great looking game. That said, the story is perhaps a little out of balance, with the game and puzzle moments often feeling detached from the ongoing narrative. That said, once you get to the Third and Fourth episodes (Books), the pace really picks up, creating a feleing of greater eveness between game and story.
The decision making moments are really the highlight of the game for me, though - there's a feel of ongoing consequence to the choices you make. Perhaps the story always ends up in a similar place, regardless, but the game does a much better job of integrating your choices into the ongoing narrative than something like The Walking Dead, where your decisions often feel peripheral and meaningless to the story. For anyone who likes a 'Choose Your Own Adventure' Dreamfall Chapters can't come more highly recommended.
For non-adventure gamers I would recommend the game with a few caveats. Obviously it's a beautiful production, but the mechanics of the game offer little flexibility in terms of exploration. Yes, the worlds can be big, but there's ultimately little to do in them besides complete tasks associated with story progression.

1.  It is free.  No microtransactions. Just Free.
2.  It's an attempt at a cool idea of turning your desktop into a 3d space where you can turn all your programs and jpegs and whatever else into "physical" objects.
3. But really it's not too practical for it's intended purpose.   Instead it's just a fun way of showing off your collection of games and jpegs in a virtual environment.   You're better off running your (newer resource-demanding) games with as few programs running in the background as possible.
4. Currently there is no way of running this program while offline.   Since it is free and multiplayer is optional, it makes no sense to me for the always online requirement.  Always online requirement is not practical for the "virtual desktop" idea either.
5. For the "virtual dektop" idea to really work, it would need the option to be able to load right after windows loads at boot.  It needs to integrate the system clock/system trey.
6. You can host your virtual desktop for people to join and look at your stuff.  But that's about all they can do.
There's no harm in trying this out.  I'm sceptical that it will reach it's potential as a useful "virtual desktop" but as a DIY virtual showcase and gallery for your games and jpeg collections it's pretty cool.

What can be said about Red Faction II? The original Red Faction was quite a success (in terms of quite positive reviews and sales) so a sequel was eventually determined to come out soon. Originally a console game and later ported to the PC, it tries to outmatch its predecessor with more action, more vehicles and with a definitely more stupid storyline. What's the final result?
Of course it's not as good or original as Red Faction I. The charm of sneaking around in a Mars colony is nowhere to be found anymore (there's really no link to the story of the first game), the gameplay got definitely dumbed down and the level design is extremely linear. To make it worse, you can no longer make use of the legendary GEO MOD engine as in Red Faction I. You are partly able to blow out some walls or pillars, but that's all. GEO MOD my♥♥♥♥♥
Nonetheless I must admit that riding vehicles or blowing away enemies with your yellow grenade launcher can be quite fun. The focus definitely lies on action and that's not necessarily a bad thing. On the other side the cons really let you down after all.
The Good:
+ Non-Stop action
+ Many vehicles
+ Many weapons
+ A not so bad second half of the game
The Bad:
- Dumb, repetitive gameplay
- Linear level design
- Boring, foreseeable story
- A horrible first half of the game
- No real replay value
- No real multiplayer available, only a bot mode
The Ugly:
-- Non-skippable ingame cutscenes (I HATE that, seriously)
It's really hard to recommend this game in retrospective. It's an ugly console child with a horrible first half and a more interesting second part. If you still decide to buy it, at least do so during sales or via the Red Faction Collection.

Interesting idea but I only see it being useful to certain people:
1. If you have your TV hooked up to your PC and are playing from the couch with a controller
2. You are part of a large group that has a server on this game where you can hop in and see what everyones playing
3. You are a fanatic for decorating virtual houses (but then why not get Garrys Mod?)
4. You are a more visual kind of person and prefer to see virtual objects rather then a list of games in steam to get an idea of what you have to play
What is there is good but again not very practical if you have a semi organized computer and use Steam. I really wish I could just give it a sideways thumb vote because it's not bad but it's also not great.
Honestly if I ever find myself in a situation where I begin to use Steam in house streaming I will probably reinstall  to use it for that.
Pros:
* It's an interesting take on the virtual desktop idea
* Great for organizing games like ROMS that don't have launchers of their own typically, lets you see exactly what ROMs you have and pick one out and launch right into it
* If you know how to use Hammer you could make your own maps to decorate
* Can use maps from pertty much any Source Engine game
* Multiplayer is an interesting idea
* Unlocking new props and maps was a good idea and was probably the main reason I stuck it out for two hours
* Decorating a house in your video games and art assets is kind of relaxing
Cons:
* It does take resources away from your PC that could be used towards the game you are intending to launch with it
* The web browser needs work
* The menu graphics are not great, they don't have good anti aliasing and look like they are from the year 2000
* Initial load time was long
* Prop menu could use some work
* I couldn't delete items where I had messed up the settings for (forgot to tell it that it was a ROM and what emulator to use) and everytime I tried to just remake it instead it would jump back to the one that was already created
* Joining a multiplayer server took way to long due to needing to download every custom asset on the server
* Selecting one object would change the screen of all other objects to the screen of the selected object

I've played Space Engineers, StarMade, Robocraft and the like, but From The Depths is by far the most varied and fun of the voxel vehicle construction games. Unlike Space Engineers, you aren't limited to a very narrow group of craft. Unlike StarMade, almost every system is customizable at the build level. Unlike Robocraft, there's no progression walls or hard limitations. You can build ships, submarines, helicopters, airplanes, airships, spacecraft, hover-fortresses, land structures, and recently, tanks. You have choices of multiple different types of armor, you're got heavy, strong, light, buoyant, and even ethereal blocks to work with. There are cannons, mortars, missiles, torpedoes, bombs, rockets, lasers, and even particle accelerator weapons! To top it all off, the building system of the game is the absolute best there is. It's almost entirely keyboard based, allowing quick, efficient construction, along with symmetry and fill tools. The possibilities in this game are truly and utterly endless.

Possibally the best games you can build warmachines in, From the Depths is just amazing.  If you think it is something you can be commited to and keep playing, get it, you will not be sorry.  However, if you think you are not going to like, I wouldn't get it.  The game tells you, "Science has proven rage-quitting can be reduced by learning how to play," and that is completely true.  You have to learn how to build things like engines or else you won't be able to play without losing.  Once you learn the game, it's one of the best experiences you cna have for the sort of thing.

From the good of voxel building games and homage to the building spirit alike, this is a tinkering title you must have in your library. Whether you take the gameplay at face value or proivde your own deeper reasons to play on the planet - From the Depths just manages to be the right kind of openess and demanding of your input. There's a distinct gravity when the idea of the tutorials are non-intrusive yet "you're going have a bad time" noted about the main menu. It's almost like a conterbalance for the thirsty builders and head-canoners who come with ideas on bated breath.
In other words, its a game that respects what you want to get into. Its learning curve can come off deceptively harsh, being a storm wind at your front, when after you chime with the game rules, is really the wind in your sunbathed sails. I barely can begin to stress  how emergent the gameplay is and can already become. My play hours are no compare to the scrawls of paper holding designs, logistics, and strategies to reach that meta level of enjoyment, This living toybox is near a 4X game if you are immersed enough. Moveover, Brillant Skies map, naviagation, and tactical screens are great barebones look at the "real time true strategy" genre layered in it. And a reminder, at time of typing the game is Early Access and a steal when a sale is going on.
From the Depths is a gem tried and true. Every notable build and action has excellent feedback sublte and large. This fact shining the most in the Campaign as the goal  lends a real-time affair to getting resourcing and building right. It's rare in a game a player builds and modifies efficiency -itself- , something any peak performer would droll at when the engines are running. And I think that's a summary right there, an engine you keep feeding and it keep providing. And you the player in turn are the same for the game. This duet is really a hallmark to what makes open sandbox (especially voxel-based) a key game type in this era.
Get this game, please - the enlightenment and enjoyment is that one heavy tool the yields just right in hands, and what ever you make feels like dawn break gold.

Split/Second is a year 2010 arcade racing game, which goes faster than NFS right from the start, and giving much more king-sized demolition than the Flatout. With that said, it is a mediocre game, which can be fun, but not for long. There are enough of breathtaking sequences, but they satisfy much better from the backseat, on youtube, rather than playing that yourself.
No doubt, it is an engrossing moment, when in the middle of race a transatlantic Boing crushing right on your head. And it is even better when you dodge this flight in the last second. Too bad, but for the most time of gameplay, you'll be the one under the blast and not one around it.
Of course, like almost always, there are non-optimal controls. But, what is more, there are too little field for player to tweak the race for own benefit, but to choose a car to drive. Those cars provides a little of variety in proportions between speed, acceleration, and so on, but, in the most cases, you'll be driving two, maybe four cars through the whole game. All other variants are just "for show", for "big numbers", and not for real variety and usability. You can't really tune cars for your style of driving or for certain circumstances, that is the first real downside.
Second big mishap is AI, which will always be one step ahead of you, even after you managed to blow all and everything around you in little pieces. Just the few seconds later, it will be you who'll be ripped apart, without any chance to dodge.
Yeah, about demolitions, dodging and racing in general. The main feeling from racing is the same as with NFS games - you can push from borders without loosing speed, you almost not need to slow down in corners, and yet catching the track just fine. But when it comes to dodging the explosions... It turns out that their physical modelling is very far from natural. For a thousand times you'll be thinking you are ways away from blast, but will be in flames an instant later.
And the fourth nail is the bad optimisation. I have a dvd with that game which works much better than "always updated" steam version. There are a major problem with missable/breakable save games, which made so many people raged there on steam. Blast the DRM!
With all that said about downsides of the game, I'm still vouching that you may try it. Especially if you buy it with some major discount about 80% of price... I'd say that Blur, the classmate of Split/Second, is much better, and should be picked first, for much more enjoyment... But Steam not selling Blur anymore. So if you are into arcade racing, but get tired of NFS and Flatout series both, get Split/Second! It'll give you some fresh air, if only for two or three nights... It's still better than nothing, right? And what a marvelous explosions you'll taste there!
Overall mark - 6.95/10 - best when under 5$ price, even better in some bundle.

A massive overhaul of the combat system without forgetting tricks learned, optional quicktime system, across the board admission that they made mistakes with the first game, and a demonstration that they can learn from them. The only problem this game has is the menu interface, which doesn't allow multiple saves or easy access to an actual title menu. But it doesn't hurt the actual content of the game.
Graphics: 9/10. Only deducted points is for some weird-looking hair and particle animation touching on the uncanny valley, but it's otherwise a gorgeous, nigh perfectly beautiful game.
Sound: 10/10. The score is wonderfully emotional and puts you in the middle of each moment. You'll find yourself humming along with the rat theme, and gratified during the main theme's return in key moments.
Gameplay: 9/10. It's not castlevania anymore, but I'm not complaining. The tricks they picked up from Devil May Cry combine well with other improvements, and mesh in the Symphony-esque metroidvania world. No more is the whip the only useful weapon, no more is spamming R1 the easiest way to end fights. No more are quicktime events required, but neither are they abandoned, for those who enjoy them. And they skip function works beautifully, at no point during even cutscenes do they feel forced, nor does the lack of them feel depriving. A good status quo. But it looses a point for not having a heart system, or a means to deal with stealth sections as a combat option. Sorry, series fidelity is one thing I'm big on, and Castlevania isn't a stealth game, neither is it Devil May Cry. That said, the stealth segments are still very well designed, just a littlle immersion breaking when you're playing as the Prince of Darkness, whom the devil and death both fear.
Replay: 9/10: Postgame, Newgame+, and some really enjoyable once-through sequences, with a train sequence early on being a standout, and a few of the boss build-ups having that effect as well, make for a game that you won't feel a need to give up for awhile, and will always be willling to dig out in a year for another run. No complaints, only point deducted is thanks to Dark Souls moving the goalposts (and Dark Souls II doing it again,) for replay value in recent years by evolving the new game+ formula, and there should have been an attempt to learn from their methods. Great games learn from each other. This applies to all games developed after a previous game. You don't need to change your self-entity, but cool tricks should not be ignored.
Story: 10/10 Yes. On par with the first, with a slightly more Castlevania-y feel, despite your role as the series villian. No more pacing problems. Just awesome. There is emotion, forshadowing, character depth all done wonderfully. If I can make a complaint, it is only that some character arcs require a knowledge of the much-less-enjoyable first game to fully appreciate, but watching a youtube cutscene compilation will fulfil your need.
Overall: 94/100. If you're into the genre, if you're into the series, heck, if you're into just good storytelling in general, give this game a shot. If you're scared, wait for a steam sale. It's optimized wonderfully, so hardware shouldn't be a big problem.

I've really enjoyed this game so far, having completed the four episodes currently released. While Dreamfall Chapters is very much a slow-boil of a story, I also enjoy the amount of time I got to spend in the locales, just soaking in the lushly designed ambience. This is a great looking game. That said, the story is perhaps a little out of balance, with the game and puzzle moments often feeling detached from the ongoing narrative. That said, once you get to the Third and Fourth episodes (Books), the pace really picks up, creating a feleing of greater eveness between game and story.
The decision making moments are really the highlight of the game for me, though - there's a feel of ongoing consequence to the choices you make. Perhaps the story always ends up in a similar place, regardless, but the game does a much better job of integrating your choices into the ongoing narrative than something like The Walking Dead, where your decisions often feel peripheral and meaningless to the story. For anyone who likes a 'Choose Your Own Adventure' Dreamfall Chapters can't come more highly recommended.
For non-adventure gamers I would recommend the game with a few caveats. Obviously it's a beautiful production, but the mechanics of the game offer little flexibility in terms of exploration. Yes, the worlds can be big, but there's ultimately little to do in them besides complete tasks associated with story progression.
