It's pretty hard to really 'review' this early access game.  I'll be honest with you, IMO this game seems like it's one of those that will just never -not- be early access.  But what is here in this game so far is simply fantastic.  I almost missed it, too.  One of my friends introduced this game to me.  At first, even then, I kind of just dismissed it.  I played a little and was kind of intimidated.  Almost a full year later, I tried again, and stuck with it.  Watched some Youtube videos and learned a lot.  Now it's one of my favorite games.
There's really no other game like this on the market for now.  I guess it's more akin to something like Robocraft than anything else, just not as a lobby-based multiplayer game.  Oh, and there's a lot of water in this game.  Like, a lot.  Hence, the title.
From the Depths isn't easy to get into.  Luckily, the developer's recently added a bit of a tutorial system that goes over a lot fo the mechanics in the game to help get you started.  There are a few Youtubers that have guides and walkthroughs as well.  If you're interested, I recommend looking up IreLAN Gaming's Youtube channel, there are a bunch of videos by him that explains a lot and does some interesting builds.
Let me give an example of the complexity of this game for you.
Take a metal block, add a propeller to it.  Doesn't work.  Propeller needs power.  Build an engine.  Oh wait...  that involves placing an engine block, placing crankshaft parts, putting pistons on the crankshaft.  That'll work and give you power, but you can get even more power by adding fuel injectors, or adding carburetors and slapping superchargers or turbochargers on 'em.  Don't forget to pipe the exhaust out to cool it all, if it gets too hot it'll lose effeciency at high loads and eventually stop working if it overheats.  There are radiators you can slap on, too.
The engine isn't working?  Oh yeah, you'll need fuel.  Don't have fuel?  Have to get some oil.  Make a refinery to turn it into fuel.
So!  Now we have an engine, with fuel, which is now powering the propeller.  But the metal block isn't very hydrodynamic, is it?  Turn that thing into an actual boat, because water and air resistance is a thing in this game.  Sloped and angled building materials are very important to minimize resistance in order to maximize speed.  Now the boat's top heavy and keeps flipping, so add a keel.  Now, to turn the boat you need a rudder.  Boat's getting a little heavy, add some more propellers.  Hell, add some wings to the ship, equip some jet thrusters to the back, and turn it into an airplane.  Hell, put some ion thrusters on various parts of the ship and now you can fly it into space and use it a a satellite or space ship.
Seal up the hull, add some airpumps, use PID controller blocks to set the ship's AI to keep it at a certain level in the water, keep it from rolling or listing too much, and turn it into a submarine.  Add some wheels, drive it on land, call it a tank.
Oh, wait, we haven't got into weapons or AI.  Well, this "review" is getting long enough as it is...
The sheer 'Depth' of this game is fantastic.  It's easy to get into, mess around, and just keep building and building.  My first ship was a massive, terrible Frankenstein's monster of a ship that could hardly float.  My more recent ships have been sleek, fast, well armored, and pack a punch.  The iterative design is awesome.
The game's being developed by a very small team, and there's really only one programmer working on it.  The love for the game is obvious, and he's always adding more to the game while improving what's already there.  The game is far from perfect, and the larger battles will slow down even powerful machines becuase of the sheer volume of what's being constantly calculated.  The game has some rough edges, and like I said before the UI is pretty rough, but it is getting better.  The game obviously isn't for everyone, it's very focused on the combat.
Definitely worth the price, IMO.  Especially if it goes on sale.  Like now.  Steam Summer Sale.  Get it. $6.00.  Game's a steal for that much.
P.S. From the Depths does have multiplayer.  It's not as stable as singleplayer, but it's nice to have.

This is the fourth game in this series, and the closest to a sequel of the first game House 1000 Doors: Family Secrets. (I have played all 4 games in the series, in order.)  It is stand alone, as is, but the series storyline might confuse a player as the game briefly refers to previous game adventures in single "throw away/reveal" lines depending on how much of the series storyline is known.
The story: The Palm of Zoroaster, a cursed orb, has been destroying things, people and quite possibly civilizations (or at least, select parts of it) for centuries.  Your job is to destroy the orb.  (No spoilers because there are some if one has been following the series storyline.)  Learn the orb's history, witness its destruction, and of course discover how to destroy it and gather the means to do so.
The game is set up with an introduction/tutorial, four adventure chapters, and the final conclusive chaper.  I rather like this setup which is different then other HOs with a much more linear storyline.  What changed in this game from the first game (Family Secrets) is the player does not get to choose which adventure to embark on first.  For this game and storyline purposes it is perfect though.
Hidden object scenes, mixed with some head scratching puzzles and the usual standard puzzles, plus some point and click and a chapter by chapter accumulate and use inventory.  Nothing too hard or tear your hair out challenging.  Game comes with a walkthrough the player can access if they get stuck in game or on a puzzle.  Every puzzle has a skip option and sparkles on needed objects or mini puzzle scene.  Unless playing in Hard mode.  There are three game modes available, in-game achievements, wall papers and a bonus chapter.
Warning: If you are hunting for those elusive extra "hidden/ghost/shape shifting" objects make sure you have them all before leaving the introduction or adventure chapter because you cannot go back once the chapter is finished. (Except in a new game).
Opinion: I like the series, therefore I like each game.  The overall concept is interesting and lends itself to innumberable further games.  The only thing I did not like in this game was the end.  I was expecting a much longer cut scene.  It ended and I thought "Wait, that is it."  The adventure ended, the game ended, but the end felt truncated.  Ah well the bonus chapter made up for the abrupt conclusion.

While you're chasing your goal the game spawns an endless amount of other enemys, but always in a fair number. They can drop special powerfull weapons you can collect and use for a short amount of time. And of course they also get harder aswell over the course of the game.

As simple as it sounds, as much fun the game is. The Arenas are all different and require their own tactics. The gameplay is fast and fluent, and if you die, you can make your next try within seconds. For the little price the game costs, if offers a lot of gameplay.

If you like Twin-Stick Shooters I can fully recommend Turret Terminator to you.

It's a fun enough game for what it is. But don't pay full price for it.
Basically ask yourself: Is it $5?
- If yes: buy
- If no: don't buy
Maybe they'll do more with it later, but it seems like this is pretty much it.
The game is fun enough for what it is. What it is NOT unfortunately, is Civ In Space.
Even the actual starships, the ostensible focus of the game, aren't particularly interesting. You get some buttons to push to make some aspects of the ships better in exchange for resources, or worse and get some of those resources back. The tactical combat actually IS interesting and requires that you think about what you're doing. Unfortunately there's a very real potential for you to just become an overpowered titan of the galaxy here and roll mindless over whatever your opponents throw at you. This can happen entirely by accident.
There's no diplomacy to speak of. No meaningful relationships with other faction leaders. And no real way to negotiate for... anything really.
The planets themselves are pretty boring, conveying some numerical advantages to you by existing. They're less like planets full of people and more like buildings in a strategy game. They're there to provide resources and some of them can house wonders. That's all.
Overall, it's a fun game, but a barebones one. Don't pay full price for it.

Starships is a game with a lot of potential, but falls short of what it could be. The game lacks a decent tutorial outside of standard tooltips, but the gameplay is fairly shallow without too much curve. Most of the non-combat gameplay is simply buying improvements/investments for better resources, which you can use to buy improvements and investments.
The battles themselves are largely a matter of flying in and out of cover, shooting targets from behind/the side and randomly crippling their abilities while they do the same to you. Torpedoes can be used to created delayed explosions, granting you a degree of control over enemy movement, and there's some shenanigans with cloaking and radar.
The maps are very similar, with the main features being shifting asteroids and portals that randomly teleport you to other portals. The former are very simple: red and green circles let you know that every turn, a path will be opened or closed. The latter is more of an annoyance than anything, due to the random aspect and the game's willingness to send your ship through one if you don't carefully plot your movement across individual hexes.
The game is connected to Beyond Earth, itself an iffy prospect at the time of writing. Completing tasks in BE will unlock bonuses in Starships, and vice versa. The BE unlocks are generally underwhelming, save for Pioneers. You can also choose to "continue" a BE save in Starships, playing as your chosen leader and maintaining the same diplomatic relations with AI leaders, though this is pointless with Starships being a step down from BE.
Ultimately, Starships isn't a particularly deep or intriguing game. The visuals and music aren't bad, and the missions have decent variety, but everything else is lackluster and the options are barebones. There's no multiplayer, no option to continue after winning, and no real depth.
It might be worth a look on Steam sale, particularly if you don't want to get a BE mod or mess with XML files to unlock the bonuses, but Starships can't break from the orbit of its iOS port origins.

Mercury Steam's hack and slash take on Konami's long running vampire slaying franchise proved to be a bit divisive by rebooting the franchise's lore and staying away from the loot gathering of the massively successful side scrolling titles starting with Symphony of the Night. With Lords of Shadow 2, Mecury Steam is drawing their controversial take on the franchise to a close, putting players in the worn out boots of Dracula himself as he faces off against Satan and his army of minions. Attempting to inject a bit of metroidvania design and hopping back and forth between Dracula's castle and modern times, is this the compromise between the side scrolling titles and the foundation laid by Lords of Shadow?

After a recap of the events of Lords of Shadow and Mirror of Fate, players are treated to an epic prologue that has Dracula defending his less than humble abode from a tremendous siege which culminates in an encounter with his son, Alucard.  The game then flashes forward a thousand years to find a very weak Dracula awakening in a cathedral in modern times greeted by Zobek. Zobek offers Dracula the chance to end his cursed existence in exchange for the death's of Satan's acolytes. In typical video game fashion, Dracula must regain his lost powers and battle a few inner demons in addition to Satan's minions. While the sections that have Dracula revisiting his castle provide some appreciative depth and introspection, the plot unfolding in modern times is rather underwhelming and even a bit silly. The game is at it's narrative peak when it recaptures the spirit of Gabirel's sober journey in the first game, reflecting on Dracula's numerous sins and the decimation of the Belmont family.

Perhaps the largest change to Lords of Shadow 2 comes in it's structure. Dracula moves between present day and his castle and, eventually, players can revisit areas previously explored. It makes the game more metroidvania-like thank it's predecessor but hoping back and forth between the two areas leaves the geography feeling fragmented and backtracking only becomes available much later in the game making this still feel somewhat like a linear level based affair. Combat remains largely intact from the previous games with light and dark magic now complimented by two additional weapons: the chaos claws and the void sword. These along with Dracula's shadow whip can be upgraded by purchasing various moves and utilizing them. It's a system that rewards using your entire move set and is an excellent addition to a genre where many rely on a couple effective all purpose combos. Relics have been added as consumable items that give Dracula the ability to restore his health, transform into a dragon for massive damage and gain extra experience.

Tragically, the gameplay does take a major step back when it comes to the puzzles. Standing in for the first game's brain teasers are a gauntlet of stealth bits that have Dracula posessing enemies, cowering in the shadows and transforming into a rat in order to navigate small cracks and crevices. Most of these are easy and don't feel rewarding in addition to being at odds with playing as a powerful and feared vampire. A couple of the stealth sections can prove to be frustrating and one visit to a forum exposes one pre-boss fight stealth section as a stopping point for many. Boss fights are also completely unchallenging which is a shame since Lords of Shadow provided an excellent difficulty balance.  Fortunately, those who invest in the DLC will be treated to gameplay and puzzles that are more in line with the original Lords of Shadow making it an excellent piece of content for fans even though it's narrative additions are minimal.

On the PC, Lords of Shadow 2's beautiful art direction is showcased by higher resolution textures and runs silky smooth at 60fps. Despite the fact that it doesn't offer the lastest graphical bells and whistles, this Direct X 9 title is more than pleasing to look and all of it's details can be appreciated since the fixed camera of the first game has been ditched. The Castle in particular is a stunning place to be and it becomes almost frustrating that the entire game doesn't take place there since the modern city seems a bit bland in comparison. Enemies can also be a bit bland and repetative but the bosses generally make up for this minor short fall. The soundtrack to Lords of Shadow 2 is also magnificent with beautiful somber orchestral compositions and delicate piano pieces. It adds a huge amount of ambiance to the game and is perhaps this year's best soundtrack.

Lords of Shadow 2 is unequivocally not as good on the whole as it's predecessor though it shows a few major improvements that are easy to appreciate. It's a lengthy experience that offers superb combat, excellent visuals and a top notch soundtrack. For a Castlevania fan, it generally outweighs the lame stealth segments, repetitive enemies and underwhelming open world design. Even for it's biggest detractors, the Lords of Shadows games are proof that Castlevania can exist in three dimensions.

I have been a fan of the Castlevania Saga since its very early days on the nintendo consoles. Seeing the first LoS on my gaming rig made me salivate and I was not disappointed. Awesome storyline, great voice acting and a perfect mixture of puzzles and action bathing in a dark graphical and musical atmosphere.
Now here comes LoS2 and I was ready to sharpen my holy swiss army cross against a legion of blood suckers again... which... you don't get to do per se. Now, don't get me wrong, I wasn't upset about the choice of having to play as Dracula. I wasn't bothered by the rather mind boggling flashbacks and choices for his resurrection. What DID make me quite mad, was the lack of consistency of the story compared to the prior game. Plot holes scattered all over, questions about some enemies which remain unanswered (you know, those mechanical ones...). Quite honestly, by trying to give you more freedom by opening up the "world" and let you travel back and forth to reach secrets you could not get before acquiring specific powers, the developers actually have damaged the game rather than improving it. I found myself running around like a vampire on the beach at noon all over the place to end up at random places for not much more than a couple of XP. Rather disappointing.
But frankly, the game gets better the more you play it and old Fangs gets his powers back to kick to serious booty. Puzzles, action, frantic action, lots of blood and body parts flying around. Seriously entertaining. And the end is satisfying.
Overall, it's a notch down compared to LoS, but not a complete disaster. Much could have been done to make it more engaging and gripping if the story had been more consistent. But aside from that, I'd say that I would recommend this game nonetheless, especially on sale. It's good. Not jaw dropping awesome but solid.

First off, let me reiterate what every other reviewer has already said: this is primarily a building game.
If you liked constructing spectacular things in Minecraft, this game is for you.
If you liked making your very own space station/craft and fighting for survival against other ships in Space Engineers, this game is for you.
If you want to build a fully functional 2:1 exact replica of the Starship Enterprise, IJN Yamato, or the Seattle Space Needle... well, you better have some serious power in that processor or you won't survive the lag of 60,000 voxel blocks, but otherwise yes, this game is DEFINITELY for you.
There are very few limitations to what you can build in FtD, and nearly all of it is interactable and functional.  Which brings me to the second most dominant part of this game: combat.
No, you will probably not do much with your in-game avatar besides riding your creations into battle.  You can try to speed across to an enemy ship in a fast boarding craft and take out it's AI, thus capturing it, but the risk of getting fragged by either your side or theirs is immense.
But none of that really matters when you can sit in the bridge of your very own space battleship and watch a broadside of nine 2-meter diameter shells arcing gracefully through space towards the enemy while their missiles hammer your hull mercilessly.  Or watch as the laser defences that you so carefully laced throughout the hull flash in response, blowing up missiles left and right.  Then you can take the helm and slowly turn the ship to face the enemy, carefully lining up your cursor on their ship before firing the massive Particle Accelerator Cannon in your battleship's nose.  You can experience the power of an EMP wave shimmering across their entire hull, followed by the satisfaction of watching the entire enemy ship slowly disintegrate because its AI died in the blast.
Space combat not your style?  Go build a tank and fight some of the land behemoths in the alternate, player-made planets and factions that the devs include with the game.  Or build a triple-decker ship-of-the-line, turn the weather settings to "bad," and have a duel in the middle of a thunderstorm with one of the many age-of-sail ships made by players in the forums or the workshop.  Build fighter jets and watch them zip across the skies, firing missiles and colliding with each other, or for more Danger Zone excitement, put one of the excellent player-made LUA codes in your jet and watch a cinematic dogfight take place overhead.
I could go on and on about this game.  Yes, the learning curve is hell on wheels, keels, and wings, but if you truly enjoy building for aesthetics, combat, replication, invention, or any other kind of dedicated creative mindset, this game is beyond worth the hours spent learning.  At 175 hours, I am still learning new aspects of systems that I thought I had mastered, and more content is constantly being added, updated, and improved.  New missions, new systems (WARP DRIVE HYPE!), new mechanics, and of course, the always-helpful and amazing player base make this game worth every minute I've spent in it.
I will say this as a warning:  do NOT buy this game if you are not prepared to spend a LOT of time learning it.  At least one weekend is the minimum you will need to really grasp what's going on in this game, and if you try to jump right into the Campaign, you will almost certainly be obliterated the first time around.  It is the biggest learning curve I've ever climbed, but if you're anything like me, the view at the top is so worth it.

OutDrive reminds me of my old casette player back in '95. It was broken so I had to hold the "Play" button to listen to the music I was into. On one hand it made me feel uncomfortable, on the other - I had great time listening to my favourite tracks.
Same kind of feeling I have with OutDrive - the gameplay is bad, at point I can say this is hardly a game at all. Your DeLorean handling is awful, physics are non-existent and there's no controller support (for the game like this - almost a crime). The other big problem I had is the lack of any motivation to play. There's no rewards - no achievements, no ladder to compare your results with other players, no story (I don't count the intro movie), no new cars or new maps. nothing. If you add the fact OutDrive is too easy - you'll have no problem getting over 20+ minutes in single run.
I can't say graphics is good, cause it is not. But the design is good - lots of neon and polygon-like surronding give this 80's feeling.
The part game shines - is the music (not the sounds - they are bad). The OST consists of synth/retro-wave tracks and there are LOTS of them (played for 3 hours and heard the same music once or twice). So if you're a fan of the genre (like I am) you'll have good time listening to it.
Just like i said - OutDrive reminds me of my old casette player, except it's not broken. It's hard to really accept OutDrive as a game, cause it feels more like WinAmp visualization came to life.
Can i recommend it? Yes, if you're into that genre of music. For the price it's awesome deal.
If you want good racing game and not a BIG fan of such visuals or music - stay away. You'll get bitter aftertaste.

The "House of 1000 Doors: The Palm of Zoroaster Collector's Edition" is a bit short (6.3 hours base game + 2.2 hours Bonus Chapter = 8.5 hours total), but not unduly so for this type of game (casual point-and-click Adventure Hidden Object Game (HOG)).  The story is a bit weaker than the norm for the genre, but otherwise, t's pretty much standard fare for a HOG:  good graphics, fun puzzles, acceptable voice acting.  The $10 list price is a tad high for it's length, so I'd wait for a sale to buy it or get it in a bundle (the Sinister Stories Bundle is how I got it).  Still, I'm recommending it.

The Palm of Zoroaster is the second installment of House of 1,000 Doors series by Alawar Five-BN. Previous installment of the series: Family Secrets.
Game Menu Option: Two section – Volume and Miscellaneous settings. The volume section has the following: Music, Ambient Audio and Sound Effects. The miscellaneous section has the following: Screen Resolution, Full-screen, Wide-screen and Window cursor.
Game Difficulty Modes: Two game difficulty modes – Casual and Expert
Cinematic/Dialogue: All cinematic scenes can be skipped if you do not want to watch them. The skip option given. Only if you don’t want to sit through listening the entire dialogue.
Game Voiceovers: Nothing much can be said about the voice-overs asides from that they are well done.
Game Music/Sounds: Nothing much can be said about the music/sounds asides from that they fit well with the game.
Game Graphics: Nothing much can be said about the graphics asides from that they are nicely drawn.
Inventory Panel: There is no option for locking it in place nor it is stationary; it slides up whenever the mouse cursor hovers over it.
Notebook: Information/Clues/Story recorded in here. That helps the player to progress further in the game.
Map: Interactive map with various indicators such as tasks and current location. You can also use the map to jump to another location and back without trekking through several screens.
Hidden Object Gameplay: Traditional word list with some and/or no interaction required.
Puzzle Gameplay: Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve. There is a skip button if the puzzle(s) becomes too tasking to solve.
Game Length: There are eight chapters of the main portion of the game. One chapter in the bonus portion of the game. There are nine total chapters in the game.
Game Ending: The main portion of the game has an ending. The bonus portion of the game extends it a bit more.
Game Extras: This section is lock until the main portion of the game is completed.
Game Concept Art/Wallpapers: 13 Concept Art in total and 9 Wallpapers in total.
Game Walkthrough: available at the start of the game. It can be access during gameplay.
Game Collectables: There 46 beyond objects (morphing objects) to collect throughout the main portion of the game.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The story may be rich, but many of the missions/puzzles are designed in such a silly way that they ruin all the fun of the game.
For example, in Book Two, when Zoe walked out from the home, she was stopped by a robotcop, asking her who and where she was going to meet. If Zoe selects to resist, then most of the streets will be locked down. As the map system is terrible and I was not familiar with the streets, I spent two hours trying to find a route to get to the mission location (i.e., Dr. Roman's apartment) but just in vein. Eventually I had to give up and restart the mission all over again and change my response to the robotcop so that there would be less streets being locked down and so I could find the way to Dr. Roman's apartment. I was really pis*ed off by this "route-finding" mission.
Furthermore, at the beginning of Book Three, what's the point to ask the player to collect the 9 drawings hidden everywhere in the house? What's the fun about it? Has anyone really enjoyed spending a couple of hours wandering around every room of the house for I-don't-know-how-many-times just to search for those well-hidden pieces of paper?
Stupid things/missions like these keep making me to think whether I should continue to waste my life on this not-fun-at-all game. At the moment, I barely found all the 9 drawings by following the hints given in the Boork Three Walkthrough. I have a feeling that I will quit playing this game very soon.
